Preface to the Carved Edition of the Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the father of all sūtras; among those who have mastered its exegesis, Tiantai alone attained its true essence.
Among the descendants of Tiantai who have excerpted his commentaries to annotate the sūtra text, there have been five families throughout antiquity and modern times.

These include: the sub-commentary by Master Wei of Siming in the Song dynasty; the annotated commentary by Master Lun of Keshan; the annotated commentary by the lay practitioner Xu Xishan of the Yuan dynasty;
the annotated commentary by Master Ru of Shang Tianzhu Monastery in the Ming dynasty; and the syncretic interpretation by Master Ouyi Zhixu of Gushu. This is it.

The world has long circulated the Four Books (Sishu) by Master Lun and those who followed him, yet it was not known that there existed the *Rushi Renshu* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) by Master Wei.
In the spring of the year Yihai, while I was lecturing on the *Wenju* at the foot of Mount Tai, a certain Mr. Shu arrived carrying this commentary.

He requested that I oversee its carving for publication. Delighted, I read it; it excerpts the essentials of the *Shuji* (Subcommentary) in a manner that does not resemble the abridgments found in the Four Books.
In some instances he altered the phrasing, and in others he rearranged the wording, making it easier for readers to understand;
this is truly of great benefit to beginners. Alas! This book was originally composed prior to the Four Books, yet now it circulates after them.
Is this not what is meant by saying that manifestation and concealment occur according to their time? Thus, I have inscribed this upon it for the sake of the book’s lineage and carved it at its head.
Written respectfully by the śramaṇa Kōken on the final ten days of the ninth month of the year Tenpuku Jinchū (1717).
The First Fascicle of the Commentary on the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma.
Regarding the term "Wondrous" (Miao): "Wondrous" means inconceivable. Regarding the term "Dharma" (Fa): it refers to the provisional and real dharmas of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses.
"Lotus Flower" (Lianhua) is a metaphor for the provisional and real dharmas. This is because the Wondrous Dharma is difficult to understand.
Metaphors are easily illustrated; moreover, the underlying meaning is manifold. To briefly approximate the preceding and following sections, they are combined into six metaphors.
First, the lotus for the sake of the flower illustrates the establishment of provisional means for the sake of the ultimate truth. As the text says:

"Knowing the supreme tranquility, yet by the power of skillful means, although various paths are shown, in reality they are for the Buddha-vehicle. Second, the blooming of the flower illustrates the opening of the provisional. The lotus appears...
The analogy illustrates the reality (*tattva*). The text says: "Opening the gate of expedient means (*upāya*) to reveal the true aspect.

The falling of the three flowers represents the setting aside of the provisional (*prajñapti*), while the formation of the lotus represents the establishment of the real. The text says: "Directly abandoning expedient means, he speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way.

Furthermore, the lotus represents the fundamental (*mūla*), and the flower represents the trace (*vyañjana*). From the fundamental, the trace is extended; the trace depends upon the fundamental. The text says: "I truly..."
The time since I attained Buddhahood has been as long as this; yet, in order to teach and transform sentient beings, I have spoken thus: "I left home at a young age and attained *sambodhi*.
The two metaphors of the blooming flower illustrate the manifestation of the trace, while the metaphor of the lotus appearing illustrates the revelation of the source. As the text says:
All the world says that I have only now attained the Way; however, since my attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless, nayuta kalpas have passed.
The falling of the three flowers is a metaphor for the abandonment of traces, while the formation of the lotus is a metaphor for the establishment of the foundation.

As the text says: "The Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is always thus; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is entirely real and not false. For this reason, the Sublime [Dharma] was first manifested.

The Dharma. Next, it is likened to the lotus flower: it sweeps away the attachment to the provisional teachings of the "City of Manifestation," abolishes the stagnant emotions of the "Thatched Hut," opens the gate of skillful means (*upāya*), and reveals the wondrous principle of ultimate reality.
It brings together the minor practices of all virtues and returns them to the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) of vastness.

Sentient beings of superior, middling, and inferior faculties are all granted the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). It brings forth the skillful ingenuity of the various sages and manifests the original [nature].

Because the subtleties of the ground are profound, the path increases and birth diminishes; his station is adjacent to Great Enlightenment. Throughout his single period of transformative guidance, both principle and phenomenon are perfected.
It is with this in mind that the analogy of the lotus is employed. Furthermore, he reveals the secret and profound treasury, which is termed "Wondrous" (Myō);
he demonstrates the correct track of the provisional and the real, and is thus titled "Dharma" (Hō). He points toward the fundamental fruit of the remote past, serving as a metaphor for...
It is likened to a lotus to illustrate the perfect Way of non-duality; it is further compared to a flower to describe the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
It reveals the wondrous principle of reality to describe its essence; it returns to the single vehicle of vastness to describe its school;

it sweeps away attachments to the provisional teaching of the "transformed city" to describe its function; and it brings the period of transformation to completion to describe its teaching. Sound itself constitutes a Buddha-work—thus it is called [the Lotus Sūtra].
This constitutes the *sūtra*. "Sūtra" (*jing*) is what is called *sūtra* in foreign lands; it is the general name for the holy teachings.

There are fifteen meanings for both the translated and untranslated terms, which are fully detailed in the *Xuánwén* (Mysterious Text). "Volume" (*juàn*) means to roll up and unroll. "Chapter" (*dì*) means position;
being at the head of a series of sequences, it is called the "first."
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
with commentary and records by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe;
and annotated by the Śramaṇa Daowei of Siming.
The Introduction Chapter, First, of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Regarding the five characters of the title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they constitute the general heading; their detailed explanation is found in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), as briefly stated previously.

As for the specific title of the "Introduction Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), I shall provide a brief exposition below. "Introduction" (*xu*) is defined as "preface. This refers to the sequence of stages, the roles of host and guest, and the entirety of the questions and answers. All...

The meaning of "xiangxu" (orderly sequence) is as explained in the following text. The two types of sequence—the general and the specific—are used to distinguish between the internal and the external.
Furthermore, it may also mean "tranquil and orderly," which carries the sense of being neither hurried nor leaping over one's turn; thus, both the general and specific sequences share this meaning.

This is because it follows the correct sequence. This is an explanation based on the etymological definition of the word. If one follows the meaning according to the sūtra compiler, there is a sequence;
thus, it is described as "sequence" (*anukrama*). First, regarding "sequence": the five matters, beginning with "Thus," are placed at the head of the sūtra; this is termed "sequence.
It is the "General Introduction" (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*), extending from "Thus have I heard" up to "sat down to one side. All of these...

The first is called the "General Preface" (*sāmānyanidāna*). Because it universally precedes the beginning of all sūtras, it is termed the "General Sequence. Second is the "Circumstantial Preface" (*pratyekanidāna*), which refers to the specific introductory section.
For instance, from the words "At that time, the World-Honored One" until the end of this chapter is named the Specific Preface.

This is because the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious signs serve as the specific occasion for the commencement [of the teaching]; thus, it is called the "Circumstantial Preface. Third is the "Narrative Preface," which [arises] from the light...
[The Buddha] illuminates and beholds eighteen thousand lands. Maitreya, harboring doubts, poses questions; Mañjuśrī, citing ancient precedents, provides answers.
For the sake of the assembly, he resolves their doubts and serves as the prologue to the formal exposition; thus it is called the "Introductory Narrative" (*nidāna*).

One should know that the single character "introductory" (*xu*) encompasses these three meanings. The first is the general term for the introduction; the latter two are specific terms derived from "narration. As for the general term:
Thus, at the beginning of all sutras, these five matters are established to authenticate the Buddha’s scriptures and to refute the heterodox views of outsiders that they are not so or are otherwise.

The conditions for their arising will be clarified in the text below. Regarding the second and third [types of] introductory sequences (*nidāna*), they specifically clarify the particular sutra and do not apply in common to other sutras;
therefore, they introduce the causes and conditions for the commencement of the formal teaching, thereby distinguishing this sutra eternally from all others.

Therefore, it is called the "Specific Introduction" (Bie xu). Furthermore, one must understand that while the "General Introduction" (Tong xu) applies to all sections (bù), the "Specific Introduction" pertains to a single section.
Moreover, the General Introduction applies to all sutras, whereas the Specific Introduction pertains to a single teaching, such as this present sutra.

Within this sutra, the section and the teaching are pure and singular, without admixture—whether contrasted with or associated with the partial and the perfect, the small and the great—it exclusively reveals the provisional to manifest the real; it is a pure, wondrous, and perfect sutra.

The "Separate Introduction" (Pratyanupūrvaka-nidāna). It is called the "Separate Introduction" because it pertains specifically to one teaching. Furthermore, while the name "General Introduction" (Sādhāraṇa-nidāna) is general in scope yet distinct in its essence, the "Separate Introduction" is distinct in its particulars yet general in its meaning.
Because its meaning is general, all sūtras universally possess a Separate Introduction; because its essence is distinct, the Separate Introduction belongs specifically to the present sūtra.
Thus, we know that for this sūtra, both the General and the Separate Introductions are distinct, as the *Lotus Sūtra* transcends the teachings of the single lifetime [of Śākyamuni].
Among all the sūtras, this one stands apart as belonging uniquely to the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).

Because it is not related to other sūtras in such ways, it can truly be called the "prologue" (*nidāna*) to the "main body" (*śarīra*), and the "main body" to the "prologue. If one grasps this meaning, the entire work will be brilliantly clear.

The following text provides the formal explanation; since it is already encompassed by this [principle], it need not be explained again. As for the term "chapter" (*parivarta*), it refers to the middle...
The Āgamas refer to this as *varga*, which is translated here as "chapter" (*pin*). The meaning of "chapter" is general;

since it applies to all the subsequent chapters, I shall not further explain the word "chapter. One should know that while the term "chapter" is general, the title of the "Introduction" (*Nidāna*) is specific, as it constitutes a single distinct chapter.
A "chapter" (*varga*) is so named because items of similar meaning are gathered together into a single section. Now, regarding this "gathering":

Whoever compiled these [sections] titled them as chapters, as seen in the following scriptural text. These are either words spoken by the Buddha himself or the words of the compilers who recorded the sutra.
Regarding those said to be spoken by the Buddha himself, as the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" states: "The Buddha addressed Śrīkūṭarāja:
'If there are those who hear this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" and can rejoice in it, etc. It further says:
"O Śrīgarbha, I entrust this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja' to you," and so forth, including the passage "upholding this chapter," etc.;
these are the words spoken by the Buddha himself regarding this chapter.

If they were the words of the compiler, as in the case of the "Chapter on Gadgadasvara," the "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara," or even the "Chapter on Exhortation," these would all have been inserted by the one who compiled the sūtra; they are not [the Buddha's own words].

This refers to the person who translated [the text]. Since the various chapters (*parivarta*) were already complete within the Sanskrit original of this sutra, and were all established by the compilers (*saṃgītikāra*), it is clear that there was no translator.
"Chapter" (*dì*) signifies a location; "one" (*yī*) is the beginning of a numerical sequence.
Because it stands at the beginning of the various chapters, it is called the "First. It must be preceded by both the general and specific introductory sequences (*nidāna*) at the head of the sutra.
Thus, only with twenty-seven chapters can it be called a *sūtra*. Because the introduction follows the main body, both are collectively termed a *sūtra*;
therefore, the proclamation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus Sutra) does not pertain solely to the orthodox teaching (*śāsanamūla*).

Since all twenty-eight chapters are equally named "Wondrous" (*miao*), within each chapter the essence (*tǐ*) and other [attributes] are fully present, and beneath every sentence the name "Wondrous" is universally applied. Thus, the four aspects—teaching (*jiao*), practice (*xing*), person (*ren*), and principle (*li*)—are all...

Because it is titled as "One," the sequence of its transmission within a single school can be understood through three stages: the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination. From the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, all constitute a single body;
the twenty-eight chapters are all collectively termed "Wondrous. This ensures that the wondrous purport is not lost, allowing for a slight semblance of broad propagation.
Therefore, it is called the "Introduction Chapter" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is so. This refers to the essence of the Dharma as heard, which is one of the five matters.
Thus, it points to the entire section as the essence of the Dharma heard, because it is distinct from the Main Body and the Circulation; it may also include the Separate Introduction.

Thus, the "Doubtful Questions" and the "Innumerable Meanings" are both generally termed "Hearing" (*śruta*). Because flowers rain down and the earth trembles, these are explained according to what they symbolize;
as both universally symbolize "hearing," the entire sutra from beginning to end constitutes the essence of that which is heard.

This should be understood by way of the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) of causal conditions. Therefore, one knows that "Thus have I [heard]" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is placed at the beginning of the sutras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Thus it is. The Way of all Buddhas is the same; not contending with the world is itself joy, which is called the *lokasaṃvṛtisatya* (worldly standpoint).

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By citing time and place, one causes people to give rise to faith. When a sutra possesses such [features], faith can arise. 'Place' refers to places like Gṛdhrakūṭa, which remain accessible even to the present.
By relying on time to manifest the flavor [of the teaching], one causes those places that are no longer accessible to become manifest. Thus, faith arises.

True faith is precisely what constitutes the *puruṣa-saṃtāna* (the teaching for people) of this present sutra. Furthermore, the two characters "A" and "Ou" (阿歐) used to refute the non-Buddhists mean "not so" or "not thus";
this interpretation is also valid. If one follows this present sutra, it refutes the former teachings—including those that are merely partial or limited—and does not simply refute external names;
this is the *pratipakṣa-saṃtāna* (the teaching for remediation). Moreover, as for the term "thus" (*evam*):

These are words of faith and compliance. Through faith, the principles one has heard are harmonized; through compliance, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected—this is precisely the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, know that the four *siddhāntas* encompass the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma. This is why they are employed here.

If there were no such interpretation based on these causes and conditions (*nidāna*), it would not differ from the externalist calculations; how much less so when the language of causes and conditions is universal, pervading the entirety of the One Transformation?
Therefore, one must know that the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold purposes) of this present great matter are not merely other forms of responsive manifestation (*saṃgēna*).

The revelation of the four *siddhāntas*—the single Way without exterior—is something of long standing that does not appear in other sutras. The four *siddhāntas* of contemplating the mind (*citta*) encompass everything within a single contemplation.
If one grasps this meaning, only then will one understand the intent of the sutra. It is unknown what kind of text Ānanda transmitted from the Buddha in this present sutra, and what it elucidates.

These are equal. One cannot transmit the sudden through gradual texts, nor can one express the perfect through partial texts. If transmission and expression are erroneous, then the text is inadequate;
if the text is inadequate, then the principle is not correctly realized. This meaning is difficult to clarify;

I shall now briefly explain it by provisionally resorting to the gradual teachings to distinguish their significance. If the Buddha clarifies the conventional, there are words and letters; in the ultimate truth, there are none.

Regarding "words": Ānanda transmitted the Buddha’s words concerning conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) in written form; these do not differ from what the Buddha spoke, and are therefore called "thus" (*iti*).
Because one realizes the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by means of these conventional words, they are called "this" (*evam*).

This refers to the opening formula "Thus have I heard" at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka sūtras of the Hīnayāna, and not to the present sūtra. As for the Buddha’s teaching that "form is emptiness, and emptiness is form," [it is as follows:]

Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; they are non-dual and without distinction. That emptiness and form are not two is "Thusness" (tathatā); that reality is found within phenomena is "Suchness" (yathābhūtam).

Ānanda’s transmission of the Buddha’s words being no different [from the truth] is "Thusness"; that the expressive signifier is identical to the expressed meaning is "Suchness. This is the beginning of the Mahāyāna.
The opening of the sutras of the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-yāna) is likewise "Thus. Yet this is not the "Thus" of the present sutra. If the Buddha speaks of arising...
Death has limits; Nirvana is limitless. To emerge from birth-and-death is to have limits; to enter Nirvana is to be limitless.
To emerge from the limitlessness of Nirvana and enter the Middle Way—Ānanda transmitted this, and it is no different from what the Buddha taught;

it is thus (*tathatā*). From the shallow to the profound, there is nothing that is not called "is. This is precisely the beginning of the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, "Thus," which does not belong to the present [teaching].
This is the Sūtra. If the Buddha taught that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa, it is also the Middle Way; how much more so, then, is nirvāṇa not the Middle Way?

True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the true nature (*bhūtadhātu*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) pervade all places, such that there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma.
Because Ānanda transmitted this without differing from the Buddha, it is called "Thus" (*tathā*). Because it is thus and immovable, it is called "Is" (*iti*). Thus:
This is the Perfect Sūtra. Now, first, it is thus: one should know that this present sūtra is thus.

It transcends all teachings—those of the sudden, the gradual, the secret, and the indeterminate—and reveals the provisional to manifest the Real; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle, with no second or third.
Only then does this present sūtra transcend the "thusness" of the eight teachings; only then is it what is heard in this sūtra. If one hears this...
The sutra says: While listening to the teaching at that very assembly, the practitioner, in accordance with what they hear, immediately illuminates their own body;

their awakened mind becomes clear and pure, and they immediately gain faith in their own mind—this is called "seeing the Buddha. When the factors of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) are clearly distinguished, this is "seeing Śāriputra.
When all the various factors are clearly distinguished, one sees the assembly of bhikṣus. When the mind of compassion is pure, this is "seeing the bodhisattvas. Thus says the sutra.
He said: "If a person believes what you have said, they will immediately see me, the assembly of bhikṣus, and all the bodhisattvas.
By observing the mind, they will see the essence of their own mind. When it is manifested in this way, one is then exempted from counting the treasures of others."
"I have heard.
Regarding "I have heard," this refers to the second person capable of upholding [the teaching], namely the Venerable Ānanda.
The Sūtra states that there are four types of Ānanda: first, Ānanda, which is translated as "Joyful" (Huanxi); he upheld the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna. Second...
First is Ānanda-bhadra, which in this language means "Joyous Sage" (Huānxǐ Xián); he received and upheld the initial gateway of the Mahāyāna, the Common Teachings, and the Miscellaneous Piṭaka.
Second is Ānanda with the title "Holding the Treasury" (Chízàng Ānán); he upheld the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Third is Ānanda-bhaga.
This is called the Ocean of Joy. It upholds the Buddha-treasury of the Perfect and Sudden [teachings]. This refers to the present Ānanda. Now, as for this Ānanda:

his faculty of hearing is unimpaired; the sound is within the range of audibility; and he applies his mind with the desire to hear. Because these various conditions harmonize, it is said, "I heard. Question: One should say "heard by the ear";
why then do you say "I heard"? Answer: I am the master of the ear. By mentioning "I," [the self is indicated].

This refers to the gathering of all conditions (*pratyaya*). Regarding these "all conditions," it means that by relying on the power of Ānanda’s vow and the Tathāgata’s past vows, when sentient beings after the parinirvāṇa possess the capacity to be awakened, they are then able to bring about the harmonious integration [of conditions] so as to hear.
Thus, it is said: "I" am the harmony of all conditions; only through this can "I" hear. Therefore, it is called "I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). Furthermore, there is another explanation:
The Treatise says: "Ordinary persons have three kinds of self: the self of views, the self of pride, and the self of names.
Those in training (śaikṣa) have only two kinds; they lack the self of views. Those beyond training (aśaikṣa) have only one kind: merely the self of names.
If it is said that Ānanda was one in training, he was thus free from the false self and was able to subdue the self of pride, yet he followed worldly convention and was called by name.
"I am without fault. Speaking in terms of the provisional teaching (*yōkyō*), the Sūtra says: "Ānanda’s face was like the pure full moon; his eyes were like blue lotuses.
He personally received the Buddha’s instructions as one holds up a perfect vessel, and he transmitted them to transform others as one pours from one jar into another.
To hear the Dharma through such transmission is the "I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) of the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna; it is not the "I heard" of the present Sūtra.
If one says that it is beyond the four propositions—self, non-self, both self and non-self, neither self nor non-self;
as well as "mine," "not mine," both "mine" and "not mine," and neither "mine" nor "not mine"—then it is beyond these four propositions.
Only then can it be called "selflessness. Within the Buddha’s True Dharma, there is no self. Who heard this? This Venerable Ānanda dwells on the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*);

he has attained emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and his faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue do not leak. He is the one who transmits and upholds both the teachings already heard and those not yet heard;
this refers to the "I heard" of the Venerable Ānanda of the Initial Mahāyāna Shared Teaching, and not to that of the present sutra. If one says...
"Ānanda, the one of great learning, knows 'self' and 'non-self' as non-dual. Yet he also discriminates between both 'self' and 'non-self.

This Ānanda, the Keeper of the Treasury, possesses vast capacity for receiving and retaining [the Dharma], like a great cloud holding rain. This refers to the Ānanda who was the recipient of the *An-wen-wen fa* (The Dharma Heard by One Who Does Not Hear);
he is the Ānanda of the Separate Teaching (*prātipakṣika*), not the one in this present sutra. If it is said that Ānanda knows 'self' and 'non-self'..."
I am dual, yet not dual. Acting as an attendant through skillful means, I transmit the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom.
With a voice of mastery, I transmit the provisional and the ultimate; I am able to discern the permanent and the impermanent, and I know that the Tathāgata never fails to preach the Dharma.
This is called the Bodhisattva Ānanda being fully endowed with great learning. Therefore, he is like the vast ocean of the Buddha-Dharma.
This flowed into Ānanda’s mind. It is precisely this that constitutes the ocean of the present sutra;

it is Ānanda who upholds this wondrous Dharma which was neither heard nor not heard—namely, the "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) of the present sutra. Question: Ānanda was born on the very night the Buddha attained the Way.
He attended the Buddha for more than twenty years. Was it not the case that he had not heard [the teachings] before attending the Buddha?
Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When Ānanda was compiling the Dharma, he said of himself: 'When the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma, I did not see it at that time;

I heard it thus through successive transmission. One should know, therefore, that he did not hear everything. Some say: "Ānanda attained the Buddha’s awakening-samādhi (*buddhabodhi-samādhi*), and by its power, [he heard everything]."

One can indeed hear it oneself. The *Bao’en jīng* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states: “Ānanda requested four vows, among which he wished that the Buddha would preach again those sūtras he had not yet heard.
It further states: “The Buddha secretly spoke them for him with his own mouth. The *Tāi jīng* (Sūtra on the Womb) also states:

“The Buddha extended a golden arm from his golden coffin and once again manifested for Ānanda the signs of entering the womb. If even the signs of the womb could still be seen, how much more so the sūtras he had not yet heard?”

One should know that all [teachings] of the previous sutras have been heard. However, those who hear the sutra today perceive within their own minds whether there is a self or no-self, and whether they have heard it or not.
They realize that all phenomena (*dharma*) are emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
If they discern no-self yet experience "I" hearing what was not heard, they understand that all phenomena are conventional designations (*prajñapti*). If they know both self and no-self as two...
Second: Although non-dual, it appears as dual. To perceive within one’s own mind that which is neither heard nor unhearing—the wondrous Dharma complete in a single thought—is itself the Middle Way;
this is the realization of the meaning of "I have heard" within one’s own mind.
"At one time.

This is the third [element], the harmony of hearing and retaining. Regarding the phrase "at one time": it refers to the fifth [occasion], when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached to reveal the ultimate truth by opening up the provisional.
It is the supreme moment of the Dharma King’s auspicious manifestation, a most excellent "one time," and not the former periods of the "combined" or "exclusive" teachings.
The time when the great and small paths are brought together is precisely the moment when this sutra’s single great cause and condition opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
at that one thought-moment, those who hear the sutra immediately illuminate their own minds.
This is precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; for sixty kalpas not to depart from a single kṣaṇa is precisely the wondrous moment.
The Buddha was dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha.
This refers to the fourth [aspect]: the Teacher who can expound [the Dharma], as well as the locus for hearing and retaining it.

Here, rather than treating them separately, the Buddha and the locus are combined; therefore, the present explanation follows this synthesis. Now, the Buddha is neither moved nor emerges from the *dharmatā*. Why is this?
Because the Buddha is able to realize that the *dharmatā* and afflictions are fundamentally non-dual in nature, which is itself *bodhi*.
There is no movement, for one is able to realize that birth and death are themselves nirvana.

There is no emergence, yet for the sake of sentient beings, one enables them to perceive through responsive manifestation. Without moving, there is movement, demonstrating the severing of the causes of birth;

without emerging, there is emergence, crossing the ocean of birth and death to transform the multitudes of the nine realms. Thus, the Buddha-body appears in the world; yet, in the Tathāgata, there is in reality nothing [of this].
"Movement" means to emerge. Regarding the term "Buddha": in Western India it is called *buddha*, which here is translated as "the Awakened One" (*jue-zhe*) or "the Knower" (*zhi-zhe*).

It is termed "knower" in contrast to delusion, and "awakened" in contrast to ignorance. These names are established provisionally for the sake of sentient beings; thus, there are three meanings of awakening, namely:
self-awakening (*zijue*), because the Buddha is able to awaken to all phenomena himself through the six perfections and myriad practices.
It is because it aids in the fulfillment of the distant [stages] and does not require passing through incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) that one achieves wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
One establishes all children within the secret treasury and dwells therein oneself; therefore, it is said that "one's own awakening and the awakening of others fulfill the practice of awakening.

What is called a Buddha is named "Awakening" (*bodhi*); this name for awakening applies universally to the Buddhas of all teachings—whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, partial (*pradeśika*) or perfect (*pariniṣpanna*). It should be understood thus.
Know that this present sutra is precisely that which reveals the ultimate by opening the provisional, and distinguishes the superior by means of the inferior.
It manifests the Honored and Extraordinary Body, which is inconceivable, possessing the characteristics of empty space, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, and free from all discrimination.

This is not like the form of the old bhikṣu of eighty or sixteen feet from days of yore; rather, it is a body that, through a single thought-moment of correspondence, sits upon a lotus throne to receive its office.

Because in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* prior to this [text], the three Buddhas were separated from the clear [teaching] and isolated from the partial and small [teachings], they have now come to the present sutra.
From the inferior, the superior is distinguished; that is, the three are one. From the perspective of the superior, it is not meant that the Great Void is called the Perfect Buddha.

Therefore, only upon reaching the present sutra does one know that the past [teachings] were actually pointing toward this. Only the Buddha has fully exhausted [this truth]; these words are thus grounded in reality. If one is to contemplate and understand this, one should contemplate as follows:
One's own mind is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; it is the ultimate Tathāgata of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

Because one’s true wisdom is in profound resonance with this reality, all of life is entirely Buddha. Having grasped this principle, the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-vidha-yoga*) are distinguished, thereby avoiding the reproach of self-deprecation and eliminating the fault of overweening pride.
This concludes the brief explanation of "Buddha. As for what is called "abiding," the Buddha-body is...
One is able to dwell. The Sahā world is that which is dwelt in. It is not merely that the body relies upon the land; rather, the mind and its phenomena also rely upon one another.

If one were to explain the meaning of "dwelling" solely by means of the physical body residing in the land, then for great Bodhisattvas, whose spirits have no fixed location, such an explanation would be insufficient.
Is it then that there is no abiding at all? You should know that this present sutra is able to abide in the place of abiding.

It is not like the former [teachings], which analyzed the substance of dharmas in sequence and involved an abiding characterized by both subject and object; rather, it reveals the provisional to manifest the real through the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Abiding in the Secret Treasury refers to the city of Rājagṛha; this is the eternally quiescent light, the dwelling place of the Buddha.
This is because one abides within the objective realm by means of the dharma of non-abiding.
Not only does one perceive the Buddha’s abiding in suchness, but one also perceives the dharma-realm in which one's own mind abides. As for "Rājagṛha," in India it is called Rājagṛha-kāla; this...
It is called the City of Rājagṛha. The name of that country is Magadha, which here means "Non-injury," because there is no law of execution or killing there.
It is also called Makhādeśa, which here means "Heavenly Net"; this is the name of the king, and the country is named after the king.
The king begot a crown prince named Pāṇḍava-pāda. Later, he succeeded to the royal throne and, together with the minor kings of a thousand small kingdoms, constructed this palace.
The circumference of the inner city was one hundred and fifty *li*. The detailed account of its origins is as found in the *Renwang Dajing Lun* and the *Fahua Wenju*;
for fear of excessive prolixity, it is not recorded here. Nevertheless, this Royal Residence (Rājagṛha) is visible to all the great assemblies.
It is the same. Some see a forest of *sāla* trees, with sand, grass, and rocky walls; this is what those of the Tripiṭaka school perceive.
Some see it as pure and adorned with the seven treasures; this is what those who have entered the Mahāyāna generally perceive.
Some see it as the place where the Buddhas of the three periods of time travel; this is what the distinct bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna perceive. Or they see it as...
The inconceivable realm of all Buddhas is the true essence of reality (*dharmatā*). This is precisely the vision of the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna;
it is what is elucidated in the *Xiàngfǎ juéyí jīng* (Sūtra on Resolving Doubts during the Semblance Dharma).

Since there are four kinds of that which is dwelled in, the Buddha-body that dwells therein must likewise be fourfold. If one contemplates the mind to perceive Rājagṛha, "King" (*rāja*) refers to the King of the Mind.

The "house" is the house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Because the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the sovereign of good and evil, it constructs this indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) house.
If one can analyze and empty the house of the five aggregates of one's own mind, that emptiness becomes the city of Nirvana. This contemplation is shallow.
To view [the five aggregates] as mere earth and wood is the beginning stage of the Hīnayāna.

If one realizes that the house of the five aggregates within one's own mind is itself empty, and that this emptiness is the city of Nirvāṇa, this is what is illuminated by those who have attained penetration.

If one contemplates the house of the five aggregates within one's own mind and, through the cessation of this form (rūpa), attains eternal form, and applies the same to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, then one perceives the eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
The four virtues being "the dwelling place where all Buddhas roam" is a specific meaning unique to the Mahāyāna. The three meanings mentioned above are none of them the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
In this present sutra, one should contemplate that the house of the five aggregates (skandhas) within one's own body is itself the *dharmatā-tathatā* (the true suchness of phenomena).
This *tathatā* is devoid of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. All sentient beings and their lands are themselves *nirvāṇa*.

The "Pan" (槃) cannot be extinguished again; it is the dwelling of ultimate emptiness and stillness, which is Great Nirvana. This is called seeing the true substance of the Tathatā within the palace of one's own mind-king.
Thus, although one hears the characteristics of dharmas in the sutras all day long, one has never heard of the characteristics of dharmas [as inherently existent].
Therefore, it is said that there is no departure from words and letters, for this is the characteristic of liberation. As for what is called Mount Qi (耆山), this...
It is translated as "Vulture Peak" (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) because the shape of the mountain resembles a vulture; thus, the peak is named after the bird. The *Āgama Sūtras* state:
"The Buddha was at Vulture Peak and addressed the bhikṣus: 'For a long succession of kalpas, the Buddhas of the three periods of time have all shared the same name, Vulture Peak.'"

Furthermore, there are other names for it. Do you know them? It is also called Mount Guangpu (Extensive and Universal), also known as Mount Fuzhong (Carrying the Heavy), and also said to be Mount Xiankue (Immortal Cavern).
It is a place where arhats, bodhisattvas, and various immortals possessing supernatural powers constantly reside. A detailed explanation is provided in the *Tiantai Wenzhu*.
Question: When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and heaven and earth are cleared away, how can there be Buddhas before and after?
"Do you dwell on this mountain together? He replied: "When the subsequent kalpa is established, the original characteristics will reappear;

only those who have attained supernatural powers (abhijñā) know this, for it is not something understood by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). If, upon hearing that [the Buddha was at] Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, one wishes to illuminate one's own mind," [one should do so].
One should contemplate one's own aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as being as insentient as a mountain. As the Sūtra says: "This body is insentient, like grass, trees, tiles, or pebbles.
One contemplates the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the spirit and the other three aggregates as the vultures.

Thus, regarding one's own five aggregates, one sees the Spirit and Vulture Peak (*Śrī-Gṛdhrakūṭa*) that is being contemplated. Furthermore, all objects of contemplation do not transcend the five aggregates; although this mountain is...

Regarding the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment): relying upon this to contemplate the *sahaja-vipāka* (intrinsic retribution). If one contemplates this Gṛdhrakūṭa as being impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, this is the meaning of the Tripiṭaka (Śrāvaka) teaching.
If one contemplates this Gṛdhrakūṭa as "form is itself emptiness," this is the intention of the Shared Teaching (Pratyekabuddha).

If one contemplates the essence of the Gṛdhrakūṭa as wisdom-nature, adorned with the wisdom of the *bodhi-bīja* (cause of realization), and contemplates the gathering of the Gṛdhras as adorned with the merit of the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause), [this is the Mahāyāna].

Yan: To contemplate the mountain as the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the unmoving primary cause (*hetu*). That which is called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyakośa*) refers specifically to the Mahāyāna meaning of the Bodhisattva.

In this sutra, contemplating one’s own Vulture Peak within a single mind, the three causes are instantaneously present—neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor distinct—and this is called the "Secret Treasury. This is precisely seeing that one's own mind is eternally abiding.
Within this context, the Great Sutra says: "Adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom," which means one abides on Vulture Peak oneself.
By means of this, one delivers sentient beings, causing others to likewise abide on Vulture Peak; thus it is called "settling all children.
This Mahayana method of complete and sudden contemplation is fully detailed in the Ten Objects and Ten Vehicles of the Tiantai *Zhi Guan*. It involves driving the great white ox.

Neither moving nor emerging, one mounts this precious vehicle and proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). This is not something that can be attained through the application of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Since the subsequent scriptural text is extensive, I shall not provide a detailed commentary or a fourfold interpretation for each point.
Rather, I shall use the aforementioned meanings to run through the various passages below, so that every sentence and every word may be clearly understood. Herein, in advance...
This is merely indicated; it is not further explained in detail. For a thorough and clear understanding, one should consult works such as the *Fahua xuanshu* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
If you wish to know this in detail, please seek those teachings. As for the scripture’s mention of "the middle":

because the Buddha abides in the Middle Way—ascending to heaven at midday, descending from heaven at midday, being born in the Middle Kingdom, and entering parinirvāṇa at midnight—all these signify the Middle Way. Now, dwelling in the mountains, he preaches the Middle Way.
The teaching is that which is manifested. △ From here below, from "Mahā... up to "retreated to one side," all constitute the fifth section:
the retinue who hear and uphold [the Dharma]. This consists of three parts: first, the śrāvakas; second, the bodhisattvas; and third, the miscellaneous assembly.
Regarding the sequence in which they are listed, there are both practical and doctrinal reasons. As for the practical reason, it refers to their physical proximity and distance; the śrāvakas...
Their physical forms transcend the mundane net, and their traces are close to those of the Tathāgata. Because they have personally realized the sūtras, they are listed first.
The gods and humans differ in form and attire, and their traces do not consist of serving [the Buddha]; because they have realized the sūtras only distantly, they are listed later.

As for the Bodhisattvas, their forms do not conform to conventional decorum, and their traces have no fixed location. Since they are neither like the laity nor identical to the monastic community, they occupy a position between the two.
This refers to the "intermediate state" (*antara*). According to one interpretation, *śrāvakas* delight in *nirvāṇa*, while gods and humans are attached to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);

each has its own partiality. The Bodhisattva neither delights nor is attached; dwelling in the middle, he seeks the ultimate source. Thus, he exists between the two. This was the view of the ancients and the *Śāstra-vyākhyā*.

All of these are merely offered as explanations based on such considerations. Within the section on the Śrāvakas, first the assembly of those with many acquaintances is listed, followed by those with few acquaintances, and finally the assembly of Bhikṣuṇīs.
From here, the scriptural text is divided into six major sections for detailed explanation.
This concludes the section on the assembly of Śrāvakas.
"Accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus.
This is the first instance of a category. "Category" (jùlèi) refers to those who belong to the same class as the great bhikṣus; it is like a group or multitude.
These are all individuals known to the public, belonging to the class of those with high reputation and great virtue. Therefore, it says "accompanied by" (yǔ). "Accompanied" means together with.
These are explained through seven shared meanings: namely, sharing the same time, the same place, the same precepts, the same mind, the same views, the same path, and the same liberation.
If one follows the subsequent praise of virtues, these seven all pertain to the "Small" [Vehicle] at the Deer Park.
However, if one discusses those who have already attained prediction, these seven are entirely the "Perfect" [Vehicle] of this present sutra, all belonging to the "Great" [Vehicle].

"Because of the identical wondrous resonance and so forth," it is able to bestow this upon Ānanda and, by extension, upon the great assembly; a detailed explanation is provided in the *Shuji* (Commentary).
Regarding the term "Great" (*mahā*) in the Sūtra, the *Śāstra* explains that there are three meanings of "Great":

First, "Great" refers to being honored by the lords of heavenly realms and emperors, kings, and great personages; thus it is called "Great. Second, "Superior" refers to rising above and transcending the ninety-five [non-Buddhist] paths.

Because it stands outside the various non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), it is called "superior" (jaya). Third, regarding "many meanings" (bahu-artha): it is called "many" because it universally knows all internal and external scriptures.
Furthermore, each [of these] should be threefold: namely, greatness of the path (mārga-mahattva), greatness of function (prayoga-mahattva), and greatness of knowledge (jñāna-mahattva).

This applies equally to both superiority and multiplicity. "Path" refers to the cultivation and nature of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna); it is superior to all non-Buddhist omniscience. "Function" refers to the cultivation of the common [practices].

Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): [The text] surpasses the non-Buddhist practitioners of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) who know that they are practicing the foundation of mindfulness of objects;

it also surpasses the many non-Buddhist practitioners of the four Vedas. Furthermore, one must discuss the meanings of "great," "many," and "superior" through the alternating application of the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), clarifying what is realized within the minds of the various assemblies and illuminating the varying depths of their realization of principle.
Setting aside the partial and the small for now, I shall briefly clarify the "great companions" of this present sutra. Directly...
Proceeding upon the Middle Way, one contemplates that the nature of one’s own mind is as vast and expansive as empty space;

this is called "Great. By simultaneously negating both extremes, one enters the ocean of quiescent extinction; this is called "Supreme. By simultaneously illuminating the two truths, it possesses great capacity for inclusion—within a single mind are all minds, inconceivable;
this is called "Many. Because these three meanings are present, it is termed "Great. As for "Bhikṣu," there are the two [versions] by Sengzhao and Kumārajīva.

The Master explains [the term *śramaṇa*] based on four meanings: first, one who seeks alms for a pure livelihood; second, one who destroys afflictions (*kleśa*); third, one who is able to maintain the precepts; and fourth, one who terrifies Māra.
The *Śāstra* (Treatise) explains it according to three meanings: first, terrifying Māra; second, destroying evil; and third, seeking alms.

Here, we follow the explanation of the *Śāstra*, as the translations by Zhu Fashu and Kumārajīva do not encompass both the initial and subsequent stages, whereas the *Śāstra* encompasses both. This is like the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* performed at the time of initial ordination.

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act). By the power of the unmanifest precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*), one universally overturns all evils; even up to the cultivation of dhyāna, giving rise to the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*) and so forth, is called "destroying evil.
If, at the initial shaving of the head and reception of the precepts, one cultivates concentration and wisdom to subdue and destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "frightening Māra.
If, at the initial departure from wrong livelihood, one sustains oneself by begging for alms, cultivates concentration and wisdom, and seeks the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), it is called "begging."
The term "bhikṣu" (monk) possesses three meanings that apply equally to both the initial and final stages.

One should also explain these three meanings of bhikṣu by way of the four teachings (*catur-yāna*) and their provisional and ultimate aspects (*honjaku*), but for fear of prolixity, I shall set this aside for now.

If one perceives these three meanings of bhikṣu within one's own mind, one contemplates one's own single mind as pure as empty space, unimpeded by the shackles of the two extremes. This is the great wisdom of equality, which abides nowhere.

Non-attachment is itself called "leaving home. Sustaining oneself through the sublime contemplation of the Middle Way and thereby nourishing the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body is what is meant by the meaning of a "beggar" (bhikṣu) who has seen his own mind.
If one contemplates that the afflictions of the five abodes within one's own mind are themselves bodhi, this is it.
This is called "one's own mind breaking through evil. If one contemplates one's own mind, all extremes and inversions are none other than the Middle Way;
this is precisely what terrifies Māra. This is seeing a bhikṣu within one's own mind.
As for the term *saṃgha*, in India it is called *saṃgha*, which here means "harmonious assembly. A single person is not called a harmonious assembly; from four people upward, it is so named.
Harmony. Harmony of matter means there is no separate assembly; harmony of Dharma means there is no separate principle. The *Śāstra* clarifies that there are four kinds of assemblies:
first, those who do not rely on pure livelihood, called the assembly of the precept-breakers; second, those who do not understand the laws and regulations, called the assembly of the ignorant;

third, those with the five expedient means, possessing shame and remorse, called the assembly of the conscientious; fourth, those with the patience for the suffering of dharmas, called the assembly of the true. Furthermore, the four teachings must be required.

The section distinguishing the provisional and the ultimate regarding the assembly is concise. If one can illuminate the Way within one's own mind and enter the stage of semblance, yet has not yet manifested the truth, feeling shame before the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning and guilt before the various sages, this is called the assembly that feels shame and guilt within their own minds.
If the truth is manifested, they are the assembly of reality. Those who do not rely on contemplative practice are called the assembly that breaks the precepts; they do not understand contemplation.
"Characteristics" refers to the multitude of the deluded; such is the interpretation.
"Not a numerical characteristic" means twelve thousand people together.
This is the second general indication of the great number of the assembly of many renowned disciples (*bahujñāta*). Question: Regarding all the enumerations of the assemblies...

Question: Why is it that the number of those who have attained the Way is necessarily complete and without deficiency? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), in its commentary on the "Five Thousand" section, states:

"Whether exceeding or falling short, they all remain within the general category. If one examines one's own mind and sees twelve thousand, this means observing the twelve bases (*āyatana*) of one's own aggregates (*skandha*).
Each base possesses the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), and each realm, in turn, possesses... [the rest of the sentence continues with the recursive structure of the realms].
The ten realms; each realm contains ten [realms]. Such phenomena are thus fully present within a single sense-base (*āyatana*), comprising a hundred realms and a thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*).
The twelve sense-bases thus constitute twelve thousand dharma-gates. This meaning must be understood through the *Tiantai Zhiguan* (Tiantai’s Calming and Contemplation).
Even if there were one dharma up to ten million dharmas, all would be seen within a single mind.
Through the gate of mastery, throughout an inexhaustible period exceeding all measure, the mind is fully revealed and illuminated; this is the fundamental intent of the Buddha’s teaching.
"All are arhats. This third section clarifies the stage of those who know the Dharma. "All" refers to the twelve thousand people mentioned above.
Regarding the term "arhat," there are two senses: first, it has a translation; second, it is a term without a [direct] translation. As for having a translation, it is as follows:

There are three meanings. These are: non-attachment (*asaṅga*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), and worthy of offerings (*arhat*). Because the mountain of the ninety-eight latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) has been exhausted, it is called "non-attachment.
Because the husks of ignorance have been shed, one will not receive the retribution of birth and death within the field of future lives; thus, it is called "non-arising.
Because one possesses the merits of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa-guṇa*), one is fit to serve as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for humans and devas; thus, it is called "worthy."

These three meanings are those for which there are translations. If there were no translations [for these meanings], it is simply because the single term *arhat* contains the aforementioned three meanings;
therefore, it is not translated, but is merely called "Arhat. The above explanation has been given primarily by way of the fruit (*phala*).
Within the causal stage (*hetu*), there are likewise three meanings as previously stated. Furthermore, the single term *arhat* has three types: first, the Arhat of Wisdom (*prajñā-arhat*);...
Liberation. Second is called "liberation through both parts" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). Third is called "great liberation free from doubt. These three types are all termed *arhat*.

One should further distinguish them according to the teachings; let us set that aside for now. The preceding explanation of the three meanings of the translation [of *arhat*] was an explanation based on their qualities (*guṇa*).
If we discuss it in terms of these qualities, not only do the *arhats* of the *Tripiṭaka* and *Shared* vehicles possess these three meanings, but the manifested (*nirmāṇakāya*) Buddhas do as well.

The two types of Arhats—those who have distinguished themselves from the Path and those who are Perfect—likewise possess these three meanings. It is not only the "killing of thieves"; there is also the "killing of the non-thief.
That which is the non-thief is Nirvana, and this too must be destroyed; this is precisely the meaning of "killing the thieves.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) is non-arising, yet it is still termed "arising. Now, one does not arise within arising, nor does one arise within non-arising; this is called [the ultimate].
It is unarisen. It is not merely that which is worthy of offerings; it is also that which provides offerings for all sentient beings, thereby fulfilling their needs.
This refers to the virtues of the three meanings—correspondence, transformation, and so forth—pertaining to the first stage (*bhūmi*) and the first dwelling (*vihāra*).

Thus, its fundamental nature is the great wisdom of equality, wherein there is neither destruction nor non-destruction. It is able to manifest traces within the various teachings as unarisen, fundamentally realizing liberation, and being free from thieves.

He is not a thief; he manifests as a slayer of thieves. Having fundamentally attained the Dharma-body, which is neither subject to nor exempt from response, he is able to manifest as one worthy of offerings.
One should know that if one relies on one's own mind and employs the subtle contemplation of the Middle Way to slay the thief of ignorance, the mind of the Two Vehicles will not arise.

One should make offerings to such a person as one would to the World-Honored One. Furthermore, it is said that making offerings to the Buddha and Mañjuśrī is not equal to providing a single meal to one who practices the Vaipulya sūtras.
It is also said that if one slanders or praises the Buddha, the resulting demerit or merit is still light;

however, if one slanders or praises a holder of this sūtra, the demerit or merit is extremely grave. Why is this? Because the Buddha has no thought of food and has long since departed from the eight winds [of worldly influence]. He does not...

Regarding benefit and harm: to bestow [offerings] upon those who uphold the sutras preserves their physical bodies, prolongs their karmic life, gives birth to the Dharma-body, and increases their wisdom-life;
therefore, it is beneficial. To disparage them gives rise to affliction, regret, and remorse, whereby one loses the opportune moment and cannot be saved;

this constitutes great harm. This is explained in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) regarding the non-arising of the three meanings; as for the response, one should make offerings. Vasubandhu points this out.
This first line, "The state of illumination," is a general praise of his virtues; the following five lines are a specific praise of his virtues. This is how Tiantai received and applied [the text]:
"All outflows are exhausted; there are no further afflictions. He has attained his own benefit and ended all fetters of existence; his mind has attained mastery."
These five phrases separately praise the three virtues of the Arhat: being a slayer of thieves (*arhat*), being worthy of offerings (*arhan*), and being non-arisen (*anupapatti*).

The first two phrases praise the virtue of being a slayer of thieves. Regarding the term "all outflows" (*āsrava*), there are three outflows: first, the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*), which refers to all afflictions of the desire realm with the exception of ignorance;
second, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), which refers to all [afflictions] of the upper realms—the form and formless realms.
Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*): excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), the third is the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), which refers to the ignorance of the three realms.

Furthermore, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states: "It is called an outflow because it causes one to lose the Path. The Vinaya says: "A deluded person creates karma, opening the gates of all outflows. This explains "outflow" (*āsrava*) in terms of its cause.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Falling into birth and death is called an outflow. This explains it in terms of its result, as it arises from the creation of karma.
Because of this cause, one loses the life-force of wisdom and falls into the bitter fruit of birth and death; thus, the Dharma-body perishes.
Having lost the life-force of wisdom and forfeited the Dharma-body, one has lost the Way. This is like the ruinous loss of a precious treasure.

Due to this loss of the Way, the "outflows" (*āsrava*) and so forth act as the moisture for karma, which in turn summons the defilements that provide the moisture—namely, the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*), including the floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*).

The *paryavasthānas* and *nīvaraṇas* afflict the practitioner. Since the Arhat has severed these, both the moisture (*ārdra*) and the moistened (*ārdrita*)—namely, karma and its concomitants—are entirely exhausted.

Therefore, the first two phrases correctly praise the single virtue of being a "slayer of thieves" (*vadhaka*). Next, the phrase "having attained" (*prāpta*) correctly praises the single virtue of being a "worthy of offerings" (*arhat*).

Because of the aforementioned slaying of thieves, the merit of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) is established; abandonment necessarily entails wisdom, and once this merit is perfected, one's own benefit is realized. Thus [the text proceeds].
"He is worthy of offerings. Next, the two lines beginning with "exhausting all" praise the virtue of non-arising.
"All existences" refers to the twenty-five places of birth; "fetters" refers to the twenty-five causes of birth. When the cause is exhausted, the fruit perishes.
The praise of "non-arising" is indeed clear; it should not be a praise for "slaying the thief.

An Arhat should only be one whose fetters are exhausted; he should not yet possess "exhaustion" [in the sense of finality]. As for those who speak of "exhaustion," they are describing the fruit within the context of the cause. Furthermore, this exhaustion will occur before long.

That all fetters are exhausted results from the perfection of both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Because concentration is perfected, the mind attains mastery; because wisdom is perfected, [wisdom...]
"Attaining mastery" means being fully endowed with concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), a person of "double liberation" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
"The birth of certainty is exhausted" is a praise of the virtue of non-arising (*anutpāda*). These five preceding phrases are a specific praise of the three virtues of the Arhat.
One should know that all Śrāvaka Arhats were originally ancient Buddhas; for example, Subhūti was originally [a Buddha of] the East, the Blue...
Nāgadatta Buddha. Śāriputra was originally the Golden Nāgadatta Buddha; he manifested as a śrāvaka to assist in the transformation of Śākyamuni.

Although he appeared to have the outflows of afflictions in his fundamental state, the source of these flows had long since been exhausted. He realized Great Nirvāṇa, which is fundamentally non-arising.
Having long realized the Dharma-body, wisdom, and abandonment, as well as the merit of the true mark, he is fundamentally one who has perfected his own benefit and is worthy of offerings.

This is his virtue. Originally, he attained the twenty-five samādhis, destroyed the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), and manifested the true self, possessing the eight kinds of sovereign mastery.
This was his fundamental act of slaying the thief [of ignorance]. Today, he traces his manifestation to display the merits of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Worldly people do not understand the intent behind the teachings—the skillful means of manifesting traces to guide sentient beings—and see only that various sutras sometimes disparage the voice-hearers (*śrāvaka*).
Hearing such talk, they claim that [the Arhats] are truly like "spoiled seeds" and the like;

they even emulate those who disparage Śrāvakas and deceive Arhats, causing ordinary people throughout the world to habitually corrupt both their minds and speech by slandering and reviling the Noble Assembly, thereby harming themselves and burdening others.
How tragic! One should know that the sixteen *arhats* and others of the four great elements, once the *Lotus Sūtra* had revealed and clarified the Dharma, have all already attained Buddhahood;
they are true *śrāvakas*. By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, they cause all to hear.
While the compiler of the sūtra praised their virtues based on their past state, now that this present sūtra has arrived, they have all become great *bodhisattvas* and the like. Today we hear [this].

As for the Sūtra: those who wish to see that their own minds are endowed with these three virtues should employ the correct contemplation of the Middle Way to illumine their own minds, so as not to fall into the two extremes of emptiness or the provisional.
When afflictions are extinguished without being extinguished, this is precisely the "slaying of the thief.
To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the "Supreme Samādhi. The treasury of robes, jewels, and pearls is fully understood within a single mind.
This is one's own property; it is the vision of one's own mind as one's own benefit and as that which is worthy of offering.

If one illuminates one's own mind and correctly contemplates the Middle Way, one severs the thieves of the fetters and also abandons the two extremes. When the Middle Way itself does not remain, the mind is no longer bound by objects or contemplation.
Therefore, it is called "sovereignty. Without severing afflictions (*kleśa*), one enters *nirvāṇa*; this is the meaning of non-arising.
There is no need to seek it afar; within a single moment of mind, one suddenly perceives the three virtues.
Their names are as follows.
From this point downward begins the fifth list of names. Below, I shall explain these names; for now, I will first indicate the intent behind citing them.
Regarding the brief mention of twenty-one venerable ones: although all the Buddha’s disciples were fully endowed with manifold practices, [the text]...
They conceal their perfect capabilities and each receive a name based on only one virtue because they wish to attract beings according to their particular inclinations.
Thus, some sages may have initially been among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) in order to refute them;

or they may have been born among the Śākyas in order to subdue them, acting as guides and leaders to draw them in—just as Śāriputra entered the womb [of a courtesan] or Kāśyapa established his ascetic practices.

Regarding his retinue, teachers, and friends—whether they were antagonistic or compliant, whether they were the transformers or the transformed—the traces left by the various sages are shown not to have been bestowed in vain.
As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*: some established fasts and built merits, constructing dwellings; others subdued non-Buddhists.

They skillfully attend to the sick; they travel about to transform people; they settle affairs and remain composed with folded hands; they delight in wearing fine garments, yet feel no shame in wearing tattered rags;

they have no satiety in eating; their speech is coarse and rugged. Whether nuns or laypeople, all are great manifestations of expedient power (*mahopāya*), each excelling in the manner of attracting sentient beings.
Like the bhikṣu Cunda, they are all renowned as eminent elders possessed of virtue.
The Great Man is accompanied by his followers: Śāriputra is accompanied by those of profound and sharp wisdom;
Maudgalyāyana is accompanied by those of great supernatural power. Each presides over a specific virtue. To understand their titles, one must recognize their respective practices;

these names are established based on their virtues, and there is nothing they cannot penetrate. Generally, when explaining the causes and conditions of these meanings, most rely upon the initial teachings. This is because...
This is because it marks the beginning of the response to the stimulus. Each point must be explained through four aspects of meaning;
some may be omitted or retained, with the aim of avoiding prolixity and being concise. Thus, Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
Kauṇḍinya is his clan name; it is translated as "Fire-Vessel. He was of the Brahmin caste, whose ancestors served the fire, and from this they derived their lineage.
Fire has two meanings: illumination and burning. Through illumination, darkness does not arise; through burning, material things do not arise.
Thus, he took "non-arising" as his clan name. *Ajñāta* is his personal name; it is translated as "Already Known," and is also called "No [Ignorance]."
This "knowing" is true knowing; it is designated by the name "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*). As the Sūtra says:

"Within my Buddha-dharma, Cunda the Bhikṣu was foremost in being broad-minded, compassionate, and widely learned, as he was the first to receive the flavor of the Dharma. Thus, he was named "Aññā" (Known).
Drawn by the two vows of both the Buddha and himself, he previously attained non-arising, like one who has long been asleep through a great night. There was no...
A person can awaken. Before the sun has risen, the morning star appears first. The Bhikṣu Cunda was the very first to see the Buddha and attain the Way.

He was the first to hear the drum of the Dharma; the first to don the incense of the Path; the first to taste the nectar of immortality; the first to enter the stream of the Dharma; and the first to realize the True Truth.
Among all those who have attained the Way in Jambudvīpa, he stands foremost before all devas, humans, and Arhats.
He attained the Way; this is why Aññā-Koṇḍañña sits at the head of the assembly, for there is something therein that manifests his realization.

For a detailed account of the origins of Aññā Koṇḍañña, as well as an extensive explanation according to the teachings on the fundamental and trace aspects, and the contemplation of the mind according to the first three teachings, one should consult the commentary (*śāstra*). Those who require it should seek it therein.

If those who now hear and practice this sutra wish to realize the wisdom of the non-arising of their own minds, they should directly contemplate their own single mind as the mirror of the Dharma-realm, perfectly round.
Herein, the middle way is the non-duality of object and wisdom;
one does not contemplate front or back, nor ignorance or true wisdom, nor various forms and appearances, nor grasp at various reflected images. One simply contemplates the sphere.
It is perfect, without boundaries, without beginning or end, without light or darkness, neither one nor different.

It is like a perfect reflection that does not grasp the appearances of the ten dharma realms; it is without good or evil, heterodoxy or orthodoxy, and likewise lacks such distinctions as great or small.

All things are utterly extinguished; there remains only the true mark (*dharmatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the Buddha-dharma. Whether form or fragrance, nothing is not the true mark.

Cultivation and nature are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*); the interior and exterior of the mirror are one. One is thus free from the conceptual distinctions and emotional attachments of the three teachings.
With non-conceptual wisdom, one illuminates the non-conceptual object with perfect clarity; in principle, there is neither light nor darkness.
When the present mind and its objects are extinguished, this is itself the *dharmatā*. One should know that the Four Noble Truths constitute the great totality of all Buddha-dharma.
Whether extinguishing or illuminating, there is nothing that is not the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), for the essence of the true mark is free from both extinction and illumination.
The total cessation of illumination is inconceivable. Therefore, the suffering of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
It is called the Dharma-body because it is not something manifested; the very substance of the hindrances is the Dharma-body. Greed, anger, and delusion are themselves *prajñā*.
It is not called *prajñā* because it is capable of illuminating; rather, there is nothing to be illuminated, for its nature is inherently luminous.

That which binds through karmic activity is all termed "liberation" (*vimukti*). It is not that liberation is attained by severing bonds, nor is there any substance to be bound, nor is there any agent that binds;
therefore, it is called liberation. Liberation is the non-arising of karma, and *prajñā* is the absence of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Birth. The Dharma-body is precisely suffering that does not arise. These three non-arisings are the one non-arising; this one non-arising is the three non-arisings.
They are neither three nor one; they are neither concurrent nor distinct. One merely contemplates that the principle is thus; one does not contemplate the removal of defilement.

The essence of defilement is itself void; its original voidness is called cessation. Therefore, the wondrous essence ceases, and the name "removal" is not established. This is the essence of the hindrance.
This is precisely virtue; it does not depend on being transformed or eliminated. It is the very seeing that the mind’s arising is itself non-arising.

Upon first hearing the name of Ājñātakauṇḍinya’s non-arising, one understands that the principles of all subsequent noble ones are likewise so. Because he was the foremost, the general outline is briefly indicated here.
If one is not deluded regarding the provisional and the real concerning Ājñāta, one may use this perfect contemplation to dissolve [the obstacles] within this sutra.
The five Buddhas and three cycles of the *Honji-suijaku* (original and manifested traces) are all the great essence of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

The entirety of the *Lotus Sūtra* can be understood within the space of a single inch-square. Were it otherwise, the name "non-arising" would be established in vain, and the principle of non-arising would never be realized.

By briefly pointing out these general directions, the contemplative objects (*vipaśyanā-viṣaya*) of the entire dispensation may be recognized; for a full and detailed account, refer to the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue*.
In the section on "Observation": Regarding Mahākāśyapa—*Mahākāśyapa*.
*Mahā* in Sanskrit means "Great" (*mahat*). *Kāśyapa* means "Tortoise-clan" (*kūrma-gotra*).

His ancestors studied the Way, and a numinous tortoise responded by bearing a celestial chart for them; because they followed virtue and established their clan, they were called the Mahā-kauravya (Great Tortoise) clan.
They are also called Ābhāsvara (Radiant Wave), or Piṅgala (Drinker of Light), named for the fact that their bodies possessed such radiance that they could outshine other objects.
They are also named Pippala, or Pippalāyana, and so forth, deriving these names from trees. [This was] his father and mother.
He prayed to the tree deity and obtained this son, who was named after the tree. Kāśyapa possessed ten great merits;
his family was so immensely wealthy that even King Bimbisāra and the sixteen great kingdoms could not rival them as neighbors.
His body was of pure golden hue, surpassing Jāmbūnada gold, and he was endowed with thirty of the marks of a Buddha. The radiance of his body shone far beyond one yojana.
However, she was lacking the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*) and the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Because the golden image of the stupa had become damaged after the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, she begged for gold from a poor woman during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha to restore it.
For ninety-one *kalpas*, her body remained constantly golden and her mind constantly experienced bliss. Finally, she took birth in the kingdom of Magadha in the family of a *nyagrodha* brahmin.
Born into a noble family, he feared that by surpassing the king he might incur punishment, so he reduced his plowing by one; he used only nine hundred and ninety-nine pairs of oxen for a golden plow.
Furthermore, a sutra states: In his household there were woolen cloths (*karpāsa*), even the lowest grade of which was worth a hundred thousand taels of gold.
When driven into the ground seven feet deep with a nail, they would not tear or break, remaining exactly as they were. There were sixty such treasuries.
Gold grain: one storehouse held three hundred and forty *hu*. Regarding such storehouses and granaries, he renounced this family estate. Furthermore, a sutra states:
"By offering barley rice as alms to a Pratyekabuddha, one shall receive pleasure for a thousand rebirths each in the Trāyastriṃśa and Tuṣita heavens, and one's body shall be entirely golden.
Thus, when the devas requested the compilation of the canon, they praised him, saying: "The Elder has already eliminated desire, hatred, and pride; his..."
His form was like a pillar of purple-gold, majestic from top to bottom and peerless in its excellence. His eyes were clear and pure like lotus flowers.

Furthermore, he took a wife of golden complexion; yet they lay together without desire, renounced their lives to enter the homeless state, and donned priceless robes which he cut to make his saṃghāṭī.
Four pieces of fine cotton cloth he offered to the Buddha as a seat. Thus he renounced three times, peerless in the world.
This constitutes the relinquishing of what is great. Furthermore, while in the village of Vṛji, he encountered the Buddha and offered him a priceless precious robe.
The Buddha gave it to him in exchange for his own rag-robe (pāṃśukūla). This robe was the great robe of the Great Sage; moreover, it was very coarse and heavy. Yet Kāśyapa said:
"When I receive the Buddha’s robes, I regard them as a teacher and as a stupa; I have never used them as a pillow, much less [given them away]."
He lay down on his side. Just as this great robe (mahāsaṃghāṭī) was a great advance in my practice, it is therefore called "receiving the great.
Furthermore, in the village of Vajji, he first heard from the Buddha the teachings on superior morality, concentration, and wisdom, and immediately attained the state free from outflows (anāsrava).

He undertook the practice of alms-gathering and observed the twelve dhūta ascetic practices, never abandoning them even as he grew old. Later, the Buddha said to him: "You are now advanced in years; you may abandon the practice of alms-gathering."
Regarding food: one should return to the community to receive alms-food; one may discard coarse and heavy rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) and accept light, dyed garments from laypeople.
