Kāśyapa said to the Buddha: "If the Buddha does not appear in the world, I shall become a Pratyekabuddha and practice the dhūta austerities for the rest of my life."
I now dare not let go of the Dharma I have practiced to further study anything else. Moreover, it shall serve as an illumination for future generations;
for it is said that in the future, the Elder Kāśyapa will be praised by the Buddha, and I shall then practice difficult and arduous austerities.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! This is what constitutes great practice. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

After Kāśyapa, who had long practiced the dhūta austerities, his hair and beard had grown long and his robes were tattered. He approached the place where the Buddha was staying, and the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs gave rise to arrogance.
The Buddha commanded Kāśyapa to take half of his own seat and sit together with him. Kāśyapa did not consent. The Buddha said, "I have..."
The four dhyānas: through meditative concentration, the mind is stilled; from beginning to end, there is no depletion or loss. Kāśyapa is likewise so.
I possess great kindness (*maitrī*), which benevolently covers all; you are also like this, for your essential nature is also kind. I possess great compassion (*karuṇā*).
You shall likewise deliver and save sentient beings. I possess four samādhis of the divine: first, formlessness; second, immeasurable intent; third, the accumulation of purity;
and fourth, non-retrogression. You shall likewise possess these. I possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*);

you shall likewise possess them. I possess four concentrations (*dhyāna*): first, the concentration of meditative absorption; second, the concentration of knowledge; third, the concentration of wisdom; and fourth, the concentration of ethical discipline.
"You are also like this; your merit is no different from mine. For what reason do you not sit?

When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s praise, their hearts were struck with wonder and their hair stood on end. Kāśyapa then sat down. For the sake of the great assembly, the Buddha recounted the causes and conditions of the past:
"In the past, I was a noble king named Mandhātṛ, whose talent was peerless. At that time, Kāśyapa was a deva..."

Śakra, in admiration of his virtue and conduct, dispatched a chariot drawn by a thousand horses and constructed a gate to welcome the King. The Lord of Devas came out to receive him and sat together with the King;
after they had enjoyed each other’s company, he escorted the King back to the palace. Formerly, Kāśyapa invited me to sit upon the seat of birth and death;
now that I have attained Buddhahood, I repay his past kindness by inviting him to sit upon the seat of the True Dharma. For this reason, I commanded him to sit.
When he was in the presence of the Buddha, gods and humans all regarded the Buddha as their teacher. Kāśyapa immediately rose and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, saying, "The Buddha is my teacher;
I am his disciple. Furthermore, Kāśyapa preached the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs, delivering a lion’s roar that was highly commended by the Buddha.
Moreover, among the great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty-four great disciples...
There was one named Weida (位大), the abbot of five hundred mountain monasteries and the presiding *sthavira* for administrative affairs in Jambudvīpa.
After the Buddha’s cremation, four *pātra* trees grew from the site of the ashes;

these symbolized Kāśyapa’s compilation of the Dharma of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, namely the Tripiṭaka and the Four Āgamas. Regarding the Tripiṭaka, Sengzhao’s preface states: "The ultimate principle is transcendent..."

Regarding conventional designations, the worthy and holy remain profound and silent; yet the profound principle is not transmitted without words, and thus Śākyamuni established his teaching through them.
He restrained the body and speech through the prohibitions of the Vinaya, and clarified good and evil by guiding others through the Sūtras.

He expounded the profound and subtle, discerning them through the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). This clarifies the Three Piṭakas of Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom. As for the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* (Four Āgamas):
the *Ekottarika-āgama* elucidates the causes and effects of humans and devas; the *Dīrgha-āgama* refutes false views; the *Madhyama-āgama* elucidates profound meanings;

and the *Saṃyukta-āgama* elucidates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). All of these are the achievements of Mahākāśyapa. To discuss them individually: Kāśyapa recited and brought forth the Abhidharma.

Dharmatara. Therefore, the Great Collection was compiled now. After the Tathāgata’s passing, the Dharma was entrusted to Kāśyapa, who was able to serve as a refuge for all beings, just like the Tathāgata himself.
As the Buddha said: "If there are practitioners of dhūta asceticism..."
My Dharma will then endure; if such a person did not exist, my Dharma would not endure.

Kāśyapa is able to shoulder the Buddha-Dharma and cause it to remain for a long time, until the coming Buddha. Having completed the entrustment of the Dharma and the transmission of the robe, he then enters parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said that he is great in upholding the Dharma. As for those who practice the twelve dhūtas: first is the renunciation of fine clothing; seeking them is difficult, and obtaining them—
First, there are many fears at that time; if one misses the proper occasion, remorse and distress arise.

Second, regarding rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), they are free from the five fears of water, fire, thieves, kings, and calamities. Third, if one possesses many robes, the labor of sewing, mending, and washing is also great;

therefore, one keeps only the three robes. Fourth, if one were to eat within the monastic community, one would have to attend to monastic affairs; therefore, one practices alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*). Fifth...
1. If one accepts leftover food or small snacks, it will disturb the mind and cause the time [of practice] to be lost;
therefore, one eats in a single sitting. 2. Excessive eating is difficult to digest and gives rise to sleepiness and indolence; eating too little leads to hunger, exhaustion, and lack of strength;

therefore, one observes moderation in food. 3. Having many vessels to wash and maintain causes much interference; therefore, one eats from a single bowl. 4. One would require drinks and undergo labor [to obtain them]; therefore, one does not drink beverages. 5. Nine...
1. Because of attachment to dwellings, one stays under a tree. 2. Because of further attachment to staying under a tree, one stays in a cemetery. 3.

Because of the arising of sorrow and grief in the cemetery, one stays in the open air. 4. If one lies down to sleep, one's efforts are wasted and laziness increases; therefore, one practices constant sitting.
These twelve kinds of practice are praised by the supreme sages. Those who hear this sutra today have the honor of being included among those in the stream of the Way;
having heard this sublime Dharma, will they not examine their own minds and conduct? Furthermore, these are called the "Twelve Shakings.

One must explain them one by one according to the provisional and ultimate teachings (*honjaku*), as well as the meditative characteristics of the three preceding teachings, just as in the commentary (*sho*). If those who hear the sutra wish to...
One perceives within a single thought-moment the shaking off of the afflictions of the five abodes;

as one shakes them off, and even until all are shaken off, they are none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*). This is the practice of the Tathāgatas, which surpasses the pure practices of all bodhisattvas;
it is precisely the perception of one’s own own ascetic practice (*dhūta-guṇa*).
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and Nadī-Kāśyapa—these three Kāśyapas share the same clan name as previously explained for the Śākyas. *Uruvilvā* in Sanskrit means "pumpkin-grove.
*Nadī* means "river" or "stream. *Gayā* is the name of a city located some distance from Rājagṛha.
Seven *yojanas* to the south, all of which are named after their locations. During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, they were brothers who together erected a pillar for the *caitya*.
The elder brother served as the teacher of King Bimbisāra and had five hundred disciples;

each of the two younger brothers had their own following of two hundred and fifty people, and they all practiced the Dharma of their elder brother. The Buddha performed ten kinds of miraculous transformations, namely:
The venomous dragon could not strike him; the dragon’s fire could not burn him; the waters of the Ganges could not drown him. He took fruit from the three directions and rice from the north;

even when [the king] knew he was being treated with contempt and withdrew, and when he knew [the king] missed him, he would immediately return. Fires were extinguished and failed to ignite; axes were raised but would not descend.
Having witnessed these various miracles at first, his heterodox attachments remained unaltered, and he declared: "Though Gautama possesses such spiritual powers, they do not equal my own Way."
“True,” [the Buddha] said. “Did you not say, ‘Are you a blind man whose eyes see nothing? Yet you saw all these divine transformations and insisted that you were truly enlightened.
You are no arhat, nor have you attained the Way. Upon hearing these words, Kāśyapa was suddenly awakened;
both master and disciples submitted, left their homes to follow the Buddha, and when his thousand disciples heard the call “Come, well-come,” they became śramaṇas.

[The Buddha said: "Phala. Furthermore, the Āgama Sūtras state: 'The bhikṣu Uruvilvā is foremost in being able to protect the fourfold assembly and provide them with the four requisites so that they lack for nothing.
The bhikṣu Nadī is foremost in the tranquility of his mind, having subdued all fetters through diligence.
The bhikṣu Gayā is foremost in observing and understanding all dharmas, being entirely without attachment.'"
He is most excellent at transforming and guiding others, being foremost among them. You should know that Uruvilvā was originally the forest of the three virtues of Prajñā;
Gayā was originally the immovable city of the realized Dharmakāya; and Nairañjanā was originally the water of liberation.
It purifies all defilements. Its traces show it dwelling in forests, cities, and waters to deliver sentient beings.
Those who hear this sutra today illuminate their single thought-moment, correctly contemplating the nature of the mind. It is unmoving in the Middle Way, like a city wall defending against enemies.
Furthermore, the nature of the mind is profoundly still and unmoving, yet it moves like water to cleanse all inverted views. Moreover, it obstructs and illuminates the withered nature of the mind.
Its flourishing is like a lush, verdant forest. The three dharmas mutually support one another, being neither identical nor separate.
Thus, one directly perceives one's own mind as the three contemplations, a single essence of brothers.
Śāriputra. "Śāriputra" is a name;
in full, it should be called Śāriputra-ra. This is translated as "Son of Śāri" (Shizi) or "Son of the Pearl" (Zhuzi).
He is named "Son of Śāri" because his mother possessed a beautiful body, and he was born from that body. Furthermore, his...

The mother was exceptionally intelligent, surpassing all other women. The mark of such intelligence resides in the pupils of the eyes; because it arises from those "beads" (pupils), they are called *putra* ("beads").
At that time, people designated the mother by means of her son; thus, both names were derived from the mother. He was also named Upadeśa, which translates as "Exegesis.
His father was thoroughly versed in the classical texts; he bound his belly with iron plates and carried a fire upon his head.

He donned the crown and walked alone through Rājagṛha, beating the drum of debate. Since the National Preceptor Dhara knew his past history, he feared that if [Vatsa] were to defeat him in debate, his own fortune would be lost;
thus, to avoid this ill omen, he gave him his daughter in marriage. Having won the wife through debate, the son was named Śreṇika (the "Victorious") to manifest his father’s virtue.
Furthermore, "Śre" signifies the father and "ṇika" signifies the mother; as it manifests both parents, it is called "Śre."
He was named Upatiṣya. "Upa" means near; "tiṣya" means son. His clan name was Kauṣṭhila, and he was originally of the Brahmin caste.

Initially, while on the road, he saw Ājñātakauṇḍinya’s dignified and orderly deportment, and thus inquired about his teacher's doctrine. Ājñātakauṇḍinya replied: "All phenomena arise from conditions; therefore, one speaks of causes and conditions.
These phenomena, their conditions, and their cessation—this is how my teacher has taught. Upon hearing this once, [he immediately attained realization].
Having attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, he came to the presence of the Buddha. Within seven days, he had thoroughly mastered the ocean-like depths of the Buddha’s Dharma;
on the fifteenth day, he realized the fruit of *aśaikṣa-arhat*. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"In my Buddha-dharma, Śāriputra is foremost among those whose wisdom is inexhaustible and who resolve all doubts. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra praised him, saying:
The carriage [was used] for the second time in discussion with the World-Honored One, until he wrapped his robe around it and placed it upon his head.
For seven days and seven nights, Śāriputra delivered a lion’s roar based on a single phrase spoken by the Buddha, further producing extraordinary flavors and extraordinary phrases.

His eloquence is inexhaustible; how could the wisdom and eloquence of Śāriputra ever be exhausted? It is for this reason that the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) calls him the "Great General Who Turns the Wheel of Dharma on the Right Side.

This refers precisely to that meaning. Furthermore, he possesses nine kinds of meritorious qualities: former skillful means (*upāya*), innate wisdom (*jāti-jñāna*), entrusted eloquence (*kṣipta-pratibhāna*), debate (*vāda*), marvelous arts (*kauśalya*), entry into the Path (*mārga-praveśa*), remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*), universal salvation (*parigraha*), and the general application of interpreting meanings (*artha-vyākhyāna*). These are not [to be found elsewhere].

This is fully recorded; the details are as analyzed in the commentary. Those who hear the sutra today, desiring to attain their own benefit, should contemplate that their own deluded thoughts are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—neither identical nor different.
Yet these characteristics of identity and difference are subsumed within the three contemplations of a single mind, which encompass all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This illuminates that within the mind, the single wisdom is all wisdom, and all wisdom is the single wisdom—not one, yet not many.
This wisdom is not all-encompassing wisdom. This is the seeing of one's own mind, Śāriputra.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana—Maudgalyāyana is a clan name; this is translated as "Praise and Recitation," or "Radish," or "Horse-bean."
This was the favorite food of the ancestral ṛṣis, and thus it became the name of the clan. *Kulada* is the name of that tree;

because he obtained a son through praying to the tree deity, he was named after it. Maudgalyāyana possessed the art of calculation and his mastery of the marks of physical characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) was equal to that of Maudgalyāyana.
To distinguish him from those with the same name, he is called Mahā-Maudgalyāyana. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among my disciples..."
Among those who travel through the ten directions by means of supernatural powers and light-footed levitation, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is foremost.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent and insight; Maudgalyāyana was valued for his noble spirit and vigor. Their wisdom and arts were comparable, and their virtuous conduct was identical.
They were called the 'Great Generals' who turn the Wheel of Dharma at the [Buddha’s] left side. This was because in the past, they had once assisted a Pratyekabuddha."
Shaving his head, washing and dyeing his robes, and sewing his *kāṣāya*—these were all for the sake of attaining supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

His subduing of the non-Buddhists, taming of the two nāgas, censuring Devadatta, excluding the unworthy from the assembly, stopping his chariot to inquire after medicine, converting Śakra, humbling arrogance, proclaiming the Buddha’s fame, knowing the Buddha’s intent, and the nine kinds of merit are recorded in the commentary; they are not described here in full. Those who hear this sutra should...
Illuminating one's own mind, the three truths are profoundly still. Without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation, one manifests great spiritual powers.
Within a single mind, suddenly there are all minds; observing all minds, they instantly vanish into non-existence. The mind is neither existent nor non-existent; all phenomena are immovable.
His supernatural powers were as swift as the wind; they were the supernormal powers of his own mind.
Mahākātyāyana—Mahākātyāyana means "Ornament" (in Chinese), because he was skilled in composing verses and eulogies; he is also called "Fan-sheng" (Fanning Cord). This son...
At the time of his birth, his father had already passed away. This boy obstructed his mother from remarrying, like a fan tied with a cord;

he was also named Kāla, which here means "Superior in Thought. "Thought" (cintā) is a mental factor associated with wisdom; because his capacity for deliberating on principles was powerful, he received the name "Superior in Thought."

These are all names derived from their surnames. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that there was a non-Buddhist who adhered to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), asserting that there is no future world.

There were ten rounds of questions and answers in which various doctrines were extensively expounded. The non-Buddhist then submitted, offering praise, saying, "Venerable sir, your wonderful exposition is excellent!
Furthermore, he was able to convert him to the precepts; he caused a butcher to receive the one-night fast (*upavāsa*).
The courtesan who observed the daytime precepts later received her retribution by each obtaining auspicious marks.
Furthermore, she debated the principles of worldly treatises with a Brahmin, whereby the Brahmin was able to distance himself from dust and defilement. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"In skillfully discerning meanings and expounding the teachings of the Way, Kātyāyana is foremost. Those who hear this sutra should contemplate it through the three truths.

Wisdom investigates the relationship between mind and objects; for objects can give rise to wisdom. Through repeated investigation and scrutiny, the single mind attains sudden enlightenment, and its principles become clear.
This is precisely what is called the mind’s own contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Aniruddha. *Aniruddha* is also called Anuruddha and also called Aniruddhu; these are merely differences in the Sanskrit pronunciation.
This [name] means "Free from Poverty" (*apagata-nirdhana*), also called "As One Wishes" (*yathākāma*), and also called "Not Obtained by Hunting. It is not that he obtained it by hunting.
Therefore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: During the final dharma period of Buddha Puṣya, there was a famine in the world.
A pratyekabuddha named Liṭa went out to beg for food, but his bowl remained empty and he obtained nothing. A poor man saw him and felt deep compassion, saying:
“Can a noble person accept some tares? He then offered the tares he had been eating to him. After the Pratyekabuddha had finished eating, he performed the eighteen transformations.
Later, while the poor man was gathering tares, a rabbit leaped onto his back and turned into a dead man.

Having no companion, the man escaped. Waiting for darkness, he returned home; when he laid [the corpse] on the ground, it became a golden man. As he pulled at its fingers, they grew back immediately; as he used its feet, they emerged instantly.
One could take from it without end. Even if wicked people or evil kings wished to come and seize it, they would see nothing but corpses;
yet, what the poor behold is purely gold and jewels. For ninety-one kalpas, his retribution was thus sufficient, and he was therefore called "The One Without Poverty" (Aparājita).
This is what is meant by "as one wishes. His clan name was Gautama, which here means "Pure and Virtuous"; he was also called Śākyan, which refers to a noble lineage. This...
He was the youngest son of King Droṇodana, named Aniruddha.
He was the nephew of King Śuddhodana, the cousin of the World-Honored One, the elder brother of Ānanda, and the uncle of Rāhula; he was no ordinary man.

Because of his diligence, he remained without sleep for seven days and seven nights, his eyelids not closing at all. For sleep is the nourishment of the eyes; since he had not slept for seven days, [his eyes became blind].
His eyes lost their pupils; he had forfeited his fleshly eye. The Buddha, together with eight hundred bhikṣus, prepared three robes for Aniruddha.
The Buddha personally stretched and cut the cloth, while the bhikṣus sewed them; they were completed in a single day.

The Buddha preached the precepts concerning deportment, such as walking and standing together, and immeasurable people attained the Way. The Buddha then instructed him to seek the divine eye, focusing his mindfulness upon its object. (4)
A great, pure form emerged from half his head, penetrating both the interior and exterior of obstructions so that he could see clearly through both light and darkness.
He said to the Brahma King: "I see Śākyamuni’s great trichiliocosm as if looking at a fruit in the palm of my hand. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Within my Buddha-dharma, among those who possess the divine eye of penetrating vision, the bhikṣu Aniruddha is foremost. This refers to the divine eye.
There is the arousal [of the mind] and the cultivation [of the path], as briefly explained in the commentary.

One should know that the *tathatā* (suchness) of the primordial abiding and the *divya-cakṣus* (divine eye) perceive the Buddha-lands through the aspect of non-duality. For those who hear the sutra, there is a profound resonance with true wisdom; thus, the ordinary person’s physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is itself the Buddha-eye.
Perceiving it through the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom within the causal stage, one realizes that only the Buddha is non-arising—this is the four eyes.
This is what is seen by the two wisdoms; it is the vision of the Buddha-eye’s true emptiness, profound stillness, and silence. Therefore, the sutra below states:
"With the eyes born of one's parents, one sees the entire trichiliocosm. If even one's own physical eye is already the Buddha-eye, how much more so the divine eye?
This can be understood from this.

Kapphiṇa, Kapphiṇa—this is translated as "Lunar Mansion" (Mansion). Because his parents prayed to the lunar mansion *kṛttikā* and were blessed with a son, he was named after that mansion (*kṛttikā*, pronounced *xiù*).
This was his name at birth. Furthermore, when this bhikṣu first left the household life, he had not yet seen the Buddha. At that time...
He headed toward the Buddha’s dwelling. Midway there, as evening fell, he encountered rain and took shelter in a potter’s house, using straw for a seat.
That night, another bhikṣu also came to take shelter, following after him. The first bhikṣu immediately pushed his straw mat aside to give it to him so they could sit together.
The later-arrived bhikṣu asked the one who had come before, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am seeking the Buddha. Thus spoke the later-arriving bhikṣu.
He immediately preached the Dharma for him; the words [of this teaching] are found in the Āgamas. [Kapphiṇa] suddenly attained the Way.
Later, that bhikṣu was none other than the Buddha himself. He stayed in the same room as the Buddha and came to behold the Dharmakāya. He was named Kapphiṇa after the place where he attained the Way.
His presiding deity is King Vaiśravaṇa, who holds a parasol following behind Kapphiṇa. Since his presiding deity has been honored, his position among the lunar mansions can be known.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma, among those who well know the stars, the sun, and the moon, Kapphiṇa is foremost.
One should know that originally he co-resided with the Tathāgata in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet in his provisional manifestation, he appeared as the constellation Rohiṇī.

Those who hear this sutra should contemplate the five aggregates as a dwelling; they are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. To penetrate the three paths of suffering and so forth is itself the Dharma-body. It is complete.
The retribution for his past deeds is thus fulfilled; the four virtues are ever-present. This is called "the mind itself seeing the lunar mansion Rohiṇī.
Gavāmpati—this is translated as "Chewing like an Ox," also as "Ox King," and also as "Ox Tracks. In the past, for five hundred lifetimes, he had once been a bull.
The Buddha once passed through another’s field of grain and plucked some stalks to examine whether they were ripe or raw. Later, he had an ox compensate for this.

Even though the ox had already finished eating, it would constantly engage in empty chewing. Now that [the Buddha] has attained the fruit of Arhatship, he still possesses residual habits (*vāsanā*). Ordinary people merely observe outward appearances and do not know of one's virtue;
if one laughs at an Arhat, one incurs sin. To avoid being ridiculed by others, he often dwells in the heavens.
The heavens know one who possesses virtue; they do not laugh at his physical form, for he delights in dwelling in the celestial realms.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa convened one thousand great arhats to compile the Tripiṭaka. He dispatched a junior monk to summon Kauṇḍinya, asking him:
When the Buddha and his preceptor were both answered as having entered parinirvāṇa, he immediately said: "Where the Buddha dwells, I dwell; where the Buddha passes away, I pass away.

He did not descend further into the celestial palaces, but manifested as a stream of water flowing through the four paths until it reached the place of Mahākāśyapa. The sound of the water spoke this verse:
"I bow my head in homage to the Wondrous Assembly, The Sangha of foremost and supreme virtue. Hearing that the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, I have followed him to depart. Great Elephant!"
Once the elephant has departed, the cub follows it and immediately enters extinction. Those who hear this sutra should contemplate the subtle and wondrous principle within their own minds:
walking with steady and upright steps, yet as swift as the wind; therein they will immediately perceive their own mind as the Brahmā-vehicle.
Revata. Revata is also called Revata;
this means "constellation," or "the constellation Śravaṇā," or "artificially assembled," or "always making sound.
His parents prayed for a son from the stars, and having obtained their response, they named him after the star.
Although he had left the household life, he still followed his original name and spoke of "provisional aggregation" and so forth.

Once, while staying overnight in an empty pavilion, he saw two ghosts contending over a corpse. The details of this incident are as cited in the commentary. The monks said, "This man is easy to deliver.
They told him, "Your body was originally the remains of another; it does not belong to you. Immediately, he attained enlightenment and realized the fruit [of the path]. His merit increased.
One version states: Regarding those who sit in meditation and enter samādhi with minds free from confusion, the Bhikṣu Liyue (Revata) is foremost.
One should know that he fundamentally abides in the *Rajanimiṣa-samādhi*. If one illuminates one's own mind, the Buddha and sentient beings are of one essence without distinction;
within this single mind, one perceives the Buddhas of the ten directions as numerous as the stars appearing at night, and thereby sees one's own detachment.
It is "transcending. Pindola Bharadvāja:
*Bharadvāja* means "residual habit" (*vāsanā*). For five hundred previous lifetimes he was a Brahmin, and his residual habits remained haughty.
While crossing the Ganges, he rebuked the water spirit, saying, "You little maid, stop the current! The spirit of the Ganges immediately divided the waters into two streams.
Later, the spirit came to complain to the Buddha. The Buddha ordered Vatsa to offer an apology; he then joined his palms and apologized, saying, "Little maid, do not be angry.
The great assembly all laughed. He apologized and yet continued to scold her. The Buddha said, "This is merely his habitual practice; in truth, he has no ill intent."
Regarding "arrogance": the *Ekottarika Āgama* states that among those who sit in painful austerity under trees, avoiding neither wind nor rain, the bhikṣu Vatsa is foremost.
One should know that while his fundamental dwelling was always in the bliss of the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*), he manifested outwardly a mind of pride and harsh speech.
One who hears the sutra clearly understands that both harsh words and gentle speech are dharmas of an inherently evil nature;
such a person immediately perceives their own self as the bhikṣu Vatsa. Bhādravudha.
Bakkula means "Good Appearance" (*Sukhavarṇa*) in this language; alternatively, it refers to his "lofty form" or being "greatly robust.

Because his physical appearance was upright and handsome, he is called "Good Appearance. In the past, he offered a single *harītakī* fruit to the Saṅgha; consequently, his body has always been free from illness.

He was one hundred and sixty years old and possessed five instances of the retribution of non-death. In the past, his stepmother once placed him on a hot griddle, threw him into a cauldron, cast him into water, and gave him to large fish to eat;
yet he did not die even when cut with a knife. This was because he upheld the precept against killing and adorned himself with the four other precepts, maintaining them firmly without violation.
He did not avoid fire or water. Although other people may uphold the five precepts, they often break and violate them.
Therefore, his body always delighted in stillness; he constantly dwelt in seclusion, never even speaking a word or two to others.

Unstained by the six sense objects, he remained perpetually in meditative concentration, never once becoming distracted. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "His lifespan was exceedingly long, and he never met an untimely death.
He always delighted in seclusion and did not dwell among the crowds. Bakula was foremost in practice."
If one illuminates one's own faculties and sense objects, all phenomena are the tranquility of the three truths; this is called "the contemplation of the mind seeing the sublime countenance.
Mahākoṣṭhila—Mahākoṣṭhila means "Great Thigh"—constantly engaged in debate with his sister, and he always prevailed over her in these discussions. Because of this...
Śāriputra’s elder sister was pregnant; in debate, she could not defeat him.

Realizing that the wisdom he carried in her womb would surpass his own eloquence once the nephew was born, she immediately left the household and traveled to South India to study the eighteen scriptures. The people of the time mocked her for doing so.
"Difficult to penetrate over successive lifetimes; not to be hoped for in a single life. He sighed deeply and said, "At home I am surpassed by my sister; on the road I am slighted by others.
He vowed to study without ceasing, having no leisure even to trim his nails. People of the time called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail).

When he had finished his studies, he returned and asked his nephew, "What has become of you? His nephew replied, "I have become a disciple of the Buddha. At this, he became greatly arrogant, saying, "I—"
The nephew was eight years old, and his voice resounded throughout the five regions. A śramaṇa asked, "By what skillful means do you convert my sister’s son?

He went directly to where the Buddha was. After reflecting for a long time, not a single dharma entered his mind. He said to the Buddha, "I cannot endure any dharma. "Endurance" has the meaning of peace.
This meant that he claimed he could destroy all dharmas so that they could not find peace; thus he spoke of "one."
He claimed that all phenomena are not endurable. The Buddha asked him, "Do you see this as being endurable? This resulted in a double defeat for him:
if he saw it as endurable, it contradicted his previous statement that all phenomena are not endurable; if he saw it as not endurable, he had no way to overcome the Buddha.
After reflecting for a long time, he lowered his head and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"The Heavenly King Virūpākṣa of the south constantly attends him holding a parasol; he has attained the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) and is able to resolve all difficulties. Koṭīviṃśa is foremost among them;
today, the one who upholds this Sūtra, having illuminated his own mind and being endowed with the two adornments, shall behold Mahāmudgalaputra."

Nanda. As for Nanda, he is also called "Cattle-herder. Because King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the bhikṣus for a three-month summer retreat, the king told the cattle-herder to deliver milk [to the Sangha] throughout the entire three months. When the king had him come to see the Buddha, he then spoke [to him].
A contemporary said: "I have heard that the Omniscient One was once the son of King Śuddhodana. Having been born in the royal palace, he was quite familiar with the work of tending cattle.
He then questioned the Buddha, who explained eleven matters for him as detailed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Consequently, he resolved to leave the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*). Because his name was derived from his former cause, he is called 'Tending Cattle' (*Gopaka*). If one contemplates..."
Regarding the mind: as in the previous examples of the "ox-chewing" contemplation and the contemplation of the mind, [the case of] Sundarananda—Sundarananda.
Nanda is as before; Sundara means "good-loved," and is also called "Undefiled."
He was born on the ninth day of the fourth month. His appearance and bearing were exceptionally distinguished. His wife’s name was Sundarī;

she was exceedingly beautiful, and they never left each other’s side for even a meal or a breath. While the Buddha and Ānanda were walking along the road begging for food, they arrived at the gate of Sundarī.

At that moment, she was eating with her husband atop a high tower. She immediately rose to welcome the Buddha, took his bowl, and offered him rice. The Buddha then returned to the Nyagrodha Garden. The Buddha—
He said to Ānanda, "Have Nanda bring it himself. Ānanda conveyed this command and received his instructions. The wife said, "My lord, you must return to eat together;
I shall send food to offer to the Buddha. The Buddha ordered him to shave his head. Grasping his fist, he said to the barber, "Do not bring the blade near the crown of the King of Jambudvīpa’s head!
Though the Buddha pressed him, he could not stop him, and so he shaved his head. The next day, the Buddha [with him]...
Five hundred bhikṣus were invited to stay and guard the monastery, yet they intended to flee. The Buddha ordered them to bolt the doors and sweep the floors;
he had the doors closed on the north and south, so that as they swept this side, that side became dirty. Fearing the Buddha’s return, they immediately fled back home.

On the road, they encountered the Buddha and hid their bodies behind some trees. The trees suddenly rose high into the air. Seeing this, the Buddha called for them to return. He asked them why [they had fled].
Therefore he departed. He replied that he had left his wife yesterday and was waiting for her return to eat together; he had merely forgotten his wife as he went.

The Buddha was about to travel to the heavens and the hells, through which [the disciple] attained the fruit of sainthood. He was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha. When he entered among the assembly, those who did not recognize him would say, "The Buddha has come.
There was a heterodox practitioner who was so clever that the people of the country called him a "wise man," and he was [a match for] Śāriputra.

In debate, he was rendered speechless. Desiring to leave the household life for the Buddha-dharma, he saw that Nanda’s appearance was exceptionally magnificent and sighed, saying, "The wisdom of this short-statured bhikṣu is difficult to fathom;
how much more so for one as grand as this! Nanda was then ordained and left the household life, later attaining the fruits of sainthood.
Those who hear this sutra should illuminate the craving of ignorance and thereby perceive the excellence of nirvāṇa within their own minds.
"Venerable.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra—*Pūrṇa* means "Fulfiller of Vows," *Maitrāyaṇī* means "Compassion," which is the name of his mother; [the remainder refers to] his father.
At the Full River (Pūrṇa-nadī), he prayed to Brahmā for a son. It happened to be the time when the river was full.
Furthermore, he dreamed that a vessel made of the seven treasures, filled with jewels, entered his mother’s womb. When the mother conceived the child, the father’s wish was fulfilled;
therefore, the boy was named Pūrṇa. His mother’s name was Mitrā-ṇī. "Ṇī" means "woman. In that region, women are generally called "ṇī" and men are called "na. Since this was so...
Because he was born from Maitrī, he is called the Son of Maitrī. My father’s name is Pūrṇa and my mother’s name is Maitrī;
thus, fellow practitioners of the holy life call me Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. This is how I received my name from my parents.

If it were derived from myself, it would be because this person skillfully knows both internal and external scriptures, knowing nothing that is not known; this would be naming him "Pūrṇa" based on his own wisdom. (From the *Ekottarika Āgama*)
It is said: "He is well able to expound extensively and discern the principles of meaning; he is foremost in fulfilling vows. It is further said:

"Among those who preach the Dharma, he is the most preeminent. When he wished to return to his native land, people were hostile toward him; yet he was able to practice patience even when people insulted or humiliated him.
When struck with fists, beaten with staves, or cut by blades, I shall consider myself fortunate to be free from the poisonous vessel of the five aggregates;

this is called the fulfillment of the practice of patience. It is praised by the Great Wise Śāriputra, and all fellow practitioners of the holy life should wrap their robes around it like a crown upon their heads.

Anyone who sees it will obtain great benefit; if one reflects upon it with a single mind, the four great vows and the four [immeasurables]— [Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary excerpt from a Buddhist commentary or liturgical text. The final line "四弘四" likely refers to the "Four Great Vows" (caturmahāpraṇidhāna) and the "Four Immeasurables" (catvāry apramāṇāni).]
"Subhūti, when one fully possesses these truths in a single thought-moment, benefiting both oneself and others, all things will be abundantly provided for;
this is the fulfillment of one's own heart's aspiration. Subhūti, [it is thus].
Subhūti—whose name means "Born of Emptiness"—was so named because at the time of his birth, all the family storehouses, treasuries, and vessels were empty.
When consulted by a diviner, it was declared auspicious; thus he was called "Born of Emptiness. Because he constantly cultivates the practice of emptiness, he is said to possess "virtuous karma."
If one makes offerings, one shall obtain superior rewards in the present life. Therefore, Subhūti always delights in dwelling in secluded forests, stone caves, and places of tranquility;
he constantly enters the samādhi of emptiness. When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, people from all over the land flocked together, vying with one another to pay him homage.
Yet Subhūti sat upright in his stone chamber, contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena, observing that form is not the Buddha, and so on, up to consciousness is not the Buddha.
"The Buddha is not the eye; even the mind is not the Buddha. At these words, she suddenly awakened to the Way. The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇī Padmā:

"It was not to you that she previously prostrated; she prostrated to the form-body (rūpakāya). Subhūti, however, previously beheld the dharma-body (dharmakāya). Thus spoke the one who heard the sutra.
One should illuminate one's own mind; it is not within, nor without, nor in between, nor does it exist as a self-entity. It is profoundly still and pure;
this is the very sight of one's own Dharmakāya, which arises from emptiness.
Ānanda. "Ānanda" means "Joy" (歡喜) and is also called "Untainted" (無染). King Śuddhodana was told by a celestial messenger, "Your son shall become a Buddha.
Shortly thereafter, a minister reported: "Last night, heaven and earth shook violently; the Prince has attained Buddhahood. The King was greatly [elated].
He was named Nanda (Joy) because when King Śuklodana’s ministers announced the birth of a son, the entire kingdom rejoiced; thus he was named Nanda.
Ānanda was so handsome that all who saw him were filled with joy. As stated in the *Madhyama Āgama*:

"If the fourfold assembly hears whatever Ānanda speaks, whether much or little, or if they observe his silence, his walking, standing, sitting, lying down, his advancing, retreating, moving, or turning, there is none among them who does not feel joy."
On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha was born on the day he attained enlightenment; later, he left the household life. The Buddha sought him out to serve as his attendant.

Maudgalyāyana conveyed three vows [on Ānanda's behalf], foreseeing that there would be censure and suspicion. The Buddha immediately granted his seal of approval. The Buddha said, "Ānanda is superior to my previous attendants."
The former attendant understood upon hearing the teaching; now, before the Buddha has even spoken, Ānanda already understands the Buddha’s intention.
He is fully capable of discerning whether [the Dharma] should be given or not; therefore, the Tathāgata joyfully entrusts the Dharma to Ānanda.
The four heavenly kings each offered a bowl to the Buddha, whom the Buddha stacked and pressed together so that they merged into a single bowl, yet the four rims remained distinct. This is the bowl.
It was too heavy. Ānanda joyfully bore it without weariness. The *Madhyama Āgama* states: "Ānanda attended the Buddha for twenty-five years;
of the eighty thousand *khandas* he heard, he recited them all without error, never asking about a single phrase a second time."
His power of mindfulness was joyful. Furthermore, when Ānanda followed the Buddha into the dragon palace, he beheld devas, humans, and nāga maidens, yet his mind remained free from defilement;

thus he was named "The Undefiled" (Anāsrava). The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "He knows the proper time and understands things clearly; wherever he goes, he is without doubt; what he remembers he does not forget;
he is widely learned and profoundly insightful; he is capable of receiving and upholding [the teachings]. Ānanda is foremost in these qualities. He made a vow to enter nirvāṇa while sitting.
In the Ganges River, he entered the *Vāyu-vikṣobha* (Wind-Arising) Samādhi and divided his body into four parts:
one for the devas, one for the nāgas, one for Vaiśālī, and one for Ajātaśatru. From his mouth he uttered subtle and wondrous words, praised by the World-Honored One and beloved by devas and humans:
"Those who now hear this sutra should illuminate their own minds as being immediately empty and provisional."
Within a single thought-moment of mental dust, the Tathāgatagarbha is fully present. To uphold the Buddha-dharma is to remain inseparable from every kṣaṇa.
By shattering the dust of one's own mind, the great scripture emerges; therein, one immediately beholds Ānanda, the Upholder of the Dharma, within one’s own heart.

Rāhula. "Rāhula" means "obscuration" or "covering. When Śākyamuni was a crown prince, he sought to leave the household life with his father's permission, but his father would not grant it, saying, "If you have a son, I shall allow you to go forth.
The Prince then pointed his finger at the queen’s womb and said:
"Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son. After the Buddha had left the household life, Yaśodharā became pregnant.
Once the Buddha had departed, the consort unexpectedly conceived. All the Śākyas were enraged; they wished to punish her and kill her, so they set fire to a pit of burning coals.
Yaśodharā, cradling her child, made this great vow: "If this is not my true son, let mother and child be consumed by the flames. If he is truly my offspring, may Heaven [protect us]."
To provide proof, he immediately took his son and threw himself into the fire. The pit was transformed into a lotus pond, and lotuses supported his true body.
Only then did the king and the people cease their doubts. There are ten meanings for the term "obscuration" (*āvṛti*), as fully explained in the commentary. The Buddha then commanded Rāhula:
He shall not enter parinirvāṇa; he awaits the total extinction of my Dharma. Even now he still dwells in the world and has not yet entered nirvana.

As for those who hear this sutra, if they illuminate their own single mind with the threefold wisdom and obstruct the delusions of the five stages so that they do not arise, they will immediately see Rāhula within their own hearts.
Thus, these great arhats and others who are well-known to the multitude—this constitutes the sixth assembly of those with many acquaintances.
Some say that "knowing" (*jñā*) is simply "cognition" (*vijñā*);
others say that hearing the name is "knowing," while seeing the form is "cognizing. Seeing the form is "knowing," while seeing the mind is "cognizing. [The term] "Great" (*Mahā*) refers to the Arhat.
The explanation is as before. This concludes the section on those with many acquaintances.
Furthermore, there were two thousand persons, both learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
This is the second group of those with few acquaintances within the initial assembly of *śrāvakas*; it mentions only the learners and those beyond learning.
Regarding their rank and number, their names are not listed and their virtues are not extolled; from this it can be verified that they are called the "assembly of those with little knowledge.

However, the holy and the mundane are separated, such that the mundane cannot fathom the holy; this is what is meant by "separation. It does not mean that the holy do not interact with the mundane at all—this would be true separation.

If one were to judge the mundane by the standards of the mundane, only then would one recognize those who interact; how much more so when judging the mundane by the standards of the holy? This is the principle.
Sever all worldly associations. Once such friendships have been severed, one cannot judge the extent of what is known or recognized based on the capacity of an ordinary person;
rather, one must equally sever all ordinary ties. One must not take being known by many people as the high, ultimate reality, nor take being known by few people as the low, provisional trace.
Therefore, know that whether one is widely known or little known [is of no consequence].

Regarding the fundamental and the manifested, the provisional and the real, each possesses its own underlying principle. Therefore, the various sages, in order to guide ordinary people and those of inferior capacity, manifest forms that correspond to their own kind.

Since the karmic conditions of beings are not uniform, they receive them according to their respective types. If there are those among the common folk whose aspirations reach for the lofty and who admire the distant, they are guided by means of extensive knowledge.
If there are those who conceal their names, hide their virtues, and practice self-effacement, they are guided by means of limited knowledge. Thus, they accord with the multitude.

Birth has various distinctions, yet one does not lose its fundamental basis through the traces of much or little. Question: Traces must have a basis, and expedient means must lead to the ultimate reality.
Your previous explanation of the śrāvakas—both the many and the few assemblies—is based on the distinction between the fundamental and the trace;
originally, they are all great expedients. If this is so, then there would be only that which leads, and nothing led. Answer: It is indeed as you have asked. Moreover...

According to the explanation based on the Dharma, when Śāriputra alone received his prediction at the beginning of the first cycle, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings were all filled with joy;

thus, there were certainly those who were led by this influence. Nevertheless, in order to establish the four interpretations, it is necessary to encompass both the primary (hon) and the derivative (jaku) meanings.
Since these primary meanings differ, they must be distinguished. If one has already entered the stage of the Perfect Teaching, one is capable of leading others...
Human beings are perfected through the two groups of those who have initiated [the path] and those who influence it; they are clearly, by their very nature, Bodhisattvas.

Beyond this, those who have once developed the Great Mind are also called Bodhisattvas. If one has fundamentally remained in the Lesser Vehicle, yet has never developed the mind [for enlightenment], they are all nonetheless called Bodhisattvas according to this Great Sūtra.
Thus, regarding the twenty-one honored ones mentioned above, both their fundamental and provisional aspects are present in detail.
The *Xiaoshu* (Explanatory Commentary) provides a fivefold analysis of the stages of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*). First, the learner; second, the non-learner;

third, the non-learner who is also a learner; fourth, both learner and non-learner; and fifth, neither learner nor non-learner. These five categories are correlated with the four teachings (*catvāra upadeśāḥ*).
Regarding the meaning of the afflictions to be abandoned through both subject and object, the details are found in the *Shu* (Commentary). As for those who hear the sutra:

if they reflect upon their own minds and correctly contemplate the Middle Way—neither taking up the two extremes nor abiding in the middle—such that both medicine and illness are extinguished, this is the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

To be able to contemplate in this manner is what is called "learning" (*śaikṣa*). This concludes the brief explanation of the text. However, the *Tiantai Shuji* (Tiantai’s Commentary and Notes) explains it as follows:

Regarding the assembly of śrāvakas above, each is individually examined through the four methods of interpretation—causality (*nidāna*), teaching (*śāsana*), origin and trace (*honji-suijaku*), and contemplation of the mind (*kanjin*).
Although these have been fully applied, following this text, there is once again a comprehensive explanation in two parts: the general and the specific.

This encompasses the meaning of the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s teaching, manifesting his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and the subtle refinement of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). His work of shadow-like transformation is complete; his companions for rebirth have ceased their transformation.
By distinguishing [this assembly] from the śrāvakas listed in other sūtras, one clearly reveals that the multitude enumerated in this present sūtra all possess wondrous capacities.
This is especially true for the śrāvaka disciples—whether manifest or hidden, great or small, leaders or followers.

He displayed both silence and eloquence; there was both contraction and expansion. Some grew weary of the external and delighted in the internal, while others turned their backs on the Great Vehicle and headed toward the Small.

He led those of the Small Vehicle into the Great, and brought those with partial views back to the Perfect. From the cause to the fruit, all was for the sake of sentient beings, acting as the seeds, the ripening, and the liberation across the past, future, and present.
Having traversed many lands and experienced diverse times and places, this was truly because the capacities and conditions of beings were not yet equal in their degree of ripening. Now...
Having gathered all together, when comparing the past with the present, it is made so that the teachings of the present—both the Dharma and the people—are perfected and beautiful.

Therefore, for each and every person, the fourfold interpretation is fully applied. Now, having understood the capacity of the faculties and the response of the Buddha—from the external to the internal—and subsequently entering the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, whether through the two gates of the Original and the Traces, or through awakening and entry at first or later, all rely upon guidance, influence, and inspiration. Upon hearing even a single phrase, if a person...
If all phenomena can serve as catalysts for transformation and are entirely suitable for contemplation, then even for a single person, a multitude of explanations must be provided.

How much more so for those of future generations who are to hear the names and initiate practice, receive the teachings and recognize the essence, contemplate the traces and behold the source, and investigate their causal conditions.

It illuminates extensively from beginning to end. If one grasps this intent, then regarding a single person and a single phrase of a sutra, one can take it as the object for seeking the supreme fruit of Buddhahood;
one can recognize the capacity of those to be transformed below; one can understand the methods of the sages' transformation;
one can comprehend how ordinary beings receive benefit; one can master the similarities and differences of names and meanings; and one can know practice.

The principles are thus distinct. One can thereby know that contemplation is accomplished according to what one hears; one can understand that the traces lead back to the fundamental person and phenomena;
one can believe that the transformative work is long-lasting; one can look up to the sagely grace as difficult to repay; and one can know that sentient beings are difficult to transform.
One can thus know that comprehending the principle is extremely difficult; others do not see it and regard it as mere overgrown weeds.

If one attains this present intention, then whenever one hears of any dharma, any event, any person, or any practice in the various sutras, one will understand how all Buddhas in the lands of the ten directions and three periods of time employ their teachings.
Although their manifestations differ, the principle of the gateways for contemplation and cultivation remains no different.

This is distinct. One who has wondrously grasped this meaning will find that the four modes of deportment and the three types of action provide a basis for the cultivation of contemplation; how much more so must one discern the similarities and differences regarding the subject of contemplation?
The commentaries and records of the Tiantai school explain this in exhaustive detail and with perfect clarity; those in need should seek them there, as they cannot be fully set forth here.
This concludes the explanation of the initial assembly of *śrāvakas*. Below follows the third section: the listing of the assembly of nuns.
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was accompanied by her retinue of six thousand.
She is listed first as Prajāpatī, which is translated here as "Great Love-Way" (Dà'àidào); she is also called Gautamī, which means "Mistress of the Multitude.

One should know that while her fundamental abiding is in the dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), her provisional manifestation is that of the mother who gave birth to the thousand Buddhas. She nurtured and raised them.

The Master asked: "For what reason is the name Mahāprajāpatī explained through the Perfection of Wisdom (*Prajñāpāramitā*)? Furthermore, she was not the Mother of the Buddha; why then is she interpreted as the 'Mother of the Buddha'?
It is because only by possessing wisdom can one truly be a 'Lover of the Way' (*prajāpati*). Since she loves the Great Way, her wisdom-perfection is likewise great.
Moreover, while all ordinary women are capable of bearing children, it is for this reason that she is metaphorically designated as the 'Mother of the Buddha' after the manner of Vimalakīrti."
The meaning of this is that they are the sons of the Teacher born from within one's own mind; "six thousand" refers to their number.

If one views them from the perspective of oneself, by correctly applying the ten kinds of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) according to the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, and distinguishing them by way of the realms (*dhātu*), they constitute six thousand.
Rāhula’s mother, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, was also there together with her retinue.
Yaśodharā is designated by her son; this is translated as "Flower-Color" (Huá-sè) or "Fame" (Míng-wén), or sometimes left untranslated.
She was gentle, kind, respectful, frugal, and yielding, and her virtue equaled that of the Crown Prince. Nevertheless, while at home, she was the wife of the Bodhisattva.
He was known among devas and humans as the leader of the community of nuns who had left the household life, and his rank was that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). Question:
In this sutra and in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said that Rāhula is the son of Yaśodharā; however, in the two sutras, the *Adbhutadharma* and the *Sutra of Auspicious Responses*...
As for the claim that this is the son of Gopī, what does it mean? Indeed, the *Dvādaśa-caryā-sūtra* (Twelve Years of Wandering Sūtra) mentions three wives:
first, Gopī; second, Yaśodharā; and third, Mṛgajā. Alternatively, that sūtra may have mentioned only the senior mother [Gopī], whereas this sūtra mentions Yaśodharā as the one who gave birth.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "Gopīta was a precious woman who was barren."
This is none other than Gopī; thus we know for certain that she is indeed Yaśodharā’s daughter. △ Below this, the third assembly—the bodhisattvas—shall be explained.

From this point in the sūtra down to the mention of the "eighty thousand [attendants]," this constitutes the second listing of the bodhisattva assembly among those who have heard and retained the teachings.
This section consists of six parts: first, clarifying the character and affinity of the bodhisattvas; second, [the rest follows].
This provides a general outline of the various major numbers: first, the three stages; second, the praise of virtues; third, the listing of names; fourth, the conclusion.
Regarding the "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva," these five characters—*bodhisattva-mahāsattva*—constitute the initial category. As for the term "category" (*qìlèi*), it refers to...
These are the kindred of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. If the Sanskrit were preserved in full, one should say *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*.
Master Kumārajīva, avoiding prolixity, omitted the two characters *ti-duo* (埵). *Bodhi* here means the Way;
*sattva* here means mind; *mahā* here means great. All these individuals seek...
It is the vast and great path. Furthermore, because it brings sentient beings to maturity, it is called the "great path mind" (*mahāyānacitta*).
Both are of the same category as the great path mind; therefore, the subsequent scripture says: "When a bodhisattva hears this Dharma, the net of doubt is entirely removed.
If a bodhisattva does not hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they are not practicing the bodhisattva path well; if they hear this sutra, they are practicing it well."
This is the path of the bodhisattva. The *Śāstra* (Treatise) asks: "The bodhisattva is subsumed within the fourfold assembly of both the ordained and the laity;

why then are they listed separately here? The answer is: "There are bodhisattvas who fall among the fourfold assembly, yet there are members of the fourfold assembly who do not fall among the bodhisattvas."

Because they have not yet resolved to attain Buddhahood through the Great Mind, those who now separately listed as being of the same kind—those who have indeed resolved to attain Buddhahood through the Great Mind—are called the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, according to the subsequent praise of their virtues, which does not involve provisional [teachings], these are all individuals who have attained realization and serve as witnesses;
they are not merely ordinary people. Moreover, there are many types of Bodhisattvas, ranging from partial to perfect; one must therefore distinguish them according to the teachings.

To distinguish and clarify the bodhisattvas of this present sutra: those who hear this sutra should contemplate their own minds. That which simultaneously illuminates the two truths through the Middle Way is called "Great" (Mahā).
That which penetrates to the fruit of Bodhi is called the "Way" (Mārga). That which destroys the afflictions of the five abodes is called "sentient beings" (sattva).
This is precisely seeing within one's own mind the Great Way-mind sentient being. Furthermore, this is the original ground of all bodhisattvas.
They are difficult to fathom. Some abide at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), while others are equal to the Dharma King.
For example, Mañjuśrī was originally the Buddha Uṣṇīṣaśirītarāja, yet in his manifested trace he succeeds Śākyamuni; the rest may be understood accordingly.

By the power of the *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*, they project their shadows and manifest their forms, employing the inconceivable wheel of speech to gather and transform beings, preaching extensively according to what is appropriate. One can only...
It is known by the mind; it cannot be explained through words. It is like using a hammer and an anvil to forge various pieces of raw metal.
"Eighty thousand people"—this is the second indication of a large number. Yet, in other sutras, the assemblies are very numerous; why are those in this sutra so few?

Yes. These are merely listed according to necessity; they are stated as a general number. Thus, one should know that the opening of the secret treasury here does not involve provisional or inferior teachings, nor is it necessary to list a multitude of followers.
Nevertheless, those who attain the Way in this Root Chapter are many times greater than in other sutras.
It is like a king discussing secret matters: he cannot consult with everyone throughout the land at once, but must select them according to necessity. As for those who contemplate the mind:

Illuminating a single wholesome mind, it encompasses the ten dharma-realms. As these ten realms interact with one another, they encompass a hundred dharma-realms and a thousand natures and characteristics.
Within the mind, there are ten wholesome minds, which together constitute the ten thousand dharmas as the object of contemplation.

Taking the Eightfold Noble Path as the subject of contemplation, and through the mutual correspondence of subject and object, they combine to form eighty thousand dharma-gates. Thus, one directly perceives the Great [Dharma] within one's own body.
The "mind of the Way" refers to the assembly of eighty thousand bodhisattvas.
They all [abide] in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the third clarification of the ultimate stage bordering on perfection. *Anuttara* here means the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-mārga*). It should...
Following the subsequent passage, one establishes the three stages of non-retrogression for the practice of the higher rank.

This must further be analyzed and determined according to the teachings to reveal that the Perfect Teaching of the present sutra possesses all three forms of non-retrogression. One should contemplate that the dharmas of one's own single thought-moment are themselves the Dharma-body;
this is called "non-retrogression in mindfulness. Realizing that one's own bound karma is itself liberation, one becomes endowed with all gates of practice.

This is called non-retrogression in practice (*caryā-avaivartika*). Realizing that one’s own afflictions are themselves bodhi, and because one is free from the two deaths through *prajñā*, it is called non-retrogression in status (*avasthā-avaivartika*).
This is the realization of the three paths within one's own mind, thereby accomplishing the three stages of non-retrogression.
From "non-retrogression" below, up to "able to deliver sentient beings," there are thirteen phrases; these constitute the fourth praise of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*).
This is virtue (*guṇa*). One should know that a phrase (*pada*) is defined by the completion of its meaning, regardless of the number of syllables it contains.
"Non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*):
here, the three characters forming the first part clarify the stage (*avasthā*), while the subsequent part constitutes the praise.

"Virtue. This single phrase has a meaning that belongs to both [sections]. Having previously used this meaning to complete the explanation of the three non-regressions within the stage, we now proceed to the latter part to correlate it with the first stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The first stage is named "Joyful," because one rejoices in not regressing and not falling into the two extremes, thereby entering the Middle Way;
thus, one returns to relying on a single thought-moment to possess the three non-regressions. Therefore, one should know that this is a praise.

This refers to the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). On this stage, one is perfectly free from the three defilements, perfectly brings forth the three types of wisdom, and is perfectly luminous and perfectly transformative.
With a single thought-moment, one makes offerings and perfectly plants the roots of virtue, for which the Perfect Buddhas offer their praise;

the subsequent phrases should each be understood according to this principle. This is merely one approach, established vertically according to the context of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), intended to facilitate understanding in accordance with the inclinations of practitioners.
Because it is for the sake of explanation. For now, let us explain the meaning of each individual phrase according to the vertical (sequential) method.

If this is so, why does this perfectly wondrous sūtra vertically praise the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as distinct developmental positions? Answer: First, because it relies upon the fundamental [stages]; second, because it demonstrates their identity;

and third, because it accords with the categories of the *Śāstra*, such as the "Gate of Gathering Affairs" (*viniścaya-saṃgraha-mukha*). The horizontal (simultaneous) explanation of the perfect meaning will be self-evident in the subsequent text.
"All have attained dhāraṇīs.
This single phrase praises the second bhūmi. The second bhūmi is named "Stainless" (Vimalā); it obstructs all evils and penetrates all virtues, which is precisely the meaning of *dhāraṇī*.
Thus, one knows this refers to the Stainless Ground.

"Skill in eloquent exposition" (*pratibhāna*)—this single phrase praises the third stage. The third stage is called the "Stage of Radiance" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*); because of the internal radiance of wisdom, one is able to speak externally.

If one wishes to know where wisdom resides, it resides in speech. Since there are various kinds of speech, skillful exposition is the most excellent; therefore, we know that this praises the third stage.
The Stage of Clarity (*Prabhākarī-bhūmi*).

"Turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma"—this single phrase praises the Fourth Stage. The Fourth Stage is named "Blaze" (*Arciṣmatī*); it can destroy darkness and can also burn the wick. It turns the Dharma...
The wheel destroys its own delusions like a burnt wick, and dispels the darkness of others' confusion like the removal of gloom; this praises the fourth stage, Arciṣmatī,
wherein one makes offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.

This single phrase refutes the fifth [objection]. It is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (Duranjayā). On this ground, one attains profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and employs the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*).
Because it is difficult to conquer and difficult to equal, in a single thought-moment, one reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas.
This is the praise of the fifth ground.
"In the presence of all Buddhas, one plants the roots of all virtues.

This single phrase praises the sixth stage, named the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*). Because one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one is able to make offerings to all Buddhas;

this merit serves as the provision for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). When this knowledge of all modes manifests before one, wisdom becomes the root of virtue. It is like planting seeds in the earth; thus, it is known that this is a praise.
This is the sixth stage.
It is constantly praised by all Buddhas.
This single phrase praises the seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi. In this stage, the two wisdoms and skillful means transcend everything.
Extensively cultivating benefit accords with the Buddha’s mind; thus, one knows this praises the seventh stage.
"Cultivating the body with compassion"—this single phrase praises the eighth, the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). With right wisdom unmoving, one does not emerge from the triple world, but merely...
To permeate the body with loving-kindness, one should enter the five realms of existence; to permeate the mouth with loving-kindness, one preaches the Dharma for others;
to permeate the mind with loving-kindness, one establishes skillful means. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* fully permeates these three karmas; this praises the eighth stage.
"Skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom.

This single phrase praises the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). "Profoundly penetrating the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and wondrously reaching the fundamental source"—this description is most appropriate.
Thus, it is known that this praises the ninth stage.
He has attained great wisdom and reached the other shore; his fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and he is able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
These four lines praise the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*). His *dharmakāya* is like space, and his meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is like a great cloud.
Wisdom is like a great rain; thus, the first phrase praises the Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).

The phrase "reaching the other shore" praises the internal virtues within this stage. It refers to reaching the other shore of the three truths; speaking of the fruit within the cause, it indicates that one will reach it before long.
As for the phrase "fame widely renowned," this praises the external virtues of this stage. Because these internal virtues are profound and vast, they result in—
"Causing one's fame to be heard everywhere throughout the immeasurable [worlds]" refers to the harmony between the internal and the external.

"Able to deliver sentient beings"—this single phrase praises the superiority of this stage (*bhūmi*) over the preceding stages in terms of delivering sentient beings; thus it is called "able to deliver. These four preceding phrases all praise the tenth stage.
However, while all the aforementioned stages fully possess various virtues such as the internal and external, these have been explained here by way of their prominence.
This is done for the sake of convenience regarding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), so that one may explain according to the inclinations of people and facilitate easy understanding.
This concludes the vertical explanation of the thirteen phrases as praises of virtue based on the ten stages.

If explained horizontally, these thirteen phrases praising virtue proceed directly from the perspective of the first stage (*prathama-vihāra*)—the stage of initial resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*)—whereby a single resolve is all resolves, transcending the two extremes, transforming the ordinary and surpassing the holy, and entering [the path].
The Middle Way: his mind is quiescent, and with every thought-moment he flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), which is called attaining non-retrogression.
In the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), he eliminates and distances himself from the obstacles of grasping at signs, ignorance, and nescience;

he maintains and penetrates the three virtues of *prajñā*, liberation, and the *dharmakāya*. Therefore, it is said that he has attained *dhāraṇī*. The merit of the first stage’s oral secret of preaching the Dharma is [inexpressible].

It is called the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*). Abiding in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), one is able to manifest as a Buddha in a hundred worlds, preaching the Dharma to transform and teach sentient beings;

this is called turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma (*avaivartika-dharmacakra*). Abiding in the first stage, one attains inconceivable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and is universally able to serve all Buddhas throughout the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
this is called making offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Abiding in the first stage, one attains the foundation of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It is able to...

Planting the roots of virtue, the first stage (Prathamabhūmi) opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; knowing that one’s own Dharma is identical to that of all Buddhas is called "being praised by the Buddhas.

In the first stage, the body of form manifests universally, responding throughout the Dharma-realm; this is called "cultivating the body with compassion. In the first stage, one enters the secret treasury;
this is called "skillfully entering the Buddha-wisdom. In the first stage, the three wisdoms are unified within a single mind, free from all obstructions.

Because it is unobstructed, it is called "penetrating great wisdom. At the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), one partially attains the ultimate realization of both phenomena and principle; this is termed "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*).
The perfect virtues of the first stage are truly in accord with their names, as expressed in such passages as "the name is universally renowned.

This first stage is able to serve as the locus of reliance for the ten realms of existence, establishing and protecting them; thus it is called "able to deliver sentient beings. This is the beginning.
Abiding in this one stage, there are furthermore immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable varieties of merit; these have been briefly extolled in thirteen phrases.
It is the same for the second stage up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The initial letter 'A' possesses the merit of forty-one letters, and the final letter 'Ḍha' likewise possesses the merit of all letters; so it is with those in between."

It is likewise. If one wishes to illuminate one's own mind and perceive its manifold virtues, one need only contemplate the threefold contemplation within a single mind as perfectly clear and luminous;

then one will perceive the aforementioned three stages of non-retrogression, the three *dhāraṇīs*, the three types of hearing and retention, the three kinds of unimpeded eloquence, the three kinds of *dharma-cakras*, the Three Jewels as a single essence, the three kinds of compassion, and the Buddha-bodies of the three teachings.
Wisdom. The three truths. The single mind and the three contemplations possess immeasurable merits that cannot be fully described; how much less could the thirteen phrases ever be exhausted?

To summarize: it is because one has attained thorough penetration and clear illumination of the non-retrogressive single mind and three contemplations, up to the point of seeing one’s own mind and contemplating sentient beings with the single mind and three contemplations, and even thereby attaining the deliverance of sentient beings.

Because of the single mind and the threefold contemplation (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*), one is finally able to attain, up to and including, the non-retrogressive single mind and threefold contemplation. These are mutually inclusive and interpenetrating;

the intermediate phrases may be understood by analogy with this principle. The three contemplations are without distinction; they appear different only according to the specific phenomena they address.

The wondrousness of the perfected virtue of contemplation cannot be divided or separated. Even a single phrase of the *Hīnayāna* is said to be inexhaustible, let alone that of a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). One...
The mind suddenly attains clarity, perceiving its own various virtues. This concludes the fourth section, the praise of virtues.
Its title is as follows:
this serves as the general heading for the fifth section, which enumerates the names of the eighteen bodhisattvas. Now, the names of the various great beings (mahāsattvas) are listed below.
As for the name: it may derive from a dharma-gate, or from virtuous conduct, or from original vows; it may be hidden or manifest, real or conventional, principal or auxiliary.
Unlike the traces of the śrāvakas, which are prominent, this [name] is not so prominent;

yet it must encompass all teachings and thus stands at the head of the present sutra. Its meaning must reside in the Perfect [Teaching]. Although it is but a single name, it is complete and lacks nothing.
Regarding the meaning of the measure [of the text]: I shall now explain it according to the various sūtras and the *Contemplation of the Mind* (*Guanxin lun*), following the sequence of the text.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is here translated as Miaode (Wondrous Virtue).
In the *Muxing jing* (Sūtra on Non-action), he is named Manshushili; in the *Puchao jing* (Sūtra of Universal Transcendence), he is called Roushou. These are the Sanskrit terms.

They are not the same. There are three meanings for explaining his name. First, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "He clearly perceives the Buddha-nature, just like Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī) and others.
This establishes the name "Wondrous Virtue" based on his realization of the nature (*dharmatā*). Second, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Cintavistara-sūtra*), it says:
"Although he speaks of all phenomena, he does not give rise to the conceptualization of phenomena; because he does not give rise to the conceptualization of non-phenomena, he is called 'Wondrous'."
Virtue (*guṇa*). This refers to observing according to what has been taught; it is a name established based on conduct that accords with one's words.
