Third, as the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "I vow that when I practice the bodhisattva path, all sentient beings whom I transform shall first attain perfect enlightenment throughout the ten directions," and so forth.
The Buddha Ratnagarbha said: "The merit you have performed is exceedingly profound; I grant that you shall take a wondrous land. For this reason, [he is called Amitābha].
I shall name you Mañjuśrī. This is because your benefit for sentient beings is vast, the stages of those you transform are high, and your practices and vows are lofty and expansive;
all are sublime. You have obtained the name "Wondrous Virtue" (Mañjuśrī) from these vows. The two characters for "Bodhisattva" are explained as before. That sūtra states:
"In the north, in the world-realm called Abhirati, you shall become a Buddha named Saṃbhavaguhya-maṇi."
The Buddha Ratnākara still exists in the present. Those who hear his name shall extinguish the four grave offenses.

Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that there is a Buddha named Dragon-Species Supreme Honored King Tathāgata, who is also Mañjuśrī, manifesting for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and aiding all things.
This was to influence the ears of Śākyamuni. Yet, why does Mañjuśrī occupy the foremost position among the bodhisattvas?
Because he was able to resolve Maitreya’s doubts within the introduction, he serves as the primary catalyst for this entire sutra.

Furthermore, at the abodes of twenty trillion buddhas, he likewise initiated inquiries on behalf of the assembly; thus, he is placed at the head of the eighty thousand [bodhisattvas]. Those who hear the sutra today—

When you illuminate the rationality of your own mind— the treasury of the three virtues— neither following them vertically nor horizontally, you will immediately perceive the wondrous virtue within your own heart.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
In the language of India, he is called *Bhalaṅkateśvara*; in this [language], he is called Guanshiyin (Avalokiteśvara). The *Siyi jing* (Saṃghāṭasūtra) states:
"If sentient beings see him, they immediately attain certainty regarding Bodhi; those who invoke his name shall be freed from all sufferings. For this reason, he is named Guanyin.
Furthermore, the *Beihua jing* (Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra) states: "If there are sentient beings suffering who invoke my name, their minds..."
"Those who remember me"—because they shall hear and see through my divine ear and divine eye—if they cannot escape suffering, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha Ratnagarbha said: "Observe all sentient beings and give rise to great compassion; from now on, I shall name you Avalokiteśvara.
This title will be explained more extensively later in the Universal Gate Chapter. Those who hear this sutra [shall be illuminated].

The three wisdoms within one's own single mind are called "contemplation" (*guan*); the three truths are called "the world" (*shi*); and the three contemplations are the original name for "sound" (*yin*).
This is precisely seeing the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara within one's own mind.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the *Siksasamuccaya-sūtra* states: "Wherever I set my foot, the trichiliocosm and the palaces of Māra tremble;
thus I am named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. This explains "sthāma" (power) in terms of majestic might. Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "I vow..."
"My world shall be no different from that of Avalokiteśvara and others. The Buddha Ratnagarbha said, "Because you have made a vow to take up a great trichiliocosm, I shall name you Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
This explains 'power' (sthāma) in worldly terms: by means of this power, you shall take up the world without contradicting your resolve.
Because your resolve is so vast, the Buddha grants you this prediction. Your vow to take up the world is also called [Mahāsthāmaprāpta]."
Worldly Aspiration: Those who hear this sutra take the three types of cessation—namely, the realization of the true nature within the single mind, equality, and so forth—as their foundation.
By casting themselves into the ground of the three truths, they cause views and attachments to collapse; thus, they immediately perceive their own minds as Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Regarding the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence (*Sadā-vīrya*), the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva, for the sake of a single sentient being, follows after them for immeasurable kalpas without abandoning them;
even if the being does not undergo transformation, he does not harbor a single thought of forsaking them. Body and mind advance together. If one illuminates one's own mind..."
The *dharmatā* of ignorance is neither identical to nor separate [from it]. One sees within the mind the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence and the Bodhisattva Unceasing.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Cintaviṣaya-vikurvaṇa-sūtra*) states: "Take *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-sama* kalpas as one day and night; thirty such days constitute a month; twelve..."
A month constitutes a year. After passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one may encounter a single Buddha.

Encountering Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in this manner, one practices all the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and cultivates meritorious virtues; only then does one receive a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).

The mind never ceases its effort, and for this reason it is so named. Now, those who hear this sutra should reflect upon their own minds: they should not dwell in emptiness, but rather, as if there were no Buddha present, they should emerge into the provisional realm.

One does not abide in the provisional. Just as when there is a Buddha, one enters into it without abiding within it; just as when receiving a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), one should illuminate the three truths.
The mind-nature is eternally abiding; this is precisely the non-ceasing within one's own mind.

Regarding the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the *Puychō kyǒng* (Sutra of Universal Transcendence) states: "Clad in the armor of supreme virtue, even the Buddha cannot thwart or defeat him. This explains "palm" (*pāṇi*).
Being clad in supreme armor, one firmly grasps the Dharma-body; hence it is called "palm. Now, in explaining the Mahāyāna, one always employs the true mind.
It penetrates all wise minds. For the sake of others, it expounds the world-transcending, supreme, and most precious jewels, with a heart free from greed or attachment.

Interpreting "jewel" according to this, if one illuminates one's own mind, it is precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; thus one is able to grasp the jewel of the three truths within the nature of the palm.
This is one's own precious palm. Regarding the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka* (Compassionate Lotus Sūtra) states:
"I vow that during the times of suffering at the end of the kalpa, I shall protect and deliver all beings from the calamities of war, pestilence, and famine."
"O Great Physician King," said the Buddha Ratnagarbha, "I shall now name you Bhaisajyarāja.
If you illuminate your own mind with the three contemplations to treat the grave illness of the three poisons, you are yourself the Bodhisattva Bhaisajyarāja."
The Bodhisattva Courageous Bestower, the Bodhisattva Jewel Moon, the Bodhisattva Moonlight, the Bodhisattva Full Moon, the Bodhisattva Great Power,
the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Power, and the Bodhisattva Transcender of the Three Realms.
These seven bodhisattvas all share the name Ratnakūṭa (寶積). The commentaries and records lack an explanation for them, and I have not yet consulted other sutra annotations.

As for Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, this is translated as "Good Protector" (善守) or also as "Worthy Protector" (賢守). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samantabhadrotsāhana-sūtra* (思益) states: "If sentient beings hear his name, they will certainly [attain liberation]."
Having attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*, he is named "Well-Guarded" (*Sugupta*). *Pratyutpanna* is also called "Well-Protected" (*Sugupta*) or "Skillfully Guarded," causing one not to fall back.
If one contemplates the Middle Way within the mind, such that among all virtues it is not moved by the three delusions, one then perceives the "well-guarding" within one's own mind.

Maitreya Bodhisattva—here translated as "The Kindly One" (Cishi)—takes "Kindly" (Ci) as his clan name. His personal name is Ajita, which means "Unconquerable. The *Siyi jing* (Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra) states:

"If sentient beings see him, they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Compassionate Mind; therefore, he is named 'The Kindly One' (Maitreya). The *Xianyu jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish) says: "In the past..."
When he was a king, seeing the elephant upon which he rode, his lustful mind became intensely inflamed. The elephant trainer touched the top of the elephant’s head with an iron hook;
seeing this, [the king] gave rise to a heart of compassion. Now, as one in the position of succession to Buddhahood, he likewise does so.

Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that he made a vow to protect sentient beings amidst the kalpas of swords and fire. Through the permeation of the power of this original vow, he gives rise to compassion upon seeing suffering. If one contemplates oneself...

The mind, being in the Middle Way without conditions, is itself Great Compassion. By the power of the roots of goodness of this compassion, all mental factors are made to enter into the Dharma of Great Compassion of the same essence.
Departing from all that is unwholesome, one then beholds Maitreya within one’s own mind.
The Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa:
the commentary and records lack an explanation for this.
The Bodhisattva Śāstṛ.

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "Toward sentient beings who have fallen into wrong paths, one gives rise to great compassion and causes them to enter the right path, without seeking any reward for such kindness;
therefore, one is called a 'Guide' (*nāyaka*). He was a lay householder from the country of Śrāvastī who caused others with wrong views to all enter the right path.
If one contemplates the mind as being emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, one guides all practices so that they do not fall [into error]."
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is itself the guide of one's own mind.
Thus, there were eighty thousand such Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas present together.
This concludes the sixth summary of the count. The second section, the enumeration of the assembly of Bodhisattvas, is finished.
"At that time" refers to the very moment [the teaching was given]. The following section concerns the third group among those who hear and uphold the Dharma: the miscellaneous assembly.

Ancient commentators say this is an assembly of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), yet within it there are noble ones (*ārya*); for example, the eight nāgas are bodhisattvas of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). How much more so, then, [for others]?
Originally, those present at the Avataṃsaka Sūtra assembly all attained inconceivable liberation; they cannot be called "ordinary" (pǎn).

The old term "secular multitude" (súzhòng) is used here because there were practitioners of the Way among them, such as those led by King Ajātaśatru; it was not exclusively a secular crowd, so they cannot be called "secular."
The old [translation] says "the assembly of devas and humans. However, this assembly also contains dragons and ghosts, so those terms are not entirely appropriate.
Following the tradition of Tiantai, they are called the "mixed assembly" (*zazhong*), which encompasses all intended meanings. What is the meaning of "mixed"?

It refers to the eight classes of beings comprising the five destinies (*gati*) and the two realms of form and desire; hence it is called "mixed. In terms of external appearance, there are the physical forms and attire resulting from the retribution of the five destinies.
"Differentiation" is also termed "mixture. With respect to the internal [practitioners], there are those who have realized the principle and those who have not yet attained the Way;
the multitudes of the five destinies possess the capacities for the four *siddhāntas*. As their essential natures—whether partial or perfect—are intermingled with one another, it is called "mixture.
This refers to the initial stage when the true teaching has not yet been heard. However, once the meditative vision arises, all become one in humanity, being purely equal and without mixture.
Such is the meaning of "mixed. How could it be judged merely by the physical forms of ordinary people?

Nor can it be judged by the five types of practitioners or by gods and humans. Because this assembly includes those who have attained the Way, those who have realized the principle, and various capacities across the four teachings, it is called a "mixed assembly."
Śakra Devānām Indra, together with his retinue of twenty thousand devaputras.
Among these eight groups, the first lists the Lord of the Desire Realm and others;

he is sometimes called Candira, which translates as "Capable of Acting," because he acts as the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven of the Desire Realm. Trāyastriṃśa is the dwelling place, located upon Mount Sumeru.

On the mountain peak, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven extends across thirty-three [peaks]. A detailed explanation is as found in other sūtras and śāstras. For now, I shall explain the "attendants" (*sahāya*);
since they are not essential to the location itself, they are omitted here. This applies to all subsequent bases as well. As the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
A bhikṣu asked the Buddha, "For what reason is he named Śakra Devānām Indra? The Buddha replied, "In a former life as a human being, he practiced sudden, spontaneous giving;
as a karmic retribution, he became a lord of devas and was named Śakra Devānām Indra. Śakra has a thousand names, each of which has its own cause, but they are not fully enumerated here.
Because he is the sovereign of this realm of desire, he is listed first. This should be understood according to the teachings."

Explanation: One receives the prediction of enlightenment through Prajñā and is named the World-Honored One Without Attachment (*Asaṅga*). It should be known that he fundamentally realizes the merits of the thirty-three stages;
his traces abide upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, where he dwells together with the gods of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*) and partakes of the nectar of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
If one penetrates one’s own mind and forgets the dharmas of the aggregates and mindfulness, this is precisely the eternally abiding true mark, like the nectar of the heavens.
"Lu" (Lù) refers to Śakra himself. "The twenty thousand [deities] and so forth" refers to the retinue led by Śakra; this can be understood through reflection.
Furthermore, there were the Devaputra Moon (Candraprabha), the Devaputra Universal Fragrance (Samantagandha), and the Devaputra Jewel Radiance (Ratnaprabha).
These three sons of gods are the inner ministers of Śakra, similar to the positions of the various high officials (*kṣatriya* or *amātya*).
Alternatively, they are said to be the sons of gods of the Three Luminaries: the one named Moon is the Moon Devaputra, who is Ratnaśrī and is the manifestation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
Pūrvagandha is the Tārakadevaputra, who is Gaganagañja and is the manifestation of [Avalokiteśvara]; and Ratnaprabha is the Sun Devaputra.
The Son of Heaven is this Jewel-Mind (Ratnamati). He is the manifested trace of Avalokiteśvara. Both his manifested traces and his name appear in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues of ten thousand sons of gods, [were present].
These Four Great Heavenly Kings are the external ministers of Śakra, like military generals. There are four of them:
the one in the east is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which means "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó) and is also called "Pacifier of the People" (Ànmín).
He dwells atop the Golden Mountain on the middle slope of Mount Sumeru and constantly leads two classes of spirits: first, the Gandharvas; second, the Piśācas. Next...
In the south is Virūḍhaka, here translated as the Heavenly King of Increase. He dwells on Mount Vaiḍūrya and leads two classes of spirits: first, the Piśācas; second, the Kumbhāṇḍas.
In the west is Virūpākṣa, the Heavenly King, here translated as "Evil Eye.
He dwells on Mount White Silver and leads two classes of spirits: first, the Nāgas (poisonous dragons); second, the Piśācas. In the north is named Virūpākṣa... [text truncated]
The Heavenly King of Śramaṇas, here called "Much-Hearing" (Skt. Vaiśravaṇa), dwells on Mount Crystal. He leads two classes of spirits: first, the rākṣasas; second, the yakṣas.
As for those spirits he leads, he does not allow them to afflict people; therefore, he is named "Protector of the World. In essence, he abides in permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
in his provisional manifestation, he appears as one of the Four Heavenly Kings who protect the world.

The Devaputra Īśvara and the Devaputra Maheśvara, together with their retinue of thirty thousand devaputras, constitute the Īśvara Heaven, also known as the Nirmāṇarati (Heaven of Delighting in Emanations).
This is the fifth heaven of the Desire Realm. Yuanhui’s Commentary states:

"Delighting in Emanations" means that although the various implements of pleasure obtained as karmic retribution are still coarse, they further employ supernatural powers of karma to transform them into subtle and exquisite forms.
Because one freely enjoys objects, it is called "mastery over transformations" (*nirmāṇavaśitā*).

As for "Great Mastery," this refers to the sixth heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which is the pinnacle of the heavens within the desire realm. When one wishes to obtain objects, one can personally transform the five sensory desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).
Furthermore, other deities, knowing what is required, manifest them on one's behalf; thus, when the five desires are employed, they are immediately sufficient.
Therefore, he receives the name "Great Sovereign" (Maheśvara). Between these, there are further two heavens, Yāma and Tuṣita, which do not appear in this sūtra;
they have been omitted for brevity. This concludes the enumeration of the celestial hosts of the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
Śikhin Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World:
this and the following list the second group, the deities of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the term "Sahā," it is translated here as "Endurance Land" (*saha-loka*);
because the sentient beings therein abide in the ten non-virtuous actions and are unwilling to renounce them, the land is named after its inhabitants, and is thus called [the World of Endurance].
Regarding the "Land of Endurance" (Sahā): The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that it is called Sahā because the sentient beings therein endure the three poisons and all afflictions;
hence it is named the Land of Endurance. It is also called "The Mixture," as the nine realms of existence dwell together there.
This is a brief explanation of the Sahā world. As for the term "Brahmā," this is translated as "Free from Desire"; having eliminated the delusions of the lower stages, one ascends to the Form Realm.
Therefore, he is named "Free from Desire" (*Vītarāga*). He is also called "Highly Pure" (*Brahmapurohita*). Śikhin is also named Śikhidhvaja; this is a name for fire.
Because this king cultivated the meditative concentration of the fire-light (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) and thereby destroyed the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, he was named after this virtue.

Although the sutra designates him as the Brahmā King, thereby indicating his status as a lord of devas, it further refers to him as Śikhin. The commentary explains that [the name] is due to the *śikhā* (topknot).
He becomes a Brahmā King; "Śikhin" is his name. This citation of his rank serves to reveal his name, referring to a single individual.
Abiding in the intermediate dhyāna, he possesses vitarka and vicāra within, and speech without. If he practices dhyāna alone, he becomes a Brahma-minister (Brahmapurohita);
if he adds the four immeasurable minds (apramāṇa), he attains leadership as a King. Thus, this first dhyāna contains three heavens; here, only its king is mentioned.
This includes the other two heavens:
the Ābhāsvara (Radiant) Mahābrahmā and so forth, together with their retinue of twelve thousand devaputras.

As for "radiant," this refers to the three heavens of the second dhyāna, all of which possess radiance; these three heavens are so named because they have for the first time departed from [the realm of]...

Because one seeks out and contemplates the faults of internal coarseness (*vitarka* and *vicāra*), causing the body to produce sublime light, these realms are given the designation "Radiance" (*Ābhāsvara*).

As for the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it refers to the three heavens of the third dhyāna and the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna; however, the author of the Sūtra has omitted them here for the sake of brevity.

If one were to explain the names of these eighteen heavens in detail, such as their correspondence with the bodies and lifespans of their inhabitants, it would be exactly as described in the *Abhidharmakośa*. This is not [the case here].
This may be explained. This concludes the enumeration of the assemblies of the gods of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

As for the failure to enumerate the assemblies of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is because their discipline is strict while their vehicle is slow, as illustrated by the four-line verse; thus, they do not participate in this assembly.
There are eight dragon kings.
This marks the third set of eight dragon kings. This is the general enumeration of their number; the following lists their eight names:
Nanda Dragon King and Upananda Dragon King.
The first was named Nanda, meaning "Joy," and the second was named Upananda, meaning "Excellent"; they were brothers who constantly protected the kingdom of Magadha.
Rain fell in its proper season, and the land never suffered from famine. King Bimbisāra held a great assembly once a year;
when the common people heard of it, they all rejoiced, and the name was subsequently established based on this. These are the very ones whom Maudgalyāyana subdued, who now dwell within the ocean.
These eight dragon kings obtained the Dharma-gate of the Inconceivable Liberation from within the *Avataṃsaka*.

Originally, they were Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage who manifested their traces by appearing in this world. Each should be understood according to their fundamental reality (*hon*) and their manifested traces (*seki*).
One should know that while their fundamental abode is the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), their traces reside within the ocean. Their contemplative understanding will be explained later.
Sāgara, the Dragon King, is the one praised in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
He derives his name from dwelling in the ocean; some say he is named after his country.
Originally abiding in the great ocean of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, his traces are found in the vast blue sea.
The Dragon King Sāgara (translated here as Duōtóu,

"Many Heads") dwells within the waters. He fundamentally abides in the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body, yet he manifests the appearance of having many heads as a provisional trace.
The Dragon King Takṣaka—

here translated as "Poison-Observer" (Shidu) or "Many-Tongued" (Duoshé)— originally dwells in the Dharma-gate of Eloquence in Expounding the Dharma (Leshuo Bianfamen), yet he manifests his traces as one with many tongues.
The Nāga King Anavatapta takes its name from the lake.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, there is a lake on the summit of the Snowy Mountains called Lake Anavatapta;
this nāga king constantly dwells within it. The nāgas of Jambudvīpa have three afflictions, namely: hot winds, hot sands, and [hot] sand.
The Golden-Winged Bird (Garuda) enters the palace and dwells in that pond, free from the three afflictions; therefore, it is named the Pond Without Heat (*Anavatapta*).

One should know that while its fundamental abode is the bliss of purity, selfhood, permanence, and coolness (*śītalānanda-ātma-viśuddhi*), its manifest location is the Cool Pond, where it avoids the diseases of the three poisons.
The Nāga King Manasvin—
here translated as "Great Body" or "Great Power"— when the Asuras churned the ocean and submerged the city of Sudarśana, this dragon coiled his body to stem the waters of the sea.
Originally dwelling in the Boundless Body (*Anantakāya*), he manifests in these forms of Great Body and Great Power.
The Utpala Dragon King and others, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
"Utpala" translates here as "the dark-colored lotus pond. These dragons dwell within this pool and are named after it.
They fundamentally abide in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, yet they manifest their presence in this pool. The *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that the dragon is for all... [text continues]
The realm of the devas. When the devas and asuras raise their armies, the devas first dispatch dragons to fight; thus it is known that they are governed by the devas.
These dragons and others are included within the category of animals.
There are four Kinnara kings;
these constitute the fourth row of the Kinnara assembly. This is a general indication of their number.
As for the "four Kinnaras," they are also called Caturdāras, which here means "Doubtful Deities. They resemble humans but possess a single horn; therefore, they are so named.
These are humans and non-humans; they are the gods of celestial dharma and music who dwell upon the Ten Jewel Mountains as enumerated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Their bodies possess extraordinary marks, and whenever they perform music, the Buddha preaches the Dharma. The various devas then play stringed instruments, sing, and play the pañcaśīrṣa lute while chanting verses on the Dharma-gates.
The Kinnara King Dharma, the Kinnara King Subhadharma, the Kinnara King Mahādharma,
and the Kinnara King Dhāradharma, each accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.

The *Dharma-kinnara* plays the sound of the dharma of arising and ceasing; the *Sūkṣma-dharma-kinnara* plays the sound of the dharma of non-arising; the *Mahā-dharma-kinnara* plays the sound of immeasurable dharmas;

and the *Dhāraṇī-dharma-kinnara* plays the sound of the unconditioned dharma. Since these various *kinnaras* have experienced the five flavors, the sounds of the dharma they play must pervade the four teachings.
As the *Mahāvṛkṣa-sūtra* says: "The Great Tree Kinnara King, together with immeasurable *kinnaras*..."
Together with immeasurable *gandharva* devas, they played eighty-four thousand pure and wondrous musical tones as they approached the Buddha’s dwelling.
As the strings and songs were set in motion, their sound shook the great trichiliocosm; Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, surged and subsided, rising and falling.
All the *śrāvakas* rose from their seats as if performing a dance. When Kāśyapa was questioned, he replied that it was not his original intention.
Thus we know that he is able to produce the distinct and perfect Dharma-sounds, causing all the śrāvakas to be unable to remain at ease. One should know that his fundamental abiding is inconceivable;

without arising from the samādhi of cessation, he remains in meditative concentration with palms joined, praising the King of Dharma. Within his manifested traces, he employs stringed and wind instruments to sing the praises of the Ten Powers.
That the present sutra does not list as many [powers] as those enumerated in the Mahāvṛkṣa-paripṛcchā serves as verification of what was heard in reality.
Because it is unchanging, the fact that [the syllables] *jin* and so forth are all fourfold indicates that the Four Teachings may be known.
If one realizes that one's own voice is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, thereby accords with the Three Truths, this is precisely praising the Buddha.
There are four Gandharva kings;
these constitute the fifth row of the Gandharva host. As for the term "Gandharva," it is translated here as "Fragrance-Sniffers" (*xiūxiāng*);

they take fragrance as their food, and are also called "Fragrance-Bodies" (*xiāngyīn*) because fragrance issues from their bodies. They are the deities of worldly music belonging to the realm of the Heavenly Emperor.
This is a general indication of the number.
Regarding the Gandharva King *Ratana*:
"Ratana" means a banner or a pole; it refers to that which takes a banner as its object, namely a wooden staff.
The Gandharva King of Musical Sound.
As for "musical sound," it refers to drums, cymbals, strings, and wind instruments.
It is the beautiful Gandharva King.
As for "Beautiful One" (Rucirā): among those who have overturned the [four] perversions, she is of the most excellent class.
Ruciraghoṣa, the Gandharva King, was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants. As for "Beautiful Sound" (Ruciraghoṣa):
he is the most excellent among those who play stringed and wind instruments. This concludes the explanation of the four hosts of Gandharvas.
There are four asura kings;
they constitute the sixth rank among the asura hosts. As for "asura," this is translated as "no-wine. They gather flowers from the four continents, intending to ferment the great ocean into wine;
however, due to the karmic power of the fish and dragons, the flavor does not change. Out of anger and jealousy, they take an oath.
Because they have severed [the faculty of shame], they are said to be "without wine" (lit. *asura*). They are also called "not upright. These deities are deceitful and crooked;
this *asura* realm is also subsumed within the two realms of ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*). If they dwell by the seashore, they are subsumed under the realm of ghosts;
if they dwell at the bottom of the great ocean, they are subsumed under the realm of animals. This is a general enumeration of their numbers.
Bali Asura-rāja—here translated as "The Bound," or "Bound in Five Places"—is so called because he is bound by five evil objects around his neck from which he cannot escape.
He is also called "The One with Bonds" because he was bound by Śakra; thus, he is named "The Bound."
The asura king Khara-karṇa—
here translated as "Broad Shoulders" or "Evil Shadow"— is the one who surges forth from the ocean.
The asura king Vemacitra...
This is called Śucīndra; he is the father of Śacī. Because Śacī slandered her father, he subsequently went to war with Śakra.
He kicked up the waters of the ocean and attacked the city of Sudarśana with his hands, yet by the power of the Prajñā mantra, Śakra was unable to harm him.
The Asura King Rāhu was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
"Rāhu" is translated here as "Obstructing-Holder," for he obstructs the sun and moon. He belongs to the species of animals;
he can transform his body to a height of eighty-four thousand *yojanas*. His body is adorned with precious jewels. When the sun emits light that shines upon his eyes, he raises his hand.

He covered the sun with his palm, obscuring it. Whenever he was afraid of the sun and moon, he would increase the size of his body and hiss at them with his breath, causing the sun and moon to lose their light.
They came to complain to the Buddha, who told them, "Rāhu, do not swallow the sun and moon."
Upon hearing the verse, Rāhu’s limbs trembled and his body broke out in cold sweat; he immediately released the sun and moon.
Then, seeing that Rāhu had released the moon out of fear and trembling, Bāli asked, "For what reason are you now so fearful and uneasy?
He replied, "If I had not released the moon in accordance with the Buddha's words, my head would have split into seven pieces by the power of the Buddha over sentient beings."
By the power of the sun and moon, they cannot harm the sun and moon.

Seeing a Buddhist stūpa being consumed by fire, he carried water to extinguish the flames and vowed to obtain a great body, the foremost in the desire realm, and to be born in the City of Radiance (*Prabhāpurī*) as the lord Rāhu.
In the southern continent, within the Vajra Mountains, there is a palace where he rules over a domain of six thousand *yojanas*, with rows of trees spread throughout.
In a single day and night, one undergoes suffering three times. That the instruments of torment enter the palace of one belonging to the four evil destinies is precisely due to this.
If one illuminates the mind, employing the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way to simultaneously negate the emptiness and quiescence of the dharma-realm, this is called "obscuration.
When the three contemplations sever delusions, it is like seeing clashing armies. To state the essence: to penetrate one's nature...
This is a section on unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*). The account of devouring the moon originates from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The commentary on the text is found within the *Āgama*.
There are four *garuḍa* kings;
this refers to the seventh enumeration of the *garuḍa* hosts. This first introduces the subject: as for the term *garuḍa*, it is as follows.

These are called *garuḍas* (Golden-Winged Ones). Their wings are of a fused golden color. On a great tree to the north of the great ocean, to the east of the tree is the palace of the egg-born *nāgas*, and there is also the palace of the egg-born *garuḍas*.
To the south of the tree is the palace of the womb-born, to the west the moisture-born, and to the north the transformation-born;
on each of these four sides there are palaces for both *nāgas* and *garuḍas*. The distance between the two wings of a bird is three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand *li*.
This bird possesses divine power: the male transforms into a celestial son (*devaputra*), and the female changes into a celestial maiden (*apsaras*).

Having transformed themselves, they turn their dwelling place into a jeweled palace, where there are also foods of a hundred flavors; yet they require the dragon as food. Those of the world say that Zhuangzi called it the *peng*;
that the *peng* travels with its wings supported by all other birds, and that it is also called the phoenix (*fenghuang*), is erroneous. The phoenix does not tread upon living grass.
They eat the kernels of bamboo and nest in milk-trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*). As for the *garuḍas*, how are they classified? This passage concerning birds is cited from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
It refers to the Great Majestic *Garuḍa* King.
*Garuḍa* is explained as before. "Of great majesty" (*mahātejas*) means that his majesty surpasses all others.
The *Garuḍa* King of Great Body (*Mahākāya*) refers to one of a great multitude.
The Great Pūrṇa Garuḍa King and the Yathākāma Garuḍa King,
each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues, [arrived]. Because the nāgas constantly satisfied their desires, they were called Yathākāma.
As for the "wish-fulfilling" [jewel], it is because the neck possesses this pearl. The lifespan of these birds is eight thousand years;
when their lives end, their hearts strike the wind-wheel and pierce through the summit of the Golden Mountain, becoming wish-fulfilling jewels. When dragons obtain them, they become kings;
human kings likewise have the power to move these pearls.
King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, together with several hundreds of thousands of retinues—this constitutes the eighth assembly of people.
"Vaidehī" is translated here as "Contemplation"; she is the mother.
Her father’s name was Bimbisāra, which means "Shadow-Real. Ajātaśatru is the son; this means "Unborn."
"Enemy. While his mother was pregnant with him, she constantly harbored ill will toward King Piṃśa; thus, he was named [Piṃśa] because he was already malicious even before birth.
Alternatively, he was called Vālika, which means "Fingerless. When he was first born, physiognomists declared him to be inauspicious.
The king ordered him to be thrown from a high tower, but he did not die; he merely lost one finger and was thus named "Fingerless. [From the *Puchao jing* (Sutra of Universal Transcendence).]
The Sūtra states: Ajātaśatru, having repented before Mañjuśrī, attained the *kṣānti* of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
At the end of his life, he entered the Piṇḍala hell; as soon as he entered, he emerged, was born in a Buddha-land above, and attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.
When Maitreya appears, he will return to this world, known as the Bodhisattva Acala, and later shall become a Buddha named Śuddhalokadhātu Tathāgata.

Having attained the patience of gentleness (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) and being included among the pure assembly of those who hear and uphold this sutra, it was only upon reaching the time of nirvana that the sores on his body first broke out;

he then repented for having attained the first fruit of the path. Thus, one should know that these traces were merely shown to lead away those who commit crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).

One must not be deluded by the traces and thereby confuse them with the fundamental reality. If one illuminates the mind, one sees that craving is the mother and ignorance is the father; to destroy these is what is called "immediate retribution."

The contrary is itself the compliant. By practicing what is not the Way, one attains penetration into the Buddha-way. This concludes the eightfold sequence of capacities among the miscellaneous assembly. Question:

Since the Buddha preaches the Dharma while within the human realm, why is the enumeration of the human assembly so small? Answer: The text is abbreviated and does not record them; in reality, they are not few.
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* serves as the introduction to this scripture, and its text states: "And all the minor kings..."
The Wheel-Turning Sage King refers to the four types of wheel-turning monarchs. The kings, ministers, subjects, men, women, and their retinues were indeed vast in number. Question:

Celestial beings, humans, dragons, and ghosts all came to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma. Yet, as for the single realm of hell and the single sphere of the formless, for what reason are they not included in this assembly? Answer: The ascent and descent among the various realms of existence depend upon one’s observance of the precepts. Since those in hell are bound by the weight of their transgressions and those in the formless realm have transcended sensory perception, they do not participate in such assemblies.

Furthermore, the purpose of these gatherings is to propagate the teachings and transform sentient beings; therefore, those who are currently undergoing karmic retribution or who lack the capacity for sensory engagement are excluded. As for the noble ones in the formless realm, they abide in meditative absorption and are detached from worldly phenomena; thus, they do not attend such assemblies. It is solely because the conditions for such a gathering are absent that these categories are not listed.

Regarding the upholding or violating [of precepts], there are differences in the urgency with which one mounts the vehicle; there is the distinction between seeing the Buddha and not seeing him; there are degrees of coarseness and subtlety in maintaining the precepts;

there are superior and inferior rewards; there are Great and Small vehicles; and there are provisional and ultimate ways of seeing the Buddha. To distinguish the precepts and the vehicle, they are briefly divided into three grades: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
Furthermore, based on a single phrase from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, these are expanded into four categories: first, those who possess both the vehicle and the precepts.

First is those for whom the practice is urgent: these are the devas and humans who hear the Dharma now. Second is those for whom the precepts are lax but the vehicle is urgent: these are the animals and ghosts who hear the Dharma now.

Third is those for whom the precepts are urgent but the vehicle is lax: these are those in the formless realm who do not come. Fourth is those for whom both the precepts and the vehicle are lax: these are those in the hells who do not come.
Why is it that other sutras list the formless realm and the hells [among those who come]? It is because the vehicle is divided into three categories.
In other sutras, they are listed; this is merely because those of the Middle and Lower Vehicles are hasty. They are not listed here because those of the Supreme Vehicle are leisurely;

they are unable to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and see the Buddha. One should know that blessings are easy [to obtain] while precepts are difficult; precepts are easy [to obtain] while the Vehicle is difficult.

Because those who have not come to this sutra are numerous, I shall provide a broad explanation of these four phrases as found in the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, interpreting them through seven meanings;

those in need should consult it. If one grasps this intent, then by means of these four phrases, one may examine each of the human and celestial beings, the eight classes of spirits, and the various capacities of sentient beings within the six realms—whether they encountered the Buddha themselves or others, the time and place they heard the Dharma, and whether their attainment of the Way was swift or slow—across all the sutras.
By examining the presence or absence of the various assemblies [in the sūtras], one may verify the place where one’s own self will be reborn in the future.

The causes and effects of the three periods of time are as unerring as a seal; they can be clearly discerned. Those who hear this sūtra now should examine their own hearts and reproach themselves according to the preface of the sūtra.

How could I not feel shame before the True Dharma? At this auspicious assembly where the Way is attained, those who number more than the dust motes of a great trichiliocosm fail to join the ranks of the elect;

I am deeply ashamed of my own lowly state. Relying on what I have now heard and seen, may the seeds of bondage be transformed so that consciousness may be entrusted to the Wondrous Vehicle, ultimately reaching the other shore.
I further pray that all Buddhas provide secret assistance, so that awakening may be manifested in this very life, and that both self and others may enter [the path] together to repay their kindness.
The grace of the Dharma is impartial in its sacred discernment; may it bear witness to this sincere aspiration.
Each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
This extensively establishes the common preface, which begins from "Thus have I heard" and concludes directly here; all such passages are termed the General Preface (Tongxu).
[End. Now, this general introduction (*pūrvapīṭhikā*) originates from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. It says that when the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"What words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras? The Buddha replied to Ānanda: "One should say: 'Thus have I heard.

At one time, the Buddha was in such-and-such a region, in such-and-such a country, together with such-and-such a great assembly. This is not only the case for my own Dharma; it is likewise for all [teachings] of the three periods of time."
All Buddhist sūtras begin in this manner; therefore, it is called the "General Preface" (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*), as it appears at the head of every scripture.

Furthermore, these five elements—beginning with "Thus" (*evam*)—universally precede both the "Main Body" (*mūla-bhāga*) and the "Circulation" (*parīndanā*) sections of a single work; thus, by saying "Thus," one refers generally to the entire text.

"I heard" (*śrutaṃ mayā*) indicates that the one who hears the entire work is the same throughout; likewise, the time, place, principal teacher, and retinue remain invariably consistent from beginning to end.

The "Introduction" (tu) encompasses the entire section and is also called the "General Preface. This is the meaning of Zhiyi’s *Chān'ān Biejì* (Zhiyi’s Separate Record), which explains the scripture according to the first three sections.
It is also called the "Postscript to the Scripture" because it was compiled after the preaching of the scripture;

it is also called the "Preface to the Scripture" because the Buddha entrusted it to be placed at the beginning of the scripture; and it is also called the "Preface of Authentication and Faith" (*zhèngxìn xù*).

It is also titled "Preface to the Refutation of Heresies," as explained previously in the corresponding section. However, the general preface (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*) of the present sutra transcends the [teachings of] a single lifetime;

its distinctions are as previously stated. This concludes the explanation of the general preface. From the passage beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One" down to the end of the chapter is called the specific preface (*asādhāraṇa-nidāna*).
It is termed "specific" in contrast to the "general. Furthermore, regarding this particular teaching, they are distinguished in relation to one another.

Regarding the statement: from the perspective of the Buddha and his disciples, both before and after the sutra, the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*) applies to both the general and the specific, while the specific introduction (*asādhāraṇa-nidāna*) applies only to the specific.
Furthermore, if one follows the Tathāgata’s final testament, then the general introduction applies only to the general and the specific introduction applies only to the specific.

However, regarding the sutras that have come down to the present since the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when compared with those of former masters, this specific introduction has a distinct meaning while simultaneously encompassing the general, as it generally recounts the past.

Therefore, it is found only in this present sutra. While the general introduction (*sūtra-nidāna*) is common [to all sutras], its meaning is distinct; this distinction lies in the "present" and the "past. All sutras are thus.
One should know that in this present sutra, the two introductions correspond to one another, their designations being self-evident.

Within this present sutra, when it speaks of a general narrative of the past, it refers to the repeated narration of the manifestation of the Dharma; regarding the emission of light, it illuminates both the gradual and the sudden teachings. Only this...

The "Flower Land" (Huā-dì) specifically represents this scripture; its esoteric intent has not yet been proclaimed. Upon entering meditative concentration, the meaning encompasses both opening and closing.

When the multitude rejoices, their delight and movement differ from the past; compared to the past, they are now different. Doubt and reflection arise simultaneously, as conditions from the past and present lead to hesitation regarding the future.

In the response and questioning, the three commonalities are extensively set forth, universally encompassing the teachings of a lifetime. Since the intent of the sutra is profound, the prologue is likewise distinct.
It is constant. Therefore, while other sutras initiate [the discourse] directly, this text consists of five parts: first, the assembly; second, the manifestation of auspicious signs;

third, the arising of doubt; fourth, the posing of questions; and fifth, the answering of questions. First, I shall provide a general explanation of these five parts, which requires the fourfold teaching (*catur-yāna*).

Regarding the first, the causal conditions (*nidāna*), Guangzhai’s commentary explains that there is both a reverse and a direct order of arising; because the assembly has gathered, the [signs] are manifested.

The auspicious omen (*śrī*), up to the answer resulting from a question, the answer resulting from a question, and even the auspicious omen resulting from the assembly of the multitude—these constitute a reciprocal causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) linked like a chain of hooks.
Yet, while the introduction to the primary meaning remains unmanifest, this direct explanation of causes and conditions alone is already unclear;
how much more so for the second, third, and fourth conditions, which lack any discernible purpose. What, then, is their intended meaning?
This refers to expressing "four and one. It is revealed by a single sūtra, for it does not go beyond these four. This [text] likewise uses the doctrine of Guangzhai to refute Guangzhai;
yet, according to our own Master’s own doctrine, it should express that all ten wonders are one. Now, we clarify the five prefaces; the preface to the "Middle" (Zheng) is the "four and one.
The first [preface], "Assembling the Multitude," describes the person: because many people have harmoniously combined, it has reached the present day.

Because they are identical, this is the world. The manifestation of auspicious omens (prātihārya) illustrates the identity of principle; each of the six omens does not fail to manifest the central meaning, and thus this name is most appropriate.

This is the primary truth (*paramārtha*). The narration of doubt and reflection illustrates the identity of practice; the purpose of the practitioner’s coming into being is to produce goodness in sentient beings.

By engendering doubt and giving rise to reflection, one causes all practices to be perfected—this is what it means to be a person. The question-and-answer section illustrates the identity of teaching.
Because questions are answered, doubt is removed and the teaching arises; thus, question and answer constitute the teaching for the removal of doubt, which serves as the remedy.

To speak briefly of its general purport, the assembly and so forth each possess the "four ones," and it is through this manifestation that the causes for the arising of the "contrary" and "conformable" [teachings] can be established.
If it were otherwise, why would Mahāyāna sūtras not assemble a congregation? Why would they... release?
Light, rain, flowers, and the shaking of the earth occurred; yet, no great doubt arose. Please answer; there is no need for [Maitreya] Subhūti to respond.

When answering a question, one does not cite three identical [precedents]. Although it has not been explicitly stated here, by means of the inquiry arising from doubt and the subsequent response, one will come to know it later.
Thus, prior to the light, rain, and flowers, it was already established that this is certainly extraordinary; and prior to the definitive statement, the assembly did not gather in vain. Although...

Having previously heard the *Anantārtha* (Infinite Meanings), one remains settled and undistracted; knowing that what was heard has not yet been completed, one realizes that concentration arises after the flowers fall upon the ground.
What is taught is not insignificant. By comparing the beginning and the end, one should know that the flowers on the ground are likewise distinct.

Through this hearing of the Dharma, the person of the One Vehicle is manifested; through the manifestation of these omens, the principle of the One Vehicle is revealed. To manifest this principle, [the flowers] arise...
The answers to these doubts demonstrate that the teaching and practice are present herein; human principles are perfectly manifest. Furthermore, from within the auspicious signs:

the preaching of the opening of the sutra represents the harmony of the teaching; entering into meditative concentration represents the harmony of practice; the emission of light represents the harmony of principle; the rain of flowers represents the harmony of the stages;

the shaking of the earth represents the harmony of the removal of delusions. These collectively constitute the perfection of the person, for which there is indeed a profound reason. Thus, it is said in the *Tianbiao* (Heavenly Manifestation): [End of fragment].

First is the Heaven of Meaning (Arthadhatu). This refers to the ground of the true mark (lakṣaṇa), which, although it possesses manifest signs, was beyond the comprehension of the assembly at that time.
Even when they heard the opening of the sutra, they did not yet know that this opening originally signified its convergence; how much less could they have known the fixed principle and so forth?

Therefore, it was only by waiting for Mañjuśrī to lead them there that they finally realized that the path of transformation was no different [from their own]. One must understand that the original purpose of giving rise to doubt was...

Establishing the practice: the practice of resolving doubts is so named because it cites ancient teachings to demonstrate their consistency. Thus one comes to know that the present Buddha is now preaching the single teaching, thereby enabling those in the assembly to become followers of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Only in this way can the present sutra serve as a gradual path toward the ultimate, acting as the initial sprout for the revelation of the truth.
If it were otherwise, to claim in vain that the introduction explains the meaning of the *Lotus Sutra* would ultimately fail to manifest its intent.
This is merely an explanation by way of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Second, regarding the classification according to the teachings (*yāna*): this introduction introduces the main body;

it does not belong to the *piṭaka*, the *tong* (Shared), or the *bie* (Distinct) teachings, but rather to the present Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). For the time being, following the principle of "abolishing the provisional," it says it is not the *piṭaka* and so forth.

First there is abolition and subsequently there is revelation; such is the natural order of principle. Thus, by traversing the teachings and excluding the three [lower ones], one has still not yet reached the One. Once the revelation and manifestation are complete, there is no longer...

This is not a King of Sutras. Third, regarding the analysis in terms of the fundamental and the manifested (*honji* and *jakuji*): if one uses the introduction to elucidate the fourfold "one" of the original ground within the Chapter on the Lifespan, it can also serve as a preliminary indication.
Thus, we know that this introduction explicitly reveals the four aspects of the manifested stage while implicitly revealing the four aspects of the fundamental stage;

for that which was accomplished long ago does not transcend these four. Fourth, regarding the analysis through the contemplation of the mind: since all [aspects] represent the One, the contemplation of principle is easily realized.
I shall now briefly describe them. The three truths within one mind constitute the unity of principle (*li*). The three contemplations within one mind constitute the unity of practice (*xing*).
The person who is able to perform these contemplations constitutes the unity of person (*ren*). The sutras that expound the objects of these contemplations constitute the unity of teaching (*jiao*).

Furthermore, when constantly contemplating the three virtues (*san-de*), both subject and object are fourfold: the *dharmakāya* is principle; the *prajñā* is teaching; and liberation (*vimukti*) is practice.

Furthermore, the harmonious union of these three dharmas constitutes the provisional person, which is precisely the Tathāgata of contemplative practice (*guanxing*). According to the six stages of realization, each stage consists of the "four-in-one";
within every thought-moment, there is the "four-in-one" of every thought-moment. A single form and a single fragrance are none other than the four-in-one.

Contemplative practice such as this is the true *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. When mind and phenomena mutually give rise to one another, this is the contemplation of causes and conditions (*yinyuan guan*).
The fourth [aspect of] the fourfold one is the fourfold one according to the teachings and contemplation (*jiao-guan*).

"Already attained from long ago" refers to the fourfold one according to the original ground (*ben-di*) contemplation. This concludes the general explanation of the five prefaces based on the four teachings.

Next, in the detailed explanation, regarding the first section—gathering the assembly—there are two parts: first, the dignified demeanor (*wei-yi*) of the assembled assembly; second, the offerings (*gong-yang*) presented by the assembled assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly.
This first sentence describes the majestic deportment of the assembled multitude. To say "at that time" (*er shi*) is intended to manifest the moment when the six auspicious omens appeared.

As the ancients said, those who speak of "the time the assembly gathered" do not grasp the essential meaning of the words. Generally, whenever the term "at that time" is used, it refers to the conclusion of a preceding event.

"The beginning of the subsequent matter" refers to the period prior to the manifestation of the six auspicious omens. It indicates the time when the assembly first gathered as he was about to preach the *Anantaparyāya-sūtra*.

If one were to say "when the assembly has gathered," it would be improper to say "the assembly has gathered and they surround [him]," as in the opening of the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*), which points directly to the moment Mañjuśrī has finished answering the questions. It cannot mean that the Buddha has arisen from samādhi.
Phrases such as "at that time" (*tadā*) and "thereupon" (*atha*) all refer to the period following that moment.

If one were to say, "After the assembly had gathered, he then preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*," it would be understood as a specific discussion (*pṛthag-vyākhyāna*), referring to the time when he intended to preach the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.

Generally speaking (*sāmānya-vyākhyāna*), these terms may point to the time before the Buddha had yet definitively set out [to preach]. Initially, the fourfold assembly surrounded him, and flowers rained down.

The earth shook; thus it is said, "At that time, there was rain from the heavens," and so forth. The reason for stating again, "At that time, there was rain from the heavens," is to specifically point to the period following his entry into meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Although this is a minor matter, such instances are indeed numerous; the significance of these events is by no means slight.
Therefore, it is intended to bring about universal cognition. As for the term "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān), this is merely a specific citation of one of the titles of the Transformation Master.
Regarding the "fourfold assembly," some say they are the four consisting of devas, nāgas, and so forth; others say the four consisting of Brahmā, Māra, and so forth.

Although there are such enumerations—including the distinction between great and small, guests and residents, ordinary and holy, those who oppose and those who follow, provisional and real, speech and silence, ancient and modern, subtle and manifest, common and distinct, as well as the combined and the solitary—none of these definitively resolve the fundamental principles of bestowal and opening.
[The previous classification] has no definitive basis. Furthermore, it is said that there are two types each for the ordained and the laity, making four assemblies in total;
this designation is restrictive and its meaning is not comprehensive. Now, our Master further divides each of these four groups—beginning with the ordained—into four sub-categories:

first, the initiator; second, the one who is the primary recipient of the teaching; third, the shadow and echo; and fourth, the one who establishes a karmic connection. By establishing these four categories, [the classification] becomes universal.
These four categories subsume the ten pairs mentioned above; from ordinary beings and sages to their original and manifested forms, each is distinct and without confusion.

As for the arising of these four: although the capacity [of the audience] may be awakened, it must rely on a preliminary guide. Once the guide has awakened that capacity, the "echoes and shadows" (the manifestations) flourish and spread.

Those who possess none of the three benefits are the assembly for planting the seeds of affinity (*karmic connection*). As for the initial initiator, they possess skillful means and wisdom, knowing the capacity and knowing the timing.
To strike, raise, and set in motion, thereby accomplishing benefit—like a great elephant felling a tree so that its young may be satiated—is what is meant by "initiation.
This refers to initiating the assembly, manifesting auspicious signs, and even initiating questions and answers; all such instances are termed "initiating the assembly.
Second, as for those who are "appropriate to the occasion": they have planted roots of virtue in the past, and when conditions converge, their time has ripened, like an abscess ready to burst.

Huì (Huìzong) did not rise from his seat; upon hearing [the teaching], he immediately attained the Way. These are called the "audience who responds to the occasion. Third, the "influential and responsive" (yǐngxiǎng):
the Buddhas of antiquity and the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas conceal their perfect and ultimate nature to assist the Dharma King, like the myriad stars surrounding the moon.
Although they act without deliberate effort, they provide immense benefit. These are called the "influential and responsive audience. Fourth, those who "form karmic connections" (jiéyuán). Form...
This refers to the initial establishment of the capacity for awakening through structural organization; conditions serve as the auxiliary support that enables its final fulfillment.
Thus, it constitutes the first sprout of the three virtues to be cultivated and attained in the future. Power lacks the capacity to guide or stimulate;

virtue lacks the function of subduing objects or imposing solemnity. Furthermore, because past roots were shallow, being shrouded, leaking, defiled, and mixed, the three types of wisdom did not arise in the present.
Although people in the world may see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, if they derive no benefit from the four *siddhāntas*, it merely serves as a causal condition for their future deliverance;

these are called the "assembly for establishing connections. This refers generally to those of the six sense faculties at the five stages (*pañca-vastu*), while specifically it refers to the group of five thousand who rose and departed.
Although they lack the three types of wisdom, the seeds have been received within their consciousness to serve as the conditions for the "tying of the jewel. This is the first assembly: the bhikṣus.

Since this is so, it is the same for the other three assemblies; together they constitute sixteen assemblies. This is analogous to the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, when the princes gave a supplementary exposition;
these were the "assemblies that initiated [the teaching]," excluding those who had already initiated it, as well as the various great bodhisattvas.
The rest were all members of the assembly who were influenced by [the Buddha’s] radiance; upon hearing the Dharma, they attained the Way.

They were precisely those who were suited to the occasion when he heard the Dharma but had not yet been delivered, and thus encountered him life after life until now—some of whom currently abide on the stage of a Śrāvaka. These were the members of the assembly with whom he formed karmic ties during that time.
At the time of that Buddha, there were still sixteen groups of four each; since the path of the Buddhas is the same today, how could it be otherwise? Thus says the Sūtra.

From the perspective of the general conception, one simply speaks of the "four assemblies. If one were to speak directly only of the "four [groups] beginning with the bhikṣus," what is encompassed would not be exhaustive.

This concludes the explanation by way of causes and conditions. These are the sixteen assemblies of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); they may also be understood by analogy with the three other teachings.

Regarding the "original and the trace" (*benji*): for the time being, this is based on essence and function; that is, the original state dwells in the most honored and ultimate, while the trace manifests as the sixteen assemblies. As for the "contemplation of the mind":

Investigating the object and practicing contemplation occurs within the stages of the "name" and "contemplative practice" (nāma-kalpa and prayoga-kalpa), where one immediately forms a karmic connection (*karmabandha*). Upon entering the stage of "semblance" (*pratirūpaka*), one becomes a suitable recipient (*yathābhavyatā*).

In the stage of "partial truth" (*tattva-amśa*), one becomes a catalyst for the "influence" (*prabhāva*) and "response" (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, the stage of partial truth is divided into two further meanings.
If they are those who have entered previously, they are merely termed "echoes and shadows" until, upon hearing the sutra, they transcend and enter the subsequent stage; the intention is likewise so.

If they are those who enter anew, they obtain this as a response to their capacity, and are also "echoes and shadows" as well as "instigators," just like those followers who vowed to propagate the sutra.
Furthermore, the departure of the five thousand [monks] was also for the purpose of forming karmic connections; thus, one knows that it is not exclusive.
The five grades. Now, I shall explain them at leisure based on the contemplative practice (*guanxing*). Furthermore, Master She stated: "Tiantai established the 'echo and shadow' assembly and others;
while there is a doctrinal meaning, there is no textual basis, so they cannot be relied upon as authoritative. One should know that Master She had not fully mastered the scriptural texts.
The Sūtra cites Mañjuśrī and Maitreya; are they not the initiators? The three cycles [of teaching] resulting in the attainment of predictions;

are they not the primary audience (*yathābhavya*)? Aside from the initiators, the other great Bodhisattvas; are they not the supporting witnesses (*pratyaya*)? Aside from the primary audience, those such as Ānanda and others; are they not like the attendants?
Is this not indeed the establishment of a karmic connection? Therefore, that which is listed in the present sutra is precisely its textual expression.

The necessity for the four factors—such as the "initiation" (*pratisthāpana*) and so forth—is its underlying meaning. Since both the text and the meaning are present, they certainly may be relied upon and followed; how much more so in the midst of a diverse assembly!
Although there is no striking or shaking, it can still lead; thus, it is collectively termed "initiation. Although it is not a permanent adornment, it can still provide assistance;
thus, it is collectively termed "influence" (*chāyā*) and "echo" (*pratiśrutkā*). That the eight classes of beings rejoice is precisely what accords with their capacities (*tatkālīna-yoga*).

Hearing this so that they may reach maturity is precisely the formation of a karmic connection (*kṣaṇa-bandhana*). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "He manifests his body within the five realms of existence," and by extension, that which he leads [others to]. (4)

Regarding the *Arthavargīya* [verses], those who claim there are no extant texts have failed to reach a profound understanding; a detailed refutation of this is found in my commentary (*ṭīkā*), so it is not recounted here in full.
As for the term "surrounding" (*parivāra*): when the Buddha first appeared in the world, people did not yet know the Dharma. A being from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven descended and manifested in human form;

having arrived, he circumambulated [the Buddha] to the right, and having circumambulated, he paid homage; having paid homage, he withdrew to sit and listen to the Dharma. It was due to this reverence shown by the deva that [the practice arose].
People take this as a model; these are the four *siddhāntas* (causes and conditions). Furthermore, "circumambulating" refers to the majestic deportment of walking in circles.

This symbolizes that when the mechanisms of the four gates are activated, one perceives the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna*). By contrasting the perfect with the partial, and by looking back at the past and present, the meanings of the four teachings are complete.
At the time of the *Anantārthika-sūtra*, it was still partial and small; only from the perspective of the ultimate meaning of the perfect now can it be considered great.

This refers to "mobility. Regarding the "original and the trace": the original is the Dharma-body, which neither moves nor is immobile; the trace is the manifestation of various teachings wherein sentient beings with differing capacities move about and circumambulate the Buddha.

Furthermore, observing the Buddha’s body, adorned with its surrounding marks and signs, and gazing up at it from all four directions to increase the concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha—this is the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind.
"Making offerings, revering, honoring, and praising.
Second, regarding the assembly gathering to make offerings: in general terms, all three types of action constitute making offerings.
In specific terms, humble and respectful prostration is called "reverence"; focused and attentive mindfulness is called "honor"; and speaking words of praise is called "praising."
[He] sighed. To bestow that upon which one relies is called "making offerings. The text here is abbreviated;
a full exposition should be as extensively explained in the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (Wúliàngyì jīng). The celestial kitchens, celestial incense, celestial bowls, and so forth, constitute "offerings.
The Great Ornament Bodhisattva (*Mahāvyūha*) and the eighty thousand great beings, with palms joined and hands crossed, constitute "reverence. To gaze up with a single mind constitutes...
This is the "Veneration. It refers to the recitation of seven-syllable verses, which constitutes praise. Regarding the current discussion on the assembly, the reference to that text is as follows:

after the assembly had gathered and the preaching of the Dharma was concluded, they remained solemnly without dispersing; he immediately entered that meditative concentration and at that time emitted light.
The heavens then rained down flowers, and the earth immediately shook in six ways. When the assembly witnessed this, they conceived doubts;
yet, despite the delay caused by questions and answers, he continued to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* from that very seat. Thus we know that the offerings of the three karmas must not differ.
Using that [detailed account] to explain this [concise one] is without fault in meaning. This concludes the explanation of the introductory section on the initial gathering of the assembly.

△ From here below, the second section, from "for the sake of all bodhisattvas" up to "the arising of stupas made of the seven treasures," constitutes the introduction concerning the manifestation of auspicious signs.
This also has two parts: first, the six auspicious signs of this land; second, the elucidation of the six auspicious signs of other lands.

Regarding the first, the six auspicious signs of this land, they consist of three pairs: namely, wisdom and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), cause and effect, and response and resonance. This is first explained in general: as for wisdom—
Pointing to one, he speaks of many. As for certainty, it consists of the objects of the truths; as for causes, they are the celestial flowers of the four stages;

as for fruits, they are the six sense bases and the shaking of the earth; as for stimulus, it is the arousal of the Mahāyāna capacity; and as for response, it is the illumination by the circular hair-tuft.

Furthermore, among these six, with the exception of the preaching of the Dharma, the remaining five occur simultaneously. Although there are differences and similarities, they collectively manifest a single principle. Yet, regarding these six...

Among these, although the first two and the latter two are intended for the assembly of that specific time, the middle two serve as the primary manifestation because they pertain precisely to cause and effect.
Thus, the flowers manifest the true cause, while the earth simultaneously represents a portion of the fruit. This exposition is provisional and manifest, following the majority;

it is definitive and intentional, following the locus where the capacity for the Perfect Teaching is about to be awakened, and the Perfect Response illuminates this accordingly. Therefore, one should know that the six auspicious omens are each distinct.

[This appears in] various sutras. Now, as for why these six are all termed "auspicious signs" (*śakuna*): the text states, "The present signs are like the original auspicious omens. An "omen" (*śakuna*) is simply a "sign" (*nimitta*).
If one were to distinguish them: that which provides a secret report is the omen; that which is extraordinary and marvelous is the sign.

What does the sign report? The subtle principle is profound and mysterious; it is exceedingly difficult to explain. Human sentiments are indifferent and unable to show reverence. First, [one must address this]...

The "extraordinary" (*i*) refers to the transformation that startles ordinary sentiment. Since ordinary sentiment is thus transformed, a sense of reverence and longing arises; therefore, "extraordinary" explains the "characteristics" (*xiang*), while "retribution" (*bao*) explains the "omens" (*rui*).

Furthermore, one should briefly clarify the six omens, which represent the retribution of the ten kinds of wondrousness (*shimiao*): the omen of preaching the Dharma represents the retribution of the wondrousness of teaching and the wondrousness of wisdom;
the omen of entering meditative concentration represents the retribution of the wondrousness of practice; and the omen of the rain of flowers represents the retribution of the [wondrousness of] rank.

The auspicious sign of the wondrous ground represents the wondrousness of the object (境界) and the wondrousness of the wondrous vehicle (妙乘). The auspicious sign of the joy of the multitude represents the wondrousness of the retinue (眷屬) and the wondrousness of the benefit (利益).

The auspicious sign of the emission of light represents the wondrousness of the response and resonance (感應) and the wondrousness of supernatural power (神通). One should know that these six auspicious signs represent the ten wondrousnesses;
they are collectively termed the "Preface of Manifesting Signs" (現相序). Furthermore, if these six signs were expanded, they would represent immeasurable wondrous dharmas. As for their locations:

In the middle [classification], there are ten; at the ultimate level of abbreviation, there is one, which expresses only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The details regarding the opening and closing of the original and the manifested (*honjaku*) are fully contained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
Since ancient times, various masters have entirely lacked this insight, which has caused those such as Guanding and others to vainly harbor doubts and offer empty responses.

If its appearance were merely like that of a dazzling spectacle for the assembly, how would it differ from a refined spirit or a non-Buddhist practitioner? Therefore, when our Master now explains these auspicious omens, they must certainly signify something profound.
Thus, this Great Matter and the Great Man produce a great stirring; those with great capacity obtain great benefit, and the Great Principle is revealed.
It requires a great retinue to assist the Great Assembly, so that all may be moved by the Great Time, as the Great Destiny reaches maturity. This could not have been otherwise.

We received the same instruction together on Vulture Peak; in this world, we have inherited it from him. How could we possibly harmonize with it? How could there be anyone who fathoms it? The general explanation of the headings is now complete.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Teaching of Infinite Meanings*, the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, which is protected and remembered by the Buddhas.
This initial teaching of the Dharma pertains to wisdom (*jñāna*). It possesses four meanings. First, to clarify the essence of the Dharma being taught:

this refers to the preaching of Mahāyāna sūtras. Regarding the term "Mahāyāna," the *Śīla-sūtra* states that there are seven greatnesses (*mahattva*): first, the greatness of the Dharma (*dharma-mahattva*).
This refers to the twelve divisions [of the canon], such as the Vaipulya and so forth; this is the present "excellence of object. Second is the greatness of mind, which refers to seeking bodhi;
this is the present "excellence of wisdom. Third is the greatness of understanding, which refers to understanding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; these two constitute the present "excellence of wisdom.

Fourth is the greatness of purity, which refers to the purification of the mind through the path of seeing and so forth. Fifth is the greatness of adornment, which refers to adorning oneself with merit and wisdom; this is the present...

1. Greatness of practice (*caryā-mahattva*): This refers to the practice performed throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Although this meaning pertains to the Tripiṭaka, there are distinctions between the "Great" and "Small" vehicles regarding the number [of kalpas].

This is the greatness of the present stage. 2. Greatness of perfection (*pariniṣpatti-mahattva*): This refers to attaining *bodhi* by adorning oneself with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Thus, the three dharmas are now marvelous. The first six constitute the greatness of the cause, while the last one constitutes the greatness of the fruit.

With this great cause and great fruit combined, they form a single Mahāyāna sūtra. This has merely introduced the seven greatnesses to establish the first five marvels within the traces [of the teaching].
Since there must be a fruit for a cause, and an object for a capacity, the former necessarily encompasses the latter; one should understand that these ten dharmas consist of cause and fruit.
The self and others constitute the essence (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma being taught. For the time being, they are identical in name as cause and effect, yet their meanings remain distinct.

By distinguishing between the inclusive and the exclusive, one must carefully discern them according to precedent before it can be termed Mahāyāna. This concludes the clarification of the essence of the Dharma being taught.

Second, the explanation of the specific names applied to that essence: the Sūtra states it is called "Infinite Meanings" (*ananta-artha*). As listed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*, there are seventeen such types, all of which...
Regarding the alternative names for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: "The Teaching of Infinite Meanings" (*Anantārthasamudgata*) is one such alternative name.

Since it is stated that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is an alternative name for "The Teaching of Infinite Meanings," we know that "The Teaching of Infinite Meanings" is likewise an alternative name for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Thus, establishing the title within the "Preface" (序) is logically faultless.
