Having previously explained the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* as the preface to the *Lotus Sūtra*, one now follows the intent of the treatise (*śāstra*) to first explain the alternative names of the *Lotus Sūtra* and then re-enter the wondrous samādhi of the *Lotus*.
If this is so, since it has already been explained previously, why is it stated again here? The answer is that the sūtra mentioned previously is clearly established [as the preface].

Preface. Now, the masters of the textual tradition repeat its name here because they wish to simultaneously rectify both the meaning and the designation; thus, by encompassing both name and meaning, they achieve a dual mastery of the preface and the main body.
To explain the intent of this treatise: the Buddha directly spoke this name and then entered this meditative absorption; therefore, it may rightly serve as the preface.

Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, the titles are all proclaimed at the outset, which does not hinder their status as introductory sections (*nidāna*).
Now, in this sūtra, Mañjuśrī cites ancient Buddhas whose name was also *Ananta-artha* (Infinite Meaning), and it further states that he shall preach the Mahāyāna sūtra named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This, too, is within the introduction; thus, the proclamation of the title is identical to that in the treatise (*śāstra*). Now, according to the commentary on that sūtra, "Ananta... [and so forth].
"Meaning" arises from a single dharma. What is called the "single dharma" is the so-called signlessness (*animitta*). Signlessness is non-sign; this is named the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
From this true mark arise immeasurable dharmas, namely: the two dharmas, the three paths, and the four fruits.
Now, the Master explains this passage: "Signless" (animitta) means the absence of the signs of birth-and-death (saṃsāra). "Non-sign" (animitta) means the absence of the sign of nirvāṇa;
since nirvāṇa itself is non-existent, it is called "non-sign and signless. This directly refers to the Middle Way, the true reality (bhūtatathatā).
Thus, one knows that the "ability to produce" mentioned in that sūtra is no different from the true reality here. The "two dharmas" refer to the sudden and the gradual. "Sudden" means...
In the sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, there are all dharmas. In the gradual teaching—namely, the Tripiṭaka, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā—there are likewise all dharmas.
The "three paths" refer to the three vehicles (*triyāna*). The "four fruits" refer to the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, the Bodhisattva, and the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Perfect Buddha is that which gives birth, while the other three Buddhas are those who are born; these are also termed the four fruits. All such dharmas are called "immeasurable."

The true nature (*dharmatā*) is the locus of meaning (*artha-sthāna*). From this single locus of meaning, immeasurable dharmas emerge; thus, the attainment of immeasurable dharmas serves as the introduction to their entry into the single locus of meaning.
Consequently, it is able to give rise to the locus of meaning. This is the specific name for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Since the immeasurable [dharmas] that arise constitute the introduction to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the single name within the introduction encompasses both directions. Furthermore, one should know that [the teaching] emerges from the one.
The "Immeasurables" (apramāṇa), although they involve the act of emerging, all generally belong to the introductory section (nirdeśa).

If the "Infinite Entrances" (apramāṇa-praveśa) are subsumed within one, although they pertain to what is produced, they all generally belong to the main body (samyaktva). Therefore, a single dharma as a locus of meaning (artha-sthāna) can also function in two directions:

the locus of meaning regarding emergence belongs to the introduction, while the locus of meaning regarding convergence belongs to the main body. Thus, when the Buddha enters a locus of meaning, his intention encompasses both paths. It is, for example, like...

The mathematician descends from one calculation to all calculations, and eliminates all calculations by returning them to the single calculation. Because he descends, he eliminates; thus, descending constitutes the sequence of elimination.
Furthermore, from one he branches out to all, and gathers all back into one; thus, opening [the manifold] constitutes the sequence of synthesis. It is the same for this [text].
To provide such an interpretation does not contradict those sūtras and śāstras, and it is also consistent with this sūtra. This is speaking according to the intended meaning.
That which is produced is itself the producer; this is merely a different name for the same thing. That which is produced by the producer constitutes the established order.

If one were to focus exclusively on the producer, how would this differ from the various masters such as Sheng (Shengzhi) and the former "One Perfect" (Yiyuan)? If one were to focus exclusively on the produced, [the same confusion would follow].
How does this differ from the commentators and the three teachings of the past? Therefore, each [approach] remains preserved, yet they both result in a dual failure.
Consequently, in our present school, the subject and object follow one another, and both meanings are established together.

If one were to focus solely on the introduction [of the Lotus Sūtra], then prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, not only was it not discussed that many are merged into one, but it was also not taught that one issues forth from the many. Thus, the *Anantamukha-sādhaka*...

I have composed this preface for the present sutra. This meaning has not been understood by the various masters of antiquity. Within my commentary (*shu*), I have extensively refuted the erroneous interpretations of the six schools;
here I shall provide a brief explanation, though the full details are contained in the commentary. This concludes the second section: the specific names of the essence.
Third, the basis upon which those who rely on it depend: as the sutra says, "the teaching for enlightening beings. It employs the locus of immeasurable meanings. By means of...

Because it teaches bodhisattvas, the "locus of meaning" refers to the principle of the Truths (*satya*). This is further explained by means of its alternative names. Teaching bodhisattvas is no different from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
thus, when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara praised the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he said: "The Dharma for teaching bodhisattvas, which is protected and remembered by the Buddhas.
Furthermore, the subsequent text states that it causes all sentient beings to likewise attain this path, and says again: [The Dharma for teaching bodhisattvas...]
"If I encounter sentient beings, I shall teach them all the Buddha-way"—this is precisely that meaning.

"Protected by those who have attained the fruit" refers to the Sūtra’s statement, "protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas. The "Place of Immeasurable Meanings" is what the Buddha himself has realized;
therefore, it is that which the Tathāgata protects with his mindfulness. As the subsequent passage states: "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna. Although he wishes to open [it]...
[The Buddha] manifested that the faculties of sentient beings were dull; having long kept this essential teaching in silence, he did not strive to proclaim it hastily.

Therefore, it is called "protective mindfulness. After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings, his body and mind unmoving.

This clarifies the second auspicious sign of entering meditative concentration. When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meaning, it was because wisdom and concentration mutually accomplish one another.
It is not that there is no wisdom without dhyāna; thus he must first enter concentration. Nor is it that there is no dhyāna without wisdom; therefore he first preached the Dharma.
Thus, he is wisdom while in concentration, and concentration while in wisdom. Whether entering or emerging, whether preceding or following, there is no obstruction between them. Furthermore:

Regarding the sequence of the ritual: there is currently a distinction between before and after. Since the Buddha occupies the supreme position, there can be no such sequence. This concerns the very nature of his embodiment.

If he had not yet expounded the *Anantārtha* (Infinite Meanings), it would be possible for him to enter this samādhi; but having already finished preaching this sūtra, for what reason does he enter samādhi? Answer:
It would be understandable if he were to enter this samādhi first and then preach this sūtra later; however, having finished preaching this sūtra, he further...
"Entering" refers merely to the introduction to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Why? Because if one does not first open [the way], there will be nothing with which to harmonize later.
Entering into the fixed state of opening serves as the introduction for the fixed state of harmony; it is called a "portentous sign.

Since the meaning within this entry into concentration encompasses two intentions, although the intentions are two, the assembly at that time saw only [the Buddha] entering concentration immediately after [expounding] the *Anantaparyāya*.

Not knowing what kind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) he had entered, nor what teaching he would expound after that concentration, the compilers further conformed to the Buddha’s intent and, when recording the sūtras he taught, simply stated "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*). When recording the concentration he entered, they added the specific location.
If one follows the meaning of the location, it serves to clarify the introductory intent by emerging from the immeasurable; if one includes the immeasurable, it...
Entering the *Arthavistara* [Samādhi]. The true lineage was secretly established; although the *Arthavistara* was added, the assembly remained unaware.

Had it been presented in sequential order—first entering the *Anantārthavistara Samādhi* and then entering the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Samādhi*—the assembly would have known it clearly and manifestly at that time.
Why wait for Maitreya’s earnestness and Mañjuśrī’s firm exhortation? Thus we know it was composed...
Preface. Its meaning becomes increasingly clear. As for "the body and mind being unmoving," this refers to being in accord with the object of focus (*ālambana*).
The fundamental source of the body is as profound and still as empty space; the nature and principle of the mind are ultimately and eternally quiescent.
Therefore, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū’s body, along with his hands and feet, was tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving; his mind was constantly serene and composed, never having experienced agitation.
Though distracted, the body is like a vajra, incapable of being moved; the mind is like space, free from discrimination.
Because the dharma of the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings sustains both body and mind, they do not move.
It is called "immeasurable" because this samādhi is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, able to know the world; from this single dharma, it brings forth immeasurable dharmas.
Furthermore, as for the one who composes the preface: the nature of the body is movement and activity, yet here it is made non-moving and non-active;

the nature of the mind is discrimination, yet here it is made non-discriminative. The meaning of the preface is thus clear. Question: The auspicious signs (praśasti-lakṣaṇa) in the original treatise are extraordinary and marvelous phenomena.
Question: Preaching the Dharma and entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is the constant practice of the Buddha; how can this be considered an auspicious omen? Answer:

Although the preaching of the Dharma was concluded, the assembly did not disperse; they remained solemn and expectant. Thus, while the previous preaching of the Dharma had brought the entire multitude together, they waited for the subsequent teaching.
This matter is extraordinary and differs from ordinary preaching; for what reason would it not be an auspicious omen? Although he entered the *samādhi* of manifestation, his intention—
Regarding the entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it differs from ordinary entry into concentration. For what reason is this not considered a portentous sign (*nimitta*)?
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī cites the six portents of the ancient Buddhas, all of which included this event. If it were not a portent in the past, how could it serve as proof for the present?
Since the principle is the same for both past and present, the ancients did not establish the teaching of concentration as a portent. This is beyond the scope of ordinary human comprehension. This...
The section on the pair of the first knowledge and concentration is concluded.
At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers,
and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
This is the second pair of cause and effect. First, it clarifies the auspicious omen of the raining of flowers; this symbolizes the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
If, within the Tripiṭaka, the cause refers to the cause of the Two Vehicles; in the Shared [Teaching], the cause refers to the common cause;

and in the Distinct [Teaching], the cause refers to the cause of the Bodhisattvas—none of these represent the cause for the Buddha of the Perfect Vehicle as manifested in this sutra. Now, the heavens rain flowers as a retribution.

That which is to be attained is the cause for Buddhahood; the cause for Buddhahood is precisely the cause of the four wheels. The small white [circle] represents the copper wheel of the *śikṣā-bhūmi* (Stage of Cultivation), wherein the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The large white [circle] represents the silver wheel of the *gotra-bhūmi* (Stage of Nature), wherein the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The small red [circle] represents the gold wheel of the *mārga-bhūmi* (Stage of the Path), wherein the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, the great red [lotus] represents the lapis lazuli wheel and the noble lineage (*āryagotra*), signifying entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
All four wheels share this same cause; since this cause arises from the center, it falls as rain from the heavens.

Because it exists within the state of the cause, it is symbolized by the flower. Yet, because the cause possesses the meaning of proceeding toward the fruit, the flower is scattered upon the Buddha. Thus it is.
As for cause and effect, who is it that experiences them? It is none other than the assembly gathered here; therefore, it says, "and the great multitude.

In the subsequent section, Mañjuśrī resolves doubts through the four phrases beginning with "blowing the great Dharma conch. Furthermore, within the formal exposition, there are the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering;
and in the parable of the great carriage, there is the passage on "wandering in the four directions. These successive sections are all of the nature of spiritual stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore...

"Knowing the flower-pillar" refers to the stage of causal practice (*hetu-bhūmi*). Question: The four wheels represent the meaning of distinct stages; how can they be used to explain the present stage of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*)? Answer:
When the name is general but the meaning is perfect, there is still nothing lost; how much more so when the name is distinct but the meaning is perfect—how could it not be applicable?
To manifest the perfect by borrowing from the distinct is as explained in detail in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation).
The worlds of all Buddhas tremble in six ways;
this is the second earthquake, which signifies the meaning of the fruit (*phala*). Both the ultimate fruit and the partial fruit may be termed "fruit.

Since both the beginning and the end are presented together, these six tremblings signify the fruit. As for the term "universal" (*prabhūta*), it refers to the three aspects of the trembling being pervasive, equal, and so forth. Thus.

It is named "Universal. Regarding the "six movements," they refer to: moving, rising, surging, shaking, roaring, and awakening. To sway and flutter restlessly is called "moving. To rise from below upward is called "rising.
To have ridges and hollows, elevations and depressions, is called "surging"; likewise, the appearance and disappearance across the six directions is also termed "surging.
To have a deep, rumbling sound is called "shaking. To emit a crashing and thunderous resonance is called "roaring. These cause all things to awaken.
This is called "Awakening. When the sutra mentions merely "shaking," it designates one [aspect] each from among the three categories of form, sound, and both.

Now, this represents the sixfold destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*) within the Perfect Teaching—namely, the six stages of abiding, practice, direction, the grounds, and so forth, up to the Subtle and Wondrous.

While the vast expanse of ignorance has never yet been invaded or destroyed, the capacities of the fourfold assembly are now about to be shattered; therefore, the earth shakes to signify this. Ignorance...
If it were to transform, it would immediately change into light; thus, throughout all Buddha-worlds, there are the six kinds of earth tremors.
This is the explanation according to the teachings (*yōkyō*). As for the causal conditions (*innen*), the *Upāsaka-śīla-viśuddhi-sūtra* states:

"When the Bodhisattva was born, the earth shook to demonstrate that his birth had already exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*). For all sentient beings who are destined to attain the Way, their afflictions..."

"It moves because it is about to be extinguished"—this is precisely that meaning. As for the "original" (hon) and the "traced" (ji), it is as when Mañjuśrī resolved his doubts by citing ancient Buddhas in response;
one who secretly grasps this intent is one who recognizes the original. It does not mean that other Buddhas manifested such auspicious signs in the past.
Yet my World-Honored One was originally endowed with this same auspicious sign; it is not merely a singular occurrence now.

If we interpret this according to the present text from the perspective of contemplative understanding, it refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). The characteristic of the earth being firm and solid represents the six faculties' state of frozen attachment, having never yet entered the path of the Mahāyāna.
The shaking of this "ground" that is difficult to move symbolizes the faculties—both pure and impure—that are about to shatter ignorance. Therefore...
This is manifested through movement. This is simply an explanation of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Furthermore, as stated in such scriptures as the *Antarābhava-sūtra*:

"Rising in the east and sinking in the west"—the east is blue and presides over the liver; the liver presides over the eyes. The west is white and presides over the lungs; the lungs preside over the nose.

Thus, the rising in the east signifies the arising of the merit of the eye faculty, while the sinking in the west signifies the mutual cessation of the afflictions of the nose faculty and the arising of the merit of the nose faculty.
When born, the afflictions of the eyes mutually cease. Since the eyes and nose manifest toward the east and west, it follows by principle that the ears and tongue correspond to the south and north.
The mind is the center; as the four directions are like the body, and the body possesses the four sense organs, so the mind universally takes the four as its objects.

Therefore, the mind is paired with the body to form the phenomena of surging and submergence—namely, surging in the center while the periphery subsides, or surging at the periphery while the center subsides. Thus, the six sense organs are paired [with their objects].
The "objects such as blue" refers to the contemplation of the twelve *āyatanas*. Furthermore, regarding the "six types of movement," within each single movement there are three kinds:

direct movement (*ṛju-kampana*), pervasive movement (*sarvatra-kampana*), and universal pervasive movement (*samanta-sarvatra-kampana*). Direct movement constitutes "movement"; the shaking of the four continents is called "pervasive movement";
and the shaking of the great trichiliocosm is called "universal pervasive movement. The same applies to the remaining five [types of movement]. Altogether, these constitute eighteen varieties.
"Movement" refers to the contemplation of the eighteen *dhātus*, which all serve to shatter ignorance.

First, it is applied to the six sense-faculties (*indriya*); next, to the twelve bases (*āyatana*); and finally, to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). These three—aggregates (*skandha*), bases, and realms—are used to contemplate the eternally abiding [nature].

This is merely a brief preservation of the numerical designations; the specific characteristics of the objects of contemplation they represent are omitted. One should know that each and every faculty is thus cultivated.
The three contemplations are like the eighteen movements; herein, we consider only the characteristics of that which moves. As for the ground moved, it is but a single ground.
Just as although there are six faculties, by means of the mind they are all sublated, so too are all [the other grounds] sublated.
At that time, the great assembly in the gathering— the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas,
yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as the various minor kings and universal monarchs—
attained what they had never experienced before. With joy, they joined their palms and focused their minds with single-minded devotion.
Contemplating the Buddha:
This is the first part clarifying the "responsive stimulus" (*ki-kan*) within the third pair of "stimulus and response. Now, regarding the auspicious signs that gladden the great assembly:

when the multitude sees the rain of flowers and the trembling of the earth, they know that the nectar of the Dharma is about to descend; their hearts are filled with exultation, manifesting the Great [Vehicle].

The occasion for its manifestation has arrived; it is thus that it responds to the supreme response-body (*sambhogakāya*). Question: Joy and anger are the common emotions of human beings. How can they constitute an auspicious omen (*praśasta-nimitta*)? Answer:
Celestial flowers delight the eyes, and the trembling of the earth shakes the mind. A Great Sūtra states: "When there is movement, it can cause the minds of sentient beings to move.
Thus, flowers and the earth are external omens, while mental joy is the internal omen. Therefore, extraordinary joy constitutes such an auspicious sign.
How can one know that this is not extraordinary? Yet, in the past within the teachings, have we not seen such signs as the rain of flowers?
Although these occurred before, you were not moved by joy. Furthermore, you were able to contemplate the Buddha with a single mind;

thus it is known that your exultation was beyond the ordinary, and so you obtained this auspicious omen. If your joy had merely moved the mundane mind (*skandha-citta*), it would have been the experience of humans and devas. If...

That "rejoicing and moving" refers to the true reality (tattva) and the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is the meaning of the *Tripiṭaka* and *Vaipulya* [teachings]. If "rejoicing and moving" refers to the provisional mind, this is the meaning of the *Pratyekabuddha* [teaching].

That "rejoicing and moving" refers to the mind of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]. Question: Since the true principle is without movement, why do you now speak of "movement"? Answer: "Movement" means "arising.
When the perfect capacity (*tīkṣṇendriya*) is about to be fulfilled, it is called "moving the mind of the true mark. This is because [the response] accords with those such as devas and humans.
"Movement," because it is directed toward the ultimate reality.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated the eastern direction until it was completely pervaded; this may also be understood as a general auspicious omen for other lands.
It illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception.
This is the third section on the "Duality of Response and Induction," wherein the Sage’s response is now clarified.

The Buddha’s emission of radiant omens signifies his establishing of teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings (*yǐ jī* 應機), thereby shattering delusions and removing doubts. However, this single passage may be analyzed in terms of its progressive and regressive aspects.

Since this passage encompasses both perspectives, its literary structure also contains both brevity and length. If one takes the shorter version, it begins from "At that time" and concludes with "pervading everywhere";
these all belong to the sixth auspicious sign of this land. If one takes the longer version, it must extend as far as the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
For now, the text is judged according to the shorter version. Alternatively, it may also begin from "shining upon the eastern direction" and continue down to...
The *Ṭa* Heaven. This half-verse from the sixth auspicious sign of this land serves as the general auspicious sign for other lands;

if it is taken as a general sign for others, one should understand that there are likewise variations in length according to the context. These manifested signs must be interpreted by means of the four methods of explanation (*catuḥ-nirukti*).

Regarding the explanation based on initial causes and conditions: the *ūrṇā* (white tuft of hair) is endowed with various merits. The *Sūtra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha* states:
"When the Buddha was first born, the *ūrṇā* was five feet long; during his period of ascetic practice, it was one zhang and four feet long;
upon attaining Buddhahood, it was one zhang and five feet long. This refers to the world-system. The interior and exterior of this *ūrṇā* are both empty, like white lapis lazuli.

The hair-tuft (*ūrṇā*) is pure both inside and out. From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, through the various practices performed in the interim, and all manner of manifestations up until the entry into *nirvāṇa*—all these merits are manifested within the hair-tuft.
This hair-tuft is situated between the two eyebrows, which symbolizes the permanence of the Middle Way.
Its soft and supple appearance symbolizes bliss; its ability to contract and expand with mastery symbolizes the self; and its whiteness symbolizes...
"Purity" refers here to the person. "Emitting light to destroy darkness" symbolizes the arising of wisdom through the Middle Way; this refers to the application of antidotes.
"Light illuminating this land and other lands" symbolizes self-awakening and awakening others; this refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Next, regarding the teaching:
although the two vehicles of the two teachings have realized the two truths, they do not know the Middle Way—this is like having two eyebrows [but no nose].
Yet it lacks the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa). Although the Separate Teaching (biejiao) knows the three truths, it cannot contain all dharmas within that tuft.
One should know that from the beginning to the end, the fact that all matters within the dharma-realm manifest within the tuft expresses the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
Furthermore, speaking in terms of partiality, these matters of the tuft here exist only in the ultimate sense. This concludes the explanation of the white tuft. Next—
Regarding the "Emanator of Light," various sutras explain the emission of light differently.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, light is emitted from each of the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of the feet up to the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head, with sixty trillion rays of light emanating from each; this is explained in detail therein.

By means of the wheel of the body, it symbolizes the pervasiveness of Prajñā. In the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*, light is emitted from the "gate of the face," which refers to the mouth; this symbolizes the Buddha’s...

The "oral secrecy" refers to the preaching of the secret treasury. In this sutra, the radiance emitted from the white tuft between the eyebrows during meditative concentration symbolizes the wheel of intention (*manas-cakra*).

Although the conditions and objects of these [three wheels] differ and the capacities and visions of beings are unequal, each one fully possesses the benefits of the three secrets and the four *siddhi*s (purposes).

Though the Buddha has throughout his entire career employed the three wheels to manifest his transformation, for every specific occasion, there is no benefit that surpasses that of the verbal teaching (*vāg-cakra*).
At the moment of his passing, light radiated from the face, signifying that these teachings would flow into future generations. For now, this is a general discussion of the emission of light;
if discussed specifically, according to various texts, it does not illuminate the formless realms, a principle identical to that regarding the gathering of the assembly.
Furthermore, there is a difference in how the light is withdrawn. The *Śātavāhana-rāja-sūtra* states: "If it is to recount past events, the light is withdrawn from the back;

if it is to prophesy future events, it is withdrawn from the front. It does not mention the recording of present events. Zhiyan (Zhang’an) says: [The light is withdrawn from the navel to record the present.]

If [the light] enters through the side, one should predict events of the present life. The Sūtra further states: if it enters through the feet, one predicts rebirth in hell; if through the ankles, one predicts rebirth as an animal;

if through the toes, one predicts rebirth as a hungry ghost; if through the knees, one predicts rebirth as a human; if through the left palm, one predicts becoming an Iron-Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*);

if through the right palm, one predicts becoming a Gold-Wheel-Turning King, as well as rebirth among the various devas; if it enters through the navel, one predicts the stage of a Śrāvaka; if it enters through the mouth, one predicts the stage of a Pratyekabuddha.

The *Jue* (Awakening) [Sutra] mentions the prediction through the entry of the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*), while the *Rouji* (Flesh Topknot) [Sutra] mentions the prediction through the entry of the flesh topknot (*uṣṇīṣa*).

Now, although this sutra emits light from the white tuft, the text regarding the retraction of that light is omitted. If the Buddha were to definitively arise in this sutra, he would certainly retract the light;

and if he were to retract it, it would necessarily be through the flesh topknot. Furthermore, it is said: "Emitting light illuminates present events; retracting the light illuminates future events. This sutra is precisely [concerned with the latter].
This treatise argues that the path of the Buddhas in this land and other lands is identical; therefore, it correctly discusses the emission of light.

If one understands that the paths of all Buddhas are identical, then through the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, one spontaneously receives the prediction of enlightenment. Thus, the emission of light is primary, while the reabsorption of light is secondary.
Therefore, it is omitted and not discussed here. This is according to the meaning of the *nidāna* (causal conditions), which concerns the emission of light by the [Śākyamuni] Buddha of six feet.

If it were the Buddha of six feet emitting light, that would be the meaning of the Tripiṭaka. If it were the Honored One of Extraordinary Marks (*vairocana*) together with the Buddha of six feet emitting light, that would be the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*p’ung*).
If it is the Honored One as a *viśvabuddha* (a solitary, transcendent Buddha) who alone emits light, this is the "distinctive" meaning.
If it is the sixteen-foot Buddha, that is, the Dharma-body of Vairocana, who emits light, this is the "perfect" meaning. As for what is called "emitting":
first, if one does not exercise restraint, it illuminates only the great trichiliocosm; second, if one intentionally activates it, it illuminates eighteen thousand worlds. This is the Tathāgata’s...
To act after deliberation is to manifest something. Since the East is the beginning of the directions, it manifests that the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) are the beginning of the stages.

Therefore, when the Dharma is preached in the Trace Gate (*jiamen*), Bodhisattvas in their birth-bodies (*janmakāya*) clearly perceive the principle and enter the Ten Abodes, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
By citing the beginning, one immediately knows the middle and the end; thus, there is nothing that is not universally encompassed. One should know that this applies to all directions as well.

Likewise, it is so for all the other honored ones. This is according to the Trace Gate (*jimen*). If one approaches the teaching from the perspective of the Origin Gate (*benmen*), the gathering of the Buddhas from the four directions signifies the preaching of the Dharma in the Origin Gate.
Regarding the *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas, who increase their path and diminish their births, there is an increase through the four stages, up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
As the text states: "Only one more birth remains. If one contemplates this as an interpretation of practice, the number eighteen thousand is based on—
Regarding the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), the treatise discusses the hundred phenomena, the realms, and the thousand natures and characteristics. The text states:

"From the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)—this constitutes the six realms of phenomena. Furthermore, by seeing the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Bhikṣus, and so forth, the ten realms are complete.

It is fully endowed with the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses; therefore, it is said that there is nowhere it does not pervade. These states of being were not yet revealed by the Buddha’s wisdom and remained latent within the eighteen [realms].

Thus, the light shines forth to signify their opening. This "opening" specifically occurs at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), where one opens the Buddha's knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
Therefore, the "ten thousand and eight thousand" signifies that all eighteen realms have been opened. This explains the pair of wisdom and concentration.

[End. From the beginning, starting with the preaching of the Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Ananta-artha* for the sake of the bodhisattvas, until this point, all constitute the first of the six auspicious omens manifested in this land.
△ Below this is the second section, clarifying the six auspicious omens manifested by light illuminating other lands.
These are summarized into three pairs: namely, the superior (sages) and the inferior (ordinary beings); persons and dharmas; and the beginning and the end.
Regarding the arising of these six: since there are sentient beings who can be transformed, there is a Buddha who can transform them;

where there is a Buddha, there is the teaching of the Dharma; where there is the teaching of the Dharma, there are disciples; and disciples are the beginning of practice, which inevitably leads to its completion.
This concludes the explanation of the downward progression. Furthermore, what is indicated here and there is that the path of the two wisdoms is identical. If...

The six auspicious omens of this land collectively report that sentient beings shall attain self-awakening (*svabodhi*). The six auspicious omens of that land collectively report that sentient beings shall attain awakening for others (*parabodhi*).
One should know that although there are six omens, light is their foundation. Light symbolizes awakened wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*);
light illuminates both this and that, signifying the two types of awakening. Furthermore, the six omens of this and that land symbolize these two [types of awakening].

The exposition of the land having been completed, I shall now explain how the paths of all Buddhas are identical. To manifest these three kinds of identity, six auspicious omens appear both here and there.
From the observation that all beings of the six realms in that land—even down to those practicing the bodhisattva path—are visible here, it is shown that the land is identical to this one.
From the passage "furthermore, they see the various Buddhas" down to "the stupa made of the seven treasures," [it is shown that the Buddhas and their teachings are likewise identical].
This means that this land being manifested here shall be identical to that land. The *Lotus Sūtra* is now likewise hidden and not yet revealed;
it merely constitutes two types of identity. Why is its present identity concealed? Answer:

If, within the light that is manifested, one were to see the *Lotus Sūtra* bestowing predictions upon the śrāvakas and proclaiming their long lifespans, then the Tathāgata would have nothing further to do below, as his transformation [work] would already be complete.

The ritual requirements were not fulfilled. Even if they had seen him receive the prediction of a relatively long lifespan, this assembly would still have harbored doubts as to whether the śrāvakas of this land would also receive predictions;
furthermore, even if they had seen him emerge from the earth, they would still have been uncertain as to what his lifespan might be.

Since these matters remained unknown, [the Buddha] concealed them all. Because they were concealed and not yet revealed, Maitreya gave rise to questions, which Mañjuśrī answered at length. [This is] complete.

The three similarities are described: the various capacities [of sentient beings] generally understand the characteristics following meditative concentration; thus, it is known that the general introduction (sūtra-prologue) is explained as being universal.
That it accords with the specific principle is due to the fourfold interpretation. That the specific introduction (verse-prologue) is distinct yet its meaning is subtle is due to the five periods.
Therefore, when the response to the matter is just concluded and meditative concentration arises, the matter here accords with the response, and only then is the text revealed.
This is the ultimate vision. This has merely briefly indicated the meaning of the auspicious signs in other lands.
From the Avīci Hell below up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above, within this world, one sees all the sentient beings of the six destinies in those lands.

This is the first vision of the auspicious signs regarding the six realms of existence in that land. Question: Seeing those six realms and so forth—why are these called "auspicious signs" (śakuna)? Answer:

Beginning with the vision of the six realms and ending with the vision of nirvāṇa, the teachings established during the five periods in that land are all instantaneously present within the light of Śākyamuni.
If what is seen is not an auspicious sign, what else could it be? Furthermore, seeing the sentient beings of the six realms is a manifestation of that [land].

The Buddha appears in the world for the sake of the five turbidities; this Buddha is likewise so. The intent of his appearance in these two lands is identical because both are characterized by the five turbidities;
therefore, his giving and other virtues are no different. This is the first instance concerning those of inferior capacity.
Furthermore, one sees the Buddhas currently residing in that land.

This vision of those second-order emanated Buddhas is an auspicious sign; it indicates that there are sentient beings with the capacity to be transformed (the "transformable") present before them, while this passage clarifies the Buddhas who perform the transformation (the "transformers").
This vision represents one member of the pair known as the "Noble One Above and the Ordinary Being Below," so it is named accordingly.
"And hearing the sutras and teachings spoken by the various Buddhas.
This clarifies the second [category], that of the person and the dharma being both middling. First, it clarifies hearing the Buddha's preaching of the Dharma;

this is the third auspicious sign in that land. This refers to seeing that Buddha initially [teach] from the single dharma of formlessness; it is not gradual, yet it is sudden, and is identical to this [land].

The intent of the *Avataṃsaka* as first taught on the Earth Stage is the same [as that of the *Lotus Sūtra*]. However, by the time one reaches the subsequent verses (*geya*), the meaning of the scripture becomes even more explicit.
One should know that the One Vehicle of the *Lotus Sūtra* is not subsumed under either the sudden or the gradual; rather, it is from within this single opening that the sudden and the gradual arise.
Thus, we know that while the *Avataṃsaka* is not itself the sudden [teaching], its sudden nature is made manifest.
Furthermore, one sees those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—those among the fourfold assembly who have practiced and attained the Way.
This vision of the fourfold assembly attaining the Way is the fourth auspicious sign; it is seeing that Buddha, who is non-gradual yet gradual.
Following the Buddha’s Flower Garland Sūtra (Avataṃsaka) in this land, he next taught the Three Piṭakas; the intent is the same. This is called the pair of persons and dharmas.
Furthermore, he saw the various causes and conditions, various faiths and understandings, and various characteristics of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Practicing the bodhisattva path.
This clarifies the third pair of beginning and end. The initial vision of the bodhisattva’s practice is the fifth auspicious sign.
Following the vision of that Buddha’s Tripiṭaka, he next taught the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, which correspond to the Buddha’s Tripiṭaka in this land.

The meaning is the same as that following the section on the "Treasury" (the *Kṣānti* chapter). Regarding the phrase "various causes and conditions" (*nānā-pratyaya*), there are both general and specific senses.

"Causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) is a synonym for "response and stimulus" (*ganying*), as explained previously. Causes and conditions apply generally to both gradual and sudden [teachings] and pervade all four periods [of the Buddha’s life].

Within these four periods, each possesses its own response and stimulus; in contrast to the present, none of these fail to serve as the causes and conditions for the teachings of the present. If one were to explain them specifically:
Regarding "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): this refers precisely to that which follows the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).

It clarifies that the shared and unshared *prajñā* (wisdom) constitute the cause, while the factors of the path—such as ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—constitute the conditions. In relation to the three types of persons, there are thus various causes and conditions.
Furthermore, concerning the various causes, conditions, and various characteristics of both the shared and unshared persons, each of these has four gates within every teaching.

Regarding the four *siddhāntas*, each gate further possesses immeasurable characteristics; this refers precisely to the meaning of the five hundred bhikṣus each explaining the cause of their own bodies.
It is the same for the four gates that are not shared [with other teachings]. If one discusses how these three arise sequentially from one another:

it is due to the causes and conditions of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*) that there is faith and understanding (*adhimukti*); due to faith and understanding, there is practice (*pratipatti*). Furthermore, to explain them separately:

This separately indicates the three teachings within the Prajñā [Pāramitā], which constitute the practice of Bodhisattvas; this is because they all achieve universal realization while simultaneously attaining distinct benefits in a hidden manner.
Furthermore, "causes and conditions" refers to the distinctions in response and resonance (*ganying*). "Faith and understanding" refers to the differences in the capacity for such resonance.
"Characteristics" refers to the variations in practice following faith. These various differences are all termed "diverse. Although...
Furthermore, although the paths differ, they do not exceed two flavors. Moreover, regarding response and stimulus, their mutual relationship varies in degree of intimacy;

thus, it is called "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya). As for the capacity to stimulate, one internally harbors and receives [the teaching]; thus, it is called "faith and understanding" (śraddhā-adhimukti).

As for cultivation, body and speech manifest externally; thus, it is called "signs and appearances" (lakṣaṇa-nimitta). Furthermore, because these are external physical forms and demeanors, they are called "signs and appearances. One should know that these causes...
The varieties of causal appearances are immeasurable; all of these are the same as this [initial case]. This is the first instance.
Furthermore, one sees various Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa, and again, one sees after the parinirvāṇa of various Buddhas that stupas made of the seven precious gems are erected for their relics.

This concludes the sixth auspicious omen seen in that land. Following the manifestation of that Buddha’s *prajñā*, he reveals the provisional to disclose the ultimate, gathering immeasurable dharmas back into the single dharma.
He proclaims his entry into *nirvāṇa*, ceases his transformative activity, and the construction of stupas begins;
his light shines upon that land, from beginning to end, reaching its ultimate fulfillment, appearing vividly before our eyes. One should know that in this land, [all things] emerge from the One.

As for the measure: it is not sudden yet sudden; it is not gradual yet gradual. Once the task is completed, one must necessarily gather immeasurable dharmas back into a single dharma, opening the provisional to reveal the real, and ceasing the transformation to return to the truth—this is identical to that land.
Although the manifestations and causal characteristics appearing in that land are of various kinds, they all ultimately converge into a single cause and a single condition.

With one and the same appearance and countenance, they all arrive at the Lotus Sūtra, where no further distinctions remain. One should know that what the Buddha of this land speaks upon arising from meditative concentration is identical to that [of the Buddhas of other lands].
Please examine the purport of the sūtras and the words of the Buddha regarding the five-period classification of the teachings.
Is this not to be believed? This concludes the third section on the unity of beginning and end. Question: Within the light, each and every thing is perceived horizontally [simultaneously].
How can it be said that there is first a sudden [realization] followed by a gradual one, and so forth, until their ultimate convergence?

Furthermore, within such perception, could there not be cases that are purely sudden rather than merely gradual? Answer: It is indeed as you have asked. At that time, the assembly only knew the cause...

One is able to see the light; yet the Great Artifice resides within the World-Honored One, and seeing it is not within the realm of ordinary perception. Nevertheless, the intention behind causing one to see is fundamentally for the sake of attaining realization through conformity.
The radiance that is emitted serves to realize the single reality (*ekayāna*). That which is distinct in phenomena and severed from principle is not touched by this light.
Since both the distant and the near are equally enabled to see and hear, how could the past and future be obstructed from sight and hearing? Thus, [the ten directions...]
From beginning to end, it is as clear as if before one's eyes. How can one measure the realm of the Sage with ordinary sentiments?

Why should it be that only the power of the Buddha, the Lord of Transformation, allows one to see it? Among those who heard the teaching together and among those who compiled this scripture at that time, there were Buddhas of antiquity who had concealed their traces therein.

Their wisdom was a mirror of that era, and they recounted these horizontal and vertical [teachings] so as to further cause those who see them to regard the sacred and the mundane as equal. Therefore...
One should know that by relying merely on the sequence of the text, the purport of the sūtra remains perfectly clear.
From the beginning—“He spoke this Mahāyāna sūtra for the sake of the bodhisattvas”—up to this point, the second section, the Preface of Manifesting Omens, is concluded.

Below this, from “At that time, Maitreya had this thought” up to “Whom should I now question? constitutes the third section, the Preface of Doubtful Reflection. This text is divided into two parts; the first is Maitreya’s doubt.
[The Buddha] reflects. Second, the two great assemblies have doubts.
Maitreya has three reflections. At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya had this thought: "Now the World-Honored One manifests signs of supernatural transformation.
By what causes and conditions does such an auspicious omen exist? Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered into samādhi; this is inconceivable and rare."
There is a matter here: this is Maitreya’s initial doubt regarding the six auspicious omens of right mindfulness. To speak of "manifesting the signs of spiritual transformations" (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*):

"spiritual" (*ṛddhi*) refers to the internal, while "transformation" (*vikurvaṇa*) refers to the external; because the internal and external differ, hearing and seeing them brings joy. This is the "world-encompassing" (*loka-saṃvṛti*) perspective. Furthermore, "spiritual" (*ṛddhi*) is a name for...

"The Mind of Heaven" (*tiānxīn*) refers to the innate internal wisdom (*nèhuì*). "Transformation" (*biàn*) refers to the manifestation of the six auspicious omens (*liùshuì*), whereby beings perceive them and give rise to goodness;

this is the "all-encompassing" (*xì*) for the sake of humans. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The Buddha abides in the non-dual dharma and is able to manifest spiritual powers (*śentōng*) to universally harmonize all things";
this is the "all-encompassing" (*xì*) for the purpose of remedial treatment (*duìzhì*). The power of the Dharma King transcends and covers all things. It is pervasive.

Kāśyapa could not fathom external transformations, nor did he know internal wisdom; therefore, there was none superior to him. This is the meaning of the "all-encompassing ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-sarva-jñatā*) based on these causes and conditions.

Now, as for those of mediocre capacity who do not know the arts, those of distracted mind who do not know meditative concentration, ordinary people who do not know the sages, lesser sages who do not know Śāriputra, Śāriputra who does not know the Bodhisattvas, and the Bodhisattvas...

The one in the position of succession does not know [the ultimate], and the one in the position of succession does not know the supreme honor. This refers to the ultimate state; in reality, those in the true rank do not know this.

This is according to the meaning of the teaching (*śāsana*). Furthermore, since Maitreya has encountered Buddhas and planted many roots of goodness, how could he possibly fail to have a general understanding?

It must be that he conceals what is manifest and reveals what is obscure, speaking of "not knowing" as a provisional means (*upāya*). This is according to the meaning of the provisional; this is the distinction between the original and the trace.
If one contemplates the mind, wisdom’s illumination is numinous and penetrating; the six sense faculties immediately manifest in accordance with the mind—this is precisely contemplating the mind.
One should then ask: "Who is it? Who is able to answer?
This was his second thought: "Whom should I ask about this doubt?
He further thought: "This is Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, who has already drawn near to and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past;
he must surely have seen these rare and marvelous signs. I shall now question him."
This is the third thought of Mañjuśrī. When the second thought arises, the first is eliminated. Since one has already attained the person [of Mañjuśrī], what need is there to think of him again?
Therefore, at that time, the third thought also ceases. Upon reaching the subsequent inquiry, only the initial thought remains;
thus, it results in but a single doubt. Question: The sutra refers to Mañjuśrī as a "Dharma Prince" (dharmarāja-putra). Regarding these various bodhisattvas...
"Who is there that is not a son of the Dharma King? He replied: "For two reasons: first, among the sons of the prince, Mañjuśrī is preeminent in virtue;
second, in various sūtras, Mañjuśrī is consistently ranked as the leader of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Thus ended Maitreya’s inquiry.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and others, all had this thought:
"This is the mark of the Buddha’s radiance and supernormal power."
Within this second section on the doubts of the great assembly, the first [part] correctly identifies the six auspicious omens.
Now, one must ask:
"Whom does this second thought refer to? The great assembly has only these two thoughts. If one looks ahead to the following verse:
This also possesses three thoughts. As the following verse says: "The fourfold assembly looks up with joy, gazing upon you and me.

If the third thought—Mañjuśrī—did not exist, why would it say "gazing upon you"? Yet he is absent from this context because [the author] intends to prioritize the one who occupies the position of the Successor (Upapadya).
There are three reasons for this priority: first, he is the Successor; second, he possesses the three thoughts; and third, he is capable of inspiring [others].
Question: For this reason, the great assembly lacks even a single thought-moment [of certainty]. Question: Mañjuśrī and Maitreya are equal in their virtue and rank;
why is there one question and one answer? Answer: This should be understood through four explanations. Generally, the capacity for awakening (the *ki*) may exist or not exist.
Although their ranks are equal, the proprieties of guest and host differ. The Sage responds to the capacity; it is impossible for one who does not ask to provide the answer.
Furthermore, as with Mañjuśrī, although he was deemed capable of inquiring after the illness, he was still rebuked by Vimaladattā; thus it is said that [the inquiry] "resides in non-existence.

This is because of the four *siddhārtha* (purposes) and their respective conditions. Moreover, among the Dharma-gates there are the provisional and the real: the provisional requires inquiry, while the real requires response.

Furthermore, regarding traces, there are those that are long-standing and those that are recent: the recent is asked about, while the long-standing is answered. Additionally, names have their own appropriateness.

This is easy to understand. Maitreya is named Maitreya (the Benevolent One); as he is benevolent toward sentient beings, he ought to ask questions. Mañjuśrī is named Mañjughoṣa (Wondrous Virtue); as he possesses wondrous virtue, he ought to provide answers.
This concludes the explanation of the third section, the introductory sequence of doubts. △ From here below, from the words "At that time" until the end of the verses.

This constitutes the fourth section, the introduction consisting of inquiries, which is twofold: prose and verse. Within the prose, there is first the narrative by the sūtra-reciter, followed by the actual inquiry.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts, [spoke as follows].
This is the sūtra-master’s narration of Maitreya’s own doubts,
as well as his observation of the minds of the fourfold assembly— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— as well as the devas,
nāgas, spirits, and others present in the gathering.
The sūtra author describes how the fourfold assembly, harboring doubts regarding others,
questioned Mañjuśrī, saying: "By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign of supernatural power occurred,
such that a great radiance is emitted?"
This is Maitreya’s general inquiry regarding the six auspicious omens in this land. Question: Since only the emission of light is mentioned, how can it be said that all six are included? Answer:

Because the emission of light concludes the auspicious omens of this land and simultaneously stands at the head of the six omens of other lands, the single instance of light is cited generally to encompass both sets of six.
Furthermore, since the subsequent verse section extensively inquires about the six omens, we know that the same applies to the prose section.
This general summary makes it clear.
He illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, seeing in their entirety the adornments of those buddha-fields.
Next, Maitreya raises a question regarding the auspicious omens in those other lands.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to reiterate this meaning, asked in verse.
This is the reason why the author of the sutra provides these verses; at the beginning of each subsequent verse, there is this same pattern of explanation. Question:
What is the intention behind the presence of these verses? The answer is: Nāgārjuna’s *Vibhāṣā* explains this through ten meanings, for the sake of the four *siddhāntas*.
First, according to the country: in India, there are traditions such as the "scattered flowers" and the "strung flowers," which correspond here to the preface and the postscript.
Second, according to differing inclinations: some prefer the scattered exposition, while others prefer well-crafted verses.

These two [points] are for the sake of the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint). Third, there are differences according to individual understanding: some attain understanding through scattered flowers, while others attain understanding through the words and phrases.
Fourth, it further expresses the Buddha’s earnest and repeated teaching. Fifth, it causes those of future generations to give rise to faith.
These three [points] are for the sake of the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint established for individuals). The sixth concerns the sequence of assembly;

the seventh concerns seizing the opponent's words and shifting the momentum of the discourse—these two are for the sake of the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial treatment). The eighth follows the capacity of those present, whether sharp or dull;

the sharp-witted realize upon hearing once, while the dull-witted realize only after it is explained twice. The ninth demonstrates that the meaning is inexhaustible; the tenth clarifies that there are sages who possess...
This discourse on the absence of fixed direction is because these three constitute the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint). There is a meaning to be conveyed through verse;
for all subsequent passages, one should follow this same principle and need not provide further separate explanations. △ There are sixty-two lines of verse.

The text consists of two parts. The first comprises fifty-four lines, which provide verses on the inquiry regarding the auspicious omens; the latter consists of eight lines, which constitute the request for an answer.

Within the inquiry, there are two sections: the first four lines inquire about the omens in this land, while the subsequent fifty lines inquire about the omens in other lands. This concludes the general outline.
Mañjuśrī, for what reason does the Guide [inquire]?

These two phrases concern the omens within this land: first, the entering into meditative absorption while preaching the Dharma. Since he is called the "Guide," this inquiry concerns his preaching of the Dharma and his entry into absorption;
it is thus a question regarding the pair consisting of supreme wisdom and meditative concentration.
The white tuft of hair between his eyebrows emits a great light that shines everywhere.
This verse praises the auspicious omen of the radiance of the white tuft of hair of the sixth holy one of this land.
Mandārava flowers and Mañjūṣaka flowers rain down, and sandalwood-scented breezes gladden the hearts of the multitude. By these causes and conditions, [the world is purified].
"The ground is entirely adorned and pure.

This one and a half verses constitute the third cause, the auspicious sign (*nimitta*). Others say that because the wind comes from the sandalwood groves, it is fragrant, and the ground is further adorned and purified;
however, this does not praise the two matters of "overflowing" (*ying*) and "increasing" (*zhang*) mentioned above. Tiantai maintains that it is not "overflowing. Indeed...
The celestial flowers are most exquisite; how could they have color alone and lack fragrance? The fragrance of these flowers is like that of sandalwood (candana); thus, it is called "sandalwood wind.

This symbolizes that through the operation of causes, one arrives at the fruit—just as flowers possess fragrance and the wind [spreads it]. This is an analogy for the fragrant wind of the virtues of the Path, which universally perfumes all things.
When the flowers gather upon the ground, the ground becomes adorned and pure; likewise, when causes give rise to fruits, the fruits become adorned and pure. Gold...
The clouds of radiance gather merit to adorn the Buddha’s body; thus, through the two elements of wind and earth, the virtues of the four flowers are manifested, from cause to fruition.
And this world shook in six ways;
this verse asks regarding the auspicious sign of the fruit manifested by the earthquake of the aforementioned fourth stage.
At that time, the fourfold assembly was filled with joy; their bodies and minds were refreshed, having attained what they had never experienced before.

This verse asks about the fifth of the aforementioned [omens], namely the "Joy of the Multitudes," which is a response to the spiritual capacity [of the audience] and a manifestation of auspicious signs (*śakuna*).
Although they do not follow a sequential order, all six auspicious signs are fully present. The above four lines of verse ask about the six auspicious signs in this land.

Below this are fifty lines, which in their entirety ask about the six auspicious signs in other lands. The text is divided into six parts; the first three lines ask about the multitudes of the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*).
First, two lines and four phrases inquire about seeing that Buddha and his preaching of the Dharma. Second, three lines and three phrases inquire about the fourfold assembly in other lands.

Next, one line and a half concludes the preceding section and opens the subsequent one. Following this, there are thirty-one lines and a half that inquire about practicing the bodhisattva path in other lands.
Finally, seven lines inquire about making offerings to the śarīras. This concludes the general outline of the sections.
The radiance from between his eyebrows illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, making them all appear like gold.

From the Avīci Hell below up to the Summit of Existence above, throughout all the worlds, the destinies of birth and death for sentient beings of the six realms, and the karmic conditions of their good and evil deeds, were all revealed.
The excellence or inferiority of the retributions received are all seen herein.

The first line of verse asks about the general intent of illuminating other lands mentioned above. From the illumination of the eastern direction upward, there are two sections: the advancing and the retreating;
these are also categorized as the general auspicious omens of other lands. According to this categorization of the verses, the light in this land [appears] at the beginning of the preceding verse.
That auspicious clouds and great light shine everywhere has already been clarified previously.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the auspicious signs of other lands" and continuing with "the light from between the eyebrows," this indicates that it is a summary verse of the general auspicious signs. In the preceding prose section, the auspicious sign of light was the sixth among the signs of this land;
by means of this, the six auspicious signs of other lands are now explained. Among the six auspicious signs of other lands, there is none without light.
[This is] seen; therefore, it must be judged as a general auspicious sign for the other land.
Master She did not establish two lands or six auspicious signs at all, but merely stated that the first half of this line is a translation while the second half is not. Alas!

Having failed to understand the intent of the scripture himself, he has needlessly cast blame upon the translator. Since it is indeed a general auspicious sign for the other land, this is why [it is not so].

This is a separate section. It is placed at the beginning of the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍgati*). The following two lines separately praise the six realms. First, the upper and lower realms are mentioned;
next, from "all worlds" onwards, the environments and inhabitants, as well as causes and effects, are fully enumerated. "All worlds" refers to the eighteen thousand [worlds].
This does not merely show the sentient beings who approach [rebirth], but also reveals the various states of existence (*bhava*) toward which they proceed. Not...
One merely perceives the excellence or deficiency of karmic retribution and also knows the goodness or evil of karmic conditions; thus, one sees the six realms of existence.

These are simply the domains where sentient capacities are grasped. Although the four lower realms and the heavens do not consist of humans, they are collectively referred to as "mortal lords" (zhǎizhǔ), which encompasses all six realms.
This is the first of the verses below.
Furthermore, one beholds the Buddhas, the Holy Lords and Lions, expounding the sutras, which are subtle, wondrous, and foremost; their voices are pure.
They emit gentle and soft sounds to instruct countless billions of bodhisattvas. Their Brahma-voices are profound and wondrous, causing all who hear them to delight.
In their respective worlds, they preach the True Dharma, using various causes and conditions and immeasurable parables to illuminate the Buddha-dharma.
This awakens sentient beings.
These four verses correspond to the second and third of the aforementioned auspicious omens; that is, what was previously "not sudden yet sudden.

In the preceding section, it was asked about seeing those Buddha-lands, which was described simply as seeing the Buddhas preaching the Dharma. Now, these verses extensively clarify the characteristics of that preaching of the Dharma.
This refers to the time when the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*) was proclaimed, intended for those of great spiritual capacity.
As for the term "Holy Sovereign Lion," it refers to the manifestation of the Vairocana Buddha in this land. "Holy" (*sheng*) is the "Sovereign" (*zhu*), hence "Holy Sovereign.

This means that while he is the sovereign of the principal and satellites throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he is specifically the sovereign among the satellites of the various bodhisattvas.

This does not concern the Pratyekabuddhas or the leaders among Arhats, nor is it the teaching of the masters of the preceding Tripitaka or the Shared Vehicle. "Lion's Roar" refers to definitive exposition.

Regarding the phrase "expounding the subtle and supreme of all scriptures," this refers to the initial illumination of the high mountain in this land—the expounding of the sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Although it is said to be inclusive of the Distinct Teaching, it was purely Mahāyāna at the outset; therefore, it is called "supreme."
Regarding the statement that "its sound is pure and produces a gentle voice": the two preceding teachings were still mixed with afflictions and thus were not pure;
because they did not reach all capacities, they are not called gentle. Regarding "teaching the various bodhisattvas and others":
this refers, for example, to the seven assemblies in this land, where there are no śrāvakas. Regarding "the Brahma-sound is profound and wondrous": these all expound the Middle Way.
Therefore, it is called "profound and subtle. That which causes people to delight in hearing it is so called because it accords with the principle and suits the capacity of the listener.
An ancient master said: "Because it arises from the great elements within the Tathāgata’s chest, it is called 'pure'; because it is free from abruptness or violence, it is called 'gentle and supple.
To explain the Buddha’s Brahma-voice by means of the physical retribution-body of ordinary beings in the realms of desire and form—how bitter this is! Each [of these views]...
Regarding the worlds and so forth: first, each consists of eighteen thousand; second, each is distinct in terms of its primary and attendant deities.
One must know with certainty that this passage should be judged as belonging to the *Avataṃsaka* teaching, rather than to the two preceding teachings or the middle samādhi.

Because these matters do not exist [there], the two teachings of the *Avataṃsaka* are called "various" across its eight gates; they illuminate the Buddha-dharma and so forth through immeasurable metaphors.
This is like the *Avataṃsaka* of this land, which begins with the words, "I first see my own body entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Therein, no three-vehicle matters exist, and this is termed "Buddha-dharma. This concludes the exposition on the *Avataṃsaka* in other lands. △ Below this is the verse:

The first vision was that the fourfold assembly attained the Way; this is the fourth auspicious sign. It consists of three parts: first, questioning the fourfold assembly of that land and immediately expounding [the teaching];
second, subsequently clarifying the Tripitaka Teaching; and third, showing that what is not gradual is yet gradual.
Within this gradual approach, there are three stages: beginning, middle, and end. Within the beginning and middle of this gradual process, there are themselves the Three Vehicles.
If there is a person who encounters suffering and grows weary of old age, sickness, and death, one preaches for them *nirvāṇa* as the end of all suffering.
This single verse is the beginning of the Tripiṭaka; it opens the Śrāvaka-yāna. This stanza clarifies the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the term "suffering" (*duḥkha*), it encompasses both cause and effect, namely the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*). "Growing weary of old age, sickness, and death" refers to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). For...
To speak of *nirvāṇa* is to speak of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). It may also be understood as the word "to speak" encompassing the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) as well;
for the path to *nirvāṇa* is the Truth of the Path, and the principle of cessation realized therein is the Truth of Cessation. Furthermore, "encountering suffering" is the general heading.

"Disgust for old age, sickness, and death" is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-parijñāna*). Because one knows suffering, one abandons its origin (*samudaya-prahāṇa*). To speak of *nirvāṇa* is to know [the cessation of suffering].
Cessation. Because one knows cessation, one cultivates the Path. This passage clearly elucidates the Four Noble Truths of the Śrāvaka Vehicle. Regarding the characteristics of the practices:
if a person encounters suffering yet commits evil deeds, their suffering will not come to an end; such are the base worldlings.
If a person encounters suffering yet cultivates wholesome deeds, their suffering likewise does not end; they loathe what is below and grasp for what is above, as [in the following example].
This refers to cases such as Nanda’s observance of the precepts for the sake of desire.

If a person encounters suffering and grows weary of its accumulation, and further grows weary of its resultant fruits, such that they are moved by the Buddha’s teaching on *nirvāṇa*, this person is able to reach the ultimate end of all suffering. Other lands also open the way for the three vehicles.
The ancient masters did not provide an exegesis of the *Avataṃsaka* prior to this passage; rather, once one has encountered suffering...

Previously, at the beginning of the Deer Park, how could there have been a text concerning each individual world? This is because within the Hīnayāna, there is no mention of Buddhas of the ten directions.
From the sudden teaching down to the initial stage of the gradual teaching, there was only the three vehicles at the Deer Park; this present text concerns the Four Noble Truths of the first vehicle.
Even down to the later passage where it says, "O Son of the Buddha," the three characteristics are clearly present. How can one not interpret the sūtra according to the five periods?
If there are those with merit who have previously made offerings to the Buddha and aspire to seek the supreme Dharma, for them he preaches the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
This single verse next opens the discussion of the Middle Vehicle (*madhyayāna*). If one makes few offerings to the Buddha, one encounters suffering and distress;

if one makes many offerings to the Buddha, although one may encounter suffering, there is merit. Thus it is said that *śrāvakas* plant the seeds of merit over three lifetimes, while *pratyekabuddhas* plant the seeds of merit over a hundred eons.
It is said they possess merit because they are compared to those *śrāvakas*. As for those whose resolve seeks the supreme Dharma, [they are] the *śrāvakas*...
One practices out of weariness with suffering; the Pratyekabuddha practices for the sake of seeking the Way.
By deeply investigating the sublime principle of dependent origination, this is precisely how the Middle Vehicle is revealed in that land.
If there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate various practices in pursuit of unsurpassed wisdom, for their sake this single verse explains the path of purity.
Hereafter, it opens the gateway to the Mahāyāna of the six perfections. Because true compassion is able to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas, they are called "sons of the Buddha.
Because they cultivate the six perfections, they are said to engage in "various practices. Because they aspire to attain Buddhahood, it is called "unsurpassed."
Wisdom. Within the six perfections there are no six obscurations, just as there is no disease within medicine; therefore, it is called the "pure path. Yet this is not ultimate purity.

Furthermore, for śrāvakas, the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) serves as the gate of contemplation; for pratyekabuddhas, the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) serves as the gate of contemplation;

and for bodhisattvas, the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*)—namely, the six perfections—serves as the gate of contemplation. Thus it is called the pure path. How much more so for the Mahāyāna of the six perfections, which cultivates various practices.
And as for the unsurpassed wisdom, it is common to all teachings. Herein, we shall first clarify that one sees [the truth] momentarily through the light;

it is not appropriate to seek the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) extensively. It suffices to briefly indicate their commonality, for this is sufficient from the perspective of principle.

If one discusses actual practice, only then can they be analyzed in detail. Below, there are thirty-one and a half lines of verse that extensively clarify the two flavors (*dvirasā*); therefore, they must be judged.
The above text concludes the section on the Three Vehicles within the Tripiṭaka concerning the Deer Park alone.
Mañjuśrī, I have resided here, and what I have seen and heard is such as this, as well as thousands of millions of other matters; they are numerous in this way.
Now I shall briefly explain this one and a half verses.
This serves both to conclude what precedes and to open what follows. "Seeing" refers to seeing the aforementioned sons of the Buddha; this is "seeing.
"Hearing" refers to the gradual and sudden teachings, all of which speak of "expounding" and "preaching"; these are all instances of "hearing."
Having seen and heard billions of matters, the Great Net is sufficiently summarized; thus it says, "it is like this.

The term "the same" serves as an abbreviation for the thousands of billions of matters, which refers back to what preceded. The phrase "and thousands of billions of matters such as these, being so numerous," etc., opens up what follows.
It is explained as a continuation of what follows; hence it says, "Now, one should know... and so forth.

The single phrase "and ten billion matters" can be interpreted in two ways, for which the metaphor of the orchid and the chrysanthemum provides the basis. This passage concludes the two preceding periods and opens up the two subsequent meanings.
△ From "Below this, starting from 'I see that land'" onwards, the fifth section consists of thirty-one and a half lines.
It asks about the various practices of the bodhisattvas in other lands. What follows below merely speaks of the "bodhisattva practice.

Since this occurs after [the teaching at] Mṛgadāva and before the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, one must, following the subsequent explanation of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, combine it with both *Sūtras* (the *Dīrgha-āgama* and the *Madhyama-āgama*), for the sake of the Dharma.

Because the characteristics of the flowers have not yet been definitively resolved, [the text] explains them with composure. Although it refers to the two *sūtras*, it mentions only the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

This is because the teachings are mostly associated with the three [periods], as the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) is identical to the three [periods] of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, while the "Lesser" (xiǎo) is identical to the Deer Park [period];
therefore, they are not specified separately. Within this, there are three parts: first, one line of general inquiry; second, fifteen lines of sequential inquiry; third, ten [lines].
The miscellaneous questions concerning the five elements and a half are hereby concluded.
I have seen that in that land, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges seek the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.

This single verse constitutes the initial general inquiry. The question asks: "Since the subsequent specific texts encompass both the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā [teachings], they should likewise include both vehicles (yāna) of the two teachings.
