Why, then, does the general inquiry seek only the Buddha-way? The answer is: It is indeed as you have asked.
However, to avoid excessive elaboration, it is treated similarly to the Deer Park [teachings] and is therefore omitted here. As for the phrase "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges":
From each of the four sides of Lake Anavatapta, a river flows forth. From the silver ox-mouth in the east, the Gaṅgā River issues;
from the golden elephant-mouth in the south, the Sindhu River issues; from the lapis lazuli horse-mouth in the west, the Vakṣu River issues;
and from the crystal lion-mouth in the north, the Sītā River issues. Each river encircles the lake once before flowing into one of the four great oceans. In...
The sands of the Ganges within are subtle and numerous; those of external paths reckon it to be a river of merit, entering its waters to wash away sins.
The Buddha also followed worldly convention and therefore constantly referred to it. Furthermore, as the Buddha frequently taught the Dharma near this river, he used it as a metaphor.
△ Below there are fifteen lines, which are divided into six parts in the sequential questions; herein lie the Six Perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).

This merely indicates the general outline. If one were to fully set forth the characteristics based on the two flavors [of teaching], it would be as detailed in the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation), fascicles 2 and 7, and the citations therein.
Regarding the first question concerning the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), there are again three points of intent.
There are those who practice giving gold, silver, coral, pearls, mani-jewels, tridacna shells, agate, diamonds, and various other treasures;
they give with joy their male and female servants, carriages, and precious decorated litters, dedicating these merits toward the Buddha-way, vowing to obtain this vehicle.

The foremost in the three realms, praised by all Buddhas; there may be bodhisattvas who give away precious chariots drawn by four horses, adorned with railings and flowered canopies, as magnificent offerings.
These four lines of verse inquire about the relinquishing of wealth, treasures, and male and female slaves. This kind of giving can be performed by both the noble and the humble alike.
As for the "precious chariot drawn by four horses," this is what the wealthy and powerful bestow; because four horses are yoked together to pull it, they are called "a team of four" (*sì*).
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who give their own flesh, hands, feet, wives, and children, seeking the unsurpassed path.
This single verse asks about the relinquishing of the body. Wives and children represent the relinquishing of the external body; for example, as when Kāśyapa gave away his golden-hued wife.
Flesh and other parts of the body represent the internal body. Since the internal body is thus relinquished, what need is there to mention the external?
Not being attached to what is received is called "renouncing one's wife. Alternatively, it refers to renouncing [worldly life] to enter the Path and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Furthermore, one sees that Bodhisattvas joyfully give away their heads, eyes, bodies, and limbs, seeking the wisdom of a Buddha.
This single verse asks about the relinquishing of life, yet does not mention the gift of Dharma; this is to defer to the *prajñāpāramitā* (the Perfection of Wisdom) that follows.
Furthermore, regarding body, life, and wealth, attaining non-destruction and permanence equal to the future limit of saṃsāra is itself the gift of Dharma;
therefore, it is not mentioned separately. The six lines above conclude the inquiry into the *dānapāramitā* (the Perfection of Giving).
Mañjuśrī, I have seen various kings who, having gone to the presence of the Buddha to inquire about the unsurpassed path, then abandoned their pleasant lands, palaces, ministers, and consorts;
they shaved off their hair and beards and donned the dharma robes.

These two verses address the second inquiry concerning the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Regarding the discussion of the precept-holder from the perspective of a *bhikṣu*: for those at home, giving is easy while maintaining the precepts is difficult;
for those who have gone forth, giving is difficult while maintaining the precepts is easy. Therefore, the precepts are clarified specifically in relation to the *bhikṣu*.

As for "going to" (*upasaṃkramaṇa*) and so forth, it signifies that one goes to no other place. "The unsurpassed path" refers to the most venerable and supreme object of inquiry. As for "the land of bliss," it refers to... [text fragment].

"Discarding what is not to be despised. "One who has shaved [the head]" signifies that both body and mind are detached. Regarding "a king who has left the household life," as stated in the *Pañcarājasūtra*:
"In the past, there were five kings whose neighboring states did not compete with one another; they were mutual friends.

There was one great king named Puhuan (Universal Peace), who practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva. Because the four remaining kings were full of intense wrong views, Puhuan took pity on them and called out..."
They came to the palace hall and enjoyed themselves for seven days and seven nights. The Four Kings said, "Our state affairs are many;
we request to return home. Pu'an escorted them himself as far as the halfway point, where he asked them, "What are the things each of you enjoys?"
One said, "I wish for the days of springtime to roam and play upon the open fields.

Another said, "I wish to always be a king, adorned with every kind of ornament, with the people as my attendants, and all who see me on the road casting their eyes upward in admiration. Another said, "I wish to have a fine wife and children of peerless beauty.
Another said, "I wish for my parents to live long, to have many brothers, and to enjoy fine food, music, and mutual companionship."

After each had finished speaking of their diversions, they turned to address Puhuan: "What is it that Your Majesty desires? He replied: "I have already explained to you that your wishes will not endure.
If you delight in spring excursions, all things wither by winter. If you delight in being king, when your merit is exhausted, another shall succeed you.
If you delight in your wife and children, one day illness may strike, and the suffering will be immeasurable. If you delight in your parents remaining forever..."
...and so forth. Once an emergency arose and he was seized by others, [he said: "That which I delight in is neither born nor extinguished; it is neither suffering nor pleasure;
it is neither hunger nor thirst; it is neither cold nor heat; it is sovereign over both existence and non-existence.
The Four Heavenly Kings asked, "Where can this bliss be sought? Where is its teacher? Puan replied, "My teacher is named Buddha; he is nearby."
At the Jetavana, the various kings were filled with joy and each went to the Buddha’s dwelling to reproach themselves for their own transgressions.

The Buddha preached the eight sufferings, and the king along with his retinue of immeasurable people attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. In the *Dīrgha Āgama*, there are accounts of four wheel-turning kings who divided a single kingdom among them, hired a barber, and then renounced the kingdom to enter the path;
the general outline is the same as this. Since it is said that he "inquired about the Unsurpassed," [it refers to the Buddha].
The Way is not concerned with minor fruits. However, as the matter of relinquishing the land is similar, I have cited it here.

This is intended primarily to clarify the meaning of what is seen, using the introductory section to represent the main teaching; the various conditions cited are merely used here to provide a general explanation.

Regarding those who don the Dharma robes, the *Sūtra of the Necklaces* (*Śrīkaṇṭhaka-sūtra*) states: "If the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, engage in conflict, they should mindfully contemplate this kāṣāya, and compassion will arise."
With a heart of compassion, he intended to ensure that the bhikṣus remained steadfast and patient, and that the lay populace would admire and yearn for him.
Like the dragon’s thread or the ox’s horn, he avoided calamity and attained liberation.
Or, seeing the Bodhisattva acting as a bhikṣu, dwelling alone in quietude, and delighting in the recitation of the sūtras.
This single verse praises the third inquiry, that of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). There are three types of patience: 1. **Patience toward living beings** (*sattva-kṣānti*):

To endure without anger when encountering wicked people or ferocious beasts in secluded forests and deep valleys. 2. **Patience toward suffering** (*duḥkha-kṣānti*): To restrain oneself and maintain one’s resolve, which constitutes the endurance of hardship.

3. **Ultimate patience** (*paramārtha-kṣānti*): To seek the path of the Buddha; this is the patience regarding the ultimate truth. Furthermore, becoming a bhikṣu constitutes the patience of ascetic practice (*duṣkaracaryā-kṣānti*), dwelling in solitude.
Seclusion and tranquility constitute the patience of birth (*utpatti-kṣānti*). Delighting in the recitation of the sūtras constitutes the patience of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-kṣānti*).

The patience of birth and the patience of suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) are found specifically in the initial teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*). The patience of the ultimate meaning also extends through the first three [teachings], though it is specifically unique to the Perfect and Distinct [teachings].
Furthermore, as in another translation of the *Āgama*: when the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, there was a brahmin who came to the Buddha’s dwelling and reviled him in various ways.
He thus troubled the Buddha. The Buddha said to the brahmin: "Suppose you were to offer various kinds of food and drink to a king and also send some to your kinsmen, but they did not accept the food;
to whom would it then belong? The brahmin replied: "It would still belong to me. The Buddha said:
"This case is exactly like that. Since I do not accept it, it returns to you. Therefore, this non-acceptance is also a form of giving."
This is patience (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, one sees a bodhisattva who, with courageous diligence (*vīrya*), enters deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way.
This single verse concerns the fourth question, the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*). Now, deep mountains are fearsome; they are not for those who are indolent or timid.

As for their dwelling place, those who possess courageous diligence can abide therein. Indifferent to external things as if they did not exist, they contemplate and cultivate the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), never ceasing from moment to moment, advancing in their quest for the Buddha-way.
△ The following two lines inquire about the perfection of dhyāna. The first line inquires about the cultivation of fundamental dhyāna;
the second line inquires about the cultivation of supramundane, supreme dhyāna. All [practitioners] generally attain these.
Fundamental cultivation.
Furthermore, seeing freedom from desire, one constantly dwells in seclusion and deeply cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), thereby attaining the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

This first line of inquiry concerns fundamental dhyāna. To say that one attains the five supernormal powers through freedom from desire refers to the concentration of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*). Moreover...

The fundamental [practice] is the liberation through detachment (*vairāgya-vimokṣa*). One also cultivates detachment through methods such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); these are the two preceding teachings.

In the Distinct Teaching (*bipākya-yāna*), it additionally includes detachment from the desires of the Two Vehicles. In the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*), it is the Middle Way, which involves detachment from the craving for dharmas that accord with the Path (*mārgānulomika-dharma-tṛṣṇā*).

Regarding the fundamental stages, higher and higher, they are explained in detail within the "Meditative Objects" (*dhyāna-viṣaya*) section of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. For those who deeply cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), [the following] arises:
The first dhyāna has nine grades; these concentrations are not yet profound. Up to the ninth grade, they become progressively deeper.

Furthermore, the nine liberations (vimokṣa), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) are each progressively deeper. Through the mastery of transforming these concentrations, one can manifest the various supernatural powers (abhijñā).
Ordinary beings possess only five of these powers; those of the Two Vehicles possess all six; and Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching defer to the Buddha.

When distinguished by the inclusion of the untainted (*anāsrava*), these are likewise referred to simply as the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). For those of the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇa-yāna*), both at the beginning and at the end, all six supernormal powers are possessed:

first, the divine eye; second, the divine ear; third, knowledge of others' minds; fourth, recollection of past lives; fifth, the power of transformation (*ṛddhi*); and sixth, the untainted supernormal power (*anāsravābhijñā*).
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas sitting in meditative concentration (dhyāna) with palms joined, praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses.

This single verse [of the text] clarifies the second stage, the supreme-superior dhyāna; this is the dhyāna of the Distinct and Complete teachings. Stillness and distraction do not obstruct one another;

they manifest various dignified postures without arising from or ceasing within the samādhi of cessation. It is like the lute of the asuras, which produces melody without being struck—this is the "conditionless" (anālambana).

There is no-thought; yet when there is resonance, form appears. Thus, one is able to praise the Buddha while in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). The two preceding verses conclude the inquiry into the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Below this, the sixth section consists of three lines concerning the inquiry into wisdom (*prajñā*). This is divided into two parts.
Furthermore, one sees a bodhisattva whose wisdom is profound and whose resolve is firm; such a person is able to question the Buddhas and, having heard their teachings, receives and upholds them all.
This single verse concerns the practice of self-cultivation. "Profound wisdom" means that one’s insight exhaustively reaches the fundamental principle.

"Firm resolve" means that one’s vows are vast and great. These constitute the two kinds of adornment; being able to question and be able to uphold [the teachings] constitutes the practice of self-cultivation.
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha, fully endowed with concentration and wisdom, expounding the Dharma for the multitudes through immeasurable parables.
Delighting in the preaching of the Dharma, they transform the bodhisattvas, shatter the hosts of Māra, and beat the drum of the Dharma.

These two verses inquire about the transformation of others (*paranirmita*). When concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are both abundant, when the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are abundant, when the four dhyānas and so forth are present, when the liberations (*vimokṣa*) are abundant in wisdom, when the nine attainments (*navasamāpatti*) are abundant in concentration, and when the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*) are balanced—only then is one said to be "fully endowed.

This is the explanation based on causes and conditions. Furthermore, while those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) have more concentration and Bodhisattvas have more wisdom, it is only in a Buddha that these are each equal; only then is he called "fully endowed."

This refers to the completeness of the teachings and their meanings. Furthermore, the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) emphasizes meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the contemplation of the conventional (*prajñapti*) emphasizes wisdom (*prajñā*);

the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) balances both. Therefore, it is said that concentration and wisdom are fully possessed. "Immeasurable metaphors" refer to the various skillful means (*upāya*);

throughout the various teachings, immeasurable analogies are cited to assist in revealing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). As for "destroying the hosts of Māra," the contemplation of emptiness destroys them.

Regarding the four māras: through the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-dṛṣṭi*), one successively destroys the eight māras; through the middle way contemplation (*madhyamaka-dṛṣṭi*), one completely destroys the eight māras, the ten māras, and all māras.

As for "beating the Dharma drum": at the initial stage of the resolve for enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), one immediately attains perfect awakening and acts as a Buddha within a hundred buddha-worlds.
This is precisely the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). It strikes the Dharma-drum of the *Brahma-paripṛcchā-śāstra*.

From the preceding section beginning with "There may be those who practice giving" up to this point, the sequential inquiries are completed. From here below, the third section consists of fifteen and a half lines;

it no longer follows a sequential order, but consists of miscellaneous questions as they appear. Question: The previous clarification regarding "what is seen" should not be considered "miscellaneous seeing. Answer: Both are indeed "miscellaneous."
[The answer is: It is seen that there are simply two different paths. From the perspective of the non-sequential, this is most consistent with what is observed;
since it is even permitted for a single vision to encompass five periods, what hindrance is there to observing both sequential and non-sequential practice? Question:

Since the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) explained above already include all myriad practices (*sāhasra-pratipatti*), why is it necessary to ask further? Is it not too cumbersome? Answer: The previous question regarding sequence was addressed from the standpoint of gradual [cultivation].
"A single path" does not mean a fixed sequence; it is not restricted to one way. Since you speak of "various characteristics," how could there be more than two paths?

Why do you say they are numerous? This sequence is disordered: the two sets of six perfections (ṣaḍpāramitā) correspond to other lands, opening up the Tripiṭaka, followed by the preaching of the Vaipulya twelvefold scriptures, which distinguish the characteristics of the six perfections. It is precisely for this reason that such a question was raised.

It is different. Within the section on miscellaneous questions, the text comprises seven points. The first two lines ask about the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*). Furthermore, there are two [points]:
seeing that the Bodhisattva remains in silent, tranquil composure while devas and nāgas pay him homage, yet he does not consider this a cause for joy.
This one verse asks about entering the dhyāna of equanimity (*upekṣā*). This refers to the fourth dhyāna as one's own practice;
it may also refer to the equanimity of forgetting both the distinct and the perfect [teachings]. It is called "equanimity" because one forgets that dhyāna.
Furthermore, one sees a Bodhisattva dwelling in the forest emitting light to rescue those in the hells from suffering and lead them into the Buddha-way.

This single verse asks about entering the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of compassion; this is precisely the transformation of others. When a Bodhisattva enters *samādhi* and emits light, they bring about various benefits.

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), there are differences according to the four teachings. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (or *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*), in its first chapter, says: "The Buddha..."
He addressed the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin: "To be able to teach sentient beings the mind of omniscience is called generosity (*dāna*).
Not abandoning the bodhicitta is called ethical discipline (*śīla*). Not perceiving the arising and ceasing of mental states is called patience (*kṣānti*).

Seeking the unattainable mind is called diligence (*vīrya*). Eliminating the coarseness of body and mind is called meditation (*dhyāna*). Being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is called wisdom (*prajñā*). These are the six [perfections] of the Tripiṭaka."
[This is] deliverance (*tāraṇa*). The second [section] says: "I declare that giving (*dāna*) is called nirvāṇa;

the foolish think it is great wealth, but it is because one enters the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Precept-keeping (*śīla*) is nirvāṇa, because there is no doing and no arising. Patience (*kṣānti*) is nirvāṇa, because every thought-moment ceases.
Diligence (*vīrya*) is nirvāṇa, because there is nothing to grasp. Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is nirvāṇa, because there is no craving."

Because of non-attachment, wisdom is *nirvāṇa*, for it does not apprehend any characteristics. This Mahāyāna universal teaching of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) is further explained in the fourth [chapter]:
"To penetrate all phenomena without anything to be relinquished is called *dāna* (generosity); to penetrate all phenomena without anything to be lost or leaked is called *śīla* (ethics);
to penetrate all phenomena without anything to be harmed or damaged is called *kṣānti* (patience); to penetrate all phenomena as equal..."
Dhyāna is the name for [the realization that] all phenomena have no characteristic of arising; Prajñā is the name for [the realization of] this.

To cultivate these six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) in such a sequential manner is the distinct teaching (bipartite vehicle) of the Mahāyāna. If, however, one does not move from this mindfulness, but possesses them all within a single mind and cultivates the six perfections instantaneously, this is the perfect teaching (round vehicle) of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva emits light to transform others, the various manifestations are not uniform; one must rely on the teachings to determine [the specific application].
This is as described in the *Sutrasamuccaya* regarding the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, who emitted light that universally illumined incalculable lands throughout the ten directions;

all afflictions and all diseases were pacified, and all who encountered the light attained peace and happiness. Even when the Buddha himself emits the light of the six perfections, those touched by it receive benefit.

One should know that within each and every dhyāna of the Mahāyāna, one must be fully endowed with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The details are fully set forth in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, so they are not cited here in their entirety.
Furthermore, I have seen sons of the Buddha who never sleep, but instead practice walking meditation in the groves, diligently seeking the path of the Buddha.
The second section consists of one line. It asks about diligence, which refers to the dharma-gates such as the mindfulness of the Buddha in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*.
"Pratyutpanna" is translated here as "the Buddha standing. This is cited as the foremost among methods for dispelling sleep, because it is practiced constantly throughout ninety days.
Furthermore, one sees those who possess the precepts, whose deportment is flawless and pure like a precious gem, as they seek the Buddha-way.
This third single practice concerns the inquiry into the precepts. As set forth in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are ten kinds of precepts.
First, the "unbroken precept" (*akhaṇḍa-śīla*) refers to maintaining the natural virtues, including even the four grave offenses, remaining as pure as one would guard a bright pearl.
One who commits an offense is like a broken pearl. Second, one who does not break the precepts maintains the thirteen [precepts] without any damage or breach;
if one commits an offense, it is like a broken vessel. Third, one whose precepts are not pierced maintains the *pāyattika* rules and so forth; if one commits an offense, it is like a leaking vessel.

These three precepts constitute the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint). Fourth, the unmixed precept (*asaṃsṛṣṭa-śīla*) refers to maintaining the morality concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Fifth, the precept that accords with the path (*anuloma-mārga-śīla*) is so named because it accords with the principle of the Truths and is able to destroy the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Sixth, the unattached precept (*asaṅga-śīla*) refers to having realized the Truth and become a noble one (*ārya*), such that one is no longer defiled by or attached to the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). Seventh, the precept praised by the wise (*jñāna-praśasta-śīla*).
These, together with the eightfold *vaiśāradya* (sovereign) precepts, are all praised by the Buddha as being based on the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others.
Thus, there are nine: the precepts that accord with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Tenth is the complete and ultimate precept (*pāramitā-śīla*), which abides in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.

The Sūtra states that "one's deportment (*īryāpatha*) is without deficiency," citing the initial precept of non-deficiency. That it is "pure like a precious jewel" refers to the tenth, the ultimate precept. The Sūtra cites the beginning here.
The subsequent and intermediate sections may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who, abiding in the power of patience, are able to endure all the insults and beatings of those with overweening pride.
In order to seek the Buddha-way.

The fourth section, consisting of one and a half lines, asks about patience (*kṣānti*). The two types of patience—patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*) and patience regarding birth (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—have already been explained as before.
Furthermore, it describes seeing a bodhisattva who has abandoned all frivolous laughter and foolish associates, who stays close to the wise, and who single-mindedly eliminates distraction.
He concentrated his mindfulness in the mountain forests for billions of millions of years in order to seek the Buddha-way.
The fifth two lines further inquire about dhyāna. The first one and a half lines clarify what must be abandoned; the subsequent half line clarifies the intention for such abandonment.
Generally, all who practice dhyāna must abandon the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), as detailed in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation). It says "abandoning playfulness" (*līlā*).
Laughter removes the hindrance of regret; being free from the retinue of delusion removes the hindrance of anger; drawing near to the wise removes the hindrance of doubt;
single-mindedness removes distraction, which is the removal of the hindrance of desire; and withdrawing the mind to the mountain forests removes the hindrance of sloth and torpor.

One who must leave behind these five hindrances does so with the intent of attaining the Buddha-way. Furthermore, as stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Kāśyapa said: "There are four conditions for urgency..."
One should flee for a distance of one hundred *yojanas* away from these four things: first, gain and honor; second, evil friends; third, evil assemblies;

and fourth, those who dwell together in much laughter, or in anger, strife, and the like. Furthermore, it is said: even if one were to strike and maim all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm, that would not constitute a grave offense;
however, if with an evil mind one causes distress to a person who has generated the bodhicitta, the sin of that act exceeds even the former. Thus it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
When traveling by boat, one must ensure that foolish people, foolish kinsmen, and fellow villagers are kept at a distance.

Or, upon seeing a bodhisattva, one should offer various kinds of fine food and drink, a hundred varieties of medicinal decoctions, and renowned garments and superior robes to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Worth millions, or even priceless robes, they offered to the Buddha and the Saṃgha in varieties numbering in the thousands of millions.

They offered sandalwood jewel-palaces and various exquisite bedding to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as well as pure gardens and groves with flourishing flowers and fruits, flowing springs, and bathing pools.
Giving to the Buddha and the Sangha—such various and subtle acts of giving, performed with joy and without weariness, seek the unsurpassed path.
The sixth section consists of five lines, which inquire about the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). The first four lines clarify the giving of four types of requisites;
the following single line concludes the perfection of giving. The first line concerns food and drink; the second, medicinal decoctions; the third, clothing.
The fourth line includes bedding, dwellings, gardens, groves, bathing pools, bridges, and fine wells—all such matters are subsumed therein.
"Kiao" (肴) refers to pickled vegetables; "shan" (膳) refers to fine food. It is unclear what specific auspicious event is intended here, yet both Master Jia and Master She take "kiao" to mean meat.
Even if the character's etymological meaning allows for the sense of "meat," why must it be exclusively restricted to that?
Regarding the character for "meat" (肉): it causes those with little knowledge in later generations to doubt [the etymology]. One should say that what is eaten which is not grain is called *yáo* (餚).
If written as [月*肴] (*yué-yáo*), it means to eat. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Shàn" (膳) refers to a complete meal; it is composed solely of the radical for "meat" and is defined as eating.
Who is it that is called "meat-eater"? Or is it said that this is meat? This statement is even more erroneous before the prohibition was established.
In the Mahāyāna, meat is prohibited all at once, with a total ban on eating meat; why discuss whether the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* prohibits it earlier or later?

Moreover, since these are all things seen within the light, how could all eighteen thousand [beings] be identical to those for whom the prohibition against eating meat had not yet been enacted? It is still...
Is it with minced meat that one makes offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha? As for what the Sūtra refers to as "famous robes" and so forth:
in this land, Kāśyapa’s *kāṣāya* was worth one hundred thousand taels of gold; perhaps such things were seen within the light.
There may be bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma of quiescence and instruct countless sentient beings through various teachings;

or one may see a bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all phenomena as being without dual characteristics, like empty space; and furthermore, one may see a son of the Buddha whose mind is free from attachment.
By means of this wondrous wisdom, one seeks the unsurpassed path.
The seventh [section] contains three lines of verse that inquire about *prajñā*. This should be interpreted according to five points. First, to directly interpret the sutra:
the first line clarifies that while *prajñā* is ineffable, it is spoken; the subsequent line clarifies that it is unobservable.
And one contemplates Prajñā: the three [aspects] and the single practice cut off the path of language and extinguish the sphere of mental activity;

it is the ineffable that is spoken, the unobservable that is contemplated—this is Prajñā. Second, regarding the explanation according to the Vaipulya period: it may be established by means of these three aspects of Prajñā.
Above, we saw the teaching of the Six Pāramitās within the Vaipulya sūtras in other lands; herein, the five [Pāramitās] follow [the first].

This is because of *prajñā*. Regarding the third pair, the explanation given during the time of *prajñā*: it may be understood as separately corresponding to the teaching of the Vaipulya sūtras in other lands;
subsequently, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* teachings clarify the flourishing discourse on the quiescence of *prajñā*, its non-duality, purity, and non-attachment.
This indicates that these two are identical. Regarding the fourth pair, the explanation by way of the three samādhis is as follows:

one may say that the dharma of quiescent extinction is the intended meaning of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) [sūtras]. Contemplating the nature of all dharmas as being like empty space is the intended meaning of the Prajñā[pāramitā] [sūtras];

this is precisely the practice of contemplation by traversing through dharmas. Since the characteristics of dharmas are non-dual, this principle truly accords with the Mahāyāna (Daxiang). If one were to...
Those who perceive the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* do so by means of this single practice of seeking the unsurpassed path through sublime wisdom.

They see only those who cultivate sublime wisdom, yet they do not see the seat of the sublime wisdom of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If they were to see that seat, they would immediately know that this sublime [wisdom] is just like that;
why then would there be any need for doubt? It is because they see only the people and do not see the seat that the entire assembly harbors these doubts.
Furthermore, regarding the fifth section, which explains [the text] in relation to *prajñā*, it may be that the threefold *prajñā* is identical to the *prajñā* found here.
However, it is not known what will be explained next; therefore, this doubt arises. The preceding prose section was concise, mentioning only six points;
yet since the verses are extensive, their meaning is revealed with perfect clarity. Moreover, what is perceived therein is immeasurable.

Examining this in detail up to the fifth [section], since the collection is so extensive, nothing lies outside of it. Question: What is the difference between the fifth explanation and the third explanation?
Answer: The third [explanation] directly takes "speaking by not speaking" and so forth as being identical to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and thus it is contrasted with that.
In the fifth [section], because within the fourth explanation the third practice is applied to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra), [the fifth explanation] is presented.
This is truly due to the two characters "Miao-hui" (Wondrous Wisdom). Yet it is said that one sees the person but does not see the seat;

thus, the first and last lines are brought back to the middle line. To observe without observing is precisely identical to Prajñā, which is the same as not seeing the seat of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Since both are cases of non-seeing, if the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* has not yet been digested, the explanation remains the same.
Regarding *prajñā*, there is thus a fifth intention. The initial instances all say "perhaps" (*huò*); the meaning lies therein.

In the preceding prose section, it merely mentions various causes and conditions for faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*), without yet distinguishing between the three flavors (*trivipāka*) and the four teachings (*caturvyavasthāna*).
Who among the commentators would know that these three practices herein contain two flavors? This question concludes the section on *prajñā*. Now begins—
Above, I have seen the bodhisattvas in that land as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; this concludes the fifth question in total.
The scriptural text concerning the practices of the bodhisattvas in other lands is finished. Below, from the passage beginning with "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī...

onwards, is the sixth question concerning the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha in that land. It consists of seven lines, clarifying how stupas were erected from the *śarīra* (relics) after the Buddha’s extinction. This is the formal verse.
In the Buddha-lands of the upper realms, Buddhas appear amidst the five turbidities; from the single dharma of formlessness, they open the gradual and sudden teachings.
Thus, there are two dharmas, three paths, and various types of practices with differing characteristics, as seen above.
Now, seeing the Buddhas of other lands enter parinirvāṇa, their disciples yearn for their virtue and erect stupas; this immediately signifies that all immeasurable beings return [to the source].
First: One emerges from the immeasurable, as has already been indicated above; that the immeasurable returns to the one is precisely the time of entering nirvana.
This concludes the demonstration. What follows consists merely of the textual sections, which, according to the text, comprise six parts.
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to his relics.
The first line generally indicates the construction of stupas after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha constructing various stūpas and temples, as numerous as the sands of countless Ganges Rivers, adorning the realms.
This second line clarifies the number of stūpas.
The precious stupa was lofty and sublime, five thousand yojanas in height, and exactly two thousand yojanas in both length and breadth.
This third line clarifies the dimensions of the stupa.
Each stupa and temple has a thousand banners and streamers, with jeweled lattices and canopies, and precious bells chiming in harmony.
This fourth line clarifies the characteristics of the stupas. The Sanskrit term *stūpa* is translated here as "square mound" (*fāng fén*). A square mound is like a tomb or burial site in this land;
the *Mahā-abhiṣeka* (Great Consecration) tradition translates it as "tomb. The halls and pavilions are like sacred edifices in this land; they are lofty.
The terraces are steep and the steps ascend; the dew-receiving pinnacles touch the clouds. These long monuments mark the pure realm, intended solely for those whose minds aspire to the Supreme Sage.
It is newly called *stūpa*, which here means a "highly manifest place," specifically the site where the bodily remains are enshrined.
The various devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans constantly make offerings with incense, flowers, and music.
This fifth section clarifies these offerings. It is because the stūpa enshrines the physical remains that those who offer worship gain great merit;
this is not the same as the case of images installed in halls or shrines. Thus, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the Buddha was approaching parinirvāṇa, there was...
The bhikṣu Brahmamā stood before the Buddha, holding a fan and fanning him. The Buddha said, "Step back; do not stand before me. Ānanda thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu has constantly attended upon the Buddha, serving him without weariness.
Now that his service is required for the very last time, for what reason does the Buddha have him dismissed? The Buddha told Ānanda: "Now, in the city of Kuśinagara..."
[The space was] twelve *yojanas* wide, yet the various devas crowded it to the point of obstruction. They resented this bhikṣu standing before the Buddha, thinking:
"Now, at this final moment, all the heavenly deities and others desire to make offerings;

yet this bhikṣu possesses such great majestic power that his radiance eclipses us, preventing us from drawing near to pay our respects. Therefore, we shall cause him to withdraw. Ānanda then addressed the Buddha.
"For what reason does this bodily radiance exist? The Buddha said: "During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, with a joyful heart, he held a torch in his hand and illuminated that Buddha-stūpa.
Because of this, his body came to possess such radiance, reaching as far as the twenty-eighth heaven. As for the bodily radiance, it did not reach that height;
since this was the case for illumination by fire, all other instances may be understood accordingly. This is the place where the śarīra resides."

The merit of such an act is not slight; yet the sin born of arrogance is among the greatest of sins. There are many such instances throughout the various sutras, though they are not the primary subject here.
I have briefly recounted one such occasion to inspire faith, rather than listing them all in detail.
Mañjuśrī, for the sake of making offerings to the śarīras, the sons of the Buddha adorn the stūpas and temples;
the realms of the land become naturally extraordinary and wondrously beautiful, like the king of celestial trees with its flowers in full bloom.
The sixth pair of verses concludes the section on offerings and so forth. As for the "celestial tree," it refers to the Pārijātaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
The intent of the sūtra is primarily to offer [relics], while incidentally adorning the realm; were it merely to adorn the realm, it would not be so.
"Why is it necessary to erect a stupa? However, in the six preceding lines, we all witnessed signs of his parinirvāṇa; thus we know that the Buddha has already entered nirvana.
Although we saw him enter nirvana, we do not understand why he spoke as he did prior to this. At that time, the assembly could not reach a decision and could not fathom the underlying reason.
Unlike the ancients who feared it might interfere with the Buddha's lifespan, they simply proceeded to construct the stupa.

Explanation of the Buddha-activities: Furthermore, since we have already seen two *sūtras* prior to this, the principles of both the Great and Small Vehicles are fully established; thus, there should be no need for further exposition.
From the beginning of the verse up to this point, fifty-four lines of verse conclude the description of the six auspicious omens in both lands.
Below this, from "The Buddha emitted... onwards, the second section consists of eight lines. This is divided into two parts: the first three [lines]...
The first five lines raise a point of doubt and request an explanation; the subsequent five lines resolve potential objections. Within the initial raising of the matter, there are three parts:
the Buddha emits a single ray of light, and I, along with the assembled multitude, behold this realm in all its various wonders and excellences.

This first line cites the events observed within this land. The white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa) serves as the basis; since the white tuft symbolizes the center and is the foundation of all dharmas, it is mentioned first.
Furthermore, because various other phenomena are seen, the term "various" (*nānāvidha*) is used. Question: It is simply stated that the Buddha emits a single ray of light and one sees this realm;
how does this ever relate to the other five auspicious omens? Answer: It is by means of the light that the places [of those omens] are seen.
The various elements of the national realm are all wondrous; one should know that light is the fundamental source of this excellence.
How much more so, then, are all auspicious omens, which likewise take the center as their basis—light itself being the center. It is the same for other lands by virtue of this light.
The spiritual power and wisdom of all Buddhas are rare and marvelous; they emit a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands.
This first line cites the matter of beholding other lands. "All Buddhas" as the fundamental principle subsumes the remaining five [lines].
By saying "all Buddhas," one part is cited to manifest the whole, specifically referring to Śākyamuni. "Spiritual power and wisdom" refers to the light itself.

This is the fundamental [principle]. "Rare" (*āścarya*) is an expression of formal praise. Prior to this, it was not so; therefore, it is called "rare. It is due to two matters that its light is pure.
When it says "emitting one pure ray of light," this praises the essence of the light. The subsequent phrase praises its function: the lands it illuminates.
Because they exceed eighteen thousand, they are termed "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*); thus, a specific number was established previously, which follows what is symbolized.
Moreover, the illumination of all directions is likewise so; therefore, it is called "immeasurable.
We have seen this and attained what we have never experienced before. O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, we pray that you resolve the doubts of the assembly.
This single line is the formal request for an answer. The first two phrases reiterate that which is illuminated, praising it as surpassing the ordinary.
The following two phrases cite the title of the vision to request the answer. "To see this" refers to the auspicious signs of the two lands;

because these differ from those of a single transformation, they are called "unprecedented. Since they are distinct from the flattery of the mundane, what is unprecedented cannot be false. "O sons of the Buddhas," etc. [is the address].
Doubtful matters are not to be taken lightly; therefore, I re-open this inquiry. This is not for the sake of asserting my own views, which is why I speak of "the assembly.
Based on this request for impartiality, the initial refutation by Mañjuśrī arises. The request says: "O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, we pray that you resolve the doubts of the assembly.
Mañjuśrī, following this, initiates the initial refutation: "You say there are doubts in the assembly, yet the assembly has never doubted. If they were to doubt..."
One should ask: "The assembly remains silent and harbors doubts; how can I resolve them? Thus, he questions Maitreya. Section Two:
Resolving Anticipated Objections, divided into two parts. First, four lines provide the direct resolution of the objections. Second, one line requests an answer.
Regarding the phrase "subduing the objection": Mañjuśrī internally formulated an objection and was unwilling to answer immediately. His intention was threefold:
first, this auspicious omen was rare and extraordinary; it could not be hastily or lightly adjudicated, as the significance of this great matter is profound and far-reaching.
Second, the assembly of wisdom is like the ocean; it maintains a spirit of humility and deference, acting as a supportive influence to inspire and encourage others.

Third, it restrains itself and withdraws slightly, thereby generating a sense of longing and veneration among the multitude, so as to protect and sustain both the assembly of those ready for the teaching and the assembly of those who form karmic connections.
The first two meanings together establish the third. It was for this reason that Mañjuśrī suppressed the objection and declined the invitation in a subtle manner. This is the text.
This is an especially difficult point of meaning. Maitreya clearly elucidates this difficulty, and his intent therein is threefold. First, the auspicious signs were great and the doubts were great;
if they were not resolved, anxiety would remain in their hearts, hindering them from hearing the True Dharma. Second, the assembly was as vast as the ocean.
The initiative rests with you, O Benevolent One. Since the entire assembly looks to you, we know that your sincere devotion is profound;
therefore, you have spoken these words to resolve our difficulties. We pray that you will grant us an answer at this time. This concludes the intended meaning of the text.
"The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy and gazes upon both you and me. World-Honored One, for what reason do you emit this radiance?

This single line represents Mañjuśrī’s initial resolution of the objection following Maitreya’s superior formal request. The previous section resolved the objection by stating that the assembly has no further doubts;
now, [Mañjuśrī] explains: "The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy and gazes upon both you and me. Regarding "and me," he intends to say: "I wish to..."
"Allow me to question you; I look to you, O Benevolent One, for your answer. This concludes the resolution of the first objection. Thereupon Mañjuśrī raised a second objection:
"The assembly all share this doubt; it is not easy to answer. We shall wait until the Buddha emerges from his meditative concentration, and then we shall resolve our doubts ourselves."
The Buddha’s son should answer at the proper time, resolving doubts and bringing joy. What benefit is there in manifesting this radiance?
Maitreya uses this second verse to resolve the aforementioned difficulty. If one harbors doubts in the heart, anxiety will not be dispelled;
therefore, one should answer at the proper time. Since it is unknown when the Tathāgata will arise from his meditative absorption, he is called "the Buddha’s son."
The response at that time was a word of exhortation, intended to prompt an immediate answer, resolve doubts, and bring joy.
Because Mañjuśrī had thus explained it, a third preliminary objection arose: "I and you both dwell on the stage of training; we wish to fathom the Buddha."
"Let us deliberate together; it is unreasonable for me alone to answer.
Is the Buddha, seated at the site of enlightenment, intending to preach this sublime Dharma, or is he about to bestow a prophecy?"
Maitreya then used this third verse to resolve the aforementioned third objection, saying:
"I too am a youth of humble mind, hesitating between the two pillars as to whether [the Buddha] will preach the wondrous Dharma or bestow a prophecy.

Therefore, it is said that regarding the wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment, he intends either to preach it or to bestow a prophecy. Because Mañjuśrī had raised this question based on this explanation, he arose.
The fourth objection: If it is as you say, then this itself resolves the doubt; why trouble yourself to provide an answer?
To manifest the various Buddha-lands, adorned and purified with myriad jewels, and to cause one to behold the Buddhas—this is no small matter.
Maitreya then uses this fourth verse to resolve the aforementioned fourth objection. The intent of the resolution is this:
how can you judge such a momentous matter based on my own state of hesitation? Therefore, he says, "He manifests various Buddha-lands; this is no small cause."
When Wenshu’s challenges were exhausted, Kuangguang also ceased. These four challenges were received by Kuangzhai from his immediate predecessor;
that predecessor received them from Master Zhao of the North of the River. Since these are the ingenious insights beyond the literal text of former sages, the present-day Tiantai masters employ them.
"Mañjuśrī, you should know that the fourfold assembly, the nāgas, and the spirits are all gazing upon you, venerable one, to hear what you will say.
With this single line of verse, Maitreya once again summarizes his request for an answer. This begins from the words: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya..."
Having concluded the desire to resolve one's own doubts, the fourth section, the Preface of the Questions, is finished.

△ From the passage beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī said to Maitreya" down to the end of the verses, it is called the Preface of the Answers to the Questions. This consists of both prose and verse; the prose is divided into four parts:
first, from "said" downwards, it is called the Answer by Reflection; second, from "Good son, since I... downwards, it is called the Brief [Answer].

The first is the "Answer Based on What Was Previously Seen. The second, from "From all wholesome [deeds] below," is called the "Extensive Answer Based on What Was Previously Seen. The fourth, from "What I now see below," is called the "Clear and Definitive Judgmental Answer.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and the various great beings, as well as the good sons...
"O disciples, as I reflect upon this, it is a reflection that serves as a thematic heading. Generally, when using the lower to fathom the higher, one can only arrive at a vague approximation;

comparing the past with the present, one cannot reach a definitive conclusion all at once. Therefore, one begins from a state of resemblance. 'Wei' (惟) means contemplation; 'con' (忖) means to deliberate."

"Contemplation" (*cintā*) means to deliberate. "The present is like the past; the past is like the present. Yet, how could Mañjuśrī, an ancient Buddha, not know that he was merely manifesting traces through contemplation?
This is an answer by way of deliberation, responding to the question posed above regarding this land.
Therefore, with the following five lines of text, he first repays the six doubts raised in the introduction.
Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, desires to proclaim the Great Dharma, to rain down the great Dharma-rain, to blow the great Dharma-conch, to beat the great Dharma-drum,
and to expound the meaning of the Great Dharma.

This section specifically concerns the response through contemplation. It answers the six auspicious signs of the preceding "Trace Gate. Regarding the phrase "desiring to preach the Great Dharma," this answers the auspicious sign of preaching the Dharma.
[The Bodhisattva] contemplates that in the past, all Buddhas preached the *Infinite Meanings* and subsequently revealed the provisional to manifest the real, subsuming the infinite within the one.
He considers that since the present Buddha has already preached the Dharma, he too must now reveal the provisional to manifest the real, bringing together the infinite...

All measures are unified in the One; this One is the Great Dharma. Regarding the "showering of the rain of the Great Dharma," this answers the previous mention of the auspicious omen of the falling flowers.

This refers to how, following the ancient Buddhas' descent of the four kinds of flowers from heaven, [beings] universally entered the perfect cause and proceeded through the stages of abiding, practicing, advancing, and the grounds.

I reflect that following the present Buddha’s raining of flowers, all these have become causes for attaining Buddhahood. Just as the heavens are neither small nor large, neither red nor white, yet they rain down red and white flowers;
so too is the ultimate truth (paramārtha): it is not something to be opened, shown, awakened to, or entered. When one perceives this principle, [one realizes it].
This constitutes the realization, elucidation, awakening, and entry [into the Dharma]. It is like a seed that sprouts upon receiving rain;
now, hearing the great rain of the Dharma, it moistens the seeds of the *dharmatā*, shatters the husks of ignorance, and opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Previously, when the flowers rained down, they already symbolized the four stages of the perfect cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) that were to be taught; thus, these four are not the fruit. Considering today’s raining of flowers...

The four rains represent the single cause that brings about the assembly at this time. This single cause must necessarily have the four stages as its basis. The four rains take the Heaven of Dharma (Dharmākāśa) as their manifesting agent.
As for "blowing the great dharma-conch," this answers the auspicious omen of the great joy in the hearts of the assembly above.

In the past, when the fourfold assembly saw such omens, their hindrances were removed through joy; their spiritual capacities were activated, and they immediately transformed their human teachings and practices according to the principle. Reflecting on this now...
The assembly rejoices. They should likewise obstruct the movement of their faculties and transform human teaching, practice, and principle.
Since that which is transformed is profound, it is called the "Great Dharma Conch. For example, by blowing a conch, one knows it is a changed signal;

so too, those who previously attained the Ten Abodes now hear the Dharma and undergo transformation, entering the Ten Practices and manifesting the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. With joy moving within their hearts, they become perfect.

The darkness of hindrances is destroyed; those who were formerly provisional beings are transformed into the present wondrous assembly. It is said that they strike the great Dharma drum, answering the auspicious sign of the earth’s trembling above.

Considering that since the previous earthquake there have been six occasions of shattering the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*), one should infer that following this present earthquake of the Buddha-ground, there shall likewise be six occasions of shattering the delusions of ignorance. Because the sound of the teaching is supremely wondrous, it is so stated.
The great drum: for example, when a drum is struck, one knows it is a warning to the troops. Now, as in the past, we have already been in the Ten Practices;

having heard the Dharma-warnings and entered into Dedication, we have awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Thus, we know that the warning to the troops must destroy the great rebels on the borders.
Since the shaking of the earth removes the ignorance within the fundamental principle, whereas the Two Vehicles have from the beginning lacked this principle entirely.
The profound benefit within the introduction was unknown to the assembly at that time. To answer the preceding omen of the emission of light, the expounder of the Great Dharma’s meaning stated:
"In the past, all Buddhas emitted white-hair light and subsequently preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; the paths of these [Buddhas] are identical.
He then inferred from the present Buddha’s emission of light that the five Buddhas share the same path, and further elaborated upon this through wide-ranging and profound discourse. Thus...
This is the exposition of the meaning. From now until then, [the practitioner] has already been in the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).

Furthermore, by hearing the Dharma again, they proceed from the Abodes into the Grounds (*bhūmi*), entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), exhausting the source of ignorance, and reaching the limits of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, it becomes profoundly deep and vast, fully perfected.

Moreover, reflecting that the present is the same as the past, one perceives that the manifestation of light already signifies that the path of revelation is identical. Therefore, with a single ray of light, both this and that are illuminated simultaneously. This...
This represents Śākyamuni; that represents the four Buddhas. Since this is the path of the Buddha, it is said that "the great Dharma and its meaning are expounded.
These five phrases all involve judging the present by means of the past and inferring the present from the past, harmonizing the text with the underlying meaning.

With the sole exception of the single auspicious sign of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), phenomena such as the raining of flowers, the shaking of the earth, and the emission of light all occur because of entering meditative concentration. This is the intended meaning.
Both [aspects] are present; there is no need for doubt. However, this initial deliberation is a response. The Great Sage’s deliberation does not involve mere idle speculation.
One should know that this initial deliberation serves as the foundation for both the concise and the extensive responses.

Therefore, Maitreya contemplates the auspicious signs to formulate his doubts, while Mañjuśrī attaches to those doubts to deliberate upon them. Thus, he reflects upon the Buddhas of the past and the present.

Regarding these six auspicious signs (*śakuna*), one should contemplate them in relation to the three subsequent cycles of the Buddha’s auspicious signs. Therefore, the answer below is given in both detailed and abbreviated forms, revealing the intended meaning according to the specific occasion;
this constitutes the skeletal framework of this sutra. Question: What is the difference between the two phrases "Great Dharma" (*mahādharma*) and "Dharma-meaning" (*dharmārtha*)?
Answer: "Great Dharma" signifies the revelation and manifestation [of the truth] within this land. "Dharma-meaning" signifies that the Way is identical here and there. This is the illumination.

In that [state], it is identical to this; therefore, it is called "expounding. These are all unprecedented within a single lifetime. It is clear that there is a basis for the answers given to the questions.
One should know that among the five phrases of the sutra, the first phrase is the general statement (*sāmānya*), while the latter four phrases are the specific details (*viśeṣa*).
As for the general statement, it refers to the "Great Dharma" (*mahādharma*). Since the following four phrases are all the Great Dharma, one knows that the latter four serve to establish the first.

This is the general summary of the phrases. As for the specific terms, they are "raining," "blowing," "striking," and "expanding," which correspond to "opening," "showing," "awakening," and "entering.
These terms such as "raining" specifically refer to that Great Dharma, causing [beings] to enter and abide therein; because they correspond to the four stages, they are called "specific.

However, in my humble opinion, these four specifically correspond to the stages of abiding (*vihāra*), practice (*caryā*), orientation (*mukha*), and ground (*bhūmi*). This is stated from the perspective of the vertical progression (*ūrdhva-artha*). If one considers each [stage] individually...
Each stage is discussed in terms of its horizontal and vertical dimensions; within each stage, from beginning to end, these are inherently complete. The raining of flowers symbolizes the four stages;
the blowing of the conch universally symbolizes the transformation across the four stages; the beating of the drum likewise universally symbolizes the fourfold destruction of delusions;

and the preaching of the Dharma encompasses both the horizontal and vertical, the profound and the vast, spanning everything from the initial raining of flowers to the ultimate meaning of the Dharma, with each element pervading all.

The迹门 (Ji-men) provides an extensive exposition; every sentence contains the intent to cause sentient beings to attain the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, such that a single stage is fully endowed with all stages.
Nevertheless, from the perspective of a vertical explanation, one may provisionally speak of "gaining benefit through hearing the Dharma" according to the differences in realization.

Now, from the perspective of entering and abiding, it is provisionally termed "the rain of Dharma," and even up to the entry into the [Bodhisattva] stages, it is provisionally termed "the meaning of the Dharma."
"O sons of good family, in the past I have seen this omen among the Buddhas of former times: after emitting such light, they would immediately preach the Great Dharma.

This refers to the brief past vision cited by Mañjuśrī as an answer to the question regarding other lands.
However, the five auspicious omens of this land do not apply to other lands; only the single omen of emitting light shines universally upon the eastern direction.

The protagonist said: "Therefore, we know that what was previously briefly seen and answered specifically concerns the *Prabhāsa* (Emitting Light) [Sūtra].

It is good. One who is capable of hearing the uniquely wondrous [Dharma] is called a "man" (nara). A man is precisely a "great man" (mahāpuruṣa); it refers to one who is able to perceive the Buddha-nature.

"Hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), and "knowing" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). These are the hearing and reflection that open up and reveal [the truth]; therefore, it is said to be difficult to believe.
The two types of wisdom must both be cultivated. As the subsequent text states: "If one hears this sutra, one contemplates and practices it.
Hearing and knowing is also the practice of the rain of Dharma. Regarding the entire body of this text, any discussion of entering the Dharma does not go beyond these two practices.
Through the two types of wisdom, one enters the various stages; for each of the two practices must possess the three types of wisdom. What, then, is hearing and knowing?
Is this the meaning of the Dharma? Indeed, "hearing and knowing that the immeasurable is gathered into the one" corresponds to the aforementioned intent of the Great Dharma;

"hearing and knowing that the teachings and principles of the three vehicles are transformed" corresponds to the aforementioned ten practices of the Dharma Conch; and "hearing and knowing that ignorance is shattered six times" [corresponds to the aforementioned stages].

"Immediately ascending to the Ten Directions of the Dharma Drum"; furthermore, hearing that the paths of all Buddhas are identical is "immediately ascending to the Ten Stages of the Great Dharma Meaning";

and hearing the revelation and instruction and so forth is "immediately ascending to the Ten Abodes of the Dharma Rain. Thus, one should know that this is a brief restatement of what was previously contemplated.
It refers comprehensively to all stages as opening up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, it is said: "difficult for all the world to believe."
Dharma. One should know that this is a pearl difficult to believe, for it was only after more than forty years that [the Buddha] finally attained faith and understanding.

For what reason is the present text pointed to as "that," while the preceding is pointed to as "this"? It is truly because, upon reflection, there are words of the present Buddha, yet there were also brief mentions of the past;
thus, by means of the present, "this" is indicated, and by means of the past, "that" is indicated. If this is so, then [the passage] regarding the extensive [past]...
There are also words concerning the past. Why are these two expressed together? However, within the extensive [explanation], the three similarities are fully described to manifest this point;
furthermore, there are words concerning the past to indicate the other [land]. △ From "These good sons" down to "your own body is it," this section of the sūtra constitutes the third part:
the extensive account of what was previously seen, answering the question regarding this land and other lands.
Regarding this question: [Manjushri] again cited what he had previously seen in the *Guang* (Extensive) version as his answer, which was even clearer than the brief version.

At that time there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,

Concentration and wisdom are virtues for one's own practice; the lamp-light is a virtue for transforming others. Because the Buddha of Benevolence (*Nengren*) possesses both concentration and wisdom, and can act for both self and others, he is identical [to the others].
Furthermore, the sun, moon, and lamp represent the three types of knowledge (*trividya*); the present Buddha likewise possesses these three knowledges.

While they are designated differently according to conditions, their essential meaning does not differ; therefore, it is said that their names are the same. If this is so, what Buddha lacks the concentration, wisdom, and three knowledges? Why [is it said that] only...

One might ask: Is the Lamp-Light Buddha (Dīpaṃkara) the same as Śākyamuni? While other Buddhas may indeed possess these same qualities, they do not equal the clarity of the meaning found in the case of Lamp-Light.

Why is this? As it says in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, when Dṛḍhamati asked about the lifespan [of the Buddha], the Buddha sent him to the east, past thirty-two thousand Buddha-fields, where there was a Buddha named Illuminating Adornment Sovereign King (Prabhāsa-vyūha-vaśavartin-rāja). [The section] concludes. Ānanda said: "As I understand what the Buddha has taught, that Buddha is merely another name for Śākyamuni.

These ten titles are the ten titles of the single essence and three bodies (yītǐ sānshēn); one must further distinguish their specific characteristics by analyzing them according to the various teachings (jiào).

He expounds the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is exquisite, it is pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life of Brahma-faring.
This is the first Buddha; the third turning of the wheel of Dharma is the same. This is because the former Buddhas likewise taught suddenly at first and gradually thereafter, all within five periods.
Regarding the "proclamation of the True Dharma, good in the beginning, middle, and end," this refers to the seven excellences of the sudden teaching during the period of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Now, as for the expression "seven excellences," it applies generally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; if one follows the perspective of the Buddha’s wisdom, they are identical.

It should be said that these are the seven virtues of the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*). Regarding the so-called "virtues of the beginning, middle, and end," these refer to the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination of the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*);
they are thus termed the "virtues of the occasion. Their meaning is profound and far-reaching; they constitute the definitive principle (*nītārtha*) of the Sudden Teaching.
The followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fathom its limits or depths; therefore, it is called "profound and far-reaching. This is the second excellence of meaning (*artha-saṃpanna*).
Its phrasing is skillful and subtle, being uttered from the eightfold voice of the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*). It directly explains the principle and delights the minds of Bodhisattvas;

thus, it is the text of the Sudden Teaching, named the third excellence of speech (*vyañjana-saṃpanna*). It is pure and without admixture, not shared with the followers of the Two Vehicles. This is...

The fourth [stage] of the Sudden Teaching is the excellence of being solitary and unique. "Endowed with" means being fully possessed of the teachings of the full letters (*pūrṇākṣara*) both within and beyond the realm of phenomena;

this is the fifth [stage], the excellence of the perfection of the Sudden Teaching. "Pure and white, free from the defilements of the two extremes" refers to the sixth [stage], the excellence of the flexibility and gentleness of the Sudden Teaching.
"The characteristics of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)" refers to the seventh [stage], the excellence of the Sudden Teaching without...

This is because it is based on compassion. This is precisely the same as what was first taught at the very beginning; it is the same as the answer given to Maitreya regarding how the Buddhas of other lands first teach the sudden Dharma.
For those who seek to become śrāvakas, he teaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to deliver them from birth, old age, sickness, and death, leading them ultimately to nirvana. For...

For those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination; for the Bodhisattvas, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the six *pāramitās*.
This is identical to the gradual teaching established after the initial sudden [teaching] of the ancient Buddhas. It does not clarify the directions [of the teachings].
What is meant by "the Prajñāpāramitā and its equals"? It is simply that they are modeled after the six pāramitās; this is merely a brief version of the two *sūtra* texts.
Regarding the previous question about those who encounter suffering and so forth, the present passage cites ancient Buddhas as also opening this gradual path to answer that question.
Next, citing those who seek the state of a *pratyekabuddha* and so forth, it answers the aforementioned question regarding those who possess merit.
Next, citing [the teachings] for the sake of the various Bodhisattvas and others, this answers the aforementioned question regarding the sons of the Buddha practicing various deeds.
This citation of the ancient Buddhas’ preaching, extending up to the *pāramitās* and so forth, clarifies that the present is identical to the past—this is the second *sūtra*.

Regarding these six *abhijñās* (supernormal knowledges) being called *pāramitās*: these are all terms from the Western land [India]. In the translations of the *sūtras* and *śāstras* made during the Qin period, there are many differences.

Briefly stated, there are three translations: some say "the ultimate fulfillment of the matter" (*shijiujing*), some say "reaching the other shore" (*dào bī'àn*), and some say "transcendence without limit" (*dù wújí*).

What is meant by "the ultimate fulfillment of the matter"? It means that when a bodhisattva cultivates these six dharmas, they are able to ultimately fulfill both the general and specific [aspects of] the *abhijñās*.
It plants the seeds of cause and effect; it encompasses all matters of self-cultivation and the transformation of others. Therefore, it is said that "the task is consummated.
Because the Bodhisattva accomplishes these six dharmas, they are able to cross from this shore of the two kinds of birth-and-death to the other shore of the two kinds of nirvana.
By means of these six dharmas, the Bodhisattva is able to traverse the vast expanse of all phenomena—the two kinds of principle and fact, both general and specific.
"Far-reaching. Therefore, it is called "Pāramitā" (Going Beyond). These are the threefold translations of the name and meaning according to the sūtras and śāstras.

First, regarding *dāna-pāramitā*: why is *dāna* called *pāramitā*? In Sanskrit it is called *dāna*; in the language of Qin (Chinese), it means "generosity" (*bōshī*). This refers to the convergence of three factors:
internally there is faith, externally there is a field of merit, and furthermore, there are material goods. When these three things come together, the mind gives rise to [the act of giving].
The practice of relinquishment (*tyāga-dharma*). That which destroys the dharma of stinginess and greed is called *dāna* (giving). It is said that there are two kinds of giving:

first, the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣa-dāna*), namely the four requisites; one is able to give away whatever is required, including wife, children, and even one’s own body and life—all these are termed the gift of material wealth.
Second, the gift of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), namely [that which is received] from the Buddhas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), or from the scriptures.
The treatise, along with its own contemplative practice, states that the mind cognizes the mundane and supramundane dharmas through hearing and seeing.
With a pure mind, the Bodhisattva expounds for others the practice of the equality of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa-samatā*). These two types of practice are called *dāna*.
As for *pāramitā*, the translation of the name is as previously explained. Because the Bodhisattva, with a pure and straightforward mind, [proceeds] at...
Among the perfections, because one is able to fully cultivate five kinds of mind, giving is called a *pāramitā*. What are these five? First, knowing the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of giving:
if the three things—the person who gives, the person who receives, and the material object—are all empty and unobtainable, one enters the correct contemplation of the true mark;
thus, by means of the dharma of non-renunciation, one is able to renounce according to what others require.
1. Not being stingy is called knowing the true nature (*dharmatā*) of giving. 2.

It is called "arousing a mind of compassion" because although a bodhisattva knows the true nature of giving—that nothing exists—they nevertheless arouse great compassion, desiring to bestow all happiness and uproot all suffering through this giving;
this is called "arousing a mind of compassion. 3. It is called "making a vow" at the time of giving.

To wish that by means of this giving one may attain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood, and not seek the fruits of retribution of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles, is called "making a vow.
Fourth, "dedication" (pariṇāmanā) refers to the act of dedicating the merit of whatever is given, at the time of giving, toward *sarvajñā* (omniscience) and toward all sentient beings;
this is called dedication. Fifth is "endowment with skillful means," which is as follows:
To be able to revolve and penetrate all Buddha-dharmas through the single dharma of giving, and to universally cultivate all practices, is called being "endowed with skillful means.

If one can fulfill these five mental states, then at that time, whatever is given, it is called "the fruit within the cause," and is also termed "the culmination of the task," "reaching the other shore," and "the infinite transcendence" (pāramitā). This is a bodhisattva.
Because one practices giving, it is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of the *dāna-pāramitā*.
Only when one reaches the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood is this *dāna-pāramitā* fully perfected. Second is *śīla*, third is *kṣānti*, fourth is *vīrya*, fifth is *dhyāna*, and sixth is *prajñā*;
each has its respective translated name and five types of mental states, all of which are *pāramitās*.

This has been explained in detail within the section on the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), though the specific characteristics have not been fully set forth there. These six [perfections] must further be analyzed and determined according to the various scriptural divisions (*nikāya*) and teachings,
so that one may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This citation demonstrates that the ancient Buddhas were identical to [the present Buddha] in their gradual approach. It refers to the teaching of the ancient Buddhas who first opened the way for the sudden and the gradual, and subsequently revealed the ultimate reality;

it concerns the beginning, middle, and end of their practice until its final consummation. This answers Maitreya’s previous question regarding the construction of stupas after seeing the Nirvana of the Buddhas in other lands.
That is to say, the present Buddha shall be the same as those of the past. This, then, cites the very first of the ancient Buddhas.

The Dharma they taught was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end.
This passage cites twenty thousand Buddhas and also answers Maitreya’s prior question regarding the names and titles of their teachings; all are identical to those of the first Buddha.

Gradually. Since it was thus for the Buddhas of the past, we know by verification that other lands do not exceed eighteen thousand; this is because beyond this number, they are not the same.

When that last Buddha was still a layman, he had eight princes: the first was named Meaningful Intent; the second, Good Intent; the third, Immeasurable Intent;
