When the princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all renounced their royal thrones and likewise followed him into the homeless life.
They resolved upon the Mahāyāna, constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and all became Dharma-preachers.
They had already planted the roots of various virtues under ten million Buddhas.
This refers to the third and final Buddha. The opening [of the teaching] gradually becomes identical [to that of the previous Buddhas].
This section concerns the "sons," clarifying that in the past he was once the eight sons of the present Buddha; this is the meaning of the gradual unfolding.

As for not clarifying the sudden [teaching], if one follows the precedent of the first Buddha and the twenty thousand Buddhas, then the meaning of the threefold identity is sufficient. The eight sons of the former Buddha are now...

The Buddha has but one son; though their numbers differ, they all emerge from and dwell together in the Land of Shared Residence (*sābhāsasāmbhogika-kṣetra*). Since this land contains both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), he manifests having sons in both cases.

While the fact of having sons is the same, there is a distinction between the "one" and the "eight" based on their response to conditions. Producing "one son" symbolizes the purity of the Single Path (*ekamārga*).

He fathered eight sons, which symbolize the Eightfold Noble Path; the significance of "taking" [a wife] and having sons is the same. However, in the past, the disciples of the Buddha left the household life having already resolved upon the Mahāyāna;
now, the disciples of the Buddha leave the household life abiding in the fruits of the Hīnayāna. How can these two be the same? Answer:

In the past, the work of transformation and guidance was completed, and the original state was revealed; therefore, it is said they "resolved upon the Mahāyāna. Now, their true origins have not yet been disclosed, and thus...

this translates as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment. "Renouncing the royal throne" refers to renouncing the position of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*). [Brahma...]

Practice refers to the practice and vows of the six pāramitās. After attaining the Way, he expounded the teachings according to the capacities of beings using the methods of his own practice, guiding and benefiting humans and devas.
The four great vows are the very essence of the Mahāyāna. This clarifies that what he had previously seen is identical to what is now [the case].
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Anantārtha*, the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas,
which is protected by the Buddhas. Having finished preaching this sūtra, he sat cross-legged in the midst of the great assembly and entered the *Anantārthavyūha-samādhi*,
remaining with body and mind unmoving.
This is precisely the ancient Buddhas sharing with this land the pair of wisdom and meditative concentration.

At that time, it rained *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, which were scattered upon the Buddha and the great assembly. The entire Buddha-world shook in six ways.
This is precisely the pair of cause and effect shared by the ancient Buddhas with this land.
At that time, in the assembly were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all others.

The minor kings, the wheel-turning sage-kings, and all these great assemblies attained what they had never experienced before; with joy, they joined their palms and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
This constitutes the first pair of responses between the ancient Buddhas and this land.

From this point, beginning with the appearance of the sun and ending with these three pairs of texts, all are instances where Mañjuśrī cites ancient Buddhas who shared the same six auspicious omens as those of the present Buddha.

The six omens manifested by the Buddhas of the past in their own lands were entirely identical to the omens of the present Buddha. A detailed explanation of these six omens for the assembly is as provided previously.
It illuminated eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception, just as these various Buddha-lands are seen now.
This is Mañjuśrī’s citation of the six auspicious omens from the other lands of past Buddhas, which are identical to those of the present Buddha.

By stating generally that they are "just as seen now," one knows that the six auspicious omens in the other lands of past Buddhas were also the same as those of the present. The above clarifies those [omens] of the ancient Buddhas.
These six auspicious omens are the same [as those previously described].
Maitreya, you should know that at that time, within the assembly, there were twenty billion bodhisattvas who desired to hear the Dharma.
When these bodhisattvas saw this radiance universally illuminating the Buddha-field, they experienced what they had never known before and wished to understand the purpose of this light.
Regarding the "Causes and Conditions" (Nidāna):
this clarifies that the ancient Buddhas harbored doubts in their introductory sections, which is the same as the present case here in this land.

However, while the Buddhas of the past clearly possessed distinct introductory sections—namely, the two sections on manifesting auspicious signs and harboring doubts—their texts lacked the three sections consisting of the assembly gathering, the posing of questions, and the answering of questions. This is the meaning [of the difference].

If one infers, they must exist. Since it speaks of "expounding the Dharma," one knows that a gathering of the assembly must necessarily take place. Since it mentions "suspicion arising," one should know that there must be questions. If there are questions, there must be answers;
however, by following the pattern of the two introductory sections (*nidāna*), the three introductory sections are simultaneously accounted for.

Furthermore, if it were recounting a past answer, there would have been no need for Mañjuśrī to expend his words. Since it does not state an answer, nor does it present a question, it is simply because [the text] does not record them.

In the past, he replied using his own words, fully recounting the beginning and end of the matter. From the initial preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* until after its final extinction, and even up to the reconciliation of the assembly, he finally composed a summary, saying:
"Now I see this auspicious sign, which is no different from that of old," and so forth, until the verse says:
"I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; his original light and auspicious signs were like this. By this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the Dharma."
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other texts, he skillfully set forth his own views by benefiting beings according to their capacities; why then labor over further words?
From the preceding section up to this point, the account of Mañjuśrī’s past experiences has been concluded, showing them to be identical to the present.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Wondrous Light (Prabhāsa) who had eight hundred disciples;
from this section [of the sutra] down to "your own body," it refers to this very person. This clarifies that Mañjuśrī’s past experiences were identical to those of the present.
The text consists of six sections, explained as follows: this first section concerns the commonality of causes in the past with the causes of the present.
He was a human being. Formerly he relied upon Wonderful Light; now he relies upon Śāriputra. Thus, the persons upon whom he relies are indeed the same.

Furthermore, in the past, when the Buddha’s eight sons studied under Wonderful Light, the Tathāgata arose from meditative concentration and addressed Wonderful Light directly, even entrusting them to him.
Now, the Buddha’s disciple Rāhula also took Śāriputra as his teacher. When the Buddha arose from meditative concentration, he likewise addressed Śāriputra.

The section on the traces (jimen) and the parables are concluded; furthermore, [the Dharma] was entrusted to Śāriputra. Thus, the past and present are identical. This person of the past is the same as this person of the present.
It is not like the erroneous interpretations of the ancient masters. As for the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa, Śāriputra is his voice.

I have heard it said: "In what way are they the same? For while his past deeds were already manifest and he was spoken of as a Bodhisattva, his present activities had not yet emerged, and thus he was regarded as a Śrāvaka.
By the time his true station was revealed, Śāriputra was indeed a great Bodhisattva. What, then, does 'the same' mean?

You must practice with single-minded diligence and remain free from negligence; for Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter, appearing but once in ten million kalpas."
This verse should likewise include the entrustment (*parindanā*). Just as in this land there is the Bequeathed Teaching (*yījiào*), the entrustment is the same:
"The sons of the World-Honored One, hearing that the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, each harbors grief and affliction; how swift was the Buddha’s passing!"
This verse should be understood in the same way. There was weeping and wailing;

as in this land at the time of the *nirvāṇa*, the disciples’ eyes were filled with tears and blood appeared all over their bodies like *bālāka* flowers. This was because they held the Dharma in reverence and possessed the resolve of those who yearn for the [Buddha].
The Holy Lord, King of Dharma, comforts immeasurable multitudes: "When I enter parinirvāṇa, you should not feel sorrow or fear.
This single line is identical to the consolation offered in this land and is also like the *Teaching Left Behind* (Śāriputraparipṛcchā), which says:
"You bhikṣus, do not harbor grief or distress," up to the passage concerning the causes and conditions already established for attaining deliverance.
This Bodhisattva Guṇagañja has already attained thorough penetration into the outflow-free true mark (*anāsrava-lakṣaṇa*).
He shall next become a Buddha, named Viśuddhakāya, and he too shall deliver immeasurable multitudes of beings.
These one and a half lines are identical to the preceding verse regarding the account of the bestowal of relics.
That night, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted; his śarīras were distributed, and immeasurable stūpas were erected.
"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, their number like the sands of the Ganges, redoubled their diligence in seeking the unsurpassed path.

These two lines above commemorate the period after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa. Regarding the phrase "the fourfold assembly having already obtained benefit, like fire being extinguished when the fuel is exhausted":
in the Small Vehicle, the Buddha takes the *vipākakāya* (retribution body) as the fuel and wisdom as the fire; wisdom relies upon the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).

When the body perishes, wisdom vanishes. In the Mahāyāna, the Buddha takes the capacity of sentient beings as fuel and his responsive manifestation as fire; when birth is exhausted, the response ceases.
Those who redouble their diligence attain liberation through this cessation.
"This Dharma Master Wondrous Light upheld the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma.
These two lines above praise those who propagated the sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
"During eighty intermediate kalpas, he extensively proclaimed the Lotus Sutra."
This verse concerns the same period of time as when the former Buddha had passed into extinction and [the disciples] were traveling.
These eight princes, having been inspired and transformed by Prabhāsa, shall remain firm in the unsurpassed Way and shall behold countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all the Buddhas, they followed and practiced the Great Way; succeeding one another, they attained Buddhahood and were granted successive predictions of enlightenment.
Finally, there was a God among Gods named Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the guide of all sages, who delivered and liberated immeasurable multitudes.
The three lines above correspond to the verses concerning the disciples who have already attained benefit.
At that time, this Dharma Master Wondrous Light had a disciple whose mind was constantly filled with indolence and who was greedily attached to fame and profit.
Seeking fame and profit without satiety, he frequented the households of the noble clans. He abandoned what he had studied and recited, falling into forgetfulness so that his mastery was lost.
For these reasons, he was called "Seeker of Fame. Yet, he also performed many wholesome deeds and succeeded in seeing countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all Buddhas and practicing the Great Way in accordance with it, he has perfected the six *pāramitās*.
Now beholding the Lion of the Śākyas, he shall subsequently become a Buddha named Maitreya, who will extensively deliver sentient beings in numbers beyond measure.
These five lines above are a verse concerning those who were to become disciples, namely Maitreya.
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you were the one who was indolent. As for the Dharma Master Wonderful Light, he is my very self now.
This single line of verse is a summary of the preceding passage that reconciles the ancient and the modern.
△ The following four verses summarize the preceding section on the clear and definitive judgment; this text is divided into three parts. First, from "I see the lamp-light" onwards, there is one line.

The first two lines of the verse above correspond to the teaching of the Mahāyāna sūtras. Next, the two lines beginning with "Now the signs are as in the original omen" correspond to the teaching of the Dharma for bodhisattvas.
Next, the single line beginning with "All those seeking the three vehicles" corresponds to what was above regarding "the Buddha’s protective mindfulness";
this can be understood from the text itself. These subsequent four lines constitute the clear and definitive response to the question posed above.
This differs from previous works in that it does not conclude with a summary verse, nor does it include the prose commentary preceding the verses.

One should understand that the final four lines of verse encompass both meanings. When reaching the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below, it merely provides an explanation by Mañjuśrī regarding Maitreya’s four latent doubts.
What, then, are these four latent doubts? Furthermore, based on the preceding text concerning Bodhisattva Maitreya...
Having first concluded the explanation of the four types of anticipated objections (*pūrvapakṣa*) raised by Mañjuśrī—

thereby ensuring that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva would certainly provide an answer to dispel the doubts of the assembly— it is now, within this context, Mañjuśrī who recites these four verses to sever the four types of anticipated doubts held by Maitreya,
so that Maitreya shall no longer need to ask further questions. As for those four types of anticipated doubts, [the first] is Maitreya’s...
There are four types of doubt: first, doubt regarding the name; second, doubt regarding the essence underlying the name; third, doubt regarding the doctrine; and fourth, doubt regarding the function.

Now, as for the first, Maitreya’s doubt regarding the name: because the preceding prose section had extensively cited how previous Buddhas had previously preached the Lotus Sūtra and provided a clear, definitive response, Maitreya harbored a latent doubt and desired to ask:
"The various Buddhas respond to the capacities of conditions... [The text continues: "...conditions."

The times and circumstances of people differ. Although the Buddhas of antiquity were named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it was not yet known whether the present Śākyamuni, upon arising from his meditative concentration, would necessarily teach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the same manner.

This is because the preceding section provided a broad answer; thus, Maitreya doubts whether the name of the teaching delivered by the present Buddha upon arising from concentration will be identical [to that of the past]. This is the first resolution of doubt.
"I have seen the lamp-light Buddha; his original radiance was such as this. By this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
This single verse is by Mañjuśrī severing Maitreya’s latent doubts regarding its name. Because of this verse by Mañjuśrī, Maitreya severed his doubts concerning the name;
yet because of this, Maitreya further doubted the substance underlying the name, for there must be a substance to a name.
There is identity in essence, and there is also that which is called "identity in name but difference in essence.

I do not yet understand what the essence signified by this name "Buddha preaching the Lotus Sutra" is intended to manifest or summon. Maitreya’s subsequent doubt concerns this very essence underlying the name.

Now, the present signs are as originally auspicious; these are the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas. Now the Buddha emits a radiance to assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Mañjuśrī uses this single verse to sever Maitreya’s doubt regarding the substance underlying the name;

thus it is said, "to assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true mark," which is precisely the substance underlying the name. Because Maitreya has severed his doubt through this, he further entertains a doubt concerning that substance.
Regarding this doctrine: who among people has realized the true nature of reality?
All you people should now know: join your palms with single-minded devotion and wait; the Buddha shall rain down the rain of Dharma to satisfy those who seek the Way.
By means of this verse on "One Practice," Mañjuśrī severed Maitreya’s third latent doubt regarding his fundamental principle;
thus it says, "The Buddha shall rain down the rain of Dharma. Because of this, Maitreya again doubted its application:
does the Buddha’s rain of Dharma only moisten Bodhisattvas, or does it also nourish those of the Two Vehicles?
"For those who seek the three vehicles, if there are any who harbor doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them, so that they are exhausted without remainder.
Mañjuśrī used this single verse to sever Maitreya’s doubts; thus it says, "For those who seek the three vehicles," and so forth.
Yet, as Maitreya successively constructed his doubts and Mañjuśrī repeatedly severed them, the matter was brought to its conclusion and the principle was fully exhausted.
He immediately grasped this within his heart; one may truly say he was skilled in question and answer, possessing both forms of adornment.

Guangzhai only knew that the aforementioned Master Zhao explained the four types of suppressed difficulties regarding Maitreya and Mañjuśrī, causing Mañjuśrī to provide the answers and thereby manifesting the excellence of Maitreya;
yet he failed to see how, in this [present] passage, Mañjuśrī explains the four types of suppressed doubts regarding Maitreya, thereby...
If Maitreya had not asked, this meaning would not have been seen; that would have amounted to suppressing the capability of Miaode (Mañjuśrī).

Master Zhanran said: "The explanation of these four passages resolving latent doubts originates from Tiantai; it was not transmitted from another commentary. I entrust this message to future worthies."

Do not suppress the long-standing traditions of others. Since the time of Master Zhaolun, for several hundred years, those who have lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* have been so numerous that they overflowed the roads;
how could this be anything other than a long-standing tradition? This concludes the text of the separate introduction (*nidāna*).

However, as for the sentient beings during the Buddha’s own lifetime, did any among them obtain actual benefit upon hearing this separate introduction? Answer: In the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination [of the sūtra], all possess the conditions for seeds to ripen.

They are liberated from the three [obstructions] and obtain great benefit. This is because those who hear [the teaching] obtain the three benefits, such as the planting and ripening of seeds. Among the five sections of the introductory narrative (*nidāna*), each section possesses distinct benefits.
As it is said regarding the "Innumerable Meanings" (*Anantārtha*), they secretly obtain the three different benefits of planting seeds and so forth;

thus, one sees the light, awakens to movement, and receives the flowers, and even in the questions and answers, all contain the planting of seeds and so on, according to their long-standing [capacity].
From afar, we have been graced by the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Having converged with the causal conditions for the Buddha-way, we encountered one another midway;

furthermore, through diverse skillful means, he assisted in manifesting the primary truth (*paramārtha*) and brought us to maturity. That today flowers rain down and the earth trembles, and that he brings us to liberation through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata—this is precisely the manifestation of that.
If one were to say merely that this is the introduction and has not yet reached the discussion of the causal seeds, it would be incomplete.
Regarding "equal benefit": this refers to the sequence within the introduction concerning the seeds, etc., of the past and future causes and effects, as well as the preceding general introduction.
This concludes the introductory section (*nidāna*) of the entire major division.

Commentary by the Śramaṇa Daowei of Siming on the "Expedient Means" Chapter, the Second, of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The explanation of the title of this chapter consists of both a brief and an extensive treatment. The brief treatment has two parts: first, the brief explanation; second, the analytical discussion. "Fang" (Expedient) means "Dharma."

"Convenience" (bian) means application. The Dharma has its squareness and roundness; application has its differences and convergences. The three provisional means are the carpenter's square and the ruler;
the one reality is the compass and the circle. If wisdom reaches the square, then one skillfully employs partial methods to accommodate and meet the needs of sentient beings.
If wisdom reaches the compass, one skillfully employs the circular method to accommodate sentient beings. This is like pointing with a finger and directing the gaze toward a specific point;
this uses a partial method to direct the gaze of wisdom. It is appropriate to use the method to explain the square, and employing it to explain the convenient.
If one points with the finger as a whole and directs the gaze toward the circular point, it is appropriate to employ the secret to explain the square, and the sublime to [explain]...
This explains the provisional means (*upāya*). To cite partial dharmas as an explanation of *upāya* is merely to follow the inclinations of sentient beings; it is not the Buddha’s original intent.
As the sutra states, he causes them to leave behind all attachments and emerge from the suffering of the triple world (*tridhātu*). For this reason, the Tathāgata earnestly extols *upāya*.

This interpretation may apply to other sutras, but it is not the intended meaning of the present chapter. Furthermore, *upāya* is a "gate" (*mukha*). A gate is so called because it is capable of providing passage.

That which penetrates what is to be penetrated—expedient means (*upāya*) and skillful strategies (*kauśalya*)—are all introductory inducements that serve as gateways to the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).

Once the ultimate reality is revealed, its achievement is due to expedient means; thus, it is named according to that which reveals it. Therefore, "gateway" (*mukha*) is used to explain "expedient means.

As the sutra says, "Opening the gateway of expedient means to reveal the aspect of ultimate reality," this may be interpreted according to other scriptures, yet it is not the intended meaning of this present chapter. Furthermore, as for "method" (*fang*):
"Secret" (*mi*) means "wondrous" (*myō*). To wondrously penetrate the principle is itself true secrecy.
Pointing out the priceless jewel within one's inner garment as being the same as the one upon the King’s head—there is but this single jewel, neither two nor different;
pointing out the hired laborer as being the son of the elder—likewise, there is neither two nor difference. Such words are secret and wondrous, as the sutra says: "Only..."
"I know this mark; the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so. "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive.

To explain it through the secret method and to explain it through the skillful means (*upāya*) is precisely the intent of this present chapter; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Skillful Means" (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*).
As for the analysis: the first explanation refers to skillful means external to the essence—the provisional power used to transform sentient beings in accordance with their inclinations.

The first explanation is also an expedient means external to the essence; it is the skillful means for transforming others through one's own practice, and it is speech that accords with the intentions of both self and others.
The latter explanation is an expedient means of the same essence; it is the skillful means of one's own practice, and it is speech that accords with one's own intention.

The first explanation of skillful means states that it is neither the agent of entry nor the object of entry; the second explanation of skillful means states that it is the agent of entry but not the object of entry;
the final explanation of skillful means states that it is the object of entry but not the agent of entry. Thus, one knows that while the names are the same, their meanings are vastly different.

People of the world do not perceive this meaning and thus offer superficial interpretations of the "Expedient Means" chapter. Question: What is the relationship between *upāya* (expedient means) and *prajñapti* (provisional designation)? Answer: They are distinguished by four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):

1. Expedient means that subverts provisional designation; 2. Provisional designation that subverts expedient means; 3. Expedient means that cultivates provisional designation; 4. Provisional designation that cultivates expedient means;

5. Expedient means is identical to provisional designation; 6. Provisional designation is identical to expedient means. Regarding "expedient means that subverts provisional designation," all four [propositions] apply.

This is the secret and wondrous skillful means (*upāya*). This skillful means breaks through the provisional that accords with the intentions of others. Regarding the breaking of skillful means by the provisional:

the provisional is the provisional of identical substance (*tongti*), which breaks through skillful means that exist outside of that substance. Their mutual cultivation and mutual identity can likewise be understood.

The first three phrases may be used to explain other sutras; the meaning of the present chapter lies in the fourth phrase. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is titled the "Chapter on Skillful Means" (*Upāyakauśalya*).
"Skillful means" (*upāya*) and "expedient means" (*kauśalya*) are non-dual and without distinction. Whether one bows the head or raises a hand, all attain the Buddha-way;
skillful expedients are entirely true reality. This concludes the brief explanation. As for the extensive explanation, it refutes the old texts by expanding upon what was abbreviated.
No commentary [is provided]. As Vasubandhu lists seventeen names, the thirteenth is "Great Skillful Means" (*mahopāyakauśalya*).

Furthermore, the *Mahāyānopāya-sūtra* clarifies ten types of skillful means; the ninth is named "Skillfulness" (*kauśalya*), which shifts those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) and causes them to enter the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*), one should know that this present chapter is the Tathāgata’s skillful means, which encompasses all things.

The Dharma is like space encompassing form, or like the ocean receiving its currents; how could the single branch or single stream of various masters suffice to explain the vast expanse of the Dharmadhātu?
Now, in clarifying the provisional and the real, one first establishes four propositions: namely, that all phenomena are provisional; all phenomena are real;
all phenomena are both provisional and real; and all phenomena are neither provisional nor real.
It is not real. All that is provisional is as the text says: "The nature, characteristics, power, substance, beginning, and end of all dharmas are thus.
Even a fleeting word is entirely provisional. All dharmas are real, as the text says: "The Tathāgata skillfully teaches all dharmas to delight the minds of the multitude.
The minds of the multitude find delight in entering into reality. Furthermore, all dharmas from the very beginning...
It is eternally characterized by quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*). Furthermore, it is said that all that the Tathāgata has taught reaches the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

It is also said that all is real and not false. Moreover, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are all ineffable, and that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are both provisional (*upāya*) and real.
As the text itself says regarding the true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, this simultaneously clarifies that everything is both [provisional and real].

Skillful means (*upāya*) is also reality. For example, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is both real and illusory. Regarding all phenomena being neither skillful means nor reality, the text states they are "neither identical nor different.
It further says: "Furthermore, one does not practice superior, middling, or inferior dharmas, nor conditioned or unconditioned dharmas, nor real or unreal dharmas.
They are neither illusory nor real; they are the true mark (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*). If all dharmas were merely skillful means, [this would be untenable].
What is there that cannot be subverted? Even if there were hundreds or thousands of teachers, each making hundreds or thousands of different explanations, none would not be provisional.
If even what the Tathāgata has taught is still provisional, how much more so the teachings of human teachers—how could they possibly not be provisional?
As previously stated, all are entirely provisional. If all dharmas were real, what would there be that could not be subverted?
Only this one reality exists; the other two are not true. There is but a single ultimate path; how could there be many ultimate paths?
As for the various masters mentioned previously, they all refuted [the notion of] entering the Real; how then could they still maintain their own sectarian strongholds?
If all dharmas are both provisional and real, then what would there be that could not be refuted? Everything possesses [both aspects].
How could provisional and ultimate truth be merely one path, rather than distinct interpretations? Within each and every phenomenon, both the provisional and the ultimate exist;
they cannot be categorized as exclusively provisional or exclusively ultimate. If all phenomena were neither provisional nor ultimate, what would there be that could not be sublated?
Why then do you create such confusion by forcefully establishing [distinctions]? Even when simply listing their names, the situation is already like this—how much more so from a distance...
Contemplating this profound insight, its vastness and sublime clarity are such as this; how much more so when discussing its underlying purport!

Now, based on the categories of the provisional and the real, ten further dharmas are opened up. Within these ten dharmas, there are eight sections of explanation: first, listing the ten names; second, their sequential arising;
third, their detailed explanation; fourth, citing scriptural evidence; fifth, concluding the ten [dharmas] as three types of provisional and real; sixth...
One distinguishes three types of the provisional and the real, which illuminate three types of the two truths. Seventh, the provisional and the real are distinguished according to various sutras;

eighth, the provisional and the real are distinguished according to the fundamental and the trace. First, to list the names: these are phenomenon and principle, principle and teaching, teaching and practice, and bondage and liberation.
Cause and effect, essence and function, gradual and sudden, opening and closing, general and specific, and the *siddhāntas*—these are the ten names.
Second, regarding their arising: from the "root of non-abiding," all phenomena (*dharmas*) are established.

"Non-abiding" refers to principle; "all phenomena" refers to facts. From principle and fact, there is the teaching; from the teaching, there is practice; and from practice, there is bondage and liberation.
Through liberation, cause and effect are established; through effect, the essence is manifested; through the essence and its function, there is gradual and sudden transformation.
Because gradual and sudden [teachings] are opened up, there is opening and closing; because of opening and closing, there is the benefit of the general and the specific.
By distinguishing these two benefits, there are the four *siddhāntas*. This is the sequence of the ten chapters. Third, regarding the explanation: the principle is the truth.
Suchness (tathatā) is fundamentally pure; whether a Buddha appears or not, it remains eternally unchanging. Therefore, principle (li) is called "real.

Phenomena (shi), such as the mind, mentation, and consciousness, give rise to pure and impure karma and are subject to constant fluctuation and instability. Therefore, phenomena are called "expedient" (provisional).

Without principle, there is no way to establish phenomena; without phenomena, one cannot manifest principle. Since phenomena possess the merit of manifesting principle, for this reason, skillful means (*upāya*) are earnestly praised.
Regarding "principle and teaching": these collectively refer to both principle and phenomena, all of which are termed "principle.

This is, for example, like how both the ultimate and conventional truths are called "truths" (*satya*). The Buddhas embody this and thereby become sages (*ārya*); "sage" (*ārya*) signifies that which is correct and real.
Desiring to apply one’s own Dharma to sentient beings below, one establishes teachings based on principle; such teaching is expedient means (*upāya*).
One should know that without teaching there is no way to manifest principle; principle is manifested through teaching. For this reason, the Tathāgata praised expedient means.

When a practitioner relies on the teaching to seek principle, right practice arises. Since practice involves distinctions of depth and shallowness in its progress, [the teaching is necessary]. Thus...
Practice is termed "expedient" (*upāya*). Since the teaching has no distinction between deep and shallow stages of progress, the teaching is termed "real" (*bhūta*).

Without the teaching, practice cannot be established; without practice, one cannot realize the teaching. Realizing the teaching depends upon practice; therefore, the Tathāgata praises expedient means.
Regarding bondage and liberation: these constitute practice. To contravene principle is bondage; since bondage is illusory and false, it is termed "expedient. Thus, it is for the sake of practice.
When one accords with principle, understanding arises; when understanding merges with principle, it is called "reality. Without bondage there would be no way to seek liberation;
yet liberation is attained by means of bondage, just as one uses a corpse to cross the sea—the corpse possesses the power to reach the shore. Therefore, skillful means (upāya) are praised.

Regarding cause and effect: the cause involves a provisional utility through its progressive advancement, and is therefore termed "expedient" (upāya); the fruit involves the final achievement and eternal realization, and is therefore termed "real" (bhūta).
Without the fruit, the cause has nothing toward which to aspire; without the cause, the fruit does not manifest of itself.

Thus, the two contemplations serve as the path of skillful means (upāyamārga), whereby one severs delusions to form the cause and enters the fruit of liberation of the Middle Way. Were it not for these two contemplations, [this would not be possible].
How could this not accord with the Middle Way? Since the fruit is achieved through causes, one praises the skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding essence (*tattva*) and function (*vṛtti*):

the preceding skillful means constitute the cause, while the entry into and abiding in correct contemplation constitute the fruit. As for the essence and function of abiding and emerging: the essence is the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), which is devoid of discrimination;
the function is the establishment of all phenomena, which differ according to their respective gradations. It is like the great earth producing various kinds of sprouts from a single source.

Without earth there is no way for things to arise; without arising there is no way for them to manifest. By tracing the current one finds the source; by investigating function, one realizes the essence.

Since function possesses the power to manifest the essence, it is praised as a skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding the gradual and the sudden: in the cultivation of causes and the realization of fruits, and in the arising of function from the essence, both possess aspects of the gradual and the sudden.
Now, in clarifying the arising of function, the gradual use of function is designated as provisional (*tāttvika*), while the sudden use of function is designated as real (*bhūta*). If...

It is not a gradual induction; there is no way to enter the sudden [teaching] directly. Because one attains the reality through the gradual, the skillful means (*upāya*) are praised. Regarding "opening and closing":
from the sudden, the gradual is opened, yet the gradual does not naturally harmonize with itself, nor does it harmonize with the sudden;

therefore, it is called "provisional" (*kevala*). By causing the gradual to reach its ultimate fulfillment, it returns to harmonize with the sudden; therefore, it is called "real" (*bhūta*). Because of the opening, there is a harmony; the opening possesses the power of harmony. From the opening...

This is called "receiving the name. Therefore, the skillful means are praised. Regarding the general and specific benefits: the general benefit is that of the "half-syllables" (the impermanent), while the specific benefit is that of the "full-syllables" (the eternal).

However, because the path of the eternal benefit is long, beings are prone to falling back or regressing; thus, the "transformed city" is used to guide them, giving rise to the thought of peace and security.
Only then does the transformation cease, leading them to the place of true treasure. If there were no benefit from the half-syllables, [this would not be possible].
One must not regard [the teachings] as being merely conventional. Since they possess the merit of partially revealing the full [truth], they are praised as "expedient means" (*upāya*).

Regarding the four *siddhāntas*: three are worldly and are therefore provisional; the first principle (*paramārtha*) is supramundane and is therefore real. Without the worldly, one cannot attain the supramundane;
it is by means of the three *siddhāntas* that one attains the first principle. For this reason, the Tathāgata praises expedient means.

One should employ four statements to explain the ten instances of the provisional and the real. Three of these instances follow the intent of other sutras, while one instance follows the intent of this chapter.
Regarding the citations of evidence: these ten meanings pervade both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings and encompass all phenomena.

To cite from the present sutra: "Not as they see the three realms do they see the three realms. The three realms are the objective phenomena; [the phrase] "not as they see the three realms" [indicates that they do not perceive them according to their conventional appearances].
The "Seer" refers to the Principle (li). All phenomena are quiescent and ineffable; this is the Principle. Through the power of skillful means, it was taught to the five bhikṣus;
this is the Teaching (jiao). If one hears this sutra, one is practicing the Bodhisattva path; this is the realization of the teaching and its practice.
Furthermore, that which you practice is the path of the bodhisattvas. Sons of the Buddha, having practiced this path, you shall become Buddhas in a future age.
Moreover, through various causes and conditions, you seek the Buddha-way; yet, simply to be free from falsehood is called liberation.
Until you have attained all-encompassing liberation, you must fully practice all the dharmas of the path possessed by all Buddhas, until you attain the fruit at the site of enlightenment. By me—

With the Buddha-eye, he observes the sentient beings of the six realms; as soon as they see my body and hear what I say, they all believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata—except for those who previously practiced and studied the Lesser Vehicle.

It is like the impoverished son who first flees, then stays among the refuse in the interim, and finally is entrusted with the wealth; or like first resting at the conjured city and later being led to the place of jewels. [This applies to] various desires and various...
Regarding nature (*dhātu*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), mindfulness, and so forth—while these generally cite an entire section as proof, we now cite a specific chapter.
Although it does not follow the sequential order, the ten aspects are fully present therein. "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;

Extensively explained through ten phrases, this elucidates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena mentioned above, clarifying and manifesting it.

First, the immovable nature supports emptiness (kong); next, the seed-nature (zhongxing) supports the conventional (su); and next, the true nature supports the Middle Way (zhongdao). Now, it is clarified that this internal nature is unalterable.

Second, humans and devas take pure karma (*śukla-karman*) as their cause. Third, the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*) take untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) as their practice.

Fourth, the bodhisattva of the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle and the Buddha take the adornment of wisdom itself as the cause.
Third, regarding the taking of the Buddha-dharma as the cause: the Buddha is neither the cause nor not the cause; this refers directly to the true cause consisting of the forty-one stages.
Thus the Sūtra says, "Riding upon this precious vehicle, one travels through the four quarters. This must also be explained according to the three truths.

Fourth, the conditions for the four realms of existence (*catur-gati*). These are the auxiliary conditions;

This is precisely taking the adornment of merit as the condition (*pratyaya*). Third, regarding the Buddha-dharma:

Those with excessive desire receive bodies in the hells; seeing instruments of suffering, they mistake them for objects of desire and immediately give rise to defiled attachment, taking these to be the habitual fruits of the four miserable destinies.
As for humans and devas, their birth as a fruit is the spontaneous recompense for wholesome minds.
Third, the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha). They take the realization of the four fruits as their fruition. Bodhisattvas also have four [stages].

First, the Bodhisattva of the Tripitaka takes the exhaustion of the fetters through the thirty-four moments of mind as their fruition. Second, the Bodhisattva of the Abhidharma (or *Abhijñā*) takes the exhaustion of all remaining residual habits (*vāsanā*) as their fruition.

Third, regarding the distinct bodhisattvas: through the provisional cultivation of contemplation, they achieve the fruit. Fourth, regarding the perfect-and-sudden bodhisattvas and Buddhas: they correspond in a single thought-moment;
the great awakening is luminous, and unsurpassed bodhi constitutes the fruit of practice. Third, concerning the summary according to the Buddha-dharma:
The Buddha is neither the fruit nor not the fruit, yet he is designated as such a fruit. This refers to that which is attained through the ultimate, wondrous, and luminous perfect cause.
As the Sūtra says, "Directly reaching the site of enlightenment," this speaks of the fruit from the perspective of the Buddha-Dharma;
yet one must also understand that taking one implies the three, and the entirety of the three is one, all of which enter into the single fruit-dharma of the Buddha in this present sūtra.

The response is as follows. Regarding the initial mental state (*citta*) as the retribution (*vipāka*): to repay a cause is called "retribution. When the causal habituation and the resultant habituation are both collectively termed "cause," they draw forth the retribution of future lives;
thus, the mind itself is this retribution that repays the cause. Second, regarding the phenomena of sentient beings, there are also four [categories]. First, the four...

Regarding the retribution of the destinies (*gati*): for example, when a person with many desires enters hell and approaches a sensual object, they immediately undergo the suffering of the copper pillar and iron bed;
this is the retribution of the four destinies. Second are humans and devas, who receive the retribution of natural pleasure due to their conditioned existence.

Third is the discussion of the retribution of the two vehicles (*yāna*). According to the original teachings of the Hīnayāna, the fruit of realization is non-arising (*anutpāda*); since the two vehicles do not... [text truncated]

Because it arises [from conditions], there is no retribution (*vipāka*). If this is so, why is it that when true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) manifests, it is called a "fruit" (*phala*) rather than being discussed as "retribution"?
Although the term "fruit" is used broadly, the term "retribution" is specific. Therefore, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), if there is a fruit, there is necessarily retribution.

If the practitioners of the Two Vehicles are also generally designated as "fruition" (*phala*), yet their retribution (*vipāka*) is not discussed— since the untainted (*anāsrava*) is that which diminishes birth rather than a dharma that draws forth birth—
and furthermore, according to the fundamental teachings of the Hīnayāna, the place of rebirth is not mentioned and thus no retribution exists; if that were so,
since those in the stages of the three fruits also attain the untainted of the fundamental teaching, how could there be seven births, one birth, or births in the higher realms?

Is this not indeed a retribution? However, regarding the three fruits that are said to have retribution, it is because residual *saṃskāra* remains inexhaustible and serves as a condition for outflows (*āsrava*) that one undergoes rebirth;
it is not an outflow-free retribution. In the original teachings of the Two Vehicles, there is certainly no doctrine of retribution.

Yet, according to the Mahāyāna perspective, even this "outflow-free" state is still termed "with outflows," because it does not eliminate the specific afflictions (*kleśa*) and thus still undergoes the birth of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body).

Thus, with the untainted (*anāsrava*) as the cause and ignorance (*avidyā*) as the condition, the land of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bhūmi*) arises. In a broad classification, the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*) indeed possess retribution.

There are likewise four types of bodhisattvas. First, the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna still possess the active afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus their retribution remains within the triple world (*tridhātu*).
Second, the bodhisattvas of the Shared Vehicle (*yōng-t'ong pusa*); from the sixth stage downward, they sever doubt in the same manner as the followers of the two vehicles. Furthermore—
First, those who do not receive retribution. Second, the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*):

regarding the sequential contemplation of the practice of the Middle Way, although these individuals have severed the pervasive delusions (*sāmānya-kleśa*), they know for themselves that there is still birth and that they receive the retribution of *pariṇāmika-vedanīya*. Thus, they possess the ten dharmas.

Fourth, the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas of the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna: their retribution is Great Nirvāṇa, which is the fruit of fruits—the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*)—as well as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and samādhi.

All things being fully complete constitutes the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*). Third, regarding the Buddha-dharma: the Buddha-dharma is neither retribution nor non-retribution, yet it is designated as such a retribution;
this refers to ultimate Great Nirvāṇa. As the Sūtra says: "Attaining the immeasurable, outflow-free, and pure fruit of retribution.
Furthermore, since the Buddha has exhausted the meaning of further birth, how could one discuss retribution? Only the Buddha alone...
When a person dwells in the Pure Land and does not undergo further rebirth, there is no retribution. In terms of the present, it exists; in terms of the future, it does not.

Both root and branch arise from conditions (*pratyaya*). Since the mind arising from conditions is empty, both root and branch are empty; this is what is meant by the equality of the emptiness of mental dharmas.

Furthermore, the root of characteristics exists only as words, and the branches of retribution likewise exist only as words; they are all merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Moreover, the root and the branches mutually represent one another.
Banner. Examining the initial marks to discern the subsequent retribution; observing the subsequent retribution to know the original marks. The initial and subsequent marks are present here;

this is discussed in terms of mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), based on conventional designations (*prajñapti*) to establish equality. Furthermore, regarding marks and marklessness: it is markless yet marked; neither mark nor markless.
Retribution and non-retribution; non-retribution yet retribution; neither retribution nor non-retribution—both enter the limit of reality (*tathatā*).

This is the equality discussed within the context of mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*). Second, regarding the phenomena of sentient beings (*sattva-dharma*), there are also four [categories]. First, the four realms of existence (*gati*).
One should know that the four realms of existence are equal in that both their origin and their end are characterized by ignorance. Since the root of evil is empty, its end is also empty;
this is equality in terms of emptiness. Furthermore, the retribution of evil exists within the fundamental characteristics and nature [of the mind]; thus, the end is equal to the root.
The nature of the primary characteristics resides within the retribution of evil fruits; thus, the origin and the end are equal.

If there were no subsequent event without the prior one, the physiognomist would not be able to predict it in advance. If there were no prior event without the subsequent one, the physiognomist would not be able to record it retrospectively.

Since the characteristics of both the beginning and the end exist, this is like the discourse on provisional phenomena. Within the four dark and evil destinies, there exists a central, substantial truth—the mind and the Buddha.

The fruit is not different [from the cause]. A single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way; this is the theoretical explanation regarding the four realms of existence and so forth.

Second, as for humans and devas, both the beginning and the end are equally the pure, ascending white dharmas. Initially, the beginning is empty and the end is also empty; this is "emptiness-equality.

Furthermore, the good karmic retribution exists within the fundamental characteristics and nature; thus, this end is equal to the beginning. This is the equality of the original nature and its characteristics.
Within the retribution of wholesome fruits, this beginning and end are equal; the initial and the final exist in mutual relation. This is equality from the perspective of the conventional.

Within the wholesome, the true principle is that the mind and the fruit of Buddhahood are not different; there is nothing that is not the Middle Way—this is what is meant by "equality" as explained through the Middle.
Third, regarding the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas, their beginning and end are explained according to the teachings, which can be understood. Third, concerning the Buddha-dharma:
The Buddha-dharma is neither beginning nor end, yet it speaks of beginning and end; it is neither beginning nor end, being ultimately empty and equal.
From the first to the last, their characteristics coexist; it is ultimately conventional and equal, fully entering the Middle Way.

It is ultimately equal within the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), ultimately the three truths, neither equal nor unequal, yet ultimately equal. Because it points to the true mark, it is thus designated: [End of excerpt]
This is the true reality (*dharmatā*). This is the Tathāgata’s own practice of the provisional and the real, which is supreme and unsurpassed.

Therefore, the heading of this chapter states "the true reality of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-bhūtatathatā*). Only the Tathāgata universally illumines these ten aspects of reality (*daśa-tathatā*), both horizontally and vertically.
It is as clear as observing fruit in the palm of one's hand. It is because ordinary beings are like those with double vision; the followers of the Two Vehicles are like those with impaired sight;
and Bodhisattvas are like those seeing indistinctly in the night, unable to discern it clearly. It cannot be described; it is understood only by oneself alone.
What others do not see cannot be proclaimed or shown. Cease, cease! Words are cut off; it is simply this. For now, let us rely on the extensive [explanation] of Tiantai.
Yan. Master Nanyue cited the Dharma, stating that there are three types [of exegesis], which he presented briefly without detail.

Tiantai further established four interpretations of his own to clarify the universal inclusion of principle (*li*). The interpretation regarding the ten realms clarifies the ultimate self-realization; the interpretation regarding the Buddha-realm clarifies the Buddha’s transformative function;

the interpretation regarding separation and combination clarifies the pervasiveness of the three virtues (*tridharmakāya*); and the interpretation regarding the various stages clarifies the correct [application]. This [latter] refers only to the correct. Correct.
It must necessarily encompass the basis. Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of "all dharmas," explaining them by means of the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

Within each and every realm, the other nine realms are mutually contained; within the one is the immeasurable, and within the immeasurable is the one. When expanded, it fills the entire dharma-realm, yet one does not know from where it comes.
When contracted, not a single dharma remains, and its location is unknown. One does not know from where...

And so they depart. Now, although ordinary beings possess [these qualities], their emotions are deluded and cut off from principle; although those of the Two Vehicles possess them, they abandon them in their quest for liberation;
and although Bodhisattvas possess them, their illumination is not all-pervasive.

Only the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, illuminate the ten dharma-realms and the causes and effects of the ten suchnesses, seeing them with perfect clarity. That only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom this is truly because of this.
Furthermore, the second [reason] is that the Sūtra states: "The Dharma accomplished by the Buddha is the foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-understand teaching.

Therefore, it is explained by means of the Buddha’s *dharmadhātu*. Just as his own practice of the provisional and the real is the most supreme—supreme in its characteristics up to its supreme retribution—it is both horizontally vast and vertically deep, with nothing superior to it.
Thus, the chapter is titled "The True Reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of All Dharmas," which is exclusively...
This refers to the Buddha’s fulfillment. The three sutras state: "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive.

Since it is said to be "difficult to conceive," it is only then able to universally accommodate all beings. Therefore, it is explained according to both separation and combination. If, within the Buddha's mind, there are the ten realms and the ten suchnesses...

All are the supreme marks, even unto the supreme fruit and retribution; they are solely this single Buddha-dharmadhātu, like the ocean encompassing all rivers, or as a thousand chariots sharing a single track.
This is the Buddha’s own practice of the union of the provisional and the real (*upāya-tattva*).

If one follows the intentions of others, there are the nine dharma-realms and the ten suchnesses, natures, characteristics, and so forth; these represent the separation of the provisional and the real in the transformation of others.

Furthermore, although the teachings for transforming others possess reality, in relation to the Buddha, they are all subsumed as provisional (*upāya*). Although the Buddha’s own practice possesses provisionality, from the perspective of others, it is all subsumed as real.
Following others, there is opening; following oneself, there is closing. Transversally and vertically, he illuminates all things; opening and closing are at his sovereign will.
Although he opens up immeasurable dharmas for the sake of transforming others, they are one within their immeasurability. Although he closes them into one, that one [remains immeasurable].

It is immeasurable; though immeasurable, it is one; yet it is neither one nor immeasurable. Though neither one nor immeasurable, it is both one and immeasurable—only a Buddha can exhaustively penetrate this.
As the *Four Sutras* state: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively penetrate it.
This must be explained by way of the six positions (*ṣaḍ-avasthā*). Such a characteristic is possessed by all sentient beings as their true reality.
The marks have existed inherently from the beginning; they are the manifestations of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Because sentient beings take these as the marks of Bodhi, they are the marks of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Such a nature is the wisdom of the original, inherent virtuous qualities, the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
All wisdom and vows remain undiminished. To speak of the original inherent virtues is to grasp the afflictions...
Affliction (*kleśa*) is itself the awakening cause (*bodhi-nimitta*). Such a substance is the inherently present Middle Way; it is the principle-substance of intrinsic purity.
These constitute the Three Virtues (*tri-guṇa*), which pervade the ten dharma-realms. Within each realm, the Three Virtues reside together within the rational nature (*li-xing*).
Therefore, the term "ten dharma-realms" refers solely to this principle. The stages of the "six identities" (*liu-ji*) are present in every single stage.

These are precisely the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) of the principle (*li*). Their status is fixed in that of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); this stage of the identity of principle is collectively termed the "True Cause" (*zhengyin*).
If one investigates these three virtues and enters the five stages of practice (*wu pinwei*), it is called "power. Upon entering the ten levels of faith (*shixin*), it is called "action.

From the stages of "entry" (*ru*) and "abiding" (*zhu*) upward, the true cultivation of the conditions and the understanding is termed the "cause" and the "condition. If one enters the stage of Buddhahood, enlightenment (*bodhi*) is termed the "fruit," and *nirvāṇa* is termed the [extinction].

Response: The first three are called the "root," and the latter three are called the "branch. Since the beginning and the end are identical in being the Three Virtues (*tri-guṇa*), they are said to be ultimately equal.
Thus, the text for the Three Virtues of the Rational Nature (*li-xing*) is found here. Now, seeing this text, one should integrate it with all other explanations.

The Three Virtues at the initial stage pervade both evil and good; they pervade both the worthy and the sage; they pervade both the Small and the Great; and they pervade both the beginning and the ultimate.
Thus it is. Though dwelling in the evil, one does not sink; though dwelling in the good, one does not ascend. Though among the worthy, one does not lower oneself;
though among the sages, one does not exalt oneself. Though in the small, one is not narrow; though in the great, one is not expansive.

Though at the beginning, one is not new; though at the ultimate limit, one is not old. Though there are distinctions among the ten realms regarding their characteristics, natures, provisional and real aspects, and their opening and closing.
There are various [distinctions]. To observe them as they truly are with the great wisdom of equality, one finds that ultimately all are equal.

If one is deluded regarding this realm, there arise the characteristics and natures of the six elements, which is termed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If one understands this realm, there arise the characteristics and natures of the two vehicles, which is termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If one realizes that this realm is neither delusion nor understanding, there arise the [characteristics and natures] of the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas.

The nature of the characteristics of the realms is the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). If this wisdom is equated with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then conventional truth is not delusion;
if it is equated with ultimate truth, then ultimate truth is not liberation. It is neither delusion nor liberation; it is the double negation of both delusion and liberation.
It is simply called "Equal Great Wisdom. This is the realm where the provisional and the real are non-dual.
Among the seven kinds of skillful means, none can, by means of non-dual wisdom, equalize the non-dual realm; only the Buddhas can, by means of non-dual wisdom, equalize the non-dual realm.
Tiantai’s fourfold interpretation stands preeminent among all predecessors. Only by interpreting the text in this manner does one truly accord with the intent of the sutra.
These ten points accord with the Dharma and are praised by the Buddha. It is for this reason that Śāriputra makes his three requests in the following text;

it is for this reason that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time reveal and manifest [the truth]; and it is because Śākyamuni conforms to them from above that there is no longer any difference between them. The great carriage serves as a metaphor for this.

This was manifested in past lives; this has been realized as the primordial foundation for a long time. It is by virtue of this that those whose faculties were impaired have now received their prediction.

From the Bodhisattva’s removal of doubts, the diminishing of births, and the increasing of the Path—from the initial generation of the mind until the final stage of the position of succession—all are contained within this.
The ten parables of Bhaiṣajyarāja praise this; the Bodhisattva’s vow to circulate [the teaching] is centered upon this. If one grasps this meaning, it is vast.
The teaching unfolds over eight years, yet it does not transcend a single thought-moment; it passes through fifty minor kalpas, yet it never stirs for even a kṣaṇa.

By this analogy, one knows that the entire dispensation adapts to the capacities of beings by abiding within the nature of the mind. Within the square inch of the heart, the entirety of the *Lotus Sūtra* is present;

therein, the Buddha-activities of the ten directions can be clearly beheld. The faculties and natures of the dharma-realm are surveyed and easily understood; thus, all that is taught according to what is appropriate is revealed.

These all point to the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha*. In this treatise, twenty phrases are employed across eighteen sections to explain the aforementioned ten aspects of suchness (*daśatathatā*).
This accords in profound harmony with the intent of the Sūtra and its fourfold exegesis. The text of the treatise is rich and abundant, yet few people understand it.

This is merely a brief summary of the commentary (*ṭīkā*), providing a rough interpretation of the Sūtra’s intent; a detailed and exhaustive explanation is fully contained within the commentary itself.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Generally, verses and prose serve as mutual expansions and abbreviations to make the meaning easily manifest; for example, the following verse on the 'ten suchnesses' is abbreviated."
If one wishes to raise up those who do not know, it would be far-reaching indeed.
The Hero of the World is immeasurable; among all classes of beings, including the gods and the people of the world, there is none who can truly know the Buddha.
These four lines are a verse summarizing the preceding words spoken by the Buddhas, praising the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real.
"The Hero of the World" in the first line summarizes the wisdom of the various Buddhas mentioned above. "Immeasurable" summarizes the aforementioned profound and immeasurable nature;

this single phrase summarizes the praise of the Buddhas regarding their real wisdom. In the preceding text, the four Buddhas were not distinguished individually, but were simply referred to as "the Buddhas."
Therefore, although it is now simply called "World Hero" (*lokanātha*), this refers to all Buddhas.

While the mere term "World Hero" might seem not to refer to all Buddhas, according to the meaning of the characters—since it is already specified as "world" (*loka*)—the term can apply to the three periods of time. As the three periods necessarily imply the ten directions, we know this verse praises all Buddhas.

This refers to the reason for transcending words, which is the object indicated in the main text. The actual prose section praising the transcendence of words is found in the subsequent verse.
"This Dharma cannot be shown; the characteristics of speech are quiescent.
These two lines are a recapitulation of the preceding passage where [the Buddha] definitively cut off words to praise the cessation of further discourse, stating that Śāriputra need not speak again.
This is because the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is not a spatial location and thus cannot be shown, and it is not something that can be expressed through language.
It is said that the characteristics of words and speech are quiescent.
"None of the other classes of sentient beings are able to understand this"—
these two lines of verse generally exclude those who do not enter [the path], namely, the persons of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).
"Except for the assembly of Bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm.
These two lines of verse distinguish those who are capable of entering; they refer specifically to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).

Therefore, it says "those whose power of faith is firm" are able to know how to enter. If that is so, why does the prose section state that only a Buddha can know how to enter, saying "only a Buddha has thoroughly [realized]..."?
[The preceding section] concludes. Why does the verse state that "through clear initial faith, one is able to know entry"?

If we rely on the names of the stages for entering the Perfect [Teaching] at the very first thought, the arousal of the mind is itself ultimately non-dual. This is because [the verse] advances by citing what resembles the stages; why then should there be any doubt? It is merely a matter of citing the beginning and the mutual [stages] in alternation.
The assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, who have made offerings to all Buddhas, whose outflows are entirely exhausted,
and who dwell in their final bodies— such persons as these cannot withstand its power.
These six lines of verse generally distinguish [the Buddha] from those of the two vehicles who do not know; as for those in their final birth, they are merely bound by the fruits [of their practice].
Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
These four lines of verse specifically cite Śāriputra’s sharp wisdom; even he could not know it throughout a single world-system.
Even if those like Śāriputra, as well as all other disciples, were to fill the ten directions, and likewise fill the lands of the ten directions—[they still could not know it].
"Exhausting their thoughts and deliberating together, they likewise could not know it.
These six lines of verse extensively state that even if Śāriputra and others were to fill the ten directions, they would still be unable to know it.
Pratyekabuddhas of sharp wisdom, free from outflows and in their final bodies, also fill the worlds of the ten directions, their number like that of bamboo groves.
Even if these were to unite their minds for immeasurable billions of eons, they would be unable to know even a small fraction of the Buddha’s true wisdom.
These eight lines of verse cannot be understood even by Pratyekabuddhas.

A Bodhisattva who has newly resolved [to attain enlightenment], having made offerings to countless Buddhas, thoroughly understands all meanings and purposes, and is also skilled in preaching the Dharma.
Suppose there were rice, sesame, bamboo, and reeds filling the lands of the ten directions;
even if they were to contemplate with a single mind and wondrous wisdom for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, they could not know the Buddha’s wisdom.
These ten phrases cannot be understood by bodhisattvas who have merely resolved their minds (*cittotpāda*). The term "resolution" is general;

it may refer to those bodhisattvas of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) during the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* who, though they have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), are termed "those who have resolved their minds.

Alternatively, it may point to those among the superior humans and devas who, having personally embraced the six perfections, employ the term "resolution" specifically to designate the distinct and general types of resolve within the Mahāyāna.
The minds of the non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, together contemplate and seek with a single mind, yet they still cannot know these four lines.
This indicates that even non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) cannot know them, for they have only severed the realm [of afflictions].

Due to internal delusions, they do not know the distinct principle. Furthermore, they do not know that even prior to the stages of the Distinct Teaching, there is the stage of realization where practice does not regress.
Again, he addressed Śāriputra: "The untainted, inconceivable, profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma—I have now fully attained it."
"Only I know this mark; the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise.
These six lines praise the aforementioned difficult-to-understand Dharma: that the Buddha is able to know the realm of the true mark (*tathatā*).
The first line, "Ineffable and inconceivable," praises the reason for its being beyond words; it summarizes the essential point by citing the realm where the provisional and the real abide.
Next is the single phrase on "profound depth. This verse praises the aforementioned "unspeakable horizontal fulfillment" of those who have attained the supreme fruit;
it is the text concerning the foremost, rare, and difficult-to-understand Dharma. Next, the three phrases beginning with "Now I...

praise the aforementioned "unspeakable vertical depth" of the supreme person's provisional and ultimate teachings; this refers to that which "only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust. Furthermore...
This clarifies that the paths of all Buddhas are identical and that they are all equally ultimate; hence it is said: "Only I know these marks, and the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise.
Furthermore, "inconceivable" means not fixed or determinate. For example, a wish-fulfilling jewel has not even a hair’s breadth of existence, yet it can rain down all manner of treasures;
the true mark (*dharmatā*) is unborn, yet it can give rise to *prajñā*. Moreover, Tiantai relies upon these six...
Verse Summary: A summary of the essential points provides four types of explanations for the ten aspects of reality (*daśa-tathatā*).

First, based on the half-verse concerning the untainted (*anāsrava*), an explanation is made in terms of the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*). This encompasses the untainted nature of all ordinary beings and sages within the ten realms and ten aspects;
furthermore, it includes the untainted aspect of the three truths and the untainted aspect of the provisional and the real. Second, based on the inconceivable...

The discussion of the half-phrase serves as the basis for opening and closing; it is the provisional that is the real, and the real that is the provisional—this is the inconceivable opening and closing.
The second part, based on the two phrases "relying on the profound and subtle Dharma," serves as the basis for providing an explanation of the Buddha’s *dharmadhātu*.
The four reliances take only the two phrases "I alone know these characteristics" as their basis.

One should understand that when explaining them in terms of the stages [of practice], the four interpretations that resolve the profound realm, as well as the citations of evidence and the foundational principles, all rely upon the Buddha’s word and accord with the intent of the sūtras.
From the beginning of the verse up to this point, the section of verses praising the two [aspects of] "reliance" and "transcendence" is concluded.

△ The subsequent three and a half lines constitute an independent verse (*gūqǐ sòng*). This precisely serves as the brief opening of the "three" to reveal the "one," thereby shaking old attachments and giving rise to new doubts;
it provides the occasion for raising these doubts to prompt a formal request for instruction.
Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas do not differ.
These two lines of verse clarify that the transformative teachings of all Buddhas, both here and there, are identical.
Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, you should give rise to great power of faith.

These two phrases exhort one to have faith. Since the Buddha speaks words that accord with reality, why would anyone hear this brief opening that reveals the One by means of the Three and yet give rise to doubt?
It is precisely to prevent those who might slander [the teaching] due to such doubt that it is necessary to exhort them to faith.
"In the long future of the World-Honored One’s Dharma, one must surely speak the truth.
These two lines clearly illustrate that all Buddhas manifest reality; this is precisely the single Truth (*eka-tattva*).

When Śāriputra heard this, he was thus filled with doubt. In truth, he had never heard such a thing before; it shook his former attachments and gave rise to present doubts, leading him to wonder: "Could it not be that a Māra has manifested as a Buddha?"

Precisely because of hearing these words, he addressed the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas: "I have caused them to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and to attain nirvāṇa."
This correctly clarifies that Śākyamuni opens [the teaching] into three; this is precisely the opening through bestowal (*pradāna*).

While the aforementioned Buddhas only clarify the manifesting of the real (*satya*), and this Śākyamuni only clarifies the opening into three, the verse briefly manifests them by clarifying one side of each in turn.
This first line is about to clarify the non-substantiality of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*); thus it says, "having attained nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the first two lines clarify the opening.
Regarding the two vehicles: the two phrases "I cause" refer to the self-cultivation of the Bodhisattva vehicle of the six perfections. How is this known?

By practicing the conduct of the six perfections, one is freed from the bonds of the four miserable destinies, yet has not yet entered parinirvāṇa for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and a hundred *kalpas*.

Thus one attains *nirvāṇa*. The term "reaching" (*dài*) means to extend far and wide. Furthermore, regarding the practice of the six *pāramitās*, because one first delivers others, it is said, "I cause them to be liberated from the bonds of suffering.
Only afterward does one personally realize the untainted state (*anāsrava*); thus it is said, "one reaches and attains *nirvāṇa*.

By inferring this meaning, one knows that this refers to the vehicle of the six *pāramitās*. Moreover, according to the subsequent enumeration, it is inferred that the Buddha employs skillful means (*upāya*).
The Power reveals the teachings of the three vehicles (triyāna). If this were not indicated, what would constitute the three?
One should not count the two vehicles twice over to make up the three vehicles.
"The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, manifests the teachings of the three vehicles.
These two lines directly refute [the notion that] the three vehicles are all false and deceptive.

Because they hear that while three are false and one is true, these śrāvakas now hear that all three vehicles are merely skillful means (*upāya*). Since skillful means are false, and since skillful means are false...
For what reason does the Tathāgata, having emerged from meditative concentration, instead praise skillful means? Therefore, the doubt raised below arises from hearing this;
thus, one wonders whether he praises both wisdom and skillful means.
"Sentient beings are attached everywhere; I lead them so that they may emerge [from suffering].
These two lines express the intent behind establishing the three vehicles. This intent is to expediently guide them away from all sufferings;

therefore, it is not the ultimate reality, but merely a skillful means (*upāya*). This concludes the verse’s brief exposition on the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one. △ Below this is...
