This is the second instance of raising doubts and requesting instruction.
At that time, within the great assembly, there were various śrāvakas and arhats who had exhausted their outflows, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others.
"The twelve hundred people.
From this point downward from the great assembly, all are titled "Resolving Doubts and Presenting Petitions.
This section of the text is the compiler’s account of the doubts of the twelve hundred.
As for the arising of the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—
this is also the sūtra compiler’s account of the doubts of the fourfold assembly.
Each [of them] had this thought: "Why does the World-Honored One now so earnestly praise the skillful means?
This, moreover, is the scribe's account of their primary doubt according to their capacity; it is a general doubt concerning the Buddha’s two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate truth.
And he spoke these words: "The Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand.
This refers to the doubt regarding the Buddha’s true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).
"Whatever he has spoken, its underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) is difficult to know; it is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
This is a doubt regarding provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). It arises from hearing that the words of all Buddhas are non-different and must necessarily speak the truth.

From this, the following doubt is born: "In the past, the Buddha taught that the wisdoms of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*) lead to the same realization without distinction; it is only a matter of whether residual habits (*vāsanā*) have been exhausted or not.
Now, he universally extols the Tathāgata’s two kinds of wisdom as being beyond my reach. For this reason, [the text] speaks of the four...
The assembly doubted the Buddha’s two kinds of wisdom.
The Buddha spoke of the single meaning of liberation, saying, "We too have attained this Dharma and reached Nirvana," yet now we do not know where this meaning leads.
This was the personal doubt of Śāriputra regarding the noble paths of the three vehicles that he had attained. He thought, "These are the true means of transcendence;
by practicing this principle, I too have reached nirvāṇa. Yet now, it is suddenly said that all are merely expedient means. I do not yet know which of these is the ultimate reality."
Therefore, it is said that one does not yet understand this meaning. This doubt arises because the preceding section refuted the three [vehicles] as being false.

Although the preceding refutation stated that all three vehicles are merely expedient means (*upāya*), the description of the doubt focuses only on the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) because their attachment is heavy and their doubt is profound;
thus, they are singled out for mention. When we reach the subsequent section on the removal of doubts, it says: "In total there are eighty thousand [beings] who seek Buddhahood."
All the bodhisattvas likewise had doubts; thus, while all three vehicles were in doubt, only those of the two vehicles are mentioned here.
This concludes the account of Śāriputra’s arising of doubt.
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing that the fourfold assembly was in doubt and that he himself had not yet fully understood, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
For what cause and for what reason do you so earnestly praise the Buddhas' foremost skillful means—the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
Since ancient times, I have never heard such a teaching from the Buddha. Now, the fourfold assembly all harbors doubts.
This section is where Śāriputra formally presents both his own and others' doubts regarding the praise of the two types of wisdom. He says:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter. For what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise this profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?"
This section constitutes the first formal request, made for the sake of resolving the inquiries of both himself and others.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, has finally proclaimed this Dharma after a long time.
These two lines praise the aforementioned doubt regarding true wisdom (*jñāna*).
[The Buddha] himself declares that he has attained such inconceivable dharmas as the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the samādhis, the dhyānas, and the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Regarding the Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment, there is no one capable of posing a question; my intent is difficult to fathom, and there is likewise no one who can inquire.
Without being asked, I shall speak of my own accord, extolling the path I have traveled—the wisdom that is most subtle and wondrous, which all Buddhas have realized.
These twelve lines of verse summarize the preceding doubt regarding provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). The explanation of "provisional" is as before:
why is it that even the various arhats who are free from outflows (*anāsrava*) and those seeking nirvāṇa have now all fallen into the net of doubt? Why has the Buddha spoken thus?

Those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha—monks and nuns, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas alike—looked at one another with uncertainty and gazed up at the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, wondering: "What is the meaning of this? We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us."
These twelve phrases summarize the doubts of the fourfold assembly regarding the three vehicles. The first phrase clarifies the arhat;
the second phrase refers to "those who seek nirvana. Here, the term "refers to" indicates that these bodhisattvas themselves seek nirvana.
Furthermore, because he intends to benefit others, he differs from those of the two vehicles; he is certainly a bodhisattva.
All of this will now be explained in detail, which constitutes the mark of doubt. The eight phrases following "he who seeks" clarify the request of the pratyekabuddhas.
Among all the disciples, the Buddha declared me to be foremost; yet now, regarding my own wisdom, I am beset by doubt and cannot discern it clearly:
is this the ultimate Dharma, or is this merely the path I am currently practicing?
These six lines clarify Śāriputra’s own doubts:
"The son born from the Buddha’s own mouth stands with palms joined, gazing up in reverence and waiting; may you utter a subtle and wondrous sound, and at this time speak according to reality."
These four lines are a verse concerning the doubts of the Buddha’s sons. Because they are able to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas through true compassion, they are called "Buddhas.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and others are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; those bodhisattvas who seek Buddhahood are approximately eighty thousand in number.
Furthermore, the wheel-turning sage-kings from ten trillion lands arrived, joining their palms with reverent hearts, desiring to hear the complete path.
These eight lines of verse summarize the shared doubts that led to the request for instruction. As for verses and prose, the meaning may be inferred accordingly.

If it is not as stated above in verse, it is either an extended passage or a mutual clarification through expansion and abbreviation; regarding matters that are not urgent for the meaning, one cannot afford prolixity.
This concludes the first section: the request for a definitive resolution of doubts for the sake of oneself and others.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak further.
If this matter were to be spoken, all the worlds—including gods and humans—would be struck with alarm and doubt."
This section, within the context of the preceding "ceasing of praise," constitutes the second instance of ceasing.

The intent behind this cessation is that if he were to speak further, the audience might become startled, doubtful, or fail to believe; therefore, he ceased. It also serves to indicate the meaning of the second cycle that follows.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will speak of this; I pray that you will speak of this. Why is this?
In this assembly there are countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya sentient beings who have seen various Buddhas in the past;

their faculties are sharp and keen, and their wisdom is clear and lucid. Upon hearing what the Buddha speaks, they will be able to believe and accept it with reverence. At that time, Śāriputra, wishing—
To reiterate this meaning, he spoke these verses:
"The Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One, please speak; have no concern. In this assembly there are immeasurable multitudes who are capable of reverent faith."

From the point where Śāriputra spoke again after the conclusion of the verse, this section of the text constitutes the second instance in which Śāriputra (Śariputra) conveys the request of the assembly.
Because they have long cultivated roots of sharp faculties, they will certainly understand; thus, he restates the matter to present his petition once more.
The Buddha again stopped Śāriputra, saying: "If this matter were to be spoken, all the worlds—including devas, humans, and asuras—would be filled with alarm and doubt;
those bhikṣus of overweening pride would fall into a great abyss. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
"Cease, cease! There is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. Those with overweening pride will certainly not show respect or faith upon hearing it.
This verse, following the Buddha’s repeated cessation of speech, clarifies the third instance of his refusal to teach.

He ceased out of concern that those with overweening pride would inevitably slander the teaching upon hearing it and thereby fall into the evil realms; it also marks the conclusion of the third set of causes and conditions for the lower [capacity].
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak; we pray that you will speak.
In this assembly, there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of those like us who, life after life, have already received transformation from the Buddha.
People such as these will certainly be able to respect and believe [the teaching], attaining peace and security for a long night, and receiving great benefit. At that time, Śāriputra—
Desiring to restate this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"O Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings, I pray you, preach the foremost Dharma. I am the eldest son of the Buddha; please deign to explain it in detail."
This assembly consists of immeasurable multitudes who are able to reverently believe in this Dharma. The Buddha has already, throughout successive lifetimes, taught and transformed such as these;
they all join their palms with single-minded devotion, desiring to hear and receive the Buddha’s words. We twelve hundred, as well as the others seeking Buddhahood, [are likewise present].
"May you, for the sake of this assembly, deign to explain it in detail. Upon hearing this Dharma, they will give rise to great joy.

From that time on, he spoke again; this was the third time Śāriputra described the great benefit of wisdom. Having restated his doubts and requested further instruction—this concludes the third section, the presentation of doubts and the request for teaching.
From the moment he arose from meditative concentration until this verse, this constitutes the formal exposition (*samyag-deśanā*).
Within this section, the initial part concludes the brief opening that reveals the One by means of the Three.
Following this, the subsequent portion shall extensively open the Three to reveal the One. This specific passage begins from the point where the Sūtra states:
"At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: 'Since you have already earnestly requested three times, how could I not speak? Below this, there are seven [sections] in total."

This half-fascicle scripture provides a correct and extensive elucidation of the "opening of the three and revealing the one. This section of the text consists of three parts: first, the teaching by means of the Dharma for those of superior faculties;
second, the teaching by means of parables for those of middling faculties; and third, the teaching by means of past-life causes and conditions for those of inferior faculties.
It is also known as the triad of principle, phenomenon, and practice. Regarding this core scriptural text, there have been many disputes throughout antiquity.
Now, following the evaluation of Tiantai, I shall analyze [the text] by means of ten principles, organizing them into ten sections.
Therefore, I have excerpted these and placed them at the beginning of the following scriptural text, so that there may be no confusion.

First, regarding the distinction between the specific and the general: in the first cycle, the specific name is "Dharma-exposition" (*dharmadeśanā*), while generally it possesses all three [modes of exposition].

For example, "The *udumbara* flower appears but once in an aeon" is the parable-exposition (*upamā-deśanā*). "If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way" is the causal-condition exposition (*nidāna-deśanā*).
Second, in the middle cycle, the specific name is "Parable-exposition," while generally it likewise possesses all three. Did I not previously say that they are all...?

For the sake of transforming bodhisattvas, he further employs an analogy: "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, he distinguishes and teaches three"—this is the teaching by way of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*).
"At the abodes of twenty thousand *koṭi* Buddhas, he constantly taught and transformed you"—this is the teaching by way of causes and conditions (*nidānadeśanā*).

If one were to claim that this passage belongs to the teaching by way of the Dharma, it would be like saying that once the elder had heard [the warning], he was already so startled that he entered the burning house; only then would it be appropriate to provide rescue. Thus...
This concerns the causal conditions (*nidāna*). Regarding the three successive turnings (*tri-parivarta*), the specific names refer to the causes and conditions of past lives;

generally, each also possesses these three aspects. "The time for my *nirvāṇa* has arrived, and the assembly is again pure; I shall cause them to enter the Buddha-wisdom" is the teaching of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*). "There was a guide" is the teaching by way of analogy (*aupamyadeśanā*).
As for why there are three turnings, it is because they proceed from the many to the primary, and from the concise to the peripheral, with the desire that their names [be established].

There is no confusion; each [teaching] is based on a single intent. Question: If the three cycles are for those of the three capacities, and one cycle contains all three expositions, does that exposition necessarily possess all three capacities?
Answer: The Dharma-exposition (dharmākhyāna) is not merely intended to accommodate those of the highest among the middling capacity.

Furthermore, there are middle and lower [capacities]. However, regarding the teaching of the Dharma itself, there are three [levels] within what is taught to oneself; the same applies to the other two cycles.

Because one wishes to clarify the persons to whom the teaching is addressed, one first clarifies the Dharma that provides benefit; therefore, the three cycles are first illustrated through both their general and specific aspects.

Second, regarding the clarification that there are both śrāvakas and non-śrāvakas, one must not hold to a partial or biased view. If one observes from the perspective of the elder’s true wisdom, there are no hired laborers;

yet, if one considers the faculties and nature of the impoverished son, he identifies himself as a laborer. According to the sutras and in light of the treatises, how many kinds of śrāvakas should there be?
First, those who have long practiced the Small Vehicle and whose path of the Small Vehicle has matured in this life, such that upon hearing the Small [Vehicle], they...
This refers to the teaching on the realization of the fruit, as stated in the *Tattvaviniścaya-śāstra*. Originally, these were bodhisattvas who had practiced the Great Path for many kalpas;
however, in the interim, they became weary of saṃsāra, regressed from the Great [Vehicle], and adopted the Small [Vehicle]. These were distinct roots of goodness.

The Buddha provisionally established the Small Teaching for them so that they might sever their fetters and attain the fruit. Since their regression from the Great was not long ago and their practice of the Small has been recent, it stands to reason that—

It is easy to understand. This refers to what the treatise calls "retrogression from bodhi. Third, because these two exist, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas secretly conceal [their true nature] while manifesting outwardly, accomplishing the guidance and reception of beings so as to lead them into the Great Way;
this refers to what the treatise calls "responsive transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).

Fourth, it is for the purpose of seeing that both the provisional and the real can bring about transcendence from birth and death, causing one to rejoice in *nirvāṇa* and cultivate the precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

Regarding wisdom: there is a slight degree of contemplative wisdom, yet one has not yet entered the stage resembling [the fruit], and having attained only a meager realization, one claims to have realized the fruit.
This is called "claiming to have attained what one has not attained," which the treatises term "arrogance" (adhimāna).

Fifth, this present teaching opens up the two types of śrāvakas—the provisional and the real—therefore, by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, it causes all to hear; these are the five kinds of śrāvakas.
Furthermore, if there were two types—those who definitively follow the Small Vehicle and those who regress from the Great Vehicle—then there would be Śrāvakas.

If one follows the Mahāyāna, it is logically impossible for them to undergo total extinction or remain forever in the "transformed city" (the provisional stage), as they must ultimately return to the "Jewel Abode" (the ultimate goal). Since this is the case for the Real, there can be no such thing as the Expedient.

If one possesses overweening pride (*adhimāna*), then they are not subsumed within either the provisional or the ultimate [teachings]. Next, regarding whether the Mahāyāna path of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) Buddha exists or not:

if he provisionally manifests as a response-body, externally displaying minor traces while internally concealing his great virtue, then from the perspective of these concealed virtues, there are no Mahāyāna *śrāvakas*.
However, if he personally reveals his origins and manifests his fundamental nature, then it is said that they do exist.
Riding upon the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he manifested his departure from that state while still appearing as a śrāvaka; this is what is called the Mahāyāna.

The primary intent of the present sutra in opening up the three vehicles to reveal the One is to ensure that those great śrāvakas who were destined for regression shall instead become Mahāyāna śrāvakas.
If this sutra had not yet been heard or recorded, there would have been śrāvakas who practiced according to the realization;

however, since it has been opened and explained through the definitive record, there are no śrāvakas in this sutra. As for the later mention of "śrāvakas," it refers to those who hear [the teaching] and subsequently regress.
This accords with the meaning of the "Preface to the An" (An-tong xu). Thus, the compilers of the sutras have traditionally applied this name.

The *Śāstra* states that while the former two [stages] were not yet mature and no prediction was recorded, the latter two received predictions. According to Tiantai’s fourfold comparison, both the proximate and the distant receive predictions. The *Śāstra* bases its account on those who received predictions while seated in the assembly;
however, we now rely on the general principle of being granted the opening [of the path]. Since both parties hear the sutra, they must both receive the prediction.
Once it was opened, there was nothing that could be disputed. The treatise addresses the doctrine of "having a remainder," yet it cannot be said to accord with the thunderous intent of the Sūtra.
Therefore, it clarifies these two points in order to determine whether that which is observed is actually existent or non-existent.

Regarding the three types of delusions having varying degrees of thickness and thinness: among those who have attained entry through the previously explained practice of reality, there are three different cycles due to the thickness or thinness of their delusions.
This indicates that their faculties (*indriya*) are either sharp or dull; all of these discuss the root-nature (*gotra*) of the Mahāyāna.

As for the specific delusions having varying degrees of thickness and thinness, they constitute four permutations: first, when specific delusions are light and the Mahāyāna faculty is sharp, one attains awakening immediately upon hearing [the teaching].

Second, those with heavy afflictions and sharp faculties understand only after hearing the teaching a second time. Third, those with light afflictions and dull faculties reach a decision only after hearing it three times.

Fourth, those with dull faculties and heavy afflictions serve merely as an assembly for establishing karmic connections. Furthermore, in the first stage, the three layers of ignorance obscure the Middle Way within the First Abode;
when the Dharma is first preached, those of superior faculties exhaust these three layers simultaneously, thereby opening [the path].
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision: those of middle capacity enter the stage of bodhisattvas and receive their prediction; those of lower capacity sever one layer [of delusion].
Next, when the teaching by analogy is given, those of middle capacity hear it and sever the three layers completely, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and entering the stage of bodhisattvas.
They receive their prediction [of enlightenment]. Those of inferior capacity advance to sever two layers [of delusion].

Next, when they hear the teaching on causes and conditions, those of inferior capacity finally sever the three layers completely, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, entering the rank of Bodhisattvas, and receiving their prediction.

Since there are differences between the beginning and end regarding the entry and abiding throughout these three cycles, one must distinguish between the sharpness or dullness of faculties and the lightness or heaviness of afflictions.
Fourth, the clarification of whether the faculties (*indriya*) are transformed or not. Generally, the mental spirit of sentient beings is unstable;
encountering adverse conditions, they transform from sharpness to dullness, while encountering favorable conditions, they transform from dullness to sharpness.

If one first encounters a Buddha and hears the Dharma, there are those who naturally transform their inferior or middling faculties into superior ones and attain awakening immediately upon hearing the direct teaching of the Dharma. There are also those who transform [their faculties] into the middling level, attaining understanding through the use of analogies. This refers to the inferior [level].

This does not change; it is only through three cycles that it is fully realized. Because the transformation [of the faculties] was already established in previous lives as the three roots, it causes one to hear the three expositions now and attain realization sequentially.
It is like cutting wood with three knives: one is sharp, one is medium, and the blunt one requires three strokes.
Although the names "sharp" and "blunt" do not change, the place where the wood is severed is the same. Question: If the three roots enter the initial [stage],...

Question: Within the stage of abiding, are there still distinctions between those of sharp and dull faculties? Answer: When the essence of true cultivation is manifested, there are no such gradations. Question:

If that is so, for those above the first stage who further initiate "conditioned cultivation" (yuan-xiu), are there still distinctions of superiority and inferiority? Answer: For those individuals at the same level, there is no longer any question of victory or defeat.
Since the essence of true cultivation is fused as one, how could there be any difference? Although it was previously clarified that the thickness of delusions must depend on—
Because of their past roots, they are clearly illuminated.

Regarding the five types of illumination, there are those who have attained awakening and those who have not. Although the former roots may have been established, it is still necessary to attain awakening.
In the sutras, it is frequently explained that Bodhisattvas constitute the superior root, Pratyekabuddhas the middling root, and Śrāvakas the inferior root. If Bodhisattvas are also included...
Do those of superior faculties attain awakening within the discourse on the Dharma itself? Do Pratyekabuddhas attain understanding within the discourse on parables?
And do Śrāvakas attain awakening within the discourse on causes and conditions? Nevertheless, the sūtras generally explain these three faculties in this manner.

As for the realization and understanding [of the truth], the meaning is not necessarily so. One should know that within each of the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma, there are instances of realization and understanding by those of the three vehicles.
If this is so, what is the intention behind the present sutra? Why is it that we see only śrāvakas attaining realization, while we do not see pratyekabuddhas attaining entry?
This is because pratyekabuddhas possess middling faculties; having encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world, they enter the path of the śrāvaka.
Because they attain awakening in accordance with their faculties, pratyekabuddhas are not separately designated; thus, the verse in the *Śāriputra-parivarta* says:
"Those who seek pratyekabuddhahood—whether bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs. Based on this text, one knows that pratyekabuddhas are included within the four assemblies (*catur-vidha-saṃgha*).
Furthermore, the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta* says: "Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who seek the voice... [The text continues].
As for those who hear [the teaching], how could those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha fail to attain awakening through conditions?
One should know that bodhisattvas likewise attain realization through three cycles.

Sixth, regarding those who have attained realization and those who have not: if the three vehicles share the same awakening, for what reason do we see only the Śrāvakas attaining realization, while the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas are not seen to do so?
Now it is explained that one who appears when no Buddha has appeared in the world is called a *Pratyekabuddha* (Solitary Realizer).

Since they hear the Buddha’s teaching on the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are called *Pratyekabuddhas* (Dependent Awakeners). Thus, they are already included within the category of Śrāvakas.
Among these, those who attain awakening and achieve understanding are not treated as separate cases. As for the Bodhisattvas who do not express their understanding:

whereas the Śrāvakas previously did not clarify their attainment of Buddhahood, this sutra now opens for them the path toward the Great Vehicle; fearing that their own understanding might be erroneous, they therefore recount it before the Buddha.
The Bodhisattvas are not like this, and thus there is no expression of understanding. Furthermore, there are three reasons for this: first, the Bodhisattva...
My original intention was to seek Buddhahood. Even if there were heterodox attachments, they would be slight; in the end, I would surely attain Buddhahood, with no concern that I might fail.
Now, having heard the teaching of the three turnings, I understand that this merely rectifies my contemplative wisdom; therefore, there is no need for me to undergo further formal realization.

Regarding the second point, that the two vehicles attain Buddhahood, there are texts on this everywhere concerning the Bodhisattvas' realization of the Great [Vehicle]. However, the teaching that the two vehicles become Buddhas begins only with the present teaching (*jiao*).

Because it was transmitted according to its essential points, it is treated here briefly. While the foreign (Sanskrit) texts may contain such passages, they were omitted and not recorded in the Chinese version.

Thirdly, as for the Bodhisattvas, their stages and practices are profound and transcendent; the various new and lesser bodhisattvas do not dare to comprehend them. This is why [the Buddha] waited until the conclusion of the discourse on the Life Span before Maitreya could fully grasp the whole.

Regarding their realization: beginning from the attainment of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and ending with the remaining one birth yet to be completed, this present sutra is fully endowed with the realizations of the three vehicles.
Seventh, regarding those who receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and those who do not:
if the three vehicles all equally attain realization, why is it that only the śrāvakas are seen to receive a prediction, while the pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas are not?

If it is because pratyekabuddhas are already included within the category of śrāvakas and therefore are not predicted separately, then there are also three reasons for the case of bodhisattvas. First, [they were] previously... [the text continues].
Having entered the stage of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one is unable to further resolve the mind [for enlightenment]; how, then, could one receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)?

Now, having awakened to and entered the Great [Vehicle], and rejoicing in this distinct decision, he is therefore granted a prediction regarding the name of his eon and his land. When a Bodhisattva resolves the mind to seek Buddhahood, their practice becomes fully perfected.
Therefore, one does not eagerly seek [enlightenment] with haste, nor does the Buddha bestow it with urgency.

Furthermore, the previous teachings that bestow predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) upon bodhisattvas at various points are also translations that follow the essential [teachings], as explained above. There are also separate predictions for the two bodhisattvas, such as Devadatta and the dragon girl;
are these not indeed separate predictions? Moreover, the "Dharma Master" chapter states: "Those who seek the state of a śrāvaka, those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha..."
"Buddhas" refers to those who seek the Buddha-way and others of such a kind.

All of them, having heard even a single phrase or a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* before a Buddha, I bestow upon them all the prediction that they shall attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*. Is this not the bestowing of predictions upon those of the three vehicles alike?

Previously, those of the two [lower] vehicles had never received the prediction of the eight signs; therefore, for them, I record their kalpas and lands, whereas for the Bodhisattvas, I record their names.

This has already been recorded previously; therefore, it is not explained again here. Such shallow and mundane records were attained as early as the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), yet they are not what the Bodhisattvas aspire to.
What the Bodhisattvas aspire to is precisely the distant prediction of the ultimate, wondrous enlightenment.

Thus, within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s "Life Span" chapter, from the initial generation of the mind until the attainment at the end of one lifetime, the wondrous cause is fulfilled and the supreme fruit is suddenly perfected. This is...
They are bestowed with the prediction of the Dharma-body. Therefore, one knows that this present sutra contains predictions for all three vehicles.

Eighth, regarding the shallowness and depth of awakening: although, at first glance, they equally shatter ignorance and enter the realization of the first stage (*bhūmi*), upon detailed investigation, there must be differences in clarity and obscurity.
Having already entered the Buddha-wisdom upon hearing the discourse on the Dharma, how could they not experience it again upon hearing the discourse through parables?

Illumination. Furthermore, having heard the principle of causes and conditions, one’s understanding naturally advances; hearing further of the lifespan [of the Buddha], it becomes even more profound and deep.
This is like a person who hears the Dharma again and finds it superior to what they previously heard; whether the teachings are single or repeated, thick or thin, can be known by comparison.

Ninth, clarifying the differences in the benefits obtained through the provisional and the real: An ancient said, "Those who practice the three vehicles with reality obtain benefit, whereas those who practice through provisional means merely serve as a means of reception and guidance for 'echoes and shadows,' and their benefit is not reckoned.
Tiantai does not hold this view; if one reaches the [Chapter on] Life Span, [the distinction is clear].
Both those of provisional and ultimate capacities receive benefit; the Path increases until it reaches its highest peak, and births are diminished until they are fully exhausted.

Standing on the verge of Perfection, with only one birth remaining—could this not be the benefit of the provisional? Therefore, at the beginning, he acts as a shadow and echo to mature those of true practice together;

later, when the ultimate fruit is taught, his own path becomes manifest. As the text says: "The profits from lending and interest spread throughout other lands. This refers to the profits from lending.

In him, there is self-benefit; through the practice of realization, he gains benefit. Because he guides others through skillful means, the merit of transformation returns to himself, and thus skillful means also gain benefit.

If it is appropriate for them to hear in secret about his long-lasting lifespan, how could he not preach the Dharma with a single voice so that sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind?
Why must one necessarily wait for the "Original Gate"? Furthermore, I myself desire to obtain this true purity.
The Great Dharma is that which benefits oneself; one should know that in this present sutra, both the provisional and the real benefit [beings].

Tenth, the clarification of those who depend on the timing [of the teaching] and those who do not: those who did not realize it prior to this point and must necessarily wait for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to realize it are said to "depend on the timing.
Those who have already understood through the teachings prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are said to "not depend on the timing. Why is this so? Because the Buddha has a manifest [teaching].

Regarding the two explanations of the Esoteric [teachings]: if one takes the Exoteric teachings as the subject, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those of the Two Vehicles had not yet awakened to the Great Way;

it was necessary to bring them to maturity through the five flavors, culminating in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Thus it is said: "The time for preaching has not yet arrived," and now, "this is precisely the time to definitively preach the Mahāyāna.
This refers to waiting for the appropriate time. If, however, one takes the Esoteric teachings as the subject, this is not necessarily so.
The complete reliance upon the five flavors occurs only at the Lotus Sūtra; prior to this, there were those who entered the Way in secret, and thus it is called "not waiting for the time.

This constitutes the great distinction between the present and the past regarding whether the time has arrived or not. If one considers the three stages [of the teaching], these too involve waiting for the time or not waiting for the time.

Likewise, within the two gates of the Trace and the Origin, there is also the matter of waiting for the time or not waiting for the time, which results in the sequential realization and entry [into the Way].

This refers precisely to that meaning. Question: In the *Mūla-śāstra*, it is stated that those of determinate nature are neither included among the secret nor the manifest, and are not subsumed under either of the two periods.
Does this mean they have lost their opportunity and will never attain awakening? Answer:

Other sūtras may describe them as having lost their opportunity, but this present sūtra does not. Although these individuals do not awaken to the secret or the manifest, they conceive the thought of having attained *nirvāṇa* and enter [into it].
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, they seek the Buddha’s wisdom in that land and are able to hear this sutra;

therefore, there is no loss of time—it is simply that they are waiting for the time to come in that land. Question: When the five thousand [monks] rose and departed from below, was this not a loss of time?

Answer: These [benefits] should be understood as the benefits received by those who propagate the sutra after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, or as those who attain liberation within the Nirvana [Sūtra].
Question: In the first week, Śāriputra requested [the teaching] for the fourfold assembly of the three faculties; in the second week, he requested it for those of middle and lower faculties.
Why, then, do you say that the Buddha taught the Dharma in three weeks specifically for people of the three faculties? Answer: This statement is not...

When it comes to invitations, they are universal invitations; when it comes to preaching, it is universal preaching. Those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom attain enlightenment upon hearing the Dharma;

those of middling faculties abide in the middle and attain enlightenment through analogies; those of inferior faculties remain at the lower level and attain enlightenment by hearing the three [vehicles]. Thus, he discerns the capacities and dispositions of all beings.

One must anticipate the underlying principle in advance. When it comes to the actual exposition, why choose between those of middling or inferior capacity? If the listener does not yet understand, one must act according to the faculties of the individual.
You should follow the meaning; how could you merely follow the words? The above ten gates are extracted from the *Tiantai Fahua jing shu* (The Tiantai Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra).

These meanings are presented in advance so that one may avoid confusion when encountering the sūtra itself. This has been explained in detail within the *Ji* (Commentary), though I have omitted it here to avoid prolixity.
Record. Those who require it should seek it therein.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "Since you have earnestly requested three times, how could I not speak?
This passage is the Tathāgata’s acquiescence. "You have [requested] thus," etc., means "how could I not speak? This is the granting of permission.
"Listen now attentively; reflect upon it well. I shall analyze and explain this section for you. This passage is both an admonition and a permission.

"Listen attentively" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); "reflect well" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and "ponder upon it" [refers to the wisdom of cultivation].
This is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). These constitute the three types of wisdom. The Great Sūtra clarifies that the four wholesome dharmas are the causes for Great Nirvāṇa;

in this sūtra, the single "wholesome spiritual friend" is the Tathāgata himself. These three phrases correspond to the three types of wisdom; therefore, the Buddha exhorted them, as they constitute the proximate causes and conditions.
△ Below this is the third section, which distinguishes those permitted among the assembly. This sūtra is divided into five chapters.
When these words were spoken, five thousand members of the assembly— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
immediately rose from their seats, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.
This is precisely the exclusion of the assembly for which permission was granted. Since five thousand were seated in the assembly, the Tathāgata had previously issued three prohibitions;
now, intending to grant permission to speak, he used his majestic spiritual power to have them depart. Therefore, this is called the "exclusion of the assembly."

Why is this? Because these people have deeply rooted and heavy karmic offenses, as well as overweening pride; they claim to have attained what they have not attained, and they claim to have realized what they have not realized.
Having such faults, they do not abide [in the Dharma].

Second, the reason for distinguishing the assembly is explained: the obstacles of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are manifold and their offenses are heavy; clinging to the "lesser" while obscuring the "great" means the roots are deep.
However, the roots of the offenses of the five turbidities alone are not yet called "deep"; it is only when arrogance and clinging are added that they are termed "deep.
To have not attained the three fruits of the path, nor realized the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), yet to claim one has attained them, is called "overweening pride" (*abhimāna*). There is...
Such "failures" refer to the three types of failure consisting of obstruction, attachment, and pride.

As for the World-Honored One remaining silent and not restraining them—his pedagogical method of departing or staying according to the three knowledges—he did not restrain them because he had previously heard the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one; these words were merely brief.
The meaning is obscure; as such, slander has not yet arisen. It would serve as a cause for binding the jewel, and its departure would be beneficial.

However, if they were to hear the extensive revelation that "three are revealed as one," it would contradict their sentiments and give rise to slander; thus, their remaining would be detrimental. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not prohibit [the departure].
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves; it consists purely of the solid and substantial.
This fourfold praise extols the excellence of those who are suited to the occasion. He states that branches and leaves are mere trifles, unfit for the purpose of a vessel;

such people cling to expedient means as if they were the ultimate, and thus are not vessels for the Great [Vehicle]. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "To cling to branches and leaves while abandoning the root."
"This person is not wise; this is precisely what that means.
Śāriputra, for such a person of overweening pride, it would be better even to fall back. Listen well now, and I shall explain it to you."
Regarding the statement, "This Ānanda withdraws from his seat; it is well that he withdraws":

since he has obscured himself with something small and, furthermore, obstructed the great light of others, his withdrawal now incurs no fault of slandering the Dharma, nor does he commit the error of hindering others; therefore, it is said to be "well.

While the upper branches and leaves had not yet been removed, the Tathāgata paused three times. Because the sincere and earnest wished to hear [the teaching], Śāriputra made four requests. Thus, master and disciple...

Examining the mechanism [of the situation], it is not merely a matter of being stingy or withholding [the teaching]. Question: The Buddha possesses great compassion; why does he not employ his supernatural powers to cause them to remain there without hearing?
Why is it that they are like those who are deaf and mute in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*? Why does he not increase the intensity of the "poisonous drum," as was done for Nandika and Vijaya?

Answer: Each has its own reason. At the conclusion of the *Avataṃsaka*, the gradual teaching was first introduced; because the attachments of the Hinayana had not yet been shattered, those in the assembly were separated from the response.
As for those at the conclusion, this is merely a provisional summary based on the records of the compilation. The old translation of the [Lotus Sūtra], fascicle thirty-seven, states:
"At that time, Śāriputra emerged from the Jeta Grove and did not see the Tathāgata’s sovereign adornments."
Regarding the manifestations, the lion’s roar, the wondrous merits, and so forth— since the great bodhisattvas and others are not seen,
and there is no eye of wisdom capable of seeing, perceiving, or forming mental conceptions of them, nor does one delight in speaking of or praising them—
this is because śrāvakas have already emerged from the three realms; thus, this is the passage concerning being like the deaf and the mute at that final assembly.

This refers precisely to the gradual [teaching] at its inception; yet it is also provisionally entrusted to a single lifetime in this Sahā world, wherein the gradual teachings are established so that their application may be communicated.
One should understand the present intent: while the *Avataṃsaka* extends to the end of the future, this very sūtra remains eternally on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
How is this different from the mutual relationship of principal and attendant throughout the ten directions?

This continues until the thirty-eighth chapter, "Entering the Buddha’s Realm," where Mañjuśrī emerges from the Hall of Good Abiding (*Susthitālaya*) together with devas, nāgas, and others, proceeds to the place of the Tathāgata, prostrates his head at the Buddha’s feet, and after making offerings, departs to travel toward the south.
At that time, Śāriputra, empowered by the Tathāgata’s strength, beholds Mañjuśrī departing.
As they were departing from the Jeta Grove, this thought arose [in them]: "We shall now go together.

At that time, Śāriputra had six thousand disciples who emerged from their own quarters, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and proceeded to where Mañjuśrī was. These six thousand individuals had all recently left the household life;
they had already drawn near to past Buddhas and were all those who had been transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī. Śāriputra...
Śāriputra extensively praised Mañjuśrī for the sake of the bhikṣus.
Mañjuśrī said to the bhikṣus, "If you are well able to accomplish the ten kinds of great resolve, you will attain the stage of Buddhahood, let alone the stage of a bodhisattva.

Since ancient times, it has been said that the *Avataṃsaka* period is long; if that were so, then the teaching following the compilation would have to wait until the arrival of the *Prajñāpāramitā* before one could attain it.
It is said that the instruction for the bhikṣus to fulfill the ten great minds is precisely the time when the teaching should be transmitted.

To summarize the meaning of these passages, they enter into the *Avataṃsaka*. Therefore, it is said that the duration is long. One should know that, when discussed from the perspective of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is nothing that is not the *Avataṃsaka*;
when spoken of in terms of the Buddha’s wisdom, there is nothing that is not the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Although this is the principle, if one considers the sequence:
If the classification were inconvenient, then all the teachings from the Deer Park should have been included.

However, because the vehicles differ in magnitude and the capacities and insights of the recipients are unequal, the Master who taught them also did not speak in a single way. Examining Śāriputra, he already had six thousand disciples;
thus, this must have been during the period of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings—how could it have been limited to the Deer Park alone? Now, the text further...
It is said: "As long as minor attachments have not been shattered, it resembles the beginning at the Deer Park.

According to the subsequent explanation of the passage concerning the elder in the *Śraddhā-viniścaya-parivarta*, this merely concerns the sequence of the faculties' perceptions regarding attachment and liberation. Now, for the sake of explanation, we shall temporarily rely on the gradual teaching, taking the end of the Great [Vehicle] and the beginning of the Small [Vehicle] as our basis.
For now, all the Buddha-dharmas must ultimately proclaim the truth after a long time; this is precisely because one intends to extinguish [deluded] transformations.
As for Pò'ān, he ought to be sent away. If both his departure and his staying would result in slander, one should follow the forceful exhortation of Xǐgēn.
If he departs now, there will be the benefit of establishing a karmic connection, serving as the cause for his future liberation;
why then allow him to stay? If he stays, there will be the harm of inevitable slander; why then not send him away? It was because of his compassion that Xǐgēn forcefully exhorted the Tathāgata.
Out of compassion, I shall now dismiss you; listen well. This constitutes the formal granting of permission (*anujñā*).
From the words "Since you have been so earnest" until this third section, the general permission has been fully granted.
Śāriputra said, "Yes, World-Honored One; I wish most earnestly to hear it.

This is how Śāriputra and the others received the command. "Wish most earnestly to hear" (yuàn lè yù wén) carries the sense of a formal request; together with the preceding [requests], this constitutes four requests.
Following this is precisely the extensive exposition of the five Buddhas' revelation of the provisional and manifestation of the real. Why is this called the "Extensive Opening"?

Yes. In contrast to the preceding [section], there are briefly three ways in which this is expanded: First, in the preceding scripture, the phrases and clauses are few; this is a brevity of text. Herein, the chapters and sentences are many;
this is an expansion of text. Second, above it was stated generally as "all Buddhas"; this is a brevity of persons. Herein, the five Buddhas are explained in detail;
this is an expansion of persons. Third, above it merely briefly opened up the three to reveal the one; this is a brevity of meaning. Herein, it is explained extensively.
This clarifies the six sections. This meaning is extensive; because it contains these three intentions, it is called "Extensive Opening.
As for the six sections: first, praising the rarity of the Dharma; second, declaring that there is no falsehood; third, opening up the provisional means; fourth, revealing the ultimate reality;

fifth, citing the five turbidities to explain the provisional; and sixth, distinguishing the false to emphasize the real. However, within these five chapters of the Buddhas, the third and fourth [sections] are consistently treated as the core.
The primary intent of this sutra consists of these six sections; the remaining four variations—whether present or absent in one version or another—converge to form a single meaning.
Furthermore, these may be briefly categorized as either general or specific. The general section begins from the emergence from meditative concentration and concludes with this verse.
The specific section is the brief opening found after the verses, consisting of three and a half lines of independent stanzas.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals;
it appears but once in a long while, like the udumbara flower."
This is the first section, which generally clarifies how all Buddhas reveal the ultimate truth by opening up the provisional. Within the verses, the first Buddha praises the rarity of the Dharma;

he praises it through both direct description and analogy. Regarding the phrase "only now is it being taught": all Buddhas appear together within the five turbidities and must first open the three vehicles.
Just as the present World-Honored One began revealing the true reality only after more than forty years—having waited for a long time and until the [opportunity] was rare—so it is here.

It is said that one speaks only when the time is right. As for not speaking for a long time, it was because people of the past were not yet capable, the time had not yet arrived, and the five thousand [who would reject the teaching] had not yet departed.
Why speak now? It is because people of the present are now capable, the time has arrived, and the five thousand have already left;
thus, one will definitively preach the Mahāyāna. Therefore, it is said that one speaks only when the time is right. Question: Take, for example, the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra. In the...
The various sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other perfect sutras all discourse upon the Buddha’s wisdom. Why, then, is it called "sparse"? Answer:

This is said in reference to bodhisattvas of dull faculties belonging to the two vehicles, as well as those taught in the *Śrāvaka-piṭaka*. First, they did not hear [the teachings] in the *Avataṃsaka*; next, they entered the Lesser Vehicle at the Deer Park;
later, they did not accept the two flavors [of the Mahāyāna]; and only now do they begin to hear them. Thus, it is considered "sparse."
"Rare. If there were bodhisattvas of sharp faculties, when would they have not heard [this teaching]? It is simply that its function as a benefit for this present sutra is one of further advancement.
In terms of the teachings, there was no lack of the Perfect and the Middle prior to this; in terms of time, both the "waiting" and the "absolute" are subtle.

Because it is pointed out here as a unique and manifest exposition, it is said to be rare. As for the *udumbara* flower, this refers to a miraculous omen; it appears once every three thousand years, and when it appears...

The appearance of the Golden Wheel-Turning King signifies that after the beings of the three vehicles have been matured through training, he then preaches the sublime Dharma and bestows the prophecy of a Dharma-King.
Upon hearing this sublime Dharma, one’s mind is immediately enlightened, and one will certainly receive the Buddha’s prophecy; this is called a "spiritual omen.
This flower definitively symbolizes the state of fruition in the future, and is therefore used as a metaphor for a precursor sign.
Śāriputra, you all should have faith in what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false.
When it is said that "you all should have faith," this is an exhortation to believe in the non-false dharma. This principle is most profound;

its principle differs from that of the past. These words are most subtle; these words run contrary to those of the past. This practice is most universal; this practice diverges from that of the past. This person...
"Supreme" means surpassing what was previously inferior. "Ultimate" (*zhi*) refers to the pinnacle of reality. Why is one exhorted to have faith?

It is because [the Buddha] wishes to clarify that what was formerly coarse is now sublime; thus, fearing that sentient beings might give rise to doubt, he proactively exhorts them to believe. How can the former be considered coarse?

It refers back to the coarseness of being a hired laborer, which has been entirely transformed into the son of an elder. Therefore, the four [sons] are sublime, having undergone no further alteration whatsoever.

Because these four [perfections] are perfected as the sublime, it is said: "That which you practice is the bodhisattva path. Fearing that beings might give rise to slander, he exhorts them to have faith.
One who has faith speaks a non-false dharma; such a person is without falsehood.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; their underlying intent is difficult to understand. This clarifies the third point:
that all Buddhas employ skillful means (*upāya*) because they wish to reveal the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

First, they describe that which is to be revealed, namely, the bestowal of [provisional] teachings. This is done because the intent is to manifest the ultimate truth; thus, they describe the purpose of employing these provisional means. First, it is explained that the Buddha-way follows...
There are three types of capacities; for those who require the teaching of expedient means, it is said that [the Buddha] "speaks according to what is appropriate.

Because the Buddha knows that the capacities of sentient beings are not yet pure and none are able to understand, it is said that "the underlying intent is difficult to comprehend. One should know that when he establishes the provisional for the sake of the real, his intent lies in the real;
these teachings are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. When he opens up the provisional to reveal the real, his intent lies in the provisional. You all—
That which is practiced is the Bodhisattva path. The Dharma of the Śrāvakas is like a hired laborer to these Kings of Sutras;
it is like a merchant’s son engaged in the business of livelihood, whereas the principle of eternal abiding is the true nature of reality.

If in the past the Real was treated as the Expedient and the name "Expedient" concealed the Real, now the Expedient is opened to reveal the Real, such that nothing exists outside of the Real. Whether hidden or manifest, the benefit lies in all beings.
The nature [of reality] abides eternally in its original source, never increasing or decreasing; therefore, it was not yet revealed.

Previously, not only was the name of the "Manifestation of Reality" (*dharmatā*) not spoken of, but there were no words at all regarding the "provisional application of means" (*upāya*). Thus, when the words for "provisional means" are spoken, one must immediately manifest the reality.
One should know that this is the essential purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the fundamental source of the teaching of reality. This is the interpretation of the meaning.
This is the ultimate destination, the treasury of all practices. If one does not realize this, then all giving and all exertion are in vain. One must understand this well.
Why is this? It is because I have, through countless skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expounded upon all dharmas.
This explains the aforementioned intention of employing provisional means (*upāya*). By citing the provisional power of the present Buddha, it explains the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas;

because their skillful wisdom is identical, this is used to explain that. The phrase "I, by means of countless skillful means" indicates that the Buddhas' opening of the provisional is also like my own.
The primary intent is to cite the Buddhas as testimony for this; therefore, this is used temporarily to explain that.
This clarifies that the paths of both [the Buddha and the disciples] are identical, as they all equally employ the provisional (*upāya*). Therefore, it must be explained.
Alternatively, it may refer to the following passage: "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination; only the Buddhas can know it.

This section concludes the preceding discussion on the opening of the provisional, using the two characters "this Dharma" (*shì fǎ*) to point back to the teaching of all phenomena (*dharmas*) and the subsequent opening [of the provisional].

Regarding the meaning of "expedient" (*upāya*): the Buddha’s intention is difficult to know; only a Buddha can fully comprehend it. When receiving the teachings according to the capacity of the recipient, what was previously called "three" is known by all Buddhas as "one.
The phrase "that is, the equality of these dharmas," etc., concludes this section of the text.

Furthermore, the fact that "the equality of these dharmas" properly belongs to the subsequent section on revealing the reality (*tattva*) is as follows: the meaning of these two lines reveals that expedient means are precisely expedient means that are identical to reality. Below...

This correctly reveals the ultimate reality. This reality is the reality that is identical with the provisional. The Buddha’s intention and the words of the sutra possess profound and wondrous significance.
This passage describes the Buddhas’ intent in bestowing and opening the provisional means.
This Dharma cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination; only the Buddhas are able to know it.
This is the initial designation of the supreme person and the Dharma within the Buddhas' correct and extensive manifestation.

By citing the non-discriminative Dharma as that which is known only by the Buddha, it shows that the Buddha, by means of non-discriminative wisdom, understands and realizes this non-discriminative Dharma. Thus...
This reveals the ultimate Dharma. Pointing toward this Dharma through expedient means is itself the revelation of the ultimate Dharma.
Why is this so? It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter.
This is the second [section] indicating the intent for transcending the world. "One great matter" refers precisely to this present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Now, the Buddhas awaken to the aspect of reality as it truly is; they appear in the world riding upon this path of reality solely to enable sentient beings to attain this very same aspect of reality.
They appear in the world for this purpose alone, and never for any other purpose. Excluding...
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—everything else is the work of Māra. Furthermore, "one" refers to the single true reality;

it is neither five nor three, neither seven nor nine, and is therefore called "one. Its nature is vast and expansive, capable of encompassing the five, three, seven, and nine; thus it is named "Great.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, they employ these majestic deportments and ritual protocols to teach and transform sentient beings. Therefore...

"Event" (*vastu*) refers to the practice for oneself and the transformation of others; both are termed "events. Furthermore, "One" (*eka*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), "Great" (*mahat*) is Prajñā, and "Event" (*vastu*) is Vimukti.
The intent of the Buddhas appearing in the world is to cause sentient beings to manifest these three dharmas as one, which is indeterminate.
This is the secret treasury; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha appears] solely for the sake of this "one great event. This is the causal condition.
This refers to sentient beings possessing the capacity for this One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); because they can thus respond, it is called the "cause" (*hetu*).
The Buddha responds by following that capacity; therefore, it is called the "condition" (*pratyaya*). This is the fundamental intent of the world-transcending One Vehicle.

As for the previous bestowal of the three [vehicles], they were merely introductory preludes to this one. It is like a person who, wishing to take something, first gives it away; although he speaks of various seeds...
The various paths are in reality but a single vehicle; this is precisely the meaning [of what follows].
Śāriputra, for what reason do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world? It is solely for the sake of the one great causal matter.
This third repetition is raised once more because, being about to provide a detailed analysis, it is brought forward again as the opening for the explanation.
Furthermore, as this is a matter of great importance that the Buddha holds in high esteem, it is mentioned repeatedly to signify that the Dharma is honored and not treated lightly.
△ Below, from "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" to [the end of] one...
The Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise. This correctly clarifies the general [teaching] of all Buddhas and explicitly reveals the text concerning reality (*tattva*).
As for this true and wondrous principle, who is able to know and see it? Only by means of the "opening" (*kai*) and so forth can one know and see it.

This is because "opening" and the others are precisely the stages of realizing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). Therefore, the Buddha explains it in terms of persons, principles, and teachings.
The "Four and One" [Practice] explains the principle of the Truth (*satya*) upon which the present sutra relies; it is the realm of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the *Fa-hua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra) explains it by way of four meanings: namely, attaining the stage of non-retrogression; knowing that the Tathāgata is able to realize the truth;

the sense of the identity of the Dharma-body; and not knowing the ultimate limit. These four types of explanations clarify the terms "opening," "showing," and so forth. Tiantai follows the sutra [in this regard].

According to the treatise, within each of the four types [of the one], one contemplates the four meanings through the gates of wisdom according to their respective stages; this section is thus explained.

This correctly reveals the text concerning reality (*tattva*). Whether viewed horizontally or vertically, all manifest the single reality. If one speaks of "revealing reality," then immeasurable phenomena are all but a single phenomenon.
Extensively, this includes all mental objects, activities, dharmas, and the entry into principle, and so forth—there is nothing that is not so.
It is not a single reality. This wondrous realm illuminated here is the true Dharma of the One Vehicle alone; how could there be four?
Although the principle is thus, from the perspective of exegesis, it would become overly diffuse and general. It is sufficient merely to contemplate and illuminate one’s own mind.
For the time being, I shall explain the sutra by means of four meanings. One should know that this true principle of the One Vehicle does not manifest in isolation.
One must employ the gateways of wisdom to contemplate the three [realms], traversing the stages they involve, so that together they may manifest the principle.
Therefore, the Buddha established four types—of stage, teaching, practice, and person—which are capable of explaining this true principle.

Thus, Tiantai followed the intent of the sūtras and śāstras to interpret them through these four meanings, ensuring that the Buddha’s appearance in the world was solely for the sake of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision within sentient beings, without obstructing the higher stages.
This exhausts the intent of the sutra by setting aside the level of ordinary beings. As for the fourfold explanation: the realization of principle arises from the stages;

the establishment of the stages arises from wisdom; the arousal of wisdom arises from the gates; and the opening of the gates arises from contemplation. Because of contemplation, the gates open; because the gates open, wisdom is perfected.
Because wisdom is perfected, the stages are established; because the stages are established, one perceives the principle; because one perceives the principle, it is called the "Unity of Principle.
Thus, it is only through each of these four meanings that one can truly perceive the text of the Sūtra. This realm of truth of the One Vehicle cannot be known or seen by ordinary means;
it can only be known and seen by means of the eye of wisdom. As for this One Vehicle, what kind of person is capable of knowing and seeing it? It should be...
The four eyes and two wisdoms cannot know or see the myriad phenomena in their dense array;

only through the Buddha-eye and the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), which are profoundly still and quiescent within true emptiness, can one know and see them. Although the essence and characteristics of the four eyes and two wisdoms are identical to those of the Buddha-eye and the wisdom of all modes, they must be distinguished in order to manifest their superiority.
As the Sūtra says: "It is for the sake of causing sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This does not depend on...
The fruit of Buddhahood is known and seen by oneself. If one speaks exclusively of the fruit of Buddhahood, one loses sight of sentient beings;

if one speaks only of sentient beings, there is no Buddha-knowledge or vision. Therefore, one must not take either side alone. For this reason, the meaning of "sentient beings" is inclusive, while the "fruit of Buddhahood" is ultimate.
This ultimate fruit of knowledge and vision enables all beings to attain it immediately; thus, it differs from other sutras. As for those who practice according to the three teachings:
Although they are sentient beings, because they do not yet possess the Buddha-eye or Buddha-wisdom, they are unable to know or see;

thus, the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision has not been achieved by them. Only those at the stages of the "name" (nāman) and "semblance" (pratirūpa) within the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna) can know and see.

Yet, even regarding their understanding and contemplation, this is not yet called "opening" in a definitive sense. Therefore, it is only upon reaching the four stages of partial realization (bhūmi) that it is truly termed "opening."

These are also sentient beings. Since they have partially attained the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom, the meaning of "sentient being" is established, and the meaning of "knowledge and vision" is likewise established.
Therefore, the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision must certainly occur from the first stage (prathamabhūmi) onward.

Were it not for Tiantai’s detailed exposition that the wondrous realm, sentient beings, the mind, and the Buddha are of one essence without distinction, how could one know that sentient beings possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
Since ancient times, the Buddha’s wisdom and insight (*jñāna-darśana*) have been taught for the sake of sentient beings, yet their underlying principle has not been clearly revealed.

Only the Great Master Tiantai, by correlating the teachings with the stages of practice and the conduct of persons, has definitively judged the Buddha’s wisdom and insight for sentient beings; thus, the principle is perfectly manifest.

Therefore, the auspicious signs in the Preface pre-emptively symbolize the falling of the four kinds of flowers from heaven, signifying that the myriad virtues all return to the same source, thereby enabling one to enter the flowers of the four stages.

One proceeds toward the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, when reaching the subsequent section on the "Exegesis of the Text," four meanings are employed, which should be used as a heading for the exegesis of the sūtra.
Among these, one meaning is explicitly revealed here; this is the first of the correct principles below.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby attaining purity.
These Buddhas are not limited to the five Buddhas alone; one must speak of all the Buddhas throughout the dust motes of lands in the ten directions.

Those who have appeared in the world have all, without exception, opened up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for the sake of sentient beings. This wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle is the fundamental intent of every Buddha.

Regarding "opening": first, in terms of stages, this refers to the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*), wherein one first breaks through ignorance (*avidyā*) to open the Tathāgatagarbha and perceive the principle of the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Why is this? Because the principle of inherent virtue (*prakṛtiguṇa*) is [obstructed] by both the pervasive and specific delusions.

That which is stained and attached consists of both the general and specific delusions, which coexist within a single thought-moment. The substance of this thought is itself [the delusion]; thus, its substance is not the principle, and its phenomena are not what they seem.
Right and wrong are one and the same; as a single substance, they act as an obstruction that is difficult to comprehend.

Those at the initial stage can achieve perfect faith through names and designations; those of the five grades can achieve perfect reception; those at the stage of semblance can achieve perfect subdual; yet they have not yet achieved severance.

This is not yet called "opening. When one internally applies contemplative practice and externally relies upon the rain of the Dharma, these assist in destroying both the pervasive and specific delusions, thereby manifesting the Tathāgatagarbha.
The cognitive vision of the cultivated nature then becomes brilliantly developed, like the sun rising and darkness vanishing so that the eyes may function;
therefore, it is called "opening. Because this cultivation based on conditions destroys delusions, it is said that one "attains purity. O Benevolent One!
The King said: "The Prajñā that enters into principle is called 'abiding. It abides in the stage of the Small White Flower within the Ten Abidings. Second, regarding wisdom:
this is the path-wisdom of the Perfect and Sudden, which perceives the true nature of the Way. This true nature is opened up within the Perfect Middle."
Therefore, it is called "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Third, as for the gate of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), this is the gate of emptiness:
when one is empty, all things are empty; therefore, it is called "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Fourth, regarding the contemplation of the mind:
contemplating the deluded thoughts presently arising is itself the principle of the three truths, which is inconceivable. When this contemplation is luminous and pure, it is termed "opening."
Within this section on the gates of wisdom for contemplating the four meanings, the stages (*bhūmi*) are explained first because they involve direct insight into the principle (*tattva*).

Therefore, they are listed at the outset; the scriptural text is likewise. One must understand that within each individual gate of wisdom for the contemplation of each stage, all four meanings are fully present.

The near and the distant mutually encompass one another, and the subject and the object reflect and manifest each other; only then does one perceive that the essence is perfect and the principle is one.
It is for the purpose of revealing to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that he appears in the world.

Regarding "Manifestation" (*śū*), if explained according to the stages (*bhūmi*): once the afflictive obstructions have been removed, the essence of knowledge and vision becomes manifest. This essence is endowed with all virtues;

the manifold virtues of the *dharmadhātu* are displayed with clarity. Therefore, it is called "Manifestation. This corresponds to the stage of the Great White Flower (*mahāśvetapuṣpa*) within the Ten Practices (*daśapratipatti*).

Regarding "Wisdom" (*jñāna*): it refers to the wisdom of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), which knows the distinctions among the various paths and modes within the ten *dharmadhātus*, as well as the dispelling of delusions and the realization of understanding.
The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Each and every one of these reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). Regarding the gates:
this refers to the gate of existence (*astimukha*), wherein "one exists" and "all exist," which demonstrates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Regarding contemplation (*vipaśyanā*):

although the opening of the middle [path] and its luminous purity are inconceivable, one is nonetheless able to distinguish emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhya*) with perfect clarity and without confusion; this is called "demonstrating."
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision are, in principle, one.
It is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to awaken to this Buddha-knowledge and vision that he appears in the world.

Regarding "awakening" in terms of stages: when hindrances are removed, the essence is revealed; the practices of the dharma-realm become clear, and phenomena and principle are harmoniously integrated, such that there is nothing further.

The second stage of progress is the non-duality of principle and quantity within the Perfect and Sudden teaching; therefore, it is called "Awakening. This corresponds to the stage of the "Small Red Flower" during the tenth stage of Dedication (*daśamī-pratipatti*).
In terms of wisdom, this is the "Wisdom of All-Knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*), which knows that all phenomena are of a single characteristic and are quiescent.
Quiescent extinction (*śānti*) is precisely the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. In terms of gates, this refers to the gate of both emptiness and existence;

that all things are both empty and existent is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. In terms of contemplating the mind, this refers to the center of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;
being three yet one, and being one yet three, is called awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is because the principle is one.
It is because he wishes to lead sentient beings onto the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that he appears in the world.
As for "entering," this refers to the stages [of realization]: when phenomena and principle have already been harmonized, one attains sovereign non-obstruction.

Flowing freely and spontaneously from the letter *a* to the letter *ṭa*, one enters the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), becoming perfectly wondrous and in accord with both reality and its extent, attaining mastery through thorough penetration.
Knowledge and vision according to measure (*yathāmātra-jñānadarśana*) can sustain all virtues; knowledge and vision according to principle (*yathābhūta-jñānadarśana*) can obstruct all delusions.
This is precisely the stage of the Great Crimson Flower (*mahāpadma*) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

From the perspective of wisdom, it is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which knows that all phenomena possess the single mark of the mark of quiescence (*ekalakṣaṇa-śāntalakṣaṇa*), and recognizes all various types of activities and characteristics; this is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Regarding the gates: this is the gate of neither emptiness nor existence. That all things are neither empty nor existent is precisely the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).

Regarding the contemplation: it is the [threefold truth of] emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle. To illuminate emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle simultaneously, while not being [limited to] emptiness, provisional existence, or the Middle, is called "entry.
Thus, from the Buddhas’ initial opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision until the final entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
