All of these are identical in principle (*li-yi*). However, regarding this section, why is it called "identical in principle"? It is so named because it relies on both the meaning and the text. As for relying on the meaning:
if there were no identity in principle, the various matters would be inverted; they would all be the teachings of Māra and would no longer be the Buddha’s sūtras.
Therefore, an explanation based on the identity in principle is required. As for relying on the text: the text speaks of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*); now, taking...

That which is known is that which is seen; what is seen is precisely the Truth (*satya*). What is known is the objective realm (*viṣaya*); the realm and the Truth are the principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, they are called the "Unity of Principle. Nevertheless, each of the four phrases—beginning with "opening"—is distinct.

When explained individually according to the gates of wisdom and stages, this is done merely to differentiate the four positions in order to manifest knowledge and vision as it is (*yathāvad-jñāna-darśana*). As the Sūtra says:
The initial resolve and the ultimate resolve are not two different things; yet between these two states of mind, the former is more difficult to achieve.

Since it speaks of "difficulty" and "ease," one knows that there must be a distinction of clarity and obscurity, as well as depth and shallowness, between the initial resolve and the ultimate resolve—just like the body of the moon.
The beginning and the end are both perfect, yet there is a distinction between the new moon and the full moon.

Although the knowledge and vision of these four stages all clearly illuminate the true reality (*dharmatā*), they differ only in their explanations of "opening" and "entering. One should know that in the knowledge and vision that accords with principle, there is truly no distinction of shallow or deep;
for within a single stage of the wondrous path of perfection, the merits of all forty-one stages are fully contained.
The opening alone fully reveals awakening, entry, and so forth; it is not a different mind.

Since this is the case for the explanation of the stages (*bhūmi*), the three aspects of wisdom-gates and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are likewise based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and possess no distinction of shallow or deep.

One must have one wisdom that encompasses the four wisdoms, one gate that encompasses the four gates, and within contemplation, one meaning that also encompasses the four meanings. The subsequent explanation of the three—persons, practice, and teaching—should also be understood in this way.
Based on these four explanations, no further distinctions will be made below.
Śāriputra, it is for this sole purpose of the one great causal matter that all Buddhas appear in the world.

This concludes the principle that the underlying meaning is one. Even in the former teachings of skillful means, one may likewise speak of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" from a doctrinal perspective.
Why is this? For example, in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood can also be correlated with opening, showing, awakening, and entering.

Although their realization of the Way is identical to that of the Perfect [Teaching], they still involve the stages prior to Buddhahood and thus do not constitute the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, the knowledge and vision of the Separate Teaching cannot be equated with it.
Sentient beings open it; those of penetrating capacity see the ground opening; those on the stage of thinness (tanubhūmi) demonstrate it; those who have abandoned desire awaken to it;
and those who have already accomplished their task enter it. For the two vehicles within the *pitaka*, this may be understood by analogy with the stages of penetration.

If categorized according to the Bodhisattva path, then the first *kalpa* constitutes "opening," the second *kalpa* constitutes "demonstrating," the third *kalpa* constitutes "awakening," and the hundred *kalpas* constitute "entering. If the sacred stages are combined, then the hundred *kalpas* are merged into the third [stage].
Awakening is achieved through [the realization of] the thirty-four minds that sever the fetters; this constitutes "entry.

Although these three teachings are explained in terms of their meanings as having stages such as "opening" and so forth, they do not clarify the Buddha’s knowledge and vision from beginning to end; therefore, they are all provisional.

Now, distinguishing by means of the specific divisions, this [teaching] is pure and without admixture, clarifying the reality of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—the great matter of the perfect fusion of the three truths. This reality is the principle (*li*).
Because it is one. This concludes the section on the unity of principle.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas.

This clarifies the unity of persons. If one were to speak according to the provisional teachings of the past, it would be said that they teach and transform those of the three vehicles; however, in terms of ultimate principle, [it is otherwise].
It is said: "He merely transforms bodhisattvas. That which the Buddha perceives in his mind is that they are his own children; there is no one among them who is not a human being.
Just as that impoverished son previously considered himself a lowly laborer, today he is revealed and realizes for himself that he is a son and truly not a hired servant.
Therefore, it is said that humans are one.
"Whatever he does is always for one purpose: solely to use the Buddha’s knowledge and insight to instruct and awaken sentient beings.
This clarifies the unity of practice. Regarding the phrase "all that exists" (*zhū yǒu*): "all" refers to the various practices of the three vehicles; they are termed "all" because they are manifold.
Regarding the phrase "always for the sake of equality" and so forth: the various practices established in the past were for the purpose of fulfilling all things;
thus, they are in fact a single matter. Where does this practice lead? It leads only to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; this is precisely the single-mindedness of practice.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings solely by means of the single Buddha-vehicle;
there is no other vehicle, whether a second or a third.

This clarifies the first [aspect], the teaching: namely, the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, which is called the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). It is the pure teaching of the One Vehicle of the Buddha-dharma.
In contrast, the three partial and inferior teachings are all termed "incomplete" (*śeṣa*) expositions; they are all of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) and are not the One Buddha Vehicle.
As for the term "no remaining vehicle" (*niḥśeṣayāna*), it must be understood according to its specific context. Why? Because once it is said that there is "no remainder," then...
Having already excluded the partial and the small [vehicles], it further states "whether two or three," which refers to the specific and the perfectly complete [teachings].

One should know that beyond the "without remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa), there are no further categories of two or three. As for the "without remainder vehicle," this refers to the current teaching’s absence of the provisional, expedient teachings with remainder found within the *Avataṃsaka*.
If there were no "two," then there would likewise be no [teachings] involving the provisional within the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Second, as for "no three," this refers to the absence of the three [vehicles] that are contrasted within the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings.

Since there are no samādhis, it can be understood that there are likewise none in the Deer Park’s minor [teachings]. Now, by interpreting the sūtra through the lens of its doctrinal divisions, the profound meaning becomes manifest.
Śāriputra, the teachings of all Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so.
This concludes the preceding section on the manifestation of reality. One should know that this applies to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
This is because it is for the purpose of revealing the One Buddha Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Beginning from this time when this wondrous Dharma was first preached, and ending here, this concludes the general section clarifying that all Buddhas have opened up the provisional teachings to reveal the ultimate reality.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable expedient means, through various causes, conditions, parables,
and modes of expression, have expounded all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
This clarifies the second chapter on the Buddhas of the Past. It specifically elucidates the teaching that opens up the provisional and reveals the ultimate through the method of giving.

However, this chapter on the Buddhas of the Past, as well as the two subsequent chapters on the Buddhas of the Future and the Present, share the same textual structure and principles as the preceding general chapter on the Buddhas, fully possessing the six meanings.

Herein, there are only the two meanings of opening up the provisional and revealing the ultimate; it lacks the meaning of praising the rarity of the Dharma and the meaning of preaching the absence [of self].

Regarding the two meanings of "falsehood" (*mṛṣā*), the former meaning is already fully contained within the preceding section. Furthermore, the latter meaning—which lacks an explicit mention of the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*)—is intended to explain the provisional (*upāya*), distinguish the counterfeit from the authentic, and emphasize the real.
These two [meanings] point to the subsequent chapter on Śākyamuni, which is the chapter on the Buddhas of the three periods; therein, all six meanings are complete.

To avoid prolixity, the Sūtra allows these points to reflect one another across the preceding and following sections. This will become clear when we reach the explanations of the chapters on the present and the future below.
This may be understood by analogy. This clarifies the disclosure of the provisional in the past.
Because these teachings are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle, all these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, ultimately attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This "Dharma" refers precisely to the provisional [teaching]. This passage truly clarifies the text that reveals the reality (*satya*) of the past;

it states that within the past itself, the three periods of time are inherently complete, and this is merely cited as a general summary. This example of revealing reality, which is superior to the preceding [section], possesses the fourfold "oneness":
first, the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*) is the oneness of the teaching. As for "hearing the Dharma from all Buddhas," who is it that hears?
The Dharma. The Dharma pervades all sentient beings; furthermore, it attains human-oneness. Ultimately, all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

That which is known is the oneness of principle (li-yi); that which knows is the oneness of practice (xing-yi). Although the textual sequence is not uniform, these four kinds of oneness are fully present.
This concludes the chapter on the Buddhas of the past.
Śāriputra, all the Buddhas of the future who shall appear in the world will likewise, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful methods,
various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
This clarifies that the third [category], the future Buddhas, likewise first bestow the provisional teachings.
Regarding the chapter on future Buddhas, one must also discuss the three periods of time oneself; this has merely been presented as a general overview, as previously explained.
These dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. All these sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This clarifies the future Buddhas; subsequently, the reality is revealed. It need only consist of two chapters, yet it must possess six meanings, as previously stated.
Śāriputra, it is said that in the present, throughout the immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, and millions of Buddha-fields in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
bring great benefit and peace and happiness to sentient beings.
This section clarifies the fourth chapter, "The Manifestation of the Present Buddhas. Herein lies the primary subject of transformation.
First, it sets forth the purpose for the Buddha’s appearance: as in the previous chapters on the Buddhas, he appears in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition;
this is likewise the case here, appearing in the world solely to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.
These Buddhas likewise, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful methods, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression,
expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
This clarifies that the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present also first bestow the provisional teachings.
These teachings are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle; thus, when these sentient beings hear the Dharma from the Buddhas, they ultimately all attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
This clarifies that the present Buddha truly manifests reality. The One Buddha Vehicle is the oneness of the teaching; the beings who receive it are one;
ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), which is the oneness of the principle known; and the means by which they know it is the oneness of practice.
Section Four, Part One. The Chapter on the Present is concluded.

Śāriputra, these Buddhas teach and transform bodhisattvas solely because they wish to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings, because they wish to awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because they wish to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Therefore, this section generally clarifies how the aforementioned Buddhas enter into principle. In the preceding text, the Buddhas were presented only through the two aspects of teaching and practice, though the meaning therein encompasses the fourfold and the singlefold (the four-in-one).

This section, however, brings forth both the person and the principle; thus, the meaning of the fourfold and the singlefold throughout the three periods of time is fully established. How could one fail to know this?
Is this text a general statement? Because the initial passage says, "These Buddhas, etc.," we know it is a general statement.
Once the Buddhas of the three periods have completed their revelation, Śāriputra, I now likewise do so; I know that sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated inclinations...
He manifests in accordance with their fundamental natures, preaching the Dharma through various causes and conditions, parables, and expressions by means of skillful power (*upāya*).
This clarifies that the present Śākyamuni is currently bestowing the teaching that reveals the provisional (*kaishen*). "I" refers to the present Śākyamuni himself.
This is what is meant. "First three, then one" is no different from the four Buddhas mentioned above; therefore, it is said, "it is likewise.

To know the fundamental nature of all sentient beings is what constitutes the response. When it says that sentient beings have various desires, this refers to the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of the five vehicles.
What is termed "desire" here is present, yet this desire arises from the faculties of the past and the latent tendencies of former lives.
The various seeds are difficult to transform; following habitual practice without abandoning them is called "that which is attached by the profound mind," and this is precisely their root.
Regarding "following its original nature," this refers to the nature that will manifest in the future. As for "root," its meaning is that which is capable of producing.
Through the roots, habits, and seeds, present desires are formed. Desire functions as the capacity to grasp objects; thus, it is able to grasp the teachings of the five vehicles.
Therefore, habitual desire becomes one's nature; thus, nature is considered in relation to desire. Nature is termed "the future," and the future in relation to the present is called "original nature.
Furthermore, these three—faculties, desires, and natures—constitute the responsive capacity for perceiving the Buddha.
Through various causes and conditions, [the Buddha] anticipates and responds accordingly, opening the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles as appropriate to their needs.
Śāriputra, all these are for the sake of attaining the Single Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
This clearly explains that Śākyamuni reveals the ultimate reality. Thus, the provisional is pointed out as being the real; therefore, it is called "revealing the real."
Why is this? In the past, when the provisional was employed, there was not even the name of "provisional," let alone the existence of the "real.

Therefore, now that the provisional is revealed, the provisional is itself the real; thus it is said, "it is thus. One should know that while the narration concerns the employment of the provisional, its intent lies in its revelation.

This is the manifestation of the Real. The Buddha-vehicle is the oneness of teaching; the principle known by the knowledge of all modes is the oneness of reality; and all [practices] are the oneness of practice.
Those who can receive this teaching are the first [kind]. One should know that as stated above, the five Buddhas revealed the provisional to manifest the real.
Whenever a Buddha appears in the world, it is without exception for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). As it is with the three periods of time, so it is with the ten directions.
If it is the same in the ten directions, then all Buddhas in all lands throughout the dust-motes of the universe first bestow expedient means and subsequently reveal the reality. This sutra...
Regarding the classification of the sections: it is purely perfect and without admixture; therefore, it is said that there are no other vehicles, whether two or three.

Thus we know that this present sutra forever transcends all the Mahayana sutras of the single lifetime [of the Buddha’s teaching], such that none can surpass it. The purport of the scriptural text is vividly and clearly manifest;
one should rely upon the Buddha’s words. The section on the Manifestation of Reality concludes.
Śāriputra, in the worlds of the ten directions, there are not even two vehicles, let alone three.
This clarifies Śākyamuni’s third instance of explaining the provisional through the five turbidities. Before raising the five turbidities, he first states their underlying intent.
Although the Buddhas above have clearly revealed the provisional to manifest the ultimate, they have not yet clarified the intent of concealing the ultimate to manifest the provisional.

One should know that the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle is pure; it is as tranquil and uniform as space, possessing not even the provisionality of "carrying two" or "carrying three," let alone the provisionality of the single Threefold or single Fivefold [vehicles] at the Deer Park. This is solely because the obstructions of the five turbidities are heavy.
Their faculties are dull; truly, they cannot be taught [the ultimate truth]. "If I were to praise the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings would sink into suffering.

While he was reflecting thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and comforted him with Brahma-sounds: "First employ the provisional means of the single fivefold and single threefold [precepts];
only then employ the provisional means of the dual fivefold and dual threefold. Therefore, it is said that within the One Buddha-vehicle, one distinguishes and teaches the three.
Regarding the mention of "two" or "three," or "five" and "three" individually, I fear that the intended meaning of what is bestowed might not be understood.
Therefore, I first establish the single reality as a premise, let alone the absence of two or three.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities and evil ages.

Having already indicated the intention of employing provisional means (*upāya*), I now wish to explain it in detail. First, I shall state the number, which serves as the basis for the subsequent explanation.
These are what are called the kalpa-turbidity, the affliction-turbidity, the sentient-being-turbidity, the view-turbidity, and the life-span-turbidity;
these are the enumeration of the names of the five turbidities.
Thus it is.

This refers to their essential substance (*tattva*). The essential characteristics of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) cannot be fully set forth; they are simply described as being "thus. Now, regarding the substance of the five turbidities:
what constitutes the substance of the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*)? The eon has no separate substance; an eon is simply a long duration of time.

This provisional designation is established solely in reference to the four turbidities (*kaṣāya*). As it says below, "the period of chaos during the kalpa-turbidity" refers precisely to this meaning.
The turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) likewise has no separate essence; this provisional designation is established based upon the retribution of views and pride.

The text states, "the defilements of sentient beings are heavy," which refers to this very point. The turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) takes the five dull fetters (*mūla-kleśa*) as its essence.

The defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) takes the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) as its essence. The defilement of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*) refers to the uninterrupted continuity of the three phases of warmth, breath, and consciousness;
thus it is said that its essence consists in the continuous maintenance of both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). This is a brief exposition of the essence of the defilements.

Śāriputra, during the period of turmoil in the *kalpa*-defilement (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), sentient beings possess heavy defilements; because they are characterized by stinginess, greed, and envy, they bring to fruition all roots of unwholesomeness.
This is a brief enumeration of the characteristics of that defilement. When the initial sutra speaks of "the period of turmoil in the *kalpa*-defilement," it refers precisely to this *kalpa-kaṣāya*.
Regarding the characteristics: for what reason is an eon (kalpa) said to become turbid? It is because the four turbidities increase and intensify, gathering together at this time;

therefore, it is called the "turbidity of the eon" (kalpa-kaṣāya). There are three types of eons—great, medium, and small—and there are also four phases: emptiness, formation, destruction, and abiding; all of these are termed "eons."

Within the four *kalpas*, three—namely those of formation, abiding, and destruction—are periods of emptiness and thus lack the turbidity of the *kalpa*. The turbidity exists during the *kalpa* of abiding. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:

"During the *kalpa* of abiding, from the time the lifespan decreases from eighty thousand years down to thirty thousand, there is still no turbidity. When it reaches twenty thousand years, this marks the beginning of the five turbidities.
A detailed explanation of the meaning of the *kalpa* is shallow and easy to understand; as it is set forth in the sūtras and śāstras, I shall not trouble you with further elaboration.
Recorded in full: If hatred increases, weapons arise; if greed increases, famine arises; if delusion increases, pestilence arises.
Due to these afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, the three minor calamities occur.

Because the three calamities arise, the four turbidities increase and afflictions flourish twofold due to the *kalpa-turba* (the turbidity of the eon) and the *kleśa-turba* (the turbidity of afflictions). These two [turbidities] arise from the eon and its afflictions.
Because of turbidity, various views become increasingly fierce. Due to the first three [defilements], sentient beings are thus turbid;

by grasping at the coarse, wretched, and evil five aggregates, they become evil sentient beings, manifesting evil and earning the designation of "filth," thereby becoming turbid sentient beings. This occurs due to the first four [defilements].

Their life-force is turbid; years accumulate to form a lifespan. As years pass, the lifespan diminishes; thus, years and lifespan press upon one another. Therefore, it is called the turbidity of life-force.
One should know that these four turbidities and the kalpa are mutually dependent; hence it is named the turbidity of the kalpa. It is like water rushing in a state of confusion.

The winds and waves rage in fury; fish and dragons thrash about in turmoil; there is not a single thing to rely upon. It is the timing that makes it so—this is called the characteristic of the kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

As the Sūtra says, "sentient beings with heavy defilements" refers to the sentient-being turbidity (*sattva-kaṣāya*), which arises from grasping at the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of form and mind.

A single sovereign lord is established, like sticky glue to which nothing does not adhere. Wandering through the six realms of existence, one takes birth in every place—sometimes poor, sometimes short;
sometimes called long, sometimes called wealthy. This is the characteristic mark of the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

As the Sūtra says, "miserliness, greed, jealousy, and envy" refers precisely to the afflictions (*kleśa*). The ocean of craving receives all flowing streams yet is never satiated; the venomous serpent of anger inhales...

Poisonous, they afflict all the world; mired in the darkness of ignorance and stupidity, they exceed lacquer or ink in their dullness. Arrogant and haughty, they look down upon others with contempt and disregard them without restraint.

Ensnared by doubt and lacking faith, they cannot be told the truth. Because of these five dull afflictions (*pañca-nivaraṇa*), this constitutes the characteristic of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
As for the sūtra’s statement, "because they have accomplished the various unwholesome roots," this refers to the characteristic of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

To perceive a self where there is no self, or a path where there is no path—these sixteen views, extending through the three times and one time, or numbering sixty-two or sixty-five, and even pervading all places and all phenomena—are like a net and resemble a dense thicket;
they entangle and distort one so that one cannot emerge from them on one’s own. This is the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
This is the mark [of the age]. As for the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*): one is born in the morning and perishes by evening; one emerges at daybreak and sets by dusk.

Like shifting waves or swirling smoke, it does not remain still for even a moment. This is the mark of the turbidity of life. However, the marks of turbidity are numerous and cannot be fully described;
I shall provide a brief explanation here, setting forth only the general outline. One should know that all five turbidities take afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) as their root. All...
From the two turbidities, sentient beings arise; from sentient beings, there is the maintenance of life. When these four pass through time, it is called the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the turbidity of the eon).

Question: If it is said that for sentient beings there are five turbidities which obstruct the Great [Vehicle], then why is it that in the *Avataṃsaka*, there are ordinary persons who have not yet eliminated the five turbidities yet are able to hear the Great Dharma?
Answer: This should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, those with sharp faculties of the Mahāyāna but heavy hindrances;
because their faculties are sharp, these heavy hindrances cannot obstruct them—these are those who first hear the *Avataṃsaka* in this land. Second, those with sharp faculties and light hindrances.
Third, those with dull faculties and light hindrances—these are those who hear the Mahāyāna in the pure lands of other directions. Fourth, those with dull faculties and heavy hindrances, such as...
In this land, those such as Śāriputra could only hear of the Great [Vehicle] after the turbidity had been removed; therefore, it is said that the five turbidities obstruct the Great.
The five turbidities hinder the Deer Park, the Vaipulya, the Prajñāpāramitā, and other teachings, as explained in detail in the Tiantai commentaries.
Regarding the heavy obstructions of the faculties, they are analyzed through the four *siddhāntas* and fourteen gates; those who require this should seek its clarification in that commentary.
"The Buddhas, by the power of skillful means, distinguish and preach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
This summarizes the preceding third point regarding the intention of manifesting provisional teachings.
"Śāriputra, if my disciples claim for themselves to be arhats or pratyekabuddhas, yet have neither heard nor known [this teaching]..."
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, perform only the work of teaching and transforming bodhisattvas. These are not disciples of the Buddha, nor arhats, nor pratyekabuddhas.

From this point until the end of this section, which provides a definitive resolution, this constitutes the fourth of Śākyamuni’s selections: the rejection of the false and the exhortation toward the real. This...
To say one has not heard and does not know is to distinguish them as not being a true disciple. As for worldly disciples, they follow the teacher’s Dharma and succeed to the transmission of the lamp.
If one has neither heard nor known [the Dharma], there is no Dharma to follow; how then can such a person be called a disciple?

In the past, the Tathāgata spoke of the three vehicles to open the way amidst the five turbidities, so that you might follow them and attain nirvāṇa. To have attained hearing and knowledge is what is meant by being a "disciple" (śrāvaka).
"Son, now that the five turbidities have been removed, I shall preach the One Vehicle for you.
If you do not hear and do not know this Dharma of the One Vehicle, yet claim to have already attained realization, you are not a true disciple. Question:

In the preceding scripture, the Buddha himself stated, "Only those who are steadfast and sincere are true disciples. Why do you now say they are not true disciples? Answer: What was said previously...
Zhen-shi (貞實) is indeed a true disciple. As for the current statement that he is not a true disciple, it is because the great is used to press the small;

"small" refers to those who claim to be true, while the "great" judges them to be untrue. Thus, by means of the great, the assembly at that time was earnestly pressed so that they might believe, accept, and understand.
If one were to claim oneself to be true, then one would neither hear nor know. "Not hearing" means not hearing the first [teaching]; "not knowing" means...
This means that they do not know how to practice the One; it is neither the True One nor the Principle One. They are not disciples, and thus they are not persons of the One.
This is a subtle refutation by means of the Mahāyāna; therefore, it says "not disciples of the Buddha," and so forth.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, these bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs consider themselves to have already attained arhatship;
they believe this is their final body and that they have reached ultimate nirvāṇa, and thus they no longer aspire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
You should know that these people are all those of overweening pride (adhimāna). Why is this?
If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing would be impossible.
This clarifies that if one does not aspire to seek [the truth] and lacks faith in this, it constitutes the arrogance of overestimation (*adhimāna*).

Previously, those who did not hear or know were dismissed as not being true disciples; now, those who lack faith are identified as having the arrogance of overestimation. This is to exhort the assembly present at this very seat:
you must have faith while seated here. Why? If you all cling to the "lesser truth" and consider yourselves to be in their final existence (*caramabhavika*), then—
There is still further transformation and rebirth in various places; you are certainly not in your final body.

Although you claim to have reached the ultimate, there remain two hundred *yojanas* yet to be traversed; you are truly not at the ultimate. To claim to have attained what one has not attained—is this not the arrogance of overestimating oneself?
If one is a true Arhat, they must believe in this Dharma. With defilements removed and faculties sharpened, they know that [their attainment] is not ultimate.

Having already believed in the present reality, they know that their body will not be reborn hereafter; thus they do not give rise to conceit regarding higher states. Knowing it is not ultimate while believing in the ultimate, they realize the unity of principle and are free from overweening pride (adhimāna);
they thus achieve the unity of practice. Belief is belief in the teaching; this constitutes the unity of the teaching.
Such a person is a disciple of the Buddha; thus, this person is one [of the true assembly]. This concludes the section on "Discerning the False to Honor the Real.

Excluding the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before one's eyes—this clarifies the exception—if the Buddha were in the world and correctly preaching this sutra, yet one did not believe or accept it, such a person would not be a true *śrāvaka*.

Those of the Han dynasty developed overweening pride (*adhimāna*). If one attains the state of an Arhat only after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is because they are biased toward provisional sutras and do not believe in the perfect teaching;
to permit such a case is not considered overweening pride.
Why is this? After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and understand the meaning of such sūtras as these will be difficult to find.
This clarifies that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, good people will be difficult to find and profound sūtras will be difficult to understand; yet one should not give rise to conceit.
Although the Buddha has entered extinction, this sūtra still remains. If one does not believe or accept it, should that not be considered conceit? Thus, [the text] provides an exemption.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, although this sūtra exists, those who can understand its words and meaning are difficult to encounter;
this has led even Arhats to lack faith and understanding, yet they should also be permitted as not being those of overweening pride.
If one encounters another Buddha, one will then attain definitive understanding within this Dharma;
this is the resolution of the doubt. [The doubt is raised: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can interpret the sūtras are difficult to find.
Those who have attained arhatship enter parinirvāṇa forever and never hear [this teaching]; will they never become Buddhas? To resolve this doubt, it says: Although such a person...

They conceive the thought of attaining nirvāṇa. After their lives have ended, they are reborn in a provisional realm outside this world, in another land, where they encounter another Buddha and hear this sutra;
thereupon, they attain definitive realization. The *Śāstra* poses a hypothetical question:
"If an Arhat receives a body from a previous life, that body must necessarily perish. Abiding in what place, then, does he fulfill the path to Buddhahood? The answer is as follows:

The Arhats have exhausted the causes and conditions of outflows within the three realms and will no longer be reborn therein. Beyond the three realms, there exists a pure Buddha-land where even the name of affliction does not exist.
In that land, in the presence of the Buddha, they hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and fully realize the path of Buddhahood.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says: "There are Arhats who, if they do not hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, consider themselves to have attained extinction (*nirvāṇa*)."

"In other lands, I have taught this matter for you all, so that you shall all become Buddhas. Since this treatise has already cited the sūtras as proof, I shall now explain the sūtra using the commentary's interpretation.
Furthermore, Master Nanyue said: "The 'other Buddhas' are the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*).

If an Arhat encounters them, he will hear the sūtra and attain definitive understanding. Moreover, when an Arhat cultivates the concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), he beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions."

By expounding this sutra, one immediately attains definitive understanding. It should be known that when it is said that Arhats recollect the Buddhas of the ten directions, this refers to those who have already resolved upon the Great Mind (bodhicitta).
If it refers solely to Śākyamuni Buddha, then this is a case where a small cause elicits a great response; it is simply the arousal of their spiritual capacity (*indriya*) that brings it about.
Within the various schools of the Hīnayāna, there are differences; some even maintain faith in the existence of Buddhas in the ten directions. That is to say—
Those of the Hīnayāna, through the power of the ultimate concentration of the fourth dhyāna, behold the Buddhas of the ten directions;

when their practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is perfected, they are moved by the Buddhas to preach this sūtra for their definitive resolution. Furthermore, ordinary practitioners who earnestly pray and repent also behold the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching to them, thereby attaining definitive resolution as well.
"Śāriputra, you all should with one mind believe, understand, accept, and uphold the Buddha’s words.
This clarifies that the fifth function of Śākyamuni is his lack of falsehood; it stops the slanderous minds of beings and encourages their faith.
This is an exhortation to believe that Śākyamuni has truly spoken. Therefore, it says: "You all should with one mind believe, understand, and uphold the Buddha’s words.
When it simply says "the Buddha," it refers specifically to Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak without falsehood.
This is an exhortation to have faith in the Buddhas' true words; therefore, it is said that "the Buddhas speak without falsehood. The Way of all Buddhas is the same.
One should increase one's faith and acceptance even further.
There is no other vehicle; there is only the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
This concludes the preceding exposition of the true teaching, stating that it is without falsehood; therefore, it is called the "single Buddha-vehicle. One should give rise to [this realization].
This is indeed true faith.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who harbor overweening pride, Upāsakas with arrogance, and upāsikās lacking faith."
Such were the fourfold assembly, numbering five thousand. They did not perceive their own faults; they had deficiencies and omissions in their precepts and cherished their blemishes.
These were those of small wisdom who had already departed—the dregs and chaff among the assembly. It was by the Buddha’s majestic power that they left.
"Such people have little merit and fortune; they are unable to receive this Dharma.

This verse corresponds to the previous section on "granting permission for the answer. Regarding the five thousand who cleared their seats, this specifically versifies the process of "discernment and permission.

Furthermore, the three faults of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), self-conceit (*māna*), and lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) are common to all four assemblies; however, among them, the two assemblies of renunciants more frequently cultivate the Path.
Having attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they mistakenly claim it to be the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*) and give rise to the pride of superiority (*abhimāna*).

Among the laity, they boast of their own excellence and frequently give rise to the pride of self-importance (*māna*). Women, having shallow wisdom, often produce deviant views; those who do not perceive their own faults possess the three aforementioned failings that shroud the mind.

By concealing their blemishes and exalting their virtues, they are unable to reflect upon themselves—such people are devoid of a sense of shame (*ahrīka*). If, however, they do perceive their own faults...

This refers to a monk who possesses a sense of shame. Regarding those with deficiencies or breaches in the precepts—namely, among the ten precepts of the *Mahā-śāstra* and the *Mahā-sūtra*, such as being "neither deficient, nor pierced, nor broken, nor adulterated"—this refers to having a deficiency in the precepts of the *vinaya* restraint (*saṃvara*).

Therefore, it is said that they are "deficient. As for "outflows" (*āsrava*), because they share in the loss associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path, they are called outflows.
To "guard and cherish one's flaws" means that, due to the absence of the Path, concentration, and so forth, evil thoughts arise within, like a jade stone containing internal flaws;

and due to the absence of moral discipline (*saṃvara*), one moves the body and speech externally, like a jade stone manifesting flaws on its surface. Because one conceals one's transgressions and thus gains [retribution] for oneself, it is called "guarding and cherishing."

Regarding the phrase "those of small wisdom" (*kṣudrajñāna*) and so forth: they do not possess the wisdom of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) or those in training (*śaikṣa*), but have only mundane small wisdom.
They falsely claim that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) to be without outflows (*anāsrava*). Because it is the smallest among the small, it is called "small wisdom."

Those who are the dregs among the assembly are the five thousand [monks] and others. They possess only mundane *dhyāna*, which is like dregs, and lack the wine of the moisture of untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative concentration.
These five thousand possess only the understanding of words, which is like husks, and lack the rice of wisdom into reality (*yoniśo-jñāna*).
By adding to them the two virtues of untainted meditative concentration and wisdom into reality, they are transformed.

Third, those whose minds were shrouded by faults were removed by the Buddha’s majestic power. These individuals possessed little merit and were incapable of hearing the Dharma; therefore, they had to be screened out and dismissed.
This assembly is now free of branches and leaves, consisting only of those who are pure and substantial.
These two lines of verse summarize the preceding statement that the assembly has already been purified. The branches and leaves are likened to those who are not suitable vessels;
as they are entirely unfit for service, the Buddha has sent them away.
Śāriputra, listen well.
This single verse summarizes the preceding exhortation and permission; that is, the previous exhortation to "reflect upon it well.
The above concludes the summary of the permission to speak. △ Below, the following shall summarize the Tathāgata’s formal response.

Regarding the opening of the provisional [teachings] by the five Buddhas, the subsequent verses summarize the gates of the various Buddhas mentioned in the prose (chángxíng), and there are four differences between them: first, those that are mutually absent. In the preceding prose...

Among the various teachings of the Buddhas, some praise the rarity of the Dharma while lacking mention of the five turbidities; the verses herein contain only the five turbidities while lacking praise for the Dharma.
These two appear alternately in preceding and succeeding sections: in the former case, the Dharma is praised first, followed by the clarification that the provisional is opened to reveal the real;

here, the opening of the provisional to reveal the real comes first, followed by the clarification that it is not in vain. Third, regarding the difference between expansion and contraction: as above...

The exhortation to believe and the statement that [the teaching] is not in vain are explained here. In the present verse section, the exhortation to believe comes first, followed by the statement that it is not in vain;

these are separated by the passage concerning the five turbidities. Furthermore, the four preceding points use Śākyamuni’s skillful means to explain and establish the provisional teachings of all Buddhas.
In the verse, the reality of Śākyamuni is used to explain and establish that all Buddhas manifest as one. Thus, there are four differences between this verse and the preceding prose.
Although these differences exist, they do not go beyond the six meanings; these six meanings are identical and pose no contradiction to the principle.
Nevertheless, they must be distinguished, and therefore they are clarified here first, so that when one encounters the subsequent text, there shall be no confusion.
The Dharma attained by all Buddhas, through immeasurable powers of skillful means, they preach for the sake of sentient beings.

Whatever is contemplated in the minds of sentient beings, the various paths they travel, their diverse desires and natures, and the good and evil karma of their past lives—the Buddha knows all these completely.
By means of various causes, similes, and the power of skillful speech, he causes all to rejoice;
he speaks sūtras, gāthās, and itivṛttakas, jātakas, adbhutadharmas, as well as nidānas, avadānas, and geyas.
The *Upadeśa-sūtra*.

These four lines and one phrase praise the aforementioned Buddhas’ correct bestowal of skillful means (*upāya*). When it says "the Dharma attained by the Buddhas," it refers to attaining various skillful means through the cultivation of the path.
It refers precisely to the skillful means manifested when the causes for one’s own practice have reached fulfillment.

"Practicing within the body" refers to the provisional means (*upāya*). From "immeasurable power" down to "power already attained," these verses praise the preceding passage concerning how the Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate, even unto the exposition of all dharmas.
Herein, the characteristics of preaching according to what is appropriate are extensively praised;

this is precisely the illumination of the capacities (*indriya*) of the nine realms, wherein the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are taught. That which is attained by the Buddhas—that is, the essence of the Dharma—is also not... [text ends]
It can be explained. By means of skillful means (*upāya*), one speaks for the sake of sentient beings; this constitutes the power of authority (*vaśitā*) in transforming others.

"That which is contemplated by the minds of sentient beings" refers to what arises as aspiration, which is termed "contemplation" (*manasikāra*); "contemplation" here refers, for the time being, to the internal mind.

"The various paths practiced" refers to the diversity of dharma-gates of the authoritative practices for transforming others, which is why they are called "various. "The many dispositions of desire" refers to...

It is said that there are seven [types of] inclinations and nine [types of] dispositions. Among these seven and nine, depending on which capacity [a being] possesses and what teaching they hear, one must adapt to that capacity;
it cannot be determined definitively. Therefore, it is called "various desires. Present delight is called "desire" (chanda); past habitual practice is called "nature" (dhātu).
Alternatively, habitual desire may become nature, and established nature may give rise to habitual desire. [This refers to] previous lives...

Regarding "good and evil karma": the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are collectively transmitted as being both good and evil. Regarding "the Buddha’s arrival at the house and the sutras":
the Buddha, by means of his skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), illuminates the dispositions and inclinations of various expedient means;

he then employs various causes, conditions, and parables to establish the ninefold division of scriptures (*navāṅga-śāsana*) according to what is appropriate for each, or sometimes the twelvefold division (*dvādaśāṅga-śāsana*). These are briefly presented within the text.
It is thus with the ninefold division. One should know that in each of the chapters on the five Buddhas, the phrase "bestowing [the Dharma]" (*shishi*) is established;

yet, it now constitutes two meanings. First, it proclaims the past bestowal of provisional means (*upāya*). Second, it serves as the locus for revealing the reality (*tattva*). Without pointing to that which was opened [by the provisional], there would be no way to speak of the reality.

Moreover, pointing to the provisional as being provisional is the intent of the provisional; now, those who are ready to receive the teaching (*pratipannaka*) know it is not ultimate. Since the reality has been revealed...
Thus, provisional and ultimate are entirely real; it is the single Buddha-vehicle alone.
Those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings and are greedily attached to birth and death do not practice the profound and wondrous path under the countless Buddhas.
"Afflicted and disturbed by manifold sufferings—for their sake, I preach nirvāṇa.

These one and a half lines conclude the intent of the provisional teaching (*upāya*). This is a long verse; it does not appear in the aforementioned [text], but is presented here as a necessary supplement.

Because their faculties were dull in previous lives and they lack the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) in this life, they are unable to hear the Great [Vehicle]; therefore, it is said that they do not practice the profound.

The wondrous Way is such that those whose karmic hindrances were heavy due to greed and attachment in previous lives, and who are now afflicted by manifold sufferings in this life, can only hear the Lesser [Vehicle].
Therefore, for their sake, he speaks of *nirvāṇa*. This concludes the verse on how the Buddhas employ skillful means (*upāya*).
I have established these skillful means to enable you to enter the Buddha’s wisdom. I have never said to you, "You shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
The reason I have not said so is that the time for such a proclamation had not yet arrived. Now is precisely that time; I shall definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna.
"These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; they have the entry into the Mahāyāna as their foundation, and for this reason I preach this sutra.
The following section is a verse summarizing the aforementioned Buddhas' manifestation of the reality.

These first three lines summarize the aforementioned "Unity of Principle," which causes [beings] to enter the Buddha-wisdom, and thus summarize the aforementioned "Great Cause and Condition" (mahā-pratyaya). "Decisively preaching the Mahāyāna" summarizes the preceding section in its entirety.

This reveals, clarifies, awakens to, and realizes the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*). Entering the Mahāyāna is its fundamental purpose; this verse summarizes the aforementioned entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

While the sutra text frequently states "this is the teaching" (*deśanā*), why does it here say "this is the principle" (*tattva*)? This is because the capacity [the teaching] manifests that which is manifested [the principle]; this can be understood by analogy with what preceded.
There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, who are gentle and of sharp faculties; having served immeasurable Buddhas, they practice the profound and wondrous Way.
For the sake of these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra; I grant this prediction to such people: in a future age, they shall attain the path of Buddhahood.

Because they have mindfulness of the Buddha with a profound mind and cultivate and maintain pure precepts, these individuals hear that they shall attain Buddhahood, and great joy pervades their entire bodies.
The Buddha, knowing their mental activities, therefore expounds the Mahāyāna for them. Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, having heard the Dharma I have taught...
Even those who [hear] but a single verse will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
These four lines and a half of verse summarize the aforementioned Buddhas and Tathāgatas, who teach and transform only bodhisattvas, thereby clarifying the first person.
The commentary above states that these are bodhisattvas who have been transformed through teaching. In the verse, various people of expedient means are extensively presented;

they all become true persons. The passage from "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure" to "therefore he preaches the Mahāyāna for them" refers specifically to those of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).

For this reason, the Buddha-son is taught the Mahāyāna sūtras; having received the prediction [of enlightenment], his mind is filled with joy, and he immediately becomes a person of true reality according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
As for those who are śrāvakas or bodhisattvas—the śrāvakas must encompass both teachings, while also including the pratyekabuddhas of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings.
As for those who attain enlightenment through conditions (pratyekabuddhas), there are some among them who encounter a Buddha.

If they are bodhisattvas—referring here to those of the *pitaka* and *āgama* vehicles and so forth—who hear even a single verse spoken by the Buddha, they will all undoubtedly achieve Buddhahood. These are the people of the seven kinds of expedient means;

from now until the end of this sutra, there are none who are not sons of the Buddha. This is the first point regarding the person who recites the verses. Furthermore, it is a sincere statement that they shall achieve Buddhahood.
Without doubt, you should know that this is the most holy and sincere teaching. You must with even greater faith accept that one becomes a Buddha through the Three Vehicles.
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for the skillful means taught by the Buddhas.
"Only by means of provisional names do I guide sentient beings, because I am preaching the wisdom of the Buddha.

This single line consisting of three phrases is a verse summarizing the preceding passage stating that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), without any other vehicle.
If the Buddhas of the ten directions preach only this one Dharma, it constitutes the "teaching of oneness" (*eka-śāsana*).
"Provisional names for guidance" refers to the teaching of skillful means (*upāya*). Since the essence of the teaching is the single reality, the three [vehicles] are provisional.

For the sake of sentient beings, the expedient devices of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and so forth were provisionally established. Now that the reality has been revealed, the text reiterates what was previously excluded to demonstrate the Buddha’s wisdom.

The sutra cites the three provisional teachings by name to reveal the single teaching of the Buddha’s wisdom; thus, the method of the "one teaching" becomes increasingly clear as it further takes up the preceding [sections].

The text states: "There is no other vehicle" (anuttara-yāna) to manifest that there is only one [vehicle], without any remaining distinct teachings such as the "round entry" (pariniṣpanna-praveśa) within the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha-yāna).
"There is no duality" means there is no duality of the "half and full" (ardha-pūrṇa) contrast found within the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-yāna).
"There is no triad" means there is no triad found within the Tripitaka Teaching (śrāvaka-yāna). Such instances of two or three are all provisional names used to guide sentient beings.

Now, there is only the single Buddha’s Perfect Teaching Vehicle (*vaipulya-yāna*). This refers to the "milk," the two "butter" stages, and the three "flavors," all of which have been completely eliminated.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, this alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. Ultimately, they never employ the Hīnayāna.

He delivers sentient beings. The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna; according to the Dharma he has realized, adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, he uses this to deliver sentient beings.
Having personally realized the unsurpassed path—the equal Dharma of the Mahāyāna—if he were to transform others using the Hīnayāna, [he would be acting contrary to his own realization].
"Even toward a single person, I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is not permissible.
These three lines of verse summarize the previous point that all actions are always for the sake of a single purpose—namely, the practice of "one.
Here, "purpose" (事) is synonymous with "practice" (行). This means that one never uses the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to deliver sentient beings; this summarizes the preceding [text].

This is the meaning of the "One Great Matter. From the Buddha’s own abiding therein until the deliverance of sentient beings, [the text] reiterates the previous point that he uses only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to instruct and awaken sentient beings.
The final line explains the intention of not delivering them by means of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
These four sections conclude the *Sūtra on the Manifestation of Reality* by all Buddhas.
If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive or mislead them, nor does he harbor thoughts of greed or envy;
having severed all evils within the dharmas, the Buddha alone is thus without fear throughout the ten directions.
This verse encourages faith based on the aforementioned exhortations of the Buddhas. The previous statement, "You all should believe what the Buddha has taught," consists of one line and two phrases;

it encourages faith by citing the inner mind of the person who has attained the fruit [of Buddhahood], clarifying that the Buddha’s mind is pure and that ignorance, the defilement of stinginess, and all evils have been severed.
Since he speaks from within this pure mind, he is to be believed.
"I adorn my body with marks; its radiance illuminates the world. Honored by immeasurable multitudes, I shall preach for you the Seal of the True Reality.

This single line sets forth the external physical marks of the person who has realized the fruit. Furthermore, it encourages faith: the Buddha’s external physical body is brilliant and distinct, its light and secondary characteristics are upright and majestic.
Since there is no darkness or delusion within, there is radiance without; thus, his speech is free from deception, and he is honored by the multitude.
"World-Honored One, when you speak of the seal of the Mahāyāna, it can be trusted and accepted. Having finished exhorting faith by citing the fruit [of the path], Śāriputra, you should know:
I originally established a vow, desiring to cause all beings to be no different from myself."
This single line cites the original cause, encouraging faith by means of the former vow:
"As I have previously vowed, it is now fulfilled; I shall transform all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way."
This single line clarifies that the former vow has now been fulfilled.

In the past, I vowed not only for my own enlightenment, but also vowed that all sentient beings would together enter the Buddha-wisdom. Now, because this vow has been repaid, it is spoken; thus it is worthy of belief.
Since the Bodhi is now fulfilled and sentient beings have likewise entered [the path], and since you yourself have personally realized the Buddha-wisdom, you may verify that my vow was not in vain.
This concludes the section on citing the reasons for exhorting faith. Question: When the Buddha first made his vow, he vowed to deliver all sentient beings.

Yet, sentient beings are still so numerous; how can his vow be considered fulfilled? Answer: The Buddha benefits beings throughout the three periods of time. For now, we shall speak generally from the perspective of a single lifetime in the present.
If he merely causes sentient beings to enter the Buddha Vehicle, his vow is said to be fulfilled. As the Sūtra says:
I am no different from them. Having finished exhorting them to have faith with these verses:
"If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way; yet those without wisdom are confused and deluded, and do not accept the teaching."
This section proceeds to eulogize the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*). The previous explanation of the five corruptions appeared after the chapter on Śākyamuni;
now, this verse-text appears at the end of the general Buddha-section and is further repeated within the chapter on Śākyamuni.

The intent is to clarify that all Buddhas appear equally amidst the five corruptions, and that they must all first teach the Three Vehicles and subsequently the One Vehicle. This single line generally clarifies that the five corruptions constitute a great obstruction. If...
The treatise states that while the turbidities do not obstruct the Great [Vehicle], those who encounter them are caused to enter the Buddha-way;

yet because the faculties of sentient beings are dull and they lack wisdom and do not accept it, it is said that they "obstruct the Great. Regarding the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*), the *Madhyama Āgama* states:

At the beginning of the kalpa, beings descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven to be born in the world. There were no distinctions of male or female, nor of noble or humble; they lived together as a collective. Therefore, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). This is based on...

First, it is named in reference to him. If one gathers the various aggregates (skandhas) and there is a provisional designation of a "sentient being," this is based on the experience of retribution during a single lifetime and is designated from its own standpoint.
If, however, one says that they are called "sentient beings" because they undergo birth in various places, [then the name applies to all].
This refers to the circulation through the five destinies by the power of karma; it is a designation based on their functional capacity, hence they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "There are ten kinds of sentient beings: namely, those that are long, short, square, round, triangular, blue, yellow, red, white, and purple.
Such beings as these, even if they were to encounter a Buddha, would still be tormented by their own suffering."
The Buddhas rescue all beings through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because compassion and suffering correspond to one another, it is said that they "meet.
Furthermore, the suchness of the Buddha and the suchness of sentient beings are a single suchness without duality; since their natures are interrelated, it is said, "I meet with sentient beings.
As for "teaching them all by means of the Buddha-way": the Buddha’s great compassion constantly pities sentient beings. If he were to teach them only the way of humans and devas, I—

I would then fall into delusion and confusion. To merely avoid birth and death characterized by blue, yellow, red, white, purple, square, round, or angular forms is not the teaching of the Buddha-way.
If I encounter sentient beings and cause them to practice only the Hīnayāna, I would then fall into stinginess and greed;
such a thing is impermissible. If I encounter sentient beings and teach them only the general and specific [aspects] of the twenty-five states of existence, I would then fall into...

Those who are remote and have lost the Buddha’s knowledge and vision do not possess the Buddha-way. From the time [the previous teachings] arrived until this present sutra, I have universally enabled all sentient beings to attain the wondrous wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), so that they may realize that all things are the Buddha-dharma and that there is nothing that is not the Right Way.

This is called teaching all through the Buddha-way, whereby the sufferings of birth and death are forever exhausted. I always speak thus; as for those who say "they lack wisdom" and so forth— *Note: The phrase "as for those who say 'they lack wisdom' and so forth" (云無智等者) appears to be a concluding remark or a transition to another section of the text.*
However, because the faculties of sentient beings are dull and their transgressions heavy, they are unwilling to accept the teaching; thus, it cannot be as you wish.

In the past, there was a Buddha named Dwelling in the Non-dwelling (*Aniśrita*), who made a vow that the sentient beings of his own land would all attain Buddhahood on the same day and at the same time as he himself entered parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, prior to the Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Equality (*Samatā*), who likewise vowed for his own land and the ten directions [to be so].

“Sentient beings would also all attain Buddhahood on the same day and enter parinirvāṇa on that very day. If there are sentient beings today and yet another Buddha exists today, how can this be reconciled?
The Buddha said, “Stop, stop! What I previously mentioned refers only to those who have attained a human body.
He asked again, “Is it possible to make a vow such that sentient beings of the five destinies attain Buddhahood on the same day? The Buddha said, “No.”

One may attain the Unsurpassed Way with a body that is not [an ideal] vessel; however, one must first transform those in the three miserable realms so that they obtain bodies as humans or devas, and only then can one fulfill one's vow. Since the three miserable realms are not wholesome paths, how could one achieve Buddhahood from them? It is like a person seeking a hoard of jewels who does not seek them in the air. I know these sentient beings: they have never cultivated the roots of goodness; they are firmly attached to the five desires, and because of delusion and craving, they give rise to affliction.
Due to the causes and conditions of various desires, they fall into the two evil realms and wander through the six destinies, undergoing all manner of bitter suffering.

Hereafter, the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) will be explained separately. These two lines clarify the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). "Roots of goodness" refers to *tathatā* (suchness) and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Because they do not rely on these roots of goodness, they do not experience greatness. To be firmly attached to the five desires is [the nature of] all...
The root of evil arises from delusion and craving; thus my illness is born, and I undergo all manner of bitter suffering.
This subtle form within the womb grows ever greater life after life. Those of meager virtue and little merit are oppressed by manifold sufferings.

This one line clarifies the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣkaṣāya*). Regarding "the subtle form of the conceived embryo": "form" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). The aggregates are called the "world" (*loka*).

Life-span maintains these aggregates and brings them into the world; from the initial stage of the *kalala* (thick curd) up to old age and death, it is therefore called "growing through life after life.

This is the characteristic of the turbidity of lifespan. The characteristics of conception are detailed as cited in the commentary regarding the body of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*).
The Sūtra states:
"Entering the dense forest of false views—whether [things] exist or do not exist, and so forth—one relies upon these various views, which comprise the sixty-two [views].
This single line specifically clarifies the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). The five views are intermingled like a dense and luxuriant forest. "Whether they exist" refers to...
The view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) and, if it did not exist, the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*): based on these two views, sixty-two [views] arise.

Alternatively, it is said that the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) postulate a self (*ātman*) through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). For each of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), there are four propositions, resulting in twenty views. These are calculated with reference to the three periods of time (*traiyadhvika*).
These constitute sixty views; together with the two fundamental views, they form the sixty-two views, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
They are deeply attached to false and illusory dharmas, firmly grasping them so that they cannot be relinquished. Arrogant and self-conceited, their minds are crooked and insincere.
This single line is a verse summarizing the passage on the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
For thousands of millions of billions of eons, they do not hear the name of the Buddha, nor do they hear the True Dharma; such people as these are difficult to deliver.
This single line of verse describes the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). The absence of the Buddha-dharma for a long duration constitutes the defilement of the eon;

furthermore, because the aforementioned four defilements converge within this period, it is called the defilement of the eon. Such people are difficult to deliver because they are obstructed by the five defilements.
Those who do not believe in the One Vehicle cannot be delivered; this is caused by the defilement of the kalpa.
Therefore, Śāriputra, I employ skillful means to teach the various paths for exhausting suffering and demonstrate to them nirvāṇa.
This one line clarifies that he provisionally taught the Lesser Vehicle because of the obstacles of the five turbidities mentioned above.
"Although I speak of nirvana, this is not true extinction; all dharmas from the very beginning have always been characterized by quiescence."
"Once the Buddha-sons have practiced the Way, they shall become Buddhas in a future life.

These one and a half lines clarify that, in the end, one is led into the Great [Vehicle]: the delusions of the three realms are exhausted, and the grasping for form is extinguished to realize emptiness.
This would not be true cessation. If one realizes that ignorance is fundamentally non-existent and eternally quiescent, this is true cessation.
Although it is fundamentally non-existent and quiescent, if one does not cultivate the Path, there is no means by which to realize this union. Therefore, it is said:
"The Buddha’s son, having practiced the Path, shall become a Buddha in a future age. This concludes the preceding chapter on the Five Turbidities.
"I possess the power of skillful means; I reveal the Dharma of the three vehicles.
Regarding this verse, the first two lines clarify that Śākyamuni first revealed the three [vehicles]; thus it says, "I possess," and so forth.
"All the World-Honored Ones preach the single vehicle path.
These two lines clarify that the Buddhas subsequently reveal the ultimate reality; they merely manifest this and that in alternation.
"Now, this great assembly should all eliminate their doubts and delusions. The words of all Buddhas do not differ; there is only the Single Vehicle, and no second.
This single line clearly demonstrates that all Buddhas first employ provisional means and subsequently reveal the ultimate reality. Their truthful words are not false; do not give rise to doubt.
The verse summarizing the Chapter on All Buddhas concludes. Below this, twenty-seven and a half lines constitute the verse on the Buddhas of the Past.

In the past, throughout incalculable kalpas, there have been immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, their total count beyond measure.
These World-Honored Ones, through various causes, conditions, and parables, and by means of countless powers of skillful expedience, have expounded the characteristics of all dharmas.
These first two lines of the verse explain the passage from the chapter on the Buddhas of the Past concerning the opening of the three [vehicles] as provisional means to bestow the Dharma.
All these World-Honored Ones preach the single Buddha-vehicle, transforming immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to enter the path of the Buddha.
This section following the verse clarifies the reality of the past Buddhas. In the preceding clarification of reality, there were only two "ones":
the one of teaching and the one of principle, which together encompassed the person and the practice. Now, within these verses, there are twenty-five and a half lines that fully represent four "ones.

The first line briefly summarizes the three aforementioned categories; all of them expound the Dharma of the One Vehicle, which is precisely the summary of the "one" of teaching. [The transformation of beings...]
"Measuring sentient beings" refers to the oneness of persons (人一). "Causing them to enter the Buddha-way" refers to the oneness of principle (理一), for that which is entered is the principle.
That which enters is practice; thus, one also attains the oneness of practice (行一). This concludes the brief verse summary. Below, the oneness is extensively elucidated by way of the five vehicles.
Furthermore, the Great Holy Lords, knowing the deep-seated desires of all beings in the world— gods, humans, and the various classes of living creatures—
employ further diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth.

Initially, these one and a half lines generally clarify the five vehicles to manifest the oneness of the One Vehicle. "The classes of devas, humans, and all living beings" cites the various vehicles to clarify the oneness of persons.
Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful means (*upāya*), it cites the various practices to clarify the oneness of practice;

this simultaneously achieves the oneness of teaching. "The primary truth" (*paramārtha*) is precisely the oneness of principle. From "by means of diverse skillful means" onwards, the true cause of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) is...

This is the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). If one employs the perfect and wondrous right contemplation, this is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and it is not called "different.

If one employs the seven skillful means of contemplation to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth, these are called "different skillful means," which cause [beings] to open up and return to the single skillful means.
If there are any classes of sentient beings who encountered the Buddhas of the past, and whether they heard the Dharma and practiced giving,
or observed the precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom— cultivating all manner of merit and insight— all such persons have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Here, departing from the previous [classification], one vehicle is manifested by means of a separate exposition of the five vehicles. These two practices separately open up the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
If explained according to the five vehicles, this Bodhisattva refers only to the Bodhisattva Vehicle of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

If explained according to the seven skillful means (*upāya*), it encompasses both the common and the distinct Bodhisattva Vehicles. Why? Because all three teachings of the Mahāyāna practice the six perfections; however...
The application of the mind differs. If one practices the six perfections with the perception of marks, this is the Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka teaching.

If it is without marks, this is the Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching. If it is neither with marks nor without marks, and one practices the six perfections in successive stages, this is the Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching.

Since we now merely list the six perfections, it is not yet known to which category they definitively belong. Referring to the preceding text, it says: "Furthermore, by means of other skillful expedients..."

This does not refer solely to the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections within the Five Vehicles; rather, it refers to the expedient means of the Bodhisattvas within the Three Teachings among the Seven Stages of Expediency (*sapta-upāya*).

While the designation "Five Vehicles" applies only to the Deer Park [the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles], the name "Seven Stages of Expediency" extends across the three flavors (*trivipāka*).
Since the practice of the Six Perfections is not restricted to a single teaching, one should know that this passage can apply to Bodhisattvas of all three teachings.

Furthermore, those who heard the Dharma in the past have all already achieved the unity of teaching; those who practiced the six perfections in the past have all already achieved the unity of practice;
such people as these have all already achieved the unity of personhood and have all achieved the Buddha-way, which is to say they have already achieved the unity of principle.
If the Bodhisattva does not clarify this, why would he need to cite the past to establish the unity of teaching? It is precisely now that he speaks of the past.
Regarding the hearing of the provisional [teachings], it was therefore necessary to open [the way].
After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, if there are people with virtuous and gentle hearts—such sentient beings as these have all already attained the Buddha-way.
This single line opens the way for both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to all enter the One Vehicle. How is it known that this opens the way for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?
It is known from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which praises the Arhat’s mind as being well-tamed and supple;

furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "Abiding in a tamed mind is the practice of the noble ones. By this, one knows that those who formerly possessed a good and supple mind have all achieved the practice of the One [Vehicle]. All...

That sentient beings are human beings is the one-ness of person; that they attain the Buddha-way is the one-ness of principle. This also includes the teaching. This concludes the opening of the Two Vehicles.
Below this, the opening of the Human and Celestial Vehicles, which also lead to the attainment of the Buddha-way, shall be presented.
After the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, those who make offerings to their relics go to billions of kinds of stupas—adorned with gold, silver, crystal, mother-of-pearl, and agate;
