This single line of verse [states]: "If one encounters another Buddha, one will then attain definitive understanding.

From the beginning with the five corruptions up to this point, this is a general summary of the preceding section on the selection of the assembly. This also clarifies that the teaching should be expounded for virtuous persons.
Śāriputra, you should know that such is the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma. Through ten thousand koṭis of skillful means, they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Those who have not practiced and studied cannot understand this.
These one and a half lines emphasize faith in the provisional [teachings] and double-bind the two meanings. The first line concludes the secret essentials, clarifying that this Dharma is thus:
first employing ten thousand *koṭi* of skillful means, and only thereafter revealing the ultimate reality.
The subsequent two phrases conclude the essence of propagating the sutra: those who do not practice and study cannot comprehend it; this specifically binds those who are unskilled.
Do not speak of this to them. Only when one encounters those who have practiced and studied can they understand it; only then may it be explained.
Since you all already know that the Buddhas, the teachers of the world, employ various skillful means as appropriate, you should no longer harbor any doubts.
The mind gives rise to great joy; one knows for oneself that one shall become a Buddha.

These one and a half lines concern the firm faith in reality. Reality and skillful means are without doubt; one knows for oneself that one shall become a Buddha. This concludes the verse on firm faith.
Furthermore, beginning from "As the Buddhas of the three periods of time... serves as the fundamental analogy for neither separation nor union. Beginning from...
The *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta* concludes here. This completes the textual exposition of the first true Dharma teaching; the remaining four chapters follow later.
*The Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Two.
*The Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
with commentary and record by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe;
and annotated by the Śramaṇa Daowei of Siming.
Regarding the title of this third chapter, "The Parable" (*Upamā-parivarta*),
it should have been placed after the verses spoken by the various devas and before the parable of the burning house; its placement here,
prior to the "Dharma-exposition" (*dharma-deśanā*) and the subsequent "Acceptance and Understanding" (*adhimukti*), is due to the translator’s editorial arrangement.
It is merely placed at the beginning of the section on "Understanding through Realization" (*parivarta*).

One must not say that it initiates the teaching for those of medium capacity, or that the "Explanation of the Dharma" (*dharmadeśanā*) and the attainment of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) serve as a prologue to the "Parable" (*aupamya*). This is merely a matter of human sentiment. If it were placed after the "Explanation of the Dharma," [it would be appropriate].

How could those of middling faculties fail to awaken? Nevertheless, although the beginning of this chapter incorporates the text of the first cycle, the current explanation of the chapter title follows the intent of the second cycle to interpret its specific designation.

As for the title "The Parable Chapter" (Puyupin), it is because the preceding extensive exposition—both in prose and verse—of the five Buddhas opening the provisional to reveal the real was intended for those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom.
When Yuanwen heard this, he attained awakening; yet those of middling and inferior capacities remained mired in delusion and had not yet reached realization.

Out of inexhaustible great compassion and boundless skillful wisdom, the Buddha further stirred the winds of instruction by moving the tree and raising the fan as a metaphor for the moon, thereby enabling them to achieve understanding; hence, these are called "parables" (*dṛṣṭānta*).
This chapter was personally proclaimed by the Tathāgata, differing from the worldly practice of using parables merely to illustrate proximate matters. [The following] illustrates what is below...

The teachings of the Dharma possess both provisional and ultimate aspects; they must not be approached with superficiality. First, there is a general explanation, followed by a specific explanation. Regarding the general explanation:
"P'i" (譬) refers to drawing an analogy through comparison; this is called a "simile. "Yu" (喻) refers to opening up the mind to bring about awakening; this is called a "metaphor.
Since these two characters are presented together, their meanings have slight distinctions. Therefore, within this realm, [the text uses] the example of a person in a chariot.
"House" is a metaphor for the profound meaning of the Buddha-vehicle beyond the realms. It was used to instruct the assembly at that time;

by relying on this [mundane] to illustrate that [transcendent], it uses the shallow to instruct regarding the deep. This is the general explanation. As for the specific explanation: it uses worldly phenomena to illustrate supramundane phenomena.
Because there once existed a father and son in the world, they now hear of the unprecedented wisdom of the supramundane and become true sons of the Buddha, leaping up [in joy].
They leaped for joy. Therefore, the sutra uses the worldly relationship of father and son as a metaphor for the supramundane relationship of teacher and disciple.

This is truly because the natural disposition (*dhātu*) of the śrāvakas and others is no different from that of the Buddha; it is only in this present sutra that this unprecedented truth is proclaimed. How is this known?
When I was secretly dispatched [to you], I still lacked the intention to serve as a hired laborer; when I received the wealth, how could I have conceived the thought that it was my own property?
It was solely because our natures were interconnected that I was thus favored by your grace of realization. My former anxieties and regrets are now finally dispelled.
When those of middling or inferior capacity hear this parable, they are for the first time called true children; only now do they truly attain [this status].
Upon awakening, his exultation increased all the more; this was because hearing the parable gave rise to genuine joy. This is the passage concerning faith, understanding, and rejoicing.
Regarding the titles of both the general and specific sections, this parable is presented according to the *loka-nirukti* (worldly standpoint) based on the theme of rejoicing.
Furthermore, by using worldly phenomena of birth as an analogy for supramundane phenomena of birth, [the Buddha] causes those who hear his voice and teachings not to lose the Mahāyāna.
As the sutra says: "The father knows the former inclinations of his sons and what various precious playthings each prefers;

therefore, he uses worldly provisions and implements as a metaphor for the supramundane phenomena of birth belonging to the three vehicles. Thus, this present sutra points back to the former three carts, which are subtle and wondrous.
This is included among rare treasures. Therefore, it is said: "The path you all practice is the bodhisattva path. Having understood the preferences of his children, he then provides the three carts;
this is because the parable is established according to the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the standpoint for the benefit of others).

Furthermore, by comparing the extinction of worldly dharmas with the extinction of supramundane dharmas, although they previously attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), they still fell into various doubts and regrets; now, having heard [of] the One...

The Great Vehicle. It begins by completely eliminating sorrow and affliction. As the Sūtra says: "I am their father; I ought to pull them from their suffering and cause them to escape being burned and boiled.
Generally speaking, although the destruction of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) has occurred in the past, there is nothing that does not eliminate evil even now.

Specifically speaking, the root of pulling one from suffering lies in the Great Vehicle; it is only now that this is attained. There is nothing that surpasses this in the ultimate elimination of evil. This is the correspondence.
The parable is taught for the sake of the *yathā-siddhānta* (the standpoint of common consensus).

Furthermore, by comparing the non-arising and non-ceasing of the great worldly carriage to the non-arising and non-ceasing of the fundamental, inherently existent nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) that transcends the world, it causes one to abide within true wisdom, thinking, "I shall certainly become a Buddha.

As the sutra says, "Riding upon this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). This is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth), established as a metaphor.
In the "Parable Chapter," one should know that the Dharma-exposition reveals the true nature (*dharmatā*). What is hidden and what is manifest?

If the long wind does not cease to blow and the moon remains ever suspended in the sky, yet those of middling and inferior capacities have not yet awakened their great potential and their deluded attachments remain obstructed, they will claim that the moon has vanished and the wind has stilled.

To address these two misconceptions, [the Buddha] moves the tree and raises the fan, thereby making the meaning of the wind and the moon manifest. Although the Dharma and the parable differ, [their intent is the same].
It is said: "The Parable Chapter" was spoken for the sake of the four *siddhāntas*. If one were to simply explain these two characters [parable], what would be the point of titling a chapter?
One should know that the Buddha, through his single sound of *śakravarti* (universal sovereignty), speaks parables; yet this single sound is exclusively the truth.

Skillful parables are combined with provisional means; through these provisional means, beings are led back to the ultimate reality. If we consider this from the perspective of the teachings, the Buddha’s original intention was to praise the One Vehicle.
However, because sentient beings were unable to bear it, he recalled the great compassionate skillful means of previous Buddhas and proceeded to the Deer Park, where he extolled the three vehicles.
Thus, those of the Two Vehicles are of middling or inferior capacity; they save themselves but their grace does not reach others. The Bodhisattva is like a bull that draws others out from the fire.
Furthermore, in the parable of the three people fearing being burned and boiled: the Śrāvaka is like a deer that goes straight ahead without looking back;
the Pratyekabuddha is like a mother deer who runs while looking back at her young; the Bodhisattva is like a great elephant that shields its body with its trunk.

"Swords and arrows" refers to the various beings emerging together as a herd; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of "escaping horses and elephants. These are metaphors from the Shared Teaching (*paryāya-yāna*).

Furthermore, those of the three vehicles who have resolved their minds [for awakening] do so recently, whereas Bodhisattvas have resolved their minds for a vast duration. Their principle is profound and their wisdom is powerful;

they sever distinct delusions, exhaust the source, and reach the ultimate nature. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The two vehicles are like fireflies, while Bodhisattvas are like the light of the sun. These are metaphors from the Distinct Teaching (*vyatireka-yāna*).

Furthermore, those who first behold my body and hear what I teach, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata at the very moment of the *Avataṃsaka*, are such persons as can be easily transformed and delivered; they require no further analogies or inducements.

For those who have not yet entered, for more than forty years I have passed through the three stages of samādhi, employing various other skillful means to assist in revealing the ultimate truth. Today, in the royal city, [this truth] is definitively [established].
He preached the Mahāyāna to universally cause all beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

He did not allow even a single person to attain extinction alone. As it is now, so it was at the beginning; as it was at the beginning, so it is now. The *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are neither two nor different.

Those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom can understand them immediately upon hearing them without the need for parables; it is only for the sake of those of middling and inferior capacities who have not yet awakened that [parables are employed].
Therefore, being deluded regarding the Dharma, they speak of the divergent paths of the provisional and the real. Their attachments stir and doubts arise;

they say to themselves, "In the past, I dwelt together with him in the stage of no-more-learning, and I was also in accord with the Bodhisattvas in the single truth. He has received a prediction of enlightenment, yet I have not yet been moistened by it."
Upon first hearing the brief exposition, they already harbored doubts as to whether this was the ultimate fruit or merely a provisional means;
whether they would remain forever small or eventually attain greatness. Even after hearing the five Buddhas speak again, their suspicions were still not dispelled.

Therefore, it was necessary today to further entice them with the Great Vehicle so that they might obtain benefit; this is called the "Parable of the Circular Cart. Furthermore, [the teaching] employs the five flavors and the seasons.

[Section]. To explain in detail will now clarify the present analogy. Question: Since this sutra is already a teaching of the Sole Perfect [Vehicle], it would suffice to explain its meaning by directly relying on the single Perfect Teaching alone.
Why is it necessary to laboriously rely on the four teachings? Would such prolixity not result in a congestion of meaning?
Answer: This is not so. It is because the great purport of this sutra—and the intent of its sections—lies precisely in the "opening of the provisional" (*kaishō*).
His merit transcends that of his generation. Without being constrained by what he has revealed, there would be no way to speak of the ultimate reality.

Therefore, just as the parable contrasts the three carts with the one cart, so too do the teachings contrast the provisional and the real, setting forth both the partial and the perfect. Were it not for this, [the distinction between the ancient and the present would be untenable].
What is it that is opened? If one were to apply the "Perfect" (yuan) alone to explain the sutra, how would this differ from the "Perfect" within the *Avataṃsaka* or the various "Flavors" (*rasa*)?

Therefore, when explaining other sutras, one uses only the [three] "Treasures" (*pitaka*) and so forth; but when explaining the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one employs the eight categories beginning with the "Sudden" (*dun*).

If the essential principle is thus upheld without error, the detailed explanation of the "Original" and "Traced" aspects is fully contained in the *Miaoxuan*. Now, those who hear this sutra should contemplate the mind.
"Emptiness is like a white ox; if it is fully equipped, it is like the body of a carriage. The above constitutes the explanation of the title, all derived from metaphors.
As for the meaning of the main text, when we reach the exegesis of the sūtra below, we shall again explain it according to the Dharma in four sections.
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy with great delight.
This concludes the second major chapter of the *Fa-shuo* (Exposition of the Dharma), the section on "Śāriputra’s Realization. Regarding the term "realization" (*ling-jie*): it means—

"Receiving" (*ling*) refers to externally receiving what the Buddha has spoken; hence it is called "receiving. "Understanding" (*jie*) refers to recounting what was heard, which is internally grasping the Buddha’s meaning;
hence it is called "understanding. These two preceding phrases describe the internal understanding of Śāriputra by the author of the sutra.
Since this internal understanding resides within the mind, it is termed "mental joy" (*yi-xi*). When this joy moves the physical form, it is termed "leaping" (*yong*).

"Leaping" (*yào*) refers to the joy of the body. Having heard the wondrous Dharma from the wondrous person and attained wondrous understanding, the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind] are all joyful.
If one encounters even a single blessing, one still rejoices and exults; how much more so when the three joys are fully present—how could one not leap for joy? The subsequent passage states:
"Now, having heard this sound of the Dharma from the World-Honored One, my heart harbors leaping joy, with the internal and external in harmony. This refers to the present life.
This is the benefit for the realm (*dhātu*). Furthermore, he changed his minor studies for the great, abandoned his poverty to inherit the estate of a wealthy family.
The text says: "Today I know for the first time that I am truly a son of the Buddha. This is the benefit for others (*pudgala*). Moreover, sorrow and regret are both dispelled;

doubt and difficulty are simultaneously removed. All internal and external obstructions are cleared away until there is vast clarity. The text says: "I have already attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)."
Hearing [this teaching] also removes sorrow and affliction; this is the benefit of the immediate antidote. Furthermore, the son of the Buddha has already attained all that ought to be attained.
As the text says: "Abiding within true wisdom, I shall certainly become a Buddha. This is the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Through hearing the five Buddhas extensively expound the provisional to reveal the real, Śāriputra and others obtained the benefits of the four *siddhārtha*s.

Furthermore, it should be understood that while those who rejoice do so at entering the stages, the Arhat has already emerged from the cage of the triple world, shattered the seeds and fruits of the four abidings, feels no sorrow when encountering harm, and feels no delight when meeting with profit;
having manifested the clarity of patience toward suffering, he has reached the ultimate stage of *aśaikṣa*.
The Three Treasuries (Tripiṭaka) were already delighted by what they had previously attained; now, they should not rejoice again.

If the three types of people equally employ the path of non-discursive speech, although their modes of refuting [substantiality] differ, their realization of emptiness is identical. Since this identical path is that of the Shared Teaching (Pāryāyika-yāna), they have already attained it long ago and likewise do not rejoice again.
If the contemplation of the two absences of self (dvi-śūnyatā) serves as the path of means, and the contemplation of the provisional (upāya-darśana) is used to dispel [delusions]...

The narrowness and meagerness of the Two Vehicles are swept away by the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which clears the clamor and turbidity of ordinary beings and transcends the faults of the two extremes;

thus one attains great joy (*mahā-prāmodya*). Yet even this is not what the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*) can compare to. One should know that the joy now attained is based on Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanwu*);
it is the "Joyful" stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) of the first *cittotpāda*, or it is the joy of progressing toward the stages, or it is the transcendence of the first ground.
It is also called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Since the three causes have been developed, it is no different from the first stage; both are named "Joy.
This is truly because those with superior faculties and sharp wisdom necessarily enter by leaping over [the stages], and thus it is also called "Joy.

Therefore, only by comparing it with the three previous teachings can its distinction be seen. The joy in this present sutra differs from that of the past; thus, it must be explained through the doctrine. Second, the two aspects of origin and trace.
Regarding the "Expositor": Śāriputra attained Buddhahood long ago, and his name is Kanakamuni. In his manifest traces, he assists Śākyamuni as the right-hand disciple of wisdom.

Beginning from his time as a non-Buddhist, he uproots error and leads others to the correct path, showing them the joy of the "milk-flavor," the fresh butter, and the refined butter to benefit bodhisattvas;
now, acting as the "cream-of-ghee" (amṛta), he enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, bringing forth joy—joy in that which benefits.

Those who further study the Buddha-way rejoice in this way; all such manifestations are merely traces of his conduct, and are thus called "rejoicing and leaping for joy," which refers to internal understanding.

Question: If it is said that Śāriputra was originally a Buddha and only manifested as a śrāvaka through traces, then according to the Dharma-exposition, only Śāriputra alone is seen to receive the prediction (vyākaraṇa).
If that were the case, then at the beginning of the assembly, there would be no one who attains the prediction through actual practice.
"Is it not the case that the Tathāgata has merely bestowed [this prediction] upon the first assembly? Answer: "Not so. As Śāriputra’s realization in the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* states:
'The Buddha, in the midst of the great assembly, declared: "I shall become a Buddha.

Since this verse summarizes the preceding prose section concerning the twelve hundred arhats, it does not refer to Śāriputra alone. However, because the Sūtra initially mentions only Śāriputra, no other names were recorded."
Regarding the passage concerning "other kalpas," "countries," and so forth: these may exist in the Sanskrit original, but the Chinese version omits them.
This is as when the fourfold assembly rejoices, saying, "We are also like this," which is identical to Śāriputra’s realization; it is identical to Śāriputra being described as perfected;
and it is identical to Śāriputra receiving his prediction. Therefore, the fourfold assembly merely sees Śāriputra’s realization, thinking, "Now we have heard the same."

The same should apply to [Śāriputra] as well. As for why the Buddha did not previously bestow a prediction upon Śāriputra, it was solely because his practice through the ultimate truth (*satyavādī*) had not yet matured, while his practice through provisional means (*upāya*) had arisen simultaneously;

thus, for over forty years, the reality was not revealed. Only upon hearing the five Buddhas’ revelation did he suddenly awaken to the wondrous principle and immediately shatter his ignorance, becoming fit for a prediction.
How could the transformative efficacy of a single lifetime’s teaching be entrusted entirely to those practicing the ultimate truth alone?
"...is it so? He immediately rose and joined his palms, gazing up at the Honored One's countenance.

These two phrases describe the external understanding. "Immediately rising and joining his palms" refers to the physical manifestation of comprehension; previously, the provisional and the real were...

Second: The two hands being apart is like palms not joined. Now, the explanation that the provisional is identical to the real is like the joining of the two palms. The joining of palms must be directed toward the Buddha.

Formerly, the provisional was not the cause for Buddhahood; formerly, the real was not the fruit of Buddhahood. Now, by explaining that the provisional is identical to the real, one perfects the great, perfect cause.
Since the cause must lead to the fruit, it is said that "joining palms and facing the Buddha. "Gazing up at the Honored Countenance" signifies understanding.

It is reality. Reality is the realm of the Buddha; it is not a provisional method (*upāya-dharma*). Gazing up at the Honored Countenance with no other thoughts expresses hearing of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*);
this expresses the understanding of the meaning. Joining the palms represents the body. This encompasses both the provisional and the real.

Gazing up and understanding the meaning of the real also expresses the understanding of the provisional. However, regarding such acts as joining the palms and gazing up—what teaching do they represent?
What was previously absent is now manifested. This manifestation is not merely the external observance of seeing the Buddha;

it is also the state wherein the mind is free from divergent thoughts, manifesting the perception of the actual realm of others and thereby opening up one’s own self-knowledge and vision. This concludes the sūtra author’s exposition on both internal and external understanding.
Next, Śāriputra spoke of his own experience, saying to the Buddha:
"Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy; I have attained what I have never experienced before."

This indicates the three types of joy. This is Śāriputra’s own account of his realization. Now, following the World-Honored One, he says, "I have seen the Buddha's body," which is called joy of the body (*kāya-prīti*).
Having heard this Dharma-sound from the Buddha's own mouth, he hears it and rejoices; thus it is called joy of the mouth (*vāk-prīti*).
Having attained what was never before, he understands the Buddha's intent through his own mind; this is called joy of the mind (*manas-prīti*). This...
This indicates the three kinds of joy. To receive [the teaching] necessarily involves all three; it is not merely a verbal reception.
Why is this so? Because in the past, I heard such a Dharma from the Buddha, seeing various bodhisattvas receiving the prediction of their future buddhahood.
Yet we were not included in this matter; we feel profound personal sorrow at having lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.

This explains the three joys mentioned above. This refers to the joy of realizing what was previously missed in a former life, as opposed to the joy of experiencing it in the present life. Regarding the phrase "formerly hearing the Dharma and so forth":

in the *Avataṃsaka* period, [the Buddha] was like one who is deaf or mute; in the Deer Park period, [the teaching] appeared to be absent. Yet, during these two periods, [the truth] was secretly present.
This was not the proper time. Hearing such a teaching as this refers only to hearing the true wisdom of the Mahāyāna within the Vaipulya (fangděng) scriptures;

it is no different from what is heard now, and is therefore described as "hearing such a teaching. Regarding the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*): this also refers to the conferring of predictions upon bodhisattvas within the Vaipulya scriptures.
The followers of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) were not included in this matter, which caused them profound personal distress. This is heard in the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra*.
To praise the great and disparage the small, and to harbor internal doubts while holding external things in contempt, is called "sorrowful attachment.
To lose one's knowledge and vision means to lose the vision of the Buddha-eye and the knowledge of the Buddha-wisdom; both of these refer to the loss of what was not previously seen.
Because one did not previously see the Buddha, there was no joy in the body; this [passage] reveals the joy now experienced by the body.
“World-Honored One, when I dwell alone in mountain forests or beneath trees, whether sitting or walking, I constantly reflect:
‘We have all entered equally into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Why then does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna? This is our own fault.’”
"It was not the Blessed One;
this was merely a lapse of speech from my past life. It serves to manifest the joy of my present verbal understanding.

This is because in my former body, while dwelling in the mountain forests, my mind clung to the Lesser Vehicle and thus I did not hear the Great Dharma; therefore, I lacked verbal joy. I have always dwelt alone in the mountain forests."

This refers to the place where one reflects upon one's transgressions, namely the mountain forests. Reflecting now upon those former days, both my outward conduct and my internal mind were entirely in error.
When it is said that we "together entered the dharma-nature," this precisely highlights the characteristics of my past faults.

This was truly because, in the past, Śāriputra and the others did not realize that beyond the nature of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there exists separately the wondrous principle of the Mahāyāna; even though they encountered the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā [sūtras], [they failed to understand them].
Upon hearing of the deeds of the Great Bodhisattvas, he thought to himself, "I was originally taught only the six perfections of a bodhisattva.

Clinging to the single principle through which he had entered, he doubted the gateway of the three vehicles. He reflected that although the Buddha had previously taught that the three vehicles differ, the true reality realized by them is identical.
Since the single principle is the same, he realized, "I have failed in my knowledge and vision; that is why I was not granted a prediction of enlightenment."

The Bodhisattva attained this and therefore received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). He adhered strictly to the literal teaching and did not truly understand the provisional application [of skillful means];
thus, he doubted the single principle, wondering whether it was lost or not lost. If it were lost, how could I have realized the principle and attained the fruit?
If it were not lost, why has he not granted me a prediction? Furthermore, he doubted that the three teachings were not identical and that the realization of the principle was not the same.

[The interlocutor asks: "Yes. Since the Bodhisattvas have received their predictions [of Buddhahood], and I too am a son of the Buddha, why does the Tathāgata show partiality by providing me with only a minor salvation?
This constitutes a fault; therefore, I now describe this deficiency and repent my error, saying: 'This is our own fault.

It is because we are deluded regarding the provisional [teachings] that it concerns neither principle nor doctrine; it is because we are confused about the single reality that it concerns neither the Buddha's partiality."

We recount our past errors and look up with gratitude to the Tathāgata; this is to acknowledge our transgressions and take refuge [in him]. Therefore, it is said that [the fault] does not belong to the World-Honored One.
Why is this so? Because if we wait for the explanation of the causes by which we shall achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...

"Bodhi is necessarily attained through the Mahāyāna and thereby one achieves liberation. However, we did not understand that these were teachings spoken according to skillful means and appropriate circumstances.
Upon first hearing the Buddha-dharma, we accepted it immediately upon encountering it, contemplated it, and sought realization. World-Honored One, from the past until now..."
Throughout the day and all night, he constantly reproached himself, thinking:

"This was the failure of my former intention; this is the joy of my present understanding. Truly, if one does not wait for the explanation of the underlying cause, there can be no genuine understanding;
furthermore, if one does not recognize the skillful means, there can be no provisional understanding. Without both provisional and genuine understanding—
Therefore, there is no intention to rejoice. Since the past loss has already been made manifest, the present gain is naturally revealed. This does not depend on external causes for two reasons.

First, regarding the non-acceptance of the past, it was not dependent upon its counterpart; as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where the sun shines upon high mountains, the wisdom of the Three Truths is illuminated—this is the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Because I did not accept this when it was offered as a counterpart to me, I incurred a loss.
Placing this before [the others], the name does not depend on its cause. Next, regarding the teachings of all Buddhas: after a long time, one must ultimately preach the truth.
I did not wait for the future, but rather, between the two pillars—at the Deer Park and the two *Sūtras*—I hastily grasped the "Small" [Vehicle].

Not understanding the skillful means (*upāya*), the provisional and the real according to what is appropriate, I did not wait for a counterpart; thus, the fault does not lie with another. Therefore...

I have often reproached myself, saying: "When one speaks of the Mahāyāna, the term applies generally to all teachings; it does not refer exclusively to the Mahāyāna, but specifically to the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna.
One should know that its causes do not transcend cause and effect, as well as vows and practice. Practice refers precisely to the six perfections.
The vows are precisely the Four Great Vows.
Now, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never heard before, all my doubts and regrets have been severed;
my body and mind are at ease, and I have attained a swift sense of peace and security.
This section concludes the three types of joy mentioned above: joy of the body is concluded by [the encounter with] the Buddha; joy of speech is concluded by hearing the Dharma;
and joy of the mind is concluded by the severing of all doubts and regrets.
Today I have come to know that you are truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma, and having attained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma.
This section concludes the three accomplishments. Thus one knows that he is truly a son of the Buddha; this is the fulfillment of the meaning of being near to the Buddha.

"Born from the Buddha’s mouth" concludes the accomplishment of speech. "Transformed by birth from the Dharma" concludes the accomplishment of mind. The sutra contains the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.

3. Explaining the text in this manner, the commentary concludes. When the text is exhausted, the principle is elucidated and its meaning becomes manifest. It is said that one "attains a portion of the Buddha-dharma";

"portion" (*bhāga*) refers here to the stage of partial truth (*satyāṃśika*), namely the first *vihāra*. Furthermore, this section of prose may be interpreted according to the four *siddhārtha* (benefits for the world):

from "From now on, from the World-Honored One... onwards is the benefit of worldly joy (*loka-saṃvṛti-sukha*). From "Why is this so? In the past, I went... onwards is [the benefit of]... [The text continues with the subsequent benefits.]
That which was previously lost is now obtained; this is the joy of humans. From the World-Honored One, I have applied the antidote to that joy since ancient times;
from this day forward, I know it to be departed—this is the joy of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, if one explains the four *siddhāntas* by way of a joyful mind:

the movement and delight [of the mind] is the worldly (*loka*) perspective; that which has never before been attained is the joy of humans (*pudgala*); the movement... [is the therapeutic (*prātipakṣika*) perspective].
Vitarka and vicāra are the antidotes; they move the physical form. When the clarity distinguishes the principle, it manifests as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The above concludes the prose section of Śāriputra’s own account.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
(These are the words of the compilers who recorded the sutra:
"I have heard this sound of the Dharma, which I have never experienced before; my heart is filled with great joy, and the net of doubt has been entirely removed."
This single line of verse summarizes the general indication of the three types of joy mentioned above. "I have heard" indicates oral joy;

"the one capable of teaching" simultaneously implies physical joy, as it refers to being near the Buddha. The remaining three phrases summarize the indication of mental joy; "I have heard" signifies its reception.
With a heart of great joy, one immediately attains liberation.
Having received the Buddha’s teaching since of old, I have not lost the Mahāyāna. The Buddha’s voice is most rare and marvelous; it can eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings.
"I have already attained the exhaustion of outflows; hearing [this] also removes my grief and affliction.
These one and a half verses concern physical joy (*kāya-prīti*). The first line concerns the body's reception; the subsequent half-line concerns understanding, which is the joy of seeing the Buddha.
The prose section clarifies the loss of knowledge and vision, while the verse clarifies that the Mahāyāna is not lost. The above discusses what is lost and what is not.
[The commentary on] "Distant" and [the verse on] "Attaining through Proximate Discourse" merely manifest one another.
Dwelling in mountain valleys or beneath forest trees, whether sitting or walking in meditation, I constantly contemplate this matter.
Alas, I reproach myself deeply: how have I deceived myself? We too are sons of the Buddha, having equally entered the dharma of outflowlessness;
yet we are unable, in the future, to expound the unsurpassed path—the golden body with its thirty-two marks, the ten powers, and the various liberations.
Though we were together within the same Dharma, I did not attain these things: the eighty minor marks of excellence, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and such merits as these;
I have lost them all. Yet, while I was walking in meditation alone, I saw the Buddha amidst the great assembly.
His fame fills the ten directions, bringing vast benefit to sentient beings. Reflecting that I have lost this advantage, I feel as though I have deceived myself.
Day and night, I constantly contemplate this matter, wishing to ask the World-Honored One whether I have lost it or not.
I have often seen the World-Honored One praise the bodhisattvas; for this reason, day and night, I have contemplated such matters.
Now I hear the Buddha’s voice preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate—outflow-free and inconceivable—causing the multitudes to reach the site of enlightenment.
This consists of eleven lines of verse. The first nine lines praise the failure to hear the Dharma due to being physically distant;
the first eight lines specifically praise physical distance while clarifying verbal reception, thereby illustrating past loss and present attainment.
The final line on "now hearing the Buddha" praises the failure to hear due to physical distance while clarifying verbal understanding, thereby illustrating past loss and present realization.

Regarding the statement "the golden color and the thirty-two marks," the commentary does not explain them. Now, following the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), I shall briefly indicate their names and characteristics.
When it comes to discussing the numinous stillness of the Dharmakāya, how could there be form, sound, mind, or consciousness that can be seen or heard?

It is solely through the power of compassion that, whenever there are those who should see [the Buddha] to obtain happiness and escape suffering, he immediately manifests his dignified marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Now, these thirty-two are generally referred to as "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*); "mark" means that which indicates something, which can be grasped and distinguished—thus it is called a mark.
The Tathāgata’s body of response and transformation manifests these thirty-two marks. By means of...
This manifests that the myriad virtues of the Dharmakāya are perfectly complete, such that all who behold him feel love and reverence;

they know there are supreme virtues worthy of veneration, and thus he is the Honored One among gods and humans, the Lord among all sages. For this reason, he manifests the thirty-two marks. Now, I shall list their names directly without the leisure for detailed explanation:
First, the soles of his feet are level and even like the bottom of a casket; second, the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet; third...

1. The fingers and toes of his hands and feet are longer than those of other people. 2. His four limbs are soft and supple, surpassing all other parts of his body. 3. His heels are fully developed, complete, and beautiful. 4.
His fingers and toes are joined by a web-like membrane, surpassing that of other people. 5. His insteps are high and well-formed, in proportion to his heels. 6.
His calves are like those of the eneya deer—slender, elegant, and beautiful. 7. Standing upright, his hands reach down to touch his knees. 8. His male organ is concealed within a sheath.
11. Like a horse-king, his body is equal in length and breadth. 12. From each and every pore grows hair that is blue-green and soft. 13.
The hair points upward, is blue-green and soft, and curls to the right. 14. His golden light is subtle and wondrous in its characteristics. 15.
The radiance of his body extends one *zhang* in each direction from his face. 16. His skin is thin and smooth, and it does not retain dust.
16. His skin is free of impurities and does not harbor mosquitoes or gadflies. 17. The seven parts—the soles of both feet, the two palms, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck—are well-filled.
18. The area between his two armpits is well-filled. 19. His upper body is like that of a lion.
20. His body is upright and straight. 21. His shoulders are rounded and beautiful. 22. He possesses a full set of forty teeth. 23. His teeth are white and pure.
24. His teeth are closely set and deeply rooted. 25. His twenty-four teeth are the whitest and largest.
26. His jaw is like that of a lion. 27. The saliva in his throat perceives the most excellent of flavors. 28.
His tongue is large and thin, covering his face up to the hairline. 29. His Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching, like that of the kalaviṅka bird.
29. His eyes are like refined gold; 30. His eyelashes are like those of a bull king; 31.
Between his eyebrows there is a white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) like *tūla* cotton; 32. A fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) is formed on the crown of his head.
These thirty-two marks are common to what is seen in the four teachings; one must know that the thirty-two [marks] in this present sutra are not those of the three preceding teachings.
This is precisely the opening of the provisional to reveal the real (the thirty-two marks). Thus, it was praised by the Dragon King:

"Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, universally illuminating the ten directions, the subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body possesses the thirty-two marks. This refers to the marks described in the present sutra.

Regarding the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), according to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha’s secondary characteristics are immeasurable; these [eighty] are merely those included within the category of form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the eighty [minor marks]: worldly sentient beings serve eighty deities; therefore, the Buddha possesses them so as to inspire reverence.

However, the intent of the current scriptural passage is merely to provide a general account of past errors. Nevertheless, each of the eighty secondary marks possesses the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) for benefiting others;
they do not necessarily pertain exclusively to the eighty deities. Thus, every single mark is nothing other than an ocean of excellence. Now, having heard this opening...

"Authority" (quan) rectifies what was previously lost, yet it does not lose the marvelous excellence [of the teaching]. "I constantly, throughout day and night": here, birth-and-death (saṃsāra) is taken as night and nirvāṇa as day.
By contrasting the Tripiṭaka with the Vaipulya, we establish the distinction between inner and outer. To say that nirvāṇa exists within birth-and-death means that it exists inside birth-and-death;
to say that it exists outside birth-and-death means that there is heterodoxy outside of birth-and-death. If it exists within birth-and-death, this is precisely the intent of the Mahāyāna. If...
That there is nothing within birth and death is the perspective of the Hīnayāna. When awakening is attained, both doubts are simultaneously dispelled;
one should know that for these noble ones, what need is there to describe their reflections on this matter, which would merely be like measuring a day and night by the transition from dusk to dawn?

Herein, one should follow the underlying significance: regarding the period of the two flavors in the former teachings, it occurs spontaneously within the mental dispositions of those with the capacity [for enlightenment].
In the darkness of the night, this doubt existed; I had not yet been able to speak openly to express it in such a way. Rather, I have recounted past failings to manifest present attainment.
Furthermore, when the Perfect and Distinct [teachings] are contrasted with the Tripitaka and Shared [teachings], both birth-and-death and nirvana are regarded as "night.
When this doubt is removed, it is called "day. When the sun rises, both doubts are simultaneously dispelled. Moreover, there are two types of people in the world: first, [those who...]

Regarding those who first establish themselves in the Mahāyāna and those who enter the Mahāyāna by practicing the Hīnayāna, if one compares their respective modes of practice, those who enter directly are inferior.
For example, those who enter from the Abhidharma are superior. It is the same for Bodhisattvas:

those who enter through the Avataṃsaka Sūtra have a weaker capacity for transformative teaching, whereas those who enter through the Five Flavors are superior. Formerly, it was said that the untainted [state] only reaches the limit of non-existence.

Only now do they finally come to know this. Upon reaching the true site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this clarifies that their former bodies were distant and thus suffered the loss of not hearing the Dharma;
it reveals that they are now near the Buddha and hear the Dharma, receiving it with their own mouths and attaining understanding.
I was originally possessed of false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins. The World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my errors and preached nirvana.
I completely eliminated all false views and attained realization of the Dharma of emptiness. At that time, I thought to myself: "I have reached extinction."

These two lines of the second verse summarize the preceding point that one does not hear the Dharma because of entering into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Holding wrong views is the attachment of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*);
entering into the nature of phenomena is the attachment of those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*). In both cases, one does not hear the Dharma.

This clarifies that while there was no oral comprehension in the past, there is now oral comprehension. From "I was once in the mountain valleys" up to this point, the verse summarizes the preceding section.
Having finished receiving this joyful understanding, he now realized for himself: "This is not true parinirvāṇa. When I attain Buddhahood, I shall be endowed with the thirty-two marks."
Revered by the hosts of devas, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, and spirits, it is only at this time that one may say [suffering] is forever extinguished without remainder.
These two lines—“Nine and a half [kalpas] from now”—express the mind’s attainment of wondrous understanding and the joy of realization.

They acknowledge that the past was not real and reveal that the present is finally real, clarifying the causal conditions upon which it depends. Hearing below that one shall become a Buddha is precisely what constitutes those causal conditions.
It is verified that in the past, he did not depend upon external causes.
When the Buddha was among the great assembly and declared, "I shall become a Buddha," upon hearing such a sound of the Dharma, all his doubts and regrets were entirely eliminated.

This single line is a direct verse summarizing the profound understanding gained during the first cycle of hearing [the Dharma]. It specifically summarizes the manifestation of the ultimate truth within the skillful means.
Upon first hearing what the Buddha had spoken, his mind was filled with great shock and doubt: "Could it be that a demon has manifested as a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?"
This single verse refers back to the time at the beginning of the Dharma-exposition in the preceding gāthās, when, upon hearing the brief teaching, doubt and regret arose.
The Buddha, through various causes, analogies, and skillful speech, caused my mind to become as calm as the ocean; having heard this, the net of my doubts was severed.
This single line of verse summarizes the preceding chapter on the Buddhas. "Various" summarizes the preceding opening of the provisional (*upāya*).

"Parables" summarize the preceding wondrous Dharma of the *pundarīka* lotus. Having heard that the Way of the five Buddhas is the same and understanding that Māra is not Māra, one understands the provisional means;
therefore, the mind is as calm as the ocean.
The Buddha has said that in the past, immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa, while abiding in skillful means, all likewise taught this Dharma.
This single line of verse concludes the chapter on the Buddhas of the Past.
The Buddhas of the present and the future, their number being immeasurable, likewise employ various skillful means to expound this Dharma.
This single line of verse introduces the section concerning the Buddhas of the present and the future.
"Now, World-Honored One, from his birth, his renunciation, his attainment of the Way, and his turning of the wheel of Dharma—all have been taught through skillful means.
This single line correctly versifies the preceding section on Śākyamuni’s revelation of the provisional teachings.
The World-Honored One teaches the true path; Māra does not possess such things. For this reason, I know with certainty that it is not Māra who has manifested as a Buddha.
Because I had fallen into the net of doubt, I thought this was the work of Māra.
These one and a half lines express repentance and self-reproach, recognizing that the fault of initial doubt lay with himself. The following verses reflect his joyful understanding and realization;
from the time he first encountered the Buddha in the past until reaching this point, these verses conclude the third section on "Receiving and Understanding."
Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice, profound, far-reaching, and most subtle, as he expounds the pure Dharma, my heart is filled with great joy;
doubt and regret are forever exhausted, and I abide securely within true wisdom.
These one and a half verses conclude the three types of joy mentioned above. The first three lines conclude the Buddha’s voice, which is the joy of speech (*vāk-prasāda*).

The next three lines conclude the joy of mind (*manas-prasāda*); since this also involves hearing the Buddha, it simultaneously encompasses the joy of body (*kāya-prasāda*), thereby concluding the three satisfactions of joy (*tri-ārṣa-saṃtuṣṭi*).
"I shall certainly become a Buddha, revered by devas and humans, turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and teaching and transforming all bodhisattvas.

This single line completes the three joys mentioned above. From the beginning of the sutra’s opening exultation down to this verse, the explanation of the Dharma as expounded by the Buddha has been concluded through Śāriputra’s realization.
From below, starting with "At that time, the Buddha said," is the third [section], the *yathābhūta* (according to reality).

Now follows the section on the Buddha’s confirmation. Herein, the Tathāgata confirms that Śāriputra’s understanding is not in vain. This passage consists of three parts: first, the past teaching of the Great Vehicle;
second, the temporary forgetting and taking up of the Small Vehicle; third, the subsequent re-explanation of the Great Vehicle.

Thus, by citing the past teaching, he describes the conditions for his vision of the Buddha; by describing how he temporarily forgot and took up the Small Vehicle, he describes his sorrowful regret upon hearing the Dharma.
The causal conditions: [the Buddha] further explains the greatness [of his teaching] to demonstrate that his realization and understanding are not in vain; this summarizes the three preceding points.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "I now speak among this great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas:
in the past, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I have constantly taught and transformed you before twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas."
"You, too, have followed me and studied under me for a long night. It was because I guided you through skillful means that you were born into my Dharma.
This was stated by Śāriputra because he had already explained his own realization;

now the Tathāgata confirms it, attesting that Śāriputra’s account of his threefold joyful awakening is not erroneous. Furthermore, herein the Tathāgata clarifies that he previously taught the Great [Vehicle].
This serves as the present occasion for seeing the Buddha; it describes how Śāriputra, having attained understanding, experienced joy in his body.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the unsurpassed path," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "The unsurpassed body refers to the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), which belong to the fruit.
Upholding the unsurpassed refers to benefiting oneself and others. Being fully endowed with the unsurpassed refers to life, vision, and precepts."
Furthermore, the unsurpassed wisdom-virtue refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The unsurpassed inconceivability refers to the six perfections (*pāramitā*).

The unsurpassed liberation refers to the ability to destroy the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). The unsurpassed practice refers to the two practices of the noble ones and the Brahmās.
These six pertain to the unsurpassed nature of the cause. Moreover, if we discuss this solely in terms of the fruit, "unsurpassed body" is the name for—
A Great Man who upholds the unsurpassed is named Great Compassion; one who is fully endowed with the unsurpassed is named One Who Has Reached the Other Shore;
unsurpassed wisdom is named All-Knowledge; the inconceivable unsurpassed is named Arhat;
unsurpassed liberation is named Great Nirvāṇa; and unsurpassed practice is named Samyaksaṃbuddha. Those who speak of the Way are Bodhisattvas.
The *Ratnavali* (Necklace Sutra) says: "The Way should be pure; defilement and turbidity are not the Way. The Way should be single-mindedness; manifold thoughts are not the Way.
The Way should be contentment; excessive desire is not the Way. The Way should be reverence; arrogance is not the Way. The Way should be self-restraint of the mind;
negligence is not the Way. The Way should be luminous manifestation; self-concealment is not the Way. The Way should be continuous connection; lack of practice is not the Way."
Non-Dharma is not the Way; the Way should be awakening. Delusion and ignorance are non-Dharma; the Way should be transformation through teaching.

Stinginess is non-Dharma; the Way is to draw near to virtuous friends. Practicing evil is non-Dharma. In this way, various aspects clarify the unsurpassed Way; thus, the meaning of the Way is immeasurable.

While the various teachings each have their own many meanings within their respective treatises, this present sutra reveals and clarifies the perfect and wondrous true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), for it is without...
The "Supreme Path" refers to the path of the Unsurpassed Buddha Vehicle; it is called the Unsurpassed Path because each and every unsurpassed aspect possesses the supremacy of all paths.

Regarding those who have followed and studied under me throughout the long night: although they underwent great transformation in the past, they had never yet shattered the ignorance within the realm of desire (the *dhātu*).
Remaining within the darkness of delusion, they followed the Buddha to receive instruction; in the past, they possessed great spiritual capacity (*mahā-indriya*).

For one at the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*), hearing even a single phrase in its entirety plants a seed within their consciousness that is never lost throughout eternal kalpas.

Although the cause of realization (*bodhi-hetu*) may be distant, it still does not perish; how much more so now, when true awakening has been attained—how could it be in vain? Thus, by citing the great teachings received in the past, he describes his present vision of the Buddha as being unmistakable.
As for the statement, "By means of my skillful means, I have brought them to birth within my Dharma," this meaning connects to two points.
If, in the past, one was transformed by the Great [Vehicle], and now gives rise to great understanding, this constitutes the condition for seeing the Buddha.
If one causes them to escape the evil realms through provisional means using the Small [Vehicle] to lead them, this constitutes the condition for hearing the Dharma.
"Śāriputra, in the past I instructed you to set your aspirations on the Buddha-way, yet now you have completely forgotten this and instead claim that you have already attained nirvāṇa.
This describes the verbal joy of hearing the Dharma; it was the Tathāgata who clearly perceived that within Śāriputra there was the forgetting of the Great and the grasping for the Small."
The aforementioned [passage] describes the intermediate state of anxiety and regret as an inducement to hear the sublime Dharma.
There are those who, having encountered this opportunity, abandon the Great Vehicle midway to practice the Small Vehicle; this is called "forgetting it midway.
If one now claims to have already attained *nirvāṇa*, this is "forgetting it all at once. Because you have forgotten your great vow, you have fallen into the anxiety of practicing the Small Vehicle.
It is regrettable that you have not yet heard this Dharma, for it would have been in vain.
Now, because I wish to cause you to remember your original vow and the path you must practice, I shall preach this Mahāyāna sūtra for the sake of all śrāvakas;
it is titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma*, the teaching of the Bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas’ mindful care.
This explains that the Tathāgata further teaches the Great [Vehicle] for them. It serves to confirm their realization and ensure that their joy is not in vain.
That it is "not in vain" means that although they previously heard of the Great [Vehicle], they did not believe in it; now, their faith is no longer in vain.

Because I now wish to cause you to recollect your original vow, I confirm your attainment of the meaning and your understanding so that it is not in vain. First, I bestowed provisional teachings to perfect the minor virtues cultivated along the way.
Thereafter, the reality is revealed to fulfill his original vow and great resolve.

This concludes the Tathāgata’s confirmation of Śāriputra’s realization and his three joys, as well as the section from "From this day forth" up to here, which constitutes the third major division of the Dharma-exposition: the Tathāgata’s confirmation.
From the verse beginning with "Śāriputra, you shall... until its conclusion, this is the fourth part of the Dharma-exposition: the Buddha’s bestowal of prophecy.
Section. Having first personally declared his understanding, and then having been confirmed by the Tathāgata, Śāriputra was therefore granted this prediction:
"Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed..."

This precisely clarifies the timing of Śāriputra’s first prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Question: If one has attained great understanding and knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha, why wait for a prediction?
Answer: There are four reasons for a prediction: 1. In the past, the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) had not received predictions, yet now they must receive them.
2. Those of middling and inferior capacities have not yet awakened; the prediction is used to encourage and spur them on. 3. To cause those who hear it...
To form a karmic connection. Fourth, to fulfill their original vows; for these reasons, they are thus recorded. Furthermore, these four intentions are fully present throughout the three cycles.
Within the middle cycle, all four intentions are also present, though in the second intention, the single character "middle" (中) is omitted, and it may simply be said:
"for those of inferior capacity who have not yet awakened. Upon reaching the third cycle, there are only three intentions, with the entirety of the second one completely removed.
Therefore, one should know that these three cycles all possess these four intentions; however, within the second intention, there is only a difference in the subsequent reduction and exclusion.
[The Bodhisattvas] made offerings to several thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, upheld the True Dharma, and fully perfected the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.

This section constitutes the second bestowal of a prediction concerning the causal practices of Śāriputra. Within the text, there is the making of offerings to the Buddha, as well as his cultivation of practice;
it states that he shall attain Buddhahood and be named the Tathāgata Padmaprabha, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata.
Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—this is the third prediction.
Śāriputra attains the fruit; from "when he shall attain" until "Flower Radiance," these are his specific titles.

The titles such as "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings) and so forth are all general designations; however, the explanations for the Ten Epithets are extremely numerous. For now, I shall interpret them according to one particular tradition:
he who is free from falsehood is named Tathāgata; he who is a field of excellent merit is named Arhat; he who knows the Dharma-realm is named Samyaksaṃbuddha;
he who possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge is named Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna; he who does not return again is named Sugata; and he who knows all realms of existence is named Lokavid.
He who is unrivaled is called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*). He who tames the minds of others is called a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

He who serves as the eye for sentient beings is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). He who knows the three groups of beings is called a Buddha. He who can destroy Pāpīyān is called Bhagavat.
The land is named Vimalā. Its terrain is level and even; it is pure, magnificently adorned, peaceful, secure, and prosperous. Gods and humans abound there.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli, with eight intersecting roads marked by golden cords along their sides.
Beside each road stand rows of trees made of the seven treasures, which are always laden with flowers and fruit.
This section constitutes the fourth bestowal of a land. "Free from Defilement" (Vimala) is its name. Its description as being "evenly bright" clarifies the characteristics of the purity of that land;
this is a pure land of cohabitation (*sahā-bhūmi*). "Level" means it is without high or low elevations; "righteous" means it is without partiality.
"Peaceful and secure," and so forth, describe the functions of the land. The passage beginning with "lapis lazuli" further elucidates the superior characteristics of the land.
The Tathāgata Padmaprabha likewise teaches and transforms sentient beings by means of the three vehicles.
Śāriputra, although the time of that Buddha’s appearance was not an evil age, he preached the Dharma of the three vehicles because of his original vow.
This is the fifth prediction regarding Śāriputra’s preaching of the Dharma, in which there are both the three vehicles and the one vehicle.

Following the present case of Śākyamuni, it is said that he likewise employs the three vehicles and so forth. However, because Śākyamuni appeared in the five turbidities, he taught the three vehicles.
Since Śāriputra’s pure land requires no further bestowal of the three vehicles, the passage of the sutra beginning with "Śāriputra" below explains the intent behind the bestowal of the three.
That land is pure and speaks only of the One Vehicle; yet, to fulfill his vow, he spoke of the three—this is both their bestowal and their abolition. Question:
At what time did Śāriputra originally vow to speak of the three vehicles? Answer: According to the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-śūnyatā-sūtra*, it was during sixty kalpas.
While practicing the bodhisattva path, he was asked for his eyes by a brahmin. He gave them to him, and as the man stepped on them with his feet, he consequently regressed from the Great Vehicle.
His resolve was that sentient beings are difficult to transform; he vowed, "When I attain buddhahood, I shall preach the Three Vehicles. Question:

Since he has already received the prediction (vyākaraṇa), why does he still pass through several more kalpas? Answer: When a bodhisattva is predicted, it is generally stated only that they have attained the realization of non-arising (anutpāda).

The above concerns the prediction [of enlightenment] for śrāvakas. This must be understood in terms of kalpas and lands; it requires the site where a response-buddha (nirmāṇakāya) attains realization and the presence of karmic conditions.
These śrāvakas have never previously practiced the path to the Pure Land; only after receiving their predictions do they establish karmic connections with sentient beings.

Because the capacities of these beings differ, the duration of the kalpas varies. Although the dragon girl was of the female form, because her aspiration for the vehicle was urgent, she first practiced skillful means.

If we discuss this from the perspective of provisional traces, it must be analyzed separately. Furthermore, regarding the various Śrāvakas whose times differ, these distinctions are made to accommodate the suitability of beings and to correspond to the varying capacities and conditions of individuals;
how could their initial stages of dwelling not be distinct? When worldly people see a Śrāvaka receive a prediction of enlightenment, they resent the length of the kalpas;
yet when they see a dragon girl attain Buddhahood, they suspect the time frame is too short. Or...
One might doubt that a minor transgression incurs such vast retribution; or one might think that a small good deed brings about such abundant merit.

One might criticize the Buddha’s teachings as being inconsistent or indeterminate; or one might reproach the Bodhisattvas for their irregular manifestations. One might hear of supreme practices spanning many kalpas and suspect that the teachings are mere fabrications;
or one might hear of the supernatural transformations of the various Buddhas and claim they are merely combined with worldly arts; or one might harbor doubts regarding the sixty [years].
A small kalpa (*antarakalpa*) is taken as half a day; or, being deluded, one may pass through countless kalpas in a single kṣaṇa.

Such false words are beyond the reach of calculation. This arises from the power of the seeds of false views being strong and the force of past conditioning being weak; thus they sit with folded hands guarding their prejudices, engaging in empty talk of right and wrong.
One should simply believe the teachings and look up to the principles—why must one rely on conjecture? To respond to conditions and benefit sentient beings is not something of this world.

Know this: one should understand that how could such a person realize that those in the first stage receive the prediction of the eight marks and become Buddhas throughout the ten directions through various manifestations?
Although there are various manifestations, they differ from the prediction regarding the Dharma-body.
If one does not cultivate practices for purifying the Buddha-land for the sake of sentient beings, for whom would one take up the land when attaining Buddhahood?
That eon shall be named Mahāratnavyūha. Why is it named Mahāratnavyūha?
Because in that land, bodhisattvas are regarded as the great jewels.
This is the sixth prediction concerning the number of eons for Śāriputra. That eon shall be named Adhastāt. Why is it named [Adhastāt]?
This is the explanation below.

Those bodhisattvas are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; they cannot be reached by calculation or analogy, and there is no one who can know them except through the power of a Buddha’s wisdom. When they wish to walk, precious flowers receive their feet. These bodhisattvas—

These are not those who have newly resolved their minds; they have all long planted the roots of virtue. Under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, they have purely cultivated the Brahma-conduct.
They are constantly praised by all Buddhas, always cultivate the Buddha-wisdom, and possess great supernormal powers.
They are well-versed in the gateways of all dharmas, upright and without guile, and firm in their resolve and mindfulness. Such Bodhisattvas fill [the world].
Regarding that land:
this is the seventh prediction concerning the number of Śāriputra’s followers; yet there are also people who possess the necessary conduct.
Śāriputra, the lifespan of the Buddha Puṣpārāma will be twelve intermediate kalpas, excluding the time when he was a prince and had not yet attained Buddhahood. Its...
The people of that land will have a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
This is the eighth prediction concerning the lifespan of Śāriputra. Since this refers specifically to his lifespan after attaining Buddhahood, it says "excluding the time he was a prince";
this is the lifespan of the Buddha himself, while the eight minor kalpas refer to the lifespan of the beings he transforms.
After twelve intermediate kalpas have passed, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha shall bestow upon the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. He will address the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati shall next become a Buddha, named Padmapratiṣṭhitagati, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha. Such shall be his buddha-field."
It is likewise so.
This is the ninth bestowal of prophecy concerning Śāriputra, based on the prophecy of his succession to the position of Regent (Upapadya).
"Puṣpadantapadavikrama" is the specific name for his status as a Regent. *Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One" (*Rulai*). *Arhat* is translated here as "Worthy One" (*Ying*).
"Homage. *Samyaksaṃbuddha* is translated here as "Perfectly All-Knowing. Among the ten titles [of a Buddha], the wording has been abbreviated;

for now, three titles are cited. From "Flower Radiance" (*Puṣpārāma*) up to "Buddha," these refer to the primary retribution (the physical body). The words following "that Buddha" refer to the secondary retribution (the environment).
Śāriputra, after the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha Puṣpārāma, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas,
and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.
This is the tenth prophecy. Regarding the Dharma-abiding and Semblance periods of Śāriputra:
the "thirty-two minor kalpas" of Śāriputra’s True Dharma refers to minor kalpas as the period during which sentient beings are extinguished by the three calamities of famine, disease, and weapons;

alternatively, it simply refers to a duration of time called a minor kalpa, such as when it is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was taught for sixty minor kalpas—this too is a calculation of time.
Therefore, we know that Śāriputra’s land is pure; it is not the external objects destroyed by the three calamities that constitute a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
In a future age, Śāriputra shall become a Buddha, a Honored One of Universal Wisdom, named Huaguang (Flower Light). He shall deliver immeasurable multitudes of beings.
This single line [of verse] transcends the third [section], which concerns the attainment of the fruit. "Universal Wisdom Honored One" (*Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhagavat*) is a comprehensive title;
"Universal" (*Samyak*) refers to Perfectly All-Knowing, and "Honored One" (*Bhagavat*) refers to the World-Honored One. Thus, it is an abbreviation of two [of the ten] titles. "Flower Light."
This is his specific epithet.
Having made offerings to countless Buddhas and fully perfected the bodhisattva practices, he realized the unsurpassed path through merits such as the ten powers.
This single line is a retrospective verse praising the causes mentioned in the second line above.
After immeasurable kalpas had passed, there was a kalpa named Mahāratnavyūha (Great Jewel Adornment).
This half-line [of verse] skips over the sixth kalpa mentioned above;
the world-system was named Vimala (Stainless), pure and free from defilement, with lapis lazuli for its ground and golden cords demarcating its paths.
Trees of various colors made of the seven treasures are always laden with flowers, fruits, and seeds.
These one and a half verses describe the purity of that land above.
The bodhisattvas in that country are always firm in their resolve and mindfulness; they have all fully perfected the superknowledges and the pāramitās.
"Under countless Buddhas, they have well studied the bodhisattva path.
These one and a half lines also constitute the seventh category of the number of bodhisattvas mentioned above in the *ullokya* (verses).
Such great beings as these were transformed by the Buddha Flower-Light.
These half-verses are a retrospective verse on the fifth method of preaching mentioned above. When a Buddha transforms others, he must necessarily preach the provisional and the ultimate teachings.
When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced worldly glory; in his very last body, he left the household life and attained the Way of Buddhahood.
The Flower-Light Buddha remained in the world for a lifespan of twelve minor kalpas, and the people of that land had a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
These two lines summarize the aforementioned lifespan.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
When the True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma shall remain for thirty-two [kalpas].
This one and a half verses summarize the duration of the Dharma’s abiding mentioned above.
The relics will be widely disseminated, and gods and humans will universally offer them worship.
This half-verse praises the *śarīra*.
All that was performed by the Buddha Padmaprabha was exactly like this. That Honored One among Two-Legged Beings is most supreme and without peer.
"That is indeed your own body; you ought to rejoice.
These one and a half lines are the Tathāgata’s concluding eulogy and bestowal of the prophecy upon Śāriputra.

"You ought to rejoice" is the explanation of his initial entry into the stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). At this first dwelling (*prathamā vihāra*), he is able to become a Buddha within a hundred buddha-worlds. His body...

If the sons [of the Buddha] were to transcend and enter the stages of practice (*bhūmi*), their merit would be twice as great. This concludes the section on the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). △ Below this is the conclusion of the verses;
this is the fifth major section of the first cycle of the Dharma-exposition, the section on the Joy of the Fourfold Assembly.
At that time, the fourfold assembly— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
as well as the great multitude of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others,
seeing Śāriputra receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before the Buddha, were filled with great joy in their hearts.
They were filled with joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
This preceding section describes the members of the assembly rejoicing and explains the names of the fourfold assembly, as was done in the general introduction (*nidāna*).
Each person removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it to the Buddha; this included Śakra Devendra, Brahmā, and other celestial kings.
Together with countless sons of heaven, they also made offerings to the Buddha with celestial fine garments, celestial *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and so forth.
The celestial garments they scattered remained suspended in the air, revolving of their own accord.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of celestial music played simultaneously in the sky, as a rain of various heavenly flowers fell.
The preceding section describes the presentation of offerings; it addresses the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, as well as the two groups of renunciants.

Regarding the "upper robe," this refers to the *saṃghāṭī*. If one discusses the three robes (*tricīvara*), none of them may be discarded, for in the Western lands (India), most practitioners possess only these three robes.
For example, in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, after three hundred bhikṣus heard the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they all...
The *saṃghāṭī* robe was used for making offerings. In the treatises, it is sometimes said that this is because one abandons personal marks (*nimitta*) for the sake of the Dharma;

or else, one may attain [realization] on that very day. If explained comprehensively, because it also includes the laity, when the words themselves turn back upon themselves, it signifies that Śāriputra has received his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) turns spontaneously; thus, cause and effect, the environment and its inhabitants, self and other—all are transformed.
For this reason, he spoke these words: "In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; now he has again turned the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma."

This section records the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings expressing their realization. It begins with the first turning of the wheel of Dharma, acknowledging the opening of the provisional at the Deer Park;
however, it merely summarizes the two intermediate flavors. From "From this day forth" downward, it correctly acknowledges the revelation of the ultimate truth today.

As for the phrase "the greatest wheel of Dharma," it refers most specifically to this present sutra, which transcends the eight [vehicles], is the supreme revelation of the provisional, and is the perfect [teaching].

It is called "supreme. "Great" refers to the four principles of humanity and so forth; or the ten categories such as the wondrousness of the object and so forth; or the three categories of mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.
Now that this sutra has opened [the teaching], it is the wheel of the single, pure, and perfect vehicle of the wondrous Dharma; thus it is named the "Wondrous Wheel of Dharma."
