At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Truths, analyzing and explaining all phenomena—the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates."
This single line of verse summarizes the preceding section on the opening of the provisional. "The five groups" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth.
Now, he again turns the most wondrous, supreme, and great wheel of Dharma. This Dharma is exceedingly profound and subtle; few are able to believe in it.
This single verse summarizes and reveals the reality above:
"Since time immemorial, we have frequently heard the World-Honored One preach; yet never before have we heard such a profound, subtle, and supreme Dharma."
This single verse is the fourfold assembly’s own account of their attainment of understanding:
"When the World-Honored One preached this Dharma, we all rejoiced; the one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, has now received the Honored One’s prediction."
We, too, are just like this; we shall certainly attain Buddhahood. Among all worlds, we shall be most honored and unsurpassed.
The Buddha-way is inconceivable; he teaches through skillful means according to what is appropriate.
These two and a half lines clarify rejoicing and so forth.
The phrase "we also act in this way" refers to Śāriputra’s realization, his being affirmed by the Buddha, and his receiving of the prediction [of enlightenment].
"Whatever meritorious deeds I have performed, whether in this life or in past lives, and whatever merit I have seen in the Buddha—may it all be dedicated toward the path of Buddhahood.
This single line clarifies dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). It is said that this clarifies dedication; above, sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) was clarified.

Among the five repentances (*pañca-pratikramaṇa*), there are only these two. Because of this, the assembly has already received their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*); they have no transgressions to repent, and they have already attained their respective portions.

Commentary: Therefore, there is no exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*). Since [the practitioner] has already reached the destination, the vow (*praṇidhāna*) is omitted; thus, the other three types of repentance (*kaukṛtya*) are absent. The Sūtra clarifies only these two.
If one considers the ultimate fruit (*paramārtha-phala*), however, with the exception of repentance, the remaining four are not non-existent. Question:
Even the great śrāvakas such as Kāśyapa and Subhūti have not yet attained liberation.

Who are these members of the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings that have attained awakening before Kāśyapa and the others? Answer: The fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings also possess three grades [of capacity].

Those of superior capacity attained understanding just as Śāriputra did; this refers to those of such caliber. As for those of middling capacity, it should be understood that they attained enlightenment following the latter two weeks.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa and the others were all practicing expedient means (*upāya*) to guide those of middling and inferior capacities who had not yet attained awakening.
This is why Kāśyapa, Pūrṇa, and the rest appeared to be as if they did not understand; it was not [that they truly lacked understanding].
This refers to Kāśyapa and others who were not yet equal to the fourfold assembly; it was to demonstrate the provisional practice, as previously explained in the section concerning Śāriputra.
From the prose of the four leaders at that time until the end of the verses, this is the "Dharma-exposition. The fifth section, "The Joyful One," concludes here.
The sutra begins from the "Expedient Means" chapter with the passage: "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: 'You have already earnestly [requested this] three times...'"
Please grant your assent; this concludes [the previous section]. Within the main body of the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon), this is the first part:
the five sections of sutra text for the teaching by Dharma for those of superior capacity are now finished.

△ From the passage beginning with "At that time" onwards, this is the second part within the extensive exposition of the main body of the "Trace Gate": the formal teaching through parables for those of medium capacity. According to the sutra...
The title of the "Parable Chapter" (Puyi pin) should properly be placed before the words "At that time" within this section, as it constitutes the formal exposition through parables.
However, the translators, in arranging the fascicle, have placed this chapter title at the beginning of the four sections of the "Dharma Exposition.

This is the second [section], which provides the formal parabolic exposition for those of middling capacity to reveal the provisional and manifest the ultimate. This section further consists of four chapters; this is the first.

These chapters precisely employ parables to reveal the One Vehicle by opening up the Three Vehicles. The chapter on "Resolute Belief" (*Adhimukti*) uses a parable to illustrate the four great beings' realization;
the chapter on "Herbs" (*Oṣadhi*) uses a parable to provide a detailed exposition; and the chapter on "Bestowal of Prophecy" (*Vyākaraṇa*) clarifies the granting of predictions.

These four chapters all belong to the middle period of the teaching and are all explained through parables. Now, regarding the text of this primary parable, there are two parts: first, the request; second, the response.
The request consists of three sections.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret;
I have personally received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha."
The preceding section is Śāriputra’s formal request, in which he describes his own state of being free from doubt.
These twelve hundred who have attained mastery over their minds formerly dwelt on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*). The Buddha constantly taught and transformed them, saying:

"My Dharma can bring one away from birth, old age, sickness, and death, leading to ultimate *nirvāṇa*. These individuals, both those still in training and those beyond it (*śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa*), likewise each considered themselves to have [attained liberation].

"I held views such as the view of self and the views of existence and non-existence, thinking that I had attained nirvana. Yet now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, I have heard what I have never heard before, and I have fallen into doubt and confusion."
This is the second instance where Śāriputra expresses his agreement with the carriage-bearer regarding their shared delusion. As companions, they share the same practice and harbor old attachments;
therefore, it was necessary for him to make this request. Under the Buddha’s constant teaching, he had previously adhered to the doctrine of the three vehicles (*triyāna*);

now, descending before the World-Honored One, he adheres to the principle of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*). Previously, he held that the three were the ultimate; now, he further maintains that the one is the ultimate.
[The two views] are true [in their respective contexts], yet they contradict and oppose one another; therefore, it is said that all fall into doubt and confusion. Question:

If even ordinary beings can attain awakening upon hearing [the teaching] once, and if the dragons and spirits were already able to cite examples and achieve understanding after hearing the five Buddhas briefly and extensively reveal the provisional [teachings], as well as hearing Śāriputra receive his prediction upon summarizing [the meaning], why do those of middling and lower capacities who practice according to reality remain suddenly so deluded? Answer: There are two reasons for this.

Regarding the meaning: first is long-standing attachment, and second is entering the stage. If one realizes the fruit through understanding, one immediately breaks former attachments; once attachment is broken, one enters and dwells [in the realization].
However, ordinary beings do not necessarily enter and dwell [in this state], as they lack such attachment. Alternatively, it may be easily understood.

For Śrāvakas, although they have heard [the teaching] but not yet realized it due to these two meanings, there are inherent differences in their faculties and dispositions within the long duration of their attachments.

Therefore, they are divided into three grades. Regarding the phrase "hearing what has not been heard before" and so forth: he heard four sections from Śāriputra that were not present in the former teachings.

By comparing these with the categories of the five Buddhas—specifically the passage "I am not the Buddha’s knowledge and vision"—and verifying his previous attainments, he knew they lacked true reality.
Whether ancient or modern, true or false, their similarities and differences cannot be distinguished; hence it is said that there is doubt.
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret."
This is the third instance where Śāriputra universally requests [the teaching] on behalf of the fourfold assembly.

Since Śāriputra has entered the [bodhisattva] stages, he must now further cultivate the practice of the Pure Land; this is the foundation of bodhisattva conduct. As the fourfold assembly constitutes the realm of those to be converted, he thus makes the request universally on their behalf.
Regarding the statement that he explains the causes and conditions: it refers to what was previously taught concerning the opening of the three vehicles and the subsequent...
This reveals the causal conditions for the one great matter. This concludes the text of Śāriputra’s request.

△ Below follows the Tathāgata’s response, which consists of three sections: first, the introduction; second, the parable; third, the exhortation. The initial introduction is further divided into two parts:
first, the suppression; second, the inducement.

At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "Did I not previously say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, through various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, teach the Dharma by skillful means, all for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
All that has been said above was for the purpose of transforming the bodhisattvas;
this constitutes the Tathāgata’s initial suppression in response to the inquiry. Here, he suppresses them to incite their indignation and vigor, so that later he may lead them forward with speed.
When [the text] says, "Did I not previously state below...," it refers back to what was not mentioned above, asking: "Is this not the provisional means? This is a reprimand and suppression.
These are my words. "All are for the sake of Bodhi" refers to the aforementioned manifestation of reality to reprove them.
"All are for the transformation of Bodhisattvas" means that whether through provisional or real [teachings], they cause all sentient beings to enter the Buddha-way and the Nirvana of Non-abiding.
I have already explained this clearly to you; why do you still cling to former teachings, remaining in delusion and darkness without understanding? The Buddha is like...
This objection is intended to suppress the text.
However, Śāriputra, I shall now further clarify this meaning through a parable, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding by means of parables.

The preceding section constitutes the introduction and consolation. Since the previous censure was so earnest, there was concern that those of middling or inferior capacity among the intended audience might become despondent and sink into self-deprecation.
Now, by permitting the use of parables, this meaning is further clarified; if one can understand them, they may still be called wise people.
This concludes the section on the "Initiation. Below this follows the actual exposition of the parables, consisting of both prose and verse.

The verse. The prose commentary further consists of two parts: first, the presentation of the analogy; second, the application of the analogy. Within the presentation, there are again two parts: first, the general; second, the specific.
Within the initial general section, there are six points.

"Śāriputra, whether it be a kingdom, a city, a village, or even down to this very house—this is the general metaphor. In the preceding verse, the provisional was briefly revealed to manifest the ultimate."

There are six analogies, all of which are called collective analogies. From the passage beginning with "Suppose there were a country" down to "servants," this constitutes the first analogy, that of the elder.
Within this analogy of the elder, there are again three aspects: first, his conduct; second, his title and status; and third, the praise of his virtues.
The first is called "conduct" (*caryā*). In the verse explaining the aforementioned Dharma, it says: "Now I am also like this. This "I" refers to me, Śākyamuni, the Lord of Transformation.
Regarding the phrase "in a kingdom, city, or village," this cites locations to manifest the name and conduct of the elder;

it applies universally to these three places. Now, the name corresponds to reality, while conduct is like the master. Conduct resides within one's own self, whereas the name is transmitted from others. Conduct possesses...

Regarding intimacy and remoteness: in terms of names, there is distance and proximity; in terms of actual practice, one is intimate; in terms of expedient practice, one is remote. When practice is intimate, the name is distant, pervading the three lands;
when practice is remote, the name is near, existing only in the Land of Common Dwelling. Within the lands of Expedient Means and True Reward, they alternate between being distant and near.
Although there are distinctions between the intimate and the distant, they mutually manifest one another; thus, name and conduct are commensurate, and others transmit them without error.

Therefore, when conduct is lofty, fame spreads far; when fame is profound, it must be rooted in intimate conduct. For this reason, he uses his dwelling place to represent him, verifying that name and conduct do not overlap.
Taking the boundaries of a realm as a kingdom is the most remote analogy, used here to liken the Tathāgata’s fruition-virtue abiding in the Land of Real Reward as his "kingdom. The Ruler...
The "governed district" (*yi*) is like the Buddha’s remaining lands (*avaśiṣṭa-kṣetra*). Within these districts, the "village" (*zhùluò*) refers to the neighboring hamlets;

being the most proximate, it is like the Buddha’s dwelling in the co-resident land (*sahabhū-kṣetra*), which serves as the village. The "elder" (*gṛhapati*) is named because his conduct pervades these three places.

Those nearby could not perceive his minor flaws, while those from afar could only admire his lofty character. His speech was free of words that should have been avoided; his conduct was free of actions that should have been avoided;

and his mind was free of thoughts that should have been avoided. His reputation and his practice were in perfect accord. A truly great man, he internally conformed to the three karmas of the Tathāgata.
He acts in accordance with wisdom, bestowing transformations according to the capacities of beings; his fame is heard everywhere, and his virtue pervades the Dharma-realm.

Once the ultimate fruit is realized, he necessarily manifests throughout the three lands. Now, following the function of these lands, we can only discuss them in terms of vertical progression, where their breadth and narrowness are unequal, in order to reveal that he dwells universally.

This is because the manifestation depends upon the reality, thereby clarifying the true state. As for "descending from the fundamental to manifest traces," prior to this day, he descended from the state of quiescence.

The essence is the fundamental realm of radiant light (*jìguāng*). It manifests traces in the three lands; yet, at the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, these traces of the three lands are subsumed and returned to the fundamental realm of radiant light.

Practice accords with the principle that is the essence, while names reach only the traces. This principle pervades the three lands, and thus the sphere of transformation necessarily encompasses them all.
Ultimately, there is no case where the practice is inferior while the name is extensive; thus, essence and function correspond perfectly, without distinction between guest and host.
Radiant and overflowing, its traces pervade the three lands. This concludes the explanation of the name "Practice" (Xing).
"There was a great elder (*mahā-śreṣṭhin*). This properly designates the title and rank of an elder.

By using the worldly elder as a metaphor for the supramundane elder, it is shown that a worldly elder must possess ten virtues to be truly called an elder; the supramundane elder is likewise so. First, noble lineage. Second...
1. High station; 2. Great wealth; 3. Majestic power; 4. Profound wisdom; 5. Advanced age; 6. Pure conduct; 7. Perfect etiquette; 8.
Praised by those above; 9. Revered by those below. Now, each of these shall be explained by correlating the worldly elder with the supramundane elder.
First, regarding those of noble lineage in the world: they are the descendants of the Three August Ones and the Five Emperors, [wearing] fox-fur on the left and...

Regarding the insertion [of the lineage] into the family: as for distinguishing those of noble birth who have transcended the world, the Buddha was born from the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) throughout the three periods of time.
As the Sūtra says, "In kingdoms, cities, and villages," being praised in these three places as great—is this not indeed noble birth?

Regarding those of high rank in the two worlds, there are the assisting ministers, prime ministers, the "salt-and-vinegar" statesmen, and the "Ar-heng" (the regents). By analogy with the world-transcending, their merit is likewise [supreme].
He attained the Way and donned [the robes]. His ten titles are infinite. As the Sūtra says, "Householder"—is this not a high station?

Regarding the wealthy of the three worlds, they possess copper hills and golden valleys, abundant and extravagant; as for the wealth of the supramundane, it is that all ten thousand virtues are fully possessed.
As the Sūtra says, "His riches are immeasurable"—is this not abundance? Fourth is the majesty and power of the world.

When the frost and dew are severe and abundant, things are accomplished without the need for strict enforcement. This is analogous to supramundane majesty: the ten powers are heroic and fierce, subduing Māra and restraining external forces.
As the Sūtra says, "Having many servants"—is this not a manifestation of majestic power? When the five mundane wisdoms are profound, one’s breast is like an armory;
when employed, they are put into action; when set aside, they are stored away. This is analogous to the supramundane single mind.
There is no wisdom he does not penetrate. As the sutra says, "He possesses many fields and houses," which refers to his strategic authority and comprehensive, magnanimous discernment;
how could this not be profound wisdom? At sixty years of age, his appearance was withered and imposing, such that all things bowed before his dignified bearing.
This is like transcending the world and attaining perfect enlightenment early on, having been so for a vast duration. When the Sūtra says "advanced in years," it refers to being elderly.
Regarding the seventh point, those whose worldly conduct is pure are like flawless white jade;

their actions accord with their words, which is analogous to the three karmas of one who has transcended the world moving in accordance with wisdom without error. When the Sūtra says "his household is vast," it refers to his virtuous conduct. Eighth, the worldly...

When the rites are fully prepared, their measured decorum and orderly sequence serve as a model for the world to gaze upon. This is analogous to the worldly manifestation of a Buddha’s majestic demeanor.
With a mind as vast as the ocean, the Sūtra says there is "but one gate," which refers precisely to the single path of ritual propriety used to instruct humanity.
Regarding the "one who is praised as supreme in the nine worldly realms," this refers to one who is revered by a single celestial son (devaputra).

By analogy, in the supramundane realm, this refers to one who is collectively extolled by the Perfectly Awakened Ones (samyaksaṃbuddhas) of the ten directions. This quality is omitted in the sutra, but it is now included by means of the term "Great" (Mahā-).

Because such a person is known by kings and great men, they are called "Great"; that is, they are those revered by superior persons. Regarding the "one who takes refuge at the lowest level in the ten worldly realms":
Thus, one becomes the object of refuge for the four seas, analogous to how the seven kinds of supramundane skillful means serve as a basis for reliance.
As the Sūtra says, "a great multitude of people," this refers to being the place where those of the four seas below take refuge. This world is endowed with ten virtues.
For example, one who possesses the ten virtues of a worldly elder is called an "elder.
This use of the title of a worldly elder serves as a metaphor for the name of a supramundane elder. By what means is such a supramundane elder accomplished?

There is nothing that does not require the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) before the fruit of spiritual virtue can be realized. Now, one must contemplate this within the mind of the practitioner before their very eyes.
The Ten Virtues. One cultivates the ten vehicles without departing from the perceptions of ordinary beings, thereby attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.

Now, regarding the ten virtues within a single mind: first, the mind capable of contemplation that causes forgetfulness of discursive thought emerges from the true reality (dharmatā) and is born into the family of the Buddha’s inconceivable realm;
this is the nobility of the mind’s lineage. Second, within a single thought-moment, one conditions...

One makes a vow based on principle that the three delusions shall not arise. Although true reality has not yet been realized, this is called "donning the robe of the Tathāgata" and "proclaiming the patience of quiescence";
thus, the stage of contemplating the mind is high. Within a single moment of thought, the three truths contain and preserve all merits.
Skillfully establishing what is called "conformity with principle" is the great wealth of this mind.

Fourth, the virtue of right contemplation within a single thought-moment subdues craving and views, eliminates delusions regarding the three truths, and attains the name of "pervasive penetration"; this is the majesty and ferocity of this mind.

Fifth, within a single thought-moment, the Middle Way illuminates both aspects simultaneously; provisional and ultimate truths are revealed together, such that nothing is obstructed or unpenetrated; this is the profound wisdom of this mind. Sixth, a single thought-moment...

Within the mind, having long accumulated roots of goodness, one is able to cultivate this contemplation of the unconditioned factors of the path (*asaṃskṛta-mārga-aṅga*). Having transcended the seven stages of expedient means, this is the "maturity of the mind.
Seventh, within the contemplation of a single thought-moment, being able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called "supreme concentration" (*adhi-samādhi*);

it causes the three karmas to be without transgression against principle, which is the purity of the mental activity of contemplation. Eighth, the stage of relying on the truth within a single thought-moment passes through...
Facing the objects of perception, one’s deportment remains without fault; this is the perfection of mental reverence. Ninth, in a single thought-moment, one gives rise to deep faith;
being able to contemplate in this way with unwavering patience, all Buddhas rejoice and praise those who uphold the Dharma; this is the reverence of the mind.
Tenth, within a single thought-moment, one does not give rise to attachment to dharmas; this causes even inferior offerings to be received from devas, nāgas, and the four classes of beings.
[The practitioner] reverently makes offerings; this is the mind’s humble taking refuge. As the subsequent text states:

"When a Son of the Buddha dwells in this stage, it is the very enjoyment of the Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. Since such a person is called a "Buddha," this is termed the ten virtues of the Elder who Contemplates the Mind.
Thus, one should know that the ten virtues on the level of fruition are all inherently present within the causal mind. [This concludes the] topical commentary on the sutra.
The Dharma’s principles and phrasing are in perfect accord. The preceding discourse on the Dharma states: "I am now also like this. Here, the elder serves as the analogy;
the Buddha’s virtues are manifest and clear.
He is advanced in years, yet his wealth is immeasurable, and he possesses many fields, houses, and various servants.
This third section, clarifying the parable of the elder, praises the elder’s virtuous achievements. Virtue is twofold: internal and external. Internal virtue consists of wisdom and strategic insight;
external virtue consists of wealth and resources. His advanced age and broad erudition regarding both the ancient and the modern serve as a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue.
The phrase "advanced in years with faculties and resolve fully matured" is analogous to the Buddha’s virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).

This single phrase regarding his advanced age is analogous to the Buddha possessing the two internal virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment within. From "immeasurable wealth" down to "servants," these are analogous to the Buddha’s external virtues, which include both general and specific categories.
The phrase "immeasurable wealth" generally illustrates that the Tathāgata possesses ten thousand external virtues. [It is] manifold.

Regarding those who possess fields and houses: the field is likened to the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom; it can sustain life, just as meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) uses the field of merit to nourish the life of *prajñā*.
The house is where one may dwell; it is likened to the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), which is the domain where Buddha-wisdom reaches its consummation.

By means of the field of meditative concentration, one dwells in the house of ultimate reality, thereby nourishing and sustaining the body and life of *prajñā*. Thus it is said, "much... [referring to the abundance of these supports].
As for "possessing": because there is no practice that the Buddha’s merit does not cultivate, his fields are numerous. If one discusses his wisdom, there is no object it does not illuminate;
thus his dwellings are exceedingly many. Therefore, it is said that he possesses many fields and dwellings.

As for the gates, they are of various kinds: briefly, there are the eighteen gates of emptiness; extensively, there are immeasurable gates of emptiness. Each dwelling has its own gate, and each gate...
They are still many; how much more so for one whose family is wealthy and whose residence is vast? Since a single residence has many gates, it stands to reason that they would be immeasurable.
A "gate" refers to a path for exiting a residence; these gates of the residence are precisely the gates of the Great Vehicle.

As for the mention of "various servants," these refer to the attendants and messengers, which serve as metaphors for the complete perfection of skillful means, knowledge, and vision. They blend their light within the six realms of existence, conforming in every way to the myriad beings.
The "servant" (kī) is the attendant of true wisdom. From the passage "From that country to this place," up to the end of the sentence "Now I am also like this"—
which concludes the explanation of the Dharma-discourse on Śākyamuni’s manifestation of reality within the first of the six general parables, namely the parable of the elder—
the parable of the elder is finished.
"The family is vast and extensive.
This single phrase serves as a general analogy for the second of the six analogies, that of the "house.

The analogy of the house corresponds to the passage in the preceding explanation of Śākyamuni’s manifestation of the ultimate truth (śuddha-satya) concerning the phrase, "for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings. Here, "peace and security" is contrasted with "lack of peace and security."
Insecurity is like the burning house of the triple world (*triloka*). Beings crowd together, yet do not emerge from this triple world; they have long dwelt within it.
Within this burning house of the triple world, beings are deluded and, clinging to their respective inversions, are consumed by the fires of turbidity.
This burning house of the triple world is governed by the Buddha. The Tathāgata already abides in security, standing in contrast to those five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

Regarding the phenomena of instability: when the potentiality [of the teaching] and the responsive capacity [of the beings] meet, it is integrated and unified from the perspective of the meaning of responding to the various capacities of those to be transformed.
Therefore, it is called "vast."
"There is only one gate.
This single phrase is the third among the six general analogies.

The "one gate" corresponds to the previous explanation of the Dharma, wherein Śākyamuni reveals the reality by proclaiming the Buddha-way through various dharma-gates; here, in contrast to that multiplicity, it is now rendered as "one."
"Gate" (*môn*) is a metaphor. That is to say, since principle (*li*) is that which is explicated by the teaching (*jiao*), the teaching belonging to principle is taken as the "gate.
Since principle is one, the teaching should likewise be non-dual. One must clarify that the teaching belonging to principle constitutes the single gate of the present context;
this is precisely the Great Single Gate, for it is "great" because it stands in contrast to the manifold. Furthermore, a "gate" refers to the gate of a house or the gate of a carriage.
There are two distinctions: the house is the cycle of birth and death within the triple world (*tridhātu*), while the gate is the path of essential departure.
It is the definitive expression of the provisional teachings; hence it is called the "gate of the house. The three vehicles are the Mahāyāna Dharma.

The "gate" (mon) is the exposition of the Perfect Teaching (enkyō). Thus, one should know that the gate of the house is the path by which one exits the burning house, while the gate of the vehicle is the path by which one enters the true aspect (jissō).
One must understand that these two gates, when contrasted according to their temporal sequence—past and present—are as follows.
In that case, the vehicle and the house would be eternally distinct. If one follows the explanation of "opening," then the two gates are not different;

since the house and the vehicle are one, how could the two gates be distinct? Therefore, the three vehicles possess both meanings: having relied upon the teaching to exit the house, they do not perceive small carts.
In the interim, all flavors have been tempered and matured. Now, he requests from his father the chariot previously promised; once requested, it must be granted.

Opening that small gate is nothing other than the Great Teaching. The minor principles beneath the gate ultimately possess no separate path. Principles are absolute and non-dual; the coarse and the subtle are one in essence.
Dharmas abide in their own stations, and the characteristics of the world are eternal. If even the three realms are thus, how much more so [the nature of reality]?
There is a distinction between them. If there were no prior difference, what would there be to discuss as being the same? Those who have sunk into suffering now all gather together;
this is precisely the single gate of the Great Vehicle. Therefore, it is said that "there is only one gate."
"Many people—hundreds, two hundred, even up to five hundred—dwell therein. This is the fourth analogy within the general parable, the analogy of the five hundred people.

It represents the sentient beings mentioned above; that is, it serves as a general illustration for the locus where those with the capacity to be converted are gathered from across the five realms of existence.
"The halls and pavilions are dilapidated; the walls have collapsed; the bases of the pillars are rotted; the beams and rafters are tilted and precarious.
This is a general metaphor for the fifth stage—where fire breaks out—within the six stages, representing the house that is being burned, which corresponds to the retributions of the six realms.

It serves as a metaphor for the "insecure" dharmas in contrast to the aforementioned "peaceful and secure" state, namely the dharmas of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). The hall represents the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

The "realm" (*dhātu*) refers here to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*). The "walls" are a metaphor for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). These walls should be understood as pervading all three realms;

there is nothing that does not constitute a reduction [of their presence]. Although the formless realm lacks the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced by the four great elements, that which is brought about by the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*) constitutes the walls.

All three realms are maintained by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). If one considers the various schools of thought, it is not the case that the formless realm is entirely devoid [of materiality].

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute form; this accords well with the purport of the sūtras. "Falling away" is a metaphor for diminution; "tipping and peril" is a metaphor for transformation. The pillar-base is a metaphor for life-force (*jīvitendriya*);

the ridgepole and beams are metaphors for mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). "Decay and rot" is a metaphor for being precarious and not lasting long. This is explained in reference to the three realms (*tridhātu*).

This general explanation covers both oneself and others, clarifying the characteristics of the burning house through concrete phenomena. To facilitate understanding, it is explained by means of a visualization:
the hall represents the lower part of the body; the upper stories represent the head and other upper parts; the walls and plaster represent the skin and flesh;
their crumbling represents senility; the bases of the pillars represent the two feet; their rotting represents impermanence; and the beams and rafters represent the backbone.

The tilting and precarious state is likened to the great end (death). Examining the subsequent verses below, it says that the surrounding obstructions and winding curves are likened to the large and small bellies;
they are also likened to the six sense organs, the six consciousnesses, the six sense objects, and so forth, which constitute the mind.
Simultaneously on all sides, flames suddenly burst forth, burning down the houses and dwellings.
This is the fifth fire within the general analogy—the fire capable of burning—which is the fire of the eight sufferings.
Because it pervades the four great elements and the four modes of birth, it is said to be "on all sides. Because all things are impermanent, it is said to be "simultaneous."
At that moment, it suddenly appears as if what was originally non-existent now exists. Originally there was no such suffering; it exists because of ignorance.
Following the principle of the Mahāyāna, [the nature of reality] is pure and originally non-existent, yet it exists now due to delusion; hence, it is said to appear "suddenly.
This meaning must be understood as the sense that saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa, and nirvāṇa is itself saṃsāra.
"The sons of the elder, whether ten, twenty, or even up to thirty, are within this house.
This is the sixth analogy among the general analogies—the analogy of the thirty sons—which illustrates the aforementioned knowledge of the dispositions and inclinations (*śayana*) of sentient beings.

While it simply says "sentient beings," the term encompasses all five realms of existence. If one takes this as referring specifically to the knowledge of the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings, it then points specifically to the three [realms].

Regarding the "Vehicle" (*yāna*): the previous mention of "five hundred" refers generally to those who possess the potential for birth [in the Buddha-way]. These five hundred all possess the *dharmadhātu-nature* (*zhengyin*).

As they were members of the elder’s household, they now represent ten, twenty, or more individuals who are distinguished by their *pratyaya* (auxiliary cause) and *pariniṣpanna-yāna* (ultimate cause).

Because they had previously practiced the Buddha-dharma, there is a natural affinity between them; this is the meaning of being "sons. The faculties of the three vehicles differ, and their dispositions and desires are not the same.
If ten are the sons of the Bodhisattvas, twenty are the Pratyekabuddhas, and thirty are the Śrāvakas.

From ten to thirty, the intent clarifies that each of the three vehicles consists of exactly ten; the text speaks of them collectively. To say "each has ten" means they all possess the nature of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*):

namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirodha-mārga-jñāna*). [Dharma-knowledge...]

The knowledge of comparison (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*): these ten knowledges are cultivated from beginning to end by those of the Three Piṭakas and the Three Vehicles.
Therefore, the practitioners of the Three Vehicles ride upon these to depart from the house; hence they are called "ten.

As for the term "or," it is because the emergence and disappearance of Pratyekabuddhas differ: they may be subsumed under the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) or the Middle Vehicle (*madhyamayāna*), depending on whether they encounter a Buddha or do not encounter a Buddha.
Because they are identical, it is said "or. This concludes the general explanation of the six parables. △ Below this are the specific parables; there are four.
First is the parable of the elder seeing the fire. Second is the parable of abandoning the small stools and employing the carts. Third is the parable of equally bestowing the great carts.
The fourth is the analogy of non-emptiness. Within this, there are four parts: first, the person who sees; second, the fire seen; third, the fear and alarm;
and fourth, the expansion of the fire previously seen.
"The elder sees.
These first three characters, "The elder sees," appear within the analogy of the first elder;
they mark out the person who is able to see, corresponding to the passage above: "I observe them with the Buddha-eye," which refers to that very person capable of seeing.
"This is a great fire arising from all four sides.
This clarifies the second observed characteristic of the fire within the analogy of the elder at the beginning. The body, sensations, mind, and phenomena constitute the four sides of the house;
from these four sides arise the four inversions of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self, which result in the eight kinds of suffering.
The fire of inverted fruits, wherein all sufferings converge, is precisely the fire that is perceived. This is illustrated by the aforementioned teaching which states:
"Sentient beings in the six realms are impoverished and lack merit and wisdom... even seeking to abandon suffering through suffering.
These are the two lines, three phrases, and four characters [of the verse]. If one knows that the body is impure, suffering, impermanent, and so forth, this is the fire of afflictions.
When it was extinguished,
he was greatly terrified and thought to himself: "Although I have been able to escape safely from this burning door,"
This is the third instance of alarm within the parable of the elder. It corresponds to the preceding section on the Dharma-exposition.

It is the passage concerning the arising of the mind of great compassion for the sake of these sentient beings. As for "great alarm": the elder is alarmed because he contemplates his son’s regression from the great resolve for goodness;
this is precisely the Tathāgata’s small response of great compassion toward those who have regressed from the great resolve.
They arise simultaneously. Because you have already renounced the Great [Vehicle], I fear that you might give rise to grave evil;
thus, I am afraid. The Elder acts for himself, yet in reality there is no alarm or fear; it is only in order to transform others that he speaks of alarm and fear in relation to the "son.

Furthermore, "alarm" corresponds to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), as one considers their lack of happiness; "fear" corresponds to compassion (*karuṇā*), as one grieves over their suffering. Although I am capable in this regard—
Regarding "those who were burned [but] safely emerged from the gate": this explains and establishes the meaning of the compassion arising from alarm and fear mentioned above.
As for the statement "though they were equal": although the elder had already safely emerged earlier, though he was safe he was alarmed;
though he had emerged, he re-entered for the sake of his children. Only then did he realize that the Tathāgata constantly dwells in great compassion, abiding in *nirvāṇa* yet not [remaining there].
Because they have departed from the three realms, they attain liberation through peace and security; this explains the nature of their alarm and fear.

If explained in terms of the capacities of sentient beings (*jī*), although they are secure—having previously seen that their children possess great resolve and were long thought to be at ease—their security will not last because of the suffering of decline and fall;
thus it is said "although" (*sui*). If explained in terms of the response (*ying*) of the Tathāgata, by the power of his wisdom, he received the teachings of the previous Buddhas.
The sublime teaching bestowed [by the Buddha] enables one to seek out the signified meaning and perceive the Truths, such that one is not endangered by the five turbidities or the eight sufferings;
therefore, it is called "peaceful" (*an*). It cannot be shaken by the violent winds of the four inversions; therefore, it is called "stable" (*wei*).

Being solemnly detached from all burdens, it is called "attaining liberation" (*chu*). Sentient beings, however, are not like this; they are consumed by the fires [of suffering]. For this reason, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, acts solely for their sake.
They are scorched by the fire of sorrow. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "From the gate that is being burned, one may emerge in safety. Question:
Since they are being burned, why is it said that they emerge in safety? Answer: Now, a gate consists of both the bolt and the opening.

Without the bolt, there would be no way to designate it as a gate; without the opening, there would be no way to pass through. While the bolt may be reduced to ashes, the opening cannot be burned. This...
This analogy is established from the perspective of the Hīnayāna. One should know that the teaching consists of both the means of expression (*vyañjana*) and that which is expressed (*artha*).
If there were no gateway of expressive discernment, there could be no teaching; and if there were no emptiness as the principle to be expressed, how could one attain liberation?

Since the teachings of the Hīnayāna’s expressive discernment do not discuss the Middle Way or the *dharmadhātu*, they are indeed impermanent; thus, the expressive means themselves perish. This is the analogy.
If the door-bolt has been burned, it is therefore called "the door that has been burned. The principle (nīti) that is expressed is not subject to destruction;

having attained what is expressed by the lower teachings of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), one is said to have "safely emerged. If one does not emerge through the door that has been burned, of what use would "safe emergence" be?
By relying upon the verbal teaching (śāsana) and acceding to the principle it expresses, one emerges through the gateway of the Buddha’s teaching.
One emerges from the suffering of the triple world and attains the realization of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said that one "safely emerges from this gate that burns.
Thus, the two meanings of "burning" and "safety" are both established. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Because the cause is impermanent, the fruit is permanent.
Furthermore, if one follows the gates of the Lesser Vehicle's teaching on impermanence, one emerges from this gate that is being burned; however, if one follows the Mahāyāna...
In the Mahāyāna teachings, the eternal presence within written words is itself liberation. This teaching is identical to the principle;

by realizing its essence, one is set ablaze yet remains unburned, and thus attains peaceful deliverance. Furthermore, if one considers this from the perspective of the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), it is an emergence through the gate of being burned.

If one considers it from the perspective of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), one realizes the nature of that which is burned and thus attains peaceful deliverance. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "First..."
He made a chest and a desk, yet he could not bring it out; he brought it out again by means of impermanence. This is precisely the meaning [of what follows].
For this reason, the Tathāgata was struck with alarm and fear.
Yet those sons, within the burning house, were attached to their play and amusements; they were neither aware nor cognizant of it, neither startled nor terrified.
Though the fire came to press against their bodies and its pain was cutting to the bone, their minds felt no weariness or distress, and they had no intention of seeking escape.
This is from within the parable of the elder; it is the fourth section, which extensively elaborates upon the fire seen in the second section.
It also serves as a reiteration to establish the meaning of being struck with terror. The phrase "those who have entered the house" refers back to the location of the people mentioned previously.

The four characters "delighting in and attachment to play" (*lèzhù xīxì*) should be interpreted in two ways. First, they shall be explained by analyzing the individual characters. Regarding "play" (*xī*):
attachment to views is called "play," which refers to wandering pleasure. "Wandering" means pervasive delight; it is likened to attachment to the delusions of views, which pervade the three realms.

Therefore, it is termed "play. Regarding "sport" (*xì*): attachment to craving is called "sport," which is also a form of delight. Although sport is likewise a delight, its scope differs according to each particular location.
Therefore, it does not pervade all three realms, because it is distinguished from the fetters of the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) by way of analogy.

Regarding the second, the explanation of the compound term: being addicted to the four views is called "pleasure" (*hī*); to lose one's merit and reputation in vain is called "sport" (*khi*). This is the combined explanation of attachment to views as "pleasurable sport.
Furthermore, being addicted to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) is called "pleasure"; to be empty-handed and gain nothing is called "sport. Thus, one undergoes birth and death in vain.
Yet there is no weariness or detachment; it is like being treated as a plaything. This combines the explanations of "playful sport" (*hikigi*) and "attachment" (*shochi*).

Why are these two explained both separately and together? Answer: Because the meaning of the two characters for "playful sport" (*hikigi*) extends to what is termed "pleasure" (*raku*), they both apply equally to the paths of seeing (*ken-dō*) and cultivation (*shū-dō*); therefore, they must be explained in combination.
Furthermore, since "pleasure" (*raku*) differs between that which is situational and that which is pervasive, they are used as metaphors for the paths of seeing and cultivation respectively.

They are not the same. Next, the explanation is provided by analyzing the individual characters. Regarding the statement "not awakening, not knowing, not being startled, and not being terrified," this should be explained in three ways.

First, explaining "not awakening" in relation to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*): sentient beings are entirely unaware of the three realms, the five turbidities, the five aggregates, and the eight sufferings;
they do not at all speak of these as the fire that burns, nor do they recognize the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). This is called [not awakening].
"Not awakening" means that sentient beings do not realize at all that the fires of the four inversions and the three poisons are inherently capable of burning;
they do not understand that fire is a phenomenon of heat. This is what is meant by "not knowing," as in the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). "Not being startled" means...
Because sentient beings do not know that fire is hot, they do not fear injury to their bodies. Since they do not recognize delusion (*moha*), how could they feel anxiety?
Since they do not recognize the origin of suffering (*samudaya*), they do not contemplate its cessation. When delusion invades the *dharmakāya*, one loses the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*);
this is called "not being startled. As for "not being terrified": since sentient beings are neither startled nor have lost the body of the Truth of the Path, they do not fear its severance.

The wisdom of life is the truth of cessation; therefore, it is said that they do not fear. Thus, ordinary worldlings are unaware of suffering (*duḥkha*), ignorant of its origin (*samudaya*), undismayed by the path (*mārga*), and unafraid of losing cessation (*nirodha*). Therefore, the Sūtra says "unaware.

This concludes the explanation based on the ordinary worldling’s ignorance of the Four Noble Truths. Next, the explanation is given according to the stage of the minor noble ones (*śaikṣa-ārya*), because they have not heard the teaching of the Four Noble Truths.

Thus, lacking the wisdom of hearing is called "not awakening"; failing to attain the wisdom of reflection is called "not knowing. Furthermore, failing to attain insight through seeing is called "not awakening";

failing to attain insight through reflection is called "not knowing. Because one lacks the vision of the truths, it is called "not being startled"; because one lacks reflection, it is called "not being terrified.
Regarding the third explanation of "seeing" in terms of the three periods of time: "not awakening to present suffering" [is explained as follows].
Due to past accumulation, they do not know that present suffering arises from present accumulation.

Since they are deluded regarding suffering and its origin, there is no path or cessation for them, yet they feel neither alarm nor fear. This is the explanation according to the three periods of time.

Although there are these three explanations concerning ordinary beings and others, in summary, all are deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths. Because they are deluded regarding the Truths, the eight types of suffering oppress their bodies; therefore, it is said:
It is not [a matter of] non-awakening and so forth. To say that "it presses upon the body and cuts to the core" means that the five consciousnesses press upon the body.
"Pressing" (*bi*) means proximity. Because the turbidity resides within the five consciousnesses, it is called "proximate. Because it cuts to the core, it is called "pressing upon the body.

At this time, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) simultaneously experiences the suffering of the objective realm; this is not the case during the first moment when there is no yet-discriminating. Furthermore, it refers solely to the substance of these five consciousnesses.

These are the eight sufferings of maturation (*vipāka*). How could one possibly go beyond these? As for "the mind not being weary or distressed": the "mind" refers to the sovereign mind-king (*citta-rāja*), which is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Although the body is oppressed by the eight sufferings, the mind does not feel weariness or affliction; therefore, this refers to the sovereign mind-king and its mental factors (*caitta*).

One cannot form a meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) by means of this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); it can only perform discrimination, thereby establishing the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
Because the principle of these three sensations is established, it is said to "touch one's very self. It is "urgent" because the pressure is extreme;

thus, every single suffering arises from the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) as they encounter their respective objects, and subsequently reaches the sixth [consciousness], where it is further discriminated and the causes of suffering are established. How, then, could this give rise to revulsion? Therefore—
There is no intention to seek escape. Furthermore, this section of the text expands upon the fire previously seen; it is a metaphor for the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

"Amusement" (*hī*) represents the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and "play" (*khi*) represents the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). They do not perceive, they do not know, and they feel neither alarm nor fear.
These four lines refer solely to delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths. Because of this delusion regarding the Truths, it is likened to the *sattva-kaṣāya* (the defilement of sentient beings).

Being pressed by fire so that suffering cuts into one's very person is likened to the *āyuṣkaṣāya* (the defilement of lifespan), wherein the five aggregates are flourishing. The mind’s lack of revulsion and its absence of the will to seek liberation is likened to the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of the eon).
From the point where the elder first sees [the fire] until this point constitutes the fourth of the four distinct analogies.
Thus ends the fourth analogy regarding the fire.
Śāriputra, that elder thought to himself: "My body and arms possess great strength;
I shall carry them out from the house using my lap, or perhaps using a small table."

From this point until the passage "looking only toward the father," this constitutes the second analogy within the section of distinct analogies: the analogy of abandoning the small stool to use the carriage.

This illustrates the aforementioned principle of "abandoning the great to employ the small. The preceding six lines and a half concern the "great" [vehicle], while the following three sections concern what cannot be attained through the "middle" [vehicle]. The first section concerns the suitability [of the teaching].
Second is the inanimate; third is the transformation through cessation. Now, the analogy is twofold, namely the two gates of admonition and exhortation, each possessing three meanings.
The passage above, from "This elder went out" to the end of the section, clarifies the initial suitability within the first gate of exhortation.
This corresponds to the aforementioned "recalling the use of the great transformation": "When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, during the thirty-seven days..."
Regarding the passage beginning with "Contemplating such matters as these," the phrase "body, hands, and so forth" is explained by the Buddha himself in the subsequent analogy:

"It is solely through the power of spiritual penetrations (*ṛddhi*) and the power of wisdom (*prajñā*. Thus, the body represents the bearing of burdens through spiritual penetrations, while the hands represent the uprooting [of afflictions] through wisdom.

Based on the merit of cessation (*nirodha-saṃbhāra*) derived from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are spiritual penetrations; based on the merit of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*) derived from wisdom, there are spiritual penetrations.

Thus there is the teaching of the Dharma. The power of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) can accomplish the *dharmakāya*. These two virtues of wisdom and abandonment enter again through the two gates of exhortation (*anuśāsana*) and admonition (*vigarha*).
Exhortation corresponds to the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals), while admonition corresponds to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial counteraction).

These two *siddhāntas* serve as the skillful means (*upāya*) for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). When the Tathāgata first intends to use the gate of exhortation to suit the capacities of sentient beings, he...
"Practice all that is good. [The Buddha] intended to bring about the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the knowledge of all modes; however, sentient beings were unable to bear this.
Next, he wished to employ the gate of admonition as a provisional means, intending to have them "refrain from all evil" so they might realize Great Nirvana;

yet sentient beings were again unable to bear this. As there was no capacity for the teaching, his transformative activity ceased. Thus we know that the application of mindfulness in the Mahāyāna consists solely of the two *siddhāntas* of exhortation and admonition. This is the divine [power].

It is through the power of penetration, wisdom, and abandonment that one does so. Thus, the preceding passage states: "Adorned with the powers of concentration and wisdom, one delivers sentient beings by means of these.

This is precisely that meaning. The previous praise of the elder for being advanced in years is a metaphor for wisdom and abandonment; wisdom and abandonment are themselves the strength of the body and hands.
Regarding the statement, "one should use a lap-cloth or a small table," the term "lap-cloth" (*niku*) refers to the *Tripitaka*.
The Dharma Master says: This is a vessel from foreign lands used for holding flowers, offered to persons of high rank to store them in.
Some claim it refers to the lapel of a robe, but that is incorrect; how could one use the sleeves to save a fire?

As for the term *yike* (衣裓), it is also consistent with the Buddha’s own analogy below, which says: "If I were to praise the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge and vision and his fearlessness, the multitude..."

Sentient beings cannot be delivered by means of this [method alone]. The Tathāgata employs supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to activate these three [vehicles] and uses wisdom (*prajñā*) to proclaim these three.

When there is no spiritual capacity, the transformation ceases; one should know that the "robe-bag" (*cīvara-kośa*) and the "table" (*mañca*) are merely different ways of expanding upon what was briefly stated.
The robe-bag is like the knowledge and vision of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); "knowledge" refers to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and "vision" refers to...
The term "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakṣus*) is synonymous with "seeing. The two characters for "knowing" and "seeing" are concise in expression yet profound in meaning.
It is like a lap-sack (*cakṣu*), which contains much within a single part; hence it is likened to a "lap-sack. The "stool" (*ji*) is a metaphorical description of being situated in the middle.

Riding upon the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) to confront the four truths (*catvāri satyāni*), it is like a stool that is slightly wider than the Dharma and provides slight stability for objects; hence it is called a "stool."
Furthermore, the "writing board" (an) is a metaphor for the One Vehicle and the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).

To explain the Ten Powers extensively, they must encompass them both horizontally and vertically, just as a writing board with many legs cannot be overturned. Thus, it is broad regarding the Dharma and stable regarding all things.

During the twenty-one days [after his enlightenment], he contemplated that he wished to preach the Buddha-dharma both extensively and concisely; however, because sentient beings were unable to bear it, he spoke of the "robe" (*cīvara*).
[He] arranged the robes upon the small tables and desks, intending to explain the matter according to his thoughts.
He further reflected: "This house has but a single door, and it is moreover narrow and small. My children are young and have no discernment;
they are attached to their play-places."

This is from the section on exhortation. Second, it clarifies that the son does not accept the exhortation; this is analogous to the aforementioned teaching of the Dharma for those without the capacity, stating:
"The faculties of sentient beings are dull," and so forth, up to: "How can they be delivered? This is the passage concerning the lack of capacity. Furthermore, he reflects once more.

Regarding the phrase "one gate that is narrow and small," this shall be further explained through both general and specific interpretations. The specific interpretation analyzes the words according to the three meanings of "one" (eka), "gate" (mukha), and "narrow and small" (saṃkucita). "One" refers to the single path of purity. "Gate" refers to the correct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which serves as the means for universal penetration. "Narrow and small" refers to those of the various vehicles who, lacking the great capacity (*mahā-ākara*), cannot be accommodated [by the One Vehicle]. Thus, it is said: "The one gate is narrow and small. This indicates that while the One Vehicle is the supreme vehicle, it is not yet the ultimate vehicle; rather, it is the vehicle that leads to the ultimate. Because it is the vehicle that leads to the ultimate, it is called the "One Vehicle. It is not that there is no other vehicle, but because it is the vehicle that leads to the ultimate, it is designated as the "One Vehicle. Furthermore, because it is the vehicle that leads to the ultimate, it is called the "One Vehicle. It is not that there is no other vehicle, but because it is the vehicle that leads to the ultimate, it is designated as the "One Vehicle. Moreover, because it is the vehicle that leads to the ultimate, it is called the "One Vehicle. It is not that there is no other vehicle, but because it is the vehicle that leads to the ultimate, it is designated as the "One Vehicle.
