△ From here until the verse, the preceding portion corresponds to the fourth section of the distinct parables above, the passage on "being without falsehood. Above...
There are two points in total: first, preserving one’s life and body; second, not deviating from one’s original intention. Each of these two has three distinct aspects.

Here, we do not combine the point of preserving one’s life and body; rather, we combine the point of not deviating from one’s original intention, which simultaneously achieves the preservation of one’s life and body. Why is this so?
The Buddha’s original intention was to eliminate the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). Once the five turbidities are exhausted, the great goodness is naturally preserved;
therefore, it is not appropriate to preserve one's entire body and life. In the preceding section, there were three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Now, we shall merely combine the two sections of the explanation and the conclusion.

Śāriputra, it is just as that elder first used the three carts to entice his children, and only afterwards gave them great carts adorned with precious objects, which were the foremost in security; yet that elder was not guilty of falsehood.
The preceding section of the text cites the parable of the three carts used as an inducement, followed by the parable of bestowing the great carts;
this first serves as a general citation to show that the [Buddha’s] initial arousal of the teaching did not deviate from his original intention, which will be formally explained and reconciled below.

The Tathāgata is also like this. He is without falsehood. Initially, he teaches the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and only thereafter does he deliver them by means of the Great Vehicle alone.
This precisely corresponds to the Tathāgata’s initial teaching of the three vehicles as an inducement, followed by the teaching of the Mahāyāna alone;
this corresponds to the preceding explanation of how it does not contradict his original intention. It refers to what was stated above: "First, he formed this thought:
'By means of skillful expedients, I shall cause my sons to emerge [from the house].'"
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable wisdom, the powers, and the fearlessnesses;
he is the treasury of all dharmas and is able to bestow the Dharma of the Mahāyāna upon all sentient beings, yet they are simply unable to receive it in its entirety. Śāriputra, for these reasons:
One should know that it is by the power of the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas that they distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle (*eka-buddhayāna*).
This section combines with the third preceding illustration to demonstrate that [the teaching] is not false; it corresponds to what was said above:
"The elder, knowing his own wealth and resources were immeasurable, wishing to benefit his children, gave them all great chariots. This combines the permission for three with the granting of one.
This is not false. The textual composition and the minor analogies provided here differ slightly from those previously mentioned.

The former intention was to enable the sons to escape; the intent did not lie in the three [vehicles]. Therefore, it was said that one wished to benefit the sons by providing them with great chariots.
Since they were not given [the chariots] after having escaped, that too was not false. The present text clarifies that when the Tathāgata appears in the world, his original purpose is...
It is called "Great" merely because those of small wisdom delight in and are attached to the triple world; thus, by means of skillful expedients, they are enticed and led forth.

Once they have emerged [from that attachment], they are restored to the Mahāyāna, which accords with their original aspiration. Therefore, it is said that he is able to bestow upon sentient beings the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
However, not all are able to receive it. In the Avataṃsaka, those who are able to receive it are immediately granted the Great [Vehicle], without waiting for the one to be opened into three.
For those who cannot receive it, through the power of skillful means, the One Buddha Vehicle is explained by distinguishing it into three.

Third, regarding sentient beings: this was not the Buddha’s original intent; therefore, by using this explanation, it is established that [the teaching] does not contradict his fundamental mind and is not false.
From the beginning, starting with the observation of all sentient beings being subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death, up to this point, the separate four analogies from above are concluded.
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
From this point until the end of the chapter, there is a second set of verses that recapitulate the preceding prose. These verses consist of one hundred and sixty-five lines, divided into two parts:
the first one hundred lines recapitulate the preceding long prose, and the latter sixty-five lines clarify the general principles.
Regarding the method of the sutra: preceding the long prose (gadya) above, there are both the opening of the parable and its application; the verses (gāthā) likewise consist of two parts.
The first, comprising sixty-five and a half lines, versifies the opening of the parable; the second, comprising thirty-four and a half lines, versifies the application of the parable.
Furthermore, the initial sixty-five and a half lines are further divided into two: the first thirty-three verses versify the general parable, and the subsequent...
These thirty-two and a half verses provide individual analogies for the six points summarized above.
Of these six points, the current section summarizes four, while implicitly including two others; it summarizes the "house," implicitly includes "one gate," and summarizes the "five hundred people."
This also includes the thirty sons. This concludes the division of the sutra.
For example, the phrase "like an elder" clarifies the elder;
it is a verse that explains the title of the superior rank, and it simultaneously encompasses the praise of his name, conduct, and virtuous qualities.
Since he possesses the virtues of a *śreṣṭhin*, it is known that his name and conduct are universally honored throughout the kingdom and its towns;

it is also known that both his internal and external [qualities], as well as his age and virtue, are supreme. Internally, this corresponds to the *Bhagavat*, who is self-aware of his own rank and title, and is fully endowed with wisdom, abandonment, compassion, and all myriad virtues.
This single phrase is a verse summarizing the preceding analogy of the elder, which states: "If in a kingdom..."
In a certain town and village there was a great elder who was advanced in years. His wealth was immeasurable, and he possessed many fields, houses, servants, and attendants—this is the case here.
"There is a great house.
This single phrase praises the vastness of the aforementioned house and simultaneously praises the fact that it has but a single gate; the detailed explanation is as before.

That house is ancient and moreover utterly dilapidated; the halls and chambers are high and perilous, the bases of the pillars are collapsed and rotten, and the beams and rafters are leaning and slanting.

The foundations and steps were crumbling; the walls were dilapidated and cracked; the plaster had fallen away; the thatched roof was falling into disarray; the rafters and eaves were askew and detached;
the surrounding enclosures were bent and warped; and all was filled with various impurities.
These three lines extensively praise the substance of the house and clarify the characteristics of that which is being burned. As it was said above: "The hall and pavilion are decayed and old;

the walls and partitions have collapsed; the bases of the pillars are rotten; the beams and rafters are leaning and precarious. Thus, one knows that these lines constitute the passage on the substance of the house.
That the house is long-standing refers to the house of the triple world (*tridhātu*); sentient beings, from time immemorial, possess the causes for the triple world.

Because the seeds of delusion have not been extinguished, they have existed for a long time since beginningless time; because they were not created by anyone in the present, they are impermanent and ultimately base.

Thus, their names are suddenly worn out. As for "the hall and house being high and dangerous," it is also said that the head is the palace, the belly is the hall, and the back is covered like a house.

Moment after moment they continue in succession; being impermanent and subject to change and decay, they are called "perilous heights. One interpretation states: the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is the hall and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the house;
that one cannot avoid falling from these is what is meant by "perilous heights. Regarding "the base of the pillar collapsing and rotting":
the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) that supports [existence] is like a pillar, and past karma is the foundation and steps. Another interpretation states: the two feet are the base of the pillar.

That which is transmuted by the three characteristics is called "crumbling and decay. Regarding "the beams and rafters leaning": consciousness is the structural framework, serving as the beams and rafters;
being destroyed by various sufferings, it is like something leaning. It is also said that the spinal column serves as the beams and rafters.
Regarding "the foundation and steps collapsing": the hips serve as the foundation and steps; the physical exhaustion of old age is termed "collapsing. The walls and partitions are ruined.
The cracked surfaces are like parched and withered skin. The flaking plaster is like a fresh coat of mud once it was vibrant and clean.
The loss of luster and the emaciation are like that flaking plaster. The thatched covering falling in disarray is like the hair and beard of an aged man, all falling away.
The weakness of the tendons and bones, and the failure of the joints to support one another, are like rafters and eaves that have shifted and fallen apart.

It is further said: The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute the walls; the skin is like the plaster and mud coating. The four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*) being improper constitutes falling into disorder.

The five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) not being sharp and failing to govern their respective objects constitutes "mismatched detachment. As for "surrounding barriers, winding paths, and pervasive impurities":
the surrounding barriers are the six consciousnesses; the winding paths are the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Furthermore, the six consciousnesses take the six [objects] as their conditions.

The sense organs (indriya) encounter great difficulty in grasping their objects; hence they are said to be "crooked. The six sense-objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) universally defile the six sense organs; hence they are said to be "filled with impurity.
The two interpretations regarding the contemplation of the mind based on causes and conditions are as explained in the commentary. The verse on the substance of the house is thus concluded.
"There are five hundred people dwelling therein.
These two lines praise the preceding analogy of the five hundred people and also praise the passage concerning the thirty sons.

This is because those with the root-natures of the three vehicles are subsumed within the five destinies. △ This praises the fifth section above, "The Arising of Fire," which consists of twenty-nine [lines].

[The section on] Practice. The main verses describe the arising of fire, clarifying the categories of things that are burned. Initially, there are twenty-two verses clarifying matters on the ground, which serve as a metaphor for the arising of fire in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This is divided into four parts. First, seventeen and a half verses clarify the categories of things burned in the Desire Realm, serving as a metaphor for the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) of sentient beings.
Next, there are six lines clarifying the causes by which the fire arises, serving as a metaphor for the arising of the five [aggregates].

The source of turbidity is explained in the third set of six lines, which clearly illustrates the momentum of the fires arising, analogous to the actual emergence of the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*).

The fourth set of six lines clarifies the characteristics of being burned, analogous to undergoing the eight sufferings amidst the five turbidities. Below, these shall be further subdivided according to the text.
The owls, crows, vultures, eagles, ravens, magpies, pigeons, and doves—these birds, when departed, are of such appearance.
There are six lines of verse that serve as a metaphor for sentient beings with the five dull fetters (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).

The first two lines above use eight types of birds as a general metaphor for sentient beings driven by the fetter of pride (*māna-anuśaya*); "fetter" (*anuśaya*) refers to those who are driven by pride.
He is a human being. Because he exalts himself and disparages others, he is like a bird whose nature is to soar high and look down upon those below.

These eight birds are a metaphor for the eight kinds of pride (*māna*) in humans. The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* clarifies the eight types of arrogance (*mada*); here, they are applied to the eight birds.

One should know that while *mada* explains *māna*, there is a distinction between the subjective and the objective: to look down upon others is *māna*, whereas to esteem oneself is *mada*. Therefore, by means of...
"Arrogance" (*māna*) refers to pride. First, the arrogance of physical vigor is like an owl; this is an analogy for "self-arrogance" (*asmimāna*), as it implies thinking "I am strong.
Second, the arrogance of noble lineage is like a *xiāo* (an owl); this is an analogy for "great arrogance" (*abhimāna*).

As the saying goes, one who is inferior to others yet claims superiority for oneself is like an owl that still preys upon its mother—how much more so for those of noble lineage! Thus, the *xiāo* serves as the analogy.
Great pride (*abhimāna*) is like a peacock. Exaggerated pride (*atimāna*) is like a vulture;

for example, when one considers oneself equal to those who are superior, just as a poor person in this world would not even deign to be inferior to Shi Chong, let alone one who is truly wealthy. Arrogance of mastery (*aiśvaryamada*) is like a hawk.
The pride of false conceit (*mithyāmāna*) is like a cloud: among those who possess virtue, one claims for oneself that one possesses virtue.

Just as even one of meager fortune would not bow before those with virtue, how much less so one who possesses power? The pride of life (*āyuṣkāmāna*) is like a crow; it serves as a metaphor for overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

1. As for "claiming to have attained what one has not attained" and "reckoning the long-lived as permanent": it is like a youth who is unwilling to respect the elderly; how much more so when one actually possesses a long life?
2. Sixth, the pride of cleverness is like a magpie; this is a metaphor for arrogance. It is like saying of others who are one's equal, "I am their equal," yet treating them with contempt.
If one wishes to slight another even when one’s own strength is inferior, how much more so when one is truly their equal? 3. Seventh, conduct...
1. *Sukha-māna* (pride of pleasure) is like a pigeon; it is compared to *māna* (pride).

It is as when one who is superior in many respects considers oneself slightly inferior, thinking that one's virtues and deeds are worlds apart from those of the exalted, let alone being slightly inferior. 2. *Varna-māna* (pride of appearance) is like a dove; it is compared to *atimāna* (excessive pride).
It is as when one whose appearance is not equal to others also considers oneself their equal, feeling self-satisfied despite being base, and being unwilling to admit inferiority.
If this were true even for Pan An, how much more so for those of beautiful countenance? These eight names for pride originate from the sūtras and śāstras;

they are used here to correspond with eight birds. This analogy illustrates how sentient beings in the desire realm give rise to the single underlying tendency of pride, being consumed by the fire of arrogance.
The two lines of this verse—“vipers, snakes, vipers, and scorpions;
centipedes and millipedes”—are metaphors for sentient beings who give rise to the latent tendency of anger (*dveṣānuśaya*) and are thus scorched by fire. There are three types of anger:
first, anger that arises spontaneously without rational basis, like inhaling [poison] without being touched. This is likened to the intensity of a viper’s venom; thus it should be known.

The *luán* (viper) is a metaphor for anger arising from irrationality; the *luán* is the black snake. The *Hànshū* refers to it as the "dark *luán*. The second type is anger based on grasping at [false] principles;
it stings upon contact. This is used as a metaphor for the *fú* and scorpion, whose fangs are venomous and which have needles upon their noses.
The third is the anger of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), which is likened to the centipede and the millipede. Those with red necks are called centipedes;
those that are not red are called millipedes, which are the same as *jijū* (crickets). This serves as a metaphor for the latent tendency of anger (*dveṣānuśaya*) in sentient beings.
Lizards, centipedes, weasels, wildcats, mice, and various other evil insects scurry about in all directions.
Feces and urine fill the air with stench, and impurities overflow; dung beetles and other insects swarm upon them.
These two preceding verses serve as metaphors for those types of sentient beings who are scorched by the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*).
Delusion arises both independently and in association with other afflictions. The geckos and the like represent the "solitary" ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) that is mere delusion.

That which dwells in a house is called a *gṛhagodhikā* (gecko), while that which dwells in a marsh is called a *śatapadī* (centipede). The *śvāvit* is a beast resembling a rat; if the character is written as *yòu*, it resembles a monkey. Furthermore...
It resembles a wildcat and also eats mice. The *xi* (mole-rat) is a small mouse that possesses a venomous sting which afflicts humans and animals until they perish without feeling pain;
it is the "sweet-mouthed" mouse. These are all metaphors for corresponding types of delusion (*moha*). As for the various species of evil insects:
From the root of delusion (*moha*), all fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) arise in their entirety.

"Running to and fro in every direction" clarifies that these proclivities condition one another; they may condition [objects] within the three realms as if crossing over one another, and their arising is as swift as running.
The line following "the foul place of excrement and urine" clarifies that the objects to which the deluded mind clings are entirely impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
"Purity": due to ignorance, one fails to understand and falsely conceptualizes purity and so forth therein, giving rise to defiled attachment. Greed and craving do not cease;
it is like dung beetles and various insects gathering upon it. This analogy concludes the section on how delusion causes sentient beings to be scorched.
Foxes, wolves, and jackals chew, trample, and gnaw upon corpses until their bones and flesh are strewn in disarray;
consequently, packs of dogs come vying with one another to seize them, emaciated by hunger and trembling with fear as they search for food everywhere.
The two preceding verses illustrate how sentient beings who give rise to the latent tendency of greed are burned by fire.
There are two kinds of greed: first, powerful greed; second, powerless greed. Powerful greed takes [objects] through its majesty and force, such as that of foxes and wolves.
Powerless greed can only beg for coarse and inferior things from others, such as that of jackals. *Cūḍāpanthaka-sūtra*.

"Chewing and swallowing" illustrates the defiled objects of greed; it is likened to a corpse because one draws things toward oneself as if chewing them, and treats them without regard for principle as if treading upon them.
It is also said that the greedy mind seizes objects according to whether they are useful or not:
seizing what is useful is like chewing, while seizing what is useless is like treading. Furthermore, when [the objects] are few, it is like chewing; when they are many, it is like...
It means to trample upon. With a greedy mind, one seizes objects; one may seize a single city or seize an entire nation. Its boundaries are like those of gnawing teeth.
That "the flesh and bones lie in disarray" means that one accumulates the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) without knowing contentment.

Furthermore, the greed of the loving mind is to crave the flesh of the five sensory objects; the greed of the perceiving mind is to crave the bones of principles and doctrines. One seeks to understand this through investigation.
Upon seeing it, he understood much; that is to say, it was merely a heap of many bones. Thus, the dogs that require bone—those that vied with one another to seize it—are those with powerful greed.
Those that pounce upon and snatch away the weak are the powerful, the influential, the wealthy, the wicked factions, and the thieves.

As for being "hunger-stricken, emaciated, and terrified," it means they are like those who are hungry and never know contentment, and like those who are emaciated because they seek but cannot obtain [what they desire]. This is the seed.

Seeking [the truth] with such diligence is like being in a state of frantic alarm. Here in this land, the Confucian masters and the followers of Zhuangzi and Laozi likewise calculate that all things are governed by fate, spontaneity, and the vital breath (*qi*);
these are all categorized as dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*). Compared to those of the Western regions, their principles are worlds apart. As the Sūtra says: "A person of many desires..."
Though wealthy, they are poor. Furthermore, among those with various views, not having obtained the food of the True Dharma is called hunger;
being unable to subdue and sever the delusions of view is called weakness; and seeking understanding everywhere is called panic.
Moreover, this is the greedy person’s longing, hoping, and expectation; thus it is said they "seek food everywhere. This metaphor illustrates how greed acts as fire toward sentient beings.
The preceding verses concerning "the classes of things being burned" are concluded.
The two lines of verse regarding "strife and seizing, snarling and barking" serve as a metaphor for sentient beings who give rise to doubt; they waver between the two extremes.

"Name" (ming) refers to doubt; it is when one has not yet determined whether something is right or wrong. "Strife" (douzheng) means that in one's mind one considers something to be right, which is called "pulling forward" (che);
or one considers it to be wrong, which is called "pulling back" (cha). Furthermore, moving forward is called "pulling" (cha), while moving backward is called "dragging" (che).

"Snarling" (zhanxi) refers to dogs gathering their lips and baring their teeth. "Barking" (haofei) refers to letting out a loud, roaring sound. This is precisely the act of speaking words to resolve the principle of what is right and what is wrong.
This concludes the explanation of how sentient beings are scorched by the latent proclivities of doubt.

The phrase "the house is terrifying" and its description of such transformations conclude the preceding section on the five dull latent proclivities (*pañca-mṛdu-anuśaya*). △ From here until the word "shrieking" [marks the end of this section].
The "Ten Verses on Summoning the Running" clarifies the classes of sentient beings scorched by the five *kleśa-pañca-dr̥ṣṭi* (five views).
The first two lines, "Everywhere there are *chī-mèi* and *wǎng-liǎng*," first summarize the five *kleśa-pañca-dr̥ṣṭi* in general;
for these views universally take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the four truths (*catvāri-āryasatyāni*) as their objects.

Because they are subject to the lower afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said that they exist everywhere. Now, ghosts and spirits possess both supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and intelligence; these are used as analogies for the sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).
Higher animals, however, lack these. Therefore, the sharp faculties are compared to ghosts and spirits. *Chī* refers to the monsters of mountains and marshes;
thus they are called *chī*. Furthermore, they are mountain deities. Those with the form of a tiger are called *chī*. *Mèi* refers to the deity of the household; [the one with] the form of a pig is...
The head-shaped spirit is called a *mei* (魅). *Chi* and *mei* are the essences of things. *Wang* and *liang* refer to transformations and anomalies of wood and stone;
it is also said they are water deities. These collectively serve as metaphors for the five *kleśa*-drives (*pañca-dr̥ṣṭi*).
Yakṣas and malevolent ghosts devour human flesh; poisonous insects and various evil birds and beasts give birth and raise their young, each protecting them with care.
Yet the yakṣas compete to come and seize them for food. Once they have eaten their fill, their evil intentions burn even more fiercely.
The sound of quarreling and contention is truly terrifying.
These three lines of verse clarify the first [of the ten] wrong views, namely the single faculty of speculative reasoning (*tarka*). A *yakṣa* is a swift-moving ghost;

it serves as a metaphor for wrong view that repudiates cause and effect. "Human" refers to a wholesome retribution; it serves as a metaphor for supramundane cause and effect, which is unmixed with afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Affliction. To deny this principle is like eating human flesh. "Poisonous insects and their kind" refers to evil retributions;
those with wrong views who likewise deny this principle are like those who devour poisonous insects and the like.
"Hatching, nursing, and giving birth": "hatching" (*fu*) refers to incubating eggs; "nursing" (*ru*) means to rear. [This applies to] beasts.
That which is produced is called "milk. According to the principles of the world, a result of the same category arises from a cause of the same category;

that is, a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) yields a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). This is illustrated by the analogy of a son resembling his father; thus it is said that the homogeneous cause is characterized by similarity.
"Preceding births within one's own category and stage" refers to the five categories and nine stages.

"Each preserves its own store" means that because a cause has the capacity for a fruit, it is called a "store" (*garbha*); because it will certainly be attained and not lost, it is called "preservation.

Furthermore, from conception and gestation to birth, this collectively explains how both good and evil possess the functional utility of cause and effect arising from one another. Human flesh is good; venomous insects are evil. [This is] false view.
Such a person’s mind denies the existence of good and evil, cause and effect, and other such matters, like yakṣas vying with one another to snatch up food.
That they have eaten their fill signifies the fulfillment of their [evil] minds. That their malicious minds blaze intensely signifies the expansion of their views of false doctrine.
The sounds of contention signify that what was accomplished within the inner mind is manifested outwardly through verbal teachings and proclaimed.
The doctrine of neither cause nor effect causes those who hear it to disbelieve in cause and effect, thereby destroying and obstructing the Buddha-dharma and falling into the three miserable realms;
therefore, it is said to be truly terrifying. This is an analogy for those types of beings scorched by the sharp arrows of false views.
The kumbhāṇḍa spirits crouch upon earthen mounds; at times they rise one or two feet off the ground, wandering back and forth and sporting wantonly.
They seize dogs by their two hind legs, throwing them down until they cry out, and placing their own feet upon the dogs' necks, they terrify them for their own amusement.
These two lines of verse in two stanzas illustrate the single fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). The *kumbhāṇḍas* are superior among ghosts;
likewise, tainted wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) are able to overcome various insects.

"Crouching on a mound of earth" refers to how faith in the ten wholesome precepts can lead to rebirth in the six heavens, which are high places within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), resembling mounds of earth. Furthermore, it refers to the practice of precepts by non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

He practices dhyāna-concentration. Initially, he attains the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*), or he attains the "not-yet-come" concentration (*anāgāmya-samādhi*). This "not-yet-come" concentration has not yet escaped the desire realm;
the summit of the desire realm is like a mound of earth. It may be one or two feet [above] it.

He attains the concentration of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-samādhi*) as if at one foot's height, and attains the concentration of the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu-samādhi*) as if at two feet' height. Having attained the ascent to the higher realms, he proceeds; however, he may also regress.
To "fall" means to be swift [in transgression]. This gives rise to the obstruction of the view of clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is like unrestrained play and sport.
"Grasping the two hind legs of a dog": the dog is a metaphor for craving (*rāga*). One interpretation states that denying the cause of suffering is like grasping the dog's legs;

denying the fruit of suffering is like placing the feet upon its neck. The accumulation of the root [cause] that invites the fruit is like the sound of the dog. The person of wrong views denies it, saying: [...denying the cause of suffering is like grasping the dog's legs; denying the fruit of suffering is like placing the feet upon its neck. The accumulation of the root cause that invites the fruit is like the sound of the dog. The person of wrong views denies it, saying:

There is no principle of suffering that can be accumulated or attained; this causes one to lose their voice. This is an explanation based on phenomena (*vastu*), which mostly pertains to the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

As for the explanation according to meaning (*artha*): if one practices the contemplation of the six aspects (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-bhāvanā*) to subdue greed, and greed does not arise—appearing as if it has been severed—that constitutes "losing one's voice.
Sensual desire (*kāma-rāga*) is the dog; applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the two legs of the dog. Applied and sustained thought...

Coming and going, one constantly dwells within the realm of craving; counting the breaths to still the mind is the meaning of "binding," as it serves to seize the feet of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*).

As for "striking": if the awakening of craving is strong, one should direct the mind toward the object of impurity and, relying on the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), subdue the awakening of craving.
The thought of greed is subdued like a dog being struck down; exhausted, it cannot utter a sound. It is further said:

practicing the contemplation of impurity is like striking a dog, which can give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) just as the dog loses its voice when struck. Regarding "placing the foot upon the neck":

although the dog may be struck and yet remain agitated and unsubdued, one must further place a foot upon it; likewise, although greed may know that it has ceased through the contemplation of impurity, greed still persists.

If the mind is not yet very still, further contemplate impermanence with the feet while adding the preservation of permanence to the neck; then fear will arise, and thoughts of craving will not emerge.
It is also said: first restrain the mind as if throwing it to the ground, then constantly bind it to its object as if placing a foot upon the neck so that it cannot rise.
One who delights in the self despite fearing dogs does so by cultivating the realization of impermanence.

A greedy mind is like one fearing a dog; because one has attained the flavor of *dhyāna*, it is called "self-pleasure. This interpretive understanding of the meaning generally encompasses both the common view and the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox.
This analogy illustrates how sentient beings, driven by the sharp fetter of attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), are burned by fire.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose bodies are tall and large; they are naked, black, and emaciated, dwelling constantly therein, emitting great evil sounds and crying out for food.
This one and a half lines of verse illustrate the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), such as the sixty-two views and so forth.

To calculate the self by extending vertically through the three periods of time is called "long. To calculate the self by extending horizontally across the five aggregates (*skandha*) is called "great.

As in the twenty types of self-view, where each aggregate is analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), these four propositions are mutually equivalent without any superiority or inferiority; therefore, calculating the self by extending horizontally across the five aggregates is called "great."
One who calculates a self as sovereign does not cultivate wholesome dharmas and thus lacks shame and remorse; for this reason, they are said to be "naked.
Because they adorn themselves with the dharma of evil karma, they are said to be "black. Because they lack the sustenance of the merit of the true Dharma, they are said to be "emaciated.
Because one who calculates a self cannot escape the triple world, it is said that they "constantly dwell therein. This refers to calculating a self.
It is within the mind that one gives voice to proclaim the characteristic of a self; hence it is said that "a great, evil sound is uttered.

Hoping that by means of this speech one might attain the fruit of the Path, one thus "cries out seeking food. This is a metaphor for those types of beings scorched by the sharp proclivities of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose throats are like needles.

These two phrases serve as metaphors for the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). That is, one regards what is not the fruit as being the fruit; for example, regarding that which is neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, and reckoning it to be eternal.
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists solely of mind, which is called a "fine throat. Neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the third [of the four formless attainments].
The ultimate limit of the realms and lifespan is called "the peril of life," yet to reckon it as permanent is called "preserving one's longevity.
This is the meaning of reckoning what is impermanent as a fruit. This is an analogy for those sentient beings who are scorched by the secondary affliction of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, there are various ghosts with heads like those of oxen; some eat human flesh, while others devour dogs.
Their hair is disheveled and matted, and they are cruel and ferocious. Driven by hunger and thirst, they shriek and run about.

These two verses illustrate the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). To conceive of a self (*ātman*) as being like a bull’s head and to rely on that self to deduce the two extremes of permanence and annihilation is like the two horns on a bull’s head.
Just as the world regards the strength of a bull as great sovereignty, so too does one conceive of the self.
To hold that "the body is the self" or "the self is the body" is to give rise to extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) based upon the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

By mutually grasping at subject and object and so forth—such as reckoning one of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as the self and the remaining four as "mine," namely as servants, ornaments, or dwellings—one establishes sixty-five views.
Due to the fault of calculating [existence] as eternal or annihilated, these views can sever mundane and supramundane roots of goodness.
It is like eating human flesh, which can sever the roots of worldly goodness.

It is as if at times one eats dog meat, and at other times one calculates [existence] as eternal, or again calculates it as annihilated, revolving back and forth like disheveled hair. Calculating eternity destroys annihilation; calculating annihilation destroys eternity.
They mutually dispute right and wrong; the strong subdue the weak, and the weak submit to the strong—all of them destroying others.
It proceeds from oneself, like the violent injury of a wild rhinoceros. Lacking the nourishment of wisdom and meditative concentration, one is driven by hunger and thirst, rushing about in haste.
This is an analogy for those who are scorched by the sharp arrows of extreme views.
Yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil birds and beasts, driven by the urgency of hunger, gaze through the windows from all four directions.
Such perils and immeasurable terrors abound.
This one and a half verses summarize the aforementioned categories of things burned by desire within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), as well as the characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

They also serve to define the characteristics of sentient beings of dull and sharp faculties; all possess outflowing minds (*sāsrava-citta*) that constantly lack the flavor of the Path, and are thus "hungry.
Because of this hunger, birth and death proceed with extreme rapidity, which is why it is called "urgent. As for the "four directions," they refer to the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*).
Although there are many [explanations], they do not go beyond four categories. Both the sharp-witted and the dull-witted possess the sense of being "hungry and urgent.

Those who "peep through a window" illustrate those who observe the principle of emptiness with a distorted view; though they yearn for the flavor of the Way and engage in contemplation, their minds are largely mired in attachment and fail to accord with the true principle.
This is like looking at the sky through a window: one cannot perceive it as unobstructed because the view is blocked by the window frame.
To perceive emptiness as biased is a partiality; emptiness itself has neither bias nor correctness. Because one peers through a window, there is no right or wrong in principle;
it is the conceptualizer who incurs error. Thus we know that, whether mistaken or correct, who among them does not claim to look up in admiration toward the Ultimate Way?

The two lines concerning "hunger and urgency" and "looking out through the four directions at the windows" collectively conclude the two types of afflictions—the sharp and the dull. The final two lines summarize the extensive discussion to conclude the refutation.
Furthermore, this dilapidated old house belongs to a single person who has recently gone out;

not long after he left, this line of verse describes the cause of the fire breaking out in the desire realm. As for the term "dilapidated and old," it is spoken in reference to [the cycle] since birth.

Therefore, throughout the preceding and following passages concerning the nation, city, and household, according to their respective meanings and contexts, whether superior or inferior, there is nothing that does not belong to the "birth" [of the Buddha];
all return to the Elder. A single color, a single fragrance—all are likewise so. One should know that the triple world is the place where the Buddha manifests his transformations;
since the moment he first resolved to attain enlightenment, he has vowed to deliver all beings. Hence it is said that [the world] belongs to this one person.
This is indeed because while the elder was at home, he was able to ensure they were careful with fire; yet after he had departed, the sons lacked understanding, and thus the fire broke out.
Internally, this corresponds to the time when the Tathāgata, as the Greatly Penetrating Buddha, constantly instructed these beings to subdue the five turbidities.
When the karmic response of sentient beings was exhausted, the Tathāgata relinquished his manifested response. Subsequently, these beings gave rise to the five turbidities.
He departs for other lands according to conditions; it is not a permanent departure, hence it is said he "goes forth nearby.

Furthermore, it is said that from the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), one no longer arises within the triple world, and thus it is called "going forth. Because he will surely return before long, it is called "nearby.
As stated in the subsequent *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Lifespan): "He frequently manifests nirvāṇa"—this is precisely the meaning of "leaving the house."
Later, in his residence, a fire suddenly broke out; its flames blazed simultaneously from all four sides.
The rafters, beams, purlins, and pillars burst with a thunderous crack, collapsing and falling, while the walls crumbled and tumbled down.

These two lines correctly praise the force with which the fire arises in the desire realm. There are two kinds: first, the extent of its reach (*śakti-bhāga*); second, its majestic power (*anubhāva*).
The extent of its reach extends even to the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), while its majestic power burns everything without exception.
Now, the two powers within this realm are likewise so. The three realms constitute the dwelling, which is vast; the five aggregates constitute the house, which is narrow and humble. Suddenly—

However, the meaning of "arising" is as explained previously. Regarding "simultaneously on all four sides," the four sides refer to the locations where the body, sensations, mind, and dharmas give rise to the four perversions, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings;
hence it is called "simultaneous. The various sufferings continue in succession and gradually increase until they become intense, which is termed "blazing together.
The rafters, beams, purlins, and pillars are also as explained previously. The severing of the life-faculty constitutes [the collapse].
"Explosive" (*pāṭa*) means the body is disintegrated by the wind-sword. Furthermore, it is said that the sounds of wailing and moaning while undergoing suffering are called "explosive";
the destruction of the sense faculties is called "disintegration. The severing of breath, the separation of bones, and the snapping of tendons constitute "crushing, breaking, and falling";
the dissolution of the four great elements constitutes "the collapsing of walls and foundations."

The various ghosts and spirits raised their voices in a great cry; the vultures, eagles, and other birds, as well as the kumbhāṇḍas, were so overwhelmed with panic and terror that they could not escape.
This one and a half lines of verse describe the signs of the burning of the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The first two phrases pertain to the *darśana-mārga* (the path of seeing);
the next phrase pertains to the *bhāvanā-mārga* (the path of cultivation). The subsequent three phrases clarify the reason why [beings] cannot escape, which is solely due to their adherence to views;
thus, it mentions *paṇḍaka* again. Furthermore, as the first two phrases provide a general enumeration, it says "ghosts and spirits, etc.," where "etc. includes insects and beasts.
The next line lists them individually; therefore, it further mentions "kumbhāṇḍas and so forth.

In the first two lines, the latter line specifically clarifies the characteristics of being burned, hence it says "loudly crying out. In the subsequent line, the latter two lines clarify that the foolish do not know how to escape.
It is precisely because they do not emerge that they burn; because they burn, they do not emerge. Therefore, they are collectively categorized under the characteristic of burning.

As for the phrase "various hungry ghosts and the like," this follows the previous analogy of the sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*) to illustrate spirits and ghosts. A person with sharp faculties may speculate on annihilation or permanence.

If one speculates on permanence, they claim that dharmas are fixedly empty: having existed, they return to non-existence, and this non-existence is itself permanence. One who speculates on annihilation claims:

It is definitively severed; there is only this one death, and no further continuation. All proclaim that this is the settled teaching, and since the matter has already been made manifest, it is said that they "raise their voices and cry out.
If, however, they are those with dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*) or those who cling to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), they originally did not conceive of such severance.
Now, seeing impermanence, they merely give rise to doubt and fear, not knowing the means of deliverance; therefore, it is said that they are "terrified and bewildered."

They cannot escape on their own. This section begins with the owls, hawks, eagles, vultures, pigeons, and doves, and concludes here; it completes the textual analogy for the fire breaking out in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

From this point downward, until the passage where the four directions become completely filled, the verses describe the events within the cave, serving as an analogy for the fire breaking out in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the interpretation of the meaning by various schools: they maintain that hatred (*dveṣa*) pervades all three realms, which is precisely what is expressed in this text.
This passage further consists of four parts.
"Malevolent beasts and venomous insects hide in holes and burrows; piśāca demons also dwell therein.
This first line clarifies the types of beings burned within the realm of form (rūpadhātu). The first two phrases illustrate the dull afflictions (mṛdu-kleśa); the next two...
The "sharp faculty" (*tīkṣṇendriya*) is like a hole; the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are like cavities.
Although they do not reach the open expanse outside the gate, one can still escape the fierce flames;

by entering these meditative concentrations, one likewise escapes the coarse evils of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Sentient beings with sharp faculties also attain meditative concentration, just as the *piśāca* ghosts do.
They dwell therein. This is an analogy for the eighteen heavens of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), which are of the same nature as those burned by beings of sharp faculties.
Because their merit is slight—this single phrase clarifies the cause for the arising of fire in the Form Realm—due to their meager merit, they encounter suffering upon being near evil.

"Pressed by fire"—this single phrase clarifies the momentum of the fire arising in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Although the Form Realm is like the interior of a hollow space, it lacks... [text continues]

Even amidst fierce flames, there is still the torment of heat; though the fourth dhyāna lacks the coarse evils of the desire realm, it still possesses the subtle suffering of attachment to its flavor.
Therefore, it is said to be "oppressed by fire."

They were slaughtering one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh; the jackals and their ilk had all already perished, while various great and ferocious beasts vied with one another to feast upon them, as foul-smelling smoke billowed and filled the area on all four sides.
These two verses clarify the manner in which the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is consumed by fire. They illustrate how those with sharp and dull faculties contend with one another.

Although the various sentient beings in the form realm who are driven by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) attain the same meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), their conceptual reckonings differ. Because these reckonings differ, they mutually affirm and deny one another as if they were harming each other.
Since they give rise to various views within the meditative absorptions, they are unable to produce outflow-free concentration and wisdom (*anāsrava-samādhi-prajñā*).

They merely cling to silence, like drinking blood; they also cling to the five branches [of the dhyānas], like devouring meat. The jackal (śṛgāla) is a metaphor for the greed of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
since it has already been severed by the future concentration (*anāgata-samādhi*), it is said that it has already died long ago. It is also called "devouring.

The greed for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is like a great predatory beast, capable of swallowing the greed of the desire realm; therefore, the four inversions and the eight sufferings [are overcome].
It is like a fierce flame. Regarding the four inversions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this suffering is like foul-smelling smoke.

It pervades body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*dharmas*), as well as the four great elements, skin, flesh, and so forth; therefore, it is said that "the four directions are filled. This concludes the analogy for the fire breaking out in the form realm.
Centipedes, millipedes, and species of venomous snakes, scorched by fire, scramble to exit their burrows.

This first line of imagery illustrates those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) who are scorched by the arising of fire; weary of the meditative concentrations of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they emerge toward the formless realm.
Disgusted by the coarse objects of the form realm, they contemplate the phenomena of the formless realm, just as the species of venomous snakes emerge when burned by fire.

The "cave. Previously, it was called the "hidden cave," which is a metaphor for the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Now, one emerges from the cave, which is a metaphor for the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
this clarifies matters concerning the "emptiness" (*ākāśa*). When it says "in emptiness," this does not refer to physical space.

Since the interior of the house was previously used as a metaphor for the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and entering the cave for the Form Realm, the open space outside the cave is now taken as "emptiness" to serve as a metaphor for the heavens of the Formless Realm. [This concludes] the previous section on the Desire Realm.
The centipede and other such creatures are used as metaphors for hatred (*dveṣa*). Applying this analogy here, it follows that hatred pervades all three realms (*dhātu*).
The Hinayana claim that there is no malice in the higher realms does not fully accord with the truth; these [beings] are of the same category as those who are being burned.
The kumbhāṇḍa ghosts seize and eat whatever they encounter. Furthermore, various hungry ghosts have flames burning upon their heads;
tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they run about in frantic agitation and distress.

This one line and a half is an analogy for the state of being burned by the formless realm (*ārūpya*). If one attains a formless concentration, one must necessarily extinguish the lower objects of perception;
yet, one immediately gives rise to attachment toward the higher realms, which is why it is said that "one takes whatever is available as food.

Even at the very peak, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one still cannot escape the various sufferings of perversion, just as if fire were burning upon one's head. There are likewise eight stages of the non-perception dhyāna.

The fire of suffering is the characteristic of being burned. The arising of divergent thoughts in the mind is called the suffering of birth. The non-abiding of every thought-moment is called the suffering of aging.
The agitation of mental formations that obstructs meditative concentration is called the suffering of illness. The falling away from concentration is the suffering of death.

Seeking concentration and not obtaining it is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. Since one does not obtain concentration despite seeking it, there must be obstacles; this is precisely the suffering of encountering the hated.

Suffering. There are four aggregates of mind, which constitute the suffering of the five flourishing aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). At the moment of losing meditative concentration, there is the suffering of separation from what is loved.
Because these fires of the eight sufferings cannot immediately sever the seeds of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is said that "the fire burns upon one's head.
Lacking untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), one is tormented by hunger and thirst; thus, one remains within saṃsāra. Therefore, it is said that one is "perplexed and distressed."
They run about in distress;
such is that dwelling. It is utterly terrifying, filled with poisonous harms and fires, and its many calamities are not just one.
This single verse summarizes, in total, the manifold calamities of the aforementioned three realms. From the beginning of the verse until this point [is the first section].
The preceding section concludes the general analogy. Below follows the specific analogies, consisting of thirty-two and a half verses.

These verses praise the second [section] of the specific analogies. There are four distinct analogies, yet here only three are praised. The first two and a half verses praise the initial passage concerning the elder seeing the fire.
The second, comprising thirteen lines, praises the subsequent passage concerning the abandonment of the small platform and the use of the vehicles.

The analogy of the great gift and the small [gift] consists of seventeen lines in the third section. The following two and a half lines provide the verse for the analogy of bestowing the great chariots.

The first two and a half lines correspond to the vision of the fire, which has three parts: first, the capacity to see; second, that which is seen; and third, the arising of alarm and fear. These are all fully included in the verses here.
At that time, the master of the house was standing outside the gate. He heard someone say these three lines.
These verses correspond to the first of the four preceding distinct analogies, concerning the person who is able to see. Previously it was explained as "seeing," but here it says "hearing";
thus, hearing is substituted for seeing. Since hearing necessarily implies receiving it from another, the statement that he was "standing outside the gate" precisely corresponds to the verse.
"Although I am able to emerge safely from this burning gate," [the text continues: "The 'Standing One' (sthita) abides on the ground of the Dharmakāya;
constantly harboring great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he desires to save sentient beings and does not dwell upon the seat of the emptiness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Nevertheless, the emptiness of ultimate truth is wisdom (*jñāna*); logically, it ought to be of one essence with compassion. Now, it is said that he does not abide in [a state] devoid of compassion."

Wisdom. Because it constantly abides in compassion that possesses wisdom, it is said to be "established. One should know that only when non-referential compassion (anālambana-karuṇā) shares the same essence as wisdom can this be so.
As for the saying heard from some: "The Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha," this refers to the Dharma of samādhi.
This Dharma is the teacher; that is, it is others. If one enters samādhi, one can perceive the capacities [of beings].
It is samādhi that enables the Buddha to see; therefore, it is said, "hearing someone say. Question: Is the True Suchness Dharma-realm (tathatā-dharmadhātu) the teacher of the Buddha?

Question: If the Samādhi of Contemplating Capacities (guānjī sānmèi) is, in essence, the Dharma—which is merely the illumination of the conventional (sāmsārika)—how can it be called a "Teacher" (śāstṛ)?
Answer: "Contemplation" (guān) belongs to wisdom (prajñā), and wisdom is itself the Buddha. Because one gives rise to illumination based upon samādhi, one attains the status of being a Teacher.

Although it is said that one "contemplates capacities," the essence of the illumination is the Dharma; it is like the Buddha’s eye of contemplation (buddhacakṣur-guāna). It is only by possessing such an eye that one is able to contemplate capacities. This is the meaning.
It is like sending someone away. Furthermore, it is said that Great Compassion is "another" (*para*). The meaning of "other" is more intimate than the meaning of "you" (*bhavat*);

yet, in relation to the *nirmāṇakāya*, the Unconditioned Compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*) is considered "you. Therefore, the Unconditioned Compassion addresses the *nirmāṇakāya*, commanding it to arise and transform sentient beings.
This is a partial analogy; it merely serves to ensure that the Dharma remains correct.
"O you sons, previously because of playing, you entered this house; being young and ignorant, you took delight and became attached.

The preceding text states, "All are of one characteristic and one kind," which corresponds to the passage on "reaching the foremost bliss. The meaning is as explained previously.

"Immeasurable billions of powers, liberations, meditative concentrations, wisdoms, and other Buddha-dharmas"—this single line of verse praises the aforementioned reason for ascending to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). As it was previously stated:
"At that time, the Tathāgata thought: 'I possess immeasurable and boundless [qualities], up to the entire treasury of the Buddha-dharmas. This is the textual passage.
Thus it is. From you, Śāriputra, until this point, the verse on the bestowal of the great chariots in accordance with the preceding [teachings] is complete.
Having obtained such vehicles, they cause all the sons [of the Buddha] to constantly sport day and night throughout kalpas, together with the bodhisattvas.
"And the assembly of śrāvakas, riding upon this precious vehicle, proceed directly to the site of enlightenment.
These two verses praise the aforementioned joy of collectively obtaining the carriage; they clarify that each has obtained a great vehicle. Previously it was said:

"At that time, the sons each rode a great vehicle and attained what they had never experienced before—something not originally expected. Now, regarding the phrase "day and night": [it refers to their constant progress].
Having first attained the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the light of the wisdom of the Middle Way is like the sun; yet because a portion of ignorance still remains, it is like night.
Having personally attained the wisdom of the Middle Way like the sun, one enters birth and death through compassion as if it were night.

Because one constantly practices these two dharmas, it is called "sporting. Since those of the three vehicles likewise enter the Buddha-wisdom, it is said that [he is together] with all bodhisattvas and śrāvakas...

Regarding the phrase "the assembly of listeners": this clarifies both self-cultivation and the transformation of others. Because one has personally attained this vehicle, it is said that one "sports day and night";
because one uses this to transform others, it is said that one is "with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Being able to transform those of the three vehicles so they may ride together upon the precious vehicle until reaching the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is the meaning.
For these reasons, if one searches thoroughly throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle to be found except for the Buddha’s skillful means.

This single verse concludes by exhorting one to have faith. Regarding the One Vehicle that has been taught, there are no causes or conditions for a third vehicle anywhere in the lands of the ten directions.
Investigating this with truth, it is found to be one and not two; except for the Buddha’s skillful means, it simply cannot be expressed in words.
Others say that bodhisattvas do not seek a vehicle, yet why does the current text state that the bodhisattvas rejoice because they have boarded the carriage?
This concludes the third verse, from "O Śāriputra" up to this point, which completes the analogy of the equal bestowal of the great carriages. △ From here below:
The instruction to Śāriputra consists of fifteen and a half verses; these are the praise for the fourth section on "the correspondence and non-falsity.
Regarding this correspondence and non-falsity, there are two parts: first, it cites [the analogy], saying, "Śāriputra, it is like that elder";
second, following the parable, it explains the correspondence and non-falsity, beginning with the three vehicles and so forth, up to: "The Tathāgata is also just like this."

"Equal," etc., refers to the synthesis (*saṃgraha*). The current text merely recites the section on the analogy within the synthesis, followed by the section on the actual synthesis itself; it then recites the synthesis and subsequently provides an explanatory illustration (*udāharaṇa*) for it.
It does not include the preceding sections that introduce the topic and so forth. Now, the recitation of the synthesis is not in vain; the fifteen and a half lines are divided into two parts.
The first three and a half lines constitute the primary recitation of the chapter heading "the synthesis is not in vain," which is further divided into two. Next, "If... [and so on].
Below, there are twelve lines of verse concerning the Bodhisattva. These verses collectively provide an explanatory illustration based on the preceding [prose], demonstrating that it is not in vain.
One should know that the preceding section by Śāriputra provides a metaphor for how his aspirations were not in vain; for his father originally intended to enable his son to escape from hardship.
He then provided the three vehicles. Having thus escaped the peril, even though he did not give the small carts, it did not contradict his original intention;
therefore, it was not in vain. The Buddha’s verse on this parable clarifies that it was not in vain. It clarifies that the Buddha’s fundamental intent was precisely to preach the One Vehicle;

however, because [beings] were unwilling to believe and accept it due to the five turbidities, he preached the Three Vehicles. Now that the turbid obstructions have been removed, he returns to preaching [the One Vehicle].
The "One Great" is precisely the manifestation of the fundamental mind; thus, the verse is not in vain.
[The Buddha] addressed Śāriputra: "You and all these people are my children, and I am your father."

This single line is included within the verse on "not being in vain. First, the father-son relationship is established to clarify that [the Buddha] fundamentally intends to bestow the Great [Vehicle].
Therefore, it says, "All are my sons," for by principle, they should be bestowed the Great [Vehicle] equally. This corresponds to what was stated in the preceding text:
"The Tathāgata is likewise; he is without falsehood."
"For kalpas on end, you have been scorched by manifold sufferings; I have rescued you all and caused you to emerge from the triple world.

This single line of verse is included within the section "The Harmonization of Non-emptiness," wherein it clearly explains the intent of the Three Vehicles as being for the purpose of removing obstacles.

Thus it says, "For kalpas on end, you have been scorched by manifold sufferings," which corresponds to what was stated in the preceding passage: "First, the three vehicles were taught to guide sentient beings."

It is so. Although I previously said that you had attained parinirvāṇa, this was merely the exhaustion of birth and death; in reality, you have not attained extinction. What you must now accomplish is solely the wisdom of a Buddha.
These one and a half lines of verse fall within the section on "Non-emptiness. They again explain the Great [Vehicle]. The first line clarifies the removal of obstacles;
the subsequent half-line fulfills the original aspiration. Since the obstacles have been removed, the original aspiration is fulfilled by bestowing the Mahāyāna Dharma;
therefore, it says, "That which should now be practiced is solely Buddha-wisdom. This refers to what was stated in the preceding text: "Thereafter, one acts solely through the Great..."
"By means of this vehicle, they deliver and liberate them. These three sections of verse together complete the section on "Non-emptiness" (不虗).

△ From here on, starting with "If there be a bodhisattva... and so forth, the verse explains the preceding section on "Applying the Analogy" (合況) by way of exposition. It further explains the previous three points. The text is divided into three parts.
If there are bodhisattvas among this assembly who are able to listen with a single-minded focus to the true Dharma of all Buddhas— though the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
employ skillful means to transform sentient beings, they are all in fact bodhisattvas.

Regarding these two lines, they are explained in conjunction with the preceding verse on "the non-futility [of the Buddha's work]," beginning with the interpretation that all are equally his children; logically, they ought to be equal.
As for the phrase "if there be bodhisattvas," this refers to sentient beings transformed through the expedient means (*upāya*) of the three vehicles;
all are children of the Buddha from whom they formed karmic connections in the past, and all likewise possess the *tathatā* buddha-nature. Therefore, it is said that they are all bodhisattvas.

From here below, starting from the verse "If a person has little wisdom," the commentary synthesizes and explains the preceding verse regarding the inability to believe and accept [the teaching] by means of the Three Vehicles.
The seven lines below constitute five parts.
"If a person has little wisdom" and is deeply attached to craving and desire—for the sake of such individuals, the Truth of Suffering is taught, and sentient beings rejoice in their hearts.
"Never before have we attained such [realization]. The Buddha’s teaching on the Truth of Suffering is truly without deviation.
These two lines, spoken within the context of the Three Vehicles, first clarify the Truth of Suffering. The first phrase indicates the cause for the teaching of suffering.
Because of their limited wisdom, they possess only worldly knowledge and are capable of teaching only the minor [truths].

The next phrase clarifies that because the accumulation [of suffering] is weighty, the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) must be elucidated. The subsequent phrase again points to the cause of suffering, and the following phrase correctly explains the teaching of suffering.
From the line beginning with "according to the hearts' delight of sentient beings," one verse clarifies that this accords with their original habits; within this, the first two phrases clarify...

The first phrase clarifies the capacity [of the beings]. The following two phrases clarify the response [of the Buddha]. Within the context of the response, it is said that there is no difference. As the *Śālistambasūtra* (Teaching Left Behind) states:
"The Truth of Suffering is truly suffering; it cannot be made into pleasure. Regarding the statement that the Truth of Suffering is taught for those of small wisdom:

among the three vehicles, the Śrāvaka is the smallest, and furthermore, the Truth of Suffering serves as their primary gateway. When sentient beings feel joy, it is because the teaching accords with their original habitual tendencies, and thus they rejoice.

Originally weary of birth and death, they sought nirvana for themselves; now, hearing that they have emerged from hardship, it immediately accords with their past habitual tendencies, and thus they rejoice.

For the sake of those sentient beings who do not know the root of suffering, who are deeply attached to the causes of suffering, and who cannot abandon them even for a moment—[it is] for these people [that this is taught].
The expedient teaching states: "The cause of all sufferings has greed as its root.
These two lines clarify the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). The first line correctly clarifies the Truth of Origination; the next half-line reveals the remedy for the Truth of Origination;
and the final half-line correctly clarifies that the fundamental fault of the Truth of Origination is [greed].
If one extinguishes craving and has no further basis for existence, such that all suffering is utterly exhausted, this is called the Third Truth.

This single verse clarifies the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). The first two lines clarify the function of the Truth of Cessation; the subsequent two lines clarify the attainment of the name "Truth of Cessation."
For the sake of the truth of cessation, one practices the path;
this half-verse clarifies the truth of the path. Herein, it precisely clarifies the four truths with effort.
To be free from all bonds of suffering is called attaining liberation. From what does such a person attain liberation? Merely by departing from delusion.
This is called "liberation.
These one and a half lines clarify that liberation through these four dharmas is not ultimate. The first two phrases reiterate liberation;
the next two phrases pose a question; and the final two phrases explain the departure from the bonds of the realms, which merely clarifies a limited or minor liberation.
In truth, they have not yet attained all liberations. The Buddha says that such persons have not yet truly entered parinirvāṇa, because these people have not yet attained the Unsurpassed Way.
It is not my intention that they should reach parinirvāṇa; for I am the Dharma King, possessing sovereign mastery over the Dharma.
To bring peace and security to sentient beings, he appears in the world.
These three lines explain the removal of obstacles. The first one and a half lines refute [the notion of a self] by means of the unsurpassed Dharma;

the next one and a half lines reveal the Buddha’s fundamental intention. When these three verses have explained that the obstacles are eliminated and the faculties of the mind are sharpened, one returns to fulfill the original purpose.
As for the mind, regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma: the Buddha’s original intention was to bestow liberation upon all beings.

Now that you have merely severed the bonds of birth and death (pariccheda), this is not yet Great Nirvāṇa, because you have not yet attained everything. Since this ultimately does not accord with my original intent, I said, "I do not wish for you to reach extinction.
Now, however, I shall cause you to attain the Unsurpassed Way and enter Great Nirvāṇa.
This is precisely the ultimate fulfillment of the Buddha’s original intention. All liberation is the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) Truth of Cessation;
the Unsurpassed Way is the unconditioned Truth of the Path. By means of these two truths, one destroys the unconditioned [notions of] Suffering and Origination.
Previously, when the Buddha wished to preach this, these sentient beings were not yet capable of receiving it. Now that their obstacles have been removed, he preaches this once again. The Buddha—

As the Dharma King, you have already attained mastery over the provisional and the ultimate teachings. Having opened up the three vehicles to reveal the one true reality, how could there be any falsehood?
From my own time as the Honored One among the Multitude of Sages above, until this present manifestation in the world, it has been thus.
This concludes the preceding section on the combined metaphors, both general and specific.

From the verse below, "O Śāriputra, this seal of my Dharma," there are sixty-five stanzas that exhort faith and promote circulation. "Faith" refers to believing whether the Buddha has spoken [the teaching] or not;
"exhortation" refers to encouraging what may be circulated and what may not. Because these two meanings are present, it is called "exhorting faith."
The text consists of two parts: first, the presentation of the two chapters; second, the explanation of the text.
"O Śāriputra, I have taught this Dharma-seal for the sake of benefiting the world."
Regarding this first verse, "proclaiming" and "not proclaiming" refers to the fact that when the Tathāgata preached this Dharma, he did so for the sake of benefiting the world.
As for "not proclaiming," for more than forty years it was not yet the time to preach it;
furthermore, because five thousand [monks] had not yet departed, he did not preach it.
In whatever direction you travel, do not propagate this recklessly.
This half-line, which marks the chapters concerning what is accessible and what is inaccessible, must not be propagated recklessly.

To speak forcefully to the wicked would cause them to fall into suffering; to fail to speak to the virtuous would cause them to lose their happiness. If, out of great compassion, you feel pity for the wicked...

It does not grant supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). If one possesses great compassion and mindfulness of the good, then one should grant such powers. This is called the chapter on distinguishing between what may and may not be granted.

If there are those who hear this and, with sympathetic joy, receive it upon their heads, you should know that these people are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive). If there are those who believe and accept it...
Those who possess this Dharma of the sutra have already seen past Buddhas in former lives, paid them respectful homage, and also heard this Dharma.
If there are those capable of believing what you have spoken, they shall be as if seeing me, seeing you, and seeing the community of bhikṣus.
Together with all the bodhisattvas, this Lotus Sūtra is taught for those of profound wisdom. Those of shallow understanding, upon hearing it, will be bewildered and unable to comprehend it.
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are beyond the reach of its power within this sūtra. You, Śāriputra, [should know this].

Even they enter this sutra through faith; how much more so the other śrāvakas? Those other śrāvakas follow this sutra because they trust the Buddha’s words, for it is not within the scope of their own wisdom.
These eight lines explain what can and cannot be spoken, clarifying the manner in which the Tathāgata benefits the world.

Generally speaking, they concern the benefits throughout the three periods of time; specifically, they concern leading the two vehicles to enter into faith and attain the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
This is an exposition based on observing present benefits for those who have already seen past Buddhas, as one observes their past virtues.
This is spoken for the sake of exposition. "I believe you have seen me" is spoken for the sake of observing the future and performing good deeds. As the subsequent passage states:

"If one has deep faith and understanding, one sees the Buddha as always present on Vulture Peak"—this is precisely that meaning. This single practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* concludes what precedes and opens what follows.
The Tathāgata observes and knows the benefits across the three periods of time; therefore, he speaks it. It is shallow [in its initial manifestation].
If the listener lacks understanding, one does not preach for them. This explains the chapter on "The Tathāgata’s Speaking and Not Speaking.

△ From the section beginning with "Pride" below, there is a dual explanation of two thematic gates. This is divided into two parts; the first consists of thirty-six lines and a half, clarifying that if one employs the gate of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one must not preach for evil persons.
This is further divided into three sections: first, citing the enumeration of evils; second, [explaining] how they will inevitably give rise to evil.
Those who slander the cause will certainly obtain an evil retribution in the future; therefore, the Tathāgata’s great compassion dictates that this should not be preached to them.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, do not preach this sutra to those who are arrogant, indolent, or who harbor views of a self. It is for the sake of ordinary people of shallow understanding [that it is kept secret].
Do not preach this to those who are deeply attached to the five desires and cannot understand it upon hearing it;
these two types of persons first create the causes for frequent evil rebirths.
Furthermore, if a person lacks faith and slanders this sutra, they sever all seeds of the Buddha in the world. Or again, [do not preach to one] who frowns with displeasure.
Yet you harbor doubts; listen now as I describe the retribution for this person's offense.

Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, whoever slanders such a sūtra as this, or seeing those who read, recite, copy, or uphold it, treats them with contempt, hatred, or jealousy—[for them, I shall explain the consequences].
Yet they harbor resentment. Listen now further to this person’s retribution for their transgressions:
these four lines and a half clarify that one will inevitably give rise to malicious slander; due to the cause of such slander, one shall obtain the evil retribution described in the following text.

When that person’s life ends, they enter the Avīci Hell for the full duration of one kalpa; when the kalpa ends, they are reborn there once more. In this manner, they continue to transmigrate through countless kalpas.
This one line and a half clarifies that those who first receive the evil retribution of the hells,
upon emerging from hell, shall fall into the realm of animals— such as dogs or jackals— with bodies emaciated, dark-complexioned, and afflicted with scabies and leprosy.
They will be harassed by others and treated with contempt and disdain by people; they will constantly suffer from hunger and thirst until their flesh and bones are withered away.

While alive, they will endure agonizing torment, and at death, they will be struck by tiles and stones. Because they have severed the lineage of the Buddha, they undergo this retribution for their sins. Or they may be reborn as a camel.
Or they may be born among donkeys, their bodies constantly burdened with heavy loads and subjected to the lash of whips; they think only of water and grass, knowing nothing else.
Because they slandered this sutra, they incur such retribution. Some become jackals that enter villages, their bodies covered in scabies and sores.
Furthermore, being one-eyed, he was beaten and pelted by various children, undergoing all manner of suffering and pain, sometimes even meeting death.
Having died there, he further received the body of a python; its form was immense, measuring five hundred yojanas in length, deaf, dull-witted, and footless.
Crawling on their bellies with contorted limbs, they are bitten and eaten by various small insects. They suffer day and night without respite;
such is the retribution for slandering this sutra.
