These ten lines and a half of verse clarify the subsequent evil retribution of falling among the animals.
Regarding the statement "cutting off the Buddha-seed in the world," this refers precisely to destroying the two causes—the *pratyaya* (condition) and the *hetu* (cause)—of the Buddha-seed.

As for what is called the "Buddha-sead," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* takes afflictions (*kleśa*) to be the seed of the Tathāgata; this adopts the nature of objective realms (*viṣaya*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* [takes] all...

The study of Prajñā by those of various capacities takes the nature of the *parigraha-hetu* (appropriating cause) as the seed of Buddhahood. This present sutra clarifies that even minor merit leads to Buddhahood;
this takes the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause) as the seed of Buddhahood. If one does not believe that minor merit leads to Buddhahood, one severs the worldly seed of the Buddha.
One should know that this sutra universally opens the seed of Buddhahood for all six realms of existence. If one slanders this sutra, it is tantamount to [severing the lineage of the Buddhas].
"It is severed. Question: "If slandering the sutras produces sin, is it not the case that the sutra serves as the condition for that sin?

Answer: "Sin and merit arise from the mind; the sutra merely acts as a contributing condition. It is like the four great elements: when they are diminished or increased, [the resulting state] is formed accordingly. However, according to the Buddha’s original intent, [the teaching of the sutras] is solely for the purpose of generating merit.
This is the fault of the deluded, not a defect in the path."
If they obtain human birth, their faculties will be dull and dark; they will be short, ugly, hunchbacked, or lame; blind, deaf, or crooked-backed;

whatever they say, people will not believe or accept; their breath will always be foul-smelling; they will be possessed by malevolent spirits; they will be poor and lowly, and will be used as servants by others.
Afflicted by many ailments and emaciated by consumption, they have no one to rely upon; though they seek the company of others, those people pay them no heed.
Whatever they may acquire, they soon lose again. Even if they practice medicine and treat illnesses according to the prescriptions, they only increase the maladies of others or even cause death.
If one is personally afflicted by illness and no one comes to provide medical treatment, such that even when taking excellent medicine, the condition only worsens;
or if others commit acts of rebellion, plunder, robbery, or theft, and one is thus unjustly ensnared by their calamity.
These seven lines collectively clarify those of low status who receive residual retribution. Below, three successive types of residual retribution are clarified.
Such a sinner shall never behold the Buddha, the King of All Sages, teaching the Dharma and transforming beings. Such a sinner...
They will constantly be born in difficult circumstances, insane, deaf, and mentally deranged, never hearing the Dharma for as many incalculable kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
wherever they are born, they will be deaf and mute, their faculties incomplete.
These three types of conduct clarify that their remaining retribution is such that they do not encounter a Buddha;
they constantly dwell in hell as if visiting a pleasure garden, and reside in other evil realms as if in their own homes—among camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs.
This is the sphere of their activity. Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses.
These two types of conduct clarify that they will again enter the evil realms;
even if they should obtain human birth, they will be adorned with deafness, blindness, muteness, poverty, and various misfortunes, as well as dropsy and consumption.
With diseases such as scabies, leprosy, and carbuncles serving as their clothing, their bodies are constantly foul-smelling, filthy, and impure.
Deeply attached to the view of self, they increase their anger and lust blazes so fiercely that they do not distinguish between humans and beasts; this is because they slander this sutra.
Such are the offenses incurred.
These four practices clarify how one may again become a human being.
Śāriputra, were I to describe the offenses of those who slander this sutra, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon. For these reasons, [one should not do so].
Therefore, I speak with certainty: do not preach this sutra among those who lack wisdom.
These two lines conclude the preceding instruction not to preach the sutra to those who are ignorant, faithless, or evil.
The above thirty-six lines complete the section on the Gate of Great Compassion, concluding that one must not preach this sublime scripture to evil persons. △ Below, from "If... [the text continues].
There are nineteen lines concerning those of sharp faculties. When explaining the propagation of the sutra, one should employ the gate of great compassion;

virtuous persons should proclaim it for others so that they do not lose the joy of the Dharma. This is the essential method for propagating [the teaching]: to harmonize these two gates and cause them to find their proper place.
This is the authentic transmission. If one does not obtain the source, it is a false proclamation. The text consists of two parts;
the first seventeen lines contain five pairs and ten pairs of characteristics of virtuous persons, which may be proclaimed and explained.

If there are those of sharp faculties, whose wisdom is clear and lucid, who have heard much and possess strong memory, and who seek the path of the Buddha—for such persons as these, one may indeed preach this.
If they have not previously seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, have planted various roots of goodness, and possess a profound and firm resolve.
For such a person, one may then explain these three practices.
First, it clarifies that for a pair of virtuous persons from the past and present, one may then explain them: those of sharp faculties constitute the present pair;
having planted roots of goodness constitutes the past member; and possessing strong memory constitutes the present member.
"I have seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas; such was my solitary practice in the past.

If there are those who are diligent, who constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, and who do not begrudge their own bodies or lives, then you may speak to them. If there are those who are respectful..."
Without any divergent thoughts, having left behind all the foolish and ignorant, dwelling alone in the mountains and marshes—only for such a person may this be taught.
These two and a half lines clarify that it is only for the second type of superior person, the "upper-lower pair," that this may be taught.
Cultivating loving-kindness is to have compassion for those below; showing reverence is to honor those above.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if you see someone who has abandoned evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends, such a person may be taught this.
If you see a son of the Buddha who maintains pure precepts like a clear, bright pearl and seeks the Mahāyāna sūtras, [to him it may be taught].
For such a person, one may then expound these three practices.
This constitutes the third pair concerning those who are virtuous both internally and externally, for whom it is appropriate to teach:
abandoning evil and associating with the good is seeking excellence externally; upholding the precepts like a precious jewel is guarding oneself internally.
If there is a person who is free from anger, upright and gentle, who always has compassion for all beings and reveres the Buddhas—such a person may be taught this.
Furthermore, there are sons of the Buddha who, amidst the great assembly, with a pure mind, employ various causes and conditions.
One who uses parables and speaks the Dharma without impediment—only for such a person may this be taught.
These three lines and a half constitute the fourth pair: self-cultivation and transforming others.
"Being straightforward and revering the Buddha" refers to self-cultivation; "speaking the Dharma through parables" refers to transforming others.
If there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of omniscience, seeks the Dharma in all four directions, receiving it upon his head with palms joined,
and who delights solely in upholding Mahāyāna sūtras— even to the point of not accepting a single verse from any other scripture— it is only to such a person that you may speak.
Just as a person with a sincere heart seeks the relics of the Buddha, so too should they seek this sutra; having obtained it, they receive it upon the crown of their head.
Such a person no longer sets their mind on seeking other sutras, nor do they ever think of the scriptures of external paths. To such a person as this, you may then preach [this teaching].
These five verses constitute the fifth pair concerning those of virtuous character from beginning to end. They may serve as the introduction for preaching the sutra;

they mark the beginning of seeking the Dharma in the four directions and requesting instruction, and they represent the conclusion of receiving [the teaching] upon the crown of one's head and practicing it with single-minded devotion—this being the ultimate reliance.
I tell you, Śāriputra: those who seek the Buddha-way and possess these characteristics could not be fully described even at the end of an eon.
Such people as these are able to believe and understand; for them, you should preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
These two lines serve as a summary. There are many who possess wholesome faith; I have briefly cited the five pairs mentioned above to demonstrate the method for circulation.
This reveals the essential points regarding what may or may not be transmitted through the two gates of compassion and wisdom.

From the beginning of this "Dharma Seal" up to this point constitutes the third major section: the intent of the chapter on Exhorting Faith and Circulation. Beginning from "At that time... [the text continues].
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret.

From the long prose through the verses, including the general summaries, detailed explanations, and parables, this concludes the first section of the four-part parabolic exposition for those of middling faculties.
Next, this chapter shall be the second section: the four great śrāvakas hearing the parable and attaining realization.
Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Three;
Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
The *Miaofa Lianhua Jing* (The Lotus Sutra), Chapter Four:
"The Stage of Faith and Understanding," with the Commentary and Notes by the Tiantai Master Zhiyi,
and the Sub-commentary by the Shramana Daowei of Siming.

In this chapter, following the Tathāgata’s completion of the formal teaching using the analogies of the four great elements and so forth for the sake of Subhūti of medium faculties, this constitutes the second section: the understanding through analogy by the four great śrāvakas.
How do they understand? They give rise to a mind of rare wonder; this is understanding through the mind. Then, rising from their seats, this is understanding through the body. And...
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "This is an understanding through verbal expression. It should be known that the four great śrāvakas have understood through all three karmas;
therefore, this is called the 'Section on Understanding. The meaning of 'understanding' is fully detailed as previously shown in the section on Śāriputra’s understanding, from which it may be known.
This chapter is a proximate understanding of the parable of the Burning House, and a remote understanding of the discourse on the Expedient Means. Having heard the parable..."
Once [the parable] is understood, one must necessarily understand the Dharma. How could there be confusion regarding the prior Dharma after having attained awakening?

Therefore, it is necessary to comprehend both the Dharma and the parable simultaneously for full realization. This is truly because faculties vary in sharpness or dullness, afflictions vary in thickness or thinness, teachings vary between the Dharma and its parables, and awakenings vary in their sequence.
Thus, prior to the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra, the śrāvakas were like pea beans; as it is said: "Hearing the Tathāgata..."
After the teaching had been given for a long time, my body became weary while I sat in the assembly;

I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and regarding the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, I lacked even a single thought of joy or aspiration. This was because at that time I had not yet attained faith or understanding.

Having come to this sutra, when first hearing the brief exposition, one’s attachments were shaken and doubts arose. Next, upon hearing the extensive teaching of the five Buddhas, one was still obscured and lacked clear understanding.
Now, having heard the parables, one is finally able to rejoice with leaping exultation; faith is aroused, comprehension is born, doubt is removed, and the principle is clarified.

This joy is the "worldly" (lokiya) aspect; the arising of faith is the "for the sake of others" (pudgalārtha); the removal of doubt is the "remedy" (pratipakṣa); and the clarification of the principle is the... [supramundane].

This is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). How much more so when, through the skillful arising of principle, one destroys evil and attains realization, wherein the four *siddhāntas* are perfectly integrated and attained simultaneously;
this is the primary meaning of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*). Because these four *siddhāntas* are all real, it is due to attaining understanding through hearing the wondrous Dharma.

This is an explanation by way of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). If, however, one explains "faith and understanding" (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) according to the teachings (*yāna*), it is spoken in terms of stages (*bhūmi*).
As for those of middle capacity: upon hearing the exposition of parables, their doubts are first shattered, and they enter the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) of the Mahāyāna.

Thus, they first realize the principle at the First Abode (*prathamā bhūmi*), which is therefore called "Faith" (*śraddhā*). At the First Abode, there must necessarily be further application of effort to advance into the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) of the Mahāyāna;
this is the Second Abode, which is therefore called "Understanding" (*adhimukti*). As the text says: "The unsurpassed treasury of jewels is obtained spontaneously without being sought."
"Today we are truly śrāvakas, for by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear.
It should be known that hearing the Perfect Teaching and entering the Perfect Stage is why this is called the 'Chapter on Faith and Understanding' (Śraddhādhimukti-parivarta).

If explained according to the principle of original and manifested aspects (honji-suijaku), these four great disciples have long entered the Mahāyāna and accomplished the Buddha-dharma; they are merely manifesting initial faith and understanding to lead those of middle capacity."

This is the "Chapter on Resolute Belief. This single chapter of the sutra is divided into two parts: first, the narrator prefaces the account with expressions of joy; second, he addresses the Buddha to recount his own experience.
Within the initial narration of joy, there is first a description of his inner state, followed by a description of his outward reverence.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented teaching— the World-Honored One’s bestowal of the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon Śāriputra—
were struck with wonder; their hearts filled with joy, they leaped for gladness.

This section is where the compiler of the sutra first describes the internal state of mind. He states that Subhūti alone is called "Life of Wisdom" (Prajñājīvita), while the other three are all called "Mahā.
Generally speaking, they are all "Great" and all possess "Wisdom"; specifically, however, Subhūti is distinguished by his realization of emptiness.

The wisdom of emptiness is their life. This is explained in terms of practice; therefore, it is called "life of wisdom" (*prajñājīvika*). Among all those possessing wisdom, the Buddha's wisdom is foremost.
The Buddha commanded him to turn the wheel of teaching regarding *prajñā*. Because he was commissioned by one who possesses such wisdom, he is called "Life of Wisdom."

This is an explanation according to the classification of teachings (*yōkyō*). Regarding the three disciples in general discussion: although they were "great" and "wise," because they were assigned fewer [verses], they did not take emptiness as the primary tenet of their practice.
This does not mean they did not receive the transformative teaching; it is merely discussed here in terms of the quantity [of verses].

The three disciples beginning with Mahākausthila have been fully explained as previously detailed. However, the reason for their attainment of joy was that they heard from afar the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Hōben-bon*).
Regarding the five-part exposition of the Dharma: it is only now that [the disciples] have realized what was previously [taught]. Therefore, they rejoice.

As for the sūtra compiler’s account of two types—namely, hearing the rare Dharma and hearing the bestowal of predictions—it may be that "hearing the rare Dharma" refers to the first four sections, while "seeing the bestowal of predictions" constitutes the fifth section. Such hearing and seeing were unprecedented; this is the reason for their joy.

Regarding the arousal of a rare and marvelous mind (*āścaryacitta*): this refers to the narration of what has recently been heard, consisting of parables, prose, and verses, each of which contains fourfold explanations—namely, the general and the specific.
Because such a rare and marvelous mind is aroused, and because the mind is thus aroused, it is termed "faith" (*śraddhā*). By means of this faith, one enters [the path].
Entering the stage of joy is precisely the meaning of the "Chapter on Resolute Belief.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms with single-minded devotion, bowed his body in reverence,
and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance.
This section constitutes the sūtra-narrator’s account of external reverence. Previously, it was said that he "gave rise to a rare mind"; this refers to the mental realization.

Now, his rising from his seat refers to the physical realization. Together with his subsequent address to the Buddha, these constitute the realization through the three karmas (body, speech, and mind).
This concludes the narrator’s account. From here on, Kāśyapa addresses the Buddha to speak for himself. First is the prose section, followed by seventy-three [verses].

One and a half verses correctly present the attainment of understanding. Next, there are thirteen verses praising the profundity of the Buddha’s grace; since this understanding arises because of the Buddha, the praise follows the presentation.
The prose commentary also has two parts: first, a brief explanation in terms of the Dharma; second, an extensive explanation by means of similes. The brief explanation also has two parts:
first, the actual explanation of the Dharma; second, a brief citation of similes. The initial actual explanation of the Dharma also has two parts: first, clarifying the past...
Because he received [the precepts] three times, he did not seek the Great [Vehicle]. Second, it clarifies that because the present assembly has unified [the vehicles], he attained it spontaneously;

first, he did not seek the Middle [Vehicle]. This section contains both a thesis and an explanation. The thesis has three parts: first, he did not seek it because he occupied the headship of the monastic community; second, he did not seek it because his secular age was advanced;
third, he did not seek it because he clung to his own realization. These will be further clarified in the text itself.
They addressed the Buddha, saying: "We occupy the foremost positions among the Sangha;
this title marks us as leaders of the community. To recount our past failure to seek [the truth]: our dharma-ordination years are already advanced, and those of later learning take us as their model.
Yet, suddenly changing our path and altering our course, we have abandoned the lesser for the greater, thereby becoming objects of reproach to those who come after us. From themselves...

To stubbornly protect that [lesser vehicle] and thus fail to seek [the Great Vehicle] involves three faults: first, by clinging to the small number of years since ordination, one is entirely deficient in the Great Dharma;

second, by not abandoning the small because one does not yet understand the opening of the Three Vehicles; and third, by being self-protective, one’s attachment to the small has not shifted, while by protecting that [other], one is confused regarding the path of the Great.
These three reasons for not seeking it describe the faults of the past.
My years have reached old age and decline.

This statement regarding the decline of my worldly years and my refusal to seek [ordination] is as follows: if one were a bodhisattva, they should single-mindedly undertake the Great Way to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
Now that I am decrepit and aged, I have no capacity for such tasks; therefore, I do not seek it. This is truly because of this single lifetime.
Regarding realization through severance: for this reason, I reproach myself for my advanced age; the seeds of failure have not yet been removed, and my unworthy views still persist.
Believing that I have already attained *nirvāṇa*, I am incapable of further effort and no longer seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
World-Honored One, in the past when you preached the Dharma for a long time, I was seated among the assembly, and my body became weary and exhausted. However—
They contemplate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet they find no joy in the bodhisattva dharmas— such as sporting with supernatural powers, purifying buddha-fields,
and bringing sentient beings to maturity.

This section indicates that because they have already realized [the goal], they do not seek further. Having previously attained the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) state of the correct position of nirvāṇa, they are unable to give rise to the Mahāyāna mind.
Because they were formerly deluded regarding the essential meaning, they merely calculated the merit of that correct position;
due to this stubborn attachment, it is difficult for the great mind to arise. It is like a high plateau or dry land where lotus flowers do not grow at all.

Having given rise to wisdom, one is established and has nothing further to rely upon or seek. This concludes the previous section on the three errors of those who received the Lesser Vehicle and failed to seek the ultimate.
△ Below this is the explanation of the preceding heading.
Why is this? Because the World-Honored One has caused us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvāṇa.
This explains the third point above: having attained the realization of nirvāṇa, one does not seek further.

Furthermore, we are now already advanced in years; regarding the Buddha’s teaching and transformation of bodhisattvas toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, we have not given rise to even a single thought of joyful aspiration.

This explains the aforementioned heading regarding his being advanced in years and presiding over the assembly of monks. Alternatively, it may refer to the fact that after he had long been preaching the Dharma, his body became weary and his mind found no joy;
thus, he did not seek to preside over the assembly of monks. Since it is stated that he was "seated," this implies he was already present.
Furthermore, considering my advanced age, I recognize that this is the meaning intended by Śramaṇa Śengshou.
We have now, before the Buddha, heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the śrāvakas.
His heart was filled with great joy; he had attained what he had never experienced before. He thought, "I did not expect that today, suddenly, I would hear such a rare Dharma.
I am deeply fortunate to have obtained this great and wholesome benefit."

This section explains the cause by which [the author] attained understanding. Because he had previously heard from afar that the Five Buddhas’ Chapter briefly opens the three vehicles and reveals the reality, he was filled with joy.
The phrase "attaining great and wholesome benefit" specifically describes this attainment of understanding;
it refers to his recent hearing of the fourfold general principles and the rare parables, through which he achieved awakening—namely, the "great and wholesome benefit" he has now obtained.
Benefit.
Immeasurable treasures are obtained without seeking.

This is a brief illustration; it serves as a metaphor for how that which was not sought in the past is now spontaneously attained—the rare Dharma-treasure that existed in the past [during the time of] Parinirvāṇa.
If one has received the teaching and considers oneself a bodhisattva, how could one have imagined that today one would receive such complete and equal bestowals?
From the initial "I then addressed [the Buddha]" until this point, the brief explanation of the Dharma through words is concluded.
“World-Honored One, we now wish to speak by means of a parable to clarify this meaning.

From here until the end of the section below is the extensive parable for understanding [the teaching]. It contains both the opening of the parable and its application to the doctrine. Now, I shall open the parable.”
Therefore, I first offer this consultation and inquiry, which is also in accordance with worldly etiquette. △ In the following extensive exposition through parables, there are five major sections.
First, from "Abandoning his father and fleeing" onwards, is titled "The Parable of the Father and Son Losing Sight of Each Other.

This closely corresponds to the general parable of the burning house above, and distantly corresponds to the brief verses of the "Expedient Means" chapter above. Second, from "The impoverished son working for wages and debts" onwards, is titled "The Father... [The text continues].
The analogy of seeing the children: the proximate meaning refers to seeing the fire in the burning house; the remote meaning refers to the skillful means where I, with the Buddha-eye, observe them.
From this third point, he immediately dispatches attendants to urgently pursue and bring them back down; this is called the analogy of pursuit and enticement.

The proximate meaning refers to abandoning the small stools and providing carts in the burning house; the remote meaning refers to the skillful means where the Great [Vehicle] is set aside and the Small [Vehicle] is bestowed. This is the fourth point.

After this, from "His mind was filled with trust" (*citta-prasāda*) downwards is the analogy of "thoroughly knowing the family business. This does not merely summarize the preceding [sections on] the near and the far;
rather, it follows up to capture the intent of the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) teachings' reprimands and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*’s transformative instruction.

From "After a short while had passed, the father knew his son’s intention" downwards is named the analogy of "entrusting the family business," which closely summarizes the previous [section on] the burning house and the bestowing of the one great [vehicle].

The carriage. The "Distant Leader" refers to the teaching of the Dharma that directly abandons expedient means. Furthermore, the fourth and fifth [sections] are combined to form a single "Leader and Entrustment" parable;
its meaning will be further clarified below. This concludes the general division of the extensive parable into five major sections.
Within the first section, concerning the loss of the father and son, there are four sub-sections: first, the son departs from his father; second, the father...
Seeking a son, he stops midway; three sons encounter the root. Fourth, the father is filled with anxious concern. Within these four sections, each contains two parts.

Regarding the first son who turns his back on his father and departs as the second [case]: first, he turns his back on his father and departs, representing the five hundred people within the general parable.
In the past, they were sons of the Great Vehicle father, but having subsequently lost their understanding, they drifted through the five realms of existence; therefore, it is said:
Whether ten, twenty, or up to fifty years [of age], they are all equally sons of the Buddha; yet because the meaning of "son" is weak, they are called "infants.

Because they have not yet established a karmic connection within their own realm, they are said to be "long-dwelling in another land. Second, those who turn back toward the source represent the collective analogy of the thirty sons.
Because these conditions possess both subtle and manifest meanings, they are called "grown-up. Since these conditions have already passed...
It is suffering. Because it is due to the Buddha’s great compassion, it is said that one "encounters [the Buddha] upon returning to one's own country. This concludes the two meanings.
Within each of the three subsequent sections, there are two subsections each; these will be clarified further below.
It is as if there were a man who, while still young, abandoned his father and fled, dwelling in another country for a long time—
perhaps ten, twenty, or even fifty years.

Regarding the first analogy, "as if there were a person," this refers to those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). Leading the aforementioned twenty children is an analogy for the practitioners of the two vehicles.
For what reason does he not lead the bodhisattvas? Because the stages and practices of the bodhisattvas are difficult to comprehend;

for now, [the father] leads them only according to the capacity of the two vehicles themselves. That they are "already young in years" means that they are shrouded and obstructed by the density and thickness of ignorance (avidyā).
Yuan Jie’s "Explanation of the Mind in the Mahāyāna Sudden and Perfect Teaching" states that because the mind lacks power, it is called "infantile.

There are two meanings to this "infantile delusion": first, being immature and ignorant; second, not yet having encountered suffering. Thus, one does not know how to return; this is what is meant by "infantile."

Regarding "abandoning his father and fleeing": following the literal text while adhering to its underlying meaning, if one explains the "poor son's escape," one interprets the text through the *half-character* (*ardha-akṣara*) dharma-gate for those of the Two Vehicles.
If one explains the "father," one interprets the text through the *full-character* (*pūrṇa-akṣara*) dharma-gate of Vairocana Buddha. Why?
Because within the house, the elder removes his jeweled necklace and puts on soiled garments; though the garments and the necklace differ, the person remains the same.
This is one [point]. It is like Vairocana Buddha, who conceals his immeasurable divine virtues and manifests a sixteen-foot golden radiance;
he holds a vessel for filth and establishes the teachings of the Three Vehicles. One should know that the "Father" is none other than Śākyamuni.

To retreat from the Great Vehicle is called "abandoning" (śe); to be self-concealed by ignorance is called "fleeing" (táo); and to head toward birth and death is called "departing" (shì). These are all spoken of according to the capacities of sentient beings.

If we judge it according to the Buddha, how could the Buddha ever abandon sentient beings? It is because they are obstructed by material objects that they do not see him; the meaning is that they have effectively fled from him. Question:

After the Buddha has relinquished his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), sentient beings give rise to delusions. This is like a father leaving his son; it is not as if the son abandons the father. Answer: [The same applies here.]
Because sentient beings do not provide the conditions for his appearance, the Buddha departs from the world; this thus fulfills the meaning of a son abandoning his father.
As for the phrase "dwelling long in another country": the *dharmadhātu* of *nirvāṇa* is the Buddha’s own country, whereas the five desires of *saṃsāra* constitute the foreign land.
Having originally sought liberation, they have instead fallen back and do not return; therefore, they dwell long in foreign lands.

As for the statement "ten up to fifty years," ten refers to the heavenly realms and fifty refers to the five destinies; this describes how a single individual undergoes the cycle through all these paths.
This concludes the analogy of the son of the Śākyas who turned his back on his father and departed, leading away the aforementioned five hundred people.

As he grew older, moreover, he fell into poverty and destitution; he traveled through the four quarters in search of food and clothing, and as he wandered on gradually, he happened upon his native land.
This son departed from his father’s presence; the second turned back toward his native land and returned, leading the thirty elder sons.

Those called "grown up" are so named because their roots of goodness have been permeated and they are gradually becoming attached [to the Dharma]. Now, as they practice their studies, these latent impressions permeate them deeply.
Having gained a slight understanding and turned toward the Way, one encounters suffering and loses happiness; thus, one seeks the supreme escape and attains maturity.
Yet, while within the three realms, not seeing the Buddha-Father is called "poverty"; failing to obtain the method for escape is likewise called "poverty.
To be scorched by the fires of the eight sufferings is termed "further distress. Those who gallop in all four directions to seek food and clothing—once the Buddha has [appeared]...
Those ordinary worldlings who have not yet emerged give rise to four views regarding body, sensation, mind, and phenomena;

therein they seek the Right Path as if seeking food, and they seek the Path of Assistance as if seeking clothing. Their wearying of suffering and their quest for principle serve as the conditions for being transformed.
"Gradually traveling until they encounter their own country" clarifies that, though weary of suffering and longing for liberation, they seek *nirvāṇa* through erroneous means;

although this is not their original intention, they nevertheless encounter a Buddha. Thus it is said "encountering [their way] toward. As for "one's own country," the meaning has been explained above.
Question: In the passage below, cities and houses are described; how are these distinguished from the "country" mentioned above? Answer: All Buddha-dharma...

Regarding "the kingdom," this meaning is broad; regarding "the city," the expression is narrow and specific. Taking the *nirvāṇa* of severed defilements (*prahāṇa-dharma*) as the city that wards off the non-righteous and resists evil is somewhat narrow.
Regarding "the house," the expression is even more intimate: taking the great compassion of same-nature (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*) as the house is closer still than [the relationship] toward a son.

However, these distinctions of breadth and intimacy are established based on the capacity of the recipient (*yogya*), by comparing the kingdom to the city and the city to the house; they all belong to the same Elder.

It is the locus of true wisdom (*bhūta-prajñā*) and likewise the basis for the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Before the manifestation of the response, the karmic conditions first strike this [locus];
therefore, it begins with the "kingdom" and extends even to the "city and house.

From the passage, "Suppose there were a person here," until "the first son turns his back on his father and departs," the initial section concerning the loss of the father and son concludes. Below this, the second section clarifies the father’s search for the son.
The analogy of the interruption also has two parts: first, clarifying that the son could not be found despite seeking him; second, clarifying the interruption itself.
Regarding the father’s prior arrival: he sought his son but could not find him.

This clarifies that the father sought his son and was unable to find him. From the point when [the Buddha] first withdrew from the Great Vehicle onward, he sought the capacity [of beings] but did not encounter it; thus, there was no meeting.
Therefore, it is said that he sought a son but did not obtain one.
He resided in a certain city; his family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable riches and treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, and amber.

Crystal beads and the like; all his granaries and treasuries were completely overflowing. He had many servants, ministers, officials, and subjects, as well as countless elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, and sheep.
His profits from lending and trade extended throughout other countries, and he employed merchants and traders.
They were also exceedingly numerous.

This clarifies that the father sought his son but could not find him. Regarding the second point, "stopping in a city along the way": this means that one does not abandon one's family business for the sake of a single child.

It is like the Buddha, who does not abandon the propagation of his transformative teachings in other regions simply because there is no receptive capacity in one particular place. They dwell together.
Since their faculties are not yet mature, they remain for the time being within the Land of Expedient Means. The statement that they "dwell in a city" refers to the Land of Expedient Means;

"whose family is very wealthy" refers to the Land of Abundant Expedients serving as a kingdom. This is called the "Middle" because it lies between the Land of Common Dwelling and the Land of True Reward.
Taking *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* as a city, dwelling in this nirvāṇa is called "stopping" (*śamatha*). Taking the true reality (*dharmatā*) as one's home, two kinds of response arise:
the inferior response corresponds to the śrāvakas and occurs only at the Deer Park; the superior response corresponds to the bodhisattvas and encompasses both locations.
Those five persons who have severed the pervasive afflictions are reborn together in that land, all becoming bodhisattvas. By means of the Buddha...
The Victorious One (the Buddha) responded accordingly. He instructed him solely in the family business of the Mahāyāna, teaching him to practice and study it.

Therefore, the father, the elder, remained here to observe and seek the readiness of his co-resident son. Not only was the meaning of the "intermediate" [stage] attained, but the kingdom, the city, and the family business were all made clearly manifest.
Regarding the "great wealth and treasures," the realm of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is the family estate, fully endowed with ten thousand virtues.
It is called "wealth. The merit of the five perfections is called "treasure," and Prajñā-wisdom is the "jewel.
Because it can lead all beings entirely into the Mahāyāna, it is called "immeasurable. Gold, silver, pearls, and so forth, refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment of the Mahāyāna.
This "upper garment" signifies the meaning of great wealth. Regarding "the granaries and treasuries being full and overflowing": that which stores rice is called a granary (*kūṭāgāra*);
the granary is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), for concentration gives birth to the one hundred and eight samādhis. That which stores goods is a treasury (*kośa*);

the treasury is a metaphor for the true nature (*dharmatā*), for it can give rise to the wisdom of the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*). Being full internally means providing for oneself; overflowing externally means transforming sentient beings. This refers to the upper garment.

The phrase "above" primarily conveys the meaning of fields and residences. As for the "servants, ministers, assistants, officials, and subjects," the servants represent the complete fulfillment of the *upāya-jñāna-pāramitā* (the perfection of skillful means and knowledge).
These adapt flexibly according to the capacities of beings, corresponding to both phenomena and principle.

This refers back to the previous mention of having many attendants. If discussed in terms of their respective positions, these include those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as well as the *pṛthagjana* (ordinary) and *sambhoga* (universal) bodhisattvas. Separately, there are three [categories].

The ten minds are all termed "servants. As for the term "minister," it may refer specifically to those taught by the Separate Teaching (Biaojiao) on the ten stages (*bhūmi*), as well as to those in the ten stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Those in the stage of the ten transferences (*daśapraṇidhāna*) are termed "assistants"; those in the stage of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) are like "officials"; and those in the stage of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) are like "commoners."
This is because one has first entered the realm of the Buddha. Furthermore, the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi) assist the Buddha in his transformative activities and subdue Māra and adversaries;

thus, they are like ministers. The Ten Dedications (daśapariṇāmanā) involve a slightly deeper engagement with principle and phenomena, and their office is closer to that of the King; thus, they are like aides. The Ten Practices (daśacaryā) proceed through distinct stages.
One cultivates the methods of dhyāna. The various activities are like those of officials; all the subjects throughout the land are none other than the King’s people.
Although they have attained the status of being "people," compared to the officials and assistants, they are still distant. This is the meaning of their relative depth and shallowness.

The mention of "countless elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, and sheep" refers to the single mind and threefold contemplation of the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna, which proceeds like the movement of an elephant. Next...

The third contemplation: the Mahayana of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) is like the movement of a horse; the contemplation of the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), the Mahayana of immediate emptiness, is like the movement of an ox;
and the contemplation for self-cultivation of the Two Vehicles of the Treasury Teaching (zangjiao) is like the movement of a sheep or a deer.
The above all pertains to what is ridden by servants, ministers, officials, and commoners; it does not extend beyond the various pavilions.

As for the "innumerable," the provisional and real dharmas are all the vehicles that are ridden. The contemplation of provisional and real wisdom is that which guides, and is thus named the horse, elephant, ox, sheep, and goat.
One should know that within the provisional and real teachings, each teaching has four gates, and within each gate there are...
Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Not only are the teachings extremely numerous, but the wisdom of contemplation is likewise not of one kind;
therefore, it is called "innumerable. Regarding "the profit of entering and exiting": duality and non-duality are "entering," while non-duality and duality are "exiting.
Furthermore, non-duality and duality are "entering," while duality and non-duality are "exiting. These two interpretations explain this in terms of the Three Truths. Moreover, there is no...

That the measure returns to oneness is entry; that within oneness there is the immeasurable is emergence. This is explained according to the two truths (*satya*). The three preceding explanations all proceed from the perspective of practice (*caryā*).
Furthermore, employing [the wisdom] for the sake of others is emergence, while employing it for one's own practice is entry; this is explained from the perspective of benefiting sentient beings.
However, the intended meaning of this passage is entirely that which is utilized by the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*). Moreover, this is the noble stage (*ārya-bhūmi*) of the Elder.

The "what is used" (the means) and "for whom" (the object) are rich in both textual expression and underlying meaning; therefore, a manifold understanding is required. To go forth from the Dharma and benefit sentient beings is termed "peace" (śānti);

to cause the merit of transformation to return to oneself is termed "benefit" (lābha). As for "pervading other lands," everything outside of the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is called "other lands.
Emerging from the land of *dharmatā*, one benefits sentient beings in the three lands, traversing non-paths and attaining thorough penetration.
The Buddha-way is precisely its meaning. Only the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is one’s own country. As for the fact that merchants and traders are also very numerous:
the various bodhisattvas are these merchants; furthermore, because they enter all three lands (*tri-bhūmi*) to seek the benefit of the Dharma, they are said to be "numerous.
Bodhisattvas of this land go to other directions to hear the Dharma, while great beings from other directions come here to listen.

The *sūtras* are like traveling back and forth to gather profit. Just as bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions benefit one another and extend that benefit to sentient beings, this is precisely their analogy.

Furthermore, the two bodies—the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*)—are like merchants who take the true Dharma and enter the three lands everywhere to transform and benefit sentient beings before returning to the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
therefore, it is said they are "very many. One should know that the Buddha himself...

The transformation of sentient beings is boundless, and it likewise causes the bodhisattva’s sphere of transformation to be all-pervasive. The bodhisattva’s transformative benefit still relies upon the Buddha as its foundation;
it is like a person in the world who causes others to manage wealth and engage in business while also engaging in business themselves, traveling among various countries.

This is fully illustrated by the accounts in various sutras of Bodhisattvas from the ten directions coming and going to receive benefit; the *Avataṃsaka* and *Mahāsaṃnipāta* are prime examples thereof.
The above concludes the section clarifying the cessation of seeking a son. What follows is the third section: the analogy of the son returning to his father.
This also has two parts: first, seeking food and clothing; second, arriving at his father’s city.
This refers to the passage beginning with "the upper fire started" and continuing through "the middle hall and pavilion were decayed and old, until suddenly a fire broke out."
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and traveled across kingdoms and cities;
this is the third section within the account of the father and son losing each other, clarifying how the son arrived at his father’s city in search of food and clothing.
Having thus internally regressed from the Mahāyāna understanding, they have encountered all manner of sufferings. Deeply giving rise to weariness and revulsion, they desire to seek liberation;
yet, their grasp of the principle is off-center, resulting in heterodoxy. Because this erroneous wisdom has permeated their minds, it is easy for them to enter the correct path.

They seek to transcend the world by taking this as the cause for perceiving the Buddha. Thus, they allow this false wisdom to secretly assist their practice toward the correct, thereby establishing it as the cause for seeing the Buddha.
Yet, they still employ the false contemplations of annihilationism and eternalism, viewing the five aggregates (*skandha*) as a village and the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as a town.
Taking the eighteen realms as his kingdom, he traversed them in search of principle; this is called wandering through various villages in search of food and clothing.
Eventually, he arrived at the city where his father resided.

Regarding "this arriving exactly at the city of the father": because one observes the realm of suffering through directed false wisdom (*mithyā-prajñā*), it assists in perfecting the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) that evokes the Great Compassion of the Buddha;

this is called "arriving at the city. The city is *nirvāṇa*. However, while the cause of suffering for non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) should result in the fruit of suffering, here, by taking up that functional capacity and being endowed with the correct seed (*samyak-bīja*), one perfumes the mind of false wisdom. Consequently, one evokes the Buddha’s correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*); this is what is meant.

One arrives at *nirvāṇa*. Since *nirvāṇa* encompasses both the partial (*hīnayāna*) and the full (*mahāyāna*), sentient beings who practice and understand [the teachings] may possess the sense of attaining *nirvāṇa*.

Although the name "nirvāṇa" is the same, its substance differs; it manifests as distinct names according to the means used to transform sentient beings, yet there is no difference in the realm of the Buddha.
Therefore, the two meanings you have reached are both established. If, when your faculties are matured, you realize what the Father has realized, this is called "arriving at the Father’s city."
This refers to those of limited capacity who first encounter the Great Response; when the principle is established, both the Great and the Small are attained.
What follows is the fourth analogy, that of the father grieving for his son. This analogy also has two parts.
The father constantly thought of his son; though they had been separated for over fifty years, he never spoke of this matter to anyone.

He merely pondered it within himself, harboring regret and remorse. Thinking to himself that he was old and infirm, yet possessed of abundant wealth—gold, silver, and precious gems—with storehouses overflowing—and that he had no offspring, he feared that once he passed away, his property would be lost and scattered, with no one to whom he could entrust it.
Thus, with such earnestness, he constantly remembers his son. This is the fourth instance of the father’s anxious concern;

it is the first thought of the suffering of having lost his son. Although previously the disciple’s capacity gradually struck the resonance of the Sage, now it is clarified that the Sage gradually gathers in the disciple’s capacity.
While the ritual of transformation and guidance is provisionally described as "anxious concern," it is fundamentally the remembrance of having lost a son.
Regarding the suffering [of this world]: since you, my son, withdrew from the Great Vehicle, the Tathāgata has constantly contemplated your great capacity from that time until now;
thus he says, "I have always been mindful of you. Since our separation, you have repeatedly forgotten [the truth] and fallen into the five realms of existence.
As your capacity has not yet matured, while the Buddha remains in the land of skillful means, we have spoken of our separation for more than fifty years.
"These" refers to the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). Because the hungry ghosts (*preta*) are distinguished and the asuras are excluded, it says "the remainder.

"Has never been spoken of" means that he has not yet explained the karmic conditions for having such a son to the ministers, assistants, and officials within the *upāya-śeṣa* (land of skillful means with remainder).

However, in that land of skillful means, there are not only those prior to the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*) or the dwellings (*vihāra*), but there are also those who have manifested their traces by attaining the grounds (*bhūmi-praviṣṭa*).

The "ascending and abiding" refers to the ministers and attendants and so forth. How could they be entirely unaware of the poor son’s disposition? It is simply that, with respect to the poor son, the time had not yet arrived;

thus, the principal and his retinue together concealed the truth and did not proclaim it, provisionally following the capacities of sentient beings, which is why it is said that he did not speak of it.

Furthermore, since the time of his appearance in the world, for over forty years—from the ancient *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vaipulya*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* assemblies—he has never addressed the great bodhisattvas by saying that these śrāvakas were originally sons of the Mahāyāna; for they were not [then considered] sons of the Buddha.

They do not understand the Buddha-dharma; some are like the deaf or mute. They place their flowers upon the seats for prostration, they cast aside their bowls and stand bewildered, or they lack any aspiration to attain it.
Because they fail in these various ways, I have not yet spoken [the Dharma] to them. As for those who merely contemplate within themselves with hearts full of regret:

This, however, explains the remote cause (*dūrahetu*). The remote cause is precisely the condition for not speaking [to him]. It is truly because when he first formed his great vows, he had not yet entered the stage of "similarity" (*sādṛśya*);
it was due to my lack of diligent instruction in former days that he failed to receive training and fled. Therefore, it is called "regret.

As for "resentment," it refers specifically to the fact that the son did not contemplate our kindness and righteousness, but instead alienated me and became intimate with others; thus, it is said he harbors resentment.

My son, it is not only that your regrets should have been stilled long ago; I also lament that your faculties were awakened too late, causing you to distance yourself from my True Dharma and become intimate with the six sense-objects.

Internally, this fails to accord with the Tathāgata’s earnest instructions for entering the stage of the ordinary person within the path of cultivation, and consequently leads to the loss of your original understanding;
hence, I speak of "regret. I lament that you lacked the resolve to be diligent and firm in purpose, failing instead to escape delusion.
He does not turn back; therefore, he speaks of regret and remorse. The Buddha has no regret. This is merely said according to the manner of his transformative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*).

When he thinks of himself as "old and decrepit," it means the period of his transformation is nearing its end and there is no one to whom he can transmit the Great Dharma—like an old man who has no son.

This refers to the subsequent intention: from his advent into the world until before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he is described as being "old and decrepit. This may also be understood from the beginning.
Regarding the formation of karmic affinity: I hope that as you grow old, before the sudden or gradual [teachings] have awakened your great capacity, you will be called "childless.
Question: The various bodhisattvas transformed by the Dharmakāya are all capable of succeeding to the position of the Buddha; why do you suddenly harbor such anxiety? Answer:
That which is manifested by the Dharma-body is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; who could speak of its aging or decay? This is not what is being discussed here.
Now, to clarify the retinue of the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), there are two kinds: first, those Great Beings of the Dharma-body who mutually influence one another;

though their traces appear as disciples, they may originally have been teachers, yet even so, they do not consider themselves aged based on this. Second, those currently dwelling together with [the Buddha].
Ordinary beings who, beginning with the transformation Buddha, first give rise to the mind of the Way are called "sons.

Just as a son succeeds to his father's vocation so that the lineage remains unbroken, if Śāriputra receives the prediction of enlightenment to become the Buddha Padmaprabha, then the Buddha-seed in one quarter will continue without interruption.
Thus, the family heritage of the Mahāyāna is transmitted from one to another. If there were no Śāriputra to be transformed, [the lineage would cease].

Regarding this pivotal moment (*tīkṣṇa*), the wealth of the Mahāyāna Dharma is currently without one to whom it may be entrusted. As for the future sentient beings, where shall the seeds of Buddhahood find their resting place?
It is precisely for this reason that I, in my old age, give rise to such sighs. "Treasury" and so forth are explained as before. "Once suddenly passing away" refers to the time of entering *nirvāṇa*.
It may also be said that when the capacity [of the recipient] recedes, the response [of the teaching] ceases. Prior to the distinction between sudden and gradual, this is also termed—
He will eventually pass away.
Then he further thinks: "If I were to obtain a son, I could entrust my wealth and possessions to him; I would then be at ease and happy, free from further anxiety.
This second thought—finding joy in obtaining a son—is the capacity for deliverance known as "obtaining a son"; [the Buddha] bestows the Buddha-dharma upon such a person.
Commentary: "Bestowing a name" refers to entrusting the wealth of the Dharma; it accords with one's original mind and is thus called "happiness.

From the beginning, starting from the analogy "Suppose there were a person," up to this point, concludes the summary of the preceding general analogies. What follows below is the commentary on the specific analogies.
From the section below, "At that time, the impoverished son went to work for hire," onwards, is the commentary on the second major section, the specific analogies concerning the father and son.

The analogy of meeting [the son] has three parts: it refers proximately to seeing the fire within the burning house, and distantly to the meaning of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) within the *Upāya* chapter.

First, the description of the impoverished son working for wages refers to the fire seen in the *Agni-gṛha-parivarta* (Burning House) chapter and the five turbidities seen in the *Dharma-paryāya* (Dharma-exposition).
Second, the father seeing his son refers to the elder’s vision in the *Agni-gṛha-parivarta* and the vision with the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) in the *Dharma-paryāya*.

The third [joy] is the fulfillment of one's wishes. It refers to the arising of great compassion within the "Dharma-exposition" (dharmadeśanā) section, following the experience of alarm and fear within the "burning house" (agnighara).
However, while both the "Dharma-exposition" and the "Parable" (aupamya) sections clarify that the father first sees the sons, this section clarifies that the sons first see the father.

If we consider the Buddha, his numinous wisdom first perceives the capacity of the beings (the "mechanism") and subsequently initiates the response; thus, it is said that the father first sees the sons. If, however, we consider...

Sentient beings must first encounter the stimulus (*nimita*) and only then receive the response (*pratipatti*). Therefore, it is said that "the son first sees the father. This interaction between stimulus and response is inconceivable;
it is neither prior nor subsequent, which is why both "before" and "after" are mentioned interchangeably. For the sake of textual convenience, I shall now divide this into two sections.

First, the son sees his father; second, the father sees his son. Within these two sections, each is further divided into four parts. Regarding the first—where the son sees his father—the four points are:
first, the cause for seeing his father, which is seeking food and clothing; second, the place where he sees his father, which is by the side of the gate;
third, the appearance of the father, sitting upon a lion throne; and fourth, the arising of fear and avoidance, regretting having come to this place.
The outline of the sections has been concluded.
World-Honored One, at that time, the impoverished son wandered about seeking employment until he happened upon his father’s house.
This is the initial cause for the son’s sight of his father within the section "The Son Sees the Father. It arose because the son was weary of suffering and yearned for joy, yet [remained] in error.
In investigating the flavor of principle, one observes that both the nature of seeing (*darśana*) and the nature of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) possess the quality of revulsion.

Cultivation is weak in its power of inference, while seeing, though dull, supersedes it when it arises. When various views arise in mutual succession, they are all capable of inferring principle; this is like the law of hiring labor, where one exchanges strength for wealth.
Although they originally give rise to false views, they still aspire to liberation from suffering. Even though their seeking is erroneous, it secretly assists the Right Path; thus, the world—

Through the gradual accumulation of such weariness, one eventually cultivates supramundane roots of goodness. Because the mundane world is easily transformed into the supramundane, it is called "hired labor.
Because one proceeds from one stage to the next, it is called "successive progression. By means of these roots of goodness, there is the principle of transition;

they are able to strike upon the Buddha’s compassion, which is why it is said that one "encounters" the father's house. This meeting occurs without prior expectation, and thus it is termed an "encounter. It is not... [The text ends here].

The mind, conditioned by worldly dharmas, suddenly feels the compassion that transcends the world; furthermore, without anticipating the worldly and erroneous speculations, it gives rise to right view and feels the Buddha’s presence.
Moreover, unexpectedly, within a small act of goodness, one enters in secret the perfect gate of the Mahāyāna;

hence it is said, "to encounter. The father is a metaphor for the Dharmakāya after the realization of the Way; the house is a metaphor for great, unconditioned compassion. [The two aspects of] the Great and the Small...

Regarding the "capacity" (indriya): they both knock on this house because there is a great capacity [within them]. Therefore, it is said below that they "see their father from afar," because there is a small capacity;
and it is said below that they "stand by the side of the gate," because there is a small capacity.

If there were only the small and no great capacity, they would not see the body of sublime marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), and the father would not say, "I now have something to entrust as my wealth and treasury. If there were only the great and no small capacity, [the same would follow].
One should not stand by the side of the gate. A son should not say, "This is not a place where I can obtain goods through hired labor.
One should know that the great capacity has not yet matured; right view is distant, while minor resonance is somewhat intimate. Being by the side of the gate implies proximity.

Therefore, following the derivative and the secondary, the meaning requires a dual engagement; following the fundamental and the great, it resides solely in the Perfect [Teaching]. From the perspective of the proximate...
[This is] a discussion. It refers to the fact that his particular capacity was already matured.
Standing by the side of the gate, he saw his father from afar;
this is the analogy for the second son seeing his father. Previously it was said that both the large and small [sons] knocked; why then is it mentioned here alone?
Does this refer to the side of the gate? It is so because, due to their minor affinity, they have previously followed that path. The "location" refers to the side of the gate;

the two contemplations serve as the means, like the two sides of a gate, both of which possess the principle of being able to see. Those with capacities for the Perfect [Teaching] see directly through the gate, whereas the Two Vehicles perceive the partial truth, and thus are said to be at the "side of the gate.
They merely use the samādhi of emptiness and the eye of wisdom of partial truth to peer in from the side.
It is the Dharma-body ear. Regarding "seeing one's father from afar," there are two kinds of correct seeing: first, seeing nearby; second, seeing from afar.
Here, it is said that while the great capacity has just begun to arise, the act of knocking and summoning is distant; therefore, it is called "from afar.
Furthermore, because the capacity is subtle and not yet met by the response, it is termed "distant."
He sat upon a lion throne with his feet resting on a jeweled footstool. All the brahmins, kṣatriyas, and householders surrounded him with reverence.
His body was adorned with pearl necklaces worth ten million pieces of gold. Officials, citizens, and servants stood in attendance at his left and right, holding white whisks.
A precious canopy covered him above, from which hung various flowered banners; fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground, and a multitude of flowers were scattered.

It is named "Flower. Various precious objects are arrayed; there is taking out and putting in, giving and receiving. Such are the various kinds of adornments, whose majestic virtue is exceptionally sublime.
When the third son sees his father’s appearance and analogy—specifically, his sitting upon the lion throne—it is precisely what is being illustrated, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The Reward Dharma-body abides securely in the principle of emptiness; being free from the two types of delusions—general and specific—as well as the terrors of the eight māras, it is said to "sit upon a lion throne.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* explains that the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) constitute the throne, signifying the place where the truth is realized.
Even when representing a lion throne in a ritual context, there is no actual form of a lion; it merely serves as a symbolic representation. Therefore...

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because the Buddha is the lion among men, the seat upon which he sits is called the Lion Throne (*siṃhāsana*), and that which he speaks is called the Lion’s Roar (*siṃhanāda*).

Although the *Avataṃsaka* section contains both distinct and shared elements, it is here designated as "Perfect Retribution" (*yuanbao*) from the perspective of its excellence and its fundamental nature;
this refers to the fundamental capacity of the recipient. Regarding the jeweled footstool supporting his feet: meditative concentration and wisdom are the feet, and the ultimate truth is [the stool].
As for "as a stand," it refers to the concentration and wisdom of non-arising, which rely upon the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the passage from "the various Brahmins" to "surrounding [him]," this is because the *victory-response* (superior manifestation) corresponds to Bodhisattvas; that is, the *Vairocana* with his distinguished body, who is perceived by those of great capacity.

If it were an *inferior-response* (lesser manifestation), it would correspond to the Small Vehicle, appearing as sixteen feet tall and clad in tattered robes, perceived by those of small capacity. Now, to clarify:
The eternal *amṛta* (supreme essence) is equal to *nirvāṇa*; the perfect and sudden *dharmakāya* is equal to the *Avataṃsaka*.

The majestic power and retinue of the elder described therein, as well as the Kṣatriyas and Brahmins who respectfully surround him, all refer to the retinue within the *Avataṃsaka*, and there is no difference whatsoever.
The characteristics of the Dharma taught are also clearly elucidated just as in that [sūtra], and likewise have no distinction. It should be understood...

One should understand the intent of the present sutra. Its purpose lies in synthesizing the beginning and the end by establishing the characteristics of the dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) as they are fully explained therein.

These are not absent from the present sutra; however, their textual expressions are preserved in an abbreviated form. Within the *Avataṃsaka* section, the forty-two stages (*bhūmi*) are not explicitly set forth.

The mastery over the primary and secondary [receptacle] worlds, the proximity to spiritual friends, and the clarification of the stages in this sutra are fully as revealed in the opening, showing, awakening, and entering of the four flowers.
Spiritual friends are exemplified by Avalokiteśvara’s wondrous voice and Bhaiṣajyarāja and Prabhūtaratna;

the primary and secondary worlds are exemplified by the distinctions of merit and the supernatural powers of the jeweled stupa—differing only slightly in their breadth or brevity. One example shall illustrate all others, as is the case with this sutra.
What is not encompassed by the term "the ten directions"? What reality is not subsumed within the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?

Such matters as the vision of the Buddha as ever-present and equal, this land as indestructible and so forth, the various adornments of halls and pavilions, the diverse pleasures and pastimes of sentient beings, and even the various characteristics of cause and effect in the *Jie mo* (迹门) section—these are for the most part explained through the text of the *Avataṃsaka*, using its numerical calculations and analogies.

The essentials are preserved in this scripture; one should extract them from the beginning of the text. [Otherwise,] they are scattered throughout various sutras. If the Great Version were lost, it would be a mere discussion of minor benefits.

As for the term *brāhmaṇa*, it means "one of pure conduct. Being of noble lineage and lofty purity, they are equivalent to Bodhisattvas who have attained Equal Enlightenment and are free from defilement.
The *kṣatriya* refers to the royal caste, corresponding to those from the first bhūmi up to the ninth bhūmi. The *gṛhapati*...
"Rich but not noble" refers to the thirty minds [of the bodhisattva path]. "Pearl necklaces" refers to the four necklaces of precepts, concentration, wisdom, dharanis, and samadhi.
These four must proceed from the ultimate; these four are that which adorns, while the body is that which is adorned.
"A value of ten million" refers to the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*), which adorn the Dharma-body.

"Officials, commoners, and servants" refers to the distinct categories of the teachings that clarify the meaning: those who receive the provisional teachings and sever the delusions common to all [vehicles] are called "commoners";

those who receive the distinct teachings and sever the delusions common to all are called "officials. If one explains the meaning according to the same category, these are likewise the provisional teachings.
The *pāramitās* are such that internally they accord with true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), and externally they accord with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.

This is analogous to the relationship between officials and the common people, wherein there is the principle of internal service and external labor. The white fly-whisk represents the function of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Standing in attendance to the right is the function of the wisdom that enters emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which brushes away the dust of the four abodes (*catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ*). Standing to the left is the function of the wisdom that enters the provisional (*prajñapti*), which brushes away [the dust of] non-existence.
Knowing the objects (*viṣaya*). These two constitute the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Middle Way; therefore, it is said that he stands in attendance.
One should know that this passage clarifies the father’s [Vairocana] and the one in the intermediate state [the Tathāgata of the Vajra Realm].

Although both are equally the retributive body of other-enjoyment (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), since this [latter] demonstrates entry into the realm of patience (*kṣānti*) and serves as the beginning of all teachings at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it is further endowed with a whisk of white hair that destroys dust and covered by compassion.
"The compassionate jeweled canopy. The preceding section described what the elder possessed; here, it clarifies what the impoverished son perceives he possesses.

"Covered with a jeweled canopy" refers to true compassion. "Hanging flowered banners" means that the flowers are the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the banners are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"Sprinkling fragrant water on the ground" means pouring down the water of the Dharma to sprinkle upon the minds of all bodhisattvas.

The ground is moistened by the dust of delusion; it is also the mind-ground sprinkled and dispersed with the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). To scatter various named flowers means to spread the seven flowers of purity:

namely, purity of precept (*śīla*), purity of concentration (*samādhi*), purity of wisdom (*prajñā*), purity of overcoming doubt, purity of knowing the path and the non-path, purity of knowledge and vision, and purity of having completed what was to be known.

As for "precept," it refers to the three types of precepts, such as the restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*). "Concentration" refers to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and others. "Wisdom" [refers to...].

"Real wisdom" means that one has severed doubt; having already transcended doubts regarding the two truths. "Purity of the path and non-path" means that while practicing what is not the path, one attains penetration into the Buddha-way.
"Purity of knowledge and vision" means that the virtue of wisdom is perfected, and one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature.
"Purity of the knowledge of exhaustion" means that the virtue of abandonment is accomplished, and ignorance is forever extinguished. "Arranging precious objects" refers to...
This enumerates the true merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*). The terms "emerging" and "entering" are explained as before. His majestic virtue is preeminently honored;
his radiance is boundless, and his physical forms are boundless. The ocean of his marks is lofty and magnificent.
This meaning must refer to the Buddha Vairocana; how could it be interpreted otherwise? It refers to the number of atoms within ten oceans of *padma-garbha* world-systems.
This is an explanation of the numerical marks and signs.
When the impoverished son saw his father’s great power and majesty, he was immediately seized with terror and regretted having come here; he thought to himself in secret:
"This is either a king or someone like a king; it is not a place where I can obtain goods through hired labor.
It would be better to go to a poor neighborhood, where there is ground for exerting one's strength and food and clothing are easily obtained.
If I stay here long, I might be coerced and forced to work. Having formed this thought, he runs away quickly.
This is the fourth [fear]: the coming of remorse. Regarding the phrase "great power and majesty":

it is called "great power" because his wisdom is vast, and "great majesty" because his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are vast; this is like the meaning of having strength in one's upper body and hands.
"Conceives fear" means that those of inferior capacity and weak faculties are timid and apprehensive of the Great Way. "Remorse comes to this point" refers to what the Buddha originally intended...

If one were to present the Mahāyāna to him, it would not accord with his capacity; he would only harbor thoughts of regressing from the Great Vehicle, and thus it is said that he regrets having come here.
As for the thought "I have secretly harbored this notion," this refers to something hidden within his latent disposition (*indriya*);

it does not mean that he has clearly perceived the *sambhogakāya* (the Body of Reciprocal Enjoyment). Or, regarding the phrase "or kings and their like": Pāpīyas is the king, and his followers are the [ministers].

The above is an explanation based on those outside [the Buddhist fold]. Furthermore, for those of inferior capacity who have severed all traces through the path of wordless extinction, where form and appearance are utterly transcended, the sight of the sublime Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body) is beyond the reach of gods and humans.
The characteristics of the Dharma taught by this body are entirely different from those of the Two Vehicles;
those of meager virtue and limited wisdom, having never before seen or heard of them, immediately claim that it is Māra or the teaching of Māra. If one...
The latter clarifies the former. Having heard the brief teaching that opens up the three to reveal the one, Śāriputra harbors doubt, wondering:

"Is this not a demon who has become a Buddha to disturb my mind? If the Great [Vehicle] had been used to teach the Small [Vehicle] from the very beginning, it would have been more than just today that he would have suspected the Buddha to be a demon.
Furthermore, the *saṃbhogakāya* is likened to a wealthy elder; the elder represents the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha. Therefore, this is the King.
[The phrase] "and so forth" [is used]. The Dharma-body is the recompense teacher (*vipāka-śāstṛ*). The teacher is like a king; many sūtras refer to this sūtra as the "King of Sūtras.
When wisdom accords with the Dharma, it means that wisdom is equal to the Dharma. Therefore, the recompense Buddha is called "equal" (*sama*).
This is the Dharma-recompense of the Mahāyāna, not a place where one gains benefit in the Hīnayāna; hence it says "or like a king, etc. Even if there are various [passages] in other sūtras...

The King of Sutras does not say, "I have already spoken; now I shall speak. Regarding the phrase "not a place where I can obtain things through hired labor," this means that those of small capacity cannot receive the Great Transformation.
"It is not like going to a place where food and clothing are easily obtained" refers to what the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says:
"One can use the Dharma obtained through poverty to deliver these inferior beings. However, the principle of emptiness does not contain [such distinctions].

The myriad virtues are not the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, it is called a "poor village. Because one-sided emptiness is praised by those of small wisdom, it is said that there is ground upon which to exert effort.

"Exertion" (si) means to release, to discharge, and to extend. That clothing and food are easily obtained refers to being able to obtain the clothing and food of *anāsrava* (outflow-free) *nirvāṇa-parinirvāṇa*.
The practice of conduct is clothing; the practice of wisdom is food. If one dwells here for a long time, or...
Seeing that I was being coerced and forced to act, I practice the path of the Mahāyāna; thus, it is said that I have "dwelt for a long time.

Originally, I was weary of and terrified of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); had I cultivated the Mahāyāna, I would inevitably have entered into birth and death and extensively studied the myriad practices (*sādhana*).
