Therefore, it is said that they are "oppressed. Originally I delighted in the Lesser Vehicle, yet now you compel me to give rise to the Bodhicitta of the Mahāyāna;
this is like being forced by violence. To abandon the Great and take up the Small is why it is said they "run away swiftly.

From the beginning, starting from when the World-Honored One first spoke, until the point where the impoverished son finished his labor for hire—this concludes the preceding section on the specific parable. Therein, one sees this great fire approaching from all four sides.

[The Buddha] rose. This concludes the passage from the *Upāyakauśalya-parivarta* (The Chapter on Skillful Means) concerning the six classes of sentient beings who are impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom, up to the text stating that they seek to abandon suffering through [further] suffering.
The four preceding sections of the sūtra constitute, in total, the second part of the "Specific Simile," ending with the text on the fire seen [by the sons].
From the section beginning with "At that time, the wealthy elder... onwards, the second [section] clarifies the simile of the father seeing his sons.
The distant reference concerns the teaching on the Dharma, where it says, "I observe with the Buddha-eye. The proximate reference concerns the person first able to see within the burning house;
this refers to the passage stating that "the elder saw [them]. This current section has four parts: first, the father sees his sons; second, upon seeing them, he recognizes them;
third, he rejoices at seeing them; fourth, their wishes are fulfilled. However, the śrāvakas are like those toward whom the father directs his gaze as if they were his children.

The analogy of the father illustrates how one who is skillfully guided may comprehend the small while encountering the great, yet fail to receive it within their own capacity. Now, the analogy of the father seeing his son is established as a subtle metaphor for the Buddha perceiving the capacities of beings;
though he does not deliberate, he is eternally aware. This concludes the analysis of the text according to the intended meaning.
At that time, the wealthy elder sat upon the lion seat—this being the place where the father first beheld his son; it was indeed a lion throne.
The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata dwells in the realm of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) free from fear, clearly illuminating the capacities of sentient beings.
Upon seeing the child, he recognized him.

As for the second instance of recognizing the child upon seeing him: the Tathāgata knew that this was a sentient being with whom he had formed a karmic connection in the past, and his heart was filled with great joy.
Regarding this third point concerning the son’s joy: the Buddha constantly observes the son’s capacity; now that this capacity has arisen in accordance with compassion, he is therefore joyful.
This very joy is the distant reception of the Dharma, which is to say, because he regards these beings as his own children, he gives rise to great compassionate heart.
Upon recently escaping the burning house, they were immediately struck with great alarm and fear, and this thought arose in them: "We have reached safety and emerged.
This illustrates that the Tathāgata manifests compassion to startle those who have fallen into suffering; thus it is called "alarm and fear. This is a metaphor for the sons receiving [the teaching];
because they are granted happiness by the Buddha, it is called "joy. One should know that while the Tathāgata extracts suffering, his fundamental intent lies in bestowing happiness. Sons...

"Receiving and delighting" and "already knowing how to extract from suffering"—the meaning of these two points is identical; they are merely presented interchangeably according to the context of the text.
He then thought: "My wealth and storehouses now have one to whom they may be entrusted. For a long time I have longed for this son, yet had no means of seeing him.
That he has suddenly come of his own accord is most agreeable to my wishes. Although I am advanced in years, I still cherish [this wealth] deeply."
This fourth father beholds his son’s fulfillment of his wish. In the past, he saw sentient beings decline from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Small;
like those seeking food in a poor neighborhood, they faced hardships in sustaining their lives. He constantly desired to give them wealth, but finding no opportunity, he could not do so.

This describes how, since they declined from the Great, they have entered the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); as the Great Dharma was no longer effective for them, he sought to employ the Small. Yet even the Small has not been achieved; thus, he gives them wealth.

It was not permitted. Today, their minor capacities have gradually begun to emerge; therefore, I employed skillful means. Now that their minor capacities have reached this point, they know that the Great [Vehicle] is not far off.
This accords with my great compassionate heart, and for this reason I rejoice. Since there is now ground upon which to entrust the wealth, the property and such are now being entrusted.
I have constantly reflected that when these sons left home, they retreated from the Great [Vehicle]; it was not merely that they were poor and lacked great riches.
Furthermore, they wander through birth and death, oppressed by manifold sufferings and pained by my great compassion; therefore, it is said that I constantly think of them.

Although I wish to rescue and deliver them, they lack the capacity [for liberation] and cannot be saved; therefore, it is said that there is no way to see them. Now, there are sentient beings with the capacity for deliverance;
therefore, it is said that they have suddenly come of their own accord. Because this accords with my great compassion, it is said that it perfectly fulfills my wishes. I...

"Though my years are old, I still remain greedy and sparing"—this explains the reason for his fulfillment of his original vow. He says "my years are old" because his transformation of one lifetime has come to an end;
yet, having not yet encountered a great capacity [for the Dharma], the teaching has not been entrusted to another.

He says he is "greedy and sparing" because he ponders from whom those of the future generation shall obtain liberation, acting thus for the sake of those who are to be saved. Now that the capacity [of beings] comes to him spontaneously, he is free from such anxieties; therefore, his vow is fulfilled.
"Such is my wish. △ Below, from "He immediately sent his attendants away," this section clarifies the third analogy: that of the pursuit and enticement.

This refers proximately to the second part of the preceding "Opening Analogy of the Burning House"—the abandonment of the stools and the provision of the carts—and distantly to the "Dharma-Exposition" passage beginning with "I first sat at the site of enlightenment," which signifies the setting aside of the Great [Vehicle] to bestow the Small [Vehicle].
This text is divided into two parts; the first concerns the dispatching of the attendants to pursue [the children].
Next, two people are sent to entice [the children]. The preceding section on the pursuit involves those with physical strength who do not employ it;

rather, the "Expedient Means" chapter provides a general admonition and exhortation as one unit. The commentary on the text is divided into three parts. Next, the "Burning House" chapter provides exhortations for departure and admonitions, each explained as threefold, though the text on their release is abbreviated.
In the prose (*gadya*), the exhortations are combined while the admonitions are not; however, regarding the text on the cessation of the transformation, [the structure remains the same].

In the prose [of the Lotus Sutra], the verses only praise the exhortations and do not praise the instructions, nor do they praise the cessation of transformation; thus, there are instances of inclusion and omission.
In the long prose section on the Burning House, the instructions, exhortations, and explanations each have three parts, which are now taken together in this text.

That is to say, "he immediately sent a bystander to run quickly and seize him" takes up the preparatory measures of the aforementioned gate of exhortation; "the impoverished son was startled and alarmed" takes up the [result] of the aforementioned gate of exhortation.

There is no affinity (*muki*). He forcibly drags [the son] back, and although there is the "Appropriate Means" (*ni-i*) in the "Admonition Gate" (*ryōjō kai-mon*), the impoverished son thinks to himself that he is innocent;

consequently, he faints and falls to the ground. This is the absence of affinity in the "Admonition Gate. From the point where the father sees him from afar, the "Exhortation Gate" (*kan-kai-mon*) is combined with the cessation of the transformation (*kise*).
This is an exploration of the Buddha’s intent: even though there is no affinity for the "Appropriate Means" of the exhortation gate, the underlying intention remains...

He did not stop, but further composed a "Gate of Admonition" as a provisional measure. When he could no longer bear the situation, he finally ceased his proselytizing. This concludes the section on the classification and correspondence of the Dharma.
He immediately dispatched an attendant to pursue him in haste and bring him back. At that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him.
This is the first part of the third section, "The Secondary Pursuit of the Two Inducements. It concerns the initial application of the exhortatory gate mentioned above.
Wisdom is that which dispels; the teaching is that which is dispelled. The meaning of principle (*li*) is primary; the meaning of the teaching (*jiao*) is secondary.

From the Buddha emerged the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras, intended for sentient beings; yet those without the capacity do not receive them, regarding them as mere milk. Therefore, it is said that the secondary is dispelled.
"Person. This is an explanation according to the teaching (*yàojiào*). Furthermore, "a bystander" refers to ministers, assistants, and the like;
that is, it means dispatching *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas to preach the Mahāyāna, such as when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* has four bodhisattvas explain the forty stages (*bhūmi*).
This is precisely the dispatching of bystanders. "Running swiftly to seize him" refers to the clear meaning of the Mahāyāna, which reveals the correct [teaching].
Directly. By employing this to respond to opportunities, one swiftly proceeds toward Bodhi; thus, it is said in the *Mahāyāna* [Sūtra] that "it is as swift as the wind.

This is precisely the point. Now, regarding the Bodhisattvas being treated as bystanders: the Bodhisattvas possess their own supernatural powers and are further empowered by the Buddha, such that they too can cause others to swiftly enter Bodhi.
This concludes the section on the method of exhortation (*pravartana-mukha*). This is the aforementioned...
The analogy is as follows: "A householder thought thus... up to "...he led them out from the house. The Dharma-exposition says:
"From the time I first sat at the site of enlightenment, I gazed upon the tree and also practiced walking meditation," up to the passage on the "subtle and supreme" [Dharma].
The impoverished son was startled and alarmed; he cried out in grievance, "I have done you no wrong! Why do you seize me?
This is the third instance of a bystander pursuing [the son] within the initial stage of exhortation, where there are two types of lack of affinity (*anādhimukti*).

Since it is evident that there is no affinity—whether because he previously awakened [to the path] but long ago abandoned it so that he no longer remembers, or because suddenly hearing the Great Teaching contradicts his mind and thus causes alarm—he does not recognize [it].
Therefore, they are startled. As for those who cry out, lamenting their grievances: in the Hīnayāna, afflictions (*kleśa*) are regarded as enemies and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as suffering.

If one were to exhort them that afflictions are themselves bodhi, they would cry out loudly, protesting that it is an injustice. If they hear that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, [they would likewise protest].
He cried out loudly, professing his suffering. Because he lacked the capacity for the Mahāyāna, he did not accept the gate of exhortation.
"I have not offended you" means, "I have not made any request of you; for what reason do you use this Great Teaching to transform me? This summarizes two points regarding the gate of exhortation.
Having failed to receive it, he ceased his transformation; as the previous analogy stated: "He further reflected that there was only one gate, yet it was narrow and small."
The Dharma discourse says: "Sentient beings have dull faculties; attached to pleasure, they are blinded by ignorance.
Thus, the messenger seizes them ever more tightly and forcibly drags them back.
This is the first of the preliminary instructions within the second section, the Gate of Receiving Understanding, from among the three supplementary sections.
The preceding explanation of exhorting toward goodness was still characterized by a degree of leniency; "I shall now speak of matters of fear" refers to urgency.
"Forcibly leading him back" means admonishing with words of suffering to cause him to distance himself from evil. Since he lacks the internal capacity [to respond], [the Buddha acts thus].
"To be externally constrained by the Great Transformation" means to be forcibly dragged back. This refers to the passage previously cited: "I shall speak to you of things that inspire fear;
this house is already burning; it is fitting that you emerge quickly at once. This is the textual meaning.
At that time, the impoverished son thought to himself, "Though I am innocent, I have been imprisoned; this must mean certain death.
He became even more terrified, fainted, and fell to the ground.
This is the second instance of a lack of capacity within the second section, the Gate of Receiving Admonition, of the third part, the Pursuit from the Side. As for "the sinner":
It is also because of compassion. Because sentient beings have committed offenses, they enter the prison of birth and death; the Bodhisattva likewise enters that prison due to their own offense.
Those of the Two Vehicles lack the mind of great compassion and are thus termed "offense-free"; yet by causing [sentient beings] to enter birth and death, they themselves are thereby imprisoned.
Lacking great skillful means, they enter into birth and death; they will inevitably and forever lose the life-force of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles.

Therefore, it is said they "will surely die. Contemplating such matters, it is said they become "even more terrified. Because their small intelligence cannot comprehend the Great Teaching, they are "faint and unconscious.
They immediately give rise to slander and will certainly fall into the three miserable realms; therefore, it is said they "fall to the ground. This is also [the meaning].
"Confused and distressed" means they are submerged in the ground of ignorance (*avidyā*).

This concludes the preceding section on how the father, despite his compassion, [observes] that the sons—down to the point where it asks "what is the house? and "what is the loss?"—lack the capacity for the teaching.
Below this, from the passage "The father sees them from afar," is the third section, which consolidates the two preceding gates of exhortation and admonition to cease the Mahāyāna transformation.

This consists of four parts: first, contemplating the transformation of cessation; second, explaining the transformation of cessation; third, the actual transformation of cessation; and fourth, the appropriateness of the transformation of cessation.

Regarding the first, there are two points: first, knowing that those with great aspirations are weak; second, knowing that those with small aspirations are strong. This concludes the division of the text.
The father saw him from afar and said to his messenger, "There is no need for this man; do not force him to come.
Among those pursued by the side, he was the third son transformed [in the process]; he was the first to contemplate transformation, knowing that his great ambition was weak.

As for "the father seeing from afar": because the child has departed to a great distance, it is called "afar. Because he is a son with whom [the father] has established a karmic connection, it is said that "he sees him.

Regarding the phrase "speaking to the messenger": in terms of the provisional teaching (*yōkyō*), the messenger is the teaching; the fundamental wisdom (*chi*) expounds the teaching, and when the wisdom perceives no receptive capacity (*ki*), the wisdom ceases and thus the teaching ceases.
In terms of the person as the messenger, he speaks to the various bodhisattvas: "There is no need to manifest your honor."

The wondrous body is made visible to those of the Two Vehicles. In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, his bodily fragrance was withdrawn so that those sentient beings would not give rise to deluded attachments.
When Samantabhadra entered this Sahā world, he contracted his body to make it small; all such instances carry this same meaning.
"Do not force those who come" means that since they lack the great capacity for awakening (*mahā-indriya*), one fears it might damage their roots of goodness; therefore, it says "do not force.
Furthermore, "one need not [rely on] this person" refers to the appropriate application of the gate of ceasing exhortation through contemplation.
"Do not force those who come" is the textual passage concerning the appropriate application of the gate of ceasing admonition through contemplation.
Sprinkle cold water on the face to cause them to regain consciousness; do not speak with them again. This refers to those of small resolve who are stubborn.

Regarding "sprinkling cold water on the face": it means one should appropriately sever the flow of water through the principle of ash, thereby removing the heat of the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*).
As for "the face," it is explained by way of "orientation": aversion toward birth-and-death is called "turning away," while orientation toward *nirvāṇa* is called "facing."
The "face" refers to the capacity [of the listener], not that the Nirvana bestowed upon them is called the face.

For one who has awakened, the Buddha opens the bestowal of the Lesser Teaching (Hīnayāna), adapting it to suit their capacity so that they may be freed from vexation and realize the Four Noble Truths.

"Do not speak with him again" means that the teaching and transformation of the Mahāyāna must certainly cease. This concludes the two passages concerning the first contemplation on ceasing the transformation.
Why is this? Because the father knew that his son’s disposition was base and inferior, while he himself was noble and wealthy—a status difficult for the son to accept.
Having recognized him as his own son, he employed skillful means and did not tell others, "This is my son."
This explains the intention behind ceasing his transformative activity. [The Buddha] was truly weary of suffering and delighted in emptiness;

yet, because they were intimately associated with the inferior and lacked a heart of compassion, they feared and found the Great Dharma difficult. Thus, he temporarily allowed them to follow their lesser aspirations, suppressing his original intent. For this reason, he ceased his transformative activity.
He clearly knows that at the sites of twenty trillion Buddhas, he had previously resolved upon the Great Vehicle; it is not that he entirely lacked the great capacity.
For the time being, the Buddha’s great transformation has ceased, yet his intention is not yet exhausted, so he awaits a later period. As for not speaking to others:

within the former teachings of the partial and limited vehicles, he spoke according to the intentions of others, using skillful means to provide protection by calling himself a śrāvaka, rather than speaking according to his own [true] nature.
The messenger spoke: "This is a bodhisattva. Thus, he ceased his transformative activity through the aforementioned door of exhortation, saying:
"Or perhaps you shall fall and be consumed by fire.
The messenger then said to him: "I now release you; go wherever you wish."
This clearly explains the cessation of the great transformation. "I now release you" means that he knew the great capacity [of the beings] was weak.
"Go wherever you wish" means that he knew their minor roots of goodness were strong. Due to these two conditions, he ceased the great transformation;
this corresponds to the aforementioned teaching through Dharma, where he said, "I would rather not preach the Dharma, but quickly enter nirvana."
The impoverished son rejoiced, having attained what he had never experienced before. Rising from the ground, he went to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing.
This is the fourth stage of the cessation of transformation according to capacity; because he was not coerced by the Great Teaching, he rejoiced.

Having avoided the grave sin of slandering the Dharma, he was spared from the three miserable realms; thus it is said he "rose from the ground. Because a small measure of goodness had arisen within him, it is said "and..."
He rises. Furthermore, previously he was suited for the Great Dharma, yet he was bewildered and unable to understand, lying upon the ground of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Now, by being accommodated with the Small [Vehicle], he may attain awakening; thus it is said that he "rises from the ground.

Within the Four Noble Truths, because he seeks the methods of the Path, it is said that he "goes to a poor village to seek food and clothing. Or, within the four [wrong] views, he seeks the methods of the Path; therefore—

This refers to the "poor district. It corresponds to the passage in the *Jie-men* (Chapter on Precepts) regarding the cessation of his proselytizing, which states: "He merely ran back and forth, looking for his father.
This concludes the section from the "Cold Water" episode above up to this point, ending the text on the cessation of his proselytizing. It begins with the passage: "He then dispatched bystanders."
This concludes the section on "guiding those nearby. From the following passage, "Now, wishing to entice and lead them," onwards, there are two types of guidance.

The first, "teaching in accordance with [their capacity]," near at hand refers to the saving of the children by means of the three vehicles within the Burning House parable; at a distance, it refers to the provisional application of skillful means (*upāya*) taught in the Dharma-exposition at Vārāṇasī.
Next, from the passage beginning "Furthermore, on another day," one takes the underlying intent to guide those who have long been illuminated upon the stages of the *dharmakāya*.

Expedient means (*upāya*). It was not at the Bodhi tree that he first realized the utility of the minor [teachings]. Having early on discerned the difficulties of sentient beings, he manifested the *vairocana-kāya* (the Honored One’s Special Form).

Thus, by intimately associating with those in soiled robes, he traced back to former events to establish his present interpretation. Question: For what reason were the four great disciples able to know that the Dharma-body had long been illuminating?
Answer: By inferring the near, one knows the distant. Had he not known from the start at the Bodhi tree that there was no great capacity [among them], [they would not have been able to perceive it].
He should descend as a spirit from Tuṣita Heaven; with perfect wisdom, he takes conception in a womb, even manifesting the presence of afflictions by taking a consort and fathering a son.

Following the thirty-four moments of mind, his final body severs the fetters. Thus it is verified that he has transcended the ocean of marks, both great and small, and is adorned with subtle and wondrous璎珞 (necklaces).

Furthermore, he has long been wearing coarse, shabby, and soiled robes sixteen feet in length. Now, regarding the first section of this lower part, which explains the "guiding" of the *Samantabhadra* teachings, the text of the "Parable Chapter" consists of four parts:
first, employing skillful means as a provisional suitability; second, knowing the prior inclinations of the mind.
Third, the three praises of the three vehicles; fourth, the fulfillment of their wishes. The "Expedient Means" chapter likewise has four [sections], and the present summary also has four.

Having completed the division of the text to indicate its structure: at that time, the elder, wishing to entice his sons, established an expedient means by secretly dispatching two men whose appearance and form—
"You, who are haggard and lack majesty, should go to that man and say to him: 'There is work here; I will give you double wages.
If the poor son agrees, bring him here and set him to work. If he asks what kind of work he is to do, you may simply tell him this."
"We hire you to remove the filth; the two of us shall also work together with you.

This is the second clarification of the text regarding the inducement of the two individuals. Within the initial section on the unification of teachings, the first contemplation is a minor proposal of what is appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "intending to entice and lead": since the Great Transformation has ceased, it would be unacceptable to leave [beings] abandoned in isolation.

Therefore, he intends to establish skillful means; thus he says, "intending to," and so forth. Regarding the statement "secretly dispatching two people": the four disciples were each assigned their own respective divisions, and as they did not involve the Bodhisattvas, he speaks of "two people.
If categorized by phenomena (*dharma*), these refer to the Four Noble Truths of Dependent Origination; if categorized by principle (*li*), they refer to the ultimate and conventional truths.

"Regarding the persons," this refers to the two types: the *śrāvaka* and the *pratyekabuddha*. One should know that "secretly dispatching" (*miqiàn*) here indicates the initial suitability for the Mahāyāna.
If one were to speak from a peripheral perspective, it would represent the Single Truth, the single teaching of the Mahāyāna, and the single person of the Bodhisattva.

Now, in clarifying the provisional means (*upāya*), the concealment of the ultimate reality is termed "secret," while the pointing toward the partial truth is termed "dispatching. In terms of the doctrinal classification (*jiaojie*), it conceals the full [truth].
"Characters" refers to the "secret. "Refuting the half-words" refers to the person: because they secretly maintain the practice of a bodhisattva within, it is called "secret";

because they outwardly manifest as a śrāvaka, it is called "refuting. Regarding "physical form": in the teachings of the two vehicles, one does not cultivate the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), but only speaks of suffering, impermanence, and impurity;
this is what is meant by a "withered physical form. Regarding the person, this refers to the various bodhisattvas.

Concealing its original essence, it manifests through provisional forms; this is not a definitive teaching (nītārtha). Lacking the ten powers (daśabala) and the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), it is said to be without majestic authority.
"You may go to him" refers to employing the Lesser Teaching (Hīnayāna) to suit those of lesser capacity.

Because the Great Teaching clarifies the true principle, it says to "run swiftly and seize him. Because the Lesser Teaching clarifies the principle through circuitous and obscure means, it says to proceed slowly.
[The Buddha] spoke: "This 'place of action' refers to the two paths of seeing and cultivation; these are the places where delusions are severed.

To 'give you double the price' means that while the five precepts and ten wholesome acts merely prevent one from falling into the three miserable realms, the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination can enable one to transcend birth and death—this constitutes one fold.
Furthermore, the six practices of the non-Buddhists can only suppress delusions, whereas now, by cultivating the Four Noble Truths..."
Thus one is able to sever delusions and attain Nirvana; this constitutes the second doubling. As for the impoverished son’s consent:

if there is the capacity [for understanding], this is consent, and the teaching is accordingly established; if there is no capacity, this is non-consent, and the teaching is not established. What is it that you wish to do?
The followers of the Two Vehicles desire only to eliminate afflictions and realize the fruit of enlightenment; they do not concern themselves with purifying buddha-lands or maturing sentient beings.
This is why it is said that [the Buddha] "hired you to remove dung.

When it is said, "We two shall also work together with you," this refers to those of dull faculties among the Two Vehicles who must rely on the teachings to practice before they can cultivate their tasks. From the perspective of principle, this means that wisdom and the truths mutually support one another.
Regarding "the person": this refers to the provisional person practicing together with the real person.

This corresponds to the passage in the preceding parable, "I shall now go and escape this harm," as well as the passage in the Dharma-exposition from "recalling the Buddhas of the past" up to "the path that I have now attained."
At that time, the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son; having found him, [the father] said, "I have already found him.

This belongs to the second section of the "Teaching through Equalization" (*zhìjiào*). Because he knew the son had the capacity (*yǒujī*), and having thoroughly ascertained that he possessed such capacity, it is said, "having already found him.

In the analogy of the sections, this refers to the father knowing that each of his sons previously had their own inclinations and that their dispositions were necessarily directed toward what they favored.
[The Buddha] was attached to [the Lesser Vehicle].
He fully recounted the aforementioned matters.

This is from the third section of the *Zhongjing lüechao* (Summary of the Various Scriptures), concerning the praise of the three vehicles as the primary skillful means for bestowing [the Dharma]. Excluding...

The dung of the origin of suffering is removed by taking the price of the Path and Cessation; this corresponds to the preceding parable where it says, "Whatever rare and precious things you may desire, I shall give them all to you.
In the discourse on the Dharma, it states: "Having reflected upon these matters, he then proceeded to Vārāṇasī. This is the text.
At that time, the impoverished son first took the wages and immediately began clearing away the refuse. When the father saw his son, he felt pity for him and marveled at this.

This is the fourth stage of the "Teaching through Equalization," concerning the reception, practice, awakening, and entry [into the path]. The phrase "the impoverished son first took the wages" and so forth refers to the acceptance of the aforementioned initial aspiration and the struggle to exit the burning house.
Those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) long for the fruit and thus practice the cause; this is why they "first take" [the wages].
Regarding "the father, seeing his son, pities and marvels at him": he marvels that [the son] does not seek the Buddha-way;

he pities him for having attained the fruit of an Arhat, for what has been lost is great while what has been gained is meager—hence the word "marvels. This concludes the section on the "Equal Teaching" within the analogy of "Receiving the Dharma.
One should know that this "Reception of the Equal Teaching" concerns, for the time being, the initial stage of the gradual teaching; it is so named because that which was received is small.

"Equaling the teaching" (*qi jiao*) refers to comprehension through the literal text. This corresponds to the section on the parable above, where the sons, upon hearing of the playthings described by their father, compete to exit the burning house.
In the "Dharma-exposition" (*fashuo*), this is termed the "turning of the wheel of Dharma" (*zhuan falun*) up to the names for the distinctions between the Dharma and the Sangha;

this constitutes the first part of "comprehension through inducement" (*yu zhong*). The section on "equaling the teaching" concludes here. From below, it is called "exploring comprehension" (*tanting*), which means comprehension by grasping the underlying intent.
The Buddha’s spiritual wisdom has shone forth from of old, and he has long employed skillful means, pursuing [his children] through difficult terrain;
it was not only beneath the tree that he first perceived the causal conditions, as has already been explained above. This text consists of four parts:

first, from "Furthermore, on another day," taking the general intent, he had long desired to apply his provisional wisdom; second, seeing his son's emaciated appearance, this is the long-known application of expedient means.

Regarding their playthings: the three liberations range from the subtle to the coarse; having long known this, they must be exhorted toward the three vehicles. Fourth, the father personally instructs his sons;
having long known this, they receive and practice that which accords with their wishes. This concludes the analysis of the text.
Furthermore, on another day, he saw his son’s body from afar through the window;

this refers to the initial section concerning the Buddha abiding in the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). First, by means of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), he had long desired to provide a suitable model for him.

The repetition of the word "initially" (*chū*) here is a term used to express gravity and emphasis. It indicates that he is about to take the essential meaning and lead [the reader] to the stage of the Dharma-body.

Having long known the capacities of both the great and the small, he employs the teachings of "one" and "three" to transform beings. To restate the Buddha’s intent, he marks this section with the word "again.
As for "another day," the two vehicles consider their own provisional means as "self" and regard the non-two-vehicle Dharma as "other";
thus, they designate the *dharmakāya* as "other. "Day" refers to time, and it also refers to wisdom; it functions in accordance with the time of the *dharmakāya*.

Wisdom illuminates the capacities [of beings]; therefore, it is said that "another day" refers to this. According to this meaning, true wisdom (real-jñāna) illuminating reality is "self," while expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna) illuminating skillful means is "other.

This is an analysis based on the individual characters (*vyutpatti*). If one further provides an interpretation by combining the characters (*samāsa*), then "receiving" according to the teaching—meaning receiving the activities of the Nirmāṇakāya—is "one's own day," while that which is not the activity of the Nirmāṇakāya is "another's day. This is in reference to transforming others.

Regarding the "teachings limited to the same" (齊教): this refers to both the Dharma and the Parable sections [of the Lotus Sūtra]. Because these pertain only to what exists according to the teachings up until the Deer Park, they are called "teachings limited to the same.
Furthermore, to explain "on other days" (*tadanyadivasa*) in terms of both one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*) and the transformation of others (*parārtha-vinaya*):

if we consider the Tathāgata, the wisdom of his own practice regarding both the provisional and the real is all termed "his own" (*ātman*). As for the Tathāgata’s provisional and real [wisdom] for the transformation of others...
All such illuminations are termed "other. Furthermore, regarding the Tathāgata’s own illumination of both the provisional and the real for himself and others:
illuminating the real is for oneself; illuminating the provisional is for others. This is the time of investigating and receiving the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

At this time, one employs the provisional wisdom that transforms others to illuminate whether the provisional capacities [of sentient beings] exist or do not exist, and to illuminate whether the provisional activities [of transformation] are appropriate or not. All of these are what is illuminated by provisional wisdom.

Therefore, it is said "on another day. If one follows this meaning, it refers to the provisional teachings; it refers to the expedient matters for transforming others, which is why the Two Vehicles speak of their own affairs.
If one probes deeper to understand it, it refers to the expedients for both self and others, which is not merely the affair of the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is called "other.

Although there are these two interpretations, both are established as "another day. Now, relying on what the Two Vehicles have understood, and furthermore following "the other," [it is said "on another day"].
The character for "sun" (*jì*) signifies that which probes and leads forth; it refers to the illumination of capacities within the *dharmakāya*, hence it is called "the other day" (*tāraka*).

"Windows and shutters" (*chuāngyǒu*) signify partiality, which is small; they represent the provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*) illuminating those partial capacities. "Distant" (*yáo*) signifies that the small has departed and the great is far removed.

Therefore, it is called "remote. As for "seeing the son": because he had previously planted great [seeds], he is designated as a "son"; since he was matched with the Great [Vehicle], it is said that he "saw" [it].
Because the window was narrow and constricted, it was not yet suitable for the Great Transformation; therefore, he set aside the Great and bestowed the Small.
One must understand that because the son was separated by the window, how could this relate to the Elder’s fault of partial vision?
Furthermore, since the Elder intended to employ a partial capacity (*ekayāna*), he remained distant from the Perfect [Teaching]; thus it is called "remote" (*yao*).
Moreover, those who "explore and lead" should also be said to belong to the "Equal Teaching," for both refer to the Dharmakāya taking hold of capacities.
Emaciated and haggard, covered in filth, dust, and impurities—this is the second sign of prior knowledge that he once possessed minor playthings;
due to his meager strength from practicing the causal power of wisdom, he is now weak.
The power of merit from cultivating causes is slight, thus one becomes emaciated; fearing internal impermanence, one becomes haggard; encountering the eight external sufferings, one becomes withered;
the four abodes are like dung and soil; and ignorance is like dust and grime.
He immediately removed his necklaces, fine soft upper garments, and ornaments, and put on coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes.
Dust covered his body, and he held a refuse-basket in his right hand, appearing as though he were filled with dread.
This third section is an anticipatory inquiry that praises the rarity of the three vehicles.

"Removing exquisite garments" is a metaphor for concealing the immeasurable merits of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), such as the forty-two stages, the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and *dhāraṇīs*.

"Necklaces" refers to the fine, soft, superior robes of the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*). The "ornaments" refer to the major and minor marks and the ocean-like array of physical characteristics. As for the appearance and attire:

When [the Buddha] was adorned with splendor, his sons were struck with alarm and fear; the followers of the Two Vehicles were not fit to behold such marks and signs of excellence, and for this reason he removed them.
He put on coarse and tattered garments and manifested a body sixteen feet tall—this is "coarseness. To cultivate the patience of birth and the patience of the Dharma is "tatteredness.
To have dust and dirt covering his body signifies that he manifests afflictions, conditioned phenomena, and outflows. To hold a refuse-basket signifies that he merely treats...
He perceives the dharmas of outflows (*āsrava*) belonging to both *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya*; this does not refer to the pure wisdom of the various stages (*bhūmi*).

The left hand is a metaphor for the Real (*tattva*), and the right hand is a metaphor for the Expedient (*upāya*). The application of the expedient is simple and easy; by means of this dharma, he severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and attains Buddhahood, and furthermore, he employs it to transform others.
His appearance of having something to fear demonstrates that he is like those who dread birth and death. Furthermore, there was the cold wind and the horse-barley.

This is merely the retribution for the seven, nine, and ten vexations. △ Below, he addresses the laborers. The fourth section provides an analogy concerning his own sons who have received instruction:

they occupy the stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) and practice the seven categories of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), thereby manifesting the manner of removing filth.
They take to heart the previous instructions, each with courageous vigor; they push and shove one another, racing together in competition and contending for [the task].
The passage on "Leaving the Burning House" consists of seven sections: 1. The analogy of the laborer, which illustrates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

This corresponds to the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). 2. The exhortation to work diligently and not to slacken, which illustrates the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
3. The command, "Ho! Man! Do not go further," which illustrates the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). 4. "Be at ease and settle your mind," which is termed "consolation."

The analogy: it illustrates the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Why are there five? [The passage] below is titled "The Analogy of the Absence of Five Faults," which illustrates the five powers (*pañcabala*).
These preceding four phrases constitute the second stage, that of the inner ordinary person (*ābhyantarapṛthagjana*).

Sixth, the analogy of the elder immediately giving his son a name illustrates the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Seventh, the passage beginning with "Though he rejoices at this encounter" is titled "The Teaching that Constantly Orders the Removal of Dung," which illustrates...
The seven factors of enlightenment—these two phrases constitute the third noble stage.
"Addressing the laborers" refers to the initial address to the laborers;
this is the teaching of the Tripiṭaka and the demonstration of the four foundations of mindfulness, which is the clearing away of filth.

This is the vessel for severing the fetters and the realm where they are extinguished. Thus, the *Śāsanānuśāsanī* (The Teaching Left Behind) states: "Constantly relying on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to practice the Path enables one to shatter the four inversions.

To experience within the burning house the fulfillment of one's aspirations and for each mind to become courageous and sharp is precisely the stage of the outsider (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) possessing the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"You all must exert yourselves; do not be indolent. By means of skillful methods, you shall draw near to that son.
Regarding the instruction "do not be indolent for a second time," this refers to diligent cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catur-smṛtyupasthāna*).
If one becomes indolent, one cannot extinguish the two evils nor give rise to the two virtues. It is through these two forms of diligence that one can generate the fire of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*)."

Pushing and shoving one another within the burning house signifies entering the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). As for "approaching his son by means of skillful means":

although the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have not yet attained the principle, the fire of [wisdom] warms the mind; it is still distant and external, and thus cannot be approached closely.
Because he had first attained the skillful means of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*), he was permitted to stay nearby.
Later, [the master] spoke to him again, saying: "Ho! Man, you shall always work here; do not go elsewhere again. I shall increase your wages.
Whatever you may require—pots, vessels, rice, flour, salt, vinegar, and so forth—do not hesitate or feel any doubt. There are also aged and infirm servants [to assist you]."
"Person": one who must be provided for by others.

"Third": *dhuk* (or *duḥ*) signifies both startling into awareness and reprimanding. In the aforementioned right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), agitation is the factor of wisdom (*prajñā-dharma*), just as a man is of a masculine nature.
The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the factors of concentration (*samādhi-dharma*), just as a woman is of a feminine nature.

Regarding "nature": it is because right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) cannot correspond with the true nature that one utters "Tut! in shock and reproach, causing the mind to abandon distraction and enter stillness;

hence it says, "O man! You who constantly go elsewhere. As for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*) and right efforts, if the movement of the mind is not single-minded, they are not called "constant.
Among the four bases of power (*ṛddhi-pāda*), concentration does not differ from its object; when one contemplates, there is concentration.

Through contemplation, [the afflictions] are severed. Because concentration is severed and focused on a single object, it is constantly one-pointed. Because it is constantly without distraction or movement, it is said:

"Do not go elsewhere again. This still occurs within the process of mutual displacement; it is precisely the stage of the *mūrdhan* (Summit) dharma. Regarding the phrase "I shall increase your price":

within the contemplation of the *uṣmagata* (Heat) dharma, one cannot yet give rise to the truth; however, within the contemplation of *yathābhūta* (as-it-is), one can give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) state. Therefore...

The words are like a price. If there is anything required—whether outflowing or non-outflowing wholesome states, the factors conducive to the Path or the Path itself—they are all sought through the contemplation of "as one wishes," and whatever is desired is immediately obtained.
The essence of the four dhyānas contains the auxiliary branches like a vessel;

the coarse aspect of emptiness of persons is like rice, while the subtle aspect of emptiness of phenomena is like flour. This is the Right Path. Within the Four Truths, there is no contemplation of sixteen truths.

Salt is always salty and vinegar is always sour; these serve as aids to the Path. Just as rice and flour are difficult to eat and must be seasoned with salt and vinegar, so too is the True Path difficult to manifest and requires the assistance of the Aids to the Path.
Do not harbor doubts or difficulties regarding this. This concludes the discussion on the True and the Aided;

it is established within the *Yirui guan* (Contemplation of Accomplishing One's Wishes), and thus one should not doubt that what is to be accomplished can certainly be achieved, just like one’s own property.
Because it is a mental construction (*saṃjñā*), one should not find it difficult. There are also those who are old and decrepit servants;

if one wishes to take direct access [to the object] to act as hands and feet, it is like employing such a servant for labor. Within the contemplation of mental objects (*manasikāra*), there is also this access, though the access is weak and inferior, being like an old and decrepit person.
Although they are no longer in their prime, they are still capable of performing labor. Furthermore, one seeks the principle through the Right Path.

The True Path is weak and has not yet been able to manifest the Truth; it requires the assistance of the Path of Skillful Means (*upāya-mārga*). The nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) serve as assistants to the Path.

These methods are also present within the contemplation of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). If one obtains these aids, they assist the True Path, and one thus becomes a person of "liberation through both" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
The above serves as an analogy for the four bases of psychic power.
"Rest your mind in peace. I am like your father; do not worry further.
Regarding "rest your mind in peace for the fourth time": this means attaining the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), which are stable, firm, and difficult to destroy.

"I am like your father" means that while patience and understanding are adjacent to the Truth (*tattva*), they are merely semblances and not yet reality; therefore, it is said "like a father. It is also "like a son. Do not worry further.
To those who are anxious, he brings peace of mind and destroys their views and afflictions.
Why is this? I am old and advanced in years, while you are young and vigorous.
When you work, you never exhibit deception, indolence, anger, resentment, or complaints; I have never seen you possess such evils as other laborers do. From this day forward—

Regarding the phrase "like a son born [to me]," and fifthly, "I am old and you are young": the Buddha dwells at the end of the Path, having already perfected both wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*); therefore, he is called "old.

You dwell at the beginning of the Path and have not yet attained wisdom and abandonment; thus, you are called "young" or "in the prime of life. This refers to the stage of the *kṣānti-dharma* (the dharma of patience). There is none [beyond this].

Regarding the five transgressions: one attains the five powers and abandons the five unwholesome dharmas. Because of attaining the power of faith, one does not deceive; because of the power of diligence, one does not become indolent;
because of the power of mindfulness, one does not become angry; because of the power of concentration, one does not harbor resentment; and because of the power of wisdom, one does not bear a grudge.
Regarding the phrase "other practitioners" (*anya-kāraka*): in a broad sense, it refers to those of external paths who seek the truth through various views; they are called "other practitioners.

In a narrow sense, it refers to those at the four stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, who have not yet escaped the five faults; they too are called "other practitioners. This text is free from the five faults, which are precisely the five powers (*pañca-bala*).
"From this time forward, like a newborn child" refers to the sixteen moments of the lower stage of patience (*kṣānti*). At that time...
The stages [of patience] are still prolonged. Although the middle stage of patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*) involves a contraction of the contemplation, it is not yet a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).

As for the worldling’s highest stage of patience (*laukikāgradharma*), it is the final momentary mind that borders upon the truth and approaches the noble ones; therefore, this stage is called "the son born according to the likeness" (*tathābhūtajāta*).
This concludes the four stages of the internal ordinary person (*adhyātma-prthagjana*).
Immediately, the elder gave him another name and called him "Son. Regarding the phrase "immediately becoming a son":
he attained the Eightfold Noble Path and entered the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga). Because he then galloped forward with vigor, it is said that he was named "Son.
Since the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma) is not long before the "Truth" (the Path of Seeing), it is said to be "immediate. — *Āgama* [Sūtra].
It is said that there are five kinds of sons of the Buddha: those in the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] and the pratyekabuddha are called the true sons of the Buddha.

For a bodhisattva, because they do not sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the meaning of "son" is not established [in this sense]. However, if one considers them in relation to the two vehicles, because they possess compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*), they may also be called "sons."
At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer;
for this reason, for twenty years he was constantly made to remove dung.
The seventh is the analogy of being constantly made to work as a hired laborer.

Although he is a son, because his contemplation is not yet complete, he still remains in the stage of training (śaikṣa) and has not attained freedom from obstacles; thus, for twenty years he was constantly made to remove dung.

Furthermore, he himself knew that he was not yet fit to succeed to the great estate, but was simply practicing according to the teachings to exhaust suffering. Therefore, it is said: "He still considers himself a lowly hired laborer."

If a person attains the first fruit [of the path] and, weary of the small, aspires to the great, such that the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened, one should immediately bestow upon them the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, there is no need to advance further to sever the remaining residual fetters; this is precisely because they do not abandon their small-scale aspirations, and thus the great capacity does not awaken.
For this reason, one causes them to rely on the teachings to exhaust all outflows (āsrava). Therefore, it is said: "For this reason, during the twenty years..."

He was constantly ordered to remove excrement. As for the statement "twenty years," this refers to one path of vision (*darśanamārga*) consisting of one liberation (*vimokṣa*) and one unimpeded knowledge (*anantarya-jñāna*), and nine paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) consisting of nine unimpeded knowledges and nine liberations; thus it is called "twenty years. This is an explanation based on summing the numbers. Furthermore, it says:

The severing of the fetters within the two paths of seeing and contemplation is called "twenty years. Furthermore, it is said that the five lower-fettering and five upper-fettering [fetters] constitute twenty years.
Again, it is said that because one still severs the delusions of contemplation within the Dharma of the Two Vehicles, it is called twenty years.
Moreover, it is said that based on the two types of practitioners, they together sever the remaining fetters; therefore, it is called twenty years. Furthermore...
Because there were those with the capacities of the two vehicles who came to evoke the Buddha’s response, he said, "It has been twenty years since I saw my son come.
If one remains in the stage of the two vehicles while the Mahāyāna teachings are being turned, this is called "managing the household affairs for twenty years.
Although the expression "twenty years" is the same in both cases, each has its own specific significance; pointing to this single phrase is precisely what constitutes the "struggle to emerge."
"The burning house of the three realms" refers to the stage of practicing the path (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

From the preceding address to the laborers up to these seven passages, this concludes the first analogy—receiving and putting into practice the long-cherished aspiration of the fourth "intimate instruction son.

Starting from the previous command to dispatch a bystander to pursue them urgently, up to this point, constitutes the third "pursuit and enticement" within the section on receiving and understanding [the teaching].
The Dharma parable concludes with the metaphor of abandoning the small couch for the great carriage; this marks the end of the textual section.

From the following passage, "From the mind’s characteristics and essence, one attains faith," onwards, is the fourth major section: the Parable of Entrusting the Household Estate. Before entering the text, four points are first indicated in advance.
The initial division of chapters corresponds to the preceding Dharma parable. The section beginning with "After this" constitutes the fourth [section]: the Entrustment of the Household Estate.

The analogy of karma: it refers proximately to the granting of the great vehicle (*mahāyāna*) in the "Burning House" chapter and so forth, and distantly to the unsurpassed path within the "Teaching of the Dharma.
This consists of two parts: first, the reception; second, the entrustment. Each of these further consists of two parts.

Within the reception of the "Burning House" and the granting of the great vehicle, there are four intended meanings, which are also the four intended meanings for revealing the reality (*tattva*) in the "Expedient Means" chapter. Regarding the two parts of the first section, the first is the characteristic of the mind.

"Embodiment of Faith" corresponds to the passage on receiving relief from calamity; "Entrusting the Family Business" corresponds to the gradual attainment of prosperity and the fulfillment of great aspirations, which corresponds to the passage on requesting the carriage.
Regarding the two points in the subsequent chapter: first, the entrustment of the family business corresponds to the passage on being granted the great carriages;
second, the receipt of that entrustment corresponds to the passage on receiving the carriages with joy. However, since the fourth and fifth [sections] are combined into a single unit, it causes...
Following the text on the Deer Park, there is no entry into the Vaipulya (fangděng) texts.

Although this is the case for the major chapters, upon closer examination, there still exist passages concerning the "avoidance of calamities" (*miǎnnán*) and so forth, which correspond to the teaching of the five periods throughout the Buddha's lifetime. These introductory sections and the entrustment (*fù*) still remain open [to interpretation].
"Leading" (ling) refers to leading [the son] in his karmic affairs; this indicates the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras. "Entrusting the wealth" occurs within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This section concludes the correspondence between the Dharma and the parable. Second, regarding the explanation of the subsequent arising: because the mind’s characteristics are fundamentally trusted, one is entrusted with the family business.
Once the family business is mastered and all knowledge and vision are fully prepared, one accomplishes the great resolve. This is due to the thorough and unimpeded nature of one's will.

Therefore, one may be entrusted with the family business; for this reason, joy arises. Having concluded [the discussion on] the arising [of joy], there are three explanations regarding the reasons for entrusting wealth.

These depend on whether [the capacity] is distant or near. If one does not first instruct [them] in hired labor and provide them with a day’s wage, how could one entrust them with the management of affairs and the handing over of wealth?
Internally, this corresponds to severing the fetters through the Tripiṭaka and becoming capable of hearing the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, thereby receiving purification.
[This is] the name. By turning the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he brings about the entrustment of the treasure.

One should know that working for wages and receiving payment is the remote cause (*dūrayukti*), while embodying faith and being entrusted with the task is the proximate cause (*āsannayukti*). This concludes the explanation of the causes for the entrustment of the treasure.

Fourth, regarding the five flavors (*pañcarasa*), to demonstrate the characteristics of the beginning and end of the exploration and reception [of the Dharma]: furthermore, within the previous analogy of the "enticement," there is the reception of the *Śaikṣa* (Equal) Teaching, which begins from...

The Bodhi tree represents the conclusion of leaving the household. Furthermore, there is the "exploring and leading" [aspect], which begins with the Dharma-body and concludes with the exhaustion of thought.
These two together constitute one beginning and end. Now, this "leading" also has two parts: first, exploring and leading through the four flavors of compassion to bring beings to maturity.
Ultimately, the entrusted wealth culminates in a single flavor. From beginning to end, near and far, these are collectively discussed as the five flavors. What are they?
Namely, the dispatching of a bystander and what that bystander says serves as an analogy for the *Avataṃsaka*’s sudden and perfect teaching;

this is the very first stage. The bystander is likened to the cow, and what he says is likened to milk. Internally, this corresponds to the twelve divisions of the scriptures emerging from the Buddha; this is the first flavor.

Using this to illustrate those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), they have no capacity to receive it; they become bewildered and fall to the ground. For their entire lives, it is like the taste of milk.
Next, the secret dispatching of two persons is explained to teach the method of clearing away filth; this is a metaphor for the period following the cessation of the Great [Vehicle].
In the Deer Park, the Three Vehicles were taught; those of the Lesser Vehicle immediately gained faith, transforming from ordinary beings into sages, like milk being turned into curd.

This internally corresponds to the *Sūtra* emerging from among the twelve divisions of the canon, which is the second flavor. Next, it clarifies that the essence of the mind’s characteristics is one of faith, such that entering and exiting [the stages] is without difficulty.
This is illustrated by the teaching of the Vaipulya scriptures following the Tripitaka, wherein the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* exalts the Great and refutes the Lesser. Second.
Those who have attained the vehicle of Great [Vehicle] do not slander it; those who have been broken down by the Small [Vehicle] do not regress.

This is truly because those of the Tripiṭaka who have severed their fetters pay the price for a single day’s labor, and thus they are permitted to indulge in praise or censure as they wish. If one has not yet severed the fetters, one is unfit to hear the exaltation of the Great;

this is like the previous "Gate of Not Accepting Encouragement. Likewise, one is unfit to hear the breaking down of the Small; this is like the previous "Gate of Not Accepting Admonition. Yet now, one does not slander.

Regarding "non-retrogression": it is because the mind’s nature is one of fundamental faith. Since the parents have already realized the Small Vehicle, they believe that the Great Vehicle is not false.
Having obtained the price of Nirvana, they do not feel resentment even when their own bodies are broken. Although it is not their own business, they neither doubt nor slander it.
This mind is pure and mature, like the production of *navanīta* (fresh butter) from *dadhi* (curd). Internally, this corresponds to the emergence of the Vaipulya Sutras from the Sūtras. Third.
This is the flavor. Next, it clarifies that the elder knows he will soon die;

this corresponds to the subsequent stage where, having attained the mind of the Vaipulya (fangděng), they believe in one another's essence and enter and exit [the teaching] without difficulty, after which the family business is entrusted to them so that they may lead the instruction and become great bodhisattvas.

He spoke of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Having already mastered the various teachings and gained a comprehensive command of the Dharma gates, his mind became clear and his eloquence grew; thus, his longing for and delight in them increased all the more.

He only regretted that he remained at the level of the Lesser Vehicle, which was not his rightful portion. "If I were further granted permission [to enter the Great Vehicle], would it not be a source of joy? he thought.
Thereupon, his mind gradually became clear and expansive, and he accomplished his great resolve. This is like refined butter being produced from fresh butter;
it is the emergence of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* from the Vaipulya sutras, the fourth flavor. Next, regarding the command given to his son as he was about to pass away:
this is a metaphor for that which follows the *Prajñāpāramitā*—the discernment of the celestial nature, the determination of father and son, and the convergence of the three vehicles into one.
Entrusting the Dharma-treasure and bestowing predictions, he expounds the teaching of the Lotus Sūtra. He reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and demonstrates the true reality.
Thus, the doubts of the bodhisattvas are removed and the śrāvakas become Buddhas; all are brought to extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.
This is like extracting clarified butter from matured cream; it is the Great Nirvāṇa emerging from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, which is the fifth flavor.

Thus it is. The four great disciples deeply grasped the Buddha’s intent and took charge of the entirety of his transformation of beings. The sequence of the five-flavored teachings from beginning to end is clearly evident in the scriptural texts;
this explicit account emerges from here. By means of the five flavors, the demonstration of taking charge of the teaching from its inception to its completion is concluded.
Regarding the passage on first assuming the family estate, it is divided into two parts: first, the mutual confirmation of the essence; second, the command to assume the estate.

Within the mutual confirmation of the essence, there are again two sections: first, clarifying the mutual confirmation of the mental aspect; second, [the patriarch] still remaining in his original position. This concludes the textual division.
After this period has passed, they come to understand one another’s minds and trust each other’s essence; thus, there is no difficulty in their coming and going.

This is the initial stage of inheriting the family business. "Inheriting the understanding of one another’s minds and trusting each other’s essence" refers to the third stage, the time of the *Samatā* (Equality).
"Mutual appearance" (*xiang*) means mutual trust. That is to say, within the Tripitaka, one obtains the price of Nirvana; since this is not false, it is now for...
The Bodhisattva’s preaching of this Mahāyāna is likewise not false; this is like a son believing his father.

The Buddha knows that such beings have already severed their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and thus will certainly not slander the Mahāyāna upon hearing it. With their untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) sharpened, they give rise to faith even upon hearing subtle teachings;
this is like a father believing his son. Because of this, they perceive the exalted and unique body (*vairocana-kāya*) of the Vaipulya sūtras and hear the Mahāyāna teaching—this is called...
This is called "entering. Furthermore, being rebuked and refuted, one still sees the sixteen-foot [Buddha] preaching the Dharma of the Small Vehicle; this is called "exiting.
Regarding these entries and exits of the Great and Small Vehicles, there is no cause for doubt or difficulty.
However, that which it abides in still remains in its original place.
Regarding this second stage of "experiencing within the realization of the characteristics of the mind":

although there is no difficulty in entering and emerging [from samādhi], one regards this as the business of a bodhisattva rather than a portion of one's own wisdom, and thus is unwilling to turn from the small toward the great.
It is like an Arhat who does not say that he shall become a Buddha in the future; this also encompasses the teachings of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the "Ghee" (Sarpis) stage.
△ From the passage beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One, the elder was ill," it is the second section, which entrusts him with the family business;

this encompasses the Buddha’s command in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* to propagate the teaching of the *Prajñā*, corresponding to the "Clarified Butter" (Navanīta) stage of instruction. Regarding this:
This consists of two parts. First, being appointed to oversee household affairs; second, receiving the appointment and taking charge. Each of these two chapters is divided into four sections.

Regarding the first four: first, clarifying the timing; second, formally appointing one to oversee household affairs; third, admonishing them to embody my intent; fourth, commanding that there be no negligence or loss.
The outline of the chapter divisions is now complete.
World-Honored One, at that time the elder was ill and knew for himself that he would soon die.
This is the first of the four [knowledges] regarding the awareness of the household affairs at the time of death; it clarifies the timing. "Soon to die" means:
Where there is a mechanism for existence, there should be birth; when that mechanism is exhausted, one should pass away, which is death. Now, the Buddha’s transformative mechanism is nearing its end;

his passing will not be long in coming. He spoke to the impoverished son, saying: "I now possess abundant gold, silver, and rare treasures; my granaries and treasuries are overflowing. As for how much is within them—"
Whatever should be taken or given, you know it all;

this is the second aspect of right livelihood, which is knowledge of household affairs. Gold refers to the specific (particular) teachings and principles, while silver refers to the general (universal) teachings and principles.

The ultimate truth elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* does not exceed these two; however, by employing both general and specific terminology, the remaining two truths are already subsumed within them.

Furthermore, when practitioners of the Two Vehicles reach this stage, they mostly achieve the general and specific [truths], yet it is said that "many" do so because, in principle, they are not actually numerous.

From various perspectives, they may also be said to be many. For example, emptiness is not merely eighteen; rather, it is called the "eighteen kinds of emptiness" when categorized according to the negation of the eighteen dharmas.
"Precious treasures" refers to the exhortation to study the Middle Way: if one understands the principle of the Middle, then all dharma-gates are indeed precious treasures.
The "granary" represents the gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), namely the one hundred and eight *samādhis*. The "storehouse" represents wisdom (*prajñā*).
The "gate" refers to the object of the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*).

It is the treasury of both the general and specific types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), encompassing all meditative absorptions and insights without deficiency. Because it is filled within and overflows without, it is called "overflowing.
Regarding the extent [of its contents], when speaking of *prajñā*, there are two gates: the extensive and the concise. A bodhisattva practicing *prajñā* should understand the concise version.
Regarding the broad characteristics: in brief they are few; in detail they are many. Practicing them oneself is "taking"; transforming others is "giving.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "You should explain this for the sake of the bodhisattvas. Therefore, it says: "You know all of this."
My mind is thus; you should embody this meaning. Why is this? Now, I and you are no different. This is the third admonition. To embody my mind:
the Buddha takes Prajñā as his mind; you, now transmitting the lamp, should speak in accordance with the Buddha’s intention.
Furthermore, those of the Two Vehicles fundamentally understand this as the emptiness of analytical phenomena; you must embody this.
The meaning is that he commanded you to transmit the teaching so as to admonish others to be like him; this is to realize the emptiness of phenomena, for the true principle is non-dual.
Previously, when you were commanded, it was thought you were transmitting the lamp to another; now you know that the Buddha has caused you to recognize the gateway to the essence.
Therefore, it is said: "You should embody this intent. When it says, "Now I and you are no different," this is the explanation of its existence.
Third: First, by being empowered [by the Buddha] to speak, he is no different from the Buddha. Second, according to principle, because all dharmas are suchness (*tathatā*), they are not different;
Subhūti’s suchness and the Tathāgata’s suchness are one single suchness, a non-dual suchness, and thus it is said that they are indeed not different.
Third, regarding the present moment, he has finally realized that the nature of father and son is fundamentally not different; whereas as for those of the two vehicles...
"You should consider yourself as having merely received an empowerment, for your spiritual capacity has not yet been transformed.
You must apply yourself with diligent care and ensure that nothing is lost or omitted.
This is the fourth injunction: do not let anything be lost. First, you are a bodhisattva; preach the teachings of Prajñā."
Do not let it be lost or wasted. Second, regarding the principle: this is precisely your own dharma; you shall employ it at a later time.
Therefore, do not let it be lost or wasted. From the illness of the elder above until this point, the instruction on entrusting the family affairs is concluded.
△ Below this follows the second section, "Receiving the Instruction and Accepting the Mandate," which is further divided into four parts.
At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the instructions and took charge of the various goods—the gold, silver, precious jewels, and all the storehouses;
this was the first instance of his formally receiving the mandate to take charge.
Yet he harbored no desire to take even a single morsel of food.
This was his second absence of longing. Although Subhūti preached the Prajñāpāramitā, he said of himself, "I have no share in it."
However, as for their place of abiding, they remain in their original position; they have not yet been able to relinquish their inferior mind.

This third stage still dwells in its original place. Although one who abides in the stage of an Arhat may aspire to the Great [Vehicle], they have not yet definitively declared their intent to become a Bodhisattva.
One who has not yet relinquished the inferior mind, though they may feel shame regarding the Small [Vehicle], has likewise not yet definitively [committed].
This refers to abandoning minor realizations.
After a short time had passed, the father perceived his son’s intent; his mind gradually became open and expansive, he achieved his great aspiration, and he came to despise his former thoughts.

This fourth father’s knowledge of his son’s intent corresponds to the parable of the neck-rope and the carriage. It signifies that the son has cast aside his former inferior aspiration and desires to seek the Great Way;
thus, the great capacity (*mahāyāna-śakti*) has been awakened. Question: When is this referred to as "a short time"? Answer:

One interpretation states that it refers to the period after the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings were concluded, when [the son] traveled and observed elsewhere, reflecting upon the Mahāyāna Dharma-gates he had received, and gave rise to a mind of longing and delight.
Regarding the investigation into what is lost and what is not lost, such reflections constitute the moment when the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened.

At this time, one is not far from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; therefore, it is said that "but a short time" has passed. Furthermore, it was at the time of preaching the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī* (The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings) that the capacity for the Mahāyāna was awakened.
How is this known? Because within the *Anantamukha-nirhāra*, the seven kinds of skillful means and the immeasurable gradual and sudden [teachings] are clarified. From...
"One dharma arises. Having heard this teaching, he reflected that the three piṭakas and the three vehicles of the past all arise from this one dharma.
Thus, these three vehicles should also enter into the One; this would then be the most proximate and brief time.

Reflecting in this way, his understanding gradually became clear and unobstructed at the conclusion of the four flavors; hence it is said, "gradually. Since there was no disparity in his spiritual capacity, it is said:
His mind became unimpeded and expansive; thus it is said that he accomplished his great resolve. This actual arousal [of the resolve] occurred at the time of the three requests.

From the passage "From the beginning, having passed above this" onwards, until the end of this section, all constitutes the first part of the fourth section, "Receiving the Entrustment," specifically the text on receiving the family estate.
Below this, from the passage "When he was about to pass away," begins the second part: the formal entrustment of the family estate.
The entrustment of the task. This further consists of two parts: first, the entrustment of the task; second, the rejoicing. The first has four sections:

1) at the time of entrusting the task; 2) commanding the son to assemble the multitude as witnesses; 3) establishing the bond between father and son; 4) formally entrusting the family estate. The division of the text is complete.
"When about to pass away" refers to the time of the first entrustment. "About to pass away" clarifies the temporal context:

it is the moment when the conditions for his transformation were nearing their end, after eight years on Vulture Peak preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and announcing his entry into *nirvāṇa*. The *Dharmadhātu-svabhāva-śāstra* states that the Buddha attained...
After this, forty-two years later, he preached the Lotus Sūtra and summoned his son, as well as his kinsmen, kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders; they had all assembled.
Within this entrustment of the task, the second point concerns summoning the assembly of his sons. As for "summoning his sons," these are those who were transformed by twenty trillion Buddhas;
they are called "sons" because their great capacities have reached maturity, and they have gathered from the ten directions like clouds.
This refers to the aforementioned fourfold assembly surrounding him. Furthermore, "assembling his kinsmen" refers to the Dharma-body throughout the ten directions.
The Bodhisattvas who are like shadows and echoes are his kinsmen. This multitude of shadows and echoes were mostly Śākyamuni’s former co-practitioners;
together with the Tathāgata, they were all converted at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas.
Since they all held the relationship of uncles and cousins toward him, he regards them as his kinsmen. As for the "Kings," these refer to all the gradual and sudden sūtras.
There is nothing that does not accord with its expressed meaning, and thus it is called the King of Sūtras. It benefits sentient beings according to their capacities;
