its arising and ceasing occur at different times, and as each section differs, they are termed "kingdoms," all of which claim to be the foremost—this is what constitutes a king.

One must know that now all these minor kings are abolished, and only one sovereign is established; therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is named the King among Kings. Furthermore, one must know this: [The text continues: ...the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is named the King among Kings. Furthermore, one must know: [the rest of the passage follows].

This sutra harmonizes all teachings. Is it not for this reason that kings are assembled? Thus, in the *Anantamukha-sādhaka-nirdeśa* (The Teaching of the Infinite Gate), they were already gathered previously.
It states: "First, the Four Noble Truths and the twelvefold dependent origination were taught; next, the Vaipulya sūtras of the twelve divisions were taught;
and finally, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the ocean-like emptiness were taught. This refers to the universal collection and integration of all sūtras.

The gradual and the sudden teachings are all brought together and entered into this scripture; therefore, it is titled "The Assembly of the King. Within this present scripture, there are no other teachings remaining.
"Section" (bu) refers to the most honored and supreme within a section, acting as the king; "teaching" (jiao) refers to the master of the teaching within that section, acting as the king.

Since the teachings are divided into Great and Small Vehicles, the kings are likewise distinguished by rank—noble or humble—and their realms by breadth or narrowness, while their subjects vary in number and their assets differ from one another.

What they produce differs; thus, within the teachings of the various schools (*nikāya*), there are two paths: the particular and the universal. The particular path bestows grace upon its own realm, while the universal path must return to the Great Kingdom.
Therefore, one knows that both the school-specific teachings and the universal teachings must be harmonized and integrated.

In the past, they were not yet integrated, like two or three petty kings within a single country, each governing the common people without having submitted to the Great Kingdom. Thus, the Teacher of Expedient Means acted as their king.

The name is not non-existent; it simply coexists within the various schools. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), the primary principle is supreme while the subordinate is weak. Once they have attained realization, they shall equally partake in this single transformation.
As there can be no two masters for a people and no two kings for a nation, those who, prior to this, either returned or did not return, were merely minor kings being assisted;
they did not govern independently after being protected. These minor kings originally had no intention of turning their backs on the superior, but it was truly due to the hearts of the people.

They have not yet returned. If the people were to return and follow them, the King’s original unified rule would be restored; one may understand this principle through analogy with the Dharma-assembly.
Those who are like the great ministers are Maitreya and the other great Bodhisattvas, all of whom are Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) beings and are thus called "great ministers.
Those from the first to the ninth stages are the Kṣatriyas, born into the lineage of the Dharma-King. The thirty minds [of the ten abodes] are the householders.
All of these have been transformed by Śākyamuni.
He then declared: "Gentlemen, you should know that this is my son, born of me, in such-and-such a city."
"Abandoning me, he fled and wandered in hardship for over fifty years. His original surname was so-and-so, and my name is so-and-so.
Long ago, while in my native city, I harbored anxiety and searched for him; now, unexpectedly, I have encountered him here. This is truly my son."
"I am truly his father.
This is the third reunion of father and son. He has indeed received instruction from me; he is truly my son.
He has attained understanding through me; he is born of me. Indeed, I have constantly taught the Great Dharma to him in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas."
Therefore, I am truly his father. Regarding "in a certain city," the texts of this sutra are more numerous in the Western lands (India), while those translated here are very few;

perhaps it refers to the ancient names of the person, the country, and the land, as in the case of the *Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū* parable, whereas here the names are abbreviated and one simply says "so-and-so.
These sentient beings turn their backs on this Mahāyāna and give rise to ignorance.

In darkness, he has fled into the cycle of birth and death; hence, it is said that he has "escaped. Having fully traversed the six realms of existence, it is said that "more than fifty years" have passed.

In the past, while in this very city, he harbored anxiety and searched for him; from the time of his abiding in the stage of the Dharma-body, he has constantly used his two wisdoms to observe and seek out those with the capacity for transformation.
Only today has the resonance between cause and effect been realized; hence, it is said that he was suddenly found "here."
It was encountered by chance.
Whatever wealth and property I now possess are all yours; the previous expenditures and receipts are known to you.
This fourth section is the formal entrustment of the family business. It is the cause for all the myriad practices of the Mahāyāna and the fruit of all its myriad virtues;

therefore, it is called "all that exists. Regarding the statement, "What was previously brought forth and sent out is what the son knows," this refers back to the instructions received in the past from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
That which was entrusted—both the extensive and abbreviated *Prajñāpāramitā*, as well as the common and uncommon dharmas—is what belongs to you.
"Know that this is yours. Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra clarifies only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and does not further elaborate upon all the various aspects of practice.
Having thus completed the entrustment of the family estate.

World-Honored One, at that time the impoverished son, hearing these words from his father, was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before, and he thought to himself:
"Originally I had no intention of seeking anything; yet now this treasure store has come to me spontaneously."

This is within the context of the entrustment of the task. Second, they attained joy upon receiving the entrustment; each mounted a great carriage as described above and experienced what they had never known before.
Previously, they looked back upon themselves and felt no aspiration for the Buddha-way, yet now they suddenly hear that they have received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood;

thus it is said that "it was obtained without seeking. In the *Tripiṭaka*, their original mind did not seek it; in the *Vaipulya* (fangdeng), they were ashamed of the Lesser Vehicle and aspired to the Greater.
Because it has been severed, he does not seek it. Within the *prajñā*, although he perceives it, he does not seek it because it is not his own portion.
It is through such non-seeking that he now attains it spontaneously. The above concludes the fourth major section, the analogy of receiving the family estate.

From the beginning with "At that time, World-Honored One, the impoverished son... up to "...having completed his hiring," the second major division, the text on the opening of the analogy, is finished.
The following section combines the text. △ From "The World-Honored One, the Great Rich Elder" onwards, this is the second instance of combining the preceding parables.
Guangzhai combined them, sometimes placing one before and sometimes after; his explanation was very brief. Now, I shall clarify the meaning according to the text.
I shall no longer elaborate. Regarding the condensation of the scriptural parables, the priority lies in grasping the meaning rather than exhausting oneself with words.

In the following passage concerning the "great wealthy elder," this corresponds to the preceding parable of the father and son who lost each other. The preceding parable consists of four parts: first, the son leaves his father;
second, the father stops halfway in his search for the son; third, the son encounters his original home; and fourth, the father’s anxious concern. Now...
By merely uniting father and son, we collectively attain the remaining meaning.
World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata; we are all like the sons of the Buddha.
This corresponds to the first analogy above regarding the father and son who have lost each other. Thus, the Tathāgata corresponds to the father above, and we all resemble him;
thus, we correspond to the sons above. There are two meanings for the term "resemble": first, taking those of great capacity as sons;

since they previously did not flee, yet they do not occupy the true stage and still dwell among the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), they are said to "resemble" [the sons]. Second, [the second meaning follows...]

Regarding those who take a small-capacity person as their child: although this small capacity resembles the root-nature of the Mahāyāna, even though both the great and small resemble one another, because the karmic connection has not been severed, the status of being a "child" is not lost.
Since the child has fled from the father, they are disparaged as "resembling" a child.

If we speak in terms of the true cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), even one who does not resemble [the father] is still a child; how much more so one who does? Since a connection has already been established, who is not a true child?

According to the account, because the son had previously fled, his father temporarily demoted him; since his status was low while his delusion was deep, the father dismissed him as being "semblance-like.

Question: The initial commentary on this chapter states that he has already "entered the truth. Why, then, is it here called "semblance"? Answer: This refers to when the son fled from his father; therefore, it is called "semblance.
At the beginning of the chapter, it clarifies the moment the son attains awakening today. Thus, your question is incorrect.
The Tathāgata has always said that we are his children.

This corresponds to the second analogy above, that of the father and son meeting. Regarding the former [meeting], there are four aspects: namely, by way of cause, location, characteristics, and so forth.
To escape [the limitations of sequentiality]. There are four ways in which the father sees his son: first, seeing the place where the son is; second, seeing and immediately recognizing him;
third, seeing the son with joy; and fourth, seeing the son’s wish fulfilled. Now, the phrase "seeing the son and immediately recognizing him" alone encompasses the eight preceding points.
Although the phrasing occurs sequentially, their meaning must be simultaneous. Is this not because the very moment the son sees the father is the very moment the father sees the son?

Because they are seen, they are recognized; even though they may flee, the trap will catch them before long. Therefore, the father is also joyful. Thus, we know that a single phrase subsumes all eight.
From here on, the passage beginning with "We [shall employ] the three sufferings" combines with the third section above, which was the analogy of the two pursuers.
Above, there were two pursuers; now, the combination likewise consists of two. In the first instance above, the pursuers were dispatched.
"Next, we pursue them again, and next, we let them go.
World-Honored One, because of these three kinds of suffering, we undergo various torments within birth and death, deluded and ignorant."
This combines with the first section above regarding the parable of sending out attendants to pursue [the deer], specifically the two gates concerning the lack of spiritual capacity (*anabhavyatā*).

In the preceding two gates of exhortation and admonition, it was first discussed individually that there was no suitable capacity; subsequently, it was discussed collectively that the two gates ceased their transformative activity. Now, these three pairs are combined for summary.
This is precisely the combination of the gate of exhortation—“Why am I being seized?”—and the gate of admonition—“I reflect upon myself as being without fault.”

Furthermore, regarding the "three sufferings": because of these three sufferings, the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) are intensified. For this reason, both [the previous] two gates lacked great-capacity practitioners; they were merely capable of being transformed by small means.
Because they are oppressed by the five turbidities, this constitutes the three sufferings. Because they are shrouded by ignorance (avidyā), this constitutes lack of knowledge.
This precisely accords with the fact that the aforementioned two gates of exhortation and warning lacked great-capacity practitioners. It was not appropriate to apply those two gates [to them].
"Appropriate" refers to those who lack the capacity for the two gates [of the Mahāyāna] and are attached to the Lesser Dharma;
this single phrase corresponds to the "small aspirations" mentioned within the previous exhortation to cease the teaching for those of the two gates. This is the preceding analogy.

There are four types of cessation through cultivation (*nirodha-vihāra*): first, cessation through cultivation by reflection; second, cessation through cultivation by explanation; third, cessation through cultivation by correctness; and fourth, cessation through cultivation according to what is appropriate.
The first section has two parts: first, knowing the great is weak; second, knowing the small is strong.
Here, we simply combine the second [part] above, which subsumes the three below as well as the first part above. Therefore, the text above regarding "correctly relinquishing" says: "I..."
"I now release you; go wherever you wish. Since I have already recognized that your aspirations are small, I let you go from this great [teaching].

This letting go is precisely the cessation of my transformative activity. Below, the two preceding metaphors of "enticement" are combined. Above, there was the "probing and leading" through the teaching of equality.
Now, combining these two intentions:
today the World-Honored One has caused us to reflect and cleanse away the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all dharmas.

This corresponds to the third section of the aforementioned *Zhengzong jiaocheng* (The Teaching of the Orthodox Lineage), which fully recounts the preceding matters by extolling the three vehicles. This is the teaching of the aforementioned *Zhengzong*.
There are four [aspects]: first, a brief illustration; second, knowing their prior intentions; third, praising the three vehicles; and fourth, fulfilling their wishes.
Here, by combining the praise of the vehicles mentioned above, one simultaneously attains the other two.
"Among these, we have applied ourselves with diligent effort and obtained the price of a single day’s wages—Nirvana.
Having obtained this, our hearts were filled with great joy; we considered ourselves sufficient and said to ourselves: 'Because of our diligent effort within the Buddha-dharma...'"
The gains obtained are vast and manifold.
This corresponds to the fourth section of the *Shangqijiao* (The Teaching of the Upper Limit): first taking the price, which is precisely the fulfillment of one's vow.
This concludes the summary of the *Shangqijiao*.
However, World-Honored One, you previously knew us.
This initial "conjunction" (he) corresponds to the parable of the son seen from within the upper storey; there were four points in the parable above, but now only three are conjoined.
The formal teaching (*dharmadeśanā*) is not conjoined here, as it is already included in the aforementioned diligent effort in clearing away the filth. Above it was said, "seen from afar," but now...
The phrase "previously known" refers to this. It corresponds to the preceding metaphor regarding suitability.
The mind is attached to base desires and delights in inferior teachings;

this second point corresponds to the preceding metaphor regarding the presence of spiritual capacity. Previously it was said that they were emaciated and haggard; now it is said that their minds are attached.
It is as you wish;
thus, [the father] simply lets you go and does not distinguish that you shall have a share of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the treasure-store.

This third point joins the preceding [section] where the sublime is discarded for the coarse; this is the praise of the three vehicles. The previous passage spoke of immediately discarding the necklaces.
[The father] further clothes [the son] in coarse and tattered garments. This refers to how [the father] now simply leaves him be and does not distinguish his share of the treasure.

This concludes the preceding section on "probing and leading. From the previous passage, "We, because of the three sufferings," up to this point, concludes the secondary pursuit of the two parables of enticement.
Below, from the passage "By the power of skillful means" onwards, corresponds to the preceding parable of "entrusting the family estate."
Above, there are "reliance" (*yiu*) and "entrustment" (*fu*); now, these combined also constitute two. Reliance is twofold: first, mutual trust;
second, delegating tasks. Now, these combined also constitute two. Trust is twofold.
The World-Honored One, through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), speaks of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

This constitutes the first point of the "Conformity with the Superior Mind, Trusting the Essence, and Drawing Near. This clarifies that, while employing the skillful means of the Three Vehicles, he reveals the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna;
thus it is said, "through the power of skillful means," he brings forth and distinguishes the Two Vehicles, and by the power of the Buddha's wisdom, he causes them to enter [the Great Vehicle].
[They] clarify the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If you do not embody this faith, how could you clarify the Buddha’s wisdom before me?
We have obtained from the Buddha the price of a single day of nirvāṇa and consider it a great gain;
thus, we have no aspiration to seek this Mahāyāna.

This concludes the preceding section on "closely following [the teacher] while remaining in one's original location. Below, there is again the section on "departing," which corresponds to the preceding section on "formally taking charge of the household duties.

In the preceding section, there were both "receiving the command" (*ājñā*) and "receiving the instruction" (*anuśāsana*); here, we only correspond to "receiving the instruction. Furthermore, this "receiving" has four aspects:

first, receiving the command; second, having no desire for acquisition; third, not abandoning what is inferior; and fourth, gradually becoming broad and at ease. Here, we only correspond to two of these: receiving the command and having no desire for acquisition.
We hope to receive it.
Furthermore, by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, we shall reveal and expound it for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
This is the initial reception of the mandate and undertaking of the task in accordance with the aforementioned Prajñāpāramitā.
Yet, regarding this [attainment], he has no aspiration;
this corresponds to the preceding "no seeking or grasping," thereby encompassing both the third and fourth [stages]. "Having no aspiration" clarifies that the Buddha exerts his majestic power.
He causes them to speak according to the Buddha’s own mind. Therefore, I have no aspiration for this.
Why is that? The Buddha knows our hearts and that we delight in the Lesser Dharma; thus, by the power of skillful means, he speaks to us in accordance with our inclinations.
Yet we did not know that they were truly the sons of the Buddha.

This explains the aforementioned lack of aspiration to attain [the fruit]; by the power of skillful means, he spoke according to the minds of those following the Hīnayāna, saying that there was no share [for them].
For this reason, we did not know that we were true children of the Buddha, and thus we did not accept it.

When the Buddha says, "By the power of skillful means, he speaks according to us," this means that the Buddha, employing the power of skillful means, taught the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) together with those of the Two Vehicles.

Because we failed to recognize his intention of non-commonality [with the Two Vehicles], we were not true children of the Buddha. The detailed explanation of the task is hereby concluded. △ Now, as for us...
"Knowing the lower" refers to the entrustment of the family business. Regarding the "upper," there are two parts: entrustment and joy. Now, this combined section also has two parts.
Within the "entrustment of the business" above, there were four items; here they are all combined into a single entrustment. This entrustment consists of two sections.
Now we have finally come to know that the World-Honored One has no stinginess regarding the Buddha’s wisdom.
From the very beginning, the Buddha was fundamentally free from any parsimony.
Why is this so? Because although we have long been true sons of the Buddha, we took pleasure only in the Lesser Dharma. If we...
There are those whose hearts delight in the Great [Vehicle]. For them, the Buddha preaches the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Yet, in this present sutra, he speaks only of the One Vehicle, whereas previously, in the presence of bodhisattvas, he disparaged the śrāvakas who delight in the Lesser Dharma. Nevertheless, the Buddha truly teaches and transforms beings through the Mahāyāna.

This explanation shows there is no stinginess; it is precisely because [beings] delight in the Small that the Great was not bestowed early on. When it says "in this sutra, the lower [vehicle]," it cites the present to prove the past.
Since the principle now is one and only, we know that the three [vehicles] of the past were not real.

It was merely because they were not yet capable that, prior to the Great, the Small mind was disparaged, with the intent to cause them to abandon the false and grasp the true. One certainly knows this is not stinginess. However, the Buddha truly...
"You have taught and transformed us with the Mahāyāna and entrusted us with the family legacy;

therefore, we say that originally we had no intention of seeking anything. Now, this great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously, and all that a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been attained."
This corresponds to the preceding "joy" and also represents the meaning of the three kinds of non-seeking.
Beginning with the great wealthy elder, this concludes the four sections within the preceding analogy.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
The verses consist of eighty-six lines and a half; the first seventy-three lines and a half versify what preceded, while the subsequent thirteen lines—

Praising the profundity of the Buddha’s grace. This section consists of two parts. The first part, comprising the initial two stanzas, praises the Dharma-teaching. The latter part, consisting of seventy-one and a half stanzas, praises the aforementioned parables.
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s voice and teaching; we rejoice and leap for joy, having attained what we never had before. Thus spoke the Śrāvakas.
One shall attain Buddhahood; this supreme accumulation of jewels is obtained spontaneously without being sought.
In the first verse of the preceding Dharma-exposition, only "obtained spontaneously" was versified, while "without being sought" was not. △ Hereafter follows the parable.

The preceding verses provide an analogy. This section consists of two parts: first, forty-one verses that provide the analogy; second, thirty and a half lines that provide the application of the analogy.
Regarding the four points of the preceding analogy—first, the loss of the father and son; second, the meeting of the father and son; third, the pursuit and enticement;
and fourth, the entrusting of the business—all of these are now versified. The first thirteen lines verse the loss of the father and son. As for the preceding [loss]...

There are four analogies for the loss [of the son]: first, the son turns his back on his father and departs; second, the father seeks the son; third, the son gradually returns; and fourth, the father longs for the son.

The present verses also consist of four parts, though they do not follow the same order. The first one and a half lines summarize the first analogy, the son turning his back on his father and departing.
The next seven lines summarize the second analogy, the father seeking the son but failing to find him. The final two lines summarize the third analogy.
In the fourth verse, his sorrowful anxiety deepens; next, in four and a half lines, he recalls the third stage, gradually returning closer to his father.
Each of the preceding four sections consists of two [lines].
It is like a young boy who, being immature and lacking discernment, abandons his father and flees, traveling far to another land and wandering through various countries for more than fifty years.
Now, first, regarding the one and a half lines beginning with "For example": this verse only describes the son turning his back on his father and departing;

it does not describe him returning toward the kingdom. In the previous section on the burning house, the term "kingdom" (*rāṣṭra*) referred broadly to the domains ruled by the elder, including cities, towns, and villages.

Here, however, it clarifies that the impoverished son transmigrates through the six realms of existence; the three realms are called "various kingdoms," while the six realms are called "fifty-odd [cities]."

This concludes the section on the years. △ Regarding the passage beginning with "His father grieved and worried," this is the second seven-line stanza. It describes the father’s failure to find his son;
as there were two parts in the preceding prose, there are now likewise two parts in this verse.
His father was filled with anxiety and sought him out in all four directions.
The first half-verse describes how he failed to find his son during that search. This "seeking in all four directions" is not the same as what occurred previously.

The former "four directions" refers to reasoning based on the Four Noble Truths. The present "four directions" refers to searching for sentient beings capable of being delivered among the four modes of birth.
Having grown weary from this search, he stops suddenly at a single city, builds a house, and amuses himself with the five desires; his household is immensely wealthy.
They possessed abundant gold and silver, mother-of-pearl and agate, pearls and lapis lazuli; they owned elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, as well as palanquins, carriages, and vehicles.
They held vast estates and many servants, and their population was numerous. Their income and profits extended throughout other countries, and they were like merchants and traders.
There was no place where he was not present. Surrounded and revered by thousands of millions of followers, he was always cherished by the king;
the ministers and noble clans all honored him together. Because of these various circumstances, many people came and went to see him; such was his great wealth and influence.
He possesses great power and influence.
These six lines and a half of verse do not mean that he abandoned his family affairs due to losing a son.

The phrase "stopping suddenly at a single city" means "suddenly exhausted"; it is a manifestation of his traces, where the meaning of "exhausted" is equivalent to "stopping. Furthermore, it also means "to stop suddenly."
This means that one does not engage in [deluded] practice; it simply refers to seeking and finding the mechanism of the "son" within this very state.
"Building a house" refers to the *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* in other lands. "Raising a house of compassion" relies upon the dwelling of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
"The multitude coming and going" refers to the bodhisattvas from various lands coming and going to hear the Dharma.
Now that I am advanced in years, my anxiety for my son increases all the more. Day and night I reflect on this, for the time of my death is approaching.
My foolish son has been gone from me for over fifty years; what shall become of the treasures and goods in my storehouses?
These two lines surpass the fourth verse in expressing the deepening of his sorrowful anxiety. The preceding passage contained two points;

here, however, it only commemorates the suffering of having first lost his son. He grieves because there is no one to whom he can entrust [his legacy]. One should know that the son has turned his back on his father and departed.
Thus, there is the suffering of losing the son, yet no joy of gaining him; the sorrow of loss and the joy of gain both reside within the father’s heart.
Therefore, at the time of loss, he already harbors joy, for he knows that the son will surely return later.

To observe the workings of karmic conditions from afar, none surpass those of the Buddha. Regarding the terms "night" and "dawn": some say that practicing for oneself is "night," while benefiting others is "dawn."
This should not be so. "Zu" (夙) means early; it refers to rising at dawn. "Ye" (夜) means evening; it refers to dusk.

Dawn represents the beginning of the transformation, while evening represents the end of the transformation. By analogy, the beginning and end of the Great Transformation can be understood in this way.

If the Buddha of six feet constantly preached impermanence, yet when his transformation was about to end, he proclaimed "extinction" joint by joint—if one were to say that his own practice constitutes "night," it would be impossible for him to [proclaim extinction] himself.
"Proceeding" also signifies that the time of death is approaching.

△ Below, from "At that time the impoverished son departed" to the end of the fourth section, two and a half lines, he recites in verse the third section above, "Gradually returning toward his father. The prose text above has two parts; the present verse likewise has two.
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing, traveling from town to town and from country to country;
sometimes he obtained something, and sometimes he obtained nothing. Starving and emaciated, sores and scabs broke out upon his body.
These two lines first provide a verse on the reason for approaching his father: it was because he sought food and clothing.

"From village to village" refers to the mutual interaction between the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), which are like villages; the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) are like kingdoms. Cultivating contaminated wholesome deeds (*sāsrava-kuśala*) is like having something acquired.
Cultivating the virtues of the Two Vehicles is like having nothing to obtain; failing to attain the Dharma-food of the Mahāyāna constitutes hunger.

Lacking great power and function constitutes weakness. Lacking great merit constitutes emaciation. The presence of non-virtuous views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) arising from these states is like sores and scabs.
"Gradually passing through [the lands], he arrived at the city where his father resided.
These two lines commemorate his actual approach to his father's city.

From the preceding "For example, like a young boy" up to this point, the commentary on the first of the four similes from the aforementioned "Opening Simile"—that of the father and son losing each other—is complete. △ Below, from "Hired labor... [the next section begins].
The first seven lines and a half of this verse praise the second analogy above, that of the father and son meeting one another.

The preceding text consisted of two parts; now, the verse likewise consists of two. The first six lines and a half praise the son seeing his father; the subsequent single line praises the father seeing his son.
In the preceding section on the son seeing his father, there were four textual segments; here, only three are versified.
Through successive rounds of hired labor, he eventually arrived at his father’s house.
This first half-verse summarizes the circumstances of seeing his father; it indicates that by means of working for wages, he ultimately reached his father’s residence.
At that time, the elder had set up a great jeweled canopy within his gate.

Seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by his retinue and attended by his guards, some were calculating gold, silver, and precious objects, while others were recording the income and expenditure of his property in written ledgers.
These second two and a half verses explain the third point above, the signs of seeing his father. The previous section clarified the location where he saw his father;
that "location" refers to the side of the gate. Now, by stating that the elder was "within that gate," the specific location is further specified.
He bestowed great jeweled canopies and the like. He perceived his father’s true form, seated upon a lion throne.

As for the statement that "the retribution is that of an elder," this means the retribution is a superior response (*viśiṣṭābhinirvṛtti*). This is because the concise is revealed through the extensive; it is as in the *Avataṃsaka*, where the physical marks, lands, practices, and vows are explained extensively.
The fundamental intent is to use this extensiveness to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby manifesting the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*). [End of] Note.
"Journalist" (記者) refers to the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) mentioned in the preceding text of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Although there are no words of prediction therein, the discussion of predictions found as a secondary discourse within the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*) chapter may also be termed a "prediction. "Bond" (券) refers to the four great vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) that promise to benefit others;
it is like a contractual agreement, for the great vows and their practice are most detailed therein. "Commentary" (疏) refers to cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
One practices; as one cultivates, one repays accordingly. As explained in the commentary, one returns [the debt] step by step until reaching Bodhi, at which point the repayment is finally complete.
Furthermore, in the *Avataṃsaka*, the bodhisattva’s practices and vows largely clarify specific numerical categories, which is termed "calculation."
The impoverished son saw his father, who was noble, wealthy, and majestic; he thought him to be a king or someone of royal rank.
Terrified and wondering at himself, he thought, "Why have I come here? He further reflected to himself, "If I remain for long, I may be coerced or even forcibly compelled to labor."
Having reflected thus, he ran away. He inquired after a poor neighborhood, wishing to go there to seek employment.
The third section, consisting of three and a half lines, corresponds to the fourth [verse] above, which describes the arising of a mind of fear and avoidance.
The Dharma-body is the king and the teacher; the retribution body is the elder. Just as with a king and his like, the above clarifies the son’s perception of his father’s appearance.

[End. △ Below, the single line concerning the elder’s departure summarizes the second section above, "The Father Sees His Son. The preceding text contains four parts: first, the place where he sees his son;
second, his immediate recognition of the son; third, his joy upon seeing him; and fourth, the fulfillment of his wish.
Now, only the first two [of the four] are versified, while the latter two are not.
At that time, the elder was upon the lion throne;
this half-verse versifies the location where he saw his son.
He saw his son from afar and silently recognized him.
These half-verses praise the preceding passage on "seeing the son and immediately recognizing him. The above concludes the second section: the parable of the father and son meeting.

From here below, starting with "He immediately commanded... and extending for ten lines and a half, these verses praise the third section: the opening of the parable regarding the pursuit [of the son].
This is the introductory prose. Now, the first three lines of verse follow upon the preceding prose. Regarding the prose that precedes the verse, there are three parts:
first, calling the son who does not come; second, calling again who does not come; third, letting go.
He immediately commanded his messengers to pursue and seize him and bring him back. The impoverished son was startled and cried out;

these first three lines of verse commemorate the aforementioned point that when calling for one’s child, if there is no responsive capacity (*mūka*), they will not come. This illustrates two meanings: the "gate of exhortation" (*kyōmon*) and the "proposed suitability" (*ni'i*) when there is no responsive capacity.
He fainted and fell to the ground.

The next line praises the aforementioned fact that he did not respond when called a second time; this illustrates two meanings: the prohibition against entering the gate and the lack of spiritual capacity.
This man clings to the notion of a self and will surely be killed; what use are food and clothing? "What has brought me to this state?"—the elder knew his son.
"Stupid and narrow-minded, they do not believe my words; they do not believe that this is their father.
These third and second lines [of the verse] summarize the aforementioned lack of spiritual capacity (*anabhijñatā*). This is a reiteration of the lack of capacity in the two preceding sections.
Because there is no capacity, the transformative activity (*nirmāṇa*) ceases; this is precisely the aforementioned meaning of "releasing and abandoning. The above constitutes three lines.
The verse concludes the preceding analogy. △ Below this, the next seven and a half lines of verse describe the secret dispatching of two men to entice [the son].
The preceding prose section consists of two parts; the present verse likewise consists of two parts. The first three lines of verse correspond to the analogy of hiring laborers.

This refers to the aforementioned "hired labor" (雇作) within the teaching of the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*. The intent of the *Saṃghāṭa* teaching, since its arrival from the Bodhi tree, was to accommodate those of inferior capacity;
thus, the meaning is that of "hired labor. The subsequent four and a half lines of verse praise the aforementioned analogy of hired labor, thereby exploring the underlying meaning of the text.

At the stage of the Dharmakāya, there is no time when he does not feel compassion; how could it ever be that he does not teach? How could he possibly wait for hired labor? This concludes the section on "initial hired labor."
The text consists of four parts: first, the employment of skillful means; second, obtaining [the result] immediately upon seeking it; third, the description of hiring labor;
and fourth, receiving payment for clearing away filth. Here, however, only the first and the last are versified.
Thereupon, using skillful means, he sent other men who were one-eyed, short-statured, and ugly, lacking in majesty and virtue. He told them:
"You may tell him that you will employ you to remove all filth and excrement, and that I shall pay you double wages."

These two lines of verse summarize the first point mentioned above: the employment of skillful means. "One-eyed" refers to being partial toward emptiness. "Dwarfish" refers to being vertically short [in stature].
This indicates not reaching the source of the true reality (*dharmatā*). "Ugly" refers to being horizontally narrow; it signifies lacking the adornment of the manifold virtues of the Mahāyāna.
Not possessing the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) is called "lacking majesty. Being different from the [four] extraordinary qualities of bliss, self, and purity is called "lacking virtue."
Upon hearing this, the impoverished son came joyfully following him to remove filth and purify the various rooms and dwellings.
This single line praises the fourth [stage]: taking wages to remove filth, which purifies the six sense-faculties and the house of the five aggregates.
The above concludes the section on the teaching. Below, the elder departs; the second section consists of four and a half lines, praising the aforementioned instruction to act.
The preceding prose passage consists of four parts; now the verse also consists of four.
The half-verse, "The elder, at the window, constantly saw his son," corresponds to the first part of the prose.
Furthermore, the phrase "on another day, arriving and seeing his son's body from afar" corresponds to the second part.
Reflecting that his son was foolish and inferior, delighting in base matters,
[the father thought of] these half-verses which describe being emaciated and haggard,
even unto being filthy and impure. Thereupon, the elder put on tattered, soiled clothes, took up a dung-removal vessel, and went to where his son was.
This single verse summarizes the foregoing point regarding the abandonment of the sublime for the coarse.

Employing skillful means, he approaches him and urges him to work diligently, saying: "Since I have increased your wages, provided you with oil for anointing your feet, and ensured that your food and drink are sufficient."
"The mats and bedding are thick and warm. Such are the harsh words [spoken]. "You should work diligently," and furthermore, with gentle words: "If you are like my own son.

These two and a half verses praise the aforementioned correct instruction on labor. Above, there are seven categories of Dharma gates; "the words" correspond to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
"Causing one to work diligently" refers to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). "Since I have increased your wages," etc. (follows below).
The first line praises the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Applying oil to the feet enables one to walk upon deep water, which is like supernatural power (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, oil can dispel wind; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is likewise free from agitation. Having food and drink in abundance refers to superior rice and flour.

A thick and warm mat refers to the cultivation of meditative concentration through observation, refinement, and perfuming, which is able to eliminate distraction and movement. Thus he spoke these words of admonition to you.
One should diligently practice the "half-action. This summarizes the fourth [chapter], "Consoling," and the fifth, "The Five Absences of Faults.

Once the faculties and powers are perfected, one is then capable of enduring harsh words; thus, one should also employ "soft speech" for the half-action. This summarizes the sixth, "Forming Characters," and the seventh, "Causing Constant Practice";
both belong to the stage of the "Son. The summary of the "Exploring and Receiving" section is complete. The above summaries trace and induce the Great [Vehicle].
The section concludes. △ From here on, following the Elder, the fortieth verse praises the fourth [section], "Receiving the Entrustment of the Family Business.
The preceding text consists of two parts; the present verse likewise consists of two. Now, the first three and a half lines praise the reasons for entrusting the business.

Next, there are six lines and a half of verse that formally entrust the task. Initially, [the child] was guided by means of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); now, likewise, there are two methods.
The elder possesses wisdom and gradually causes [the child] to enter and exit.
The first half-verse is a general summary of the characteristics and essence of the mind, which corresponds to the aforementioned "entry and exit without difficulty.

△ Below this, the second [half-verse] praises the aforementioned "entrusting the family business through the middle [son]. Regarding the entrustment of the business mentioned above, there are both "life" and "love";
here, only the reception of life is praised. Regarding the four ways of receiving life mentioned above, only three are praised here.
After twenty years had passed, he entrusted him with the management of the household affairs, showing him the gold, silver, pearls, crystal, and all other items,
and ensuring that he understood all matters concerning their income and expenditure.
This one verse and a half first summarizes the aforementioned receiving of the life-span. Regarding the phrase "twenty years," it cannot be understood in the same way as above.
In the previous case, the removal of *darśana-heya* (delusions of views) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions of thought) was termed "twenty years. Here, it clarifies the management of household affairs;

alternatively, it refers to the turning of the Mahāyāna teachings to instruct various bodhisattvas, whereby they sever the distinct delusions of the Mahāyāna—namely, the delusions of views and thought—which is termed "twenty years. Alternatively, it refers to the preaching...

The period of the *Prajñā* [sūtras] was long, lasting for twenty years. Some say that these twenty years refer to the time he resided in the stage of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) while turning the Mahāyāna teachings.
The *Renwang bore boluomi jing* (Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) states it was twenty-eight years; the detailed explanation is as provided above.
He remains outside the gate, dwelling in a grass hut, reflecting on his own poverty and thinking, "I have no such thing.
This verse praises the aforementioned state of still residing in one's original place, having not yet abandoned the inferior mind.
The father knows his son’s mind has gradually become vast and expansive.
This half-verse praises the aforementioned state of being open and at ease, and the movement of the great aspiration of the Mahāyāna faculty.

The above concludes the section on the completion of the entrustment of the task. From the line "Now he wishes to give... onwards, the second section consisting of six and a half lines praises the second main theme.

The entrustment of the family business consists of two parts in the preceding prose; now, the verse likewise has two parts. The first four and a half lines of verse correspond to the actual entrustment of the family business;

the subsequent two lines correspond to the joy of having received the entrustment. In the preceding prose, there were four sections for the actual entrustment of the task, whereas in this verse there are only three.
He does not praise the time, but desires to bestow wealth and goods; he immediately assembles his kinsmen, the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders.
The first verse praises the gathering of kinsmen until they have all assembled.
To this great assembly, he said: "This is my son. He abandoned me and went elsewhere, and fifty years have passed.
It has been twenty years since I saw him come here. Long ago, in a certain city, I lost this son; I traveled everywhere seeking him and have finally arrived here."
The second section consists of two and a half verses, which summarize and confirm the third point: the natural relationship between father and son.
"Whatever I possess—my houses and my people—I entrust them all to him; let him use them as he pleases."
The third verse summarizes the fourth section above, the "True Entrustment. The preceding three sections on the entrustment of the task are now concluded.
The son reflects: "Formerly I was poor and my aspirations were base; yet now, from my father, I have obtained great treasures as well as a house and estate."
All his wealth and possessions [he gave away], feeling immense joy at having attained what he had never experienced before.
This is the second [verse]. These two verses praise the joy of receiving the entrustment mentioned above.

From the passage beginning with "The elder possessed wisdom" up to this point, the fourth section of the opening parable—the handing over of the family estate—is concluded. △ Below, from the words "The Buddha also... onwards [the following continues].

These thirty and a half verses summarize the four preceding analogies. In the preceding section, there were first four instances of father and son losing each other, followed by two instances of father and son meeting.
Within those, there were first four instances of the son seeing the father, and four instances of the father seeing the son.

The current text is abbreviated by combining these; in the subsequent passage, the phrase "The Buddha is also like this" should be linked with the phrase "knowing that I delight in the small [vehicle]."

The upper and lower parts borrow from one another’s momentum; only through their mutual completion is the meaning fully revealed. These two lines combine the two preceding metaphors to provide a comprehensive summary.

If one were to pair "The Buddha is likewise" alone with "Knowing that they delight in the Small Vehicle," each would stand in isolation, resulting in a failure to perceive the correspondence and a lack of clarity in the intended meaning.
The Buddha is also like this.
This single phrase corresponds to the first analogy in the preceding verse regarding father and son losing each other.
This phrase must rely on the following phrase to be fully realized; because [the sons] know and delight in the Lesser Vehicle, in meaning they are "lost" to one another.

The single phrase, "Knowing that I delight in the Lesser [Vehicle]," corresponds to the preceding analogy of father and son meeting. This phrase must rely on the preceding sentence to be fully realized.

Because the Buddha knows that [the disciples] delight in the Lesser, they are able to meet one another. One should understand that this delight in the Lesser arises from having regressed from the Great.
This is why they lose sight of one another: because they regress from the Great [Vehicle] due to delighting in the Small. This is why they see one another;
thus, two phrases must be mutually established to encompass the preceding eight phrases. Knowing the phrase "delighting in the Small" is equivalent to immediately recognizing its meaning.
"I have never said, 'You shall become Buddhas.

This refers to the third of the two preceding metaphors for gradual enticement; these two sentences correspond to the first of the two sub-metaphors within that section—the metaphor of the simultaneous instruction given to those who were being gradually enticed.
Within that previous correspondence, there are two parts: first, the correspondence regarding the failure to respond when called a second time; second, the command to let go.
The present text summarizes its meaning in a general verse: "A single summoning" already encompasses the two aforementioned meanings.
Yet it says, "We have attained all outflows-free states and achieved the stage of a śrāvaka disciple of the Hīnayāna."

This single verse summarizes the preceding analogy of sending two people together to entice [the disciples]. The preceding summary consists of two chapters: "The Uniform Teaching" and "The Investigative Teaching.
Each of these two chapters contains four sections, which correspond to the appropriate capacities of the listeners and praise how the vehicle accords with their aspirations.
Now, this single line merely summarizes that intent in general; since it speaks only of achieving the outflow-free [wisdom], it refers to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
In the teachings, the term "untainted" (*anāsrava*) applies generally to all fruits; however, the term "accomplishment" (*samanvāgata*) refers only to the final stage.

Therefore, it also subsumes both sets of four [fruits]. This concludes the analogy of the "pursuing and inducing. Below this, the Buddha’s command to depart consists of twenty-eight and a half lines, which corresponds to the fourth section:
"Receiving the Family Business. The preceding correspondence has two parts: "Trusting and Entrusting the Task. Now, for the first of these, there are ten [lines].
The first eight lines and a half summarize the detailed practice; the following ten lines summarize the formal entrustment.
Within the section on receiving the mission, there are only two points: first, receiving the mission; second, having no desire for gain.
The Buddha commanded us to expound the supreme path; those who practice it shall attain Buddhahood.

Now, this first verse serves as a prologue to announce what follows. What precedes this is not found in the original [Sanskrit] text. The "supreme path" is none other than the Prajñāpāramitā of Emptiness;
there is nothing superior to it. From "I have received" (*vayaṃ... pratigṛhya*) down to the seventeenth line and a half constitutes the main body of the verse.
Receiving the command and being free from expectations, and so forth; there is no failure to relinquish, and there is thorough composure.
I, following the Buddha’s teaching, act as a great bodhisattva, employing various causes and conditions, diverse parables, and manifold expressions.
They preach the Unsurpassed Way. When the sons of the Buddhas hear the Dharma from me, they contemplate it day and night and practice it with diligent effort.
At that time, all the Buddhas immediately bestow upon them the prediction: "In a future age, you shall become Buddhas. Thus do all the Buddhas [prophesy].
The Dharma of the secret treasury is expounded solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas to reveal its actual reality; it is not for my own sake that these essential truths are taught.
These five lines of verse clarify that when the Buddha’s son hears the Dharma and attains realization during the time of the samādhi of the True Prajñā, he proceeds to teach and benefit others.
At that time, it refers to turning the teaching to transform and edify Bodhisattvas; it does not say it is for my own sake.
△ Below, it proceeds as in that [passage], for twelve and a half lines. The verse lacks the phrase "desiring to take. This text expands upon the above. Furthermore, there are two points:
like that impoverished son who, having approached his father, although he knows of all the goods, does not desire to take them in his heart.
This single verse restates the preceding analogy and applies it [to the subject]. △ From "We... below, the second section consists of eleven and a half lines;
it correctly applies [the analogy] to the absence of seeking or grasping. This is further divided into three parts.
"Although we speak of the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha, we ourselves lack aspiration;

it is likewise so. This single verse correctly praises the absence of seeking. Next, from "We... onwards, there are nine and a half lines concerning the absence of seeking due to being endowed with wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*).
This is further divided into three parts: the thesis (*uddeśa*), the explanation (*nirdeśa*), and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*). The first [the thesis] is twofold.
"We have attained internal extinction; we consider ourselves sufficient. We have understood only this matter, and there is nothing further.

This first verse indicates that because he possesses the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), he has no desire for further attainment. Regarding the term "internal extinction": "internal" refers to the essence of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since the afflictions of the three realms have been exhausted, it is called "internal extinction"; this pertains to the virtue of abandonment.
If we were to hear [of the Buddha’s deeds], such as purifying the Buddha-lands and transforming sentient beings, we would have no joy or delight at all.

The next verse indicates that because he is endowed with the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), there is nothing to be sought or grasped. Since it says "if one hears," hearing the teaching pertains to wisdom;
thus it is called the "virtue of wisdom. Because they possess only small wisdom, they do not rejoice in great wisdom. These two points together illustrate their failure.
The refutation of errors is concluded. △ The following six verses constitute the second section, which provides a dual explanation of the two preceding chapters on Wisdom and Severance.
Why is this so? Because all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent; they are neither arising nor ceasing, and there is neither great nor small.
"Untainted and unconditioned. Reflecting thus, they do not give rise to joy or delight.
The first two verses explain their abiding in a minor stage of abandonment:
"For a long night, we have been without craving or attachment toward the Buddha’s wisdom, and no longer harbor any aspiration for it; yet we remain within the Dharma ourselves."
This refers to the ultimate.
This one verse and a half explains the loss of great wisdom:
"For a long night, we have practiced the dharma of emptiness and attained liberation from the afflictions of suffering within the three realms; we now abide in our final body."
There is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
These one and a half verses re-explain the lesser severance.
Since the Buddha’s teaching has resulted in the attainment of the Way without fail, it is as if one has already attained [the goal] and repaid the Buddha’s grace.
This one verse further explains the loss of great wisdom:
although we have preached the Bodhisattva Dharma to the sons of the Buddhas so that they might seek the Buddha-way, regarding this Dharma...
"Forever without aspiration or delight.
This one and a half verses conclude the explanation that [the Buddha] himself has no desire for acquisition. The above concludes the explanation of being endowed with both wisdom and abandonment.
"The Guide saw me and set me aside; because he observed my mind, he did not initially urge me forward, though he spoke of real benefits."
The third single verse clarifies that the Buddha perceives his abandonment of me; this corresponds to the preceding section on having no desire for acquisition.

From the Buddha’s initial command up to this point, the verses conclude the "Household Affairs" section within the *Prajñā* chapter. Below this, from the ten lines beginning with "Like a wealthy elder," the verses correspond to the "Actual Entrustment of the Task.
This section has two parts: first, the actual entrustment of the task; second, the joy upon receiving the entrustment.
Now, the verses also consist of two parts. The first three lines of verse concern the formal entrustment itself; the subsequent seven lines concern the joy of having received the entrustment.
Within the first three lines, the preceding section generally combined the activity of the formal entrustment; these [lines] likewise provide a general summary thereof.
It is like a wealthy elder who, knowing his son’s inferior disposition, uses the power of skillful means to gently subdue his mind,
and only then entrusts him with all his wealth and treasures.
These one and a half verses cite the analogy and apply it to the case at hand:
"The Buddha is likewise; manifesting rare and marvelous events, he knows those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle and, through the power of skillful means, tames their minds."
He then taught the Great Wisdom.
These one and a half verses are precisely the summary of what was entrusted.
Today we have attained what we never had before; it was not what we previously hoped for, yet now we have obtained it ourselves, just like that impoverished son.
We have obtained immeasurable treasures. World-Honored One, we have now attained the Way and its fruits; regarding the untainted Dharma (anāsrava-dharma), we have attained the pure eye.
Throughout the long night, we upheld the Buddha’s pure precepts, and only today do we finally receive their retribution within the Dharma of the Dharma-King.
Having long practiced the pure conduct, we have now attained the untainted, unsurpassed, and supreme fruit.
We are now truly śrāvakas, who by the sound of the Buddha-way cause all to hear. We are now truly arhats among all the worlds.
Devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās—all among them, he is worthy of receiving offerings.

These seven verses praise the second point within the preceding section on the entrustment of the task: the joy of having received the entrustment. "The World-Honored One" refers to one who has attained the Way;

that is, one who has attained the Way of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). "One who has attained the fruit" refers to one who has partially attained the fruit of practice (*abhyāsa-phala*) of the Mahāyāna. As for the fruit of practice:

When one attains the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), the destruction of one grade of ignorance is termed the "fruit of practice" (*śikṣā-phala*). These two phrases clarify the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "in the untainted, most pure eye": these two phrases clarify the opening of the Buddha’s vision; it is the vision of the principle of true reality (*dharmatā*).
Previously, seeing the untainted did not cause one to fall back to the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); today, seeing the untainted does not cause one to fall back into the two [vehicles].
It is a vehicle. In the past, the eye of wisdom saw emptiness; now, the pure eye sees the Middle Way.

As for us who have reached the fruition of long nights [of practice], it was through formerly maintaining precepts and practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) together to manifest the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
That there is no person who receives this fruition means that within the Dharma of the Dharma King, one reaches the great fruit through the holy life practiced today. Thus, one is able to attain it.

The "outflow-free" (anāsrava) refers to the meaning of the "revealing cause" (vyañjana-hetu) that takes up the fruit. "Maintaining the precepts" refers to the meaning of the "conditioning cause" (pratyaya-hetu).
The principle seen by the pure eye refers to the meaning of the "direct cause" (hetu-hetu). "We are truly equal" and so forth refers to the true stage of the Mahāyāna.

Within the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā), although one’s single voice pervades the three thousandfold world-system, it resembles the Path but is not yet the true Path. Upon entering the ten abodes (daśa-vihāra), it becomes the true Path. True.
An Arhat possesses three meanings; here, only the single meaning of "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat) is cited.

If one does not give rise to the transformation-death (parināmi-cyuti) and slays both the general and specific delusions, this constitutes the meaning of "slayer of thieves" (caura-ghātaka). Being capable of serving as a field of merit for the ten dharma-realms, one is thus "Worthy of Offerings.
The terms "Worthy of Offerings" and "Slayer of Thieves" mutually elucidate one another. The above concludes the preceding verse on the Dharma-exposition.
The World-Honored One’s great kindness is such that, through this rare occurrence, he has compassionately taught and transformed us for our benefit.

Even throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, who could ever repay it? Whether by providing for us with hands and feet, prostrating with head and crown, or offering every form of worship, none of these can repay his grace.
If one were to carry [the Buddha] upon the crown of one's head or bear him on both shoulders for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, honoring him with all one's heart;
and furthermore, were to offer him exquisite food, immeasurable precious robes, various bedding, diverse medicinal decoctions, ox-head sandalwood, and all manner of rare jewels—
Even if one were to build stupas and temples, spread jeweled robes upon the ground, and perform such acts of offering for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
one could never repay [the debt] for the Buddhas' rare, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable power of great supernormal faculties.
Taintless and unconditioned, the King of all dharmas, he is able to condescend to this inferior state for the sake of ordinary people who grasp at signs;
according to what is appropriate, he teaches them. Regarding the Dharma, the Buddhas have attained supreme mastery; they know the various inclinations and desires of all sentient beings.
According to their resolve and strength, and as far as they are capable, he preaches the Dharma using immeasurable parables.
He discerns the various roots of goodness from past lives of sentient beings, and having distinguished through careful deliberation those who are matured and those who are not yet matured,
he teaches the three vehicles as appropriate within the single vehicle path.
These thirteen lines represent Kāśyapa’s conclusion of his exposition and understanding, wherein he praises the Buddha’s profound kindness as difficult to repay.
I privately remark that when it is said the World-Honored One’s great kindness is difficult to repay, one may speak of ten aspects.

First, from the very beginning, the Buddha established compassion, uprooting the suffering of the six realms and bestowing the bliss of the four noble ranks upon the entirety of the ten dharma realms, bringing them into the Four Great Vows; this is the Tathāgata’s chamber.
Gratitude. This first is the universal and all-pervading grace; it is the beginning of the Four Great Vows.

Second, when the Tathāgata practiced the Bodhisattva path, he instructed, taught, benefited, and gladdened others. He once taught me the Mahāyāna; although I may have forgotten it midway, my wisdom and vows have not been lost.
This is indeed the Tathāgata’s chamber—cooling and warm—a grace of great compassion that bestows happiness upon sentient beings. Third, when sentient beings encounter...
He regards only his father with suffering. The Buddha watches for the opportune moment, like a calf following its mother, fully practicing the six perfections to benefit sentient beings.

This is the Tathāgata’s chamber, which wards off cold and shields against heat; it is the grace of Great Compassion that uproots suffering. These two graces—the grace of uprooting and the grace of bestowing—are distinct.
Once one is specifically covered by these within the fulfillment of vows, then after the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), one initiates the practice.
Come! Since before I attained the Way, I have received benefit everywhere. The nature of this benefit does not go beyond bestowing and rescuing;

as for the grace of such bestowal and rescue, how could it ever be repaid? The reason it is difficult to repay is that, first, through the truth of your own practice, you caused me to cultivate the path.
Since I received your teaching, even when I fell back into the great cycle of saṃsāra, your compassion never left me; you bestowed and rescued me everywhere. This—
Third, the kindness of the dwelling: After the four Buddhas had attained enlightenment, they should have enjoyed the bliss of unconditioned nirvana;

yet they concealed their sublime spiritual virtues and employed the Dharma that accords with the inclinations of the poor, demonstrating the vehicle of humans and devas through the five precepts and ten wholesome paths.
By sprinkling cold water upon their faces, they caused them to awaken; this was the kindness of the Buddha’s robe shielding the poor from the heat of desire. Fifth, at the Deer Park...
In the middle [section], he manifested the image of an aged bhikṣu and used skillful means to approach him, providing him with a day’s wages.

This was to cover the Buddha’s robe and remove the suffering of cold and heat; it was the sixth act of giving from the *Vaipulya-samāja*. After this, they came to understand and trust one another in their inner natures.

He then rebuked, censured, and disparaged him, causing him to feel shame for his small-mindedness and to aspire toward the Great Vehicle; this was to conceal the Buddha’s robe and hide his ugliness; it was the seventh [act]. Up until the *Prajñāpāramitā* section...
I commanded him to take charge of my family estate and made him fully acquainted with all my stores of gold and silver;

this was because of the grace of the Buddha’s robe which adorned me. Regarding these four debts of gratitude, since I first received the teachings, I have forgotten both their magnitude and their details.

Having been harmonized in every circumstance and having known that my spiritual capacity had matured, I have suddenly perfected the path—both sudden and gradual—within this realm. Although I was originally intended for those of great capacity, [I have now fulfilled the purpose].
Furthermore, out of concern for my virtuous lineage, he subsequently bestowed upon me his minor teachings. He rebuked and refined me, forging and tempering me like metal on an anvil;
he humbled me by making me tend to a thatched hut and enticed me with the prospect of a wealthy family estate.

Though the sprouts of my past potential have begun to break through, they have not yet blossomed into full splendor. How can I ever repay this long-term grace? This is the fourth [instance] regarding the robe.
This is the grace [of the Tathāgata’s seat]. Eighth, it brings together kinsmen and establishes the relationship between father and son; the peerless treasury of jewels is obtained without seeking.
This is indeed the grace of the Tathāgata’s seat. Ninth and tenth: once seated upon the seat, body and mind become serene, and one swiftly attains peace and stability.
By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, one causes all to hear; all devas and humans universally respond within it.

Receiving offerings, covering [the Buddha] as his seat, and enabling me to fulfill the grace of self-cultivation and the transformation of others—these three graces first yield wondrous benefit at the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while simultaneously allowing one to benefit all beings.

That the grace of these [three], which is difficult to repay once the path of transformation is initially established, is indeed for this reason: because the chamber provides clothing, there is the grace of protection and nourishment.

Because the chamber possesses a seat, it fulfills the functions of both [providing] dwelling and extraction. The seat relies upon the robe and the chamber to enable the practice of oneself and others to be perfected.
The robe relies upon the seat and the chamber to allow the principles of the beginning and the end to be revealed. Therefore, these three meanings combine to form a great kindness.
Regarding this kindness from beginning to end, how can it be repaid? It is said that even bearing such a burden on both shoulders cannot repay it. This is what is meant. Above.
The prose and verse sections are now entirely concluded as the segment on comprehensive understanding and realization.
*The Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Four.
*The Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
with commentary and record by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe;
and annotations added by the Śramaṇa Daowei of Siming.

The fifth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," has already been explained in its general title as previously set forth. The specific title, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," shall now be explained in detail.

This chapter constitutes the third section, the "Explanatory Confirmation," within the middle-level parables for those of middling faculties. First, it is explained according to the *loka-nirukti* (worldly standpoint).
Furthermore, within this chapter, there are mountains, rivers, clouds, rain, and so forth. Why, then, is it specifically titled after "medicinal herbs"?
One must understand that the earth is that which gives birth, while the clouds and rain are that which provide moisture. Grasses and trees are what is born and what is moistened.
Since both that which is born and that which is moistened are universally useful, yet the utility of medicinal herbs is particularly potent; moreover—
The land remains much as it was, while the grasses and trees include both those of the past and the present. One should know that medicinal herbs have both general and specific aspects.
Generally speaking, the medicinal herbs of the past were all able to cure diseases; specifically, however, it is only in this present sutra that they are truly called "medicinal herbs."

Therefore, they are called "medicinal herbs" (bhaisajya-trna). These medicinal herbs are called "auspicious herbs" (maṅgalya-trna). Furthermore, regarding these medicinal herbs, from the perspective of the meaning as described, there is nothing that is not medicine.
However, if one follows Kāśyapa’s ability to comprehend them and names them after the medium-sized herbs, then one should simply call it the "Chapter on Medium Herbs.
One should know that whether the three types of grasses and two types of trees are auspicious or not depends on the past; although...
Originally born from the same ground and nourished by the same essence, yet they were unaware of this;

thus, until now, as the sutra was suddenly revealed to them, it was nothing other than a most auspicious omen, enabling them to scatter flowers with a mere snap of the fingers and thereby universally accomplish the wondrous cause, realizing non-arising within arising.

Wisdom universally accomplishes the knowledge of all modes; therefore, because its function is powerful, it is called the "Chapter on Herbs. The mention of the rain from the earth further describes its mastery over reality;
thus, there is no separate discussion of various mundane virtues, as they are all capable of counteracting evil, with the supramundane being supreme.
Among the assembly of those free from outflows, the four great disciples understood the Buddha’s parables through their own metaphors, thereby deeply harmonizing with the Sage’s intent.

Therefore, the Buddha now further uses the parable of the medicinal herbs to confirm their understanding. The Sūtra praises them, saying, "Excellent! This is truly rare," thus describing their attainment of realization and using a metaphor for these individuals;
hence it is titled the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs. One must understand that the title of this chapter conveys its intended meaning.
They are distinct; therefore, they are called "medicinal herbs. While the words refer to specific cases, the underlying meaning is universal. For now, we point specifically to the *śrāvakas*.

Although the Buddha’s intention is universal, his description of their attainment of understanding refers specifically to Kāśyapa; his description of their inadequacy serves to restore them to their original nature.

Whether universal or specific, all constitute medicinal herbs. This concludes the explanation according to the "World" (loka) interpretation. If explained according to the "Person" (pudgala) interpretation: medicinal herbs have grown in profusion for a long time.

For twenty thousand *koṭis* of eons, they remained within skillful means; now, for the first time, the truth is revealed. Having once received the rain from the clouds, the grasses and trees flourish:
their sprouts and stalks grow lush and dense on the outside, while their vital power and moisture fill them within.

This is analogous to those who dwell in the *nirvāṇa with remainder* during their final body, possessing no further aspiration for the unsurpassed Buddha-way, yet now hear this sutra. From themselves—
Riding upon the Buddha-vehicle, one simultaneously transports others. As the text says: "We of this day are truly śrāvakas;

by the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear. Because both the internal and external, self and other, possess supreme power and function, it is called the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter.
Having completed the explanation for the sake of others, if one explains it by way of antidote as well as the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*): as for "medicinal herbs," in the world...
There are three grades of medicine: the lower cures the four great elements; the middle benefits the five viscera; and the superior can restore one's years.

This is like the past, when the diseases of the four abodes were eliminated, yet one merely nurtured the body of the five aggregates and restored the years of true principle while arresting the color of change—neither of these, however, is the King of Medicine.
These medicinal herbs have, from that time until now, been shaded by the cloud of unconditioned compassion and drenched by the rain of impartial Dharma.
Thus, those who planted seeds long ago have obtained benefits without partiality; these ephemeral, lowly weeds have become the eternal King of Medicines.
By practicing for oneself and for others, all three delusions are entirely eliminated, resulting solely in the attainment of the eternal body of the Great Sage Buddha. This is an analogy.
All those who are untainted, having heard the sutra, shatter ignorance and delusion, and open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The text says: "Today we are truly the sons of the Buddha;
this unsurpassed treasury of jewels was obtained without seeking. All that a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been attained.
In the presence of the Buddha, we have received our predictions of enlightenment. Because the magnificent is used to describe the subtle, it is called "medicine" (yao).

This is the "Parable of the Grasses" chapter. Having concluded the explanation according to the first meaning of antidotes, the four interpretations above are all explained in terms of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Second, regarding the explanation according to the teachings: the grasses and trees represent the three vehicles (the three teachings), while the earth and rain represent the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*).

By distinguishing between the relative and the absolute, the present marvelous teaching is revealed. If explained in terms of the fundamental and the manifested (*honji-suijaku*), the fundamental resides in the ground of wisdom.
In the past, he bestowed clouds and rain; his traces became grasses and trees, drawing them forth to grow. Those who understand through the contemplation of the mind may infer this from the above.

This chapter provides a comprehensive account of his universal realization and understanding: beginning with the natural affinity for establishing karmic conditions, continuing through the intermediate stages of pursuit and guidance, and concluding with the entrustment of the Dharma-treasure.
From the subtle to the manifest, it explains his immeasurable and boundless great virtues and benevolence.
The chapter title concludes. The text of this chapter is divided into two parts: first, a brief exposition; second, an extensive exposition. The brief exposition is further divided into two sections:
the first provides a double expression of "well said" (sādhu); the second clarifies the realization that what was previously understood was insufficient.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples: "Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!
You have well spoken of the Tathāgata’s true merits; it is indeed as you have said."
This is the Tathāgata’s initial brief exposition establishing two points to lead [beings] to understand the provisional and the real of the Buddha.
