This should be interpreted in two ways. First, regarding the causal conditions: one "Excellent! describes his skillful means (upāya), while the parable of the burning house leads to the realization of the Real. Furthermore, another "Excellent!
describes how he leads [beings] through both locations to understand the Provisional. "He has well explained the true reality of the Tathāgata" is the description [of the Real].

Regarding "comprehending the real": this describes the comprehension of the ultimate truth (*tattva*). Regarding "comprehending the provisional": this describes the comprehension of the expedient means (*upāya*). Furthermore, if we categorize them according to the teachings:

the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s adaptation to the capacity of beings comprehends the real; the *Tripiṭaka*’s inducement comprehends the provisional; and the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/Pratyutpanna) Sūtras’ cultivation of faith [comprehends both].
The *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures’ reception of the teaching encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate; the *Lotus Sūtra*’s entrustment of the treasury discusses exclusively the ultimate.

At the beginning, Kāśyapa establishes a parable and attains realization, fully encompassing the teachings of the five periods; because his expressions are so skillful and refined, it is said that he "well expounded" [the Dharma].
All these are the Buddha-dharma; therefore, they are called "true and real. "Truly as you have said" is the principle of sealing and affirming [the teaching].
Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits. If you, all of you, regarding those immeasurable billions...
Even in an eon, it could not be fully described.
This is to state that Kāśyapa’s range of comprehension does not reach it. How does it not reach it?

It refers to regression and progression, the horizontal and the vertical, both horizontal and vertical, and neither horizontal nor vertical—all these are beyond his reach. Why is this so? Because of the Great Cloud...
Universally covering all, it bears the burden of universal coolness; the great rain falls upon all equally, and there is none that does not receive its bounty.

It causes all in the world to know and see this unprecedented Dharma. You, Kāśyapa and the others, were suddenly and simultaneously instructed to cease [your practice] and lead those of the Two Vehicles to gain benefit;
you did not speak of the "small grasses" of humans and devas, which constitutes a failure to reach those who have regressed. Furthermore, the name "Bodhisattva" signifies the superior.
Grass, as well as what are called small trees and great trees, flourish and grow luxuriantly, benefiting both themselves and others; yet they do not possess such awareness.
This is what is meant by "that which is surpassed in terms of progression. Furthermore, the ten dharma-realms collectively constitute the Buddha-dharma realm;

why then does [the teaching] only acknowledge the two vehicles while the remaining eight dharma-realms are entirely beyond its mention? This is what is meant by "that which is surpassed in terms of horizontal scope. Moreover, the seven...
Regarding skillful means (*upāya*): from the shallow to the profound, all enter into reality. The other five types of skillful means have never been mastered;
this constitutes "vertical" incomprehensibility. Furthermore, the benefit of the three periods of time has never for a moment ceased;

this is also "vertical. To pervade the ten directions and ten realms in every lifetime is also "horizontal. This is both horizontal and vertical, and it constitutes mastery that is beyond comprehension. Moreover—

Mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys—all are collectively said to be capable of producing [growth], for the earth never makes distinctions as to who shall take this and who shall be excluded from that.
Seeds of grasses and trees all rely upon the earth; they have no other support. When a single cloud gathers and hangs low, there is nowhere it does not cover densely.

A single rain has a single flavor; it makes no distinction between the withered and the flourishing. Since the universal moistening is the same, all alike attain growth. The Tathāgata’s impartiality is inconceivable.
In truth, he does not first act suddenly and later gradually, nor does he favor the beginning, middle, or end.

It is like a dragon raising auspicious clouds and raining universally upon all things. Though the rain does not fall upon the body or mind itself, it removes heat and brings about coolness. This is the Five Vehicles.
The seven stages of expedient means—spanning the ten directions and the three periods of time—are equal, vast, profound, extensive, and far-reaching;
they are inconceivable and without differentiation. This is what is neither horizontal nor vertical, beyond the reach of comprehension. Yet, as for the principle of that which is beyond reach:

It is not that [the former] completely and suddenly supersedes [the latter]; rather, it is because one looks back from the initial mind (*ādi-citta*) toward the subsequent mind (*paścima-citta*), and has not yet reached the ultimate stage (*atyanta-bhūmi*).

Therefore, it is said that "it cannot be fully explained. This is an explanation based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) regarding what has not been attained. Furthermore, the initial awakening is itself *A*; it also possesses the merits of the subsequent *Tā*.

However, this is merely the realization according to the teachings; there has not yet been the opportunity to advance to a realization that is transverse and vertical, all-encompassing. This is [an explanation] based on...
This is the explanation of the teaching. Furthermore, such expedient practice is appropriate for a Great Being (Mahāsattva).

The two preceding sections of the sūtra text constitute a brief summary of the fulfillment [of the teaching]. △ Below, the Tathāgata’s detailed exposition of the fulfillment is divided into two parts:
the prose and the verse. The prose section is further divided into two: first, the exposition of the fulfillment that reveals the One by opening up the Three; second, "Finally, you... [and so forth].

The section beginning with "Kāśyapa" concludes with a summary and praise. Initially, there is the presentation of the principle (*dharma*), the analogy, and their synthesis. Within the principle, there are two further parts.

First, the mention of the "Dharma King" serves to encourage faith without falsehood. Second, the passage beginning with "in all dharmas" correctly describes the revelation of the One Vehicle by opening up the Three Vehicles.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never false.
This is the first of the extensive expositions on the teaching of the Dharma, which cites the Dharma-King as a means of encouraging faith.
Just as a human king has no fear from without and his words within are not double-tongued, so it is with the Dharma-King: all evils have been exhausted, and his speech is sincere.
Listen! You should know that although the Buddha-dharma is vast, it does not transcend the provisional and the real; beyond the provisional and the real, there is no other dharma.

Yet, to speak of it as being immeasurable and boundless makes this meaning difficult to believe. Therefore, by citing the Dharma King, [the Buddha] encourages those, such as Kāśyapa, who have not yet reached full realization, so that they must all the more accept it with faith.
Furthermore, this serves as the basis for the analogy of the great cloud.
Regarding all dharmas, he expounds them through wisdom and skillful means;
this explains the opening of provisional means according to the teaching. "All dharmas" refers to the seven stages of expedient means as the horizontal dimension.
With respect to a single reality, this constitutes verticality (*ūrdhvatā*).

If one says it is not so, why is it that after initially resolving upon the Great Mind in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas, one subsequently adopts the Lesser Vehicle and wanders through the five destinies? Is this not verticality? Furthermore, there are the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

If even a single person possesses [these qualities], how much more so those on the seven stages of expedient means (*upāya*)? One should know that although these dharmas are numerous, when illuminated by the *pāramitā* of expedient means, there is nothing that is not fully exhausted.
By preaching according to the various sounds of their species, there is no one to whom the teaching is not appropriately adapted:

for humans and devas, he preaches the precepts and wholesome deeds; for those of the two vehicles, he preaches the Truths and Dependent Origination; for those of the Tripiṭaka, he preaches the phenomena and the *pāramitās*; for those of the Shared [Vehicle]...
The teaching on non-arising is a sequential exposition for the purpose of revealing the Tathāgatagarbha;
this is called a restatement that confirms Kāśyapa’s understanding of the intention behind the provisional establishment of the three vehicles as a skillful means.
The Dharma he teaches all reaches the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

This clarifies the teaching in terms of its doctrinal exposition, describing how it reveals the reality and brings about realization. That which is taught refers to the provisional methods (*upāya*) as being identical to the ultimate reality.
Its intent is to cause sentient beings to reach this ground of wisdom, where, in the final analysis, there is no duality; therefore, it is called "one. Its...

Its nature is vast and comprehensive; therefore, it is called "thorough" (*kṣānti*). It is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; therefore, it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). It is the non-abiding foundation upon which all dharmas are established;
therefore, it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*). This ground is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

For example, as the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* extensively enumerates all dharmas as being the Mahāyāna—that is, the true mark of the Great Vehicle—the true mark is itself the ground of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). Thus it is said.
The text states: "Only this one fact is real" refers to this stage; "the other two are not true" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*).
This is because it describes the fulfillment of the opening of the provisional and the revelation of the real (*kaiquan xianshi*) in terms of both the gradual and sudden teachings.
The Tathāgata observes and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena; he also knows the conduct of the deep minds of all sentient beings, penetrating them without obstruction.

This refers to provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). It describes the opening of the provisional to explain the teaching. That the Tathāgata observes and knows the ultimate destination is the knowledge of the medicine;

that which is practiced by the profound mind is the knowledge of the illness. Both the illness and the medicine are provisional dharmas, each having its own destination, such as the precepts and wholesome deeds, which proximately lead to the realms of humans and devas.
If one opens them up as contributory causes (*pratyaya-hetu*), even lowering the head or raising a hand [is sufficient].
The applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and so forth, lead one near to *nirvāṇa*.

If they are treated as adornments, then what you practice is the path of a bodhisattva, leading one far toward the place of jewels. Thus, from the general and specific aspects of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) onward, the routes by which bodhisattvas approach and reach their destination differ;
the Tathāgata understands them all thoroughly. Furthermore, the precepts and wholesome deeds are the bliss of humans and devas, while the [Four] Truths...
The six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are the medicine for those of the three vehicles; even the general and specific six perfections are the medicine for Mahāyāna bodhisattvas.

Because the Tathāgata can fully comprehend these, it is said that he "knows where they are headed. Regarding the phrase "that which is practiced with a profound mind," there are two kinds of profound minds:

first, those who are attached to the environment and its inhabitants give rise to the ten grave evils, which obstruct the vehicle of humans and devas; second, those who are attached to what they grasp [at as real].

As for "Dharma," it refers to that which gives rise to the four inversions, the three paths, the six obscurations, the four abodes, the five abodes, and so forth—obstructing the vehicles of the various sages.
One should know that the manifestations of the deep-seated sicknesses of the mind differ; the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom illuminates them all with unimpeded penetration.
This passage cites provisional wisdom to explain provisional teachings.
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, he thoroughly investigates and clearly understands them, demonstrating to all sentient beings the wisdom of all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

This is because it is illuminated by true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), which, according to the teaching, constitutes the realization of reality. All provisional teachings (*upāyadharma*) are such that none fail to enter into the ultimate reality.

Therefore, it is called "ultimate. Because it is that which is seen by the Buddha-eye, it is called "clear. Because it is that which is known by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), it is called "thoroughly understood.
Because it can demonstrate to sentient beings such a perfect realm and wisdom, it is called "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajña-jñāna*). Furthermore, as for this wisdom:
This wisdom illuminates this medicine and this illness, but does not illuminate that medicine and that illness; furthermore, that wisdom illuminates that, but cannot illuminate this.
Such distinctions in kind constitute provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). A single wisdom universally illuminates all medicines and all illnesses.
True wisdom is illumination. Furthermore, this also serves as a general explanation for what follows. "All phenomena" refers to the ten dharma-realms.
Each of these ten dharmas has distinct characteristics and desires; each receives its own retribution, and their ultimate destinations also differ.
To know these various phenomena in their entirety is called "knowing the illness. To know all that the deep mind is attached to is called "knowing the medicine. As for the medicine...
Regarding depth and shallowness: as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states, "With the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), one knows the mind of greed, the mind of anger, and the mind of delusion.
If one employs the medicinal remedies of all dharmas—such as the precepts, the truths, the objects of mindfulness, and the perfections—with the wisdom of suchness, one attains unimpeded penetration.

Furthermore, in the section on provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), "unimpeded penetration" refers to discussing the real (*satya*) by means of the provisional; whereas in the section on the wisdom of suchness, it says "furthermore... [and so forth].
Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*). As for "all phenomena," when discussing the ultimate in relation to the provisional, these two expressions appear alternately;

this clarifies that the ultimate is the provisional-ultimate, and the provisional is the ultimate-provisional. One should know that what is illumined by the two wisdoms consists of both the pervasive and the perfect spheres, which are penetrated without obstruction.

Therefore, one is able to expound the two teachings of the provisional and the ultimate; this is to explain the teaching by means of the wisdom. Furthermore, if one considers the final consummation...
It is neither provisional nor ultimate; it is neither differentiated nor non-differentiated. Through the skillful means of wisdom, there is provisional differentiation;
yet when one reaches the stage of wisdom, there is no differentiation. It is like the earth, which has no differentiation, yet upon it grow various kinds of grasses and trees.

This plurality is not plurality; it is precisely non-plurality that constitutes plurality. It is, for example, like discussing phenomena (dharma) by way of the mind, or discussing the mind by way of phenomena.
The mind possesses various enumerations, whereas phenomena possess no enumerations. Furthermore, the mind is not separate from phenomena, and phenomena are not separate from the mind.
Moreover, one enumerates by way of the unenumerated; it is merely enumeration that is non-enumeration. Expedient means (upāya) and reality (tattva) are likewise so. This...
This is a combined commentary. The preceding exposition of the Dharma has concluded its summary and establishment. △ From here below, the Tathāgata provides a parable.
The text describing Kāśyapa’s realization and understanding is divided into two parts: first, the illustrative parable; second, the reaffirmation and praise of the core principle.
This is also called the "Concluding Eulogy. The initial parables consist of both opening and closing sections. When opened, they comprise two parts:

first, the parable of differentiation, which illustrates the aforementioned wisdom of the provisional teachings; this has six sub-parables. Second, the parable of non-differentiation, which illustrates the aforementioned wisdom of the ultimate teachings.

Regarding the grasses and the two types of trees: because their fibers and density are unequal, they are termed "differentiated. As for the single earth and the single rain: they universally support and universally moisten all things.

Therefore, there is no differentiation. If one observes their branches and offshoots, they appear to be each distinct; yet if one investigates their flourishing roots, none are anything other than earth and rain.
Internally, this corresponds to the way the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) illuminates the seven and five as being individually different.

If the wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) proceeds to illuminate them, they ultimately return to the single reality. The single reality is the seven and five; the seven and five are the single reality. Differentiation and non-differentiation are non-existent.
"Differentiation within differentiation. This serves as a pre-indication; it will be easily understood when we reach the section below.

Furthermore, one must understand that the sequence of the six metaphors arises because there are sentient beings composed of the five aggregates (*skandha*), and thus there are the five vehicles as the herbs and trees. Because there are the seeds of the five vehicles, the dense clouds respond to the world.
Their response necessarily entails preaching the Dharma; preaching necessarily entails moistening; and moistening necessarily entails growth. Thus it is said, "Furthermore..."
The "Essential Meaning" (zōng) refers to the general purport of this chapter. It fundamentally describes the accomplishment of Kāśyapa’s realization;
within it, however, there is an extensive eulogy of the Tathāgata’s ability to know the two types of wisdom (*jñāna*), which appears as if the Tathāgata were praising himself alone.
Fearing that those who have not yet understood might think Kāśyapa did not comprehend these two wisdoms, the Tathāgata finally says: "You, Kāśyapa, are truly rare and marvelous," and further...

The preceding section is a restatement of the previous thesis (*pūrvapakṣa*). Because it recounts the account of Kāśyapa, it is called "Restoring the Thesis" (*punar-mūla*). Although it praises the Tathāgata, its underlying intent lies with Kāśyapa;
therefore, it is named "Restoring the Thesis.
Kāśyapa, it is like this: for example, consider the mountains, rivers, valleys, and terrain of a trichiliocosm.
This is the first of the six analogies for the wisdom of the provisional teachings within the section on "Distinguishing Analogies. It contains two types of explanation: the general and the specific.
The general explanation states that the "trichiliocosm" (the three-thousandfold world system) is an analogy for the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
The "mountains, rivers, valleys, and land" are analogies for the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*). Why is this? Because there is no separate dharma apart from the world.
Mountains, rivers, valleys, and gorges are formed from the earth; sentient beings have no separate dharma, for they are sentient beings formed by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

The earth is a metaphor for the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); the mountains, rivers, valleys, and gorges are metaphors for the other four aggregates, which serve as the basis of support.

Thereafter, there are plants, trees, and so forth, which likewise depend upon the five elements such as the earth, just as sentient beings do. Within these capacities, there are the faculties of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
The nature [of things] possesses the meaning of grasses and trees receiving moisture and growing. One should know that the earth and such are not identical to the grasses and trees;
the physical substance of the grasses and trees is merely named "grasses and trees. As for the seeds of grasses and trees, they have no other name;
it is simply the functional capacity to produce that is called the "seed," while the physical substance produced is called "grasses and trees. All are rooted in this.

Earth. Earth is the foundation. Internally, it corresponds to the causes and fruits of habituation (*vāsanā*). Although these depend upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the five aggregates themselves are not identical to cause and fruit.
It is by depending upon the aggregates that there exist the causes of habituation; their growth and fulfillment are termed the "fruit of habituation.
Thus, cause and fruit arise based upon the aggregates. In this way, the analogy of mountains, rivers, and land is established, just as seeds of grass and trees receive moisture.
The increase of the metaphors is thus fully accomplished. This concludes the general explanation. Furthermore, if one were to illustrate each vehicle individually through its respective metaphor:

although a mountain is high and steep, it possesses five characteristics such as depressions and elevations; even though the earth is level, it likewise possesses five characteristics such as mounds and ponds.
These correspond to the five vehicles and the five aggregates (*skandhas*). The height of the mountain illustrates the five aggregates of a Bodhisattva, while the valleys...
The Buddha is like a friend; the śrāvakas are like mountain streams; the land is like heaven; and the valleys below are like the human vehicle and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Each of these five aggregates possesses a basis for both accumulated causes (*vāsanā-hetu*) and accumulated fruits (*vāsanā-phala*), just as mountains, rivers, streams, valleys, and lands do.
All serve as the basis for seeds, the core, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the primary cause (*hetu*) and the retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*):
the three-thousandfold world system is used as a metaphor for the principle of the primary cause, serving as the universal basis for all things.

Mountains, rivers, valleys, and the soil represent the physical and mental aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*) that constitute the retributive fruit of sentient beings; while grasses, trees, thickets, and forests [represent the secondary causes].

This is like the causal conditions for the habits of sentient beings. These three dharmas are not separate from one another. The causal conditions for habituation depend upon the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas), yet the aggregates and sense bases do not transcend the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
This is because the causal conditions for habituation and the three factors of correct practice are neither identical nor separate.
Question: What is the difference between the ground and the subsequent ground? Why is there a distinction in the metaphors used here, while the lower [text] uses no metaphor at all?

“Venerable sir,” he replied, “the analogies used are distinct. The previous analogy illustrated the ultimate reality (*tattva*), whereas the present analogy illustrates the retribution-aggregate (*vipākaskandha*);
therefore, they are not the same. The various species of plants, trees, groves, and medicinal herbs that grow there differ in their kinds, and their names and forms are each distinct.”
This is the second illustration of what arises from differentiation, concerning herbs and trees. "Herbs" (卉) is the general name for grasses;
"trees" (木) is the collective term for plants. A multitude of grasses forms a thicket; a multitude of trees forms a forest. As for those whose power to cure diseases is superior:
They are called "medicines. Just as within the wholesome dharmas all are able to cure evil, the meaning of untainted wholesomeness curing afflictions is superior to that of inferior herbs and trees;
because its branches and foliage provide broad shade and its utility is great, it serves as a metaphor for the two Bodhisattvas.
Regarding "various kinds": these are the seeds of the five vehicles and the seven wholesome causes and effects; hence they are called "various. These are the "kinds.
Each has its own designation, which constitutes the "name. Each has its own essence and characteristics, which constitute "form-dharmas" (*rūpa-dharma*).
Dense clouds spread everywhere, completely covering the trichiliocosm.
This is the third simile of the dense clouds. The clouds possess form and color, which represent the sheltering protection;

in the following verse, the distant thunder represents the Buddha’s compassion, the form and color represent the Buddha’s manifestation in the world, and the thunder represents the Buddha [speaking the Dharma].
Regarding "teaching": "Mysterious Cloud" refers to the three mysteries. "Compassion" is the mystery of mind; "thunder" is the mystery of speech;
and "form and color" is the mystery of body. "Pervasive" means all-encompassing. Because it is both mysterious and pervasive, it is called "pervasive.
By means of compassion as an incense-like influence, the response-body preaches the Dharma, pervading the ten dharma realms; therefore, it is called "pervasive. *Sūtra-vinaya-yi*... [text fragment]
Regarding the signs: clouds may have five colors. If they are blue, wind is predominant; if red, fire is predominant; if yellow or white, earth is predominant;
and if black, water is predominant. There are four masters of lightning: Śarīrasvāda in the east, Śatapati in the south, Ajagara in the south, and Aśvalamba in the north.
Because these four lightnings contend with one another, there is thunder. Furthermore, because water, fire, wind, and earth contend with one another, there is thunder.

Furthermore, there are five matters. There is no rain. One should know that the cloud is a metaphor for the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), the thunder for fame, the lightning for the emission of light, and the rain for the preaching of the Dharma.
However, in this context, there is neither thunder nor lightning; this is because the subsequent verse describes the correspondence of the reflected image with the dharma.

Where there is lightning, there must be thunder; where there is thunder, there must be clouds; and where there are clouds, they must pour forth rain. Now, we do not take the case where there is neither lightning nor thunder.
The rain and the clouds that produce no rain serve as metaphors. One must understand this meaning by applying it to the body as a cloud and so forth.
Furthermore, the metaphor of the cloud should correspond to form (*rūpa*); since forms are not singular, five colors are generally cited here as a metaphor for the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*).

Moreover, the Buddha, as the teacher, is like a master of lightning; the karmic conditions of sentient beings are likewise like lightning, and their mutual resonance is like that of the master of lightning.

Regarding "fighting": when there is a responsive resonance according to the occasion, one responds with light. Furthermore, as for the five instances where there was no rain, this is because there were no occasions for the five vehicles;
thus, the Dharma-rain did not fall. This serves to explain that when there is an occasion, the Dharma-rain descends together with it, manifesting within the dense clouds. Question: [What is this?]
Regarding the six similes herein, they illustrate the distinctions [of the teaching]. Why, then, is the single rain from the dense clouds used as a simile for non-distinction?

Answer: The clouds and rain mentioned in the subsequent passage are precisely the same clouds and rain as those in this context; it is simply that here we follow the perspective of what is rained down.
It receives a distinct name. If that is so, how does it differ from grass and trees? Answer: Grass and trees receive their names solely based on the grass and trees themselves;
clouds and rain, however, derive their names as agents based on what they manifest. Therefore, they are not the same.
"At one time [they] rain down equally.

This single phrase is the fourth analogy for raining down. It illustrates the use of the eightfold voice and four analytical knowledges of the secret mouth to proclaim and rain down the Dharma-rain, thereby benefiting and nourishing sentient beings.
Its moisture pervades all: the flowers, trees, and forests, as well as the various medicinal herbs—those with small roots, small stems, small branches, and small leaves;
those with medium roots, medium stems, medium branches, and medium leaves; and those with large roots, large stems, large branches, and large leaves.
This is the fifth analogy of moistening. The Dharma-cloud rains universally upon the mental ground of seven types of sentient beings;
all seeds of the causal conditions for practice immediately give rise to the wisdom of hearing, which is called "soaking. Regarding the branches, leaves, roots, and stems: faith is the root.
Precepts are the trunk; meditative concentration is the branches; wisdom is the leaves. Because they support one another in succession, they are illustrated by this analogy.
The small roots, trunk, and so forth refer to the faith and precepts of humans and devas. The medium roots, trunk, and so forth refer to the faith and precepts of the two vehicles.

The great roots, trunk, and so forth refer to the faith and precepts of the bodhisattvas. One should know that although the five vehicles are taught, they are fundamentally intended for the single reality. How could one [fail to] accept this?
At the time of moistening, does it depart from the actual ground? However, faith, precepts, and so forth belong exclusively to the human vehicle;
lacking concentration and wisdom, they are represented by the mental factors (caitta). Thus, the four meanings are complete.
The various trees, whether large or small, each receive according to their superior, middling, or inferior nature;
though rained upon by a single cloud, they grow in accordance with their respective species, putting forth flowers, fruits, and seeds.
This is the sixth analogy for growth. The text briefly restates this to clarify that grasses and trees receive nourishment according to their respective capacities.

Just as the two causes—habitual cultivation (*vāsanā*) and retribution (*vipāka*)—of wholesome dharmas have received the rain of the Dharma, the two fruits of habitual cultivation and retribution each attain growth.

The phrase "in accordance with their seed-nature" (*gotra*) clarifies that the application of skillful means (*upāya*) accords with the capacities of beings: those of lesser capacity do not exceed their limits, while those of greater...

It does not decrease; this refers precisely to the seven kinds of causes consisting of the two types: the causes of habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*) and retribution (*vipāka-hetu*). "Flowers, fruits, blossoming, and ripening" refers to the two results:

the results of habituation (*vāsanā-phala*) and retribution (*vipāka-phala*). Flowers correspond to the result of habituation, and fruit to the result of retribution. This is a correspondence based on separated characters; one should properly say "flowers blossom and fruit ripens.
Furthermore, there are flowers that have not yet blossomed and fruits that have not yet ripened, which may also serve as metaphors for the two causes. Now...
Having taken [the seeds] and having spread them, they truly serve as the cause for two fruits. That which is attained through growth consists of three meanings:
first, to accord with their respective natures (*gotra*), which is the basis for growth; because the establishment of the teaching accords with the capacities [of beings], there is growth.
Second, each attains growth, which explicitly clarifies the nature of growth. Third, the blossoming and flourishing of flowers and fruit, which is the manifestation of growth.
The six analogies above constitute the first set of differentiated metaphors; this concludes the section on the wisdom of the provisional teachings.

△ Although the subsequent section begins with "In one land," it constitutes the second major division: the single rain falling upon one land is a metaphor for non-differentiation, revealing the One Reality.
This text further contains three parts.
"Though produced from the same ground":
this clarifies that what is produced from the ground prior to the path is produced from the ground of the mind; ultimately, it is triggered by the ground of wisdom subsequent to the path.

One should know that these names, "prior" and "subsequent" to the path, have both general and specific applications. That which is subsequent to the path is definitively situated after the fruition. As for the path...

The preceding [stages] extend down to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, in the "Expedient Means" chapter, that which precedes equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is also designated as the stage prior to the Path (*mārga-pūrva*).

Herein, it must be understood that the ordinary being at the level of the broad ground (*bō-dì*), who lacks precepts and wholesome roots, constitutes the stage prior to the Path, while the five vehicles constitute the stage of the Path itself.
Thus, the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) both prior to and subsequent to the Path is uniformly the Ground (*bhūmi*); the essence of the Ground is without distinction.

They are distinct. Nevertheless, all are capable of producing [the result]; thus we know that within the mental ground (*cittabhūmi*) prior to the Path, how could sentient beings ever lack the nature capable of production?
That they are unable to achieve [it] is necessarily because they must rely upon the ground of ultimate fruit-wisdom (*phala-jñāna-bhūmi*) subsequent to the Path to cause it to arise and be perfected.
From the moment the mind is first resolved (*cittotpāda*) until the final culmination, they all rely upon this ground of wisdom for their maturation. However, fundamentally...
It is because they belong to a single stage.
They are moistened by the same rain;
this is the second point of being moistened by the same rain. They are rained upon by the same cloud, proclaimed by the same voice, and [taught] through the Dharma-gate of the Single Vehicle.
The development of the five kinds of roots of goodness within the Path ultimately constitutes the teaching of the single voice of equality.
Although there are five [categories] according to the beings they reach, the intent of the transformation is one and the same.
Yet, among the various grasses and trees, each possesses its own distinctions.
These distinctions among grasses and trees—the three types of grass and two types of wood—receive the teaching yet remain unaware of it.
The five kinds of roots of goodness, having been moistened by the rain of the Buddha-dharma, grow according to their respective capacities;

yet they do not know that these five causes all rely upon the single Buddha-nature. Furthermore, they do not know that the teachings of the five vehicles are all Mahāyāna, nor do they know that they are the same.
"Return to the Buddha’s wisdom," because only the Tathāgata is able to know it. This is the analogy of non-differentiation.
From the preceding "For example, like the three thousand [worlds]" down to this point, the Tathāgata has completed the formal presentation of the analogies and their corroboration.

From the following section, beginning with "Kāśyapa, you should know," the text correlates the preceding analogies. The correlation of the analogies of differentiation is divided into two parts; first, the direct correlation.

Next, the application of the analogies. There are six distinct analogies; their current arrangement does not follow the original sequence, for such is the nature of the relationship between the capacity [of the recipient] and the response [of the Buddha].
Although they do not follow the sequence, there is a specific reason for arranging them here according to the order of their arising. First, it clarifies the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
Thereupon, he preaches the Dharma with the eight musical tones. In preaching the Dharma, there are sentient beings who receive transformation.

When these beings hear the Dharma, each is moistened by the Way; though their being moistened is the same, there is no lack of difference in their growth. First, the six analogies for these differences are combined as follows.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is likewise so. Appearing in the world like the rising of a great cloud, he pervades the entire world with a great voice.
The devas, humans, and asuras are like that great cloud, completely covering the trichiliocosm.

This combines with the third analogy above, that of the dense clouds, while also concurrently combining with the first analogy, that of the world-system. Regarding the combination with the dense clouds:
first, the secret of the Buddha’s body is raised to correspond to the clouds having form; subsequently, the secret of the Buddha’s speech is raised to correspond to the clouds having sound.
The Tathāgata is likewise so: his appearance in the world corresponds precisely to the manifestation of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
"In the world. This is like the rising of a great cloud; it immediately provides a metaphor to illustrate that the Tathāgata’s great compassion manifests in form to cover and nurture all beings.
"With a great voice" refers to the Buddha’s secret of speech (*vāg-guhya*), corresponding to the sound of the cloud.
"Devas, humans, and asuras" specifically names those in the three virtuous realms who receive the benefit of the secret of speech. Thus...
These are the faculties and natures of the three vehicles; the "thirty sons" refers to those who individually receive the benefit of the voice [of the Dharma].
"Like that great cloud" is an illustration that corresponds to the fact that the cloud possesses sound.

"Pervasively covering the trichiliocosm" generally indicates that all are Buddha-sons, and that they all equally receive the benefit of the secret of the mouth (the *guhyavāc*). Alternatively, one may simply correlate this with the five similes, leading to the universal...
"Throughout the world" and below serves as a combined analogy for the lands of the aforementioned worlds. "Worlds" refers to the world of lands (*bhūmi-loka*).
"Heavenly beings, humans, and *asuras*" refers to the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*) of provisional designation.

The provisional designation corresponds to the aforementioned "worlds," while the five aggregates correspond to the mountains, rivers, and valleys. From "In the midst of the great assembly" and below is... [the following section].
The second part combines with the fourth, the analogy of the pouring rain. First, the topical headings are presented, followed by the exhortation to listen and receive.
There are six topical headings.
In the midst of the great assembly, he proclaims these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct."
Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One:

you cause those who have not crossed over to cross; you cause those who have not been liberated to be liberated; you cause those who have not found peace to find peace; you cause those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa.
You know this world and the world beyond as they truly are. I am the All-Knowing One, the All-Seeing One; I know.

"The Way," "the opener of the Way," and "the speaker of the Way" correspond to the preceding rain analogy and first set forth the six topical headings: 1. The Ten Epithets, namely Tathāgata, Arhat, and so forth;
2. The Four Great Vows, namely to deliver those not yet delivered, and so forth; 3. The Threefold Clarity, namely [knowledge of] this life and future lives...

1. The World-Honored One (Lokavid), etc.; 2. The One of Single Mind and Threefold Wisdom (Ekacittatrayajñāna), meaning he is fully endowed with knowledge; 3. The Five Eyes (Pañcacakṣus), meaning he is the seer of all; 4.
The One whose Three Karmas Proceed Together with Wisdom (Jñānasahagata-trikarma), meaning he knows the Path—this refers to the non-restraint of mind;

he opens the Path—this refers to the non-restraint of body; he teaches the Path—this refers to the non-restraint of speech; he is also called the Teacher (Śāstṛ), meaning he is one who knows the Path, and so forth. One should...

One should know that these six categories of dharma-gates—beginning with the ten titles [of a Buddha] and ending with the three karmas—encompass all the dharma-gates of spiritual function on the stage of fruition as elucidated in all the teachings;
therefore, they are fully subsumed within these six. Thus, the sutra provides a combined analogy and briefly enumerates them.
Moreover, these six gates each mutually encompass one another. As for the sequence of these six: because [the Buddha] possesses the ten titles, there are the four great vows;

thus it is said, "those who have not crossed over, may they cross over. Although the four great vows are employed, if the three types of penetration (trividya) were lacking, the illumination of sentient beings' capacities would not be universal.
Only when the three wisdoms are fully perfected can one be called "penetrating. Wisdom must necessarily possess the eye; since these two dharmas are already...
With meditative concentration and wisdom as the cause, one attains the two fruits of the eye and knowledge; thus, where there is knowledge, there must be the eye.
These five categories are such that none fail to have the three karmas follow the movement of wisdom. Therefore, six categories are briefly cited to demonstrate this responsive capacity.
The Buddha himself referred to these to manifest his ability to rain down [the Dharma].
"You gods, humans, and hosts of asuras, all should come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
This is the second exhortation to beings to listen and receive [the teaching]. The Buddha’s eightfold voice articulates six kinds of dharma-gates;
speaking from the perspective of the majority, he exhorts those in the three happy realms that they should go to hear the Dharma, so that they may faithfully accept the Buddha’s words.
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma;
this is the third [analogy], which corresponds to the first analogy above concerning mountains and rivers. Sentient beings exist by grasping at karmic retribution.
Just as there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of worlds based upon mountains and rivers, so too are there the sentient beings of the ten dharma realms.
Here, we are specifically speaking of the distinctions among the sentient beings of the seven stages of expedient means, which correspond to what was explained above.
At that time, the Tathāgata observes these sentient beings—their faculties being either sharp or dull, and their diligence being either vigorous or lax.

This is the fourth [point], which corresponds to the second analogy above concerning grasses and trees. Regarding the phrase "at that time": if one discusses the beginning of the gradual process, it refers to this moment.
This refers to the time when the Three Vehicles were first taught at the Deer Park. If one discusses the intermediate period, it may be discussed at various points throughout that time.

Regarding those of dull and sharp faculties: as a general judgment, those in the three miserable realms—who possess evil causes and experience suffering as their fruit and are thus unable to receive the Way—are called "dull.
Those who, through the seven kinds of expedient means, hear the teaching and obtain benefit are called "sharp. To explain specifically: gods and humans merely receive karmic retribution and do not...
To be willing to receive the Way is called "dull. To sever delusions and transcend the realms through the root-natures of the Three Vehicles is called "sharp.

Furthermore, for a Śrāvaka to contemplate arising and ceasing is called "dull," while for a Bodhisattva to contemplate non-arising and non-ceasing is called "sharp. The sharpness and dullness of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [Teachings] may be understood by analogy.
To be negligent in the three miserable paths is called "indolence"; to observe the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds as humans or devas is...
Diligence: for humans and devas, not being weary of suffering is indolence; for the two vehicles, fearing impermanence is diligence.
Furthermore, for the two vehicles, craving realization and not seeking to become Buddhas is indolence; for a Bodhisattva, aspiring to seek the Buddha-way is progress.
One should know that the terms "sharp" and "dull" apply universally across the four and three flavors and the ten realms.
According to their respective capacities, he preaches the Dharma for them in various and immeasurable ways, causing them all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits.

This is the fifth [point], which corresponds to the fifth analogy above regarding "receiving nourishment. "According to their respective capacities" means to accord with and meet their individual aptitudes, avoiding the error of adding or subtracting;
it is like bestowing the ten wholesome paths upon those whose capacity is human, or [bestowing higher teachings] upon those whose capacity is celestial.
Bestowing the five precepts constitutes a reduction; this applies even up to Bodhisattvas, where the degrees of increase and decrease are likewise understood.
To joyfully obtain benefit means that each receives the rain of the Dharma, being universally moistened and benefiting all at once.
When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they will enjoy peace and security in the present life and be reborn in favorable realms hereafter, experiencing happiness through the Path.
They shall also hear the Dharma; having heard it, they will be freed from all obstacles and, within the various teachings, act according to their own capacity.
Gradually one attains entry into the Path;

this corresponds to the sixth "increase" analogy above. That "one is secure in the present life and will be reborn in a good realm in future lives" refers to the causal conditions for retribution giving rise to the fruits of retribution;
this corresponds to the "blooming and increasing of the flowers" mentioned above. Furthermore, one comes to hear the Dharma...
Regarding "those who enter the Path": this refers to the causal practice leading to the resultant practice, which corresponds to the aforementioned growth of the fruit.
Having heard this Dharma, it corresponds to the reason for the aforementioned growth; there is peace and security in the present life, which precisely corresponds to the aforementioned growth.
"Being born in a good realm in future lives" corresponds to the characteristics of the aforementioned growth. This is a brief explanation. For a detailed explanation, the Buddha...
Just as a great cloud universally covers all things, even those in the three miserable realms receive its moisture and grow.

As it is said regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the Vaipulya sūtras, this clarifies that even beings in the hells obtain benefit. Furthermore, various sūtras also speak of dragons, birds, ghosts, spirits, and so forth.
Hearing the Dharma and attaining the Way—like a fire being extinguished or boiling water cooling—is peace and security in the present life.
Being born among gods or humans is a favorable rebirth in future lives. Cultivating the Way among gods and humans is experiencing happiness through the Way.

This is the explanation according to the three miserable realms (*durgati*). Furthermore, if one considers humans and gods: hearing the Dharma and upholding the precepts is supported by the power of merit.

The body will not be harmed by ghosts or spirits; this is peace and security in the present life. Alternatively, a deva may be reborn as a deva, a human as a human, or devas and humans may be reborn interchangeably;
this is birth in a good destination in future lives. Being born with the capacity for awakening and understanding is to experience happiness through the Way.
If one considers the two vehicles hearing the Dharma, they attain *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder); this is peace and security in the present life.
"Peaceful" means that being born in that land and hearing the sutra is to experience happiness in a virtuous place.

If we speak in terms of a *janman-kāya* bodhisattva, hearing the Dharma preached by Vairocana Buddha and attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) constitutes peace and security in the present life.

Subsequently, being born in the world of Pure Fulfillment as an attendant of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) constitutes a virtuous place, wherein one experiences happiness through the Way. Thus it is said:

To be free from all obstacles means that in this present life one will enjoy peace and security; by acting according to one's capacity, one gradually enters the Path, which is the attainment of happiness in future lives.
One should know that within the nine realms, hearing the Dharma of the five vehicles is natural: the vehicle of the five precepts delivers one from the suffering of the three miserable paths;
the vehicle of the ten wholesome deeds delivers one from the eight sufferings of the human realm; and the vehicle of the śrāvaka delivers one from the impermanence of the triple world.
Suffering. For those who emerge from the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, there is the suffering of hearing the Dharma from others.

For those who emerge from the Bodhisattva Vehicle, there is the suffering of lacking internal sharp wisdom and lacking external marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). These constitute the five vehicles. From Kāśyapa onwards, you should know that this concludes the account of the Tathāgata.
This precisely completes the six analogies for the distinctions mentioned above.
Just as that great cloud rains upon all grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and medicinal herbs according to their respective natures.
Fully receiving the moistening [rain], each attains growth;
this is the second [section]. The "Great Cloud" section synthesizes the first analogy of the two benefits of form and sound.
The "Raining upon All" section synthesizes the second, the six-chapter Dharma-gate. The "Herbs" [section]...

The "woods and groves" correspond to the fourth [section], the receiving of transformation; it refers to the sharpness or dullness of sentient beings' faculties, their causes for indolence or diligence, and the depth or shallowness of their practice, as well as the mountains and rivers.
Just as various species fully receive moisture, this corresponds to the fifth [section], receiving nourishment and attaining the benefit of the Dharma.
Each attains growth, which corresponds to the sixth [section], the increase of peace and security in the present life.

This is an analogy. The section on combining the analogies of distinction is concluded. △ From the point where it says "The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma" onwards, the second part combines the analogy of non-distinction.
Above, the opening of the analogies consisted of three parts; now, the combination likewise consists of three, though they do not follow the same order.
"The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is of a single characteristic and a single flavor.
This is the paired heading, which corresponds to the preceding [passage on] "one earth and one rain. As for what is called "a single characteristic," it refers to the minds of sentient beings.
It is the characteristic of the same suchness (*tathatā*). This single characteristic is the foundation of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita-mūla*), from which all phenomena (*dharma*) are established.
Non-abiding and the absence of characteristics constitute non-differentiation; the establishment of all phenomena constitutes differentiation.

Differentiation is like various plants and trees, while non-differentiation is like the single earth. Although the earth itself has no differentiation, it is able to produce peaches, plums, and other vegetation.
The differences among trees and so forth are distinct; although peaches, apricots, herbs, and trees differ from one another, they share the same characteristic of solidity.

If one knows that the earth-element encompasses both peaches and apricots, one recognizes that within the real there is the provisional. Thus, one understands that non-differentiation is itself differentiation.
If one knows the firm nature of the peach and plum, one immediately recognizes that within the provisional there is the real; one understands that differentiation is itself non-differentiation.
For this reason, the analogy of the upper stage is joined with the single characteristic. "One flavor" refers to the Dharma of the One Vehicle, which equally explicates a single principle;
this is the "one rain. It is the teaching of reality (the *nītārtha*), pure and without admixture. This serves as the illustration.
Contemplate this as a single characteristic. In the past, the single reality-characteristic was skillfully opened up into seven characteristics;

within the One Vehicle Dharma, it is distinguished and taught as having seven teachings. This is because the Buddha knows that they ultimately converge into a single characteristic and a single flavor, being thus without distinction.
What are called the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation, culminating in all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This pair explains the aforementioned single characteristic and single flavor. The nature of the minds of sentient beings is precisely the three characteristics of inherent virtue.
When the Tathāgata speaks these three dharma-characteristics with a single voice, they immediately become the three flavors; this is the pair.

This explains the aforementioned karma. Regarding the "characteristic of liberation": it is the absence of the characteristic of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and furthermore, the absence of the karmic causes of the two extremes—namely, the *paricchinna* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma* (transformative).
Therefore, it is called "liberation. Thus, within the path of karma, this is the virtue of liberation. Regarding the "absence of characteristics":
it is the absence of the characteristic of *nirvāṇa*, and furthermore, the attainment of Middle Way wisdom, which is able to remain far removed from the two extremes.
Being without attachment is called the characteristic of detachment; this is the virtue of *prajñā* within afflictions, for it is the non-characteristic of even non-characteristics.

The characteristic of cessation refers to the cessation of the causes of the two extremes, whereby one attains *nirvāṇa with remainder*, and the cessation of the effects of the two extremes, whereby one attains *nirvāṇa without remainder*;
thus it is called the characteristic of cessation. This is the virtue of the *dharmakāya* within the path of suffering. These three—
Taking characteristics as the conditions for the objective realm gives rise to the practice of the Middle Way; ultimately, one attains the fruit of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*).
Therefore, it is said that one reaches the ultimate state of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Furthermore, reaching the ultimate state of the knowledge of all modes means that if one attains the cessation of the characteristics of the two extremes, then both the general and specific delusions are exhausted, and one enters the Buddha’s knowledge.
[The Buddha] sees that one practices Prajñā within the mind of *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience). There is no distinction between the initial aspiration and the ultimate goal;
therefore, it is called "ultimate. This is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha; therefore, it is called *sarvākārajñatā*. The dual explanation is complete.

From the passage beginning with "Following that existence," it clarifies that upon hearing the Tathāgata’s Dharma, one does not realize it for oneself; this explains the distinctions [between the stages].
The meaning is as follows: sentient beings are the distinction between the provisional and the real regarding mountains and rivers;
they are also the distinction of seeds. The Tathāgata is the cloud; hearing the Dharma is the rain; reading, reciting, and practicing are the moisture; and merit is the growth.
One cannot understand these distinctions [without further analysis]. Regarding the text, there are five sections.
If there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and whether they uphold, read, recite, or practice it as taught, the merit they thereby obtain,
they do not themselves perceive or know.
This is the first [point]. "Sentient beings do not know" refers to those who lack understanding. "Dharma" refers to the Dharma of hearing a single sound.
That "those who uphold and expound it differ" clearly elucidates their lack of knowledge; for their upholding and expounding are not the same, and their practices vary.

Humans and devas form interpretations based on precepts and wholesome deeds, while those of the Three Vehicles form interpretations based on the Truths, the Bases of Mindfulness, and the Factors of Enlightenment. Since these interpretations differ, this is...
Regarding "the distinctions" and "the merits attained not being self-aware": this clarifies that the five individuals each received the teaching individually;
they did not know that the Buddha’s teaching was of a single flavor and without distinction, nor did they know the seven kinds of skillful means, each forming their own interpretations.
Yet each clings to their own view as being real. This is because they do not understand the provisional (upāya), nor do they recognize the real;

it is simply that they fail to realize the non-distinction between them, for originally there is no distinction. From the section below, "The Tathāgata is able to know," onwards, it clarifies that the Tathāgata is able to know.
It briefly reduces the number [of categories] by citing ten objects of perception, which are combined into four meanings. First, regarding the four...

Knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is fourfold: first, knowledge of phenomena in relation to three dharmas; second, knowledge of phenomena in relation to two dharmas; third, knowledge of phenomena in relation to one dharma; and fourth, knowledge of phenomena in relation to four dharmas.
As for the four dharmas, they are the four factors of characteristic (lakṣaṇa), mark (nimitta), substance (dravya), and intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Why is this so? It is because only the Tathāgata knows the lineage, characteristics, and essential nature of these sentient beings.

This clarifies that the Tathāgata is able to know that sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha-lineage and its characteristics. Regarding "lineage" (gotra): the three paths are the seeds of the three virtues.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The entire host of afflictions constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata. This clarifies...
From the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*), there is precisely *prajñā*. It is further said: "The five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) are all the marks of liberation.
This means that from the unwholesome, there is the liberation of wholesome dharmas. All sentient beings are the very mark of *nirvāṇa*; they cannot be extinguished further.
This is the taking of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as the *dharmakāya*. One should know that these three paths are themselves the nature (*prakṛti*).

It is called a "seed" (gotra) because it possesses the nature of being able to produce [results]. This discussion of "seed" is based on the principle of contrasting opposing states—namely, phenomena and principle, cause and effect, delusion and awakening, bondage and liberation;
since their fundamental principle is one from beginning to end, it is termed the "nature-seed" (prakṛti-gotra).
If "seed" is discussed in terms of categories, then every instance of lowering the head or raising the hand is entirely a seed of liberation; all three vehicles [are likewise seeds].
The mind is the seed of *prajñā*. Indeed, all who possess a mind shall become Buddhas; this is the seed of the *dharmakāya*.
This seed of the *dharmakāya* differs from the aforementioned *dharmakāya* of the nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) only in its mode of being distinct or identical.

The Tathāgata is able to know these various distinctions among the seeds. Yet, all seeds are but a single kind, which is precisely their non-differentiation. The Tathāgata is likewise able to [know this].
He knows that differentiation is itself non-differentiation, and non-differentiation is itself differentiation. The Tathāgata is likewise able to know this.

Regarding the characteristics and essential nature, this is explained by way of the ten dharma-realms and the ten suchnesses; it is not recorded in full here, but may be understood by analogy with the explanation of the [ten] seeds. The Tathāgata knows them all completely.
△ From the phrase "From what he recollects" onwards, it is explained that he is able to know by means of three dharmas. These three dharmas are... the three.

Wisdom (prajñā) likewise has three aspects: first, the objects of the three types of wisdom; second, the essence of the three types of wisdom; and third, the causes and conditions of the three types of wisdom.
What does one recollect? What does one contemplate? What does one cultivate?
This first section clarifies the objects of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). What is it that mindfulness attends to? This clarifies the function of the three types of wisdom.
Mindfulness apprehends the object upon which one reflects; this is precisely the object of the three types of wisdom.
One should know that there must be wisdom that apprehends an object before there can be the object apprehended—namely, that which is heard, reflected upon, and cultivated.
What is mindfulness? What is reflection? What is cultivation?
This clarifies the essence of the three types of wisdom, which are the capacities for hearing, reflecting, and cultivating.
Mindfulness consists of recording the teachings one has heard; it is precisely the essence of the wisdom of mindfulness.
"By what dharma does one recollect? By what dharma does one contemplate? By what dharma does one cultivate?

This clarifies the causes and conditions for the three types of wisdom; that is, the three types of wisdom apprehending their objects through the union of the subject and the object in hearing the Dharma.

This is their causal condition (*nidāna*). Furthermore, because the objects and wisdom of the three types of insight (*trividya*) are joined through causal conditions, one attains the dharmas of the three insights;

this is also called a causal condition. Regarding these three vehicles and their three insights, it was previously held that there were differences in the nature of their objects and causal conditions.
This is precisely their differentiation. If one enters the perfect and wondrous threefold wisdom of this present sutra, there is no differentiation.
The Tathāgata is likewise able to know both this differentiation and non-differentiation.
By means of what dharma does one attain what dharma?
This refers to two dharmas to clarify that the Tathāgata is able to know them: by means of what dharma is the cause, and what dharma is attained as the fruit?

The various causes of the five vehicles each obtain their respective fruits; this is their differentiation. The suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of the Buddha—[are they the same or different?]
The suchness of one is the suchness of two; there is only a single cause and a single fruit, which is thus without distinction.

The Tathāgata is able to know both distinction and non-distinction. That distinction is itself non-distinction, and that non-distinction is itself distinction; the Tathāgata is also able to know this.
Sentient beings dwell in various stages; only the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are, with clarity and without obstruction.
This refers to the single dharma that can know [them]; because the seven skillful means abide in seven positions, they are called "various stages.
This is the distinction. The Tathāgata perceives them with his Tathāgata-eye as it truly is, just as all rivers flow into the ocean.

If the original flavor is lost, there is no distinction; yet when one speaks according to the intentions of others, employing wisdom and skillful means to expound the teaching, the Tathāgata is able to know the distinctions.
Furthermore, because all the teachings he proclaims reach the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the Tathāgata is able to know their non-distinction as well.
Just as those flowers, trees, forests, and various medicinal herbs do not themselves know their superior, middling, or inferior natures—
this is the third [point], which provides an analogy to correspond with the aforementioned fact that sentient beings do not realize it for themselves.
The Tathāgata knows this Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor— namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment,
the characteristic of cessation, ultimate nirvāṇa, the eternally quiescent characteristic, which ultimately returns to emptiness.
This fourth point restates the preceding summary of the Tathāgata’s ability to know—such as the "one characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and "one flavor" (*ekarasa*)—as already explained above.
It should be understood that these "one characteristic" and so forth function as conditions for discernment; that is, within the one, there are the infinite.
Ultimate *nirvāṇa* ultimately reverts to emptiness; it is one among the immeasurables. This restates the preceding point to further explain the aforementioned lack of differentiation.

Why is this? Because this single characteristic and single flavor—liberation, detachment, and cessation—if they were the essence of the *dharma* of the Two Vehicles, would still be proclaimed through words of differentiation. Now, as the ultimate *nirvāṇa* of the Mahāyāna, it ultimately...
"Returning to emptiness" means that one immediately penetrates non-differentiation and reaches ultimate *nirvāṇa*. This concludes the preceding phrases;
they all refer not to the *śrāvaka*’s *nirvāṇa* with remainder or without remainder, but rather to the perfect, ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
"The mark of eternal quiescence" concludes the preceding phrases; it is not the quiescence of the Lesser Vehicle, but rather the eternally abiding quiescence. Therefore, the previous text says:
That "all dharmas from the very beginning are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction" refers precisely to this meaning.
That they "ultimately return to emptiness" does not mean an emptiness of annihilation; rather, it is the emptiness of the primary truth of the Middle Way. The sutra text cites two ultimates:
the first ultimate reaches the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This cites the fruit of wisdom in contrast to the wisdom of the two vehicles.
This is not the ultimate. Second, it cites ultimate nirvana, characterized by eternal quiescence, which ultimately returns to emptiness.

This citation contrasts the cessation [of suffering] of the two vehicles with that which is not ultimate. Through this passage on the ultimate, one knows that it is not the emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle.
This concludes the section that restates the preceding points and provides a final explanation.
Having known this, the Buddha observes the inclinations of sentient beings' minds and protects them; for this reason, he does not immediately preach the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is the fifth [point] that severs the doubts of beings. Since the Buddha has long known that the beginning and the end are one and the same, why did he not [preach it] to the *mṛga*?

The Garden [Master] then explained the truth for him. Therefore, the Buddha now personally resolves this doubt, saying: "Observing the desires in the minds of sentient beings, I protect them according to the three *siddhāntas*.
Fearing that they might slander [the teaching], I did not explain it immediately.
This concludes the third section, from the beginning up to the passage where sentient beings hear the Tathāgata’s Dharma, within the five-part textual sequence of the "Non-differentiation" chapter.

The distinction between grasses and trees: [the Buddha] does not know what is manifest, yet he knows it. This concludes the second section on the analogy of non-distinction within the three categories.
From the passage beginning "You, Kāśyapa," onwards, this is the second part: restating the thesis and providing a description.

This is intended to resolve the doubts of sentient beings. As for these doubts: having heard that the Buddha possesses immeasurable merit, they assume that the four disciples have attained full understanding through the uniformity of the teaching.

Why must this necessarily be taken as literal fact? It is feared that at this time, the assembly, hearing the Buddha describe what Kāśyapa leads, might fail to understand the Buddha’s intent and instead claim that Kāśyapa’s leadership is inadequate.

Therefore, the Buddha personally describes his own provisional and ultimate teachings to praise Kāśyapa for being able to know that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate; though he himself leads, in reality, he encompasses all.
Although he has not yet reached the ultimate perfection of the Buddha-ground, once he has received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), he is already a "True Buddha.
From the Deer Park onwards, he has fully mastered both the provisional and the real; by the time of the *tīrthika* (the "clarified butter" stage), his mastery of karma is not in vain.

One should know that the previous praise of Śākyamuni was originally intended to praise Kāśyapa; therefore, having now resolved these doubts, this praise restores the fundamental principle. As for restoring the fundamental principle:
As in the preceding text, this has been moved and added here; it shall not appear again.
You, Kāśyapa, are truly rare indeed, for you are able to understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and you are able to believe and accept it.
Regarding this initial praise for what is rare: generally, those who possess the quality of reciprocity can derive benefit from hearing [the teaching]. For a bodhisattva, this is their own concern;

thus, their understanding is not particularly extraordinary. These śrāvakas, however, have already attained the unconditioned state of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and are able to relinquish [their attachments] to enter into reality.

This is truly rare: to be able to know how to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate. To describe his ability to comprehend and open up the three [vehicles] is to describe the passage concerning his comprehension and realization that reveals the reality.
Next, the statement regarding his ability to believe and accept is precisely the description of his comprehension and realization that manifests the ultimate truth.
Why is this? The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.

This is the meaning of the commentary that returns to the fundamental tenet. It clarifies that the Buddha speaks of three within the One Way, which is profoundly mysterious and difficult to comprehend;
yet you are able to believe and accept it. Therefore, you too are worthy of praise as being most rare and extraordinary. Zhan’an explains that [the passage] preceding—
The Tathāgata Mañjuśrī possesses further immeasurable merits that you all cannot fully describe.
Yet, the text later states, "You are truly rare," because the Buddha's grace is universally bestowed, like clouds and rain that cover and nourish all without exception.
The Buddha’s grace universally sustains all, just as the great earth brings nothing to life that it does not generate;
how could it be intended for only a single capacity or a single region? Therefore, it is said that you cannot fully describe it.

Although the Buddha’s grace is universal, sentient beings do not realize it in their daily lives, just as the three types of grass and two types of trees, though they take root in the earth and receive moisture from the rain, remain unaware of it.
"I know. That you are able to recognize these ten benefits from beginning to end is truly rare. 'To deliver those not yet delivered,' etc., describes the Buddha’s grace of the Four Great Vows;
this is truly rare. Sentient beings find peace and security in the present life, are reborn in good realms in future lives, and experience happiness through the Way;
this describes the grace of his great compassion in bestowing happiness; this is truly rare. Having heard the Dharma..."
Thus, having been freed from all obstacles, one may gradually enter the Path according to one's capacity. To describe the kindness of his great compassion in uprooting suffering is truly rare;

he surpasses the Wheel-Turning Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā, while those are but minor medicinal herbs. To describe the kindness of his knowledge in exhorting toward goodness and removing the feverish afflictions is truly rare;
he knows the outflow-free Dharma (*anāsrava-dharma*), through which one can attain *nirvāṇa* as well as the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
Realization. Among these, the medicinal herbs describe how they know and eliminate the heat of various views and cravings; this is most rare.
The superior herbs and small trees describe how they feel shame for their own smallness and aspire to greatness; they describe how they know and conceal the debt of their disgrace;
this is most rare. The great trees describe how they adorn [others]; this is most rare. This is the first discourse on the most ultimate reality.

The earth receives but one rain. To describe his knowledge of the entrustment of wealth and the seating, and the grace of the sovereign peace and bliss of body, mind, wealth, and Dharma—this is truly rare.
One should know that when the Buddha describes their distinctions and offers praise, the text for praising the ten graces is complete.
If one describes this as praising their lack of distinction, it constitutes a single great grace.

Were it not so, regarding Kāśyapa’s question in the preceding chapter—“What is the basis of the Tathāgata’s great grace?”—one must understand that Zhangan merely reiterated the thirteen verses of the previous chapter to praise the depth of the Buddha’s grace;
this is precisely his ability within this realm to know [the truth] according to what is appropriate.

The phenomena and principles of this realm encompass everything. Question: In this context, the preceding praise of the Buddha’s profound kindness—how does it differ from that of the ancients? Answer:
The ancients simply stated that the kindness was profound, without distinguishing whether that kindness was near or far.

Therefore, the preceding thirteen verses fully encompassed the beginning and end; now, because the Buddha recounts them in detail, it is truly called "recounting and completing" (shucheng). This is [the interpretation of] Zhang’an.
This assists in perfecting the profound realization of the wise. If one relies on this meaning, the Buddha originally recounted the entire history of Kāśyapa from beginning to end;
yet the assembly did not understand it at that time, so it was necessary to remove their doubts. Therefore, the commentary states that Kāśyapa was able to know [it].
If one seeks the intention of Zhangan (Zhiyi), how can the four "hidden difficulties" be considered identical or interchangeable with this? This clarifies the second [point].
The praise of the fundamental doctrine is concluded. The first section was the exposition and establishment [of the teaching], opening the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle.

These two sections together constitute the completion of the extensive exposition in prose. △ Below follows a verse section of fifty-four and a half lines, which versifies the preceding extensive exposition and establishment.
In the prose, there is the revelation of the Dharma and the parable; now, the first four lines of verse all summarize these. The verse on the Dharma-exposition consists of two parts:

first, the presentation of the Dharma King; second, the revelation. Next, fifty and a half lines of verse summarize the parable-exposition. The Dharma-exposition is further divided into two: first, the citation of the Dharma King; second, the revelation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
[This is the introduction by the compiler of the sutra:
The Dharma King who destroys existence appeared in the world.
These first half-verses praise the preceding extensive exposition of the Dharma teaching; they specifically commemorate the initial exhortation to believe based on the Dharma King’s non-falsity.
This corresponds to the passage in the preceding text: "Kāśyapa, you should know that from the Tathāgata’s [attainment]... down to 'all is not false.

△ Below this, there are three and a half lines which praise the opening [of the parable]. In the preceding text, there were two teachings and two wisdoms; now these are likewise fully commemorated. First:
The first one and a half lines praise the two teachings; the latter two lines praise the two wisdoms.

"Preaching the Dharma in various ways according to the desires of sentient beings"—this half-line praises the provisional teachings mentioned above, namely what was stated in the preceding text: "Regarding all phenomena, by means of wisdom..."
He then proceeded to expound it. The Tathāgata is revered;
