his wisdom is profound and far-reaching. For a long time he has kept this essential teaching in silence, not being intent on proclaiming it hastily.
This single line of verse summarizes the aforementioned teaching of reality. As the preceding text states: "All the teachings he proclaims reach [the ultimate goal]."
This is the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
Those with wisdom who hear it will be able to believe and understand; those without wisdom who harbor doubt and regret will suffer eternal loss.
This single line of verse summarizes the preceding explanation of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). As the previous text states: "The Tathāgata contemplates and knows all phenomena..."
The Dharma... up to its unimpeded penetration.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, one should teach according to one's capacity, using various conditions to enable others to attain right view.
This single line of verse explains above that true wisdom, through various conditions, expounds various teachings, all for the purpose of [enabling others to realize it].
One attains the right view of the Mahāyāna; prior to this, all [views] are termed wrong views. This corresponds to what was stated in the preceding passage:
"Furthermore, one exhaustively investigates all dharmas, up to and including all-encompassing wisdom. Moreover, this verse expresses the intent of the Tathāgata’s four *siddhāntas*:

"Destroying the existence of dharmas" refers to the *prātipakṣika-siddhānta* (the therapeutic intent); "according to the desires of sentient beings" refers to the *lokasaṃvṛti-siddhānta* (the worldly conventional intent).

The intention is this: there is wisdom that reaches the point of permanent loss; this is the human intention. To cause one to attain right view is the intention of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The three *siddhāntas* (doctrinal standpoints) are precisely the verse above stating that through the skillful means of wisdom, one expounds the teaching to cause the attainment of right view;
this is the verse for reaching the stage of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). This concludes the exhortation regarding the Dharma-exposition. △ Below, from Kāśyapa:
It should be known that fifty lines and a half [of the prose] correspond to the preceding parables. Of these, the first ten lines and a half correspond to the opening of the parables;
the subsequent forty lines correspond to the application of the parables. Regarding the opening of the parables above, there are two parts:

now, the first nine lines and a half correspond to the parable of differentiation, and the next one line corresponds to the parable of non-differentiation. Regarding the six types of differentiation above, they are all fully versified here, yet...
This follows the same sequence as the extended prose (gadya) illustration; it merely accords with the sequence within the application (yoga).
Regarding the first distinction, the first three lines [of the verse] correspond to the third illustration above, that of clouds and rain; the remainder will be shown in their respective contexts.
Kāśyapa, you should know this: it is like a great cloud arising in the world that covers everything. The cloud of wisdom contains moisture; lightning flashes brilliantly;
the thunder resounds afar, bringing joy to all beings; the sunlight is eclipsed, and the earth becomes cool and refreshing.

"Hanging down in dense masses, as if one could grasp them"—this verse refers to the third analogy of the cloud within the preceding section on "Opening the Similes. The cloud is an analogy for the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).

Because the response body acts in accordance with wisdom, it is called a "wisdom-cloud. Because it is able to possess the twelve divisions of the Dharma (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma*), it is said to "contain moisture. If [one considers] the response body...
He does not preach the Dharma. As for the Buddhas Suchandana and Prabhūtaratna, these clouds do not contain moisture.
His body emits great radiance like a flash of lightning, and his mouth resounds with the four analytical knowledges like the sound of thunder. The ninety-five kinds of heterodox lights do not appear;
therefore, it is said they are eclipsed. He removes the ninety-eight kinds of feverish afflictions, just as the earth becomes cool and refreshing.

That which can be grasped is the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) descending into the world; it appears as if identical to the three realms of existence, and one may have the intention to seize it, yet in reality it cannot be obtained.
This is what was stated in the preceding passage: "Dense clouds spread everywhere, covering the trichiliocosm.
This is that very text.
That rain falls equally everywhere, descending simultaneously from all four directions; it pours down in immeasurable torrents, saturating the entire land.

This verse illustrates the fourth analogy of the pouring rain. The eightfold voice and four analytical knowledges proclaim and pour forth the Dharma-rain, which descends simultaneously from the four directions and is heard by all at once;
this is also called the "fourfold equality. All sentient beings who possess a mind receive its benefit and nourishment.
Therefore, it is said that "the whole land is filled and saturated. This completes the preceding section and also completes the analogy of the mountains and rivers below;
it refers to the passage in the text above concerning the "simultaneous and equal pouring" of rain.

"Mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys" refers to the first analogy of the land mentioned above. This represents the five aggregates (*skandhas*) of sentient beings within the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).
Now, having received the rain of the Dharma, their bodies and speech become supple and soft, just as the soil receives moisture. This corresponds to the passage above: "Kāśyapa, it is like..."
This refers to the textual passages concerning the three-thousandfold world system, up to the mountain ravines, valleys, and lands.
That which arises in these remote and deep places—the herbs, trees, and medicinal plants—this verse praises the second analogy of the herbs and trees.
It illustrates the differences in the habitual causes of sentient beings, as well as the long duration of those beings.
The causes of habitual tendencies planted long ago lie hidden within the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas); therefore, they are said to be "profound and remote.

Now, having received the rain of the Dharma, they all attain development; therefore, they are said to be "that which is produced. This refers to the passage in the text above concerning "the grasses and trees that are produced," up to the words "name-and-form are each distinct," and so forth.
The various large and small trees, the hundred grains and sprouting crops, the sugarcane and grapes—all are made abundant and sufficient by the moisture of the rain.

Even the parched earth is universally moistened, and medicinal herbs and trees flourish together. From that cloud issues water of a single flavor, which nourishes the grasses, trees, and dense forests.
They receive nourishment according to their respective capacities.

This verse corresponds to the fifth analogy above regarding receiving nourishment. The mention of "a hundred grains" refers collectively to the five types of grain, which serve as an analogy for the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*).
It means that by means of a hundred virtues, one is able to produce the fruits of the five vehicles. One should know that each of the five vehicles, in turn...
The hundred virtues are the foundation. As for the causes of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, how could they exceed the ten virtuous actions?

When these are mutually adorned, they constitute the hundred virtues. Question: Do humans not possess the hundred virtues? Answer: Regarding alcohol, it serves to guard the mental ground; thus, in general terms, it is not that they do not exist.

The sugarcane is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because their essence is one, this is explained in terms of the object of focus (*ālambana*). The grape is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*); wisdom is explained in terms of what it eliminates.
It is not like the single instance of the grape; it refers to the universal moistening of dry ground, which is a metaphor for causing those who have not yet attained faith to believe.

Other instances are to be understood by applying the same principle as above. This is precisely what the preceding text says: "Its moisture universally moistens," continuing through the passage concerning the large branches and large leaves.
All the various trees—superior, middling, and inferior—each grow according to their respective sizes;
their roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, luster, and colors all attain a fresh brilliance wherever the single rain reaches.
This is the sixth illustration of "increase" from the preceding verses. It refers to the passage in the main text which says:
"The various trees, large and small, even unto their flowers, fruits, blossoms, and seeds. This concludes the six illustrations from the section on "distinctions" above.
From here on, regarding "according to its essence," this is a verse summarizing the second illustration of "non-distinction. There were three parts in the main text, but they are omitted here.
The verse speaks of a single ground; yet because that which is produced therein is inclusive [of all], it is as follows:
according to their essential nature and characteristics, and the magnitude of their individual capacities, though the moisture they receive is one and the same, each grows lush and flourishing.
This verse praises the second point above, the analogy of non-differentiation. The first two lines praise that which is produced and that which is moistened;
the next line praises the agent of moistening, which is thus without differentiation. Yet, each flourishes luxuriantly, though they do not themselves perceive this distinction.
This corresponds to the preceding text, which says: "Although they are born from one earth and moistened by one rain, yet the various grasses..."
The trees each have their differences. This concludes the analogy for non-differentiation. The above constitutes the conclusion of the verses that open the analogy.
From the following section, "The Buddha is also like this," down to the forty lines, these verses constitute the second part: the application of the analogy (*upanaya*).
Of these, the first thirty-five lines of verse apply the analogy to the distinctions; next, the five lines beginning with "Thus, Kāśyapa... apply the analogy to the [non-distinction].
There is no difference. The preceding section provides the formal application (*yoga*) of the analogy of the superior union; the subsequent section provides the illustrative application.
In the present text as well, there is first the formal application, followed by the presentation of the analogy to apply it.
The Buddha is also like this. His appearance in the world is like a great cloud that universally covers all things.
This single line of verse corresponds to the analogy of the dense cloud. The first two lines equate the body with the cloud;
the latter two lines present the analogy and apply it to the subject. As the preceding text states: "The Tathāgata is also like this," extending even to the great trichiliocosm.
This is the Dharma-text.
Having appeared in the world, for the sake of all sentient beings, he has analyzed and expounded the reality of all phenomena.
The Great Sage, the World-Honored One, amidst the assembly of devas and humans, proclaimed these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the most honored among those who walk on two feet."
He emerges from the world like a great cloud.
This verse corresponds to the second analogy of "pouring rain" mentioned above; it is the first of the ten titles among the six topical headings previously set forth.
Now, these ten titles are concise in wording yet rich in meaning. Why is this? Because "emerging from the world" [encompasses] the title of "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara*) and...

"Buddha" is the first title; "Tathāgata" is the second title, meaning one who has come well and departed well, as well as the Well-Gone (Sugata). "Arhat" is the third title, meaning one who is worthy of offerings. "Samyaksaṃbuddha" is the fourth title, meaning the Perfectly Awakened One who possesses complete and universal knowledge.

"Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna" is the fifth title, meaning endowed with wisdom and conduct. "Bhagavat" is the tenth title, meaning World-Honored One. "Puruṣadamyasārathi" is the title among devas and humans, meaning the Charioteer of Men to be Tamed.
"Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām" means the Teacher of Devas and Humans. "Lokavid" means the Knower of the World. Although these are abbreviated, their meanings are fully contained therein.
Tenth:
To moisten and nourish all withered and parched sentient beings, causing them all to leave suffering behind and attain the peace and happiness of the world,
as well as the bliss of nirvāṇa.
This verse pertains to the chapter on the Four Great Vows among the six preceding chapters. "To fill and moisten all" refers to the first great vow.
"Causing all to be free from suffering" refers to the second vow; this means being freed from the suffering of both cause and effect.

"Attaining peaceful security and bliss" refers to the third vow, as well as the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, which is the fourth vow. That the five vehicles all possess worldly bliss [is likewise included]. All...
To cause them to attain the foremost bliss.
All you hosts of devas and humans, listen with single-minded devotion; all should come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One. I am the World-Honored One.
There is none who can equal him. To bring peace and security to sentient beings, he appears in the world and speaks for the great assembly.
He expounds this pure Dharma of ambrosia, which is of a single flavor: liberation and nirvana. With a single wondrous voice, he proclaims this meaning, always for the sake of the Mahāyāna.
"And thus creates the causes and conditions.
These four lines above praise the exhortation to listen and receive [the teaching]. The preceding text says: "You gods and humans...

even for the sake of listening to the Dharma," which refers to this. Of these first two lines, the former praises the Buddha, while the latter, beginning with "for the sake of the great assembly," [praises the listeners].

Because he is able to speak as the Honored One among men, the Dharma he teaches is wondrous. Since the seven virtues all ultimately converge in the One Vehicle, he exhorts [beings] to listen and receive it.
This cites the absence of differentiation to explain away the notion of differentiation. From the time he first appeared in the world until this point—
The preceding commentary on the third analogy of pouring rain concludes here.
I observe all things as universally equal, without distinction between self and other, and free from feelings of love or hatred; I harbor no attachment.
Furthermore, they are without obstruction; they constantly preach the Dharma equally for all. As they do for one person, so it is for many.
They constantly expound the Dharma and never engage in other affairs. Whether walking, coming, going, sitting, or standing, they never grow weary or fatigued, fully satisfying the world.
"Like rain that moistens everywhere.
These four lines above correspond to the third analogy within the section on "Conformity," namely the analogy of mountains and rivers.

Just as seven kinds of sentient beings with the five aggregates are rained upon without distinction between ravines and valleys, the Buddha’s teaching is impartial; thus, there is no discrimination between self and other, yet it acts according to the presence of spiritual capacity.

This [is the case]: those without the capacity for awakening are treated as "others"; planting roots of goodness is "love," while increasing opposition is "hatred. Buddha-activities are "self," while demonic activities are "others.

That which corresponds to the former is "coming," while that which corresponds to the latter is "going. Entering into the ultimate truth is "sitting," while emerging through skillful means is "standing.

When the Buddha observes sentient beings, he regards them in this way; this is precisely the meaning of raining equally upon mountains and rivers. One should know that the Buddha’s hatred and love are thus.
It is eternally exhausted, yet without distinction between self and other; one does not love those with the capacity for this Buddha’s teaching, nor does one hate those with other capacities.
This verse corresponds to the preceding passage, which says: "At that time, countless thousands of myriads of kotis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was."
This refers to those who listen to the Dharma.
Whether noble or lowly, superior or inferior; whether observing the precepts or violating them; whether their deportment is complete or incomplete; and whether they possess right view or wrong view.
Whether for those of sharp faculties or dull faculties, he rains down the rain of Dharma equally, without weariness.
These two lines of verse correspond to the fourth analogy in the preceding "Harmony" section—that of grasses and trees.

From the noble and the lowly to the sharp and the dull, these are explained through the tradition of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). The distinctions of noble and lowly, superior and inferior, are divisions according to their respective stages (*bhūmi*). This is maintained.
"Observing the precepts or violating the precepts" refers to the explanation in terms of practice. "Sharp or dull faculties" refers to the distinction based on cultivation.
The passage mentioned above, from "At that time, the Tathāgata... down to "...diligence or indolence," is precisely this. From "All sentient beings" below, the fifth section consists of eleven lines.
It provides a verse summary of the fifth [section], the analogy of receiving moisture, divided into three parts. The first line generally clarifies the reception [of moisture].
Moistening. Next, there are seven lines concerning the place where beings in the human realm receive this moisture. The second section clarifies the reception of moisture.
The following three lines constitute the text on that which is moistened and that which moistens.
All sentient beings who hear my Dharma receive it according to their capacity and abide in the various stages.
This single line generally clarifies the receiving of nourishment. What follows below specifically clarifies the receiving of nourishment in five parts.
Those who dwell among humans and devas as wheel-turning sage-kings (*cakravartin*), Śakra, or the various Brahmā kings are the small medicinal herbs.
This first line clarifies that both humans and devas have not yet severed their afflictions; together they constitute the "small shrubs.

Knowing the outflow-free dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), they are able to attain *nirvāṇa*, give rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), and obtain the three insights (*trividyā*), dwelling alone in mountain forests.
They constantly practice meditative concentration and attain the realization of a pratyekabuddha. These are the medicinal herbs;
these two types of practice clarify the Two Vehicles, both of which possess abandonment and realization, and are thus combined as the middle-sized herbs.
Seeking the state of the World-Honored One, one should think, "I shall become a Buddha," and practice the meditative concentration of diligence (*vīrya-samādhi*). This is the superior medicinal herb.

This single practice clarifies the Three Piṭakas and the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); one who aspires to become a Buddha and transforms others surpasses the Two Vehicles, and thus stands alone as the superior herb.
Since it is said that one practices the meditative concentration of diligence, among the Six Perfections, diligence is the most supreme. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)
It is said: Generosity, ethical discipline, and patience are the constant dharmas of the world. If one wishes to cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom, one must necessarily apply diligence;
how much more so when diligence pervades all five [perfections]. For this reason, diligence is cited as encompassing the six.
Thus, we know that the two pieces of wood mentioned in the subsequent text do not pertain solely to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, those who focus their minds exclusively on the path of the Buddhas, constantly practice compassion, and know for themselves that they will become Buddhas with absolute certainty—
these are called "small trees."

These one and a half lines clarify that the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), having already severed the delusions common to both vehicles, vow to rely upon their remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) to engage with the realm of existence (*saṃsāra*) for the sake of transforming others.
Compared to those above, they are inferior; compared to those below, they are superior.

Since it is said that they "constantly practice compassion and know for themselves that they will become Buddhas," whereas the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections (Liuduo) only come to know this definitively during the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, the latter do not equal the former.

However, having transcended the two stages, one will certainly know that one will become a Buddha; thus, this differs from what preceded. It is designated by its excellence, and is therefore called the "Small Tree.
Firmly abiding in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), they turn the wheel of non-retrogression and deliver immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. Such is the bodhisattva.
This is called the "Great Tree.
These one and a half lines clarify the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), which encompasses both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.

Since it speaks of "turning the non-retrogressive wheel," those of the Separate Teaching are able to turn the Dharma-wheel at the first stage (*bhūmi*); this is "non-retrogression through mindfulness. In the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, one only turns the Dharma-wheel upon reaching the final fruit.
How could they be called such Bodhisattvas? Therefore, within the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the Bodhisattvas are superior due to their height and breadth, and are thus named "Great Trees.
Furthermore, one may correlate the three types of Bodhisattvas with three trees respectively; the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) correspond to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
The Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) refers to the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages, while the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) refers to the thirty minds.

Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the initial enumeration speaks of "three trees and two grasses," whereas the subsequent verse speaks of "three grasses and two trees. This represents a perspective that accommodates both approaches.

The Buddha teaches with impartiality, like a rain of a single flavor; yet according to the dispositions of sentient beings, what they receive differs, just as plants and trees each absorb nourishment in their own distinct way.
These one and a half lines conclude the section on "moistening by the fetters" (*saṃyojana-sneha*). They provide an analogy to explain the moisture received.
Although seven types are clarified, these seven are merely a small portion; therefore, it says below that they are like a single drop in the ocean.
The Buddha uses this analogy as a skillful means to reveal and teach a single Dharma through various words and phrases;
yet compared to the wisdom of a Buddha, it is like a single drop in the ocean.
These one and a half lines conclude the section on "ability to be moistened," clarifying that the Buddha’s wisdom is as vast as the ocean.

From the previous passage, "All sentient beings who hear my Dharma," up to this point, it is a verse summarizing the aforementioned "receiving moisture. This refers to the preceding text which states:
"According to their capacity," and so forth, up to "swiftly attaining excellent benefit. Below this, from the line "I rain down the Dharma rain" onwards, there are eight [lines].
Half of the verse [is as follows]. The sixth [section] above, "Combined Joyful Increase," also has two parts. First, the first two lines provide a general summary of the increase.
This also has two parts:
"I rain down the rain of Dharma, filling the world; with the Dharma of a single flavor, practice according to one's capacity."
This single line is a general verse summarizing the preceding analogy of growth. The preceding text states:
"When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they will gradually attain entry into the Path."

"Just as in that forest of karma, the medicinal herbs and various trees gradually increase and flourish according to their respective sizes"—this single line of verse provides a summary and commentary on the preceding metaphor. It refers to what was stated above:
"Just as that great cloud... each attains growth. This concludes the verse summarizing the analogy of growth. △ Below, from "All Buddhas... [the text continues].
The Dharma of the Buddhas is thus. In six lines and a half, it specifically clarifies the increase [of merit].
The Dharma of all Buddhas always employs a single flavor to cause all worlds to universally attain fulfillment, practicing the gradual stages of cultivation.
All have attained the fruits of the Path.
These one and a half lines clarify the increase of humans and devas, who universally attain fullness; this verse praises the peace and security of the present life.
"Gradually practicing" praises the future life, wherein one experiences happiness through the Path; this thus combines with the increase of humans and devas.
Furthermore,
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who dwell in mountain forests in their final bodies, hearing the Dharma and attaining the fruits thereof, are called medicinal herbs;
each attains growth.

These one and a half lines clearly demonstrate the increase [of merit] for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Regarding "dwelling in the final body" (*antya-kāya*), there are two interpretations. One says:

if the bodies of those of the two vehicles did not encounter a Buddha, it is not certain that they would not have further rebirths; because they encounter a Buddha, they become those in their final body—this is the meaning of "increase.
This is an explanation according to the *Hīnayāna*. If explained according to the *Mahāyāna* treatises, the two vehicles attain...
There is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Abiding in their final body, they are ripened by the five flavors of the Buddha’s teaching and attain entry into the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Upon hearing the Mahāyāna, they attain liberation; this is precisely what is meant by "increase. The Lesser Vehicle is mentioned last, as they are permitted to remain within the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna, where it is provisionally termed "non-existence," though this is not ultimate non-existence.
If they attain the equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Dharmakāya and undergo one further transformation, they shall enter the Sublime Enlightenment (*suvi-buddhatva*). Therefore...
It is said that this is his final birth.
If there are bodhisattvas whose wisdom is firm and stable, who thoroughly understand the three realms, and who seek the Supreme Vehicle, these are called "small trees."
Thus it attains growth.
These one and a half lines of verse specifically describe the growth and firmness of the universal teaching. This is the wisdom that realizes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-prajñā*);
it thoroughly penetrates the three realms and thereby exhausts all afflictions.
Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna and attain the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*). Hearing that all phenomena are empty, their minds are filled with great joy;
they emit countless rays of light to deliver all sentient beings. This is called the "great tree" that attains growth.
These two lines constitute a separate verse that elaborates upon the distinct teaching; this concludes the separate verses on the preceding analogy of distinction.
△ From "Thus, Kāśyapa," below, there are five lines which summarize the second preceding analogy of non-distinction.
This is further divided into two parts.
In this way, Kāśyapa, the Dharma taught by the Buddha is like a great cloud that rains with a single flavor, moistening human beings and flowers so that each attains its own fruit.
These one and a half verses correspond to the aforementioned "differentiation within non-differentiation.

For example, like a great cloud, with rain of a single flavor—this corresponds to the aforementioned rain of a single flavor being both without differentiation and yet distinct—as it moistens human beings and flowers.
Each attains realization; this is precisely the differentiation from the preceding verse.
Kāśyapa, you should know that by means of various causes and conditions and diverse parables, I reveal the Buddha-way; this is my skillful means.
The Buddhas are likewise. Now, for your sake, I shall declare the most ultimate truth: none among the assembly of śrāvakas have attained final nirvāṇa;
the path you practice is the bodhisattva path. By practicing and training gradually, you shall all become Buddhas.

These three lines and a half constitute the distinction between differentiation and non-differentiation. Kāśyapa, you should know that from the passage "by means of various causes and conditions" onwards, this clarifies *upāya* (expedient means);
*upāya* is precisely differentiation, which corresponds to what was previously described as "the arising [of phenomena]. Now, the phrase "for your sake" serves to reveal the *tattva* (reality);
reality is precisely non-differentiation, which corresponds to what was previously described as "one ground. As for the phrase "not those who have attained extinction":
They have not yet transcended the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*). It is spoken of as the "Two Vehicles" alone because their resolve and guarantee are firm.
Humans and devas do not regard the fruit [of their practice] as *nirvāṇa*, and Bodhisattvas do not seek realization midway.

As for this "Bodhisattva Path," when a Bodhisattva practices the path, they must also sever the pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*). You have already severed them completely; this is precisely the Bodhisattva Path. (From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*)

The treatise states: If one who has regressed from the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta) generates it again, the roots of goodness previously cultivated are not extinguished, and they will attain the same fruit as later.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the wisdom and abandonment of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) constitute the path of a bodhisattva: because the followers of the two vehicles cling to their own fruits, [the text] dismissively refers to them as "the path of a bodhisattva.

Here, "path" (*mārga*) refers to the cause (*hetu*). Question: Do bodhisattvas also have fruits? Answer: According to the *Śraddhā-vimukti-śāstra*, it is said that they "attain the path and attain the fruit."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Existence (*bhāva*) is the path of the bodhisattva; non-existence (*abhāva*) is the fruit of the bodhisattva. Why does it not say that [non-existence] is the fruit of the bodhisattva?
The answer is: this meaning should indeed be understood as such. However, what is said here—whether it be the path or the fruit—is that both are causes for Buddhahood.
The cause is itself the path. This concludes the preceding section on the analogy of non-differentiation.
From the beginning of this chapter’s prose and verses up to this point, the second part—consisting of the analogies for those of medium capacity—is complete.
This marks the end of the third section, in which the Tathāgata confirms the understanding of the four great disciples.
