The *hūragas*, humans, non-humans, and others respectfully surrounded him. Furthermore, they saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
This fourth section clarifies seeing the Buddha by following the light.
Then the Brahma Kings bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times.
They immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha until the scattered blossoms were as vast as Mount Sumeru; they also used them to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having completed these flower offerings, each offered his own palace to the Buddha and spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and bring us benefit."
"May you graciously accept and dwell in these palaces we have offered. At that time, the Brahma Kings, before the Buddha, with single-mindedness and in unison, spoke in verse:
The World-Honored One is exceedingly difficult to behold. Having destroyed all afflictions, it is only now, after more than one hundred and thirty kalpas, that we have been able to see him once.
He fills with the rain of Dharma all sentient beings who are parched with hunger and thirst. Such a being of immeasurable wisdom has never before been seen.
Like the udumbara flower, which is encountered only today; our various palaces have been adorned by the power of this light.
O World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, we pray that you will graciously accept them.
The fifth section clarifies the offering of the three karmas.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they each spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the Wheel of Dharma, so that all in the world—devas, Māras, Brahmas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—may all attain peace and security."
And thus they attain liberation. Then the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke in verse:
"We pray that the Honored One among Gods and Humans will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; beat the great drum of the Dharma and blow the great conch of the Dharma."
May you universally rain down the great Dharma rain and deliver immeasurable sentient beings. We all turn to you with this request: please manifest your profound and far-reaching voice.
This clarifies the sixth request for the Dharma.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
This is the seventh clarification regarding silent consent. The above concludes the text on the invitation by the Brahmās of the southern direction.
In the following passage, the scribe avoids prolixity and follows the preceding example to provide a general account of all six directions.
The same applies from the southwest down to the nadir;
this collectively clarifies the six directions. Herein, these six directions, together with the previously mentioned southern direction, constitute seven directions.

This is like requesting the turning [of the wheel] to correspond to the half [of the teaching] in order to clarify the full, just as the present Buddha speaks of the Vaipulya sūtras. The above all clarifies the requests for the nine directions.

The praise concluded. From here below, the invitation from the upper direction is clarified; it consists of only six sections. Because the World-Honored One spoke them immediately, there was no silent assent.
At that time, in five million billion lands of the upper direction, all the Great Brahma Kings beheld their own respective abodes.
The palace was brilliantly illuminated with majestic radiance;
this was the first clear vision of an auspicious omen, the likes of which had never occurred before.
He leaped for joy with great exultation, giving rise to a sense of wonder.
The second [section] clarifies their astonishment.
That is to say, they each went to one another and deliberated together on this matter: "By what cause and condition does our palaces possess such radiance?"
Now, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Śikhin, who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
"By what causes and conditions do our palaces now possess such majestic power and radiant light, adorned in a manner never seen before?"
"Such a wondrous sign as this has never before been heard or seen. Is it because a Great Virtuous One (Mahātmā) is born, or is it because a Buddha has appeared in the world?
This is the third inquiry regarding the manifestation of light.
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, together with their palaces,

each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively toward the lower direction to investigate the cause of these signs. There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree,
seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
The *kumbhāṇḍas*, humans, non-humans, and others respectfully surrounded him. Furthermore, they saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
This fourth section clarifies seeing the Buddha by following the light.
Then the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha;
the flowers thus scattered were like Mount Sumeru. Having made this offering of flowers to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree, they each presented their palaces to the Buddha, saying:
"May you look upon us with compassion and grant us benefit."
"May you graciously accept and dwell in these palaces we offer. Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma Kings, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse:
Excellent is the sight of all Buddhas, the Holy Honored Ones who save the world; they are able to exert effort to deliver all sentient beings from the prison of the three realms.
The Universally Wise Honored One of gods and humans has compassion for all classes of living beings; he is able to open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all.
In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, time passed in vain as no Buddha appeared. Before the World-Honored One emerged, the ten directions were perpetually shrouded in darkness.
The three evil realms increased, and the asuras flourished; the hosts of devas gradually diminished, and most who died fell into the evil paths.
Not hearing the Dharma from the Buddha, they constantly perform unwholesome deeds; their physical strength, wisdom, and such qualities all diminish.

Due to the causes and conditions of their sinful karma, they lose both happiness and the perception of happiness. Abiding in the dharma of false views, they do not recognize wholesome conduct or proper rules.
Failing to receive the Buddha’s transformation, we have constantly fallen into the evil realms. The Buddha is the eye of the world;
appearing only after a vast expanse of time, he manifests in the world out of compassion for all sentient beings. Having transcended and attained perfect enlightenment, we rejoice most profoundly.
Together with all other assemblies, they marveled at this unprecedented event, exclaiming in joy: "Our various palaces have been adorned by the power of this light;
we now offer them to the World-Honored One. We pray that you will compassionately accept them. May the merit from this be extended to all beings."
“May we and all sentient beings together attain the Buddha-way.
This fifth section clarifies the offering of the three karmas.
At that time, after five million billion Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each addressed the Buddha, saying: “We only pray that...”
The World-Honored One has turned the wheel of Dharma, bringing peace and security to many, and delivering many across [suffering]. At that time, the Brahma Kings spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One turns the wheel of Dharma, Beating the drum of the Dharma of Ambrosia. He delivers sentient beings from suffering and affliction, Revealing and showing the path to Nirvana."
I only pray that you will accept my invitation. With a great and subtle voice, out of compassion, please expound upon the Dharma practiced throughout immeasurable kalpas.

This is the sixth section, clarifying the method of invitation. According to the text of this verse, the Brahmā of the upper direction invites [the Buddha] with both the preliminary and the full [invocation], just as the present Buddha’s preaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* begins from the time of the previous Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment and his long life, continuing until now; this clarifies the distance of the karmic connection.

The preceding section concludes. △ From the passage below, "At that time, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū received [the request] from the ten directions," onwards, the text concerning the proximate causes for establishing karmic conditions consists of two parts:

first, the initial turning of the Dharma-wheel of the *ardha-akṣara* (half-syllables); second, the request by the sons to turn away from the *ardha-akṣara* and clarify the Dharma-wheel of the *pūrṇa-akṣara* (full-syllables).
The first part has three sections: first, the acceptance of the request; second, the actual turning of the wheel; third, the attainment of the Way upon hearing the Dharma. Now, this...

Within this [text], one should have explained the three vehicles, as in the text of the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*). That it is not explained here is precisely for the sake of establishing a karmic connection and revealing the truth for those of inferior faculties;
thus, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are merely omitted from discussion.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the invitation of the Brahma Kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes;

this was the first instance of a Buddha accepting an invitation. Because the Buddha accepted the invitation and preached the Dharma, the subsequent sections were able to be recited as a commentary and concluded accordingly.

Because the conditions were near, he immediately turned the Wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects—a wheel that no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could turn—namely:
this is suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

And he extensively taught the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;

name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence.

With birth as condition, there is aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;
with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases.
Cessation. With the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.
This second section correctly elucidates the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma, namely: showing, exhorting, and realizing. "Showing" refers to demonstrating its characteristics.
"Exhortation" means urging others to practice; "realization" means leading oneself to realize that [truth]. Now, the characteristics of the three turnings shall be briefly explained.
"Showing" refers to: "This is suffering," up to "This is the path. "Exhorting" refers to: "Suffering should be known; the origin should be abandoned."

Cessation (*nirodha*) should be realized; the Path (*mārga*) should be cultivated. As for "realization": "Suffering has been known by me; it need not be known again," and so on, up to "the Path has been cultivated by me;
it need not be cultivated again. A detailed explanation is as found in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

If one were to record exhaustively within this work the characteristics of the similarities and differences regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*) according to the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras, even a hundred pages would not suffice.

It may be concluded as follows: it is simply to let them know that what was previously small later becomes great, being of the same substance as this very earth; therefore, I shall not describe it further.
Furthermore, it is in relation to those on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), those on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Moreover, it is for the sake of the three turnings for *śrāvakas*, two turnings for *pratyekabuddhas*, and one turning for *bodhisattvas*; this is according to their respective objects. Why is this so? It is due to the sharpness or dullness of their faculties (*indriya*). This...
This is merely a general statement; in principle, all [teachings] throughout the various directions follow these three turnings. Why are there three turnings?

The Dharma spoken by all Buddhas reaches its full expression at three points because sentient beings possess three types of faculties (*indriya*). This is explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Question:
When [the Buddha] first taught for the sake of the five monks, how did he establish the three faculties? Furthermore, there were eighty thousand devas [present]; why...

Therefore, why are there not three faculties? Answer: Because humans and devas both possess three meanings. This is because they give rise to the three types of wisdom, the three faculties, and the three paths.
If hearing and so forth differ, these constitute the three types of wisdom; if there is a sequence in their realization, these constitute the three faculties.

The paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning constitute the three paths. The attainment of parinirvāṇa in the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu) is likewise applicable by extension, though it is not attained through the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
This concludes the explanation of the three turnings. As for the "twelve aspects" (dvādaśākāra), the first is categorized according to the teaching on the Four Noble Truths.

Second, regarding the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). First, concerning the twelve aspects of the teaching (*deśanā-dvādaśākāra*): for each of the Four Truths, the acts of indicating, exhorting, and realizing constitute the twelve aspects of the teaching, as these are the functions of the Teacher.

Regarding the twelve aspects of practice (*pratipatti-dvādaśākāra*): the arising of the four dharmas—eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening—from each of the three turnings constitutes the twelve aspects of practice.

Furthermore, the twelve aspects of the teaching are the "turner" (*pravartaka*), because all four are spoken by the Buddha and are thus capable of turning; the twelve aspects of practice are the... [the turned].

Second is that which is turned. Because it enters into that mind, it is called "that which is" (*so*). Furthermore, the practice of the twelve [links] is the wheel, for the wheel serves to crush delusions.
The twelve teachings are not the wheel, because the teaching originates from the Master of Transformation.

Moreover, since the Buddha knows the time and knows the capacity [of beings], he does not turn the wheel in vain without practice. This is merely a preliminary explanation. If one were to treat them as two...
Regarding the meaning of the wheel: as for "eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening," these four mental states are expanded in relation to the forty-eight dharmas to constitute sixteen mental states.

Specifically, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is the eye; the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is knowledge; the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) is clarity; and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is awakening.
This applies likewise to the remaining three truths, thus forming sixteen mental states. Individuals of the three faculties each attain these sixteen mental states.
Thus, they constitute forty-eight aspects. The twelve truths are the wheel of the teaching (*śāsana-cakra*), and the twelve aspects are the wheel of practice (*pratipatti-cakra*);
therefore, two wheels are established. Through the cultivation of the characteristics of both teaching and practice, they together are able to subdue delusions;

moreover, since both teaching and practice are turned by the Buddha, both teaching and practice are designated as "wheels. Furthermore, it is the wheel of teaching that is able to turn the wheel. Only...
This is the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*). That which is turned consists of the twelve teachings.

If one turns the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), there are twelve teachings that can turn it, and the practices that are turned are likewise twelve. These may apply to three types of persons or be restricted to a single person.

Now, regarding the three types of persons on the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*): those of sharp faculties who, upon hearing the turning [of the wheel], immediately give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening. Because these three types of persons are treated together, it is said that there are "twelve aspects" (*dvādaśākāra*).

One should know that when the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) who attained the realization of the truths were precisely those for whom the twelve [aspects] existed. This concludes the explanation of the twelve aspects. Next, the explanation of what cannot be turned: The Buddha said: "This Dharma-wheel is difficult to turn; no one in the world can turn it against me. Why is this so?

Because the Dharma is profound, subtle, and difficult to understand; it is not something that can be turned by anyone else. Furthermore, because the Tathāgata has already fully realized and mastered all dharmas, he alone can turn it, and no other can turn it against him. Moreover, because the Dharma-wheel is the supreme truth, free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and because it is the ultimate destination of all paths, it cannot be turned by others. This concludes the explanation of what cannot be turned.
As for this, the śramaṇas have not even heard of it, let alone know its name, much less be able to turn it. Although the pratyekabuddhas have awakened to it, they cannot speak of it verbally.
Although the brahmins have heard its name, they do not understand its principle; the same is true for Māra and Brahmā.
Therefore, the name "Dharma-wheel" is obtained solely from the Buddha. If the Buddha did not speak it, [others] would not even know its name—how could they possibly turn it?
As for "turning," it means to turn this sūtra and cause it to enter the minds of others, enabling them to attain awakening and shatter the sixty-two views;

only then is it called "turning the wheel of the Dharma. Because it lacks this meaning, it cannot be turned by Māra, Brahmā, or others. This concludes the brief explanation of those who cannot turn [the wheel].
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, they shall now be elucidated according to the expansion and contraction of the single transformation of the Great and Small Vehicles.
Regarding the Four Truths of the Mahāyāna: the first turning concerns two truths; the next turning concerns one truth; and the subsequent turning concerns no truth.

One should know that from the absence of the Four Truths, they are unfolded into four, and the four are rolled back into the absence [of truth]. This unfolding and rolling up are merely different names for opening and closing.
If the Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna take arising and ceasing as their essence, those of the Mahāyāna take non-arising as their essence.

Having completed the explanation of the Four Noble Truths, as for the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, these are likewise specific characteristics that constitute a detailed observation of the Four Noble Truths;

they consist of two causes and five effects, or three causes and two effects. If considered in terms of general characteristics, they transcend the three periods of time; they are categorized according to Suffering and its Accumulation.

Thus, there is ignorance up to old age and death; regarding their cessation through the Path, there is the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death—this is the specific designation.
Furthermore, regarding the general discussion: one generally contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination.

What constitutes the twelve links of dependent origination involving arising and ceasing for the Two Vehicles is the twelve links of dependent origination involving non-arising for Bodhisattvas. Moreover, this general discussion applies to all three vehicles.
Regarding the Four Truths: for the followers of the Two Vehicles, they are the finite Four Truths; for Bodhisattvas, they are the infinite Four Truths.
Furthermore, it may be discussed generally that those of all three vehicles equally cultivate the six perfections. Thus, the "Chapter on Setting Out" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas reach the other shore by means of the six pāramitās. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also states: "Ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles both possess [the capacity for these]."
The six perfections are merely different in name.
When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, six hundred trillion nayutas of people,
by not grasping at any phenomena, attained liberation of mind from all outflows and all attained profound and wondrous dhyāna.
He was established in meditative concentration, possessed the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations.

During his second, third, and fourth teachings of the Dharma, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and nayutas in measure, likewise attained liberation of mind from all outflows by virtue of not grasping at any phenomena.
From that time onward, the assembly of śrāvakas became immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
Regarding the enumeration:
this is the third instance of attaining the Way through hearing the Dharma. At the beginning there were few, while in the middle there were many. "Not receiving" means not accepting the four views;

this refers to awakening to the first fruit (srotāpanna). "Attaining liberation" uses the initial stage to illustrate the subsequent one, meaning that one is immediately freed from the two bonds of the "son" (the cause) and the "fruit" (the result).
They have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). As for those of profound and wondrous concentration, they are the "liberated-in-both-ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) persons.
The three sections above constitute the completion of the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma of the "half-syllables" (*ardhakṣara*).

From here below—starting from the passage "At that time, the sixteen princes all left home to become monks"—is the second request for the Wheel of Dharma of the "full-syllables" (*pūrṇakṣara*). The text is divided into seven sections.
At that time, the sixteen princes all left home as youths to become śrāmaṇeras. Their faculties were keen and sharp, and their wisdom was clear and lucid.
They had already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas, purely cultivated the brahma-faring, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The first section clarifies the prince’s renunciation. "The various faculties" refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Because these six organs are pure, they are said to be "penetrating and sharp";

this refers to the stage of semblance (*sādharmya-avasthā*). Furthermore, because the six organs function interchangeably, they are said to be "penetrating," and because they enter the realm of the Buddha, they are said to be "sharp.
"Wisdom is clear and lucid" refers to the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering. That Buddha initially taught the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) doctrine.

All these sons of the Buddha are fully endowed with the merits of the Mahāyāna. Out of compassion for those who rely on expedient means, they earnestly entreated the Buddha to reveal the provisional teachings and manifest the ultimate reality.
Together they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of great virtuous śrāvakas have all already attained [enlightenment]."
"World-Honored One, you should likewise preach the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for us as well.
Having heard it, we shall all together practice and study it. World-Honored One, our aspiration for the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision is what our deep minds contemplate;
may the Buddha himself bear witness to this."

The second section clarifies the request for the Dharma. The statement "the śrāvakas have all already attained accomplishment" indicates that their obstacles have been removed and their spiritual capacities have been activated;

it is for this reason that they make this request. When they say, "We aspire to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision," this refers exclusively to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which elucidates only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Their aspiration is directed solely toward this, which constitutes a formal request for the "full word" (paripūrṇa-vyañjana) while setting aside the "half-word" (ardha-vyañjana).
The text is as clear as this.

At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, eight trillion people, upon seeing the sixteen princes renounce the household life, also sought to renounce the household life. The King immediately granted them permission.
Third, it clarifies that the assembly he led also followed him into the homeless life.
At that time, the Buddha accepted the śrāmaṇeras' invitation, and after twenty thousand kalpas had passed,
he preached this Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*— the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas— amidst the fourfold assembly.
The fourth section clarifies that the Buddha accepted the invitation to preach the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "passing twenty thousand kalpas":

since the three [vehicles] were opened above for such a long duration, it cannot be that there was nothing occurring in the interim. According to the meaning of the subsequent text, during those twenty thousand kalpas, he must have preached the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.
The text states: "He preached the six pāramitās and various matters concerning supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Prajñā is the practice; supernatural powers are...
This applies to all such matters. The various Vaipulya sūtras mostly clarify inconceivable deeds and practices. Furthermore, the verse states, "discerning the true Dharma.
Because they are discerned, everything from form and mind up to the knowledge of all modes does not transcend the true mark (dharmatā);
therefore, it is called "true. Following the two *Sūtra* [periods], there is the teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*, which fulfills the instruction.
When this sutra had been spoken, the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all together received, upheld, recited, and mastered it.
While this sutra was being taught, the sixteen bodhisattva-śrāmaṇeras all believed and accepted it;
among the assembly of śrāvakas, there were also those who believed and understood; yet among the other beings, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, doubts arose.
Regarding delusion:
among the assembly of the fifth period, some understood while others did not. It is said that the sixteen śrāmaṇeras accepted it with faith, as did those of the two vehicles;
however, the remaining ten million all gave rise to doubt and confusion. This group of the uncomprehending was then joined by the ten...
The six sons are those who established the karmic connection for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or abandoning it;
the sixth [point] clarifies the timing of the preaching of the Dharma.
Having spoken this sutra, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and dwelt in meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
This is the seventh clarification: having finished preaching the Dharma, he enters samādhi. Yet, how could the Buddhas ever not be accompanied by concentration?

It is simply because the capacities of sentient beings were focused upon the sixteen sons, and the period for establishing karmic connections was limited to that duration; thus it remained for so long. This is precisely the point of establishing the connection.
The reason for this proximity is that because the Buddha entered meditative absorption and did not emerge, the assembly of those with doubts had no one to consult.
Therefore, the sixteen sons later provided further expositions of the sutras for those who remained uncomprehending.
Within the text, the location where he entered absorption is clarified as a quiet chamber; "entering absorption" refers to abiding in *dhyāna*; and the duration of the absorption is as follows...

These eighty-four thousand kalpas constitute the section from the Buddha’s initial address to the bhikṣus—“The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū lived for five hundred and forty million nayuta kalpas”—until the conclusion of this sutra text.

This concludes the explanation of the causes and conditions for establishing karmic connections both distant and near. From here below, beginning with “These sixteen bodhisattvas knew that the Buddha had entered his chamber,” and so forth.

The second part correctly elucidates the formation of karmic connections (*saṃbandha*). This consists of two sections: first, the formation of connections through the Dharma-exposition; second, the formation of connections through the parable-exposition.

Within the Dharma-exposition, there are again three parts: first, clarifying the mutual formation of connections in the past; second, clarifying their further encounters during the intermediate period;
third, clarifying that he now returns to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Within the first of these, there are again four sub-sections.
First, he knew that the Buddha had entered his room, which was why he was permitted to speak.

The Buddha knew that his work of transformation was nearing completion and that he would no longer need to ripen this particular group of people; therefore, he caused the prince to form a karmic connection with them.

Furthermore, knowing that these individuals would surely emerge from the prince’s influence and ultimately attain liberation, he entered meditative absorption and did not emerge for a long time. This concludes the general demonstration of the section divisions.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration,
each ascended the Dharma seat as soon as they realized the Buddha had entered samādhi.
For eighty-four thousand kalpas, they extensively expounded and analyzed the wondrous [Dharma] for the fourfold assembly.
The Lotus Sutra.
Second: The various princes further lecture on the Lotus Sutra to establish karmic connections.
Each and every one of them delivers six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, providing instruction, guidance, benefit, and joy.
Ānanda caused them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This refers to the benefit obtained by the assembly during the third preaching of the Dharma; they all resolved upon bodhicitta, which is why it is called "crossing over" (*tāraṇa*).

If, at the time of first resolving the mind, one vows to become a Buddha, one has already transcended the mundane world; this is precisely what is meant by "crossing over the seven stages of expedient means."
This is the meaning of "the other shore. △ Fourth, below, the Buddha arises from samādhi, offers praise, and exhorts faith; this section further has two parts.
After eighty-four thousand kalpas had passed, the Great Penetrating Wisdom-Victory Buddha arose from samādhi and proceeded to the Dharma seat.
Sitting in serene composure, he addressed the great assembly: "These sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras are truly rare.
Their faculties are sharp and penetrating, and their wisdom is clear and lucid. They have already made offerings to immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of buddhas;

in the presence of those buddhas, they have constantly cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya), received and upheld the Buddha-wisdom, and revealed it to sentient beings, leading them to enter therein."
This first section is the formal praise of the Bodhisattva. △ The following is the second part, the exhortation to believe, which has two sections:
"You all should repeatedly draw near to him and make offerings to him."
This first exhorts beings to draw near [to the teaching].

Why is this? If śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas can believe in the sūtra-dharma spoken by these sixteen bodhisattvas, and accept and uphold it without disparaging it, such persons shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"The wisdom of the Tathāgata regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

This second explanation clarifies the intention of the exhortation. The above section, from the point of knowing that the Buddha has entered meditative concentration, concludes the first part: the three sections on the formation of karmic conditions in the past.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These sixteen bodhisattvas always delight in preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Each of these bodhisattvas has transformed six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;

in every birth throughout their successive lives, they have been born together with these bodhisattvas, heard the Dharma from them, and have all attained faith and understanding. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they have encountered..."
There are forty trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who have not yet reached their end.

This third illumination concerns the constant meeting during the intermediate period. There are three types of such encounters. If one meets and encounters them, one will constantly receive the Mahāyāna;
these individuals have all already attained accomplishment during that interval and do not wait until the present. If one meets and encounters them...

They fell away from the Mahāyāna and were instead received by the Hīnayāna; this class of people has still not been fully exhausted even during that intermediate period. Now, they have once again heard the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

Thirdly, if one discusses only their encounter with the Hīnayāna and does not consider their encounter with the Mahāyāna, then those who were not liberated during that intermediate period would likewise remain inexhaustible even today.
These individuals first formed a karmic connection at the initial hearing of the Hīnayāna, and subsequently, during the intermediate period...
They had practiced only the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Now, having encountered the Prince, they first heard the Lesser Vehicle; these are the third type of person.
Having never before heard the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), they were previously wandering in saṃsāra, but now they receive the Great Vehicle, even attaining the Way after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
When people see that among the teachings of Śākyamuni’s single lifetime there is a portion of śrāvakas who have not yet resolved their minds [for enlightenment], they immediately...
The judgment states: "They are eternally extinguished and do not arise again. This, however, shows a failure to understand the Tathāgata’s long-term transformation of beings. Question:

If, as stated above, it takes a vast number of kalpas—numerous as motes of dust—before one finally attains arhatship, one should know that the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) must be extremely difficult to reach.
Answer: One explanation says: The Great Sage is skillful in means; relying upon the four *siddhāntas*, he makes such statements. Or...
One may speak of the Buddha-way as long or one may speak of the fruit of Buddhahood as easy to attain.
If it is to counteract weariness with the length of the path, one speaks of it as short; if it is for those who conceive a sense of ease regarding the path, one speaks of it as long.

Whether it be to arouse past roots of goodness, to accord with worldly inclinations, or so that by hearing these accounts of length and brevity one may enter the ultimate truth—it should be understood thus.
As for the statement that it took many kalpas before one could now attain arhatship, this is an expedient practice of the four *siddhāntas* intended to lead those of true practice toward the Way.
Question: What passage in this sutra accords with their preference for brevity? Answer: It is the case of the Dragon Girl.

Although no specific time period is mentioned in the "Dharma Master" chapter, it should be understood that the duration was not far removed [from their expectations]. Even within the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle...

It merely states that it takes sixty hundred kalpas; yet, even those who exit the realm after passing through eight, six, four, or two [kalpas], though differing in duration, still belong to the provisional teachings (*upāya-śāsana*).
Therefore, within the ultimate teachings (*tattva-śāsana*), the six faculties and the five grades can be expected within a single lifetime.

Even the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* speaks of attaining the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in one lifetime. Thus, Nanyue, employing the intent of the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-samādhi-sūtra*, spoke of the six faculties.

At the very longest, it will not exceed three lifetimes. Although the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) respond to the capacities of beings according to the length of their respective dispositions, when considering his own practice, [the Buddha] ultimately never remains idle with hands folded in a gesture of authority.
Question: Since the *Lotus Sūtra* is the teaching of ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), it should only speak of what is real. Why, then, do you still speak of short kalpas as long? Answer:
When we speak of the provisional and the real, we are discussing the dharmas practiced; the duration of time is merely a means to encourage and advance those who are weary.

One should know that the provisional teachings consistently speak of long periods, such as the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the immeasurable eons in various Mahāyāna sūtras;
these are certainly not to be shortened. Although within the true teaching there are both long and short durations, if one relies on the true path, the shorter duration is correct.
For example, the assembly that constantly and lightly reviled [the Buddha] passed through only four thousand billion buddhas.

All have attained deliverance. How could it be that they must necessarily pass through many kalpas of dust? Nevertheless, whether long or short depends on the capacity of the individual; how could the principle itself be so?
Since length and brevity are relative to the person, one need only be diligent in one's own efforts; what necessity is there to debate the length or brevity of another’s time?
This clarifies their meeting in the interim. △ From "The various bhikṣus... onwards, the third section clarifies the present.

On that day, he returned to preach the Lotus Sūtra. This section further consists of two parts: first, reconciling the ancient and the modern; second, clarifying the return to the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra.

The first part, reconciling the ancient and the modern, further consists of two sections: one, concluding the ancient and modern [teachings] of the Master; and two, reconciling the ancient and modern [teachings] of the disciples.
"O bhikṣus, I now tell you: those sixteen śrāmaṇeras who were disciples of that Buddha have all now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
They currently reside in lands throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma, with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as their retinues.
Two of those śrāmaṇeras have become Buddhas in the eastern direction."
The first is named Akṣobhya, residing in the Land of Joy (*Abhirati*). The second is named Sumerukūṭa. In the southeast, there are two Buddhas:
the first is named Siṃhaghoṣa, and the second is named Siṃhadarśana. In the south, there are two Buddhas: the first is named Gaganastha, and the second is named Nityanirvṛta.
In the southwest are two Buddhas: the first is named Śakradevendra-lakṣaṇa, and the second is named Brahmā-lakṣaṇa. In the west are two Buddhas:
the first is named Amitābha, and the second is named Sarvalokadhātūpadravodvegapratyuttīrṇa. In the northwest are two Buddhas:
the first is named Tamālapatracandanagandhābhijña, and the second is named Merudhvaja. In the north are two Buddhas: the first is named Meghasvara...
The second is named Cloud Sovereign King. To the northeast is the Buddha named Destroyer of All Worldly Fears.
The sixteenth is I, Śākyamuni Buddha, who has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-system.
The first section concerns the Master’s antiquity and modernity. The sixteen *śrāmaṇeras* represent the ancient; the eight directions becoming Buddhas represents the present.
△ Below is the second section concerning the antiquity and modernity of the disciples, which is further divided into two: first, the assembly of the present; second, the assembly of the future.
Now, among these, there are four.
"O Bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, each of us converted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
Having heard the Dharma from me, they set their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
This first assembly is currently present; they abide in non-retrogression toward bodhi.
Among these sentient beings, there are those who now dwell on the stage of the śrāvakas;
I constantly teach and transform them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. These individuals should, by means of this Dharma, gradually enter the Buddha-way.
The second clarifies those who regress; they are currently abiding as śrāvakas.
Why is this? Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe in and difficult to understand.
The third explains the intention behind their regression and abiding.
As for those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time—these are you, all you bhikṣus.
This concludes the fourth section, which correlates the past and the present; thus ends the first part, the text concerning the present disciples.
From here below begins the second section, concerning the future disciples, which is further divided into two parts.
Furthermore, those who will exist in the future world after my parinirvāṇa are the śrāvaka disciples;
this is the first formal assembly.
After my parinirvāṇa, there will again be disciples who have not heard this sutra, and who neither know nor realize the conduct of the bodhisattvas.
Regarding the merit they have attained, they conceive the thought of extinction and believe they shall enter nirvana;
yet I shall become a Buddha in another land under a different name. Although these people conceive the thought of extinction and enter into nirvana, in that land—

Seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, they have come to hear this sutra; they shall attain extinction solely by means of the Buddha-vehicle, for there is no other vehicle, except for the skillful means employed by the Tathāgatas in preaching the Dharma.

The second [section] resolves a doubt. A doubter says: "Those in the present who hear the Buddha preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and enter the One Vehicle may indeed be part of the stream of those with whom he has established karmic connections;
however, how can those in the future, who do not hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, yet enter into parinirvāṇa?"
How could these [beings] abandon the Lesser Vehicle to enter the One Vehicle? Therefore, the sutra explains:

"Even after their parinirvāṇa, they will ultimately hear that I am acting as a Buddha in another land and shall hear this sutra. Regarding "another land," this refers to the "remaining lands" within the common teachings of the Three Vehicles.
This constitutes two pairs: horizontal and vertical. The horizontal discussion concerns the essence of the lands and the characteristics of the teachings.

When discussing the vertical classification according to the stages of the teaching (*dharmaparyāya*), those of the two vehicles (*dvayayānika*) who have already attained mastery in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (the stage of "having a remainder") are already masters in this [teaching].
This refers to those who, from the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*) up to the Vaipulya section, have already become masters.
Re-entering the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), one becomes a person who has realized non-arising; yet this does not mean that one further uses this teaching to sever delusions.

The exception is for the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgatas in preaching the Dharma, which serves to sever doubts; these three [vehicles] are merely skillful means. In reality, there are no three.
This concludes the reconciliation of the ancient and the modern. Below, from the passage beginning with "The bhikṣus," the second section correctly clarifies the return of this day.

He preached the Lotus Sūtra. This section further consists of three parts: first, the purity of the assembly; second, the actual preaching of the Lotus Sūtra; and third, the explanation of the meaning of the previously mentioned "opening of the three vehicles.
"O bhikṣus, when the Tathāgata knows for himself that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and the assembly is pure, with firm faith and understanding..."
Having thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness and deeply entered meditative concentration, he first clarifies the purity of the assembly. Regarding "the time for nirvana has arrived":

when the Buddhas appear in the world and their work of teaching and transforming is nearing completion, they then preach this sutra—just as Kāśyapa Buddha, Candrasūryapradīpa Buddha, and others did after preaching this sutra.
He immediately entered *nirvāṇa*. After Śākyamuni finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he proclaimed that he was about to pass away.

His statement that "the assembly is again pure" signifies that his work of transformation is nearing completion and the capacities of the assembly are ready to ripen. "Ripening" refers to the fulfillment of the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*);

thus, the term "pure" indicates the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*), which is the virtue of abandonment. Regarding the phrase "firm in faith and understanding," faith refers to the four [inshakings of faith].

Regarding "unshakable faith," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: The Sūtras teach that there are four kinds of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*), namely those directed toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts (*śīla*).
These four are precisely what is realized. When one perceives the [first] three Truths, one attains two types of purity: that of the Dharma and that of the precepts.

When one perceives the Truth of the Path, one simultaneously attains [purity in] the Buddha and the Saṅgha; thus, by perceiving the Four Truths, one realizes the four verified purities. This explanation is sufficient.

They have eliminated the outflows (*āsrava*), correctly understood [the truth], thoroughly realized the ultimate reality (*satya*), and are endowed with all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). This refers to the establishment of wisdom and the abandonment [of defilements].
At that time, they are capable of being taught the Great Way; upon hearing it, they will certainly believe and accept it. This is by contrasting the Deer Park period with the time of Nirvāṇa;

only through this interpretation can the intent of the "Simile Chapter" (*Upamā-parivarta*) be properly grasped. Furthermore, "the assembly was again purified" means they had attained the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
This further serves to avoid calamities. Those whose faith and understanding are firm possess a heart that fundamentally trusts the Vaipulya teachings.
They thoroughly comprehend the dharma of emptiness; upon hearing the teachings of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they attain realization within the dharma of emptiness.
This refers to the intent of converting others through teaching, which should be explained according to the meaning of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Śraddhābhūmi*).
He then assembled the bodhisattvas and the community of śrāvakas and preached this sutra for them: "In the world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction;
it is only through the single Buddha-vehicle that one attains extinction."
The second is the correct exposition of the Lotus Sūtra. "Gathering all bodhisattvas" refers to the assembly of kinsmen and so forth; this is the preaching of this sūtra.
Regarding the previous explanation of "kinsmen," it is clear that their meaning is evident when verified by this passage:

that they are the great beings of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya-mahāsattva) who serve as the shadow and echo [of the Buddha]. "Gathering all bodhisattvas" constitutes the assembly of kinsmen, while the assembly of śrāvakas constitutes the summons.
O bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata, through his skillful means, penetrates deeply into the nature of sentient beings.
Knowing that they delight in inferior teachings and are deeply attached to the five desires, he preaches nirvāṇa for their sake. When these people hear it, they immediately believe and accept it.

The third [section] explains and opens up three meanings. Question: If there are no followers of the two vehicles who attain extinction (nirvāṇa) in this world, for what reason did the Tathāgata previously preach the provisional teachings?
Therefore, the sutra explains: "Bhikṣus, you should know that these are the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata."
He deeply understood that sentient beings possess inferior dispositions and desires, are attached to the five sensory objects, and are defiled by the five turbidities;
therefore, he first taught the three [vehicles] to enable them to break through their defilements and escape calamity, and only later taught the one [vehicle].

Since the sutra text states that there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction (nirvāṇa), how could it be claimed that a fixed nature is established? The above follows from these sixteen bodhisattvas.

The śrāmaṇera knew that the Buddha had entered the room. This is from within the section on "Formally Establishing Connections" (*shō ketsuen*). The initial explanation of the Dharma through words has concluded.

△ From the passage beginning with "For example" (*pí-rú*) onwards, this is the second explanation by way of analogy within the section on "Formally Establishing Connections. Analogies involve both opening and closing;
this text is difficult to discern, therefore it is analyzed in detail in contrast to the two preceding cycles. First, the opening analogy is divided into two parts. The first:

The analogy of the "Guide" illustrates the initial teaching and the collective formation of the great vow; it corresponds to the general metaphor of the burning house and serves as a summary verse on skillful means (*upāya*).
Second is the analogy of the "Leading Forward," which illustrates the meeting in the interim and the subsequent preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
If they were to meet in the interim and hear the Dharma from me, all would attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*. However, this is not the case.

An analogy is established for such a person. If one were to encounter [this situation] midway, those who currently abide on the stage of a śrāvaka are precisely the ones for whom this second analogy is established;
it corresponds to the separate analogy for the burning house and is the extensive verse on skillful means (*upāya*).
The initial analogy of the guide corresponds to the general analogy for the burning house and contains the six points within the concise verse on skillful means.
Furthermore, regarding this text, there are five parts. Question: In this section, the analogy used speaks only of "beginning and end.
Why does it not employ names such as "the son and father losing each other," "the elder entering the burning house in alarm," or "not in vain"?

Since the analogies are different, should they not be fundamentally inconsistent with the two previous weeks? How can they be identical to the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa)? Answer: Generally, when making an analogy...

These names are each assigned according to the convenience of their meaning. Above, they are taken to indicate the presence or absence of spiritual resonance; hence it is said that "father and son lose each other" or "father and son meet.

If one takes them to signify the initial response to a stimulus, then because [the Buddha] first accords with the capacity [of beings], it is said that [the children] are startled and enter the burning house.

Herein, it clarifies that he leads and guides all people, meeting them life after life; how then could it be said that they have lost one another? Having long since established karmic conditions, how could it be said...

This is precisely for the sake of this meaning. It is not that they failed to recognize the signs and were startled into being called by name; rather, the phrasing is not applicable [literally], yet its intent is universal.

Why is this? As for "failing to recognize the signs" and "seeing the signs," since these refer to those of middle capacity who have already attained awakening, their failing to realize it today—prior to the manifestation of the Great and Small Vehicles—is termed "turning one's back on one's father. Furthermore, it clarifies that although they see their father, they do not recognize him.

This is the fault. As for the phrase "startled entry" mentioned in the middle [of the text]: although I have turned my back on my father, my father does not abandon me; he constantly contemplates my capacity (*indriya*).

At the very moment that capacity is reached, there is thus the significance of "startled entry. If one discusses the response to this capacity, it occurs after the conditions for connection have already been established.

How could it not be as it is now in this text? Since it is stated here that they met in the interim and have now met again to attain deliverance, we know that there was no lack of losing sight of one another and being startled into entry [into the path] during that interval.

One should understand that following and pursuing arises from being startled into entry; because of being startled into entry, they meet; and because they meet, they had previously lost sight of one another. Each statement cites only one side of the matter. Great!

The essential meaning is no different. Question: Since it was previously stated that [the provisional] "follows along" (*anuvartate*) and not that it is "lost," why is the analogy of "not being in vain" (*amogha*) not applied now that a benefit has been obtained?
Answer: In the preceding sections, the opening of the provisional and the revelation of the real (*upāya-kuśala-prakāśana*) have been treated in twenty-two instances across four locations;

thus, the meaning is already manifest. The purpose of "not being in vain" was originally intended to encourage faith. Since those of inferior capacity will attain faith before long, it was not [necessary to state it here].
It must be so. For example, there are five hundred yojanas.
This clarifies the first of the five hundred yojanas within the analogy of the guide. Now, regarding the explanation of these five hundred [yojanas], it concerns the Teacher of Men and...

The sūtras and śāstras have been transmitted in various versions, and their interpretations differ widely; these details are fully analyzed in the commentaries (*śu*). Here, I shall explain according to this specific sūtra.

The three hundred realms refer to the places of karmic retribution within the triple world (*tridhātu*); the four hundred realms refer to the places of other lands; and the five hundred realms refer to the places of the land of true recompense (*sahapratipūrṇavipāka*).
This is an explanation based on the locations of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). As the analogy in the subsequent text states: "Knowing all births and deaths... and so forth.
It is clear that death itself is the locus [of this teaching]. However, the Buddha’s intent is difficult to comprehend; it must be further explained in detail.

The delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) constitute one hundred; the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) constitute two hundred; the five upper fetters (*pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) constitute three hundred; and the *rajas-aṇu* (dust-like afflictions) constitute four hundred.

Ignorance constitutes five hundred [yojanas]. The following passage provides an analogy, stating: "The afflictions are a perilous and difficult evil path. This meaning supports one another; this is an explanation based on the afflictions.

Furthermore, entering the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) enables one to traverse three hundred; entering the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) enables one to traverse four hundred;

entering the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*) enables one to traverse five hundred. The subsequent passage provides an analogy, saying: "Skillfully knowing the passage through the perilous road."
The characteristic of "blocking" refers to the mutual support of the two meanings of the five hundred [verses] regarding both cause and effect;
this is explained in terms of the contemplative wisdom that enables crossing over.
It refers to dangerous and difficult evil paths, desolate and uninhabited, places of terror and fear.
The second, the perilous and evil path, is an analogy for the causes and effects of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

The distinction between the *paricchinna-vidhvansa* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma-vidhvansa* (transformative) constitutes the peril of the effect. The five abodes of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) constitute the peril of the cause.

Because of these causes and effects, it is called an "evil path. Regarding "no people": there are two kinds of paths. First, those that are desolate and remote where no people can be relied upon; second, those where there are no people at all.
One may rely upon it; it is like having nirvāṇa within saṃsāra, or bodhi within afflictions (kleśa). Although these are vastly separated, there is still someone upon whom one can rely.

If there were no bodhi within saṃsāra and afflictions—just as there is no illness within medicine or no medicine within illness—then they would be utterly severed and there would be no one to rely upon.
Whether there is reliance or no reliance, both proceed along a desolate road.

This refers to the two vehicles of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings. As for the *Pratyekabuddha* (Distinct) and *Bodhisattva* (Perfect) teachings, they are not for those who are not of vast capacity.

This is analogous to the aforementioned masses who have not yet crossed over; because their afflictions are heavy, they find it difficult to believe in and difficult to understand the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The Sūtra says: "Regarding these sentient beings, those who now abide on the stage of the śrāvaka, I constantly teach and transform them.

This refers to the passage concerning that which is difficult to believe and difficult to understand, which corresponds to the analogy of the fire breaking out within the burning house. It is like the roots of a pillar being rotten.

The beams and rafters are collapsing and perilous; this refers to the passage where the fire suddenly breaks out. In the "Expedient Means" chapter, the passage concerning "peace and security" is in contrast to the dharmas of insecurity.
This applies when there is a large multitude.

Third, as for the case where there is a great multitude, this is an analogy for the unliberated multitudes transformed by the prince who wishes to traverse this path and reach the place of precious jewels.

The fourth [point] concerns the desire to reach the place of treasure. Because one wishes to pass through this perilous path and seek to arrive at the realization of the various [levels of] awakening, it is said that one reaches the site of precious jewels.

This is analogous to the previous exposition of the *Lotus Sūtra*, which corresponds to the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" regarding the single flavor, the single rain, the single gate, and so forth.
There was a guide, wise and discerning, who well understood the characteristics of the dangers and the passages—both open and blocked—along the perilous path.

△ Below follows the second section: The Tathāgata’s Confirmation and Bestowal of Prophecy. This section contains both prose and verse. The prose portion has two parts:

Second, regarding whether they see their original merit or not: while the multitude sees only their outward traces as being śrāvakas and cannot know that they are originally bodhisattvas, [the Buddha] asks, "Do you all see them? to address this.
"I have always praised him as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
This indicates his traces. Now, regarding these traces, he is the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.

If it were not for the wondrous fundamental essence of the Dharmakāya, there would be no way to manifest such a supreme trace. Hitherto, it has only been said that he is foremost among those who preach the Dharma with respect to his traces.
The Dharma is supreme; yet now it is not so, for he has long attained supremacy regarding the unsurpassed Dharma.
This cites the manifest traces to reveal the fundamental source.
Furthermore, he constantly extols its manifold virtues.
This indicates the fundamental ground (mūlabhūmi), the dharma-gates of the myriad practices of merit and wisdom; hence it says "various.

It has already come; there is no one capable of knowing it. This refers to the seven kinds of skillful means (*upāya*).

It is not merely that he has assisted me in proclaiming the teachings of the Half and Full [Vehicles] for a long time; rather—

Furthermore, based on the ninety billion texts, it is fully explained how they assist the Buddha in proclaiming the teachings of the five flavors to mature sentient beings.

As for the phrase "protecting and assisting in the proclamation," this refers specifically to assisting in the proclamation of the "half-syllable" (ardhamātrā) teaching, which is like the flavor of curdled milk (*dadhi*). This is the True Dharma of the Buddha.
This refers to assisting in the proclamation of the *mṛdvī-sarpis* (fresh butter) flavor of the Vaipulya teachings.

This is also like the present Buddha turning the wheel of the teaching, preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā*, clarifying the six *pāramitās*, and how they mutually encompass one another, revolving without obstruction. At the abodes of nine billion Buddhas, he likewise assisted in their proclamation.
Yang: It is no different from today. Those people of that Buddha’s world all considered him to be truly a śrāvaka.

This clarifies the fulfillment of the fruit. △ Below, the text clarifies the vast purity of the land where his vows are fulfilled. This section further divides into five parts.
That Buddha takes as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are sands in the Ganges River and makes them a single buddha-field. The ground is composed of the seven treasures;

This clarifies the first of the five aspects of the vast purity of the land: that the land is exceedingly majestic and pure, such that its surface is as level as the palm of a hand.
The sutra states explicitly that it is "like the palm," not specifically "the palm of the hand. Since the palm of the hand is uneven, it would not serve as a valid illustration.
There is a stone at the bottom of the ocean called the "Palm"; this stone does not possess even a speck of dust's worth of unevenness. It must be of this kind, resembling the "palm of the ocean.
Furthermore, the *Bhadrapāla-kalpika-sūtra* (or *Bhadrakalpa-sūtra*) clearly explains it as being like the palm of the Buddha’s hand, rather than citing the human hand.

Those born in the lower grade in the realm of Sukhāvatī dwell within lotus flowers and constantly hear Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara preaching the Dharma.
Regarding those who "feed on the joy of the Dharma": hearing the Dharma brings them joy; while actually hearing it constitutes the food of the Dharma, having heard it constitutes the food of joy.
Regarding those who "feed on dhyāna": this means they sustain themselves through the methods of meditation and have no need for solid food.

This fourth [point] clarifies that the number of the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas is exceedingly great.
That Buddha-land is thus adorned and perfected with such immeasurable merits.

"The equality of pure precepts refers to the cessation of the ten paths of wholesome action.

They will be born in the happy realms. If one dedicates this root of goodness from abstaining from killing toward enlightenment, one will certainly reach enlightenment and achieve unsurpassed wisdom.
