The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Nine: The Bestowal of Prophecies upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training.
This chapter constitutes the second section of the text concerning the bestowal of prophecies. Regarding the initial explanation of the causal conditions:

"Those in training" (*śaikṣa*) refers to those who investigate the truth and sever delusions; "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) refers to those who have exhausted the truth and eliminated all delusions. They investigate and cultivate the true principle, aspiring to and seeking supreme insight.
This is termed "learning" (*śaikṣa*). The stages of learning consist of the three fruits and four paths; it is genuine, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).

As for the fruit of Arhatship, one has thoroughly investigated the principles and reached the pinnacle of superior vision; there is nothing further to learn, hence it is termed "beyond learning" (*aśaikṣa*). The distinction between the learner and the one beyond learning is the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint).

The stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the standpoint of individual benefit), while the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial counteraction).
The stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This is the explanation of the "Chapter on Causes and Conditions. If explained according to the teachings:

to analyze phenomena and investigate the truth is called "learning" (*śaikṣa*); when delusions are exhausted and the truth is fully realized, it is called "no-more-learning. This refers to the Tripiṭaka (Hīnayāna) teaching. To realize the essence of phenomena and investigate the truth is called "learning";
when there is neither truth nor delusion, it is called "no-more-learning. This refers to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). From the shallow...

The depth of this is called "learning" (*śaikṣa*). When both the common and specific delusions are exhausted and the provisional and real principles are fully realized, it is called "beyond learning" (*aśaikṣa*); this refers to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
Investigating the *tathāgatagarbha*, there are those in training and those beyond training; the *dharmatā* and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are neither in training nor beyond training.

To both study and yet have no more to study is precisely the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). For one who contemplates the mind, among the six stages of "identity" (*ji*), the final stage is the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);
the remaining four stages are termed the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*). The stage of principle (*li-ji*) is neither learning nor no-more-learning.

Furthermore, regarding these six stages of identity, they are all collectively neither learning nor no-more-learning; from the stage of partial realization (*fenzhen*) onward, one both studies and has no more to study.

This concludes the explanation based on the contemplation of the mind. The text of this chapter is divided into two parts: first, the request for a prediction; second, the bestowal of the prediction. Within the request, there are again two sections:
first, the request made by two individuals; second, the request made by two thousand people. Within the request made by the two individuals, there are further two sub-sections.
At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula had this thought: "We often reflect to ourselves:
'If we were to receive a prediction [of enlightenment], would it not be most delightful?'"
This first section clarifies that the two men were reciting silently.
They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we too should have a share in this; the Tathāgata alone is our refuge."
Second, regarding the clarification of requesting a prediction through speech: first, an example is cited because there must likewise be a portion [for others].
Furthermore, we are known and recognized by all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras; Ānanda has constantly served as the attendant and protected the treasury of the Dharma;
and Rāhula is the son of the Buddha. If the Buddha were to grant us the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...
Regarding the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: "My vows are fulfilled, and the expectations of the assembly are also satisfied.

This is the second part of the request for a prediction made through speech; it follows the request based on expectation. Of the two, [Rāhula and Ānanda] are the most intimate. At that time, they were what the assembly expected:
Rāhula was the Buddha’s son, held in high esteem as a kinsman in the secular world, while Ānanda held the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma, being his closest relative in the path of the Way.
Regarding "Victorious" (Jina) and "Victorious Again" (Punarjina): these two individuals did not receive individual predictions; thus, the expectations of the assembly were not fully met. Question:
Whether they are "reborn again" or "victorious," they should have been included among the "Upstreamers" (Urdhvasrotas). For what reason are they recorded here?

Furthermore, if they were to be listed among the assembly, the two would have received their predictions within the count of those in the higher stages; for what reason do they reside below? Answer: They were granted predictions collectively with the twelve hundred [monks]. As for these two individuals...

This has already been treated as identical to the case of those of inferior faculties who are "stream-enterers bound to rise" (ūrdhvasrotas). Although it was recognized by many people, the intention was to lead those of inferior faculties;
now, I am merely seeking a separate record for this. Ānanda is a person still in training (śaikṣa), and Rāhula is at the stage of a disciple;
they are included in the chapter on those in training and those beyond training (śaikṣa-aśaikṣa). The two requests are concluded.
At that time, two thousand śrāvaka disciples, both those still in training and those beyond training, all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, and approached the Buddha.
With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and gazed up at the World-Honored One, making aspirations just as Ānanda and Rāhula had done.
Standing to one side, this clarifies the two thousand [devas] requesting a prediction. There is merely a silent contemplation that cites an example;

because the two intentions are identical, it is said, "just as Ānanda wished," yet there is no verbal expression, as there are no matters of repetition or superiority. Having finished the request. △ Below.
The section on the Tathāgata’s bestowal of the prediction is divided into two parts: first, the prediction for two individuals, followed by the prediction for two thousand people.
Within the prediction concerning Ānanda, there are further five sections: first, the prose narrative; second, the verse hymn; third, the arising of doubts among three thousand bodhisattvas;
fourth, the Tathāgata revealing his origins to resolve those doubts; and fifth, Ānanda manifesting his original state and offering praise.

At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Śāgarabuddhi-vaiśāradya-vaśavarti-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara."
Charioteer of men, Teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—
this clarifies the attainment of the fruit:
one shall make offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas and protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma, and thereafter attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*, he taught and transformed twenty quadrillion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* bodhisattvas,
causing them to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This clarifies those transformed by the causes of conduct and practice.
The land is named Constantly Erected Supreme Banner; its soil is pure, with lapis lazuli for its ground. The eon is named Pervasive Wondrous Sound.
The lifespan of that Buddha shall be immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
even if one were to calculate and reckon for thousands of myriads of koṭis of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one could not know its extent.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twice as long as his lifespan, and the Semblance Dharma shall remain in the world for twice as long as the True Dharma.
This clarifies the name of the eon, the title of the Buddha, the duration of his lifespan,
and the period during which the Dharma remains. Ānanda, this Buddha, King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Ocean-like Mountain Wisdom,
is praised together by immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, for his meritorious virtues.
This clarifies that [the Bodhisattvas] are protected by the Buddha's mindfulness. The above concludes the initial prose section.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

I now declare within this Saṃgha: Ānanda, who upholds the Dharma, shall make offerings to all Buddhas and thereafter attain perfect enlightenment, known by the name Samudrareṇu-jñāna-vaśavarti-rāja Buddha.
His land will be pure, named Constantly Erected Exalted Banner.
He transforms and guides bodhisattvas, their number like the sands of the Ganges. The Buddha possesses great majestic power, and his fame fills the ten directions.
His lifespan is immeasurable; out of compassion for sentient beings, the True Dharma shall last twice as long as his life, and the Semblance Dharma twice as long again.
"Countless sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, shall plant the causal conditions for the Buddha-way within this Buddha-dharma.
These five verses praise the lifespan of those transformed by the causes and fruits of the aforementioned practices, and how the Dharma will abide for a long duration.
This concludes the second set of verses.
At that time, eight thousand bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds within the assembly all had this thought:
"We have not even heard such a prediction for the great bodhisattvas; by what cause and condition do these śrāvakas receive such a definitive assurance?"
The third [point] concerns the arising of doubt regarding the eight thousand [beings]. As for "doubt," it refers to a general uncertainty:

[the thought arises that] these śrāvakas have only just today resolved their minds and yet have already received the Buddha’s prediction, with their lands becoming pure in such a manner. Previously, within the Vaipulya sūtras, it was recorded that various bodhisattvas had to practice for immeasurable kalpas before they finally received the Buddha’s prediction. Why is this so?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed them, saying:
"O sons of good family, Ānanda and I simultaneously resolved our minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha Emptiness-King (*Śūnyarāja*).
Ānanda always delighted in extensive learning, while I always applied myself with diligent vigor; therefore, I have already attained [enlightenment]."
Regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Ānanda shall protect and uphold my Dharma, and likewise protect the Dharma-treasury of all future Buddhas;
he shall teach and bring to maturity the assembly of bodhisattvas. Because his original vow was such, he has received this prediction.
The fourth section clarifies the Tathāgata’s resolution of doubts. Because the Bodhisattva above had given rise to doubt, the Buddha revealed his origins to resolve it:
"In the past, you and I together resolved the Great Mind; thus we were fellow students. Due to my diligent exertion, I surpassed you and attained Buddhahood first."
Because of his extensive learning, he still upholds the sūtras and serves as an attendant; such was his status in his original ground.
Now that he has been granted this sublime prediction, what is there to doubt?
Facing the Buddha, Ānanda personally heard his own prediction of enlightenment, as well as the adornments of his buddha-field and the fulfillment of his vows.
His heart was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before.

Immediately, he recollected the dharma-treasuries of immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of past Buddhas, penetrating them without obstruction just as he had now heard them, and he also recognized his original vow. At that time, Ānanda spoke:
The verse says:
"The World-Honored One is most rare and marvelous; he causes me to recollect the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, just as I have heard them today.
I now have no further doubt; I shall abide securely in the Buddha-way, serve as an attendant through skillful means, and protect and uphold the teachings of all Buddhas."
Fifth, the clarification of Ānanda’s manifestation of his original nature and his eulogy.
Having finished bestowing the prophecy upon Ānanda, at that time the Buddha addressed Rāhula: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood;
your name shall be Tāpīptasaptaratnapuṣpa (Treading upon the Seven-Jeweled Flower) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-carita-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi..."
O Noble One, Teacher of Gods and Humans, World-Honored Buddha, you shall make offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are atoms in ten worlds;
you shall always be the eldest son of those Buddhas, just as you are now. This is the Buddha who treads upon the seven-jeweled lotuses.

The adornment of his buddha-field, the duration of his lifespan in kalpas, the disciples he transforms, and both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma shall be no different from those of the Tathāgata King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Ocean-Mountain Wisdom. He shall also become the eldest son of this Buddha.
After this period has passed, he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this further, [spoke these verses].
He spoke in verse, saying:
"When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son; now that I have attained the Buddha-way, he receives the Dharma and becomes my Dharma-son."
In future ages, he shall behold immeasurable billions of Buddhas and serve as their eldest son, single-mindedly seeking the path to Buddhahood.
Rāhula’s secret practices are known only to me; appearing now as my eldest son, he does so to manifest this to all sentient beings.
Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions; their merits are beyond counting. Abiding securely in the Buddha-dharma, they seek the unsurpassed path.
The above prose and verse conclude the bestowal of the prediction upon Rāhula. Next follows the bestowal of predictions upon two thousand people.
The prose and the verses [conclude]. Having received their predictions, they were filled with joy.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that these two thousand persons—both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—were of supple minds, tranquil and pure, and gazing at the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Do you see these two thousand persons, both those in training and those beyond training? [Ānanda replied,] "Indeed, I do."
"Ānanda, you should see that these people shall make offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are atoms in fifty worlds;
they will revere, respect, and protect the treasury of the Dharma. Finally, at the same time, in the lands of the ten directions, each shall attain Buddhahood, all bearing the same name:
Ratnaketu Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata..."
He is the Tathāgata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. His lifespan shall last for one kalpa;
the adornment of his land, his śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma shall all be identical [to those of Śākyamuni].

This clarifies the bestowal of predictions upon two thousand people; that they shall attain the fruit through the practice of causes, and that their lands shall be named Dharmasthiti and so forth, as stated in the text.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
These two thousand śrāvakas now stand before me; I bestow upon them all the prediction that they shall in the future attain Buddhahood.

The number of Buddhas they have made offerings to is as previously described, equal to the number of atoms in a dust mote; having upheld their Dharma-treasury, they shall later achieve perfect enlightenment.
In each of the lands of the ten directions, they shall all possess the same name; simultaneously seated at the site of enlightenment, they shall realize unsurpassed wisdom.
All shall be named Ratnalakṣaṇa (Treasure-Mark), and their lands, disciples, True Dharma, and Semblance Dharma shall all be equal and without distinction.
All, by means of their various supernormal powers, deliver sentient beings throughout the ten directions; their fame is universally pervasive as they gradually enter nirvana.
These five verses are a summary of what was seen above.
At that time, two thousand learners and non-learners, having heard the Buddha’s bestowal of predictions, leaped for joy and spoke these verses:
“The World-Honored One is the lamp of wisdom; hearing the sound of this prediction, our hearts are filled with joy, as if we were being drenched with ambrosia.”

The prose and verse sections clarify that two thousand people attained the prediction [of enlightenment] and rejoiced. From the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter up to this point constitutes the primary exposition of the three cycles of the迹 (traces).
This concludes the section on the realization, understanding, and receiving of predictions, marking the end of the *zhengzongfen* (the main body of the teaching).
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Preacher.

The five chapters below constitute the section on the propagation of the provisional teaching (jimon ritsūbun). It is not merely for the benefit of those in the present age, but also serves to moisten and nourish future generations;
therefore, there are these five chapters of propagation. A detailed outline is provided below. Regarding the explanation of the title of this chapter: it should...

There are two types of explanation: the general and the specific. First is the general explanation; second is the explanation by reducing the number. In this chapter, there are five kinds of Dharma-preachers:
first, those who receive and uphold [the teachings]; second, those who read; third, those who recite; fourth, those who explain; and fifth, those who transcribe.

However, regarding these five kinds of Dharma-preachers, not a single word mentions the numbers "one," "two," and so forth. Because the tradition of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers has been established collectively by both ancient and modern scholars, we rely upon it accordingly.

The definitions established in the sūtras and śāstras vary in their extent. Therefore, this chapter is titled "The Dharma Master" in general. If one follows the *Mahā-śāstra*, it explains six types of Dharma masters:

receiving [the teachings] through the power of faith; retaining them through the power of mindfulness; reading by looking at the text; reciting without forgetting; explaining by proclaiming [the meaning];
and providing commentaries on the difficult points of the sages' scriptures—these constitute the six types of Dharma masters.

In this sutra, these practices are combined into one for receiving and upholding (*dhāraṇa*), combined into one for explaining and expounding (*vyākhyāna*), divided into two for reading and reciting (*pāṭha* and *svādhyāya*), and completed with five by adding writing (*lekhana*).

Such is the intent of the sutra; it differs from the treatise (*śāstra*) in that the names vary according to whether they are grouped together or separated. To further distinguish them as general or specific:
if discussed specifically, four persons represent self-cultivation (*svārtha*), while one person represents transforming others (*parārtha*). In the Great Sutra, they are divided into nine.
[This concludes] the section. The first four individuals lack understanding; they are at the level of disciples (*śrāvaka*), like the three *Gaṅgā* rivers.
From among the sixteen parts of the four *Gaṅgā* rivers, there is one part that possesses the meaning of analysis; up to the eight *Gaṅgā* rivers, one possesses the full understanding of a person.

These five types of people are all able to preach and are equally at the level of teachers (*ācārya*). This distinction is made specifically regarding the division of Dharma-preachers into teachers and disciples. If discussed generally, however:
If one personally practices the five dharmas, one is a Dharma Master who practices for oneself; if one teaches others the five dharmas, one is a Dharma Master who transforms others.
Because of practicing for oneself, they are generally called disciples; because of transforming others, they are generally called Dharma Masters.

Following this general meaning, it is titled the "Chapter on the Dharma Master. The initial general explanation of the chapter is complete. Next, regarding the explanation by reducing the number [of categories], there are four parts. First:
The first grouping consists of five types of Dharma-preachers, which correspond to the "Peaceful Practices" (*sukhavihāra*). The four types of Dharma-preachers are explained later.

Regarding the second grouping, which condenses these four into three types of Dharma-preachers: the first is categorized by the three types of action (*trikarma*); the second by the three gates; and the third by the three dharmas.

The first, upholding [the teachings], is mental action (*manaskarma*); reading, reciting, and explaining are verbal action (*vākkarma*); and copying is physical action (*kāyakarma*). These are discussed individually.
Vocal karma is for transforming others; bodily and mental karma are for one's own practice. Generally speaking, the three karmas as one’s own standard constitute the teacher for one's own practice;
the three karmas as instruction constitute the teacher for transforming others. Therefore, it is called the "Dharma-Master Chapter. This is the explanation based on the three karmas.
Next, regarding the explanation by way of the three gates: practicing these five dharmas to cultivate oneself results in merit and virtue.
The gate of "widely proclaiming the five dharmas to extensively benefit others" refers to the gate of transforming others (*parārtha*).

To cultivate oneself and benefit others, all in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, constitutes the gate of repaying kindness (*pratikāra*). To discuss these separately: cultivating oneself to repay kindness is called the Dharma Master of Self-Cultivation (*svādhyāya-dharmabhāṇaka*);

benefiting others is the Dharma Master of Transforming Others (*parārtha-dharmabhāṇaka*). In general terms, both those who follow the rules themselves and those who guide others are called Dharma Masters; therefore, it is said "Dharma."
This is the Chapter on the Teacher. Third, explaining the Dharma-teacher by means of three dharmas: reading, reciting, and copying are the external practices, which are the Tathāgata’s robe;
receiving and upholding [the teachings] are the internal practice, which is the Tathāgata’s seat; and explaining them to benefit others is the Tathāgata’s dwelling.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s dwelling, it is discussed separately as "crafting others"; regarding the robe and the seat, they are discussed separately as "crafting oneself. Generally speaking, however, this is not so.
Compassion covering all beings while wisdom and benefit accrue to oneself is called the "chamber. Warding off evil in others while shielding one's own faults is called the "garment.
Only by settling the mind in emptiness can one settle others; this settling of others and self is called the "seat.
These are the three dharmas of one's own conduct, and such a person is also called a Dharma Master. If one wishes to benefit beings, one must necessarily enter through compassion.

Taking the chamber as the primary focus; engaging with existence; taking patience as the foundation; and saving others by taking self-forgetfulness as the root—when one can practice these three dharmas, the Great Teaching will be proclaimed and spread.
Thus, one becomes a refuge for the world; therefore, this is called the "Chapter on the Dharma Master. Regarding the third section, which condenses the three into two types of Dharma Masters:
these refer to those who practice for themselves and those who transform others, as can be understood from what preceded. Furthermore, there are both general and specific categories.
From a specific perspective, they are distinct; from a general perspective, they interpenetrate, for both self and others are mutually capable [of the task].

Now, this section generally follows the aspect of transforming others, and is thus titled the "Chapter on the Dharma Master. Regarding the fourth point, which groups these two into one as the "Dharma Master":

it means that the Tathāgata’s practice encompasses all practices; through compassion, he uproots all suffering—namely, that of the four realms of existence, the three worlds, the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas.
"Equal suffering" refers to compassion. "Bestowing all happiness" refers to the happiness of humans, devas, nirvāṇa, and eternal abiding.
"Gentle clothing" veils all ugliness, namely the ugliness of the four abidings, ignorance, and nescience. The "empty seat" is the extinction of all marks.
That is to say: with marks, without marks, and neither with nor without marks. This practice of the Tathāgata is based on the text of the "Noble Practices" chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Specifically, this refers to the Mahāyāna Great Parinirvāṇa; Nirvāṇa is precisely the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Therefore, the three—abode, clothing, and seat—are used to explain the three virtues. These three virtues are themselves the one Great Nirvāṇa.
This Great Nirvāṇa pervades all places and pervades all phenomena; therefore, it is called "one. This is the general meaning. As for the specific meaning:
compassion gives rise to all that is good; gentleness wards off all that is evil; and sitting upon the seat sweeps away all marks.
This explains the Dharma Master in relation to the sweeping away of marks through the contrast of good and evil. Furthermore, compassionate patience establishes all things.
Merit and virtue constitute the empty seat that accomplishes all-encompassing wisdom. Wisdom is the eye—namely, the five eyes; merit and virtue are the feet—namely, the six perfections.
This pair of merit and wisdom explains the Dharma Master. Furthermore, compassion surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
gentleness surpasses all ordinary beings and non-Buddhists; and the empty seat surpasses the analytical investigation of substance and pervasiveness.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "For example, one can only be considered brave after having conquered an enemy.
This passage refutes those who preach the Dharma with partiality or deviance. Furthermore, compassion destroys the celestial Māra; gentleness destroys the skandha-māra;

and emptiness destroys the kleśa-māra and the death-māra. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "If one transforms all sentient beings and contemplates all things as empty, the Māras will find no opportunity."
This explains the Dharma Master as one who refutes the four māras. Furthermore, because of compassion, he is able to question; because of the empty seat, he is able to answer.
This explains the Dharma Master by way of possessing the two types of adornment (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*). Moreover, compassion and patience can plant, establish, and provide sustenance;
while the wisdom of emptiness can weed, destroy, and guide. This explains the Dharma Master by means of analogy. Furthermore, because of compassion, what [is there that...]?
"Separated. What can obstruct gentleness? What can cause contention over a seat? This explains the Dharma Master in terms of essence and function.

Because he brings forth the three truths, he is called the "Victorious Banner" (Jiayou-dhvaja). Because he encompasses and universally gathers all, it is called Mahāyāna; this is the practice of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, it is called the "King of Samādhis. This is an explanation based on the differences in terminology. The Sūtra states: "All wholesome dharmas have loving-kindness as their root;
patience is the foremost path; the signless is the most supreme. If one discusses the Dharma Master of Perfect Practice, his explanations are inexhaustible.
As clearly explained in the *Xuánwén*, the five perfect practices encompass all practices, even up to the four kinds [of practices].
Samādhi encompasses all practices; all practices are but a single practice. Master Shi explained this by means of the "reduction of numbers.
Having finished this explanation, he asked: "Why is it necessary to rely on three factors? Master Ming replied:

"If we consider the practical matter, one must ascend the hall, adjust one's robes, and take one's seat before one can propagate the teaching; therefore, we rely on these three. Furthermore, if principle and phenomenon are unified..."
Treatise: Generally, delusion does not exceed three types. First, delusion arises in relation to the fruit of suffering; therefore, the gate of compassion is employed.

Second, delusion arises in relation to fetters and karma; therefore, the gate of patience is employed. Third, delusion arises in relation to the principle of the Truths; therefore, the gate of emptiness is employed.

The method of application consists of three gates through which [the Dharma] is demonstrated and guided. Furthermore, in terms of principle: because those who are deluded regarding the Truth fall into suffering, the gate of compassion is employed;

because those who are deluded regarding the Conventional sink into emptiness and cling to pleasure, the gate of harmony and patience is employed; and because those who are deluded regarding the Middle Way create cognitive obstructions, the gate of emptiness is employed.
Thus, the Dharma Master has explained [the title] based on the Three Truths and the Three Dharmas. The general explanation of this chapter is now complete. Next—

Regarding the separate explanation: "Dharma" refers to the rules and regulations; "Master" (śāstṛ) refers to a craftsman or teacher. Although the Dharma may serve as a rule, its essence cannot propagate itself; it must be transmitted by means of persons.

There are five types of those who transmit the sūtras, all of whom receive the title of "Master. By upholding the Dharma, they perfect their own practice, and in all cases, they take the wondrous Dharma as their Master.

Because they take the wondrous Dharma as their Master and thereby achieve perfection in their own practice, they are called "Dharma-masters" (dharmabhāṇaka). Furthermore, there are five... [text continues].
This person is one who can use the wondrous Dharma to instruct and mold others; therefore, the Master is designated by means of the Dharma, and thus it is called the "Dharma Master Chapter.

If both following the Dharma oneself and acting as a master of the Dharma for others are equally termed "Dharma Master," then this is an explanation of the chapter based on causes and conditions (*nidāna*).
The various interpretations provided above all rely upon the Dharma-gates of the Perfect Teaching (*vimala-dharma*) to explain this chapter. This...
The general and specific explanations of the title are concluded. △ From here, five chapters follow for the purpose of circulation:

the two chapters on the Dharma Master and the Jeweled Stūpa clarify that the merit of propagating the sutra is profound and its blessings weighty, and that circulating what has not yet been heard brings immense benefit.

The chapter on Sadāprarudita cites his past propagation of the sutra to demonstrate how it benefits both self and others, thereby proving the depth and gravity of its merit. The Chapter on Upholding [the Sutra] features eighty thousand great beings.
Those who have perfected the power of patience propagate this sutra in this world; those who have newly attained the stage of "keeping in mind" (dhāraṇī) propagate it in other worlds.

Regarding the chapter on the "Peaceful Practices," the old translations speak of "receiving the regressive and circulating [the teaching]"; perhaps it was intended in this way, though it is not necessarily the case entirely.

Beginners among the external ordinary beings rejoice in these superior blessings, yet they are intimidated by the sight of the śrāvakas and feel humiliated upon hearing of the bodhisattvas; looking back at their own feeble strength, they hesitate.
Failing to benefit oneself or others, one would then fall into despondency. For such a person, the Buddha taught the "Peaceful Practices" (*Anrakugyō*);

by relying on this Dharma for propagation, one need not fear danger or suffering. Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," the World-Honored One himself speaks of the merit and blessings of propagating the sutra and commands its circulation.
In the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," the Many Treasures Buddha and his emanations both testify to and assist it, exhorting its circulation. This demonstrates [the importance of propagation].
The fifth chapter on the Dissemination concludes the general meaning of the major sections.

Second, the explanation of the bestowal of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). The karmic rewards are as previously described and may be understood accordingly. The above constitutes the section on the disciples who have received the Way;

their merit is profound and their blessings are heavy, and it is commanded that they seek its circulation. From the phrase "If, moreover... onwards, the second section clarifies the five kinds of teachers who transmit the Way.
Their merit is profound and their blessings are heavy. This section contains both prose and verse. The prose portion has two parts.

First the specific, then the general. Regarding the specific: in terms of persons, one speaks of the inferior and superior; in terms of time, one speaks of the present and future. Next, regarding the general:

Furthermore, if there should be anyone who receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,

silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music, or even merely joining their palms in reverent salutation;
The first section clarifies the characteristics of the present minor-grade teacher; these consist of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers and the ten kinds of offerings:
first, flowers; second, incense; third, necklaces; fourth, powdered incense; fifth, unguents; sixth, burning incense; seventh, banners and canopies;
eighth, robes; ninth, music and performance; and tenth, joining the palms in reverent respect.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that these people have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas.
Having fulfilled their great vows in the presence of those buddhas, they have been born into this human world out of compassion for sentient beings.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if anyone asks, "What kind of sentient beings will attain buddhahood in future ages? one should point to these very people, saying that they will do so in future ages.

They will certainly attain Buddhahood. Why is this? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, writes out, or makes various offerings—even with a single verse—of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, using flowers, incense, and necklaces as offerings to the scripture, [they shall attain it].
With powdered incense, ointment, and burning incense; with silk canopies, banners, and streamers; with robes, music, and instruments;
with palms joined in reverence—such a person is worthy of being venerated by all the world. One should honor them with the same offerings one would offer to a Tathāgata.
You should know that this person is a great Bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and out of compassion for sentient beings...
"Born here. May they be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Next, "O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that these people have already made offerings in the past," and so forth, clarifies that although their [present] merit is slight, their past roots of goodness are profound.
"Having made offerings in the past" indicates the depth of their prior causes. "Out of compassion for sentient beings, they are born among humans" clarifies their manifestation in the present.
The merit is great. From "If there were someone who asked... below, it clarifies that the retribution in future lives is heavy. △ From "How much more so...
below, it clarifies the teacher of the highest grade; this also has two parts.

Therefore, having been born in an evil age, he extensively expounds this sutra.
Next, the superior grade of merit and retribution is explained. "This person, though personally abandoning the pure [realms]" is because they are drawn by the power of compassionate vows;
yet they are still born through karma and have not yet attained supernatural powers or responses. Herein, the present teacher is concluded. △ Next, [the following] explains...
After my parinirvāṇa, there will likewise be those of inferior and superior grades. As for the two inferior grades:
if there be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, after my parinirvāṇa, is able to secretly preach even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to a single person;
First, to clarify the characteristics of an inferior teacher: such a person merely possesses a partial grasp of the meaning; they have wisdom but lack extensive learning (*śruta*).
They are only capable of speaking in private and are not yet fit to preside over an assembly; thus, they are an inferior teacher.

One who speaks a single phrase in private to a single person may indeed attain an understanding of that one phrase, yet because they have not heard widely or studied many different interpretations, they cannot [teach] before a multitude.
It is said therein: "If there are difficulties in any inquiry that remain unpenetrated, it will prevent the Right Principle from being proclaimed and propagated.
As clarified in the *Śāstra*, one who possesses wisdom but lacks learning is like a light rain without thunder.

If one wishes to expound this single phrase of correct speech, I shall first speak of it in private. Thus, we know that even within our own teachings, the extensive study of differing [doctrines] is permitted.
This meaning serves to assist the True Teaching. When there are worldly customs and secular classics that are said to "assist the True," they instead cause one to sink into the ultimate principle;
one should know that such a person is an emissary of the Tathāgata, sent by the Tathāgata, and performs the work of the Tathāgata.
The second clarifies the inferior karmic retribution for teachers after their passing. This sutra is that which was spoken by the Tathatā-jñāna (Wisdom of Suchness);

it speaks according to the principle of suchness (yathābhūta). This capacity to dispel [delusion] is the teaching. Today’s practitioners, relying upon this teaching of suchness, proclaim the principle of suchness.

This means one is an envoy of the Tathāgata. Just as a king’s messenger transmits his commands, if one accords with the Master’s intention, one is called an "envoy" (dūta) and receives the title of one who has been dispatched.
To "perform the work of the Tathāgata" means that, like wisdom, one illuminates reality as it is; this refers to one's own practice.
For the Buddha, there is no other task than the illumination of reality. Today’s practitioner, relying on the teachings, practices in accordance with them.
Principle (*tattva*) is precisely the performance of the Tathāgata’s work. One should know that *tathatā* (suchness) is principle, while illumination is termed "work.

To further explain this in terms of transforming others: first, there is suchness as wisdom and suchness as principle; transforming sentient beings constitutes the "work. Today, the practitioner is able to possess [this] greatly...

They come from within suchness. For one who performs the deeds of a Tathāgata, there is not a single phenomenon that is not true suchness;

How much more so when they extensively expound it for others amidst the great assembly!

The above concludes the separate explanation of the two types of teachers. △ Below this is the second section, which generally explains the five kinds of Dharma-preachers:
those who act contrarily incur sin, while those who act conformably obtain blessings.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there were an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, stood before a Buddha for an entire kalpa constantly reviling and abusing him,
his transgression would still be relatively light. However, if a person were to utter a single harsh word in disparagement of those, whether lay or ordained, who read and recite the Lotus Sūtra,

The first section clarifies the transgressions incurred by creating obstacles. Regarding the offenses and merits herein, one does not consider whether the field of merit is fertile or barren;

rather, the gravity of the act is determined based on the initial and subsequent states of mind. Since a practitioner at the initial stage still possesses afflictions, if they are subjected to such obstacles, [the offense is grave].
Consequently, the matters they have studied will be abandoned; thus, they incur many offenses. The Buddha, however, is impartial; evil cannot encroach upon him, so how could it create obstacles?
Therefore, it is said that their offenses are light. The same applies to making offerings. This refers to those, whether lay or ordained, who uphold this sutra.
This person has dependencies; if they receive offerings, the tasks they cultivate will be accomplished. Therefore, the merit of the donor is most excellent.

The Buddha, however, has no dependencies and is fully satisfied in all matters. Although one may present offerings, they bring no further benefit to the Buddha; thus, it is said that the recompense is inferior.
For example, if a prince is in distress, providing him with his necessities brings great merit. But if one were to insult the king...
The offenses incurred are not light; both the transgressions and the merits are grave. If one offers food and clothing to a great king, the matter is minor;

even if you wish to insult or harm him, you cannot cause him actual damage, and thus both the offense and the merit are slight. If that were the case, making offerings to the Buddha would yield no merit.

Question: Why is it necessary to make offerings to the Buddha? Is there no sin in disparaging the Buddha? And why is it necessary to establish prohibitions against such acts? Answer: It is indeed as you have asked. However, this was said in order to facilitate a comparative analysis;

thus, I previously stated that we do not distinguish between whether the field of merit is fertile or barren. If one were to judge solely by the nature of the field, the ordinary person’s field is barren while the Sage’s field is fertile;

therefore, disparaging or making offerings to the Sage should be considered more serious than doing so to an ordinary person. For now, however, let us consider the ease with which a beginner might succeed or fail.
It is said that among the eight fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), nursing the sick is foremost. Because many people feel weary of and abandon the sick, the merit of those who care for them increases.

Furthermore, superiority may be determined by the difficulty or ease of the task for a beginner. If one were to judge the field based on the specific act, how could a single patient be compared to the Great Sage or the Sublime Dharma?
Just as saving a commoner is worlds apart from making an offering to a king, the gratitude of a commoner cannot [be measured] by itself.
[This is] a concealment. The King’s grace has reached the myriad people; the four [principles of] universal satisfaction adapt to the times and cannot be standardized by a single rule.
Based on this, the merit of this sutra is supreme and its principle is peerless, such that this statement can be made. Other scriptures cannot be treated as examples in this regard.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that whoever reads and recites the Lotus Sūtra adorns themselves with the adornments of the Buddha;

they are carried upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata. To whatever place such a person goes, one should face them, pay homage, join one's palms with single-minded devotion, and respectfully offer worship, honoring and praising them with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointment incense, and burning incense.
One should offer him silken canopies, banners, pennants, robes, delicacies, and food, performing various musical performances as the supreme offerings among humans.
One should scatter celestial jewels and present the precious accumulations of the heavens. Why is this so?
This person joyfully expounds the Dharma; upon hearing it for even a brief moment, they immediately attain ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This clarifies that by following these five kinds of Dharma-preachers, one immediately attains merit. It clarifies that reciting and chanting [the scriptures] is an adornment like that of a Buddha. The Buddha...
They are adorned with meditative concentration and wisdom, for such persons are also able to cultivate concentration and wisdom. They are "those who bear the Tathāgata upon their shoulders.
To carry on the back is to bear a burden; to carry on the shoulder is to bear a load. Cultivating the essence of the Dharma-body, which is neither provisional nor ultimate, is the Tathāgata’s burden.
Being able to employ both the provisional and the ultimate through the function of the two wisdoms is the Tathāgata’s load. Accordingly...

Regarding "one who should be approached and paid homage to": the previous section clarified taking the Dharma as one's teacher; this section clarifies those who are capable of being teachers for sentient beings.

Such persons possess inclinations that are entirely in accord with the true nature (dharmatā); they are all worthy of veneration and compliance. Compliance is "approaching" (xiàng), and veneration is "paying homage" (lǐ).
To venerate and comply with them, as well as to offer worship and so forth, and to treat them as the shoulders of the Tathāgata and so on—[this is what is meant].
The Buddha has attained both the provisional and the real, as well as that which is neither provisional nor real; I too have attained these, and thus they are called "attained by the Buddha.

This means that their significance rests upon the Buddha’s shoulders and back. Furthermore, because he employs the Buddha’s dharmas of the provisional and the real, their name is said to rest upon the Buddha’s shoulders and back.
Moreover, these are always upon the shoulders and backs of sentient beings, yet they use them daily without knowing it. Other sutras are not like this; therefore, they must be explained.
If it were not so, how could those who uphold this sutra be entirely borne upon the shoulders and backs of the Tathāgata?

Therefore, this passage must be explained by setting aside its literal meaning. If one is confused regarding the provisional and the real, or the concealment and the revelation, even if one attempts to interpret it using the terminology of "provisional" and "real," one still has not grasped this sublime intent. The general explanation is now complete.
