If one should utter even a single harsh word against someone who reads, recites, or upholds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, their sin shall exceed that of the former.
These two lines of verse concern the sin incurred by those who act with hostility.
Suppose there were someone seeking the path of the Buddha who, for the duration of an eon, stood before me with palms joined and praised me with countless verses.
Because of this praise of the Buddha, they would obtain immeasurable merit; yet the merit of one who extols and praises the upholder of this sutra exceeds even that.
For eighty billion eons, one might offer the most exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile objects to those who uphold this sutra.
Yet, having made such offerings, if one should hear it for even a single moment, one ought to rejoice within oneself: "I have now attained a great benefit."
The next four lines praise the merit gained by following this [teaching].
Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have spoken, the Lotus Sūtra is the foremost.
This third section, consisting of one line, praises the supreme excellence of the sutra. △ From here below is the second part within the section on the teacher who bestows the Way;

it praises the Dharma that is upheld and the method for propagating the sutra. The Dharma that is upheld is the method for self-discipline, while the method for propagating the sutra is the method for guiding others.
This includes both prose and verse. Regarding the prose: first, the Dharma of the sutra is praised, and subsequently...
The *Gati* (Track) is initially praised in five ways: first, praise concerning the Dharma; this is also a praise by way of comparative evaluation. Second, praise concerning the person.
Third, praise concerning the place. Fourth, praise concerning the cause. Fifth, praise concerning the fruit. Because the Dharma is wondrous, the person is noble;
because the person is noble, the place is honored; because the place is honored, the cause is perfected; and because the cause is perfected, the fruit is ultimate.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"Of the immeasurable thousands of millions of koṭis of sūtras that I have spoken—those already spoken, those currently being spoken, and those yet to be spoken—among them all, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sūtra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others."
O people, this has been protected by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Since ancient times, it has never been openly proclaimed.
Even while the Tathāgata is currently present, this sutra still encounters much resentment and jealousy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa?
Regarding the initial praise within the sūtra’s exposition of the Dharma: first, the praise based on the Dharma will now be explained. This sūtra is the most supreme.

"Already" (*yi*) refers to the various gradual and sudden teachings from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (*Dapin*) onwards. "Now" (*jin*) refers to those in the same assembly, namely the *Anantamukha-saṃdhinirmocana* (*Wuliangyi jing*).
"To come" (*dang*) refers to the *Nirvāṇa*. The gradual and sudden teachings such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* all still involve skillful means (*upāya*).
It is easy to believe that the One gives rise to the immeasurable; it is likewise easy to believe that the immeasurable returns to the One.
Now, regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*: as for the Dharma, it discusses how all distinctions are harmonized and integrated into the Single Dharma; as for the person, [it discusses...]

Thus, both the master and the disciple, as well as their fundamental and manifest traces, have all existed for a vast duration. These two aspects are entirely contrary to what was previously known; they are difficult to believe and difficult to understand, being matters that are hard to encounter.
Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already been preached and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* follows after it, the latter is easier to believe.

Regarding the "Secret and Essential Treasury": it is called "secret" because it was concealed and not spoken; it is called "essential" because it comprehensively encompasses all things—namely, True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the Reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
To "encompass and contain" is to conceal. That which cannot be distributed is because the Dharma is subtle and difficult to believe; it may be transmitted only to those of profound wisdom.
To those without wisdom, it would only increase their transgressions; therefore, it must not be spoken of recklessly. As for that which has never been explicitly revealed since ancient times:

within the Tripiṭaka, it was not taught that those of the Two Vehicles become Buddhas, nor were the fundamental and manifested traces of teacher and disciple clarified. This is the case with the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sutras.

Although the treasury of the true reality (*dharmatā*) has been taught, it has not yet been taught that those of the five vehicles can attain Buddhahood; nor has the origin of the teaching been revealed to manifest its fundamental nature.
Since the various sutras of the sudden and gradual teachings have not yet been harmonized, they are called "secret. This sutra fully explains the dharmas previously kept secret;
thus, it is the opening of the secret treasury, which reveals the provisional (*upāya*). It is also itself a secret treasury, for this sutra manifests [the truth].
Indeed, this secret treasury has never been revealed before. Even when the Tathāgata encountered those who were hostile and jealous, he was unable to preach it for over forty years.
Now, although he wishes to preach it, five thousand people have immediately withdrawn from their seats. If such was the case even during the Buddha’s own lifetime, how much more so now!

How much more so for the future? In principle, such people are difficult to transform. Furthermore, regarding those who harbor resentment and envy: one who dwells upon past evils as a cause for enmity is called "resentful" (怨); one who begrudges present goodness is called "envious" (嫉).
Thus, that which obstructs and has not yet been eliminated is termed resentment, while that which takes no pleasure in hearing [of others' virtues] is termed envy. This is the general discussion.
In the Trace Gate (Jikimon), the two vehicles and the dull-witted bodhisattvas acted as envious adversaries; that five thousand rose and departed was not yet sufficient cause for regret.
In the Essential Gate (Honmon), however, those among the bodhisattvas who delight in approaching completion act as envious adversaries, such that the entire assembly remains unaware.
Why should this be considered strange? It still remains within the traces [of the teaching], and its intent can thus be seen.

O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who are able to write, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, and explain it to others—the Tathāgata will clothe them with his robes, and they shall also be protected by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions.
Reflect: this person possesses the power of great faith, the power of aspiration, and the power of all roots of goodness. You should know that such a person dwells together with the Tathāgata;
it is as if the Tathāgata were to stroke their head with his own hand.
The second [section] is a praise in terms of persons. This Dharma resides in persons; thus, those persons are noble and honored.
"Clothed by the Tathāgata" means that practicing and studying great patience (*mahākṣānti*) serves as their clothing. As stated in the preceding text, this is the "adornment of the Tathāgata.
"Protected by the Buddha" means that true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the Buddha, and true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) is the child. To revere true reality and give rise to true wisdom is—
One is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. The fourfold faith constitutes the power of faith; this refers to the Three Jewels and the precepts.
These four forms of faith must be understood according to the Perfect Vehicle (Ekayāna): the Three Jewels as one essence and the ten precepts as a single thought-moment.

These are precisely the ten precepts of non-piercing, such as the *pāramitās*. Only then does it constitute the Perfect Gate. The Four Great Vows constitute the power of aspiration, and great wisdom constitutes the roots of goodness.
Power (*bala*). Faith is faith in the principle; the principle is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Aspiration is the establishment of practice; practice is liberation (*vimukti*).
When the roots of goodness are firm and difficult to move, this is Prajñā. One should know that the power of the Three Jewels is precisely the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Were it not so, how could one be protected by the Buddhas of this world and other realms?
Contemplation: When the initial mind dwells here, it is no different from the Buddha; therefore, it is said to "dwell together with the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, through the power of faith, one cultivates ultimate emptiness, which is the wisdom of the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata takes ultimate emptiness as his dwelling, and this person, by the power of faith, likewise studies ultimate emptiness;
thus, they dwell together with the Tathāgata. This is explained in terms of what is symbolized. Were it otherwise, [it would not be so].
To dwell together with the physical body and even to touch its impure head—what benefit is there in this from the perspective of principle? Nevertheless, as for the hand rubbing the head:

this person, through the power of their vows, the power of goodness, and their own practice of the provisional and the real, acts as the responsive stimulus (*ki*). "Head" is the name for this responsive stimulus.

The Tathāgata, by means of the two wisdoms of transformation for others—the provisional and the real—is called the "hand. This hand awakens the provisional and real [wisdom] of the former person’s own practice.

Because the reality of the Dharma and the response of the practitioner meet in the Way, it is said that he "stroked his head. To stroke the head is to bestow a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

O Bhaiṣajyarāja, wherever this may be—whether it is being preached, read, recited, or written, or wherever the scroll of the sutra may reside—one should erect a stupa made of the seven precious substances, making it as high, vast, and magnificently adorned as possible. It is unnecessary to enshrine bodily relics there.
Why is this? Because within this [stūpa] already resides the entire body of the Tathāgata.
This stūpa should be honored, revered, respected, and praised with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, silk canopies, banners, streamers, music, and hymns.
If there are those who behold this stūpa, prostrate before it, and make offerings, you should know that they are all drawing near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Third, the praise of the sūtra according to its location. This Dharma resides in a specific place; thus, the place itself is noble.
Indeed, wherever the Buddha was born, attained enlightenment, turned the wheel of Dharma, or entered parinirvāṇa—places where the Dharma King has traveled—one should erect a stūpa. This sūtra...
This is the birthplace of the Dharma-body, the field where the Way is attained, the true essence of the Wheel of Dharma, and the cave of Great Nirvana.
Wherever this sutra resides, it must be honored with stūpa offerings; there is no further need to enshrine bodily relics (śarīra). As the *Śāstra* states: "Crushed bones are bodily relics;
scriptural scrolls are Dharma-body relics. This sutra is a relic of the Dharma-body; [bodily relics] are not required.
Furthermore, the *sheli* (relics) of the physical body (*janma-kāya*) are further established. Regarding the two bodies—the physical and the dharma—each has both complete and fragmentary aspects.

As for the complete and fragmentary aspects of the physical body, they are exemplified by Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna. Regarding the two types of the dharma-body, the various provisional teachings represent the fragmentary dharma-body, while the single reality of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* represents the complete dharma-body.
This is clearly revealed through the detailed analysis of the four teachings and five periods; thus, one should know that all other sutras are either complete or fragmentary.
[The two views] are roughly equal. Only this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* [sūtra] is the entire body of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
there is no other dharma, for all enter into reality. Liu Qiu’s commentary states: "Previously, taking the person as the fish or rabbit, it was equated in merit with the sixteen-foot [Buddha].
Now, taking the words as the trap or snare, it is equated in subtlety with the śarīra. This, however, is not so. If one does not distinguish between the coarseness of the words..."
Excellent! This returns to being equal in merit to the six-foot physical body (rūpakāya). How does this sutra differ from the Āgamas and the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā?

Thus we know that the commentators did not understand that "upholding" means dwelling together with the Dharma-Buddha, nor did they realize that what is upheld is coextensive with the realm of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya-dhātu).
Therefore, among the seventeen names [of the relics], it is called "solid śarīra. One should know that the fragmented-body śarīra does not receive [this name].
This is the name for "firmness.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, whether lay or ordained, who practice the bodhisattva path;

yet if they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that these persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path.
If there are those who hear this sutra, they will be able to practice the bodhisattva path well;

this is the fourth instance of praising the cause. If one has not yet practiced the bodhisattva path well, following the first three teachings is like possessing fragmented relics of the Dharma-body, which cannot skillfully deliver others.
If one enters the Perfect Teaching (Eka-yāna), it is as if possessing the entire body.
Śāriputra, this is skillful deliverance; skillful deliverance constitutes the practice of the good path. △ Below, regarding the passage "If there be sentient beings who...
and so forth, this is the fifth section: praising by way of the fruit. This text itself consists of five parts: first, clarifying the proximate fruit; second, providing an analogy;
third, applying the analogy; fourth, the explanation; and fifth, the exclusion of what is not [the case].
If there are sentient beings seeking the Buddha-way who see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and having heard it,
believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, you should know that such persons have drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

First, the proximate fruit is clarified. It should be understood that those who will certainly attain the fruit of *sambodhi* (perfect enlightenment) are called "those dwelling in proximity" within the context of the "Peaceful Practices.
This fruit of *bodhi* has as its essence the sphere of the Buddha’s eye and the Buddha’s wisdom; it is of two kinds:

first, the *bodhi* of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*), and second, the *bodhi* of the final resolve (*paścimacittotpāda*). What is here termed "proximate" refers specifically to the former.
First, one dwells in bodhi. Furthermore, with regard to the perfect fruit, one cultivates the perfect cause; when one attains a semblance of understanding, it is called "near.
The preceding section, concerning the cause, praised the cultivation of both common and specific causes; this refers to being unskilled, as one is far from the perfect fruit.
If one cultivates the perfect cause, this constitutes wholesome practice, and one is near to the perfect fruit. Now, taking the perfect, suchness-realizing wisdom as...
The cause takes this very same thing as its fruit. The True Suchness prior to the Path is the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*);
the True Suchness during the Path is the conditional cause (*ālambana-pratyaya*), also termed the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*). The True Suchness subsequent to the Path is the perfect fruit.

Therefore, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the Real Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the Real Mark. Thus says the *Śāstra*.
It is said: Initially observing the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is called the cause; having completed the observation is called the fruit.

Discussing this from the perspective of principle (*li*), true suchness (*tathatā*) and true reality have no actual cause and fruit, nor do they possess sequence. However, if one speaks in terms of the practice of sentient beings, there is indeed sequence as well as cause and fruit.

Furthermore, regarding the previous mention of "prior to the Path" (the stage before the path) and the "provisional and real" [aspects of the bodhi], these refer to what is attained through cultivation.

That [enlightened nature] is the true cause; within that very cause, the conditions and the consummation are equally established as the true cause. Cultivating the middle way of the true cause, the conditions and the consummation are likewise equally established.
This refers to the conditions and consummation in relation to the truth (the *tathatā*); it is also called the conditions and consummation that are identical to the truth.

One may also say "the conditions and consummation of *tathatā*. That "the entire nature becomes cultivation" is precisely this meaning. Only this Dharma exists; worldly dharmas cannot defile it, nor can Māras.
It cannot be destroyed; the Two Vehicles cannot extinguish it, for it is identical to the Suchness (tathatā) itself.

Here, the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is taken as the "pre-stage of the Path," and the period after the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is taken as the "middle of the Path. Within this middle stage of the Path, it is divided into two:

that prior to the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*) is the "condition" (*pratyaya*), and from the attainment of the dwellings onward is the "realization" (*pariniṣpanna*). Thus, a single stage is divided into two, which is why it is said to be "both. This refers to the state after the realization of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
This is called "After the Path. It differs slightly from what preceded it.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, parched with thirst and needing water, digs for it on a high plateau.
Seeing only dry earth, they know the water is still far off. Yet, without ceasing their efforts, they see moist soil appear, and eventually reach mud; thus, their mind—
It is certain that water must be near. The second analogy is explained in two ways:
first, in terms of the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*); second, in terms of the gate of teaching (*deśanā-mukha*). Regarding the gate of contemplation:

the minds of sentient beings, replete with all afflictions (*kleśa*), are called "high plateaus. The cultivation of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is called "digging. Only then does one realize [the truth].

The flavor of principle is like obtaining clear water. Based on the contemplation of penetration: the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśana-bhūmi) is like dry soil; the stage of Nature (gotra-bhūmi) is like moist soil and mud;

and the stage of Seeing the Truth (darśana-mārga) is like obtaining clear water. Contemplating separately by entering emptiness from the conventional, one sees only emptiness and does not see that which is not empty;
this severs the four abidings (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), which is like digging through dry soil—water is still far off. From emptiness, one emerges into the conventional, first knowing...
It is not provisional; now one knows it is not empty. By means of these two contemplations, one enters the Middle Way and is able to subdue ignorance.
One perceives moist soil, and the water is near. In the perfect contemplation of the Middle Way, which is neither empty nor provisional, one illuminates both emptiness and the provisional.

It is like gradually reaching moist mud. When the four abidings (*catur-vihāra*) are exhausted and ignorance (*avidyā*) is subdued, one attains a semblance of the perfect understanding of the Middle Way;

therefore, it is said to be "like mud. If one enters the first abiding (*prathama-bhūmi*), one gives rise to the true understanding of the Middle Way, thereby shattering ignorance, just as when mud becomes clear and still.
One then perceives the Middle Way, just as one sees clear water. The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that the Buddha-nature is like water. It should be understood thus.
One knows the sequence. Thus, water is like the Buddha-nature; because it is drawn up differently and requires long-term cultivation, it is said to be sequential.

This refers to the differing levels of depth in the contemplative characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the various teachings; one must understand their underlying intent. That intent lies in the *Lotus Sūtra*’s perfect and ultimate teaching.
Next, regarding the gate of doctrinal classification (*paryāya*): the land is a metaphor for the sūtras and teachings, while the water symbolizes the Middle Way. The teachings elucidate the Middle...
The Way is like soil containing moisture. The teachings of the Tripiṭaka have not yet expounded the Middle Way; they are like dry soil.
The Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings, while still retaining expedient means, explain the meaning of the Middle Way; they are like seeing damp soil.

The Lotus Sūtra teaching directly and manifestly explains the Unsurpassed Way; it is like seeing mud. By means of the Lotus Sūtra teaching, one gives rise to hearing, reflection, and cultivation, thereby attaining immediate awakening.
The Middle Way truly perceives the Buddha-nature; the true wisdom thus aroused no longer relies on words and texts. It is like obtaining clear water, wherein the appearance of mud no longer exists.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The body of wisdom possessed by Bodhisattvas in the Ten Abodes is not realized through another."
This is equivalent to obtaining water. There were five ancient masters who provided interpretations; they should not be followed as they are in the commentary.

A bodhisattva is also like this: if one has not heard, has not understood, and has not yet been able to practice this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it should be known that such a person is still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If, however, one manages to hear, understand, and contemplate it...
By practicing this alone, one will certainly know that one is drawing near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the third combined analogy. Within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, obtaining hearing, reflection, and cultivation is precisely the perfect contemplation of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*).
Only then can one approach the fruit. This is not [attained] through the hearing, contemplation, and cultivation found in teachings such as those on the dry or the moist.
Why is this? Because the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all bodhisattvas belongs entirely to this sutra.
This sutra opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the true aspect; it is the treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, profound, firm, and far-reaching.
No one can reach it. Now, the Buddha’s teaching transforms and brings to fulfillment the bodhisattvas, revealing it to them.
Fourth, regarding the interpretation of the proximate meaning: this section of the sutra is precisely the great purport of the "Trace Gate" (Ji-men). If this purport were to collapse...
How, then, shall this be circulated? For this reason, ancient precedents and critical evaluations are extensively cited first, followed by the present school’s formal interpretation.
The Guangzhai commentary states: "In the past at the Deer Park, the capacities of the audience were mixed; thus, the Tripiṭaka was extensively taught, yet the single principle was not clarified.

At that time, the provisional concealed the real, and the single principle was obstructed by provisional teachings. Now, at the Royal City, the great capacity is met, and the true reality is revealed."
Once the ultimate truth (*tattva*) is revealed, the former teachings are set aside. Because the former teachings are set aside, the gate of skillful means (*upāya*) is opened.
When the single principle is manifested and the true aspect is revealed, Zhanran (Zhang’an) said: "This interpretation is precisely the refutation of the provisional.
One should know that Guangzhai’s statement that "the former teachings are set aside" does not mean they are "opened"; thus, his meaning is not established. Furthermore, due to Guang[zhai]...

The Master [Zhiyi] once specifically pointed to the Deer Park in his discourse; thus we know that interpreting and explaining the words is no easy task. By the single character "remove" (*chú*), one may immediately be judged as either praiseworthy or censurable.
Some explain this as the two provisional means (*upāya*) of the body and speech of the teaching, and the two realities (*tattva*) of the body and speech of the manifestation.

Throughout the three periods of time, the Buddhas possess only form, sound, the provisional, and the real. Based on this opening and revealing, the twelve divisions and eighty thousand teachings shine forth with clarity.
However, this is understood. Zhan’an said: "This merely borrows the meaning of the 'Dragon Seal' (the *Nāgārjuna-seal*);

it still intends to subvert the provisional (*upāya*), rather than opening its meaning. Hexi Daolang said: "To directly designate the Three Vehicles as 'provisional' is precisely to open the gate of the provisional.
Previously, it was not stated that the Three were provisional, and thus the gate of the provisional remained closed; now, by designating the Three as provisional..."
"Convenient. This indicates that one [aspect] is the true reality (*tattva*). Zhanran (Zhang’an) says: "This interpretation accords with the scriptural text.

It is difficult to adopt the established doctrines of the ancients. Question: Is the provisional means (*upāya*) itself the gate? Or is it a gate because it leads to the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*)?

Zhanran answers: It possesses both meanings. That it is a gate to the true reality is easy to understand. As for its being a gate by its own nature (*svabhāva*), it is as explained in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "Seeking... [and so forth].
O Good Spiritual Friend: there are various Dharma gates, such as counting sands and contemplating the ocean; these two gates each have their periods of opening and closing.
In the past, it was not said that "three" is the skillful means, and thus that gate remained closed. Now, it is taught that "one" is the ultimate reality, and thus the gate is opened.
Furthermore, this skillful means also penetrates the true mark (dharmatā); therefore, the skillful means of the Three Vehicles constitute the One Vehicle.

The term "gate" (*mukha*) also carries two meanings regarding the true nature (*dharmatā*). First, it is called a gate because its essence is inherently void and pervasive, as in the "Gate of Non-duality" in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* or the "Gate of the Dharmadhātu" in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Second, it functions as a gate by enabling access to skillful means (*upāya*). Liu Qiu stated:
The power of penetrating all phenomena arises from the One; thus, the One serves as the gateway of skillful means (*upāya*). The efficacy of drawing beings forth relies significantly upon the Three;
thus, the Three constitute the aspect of ultimate reality (*tattva*). If one says it is not three, then the gateway of skillful means is opened;
if one speaks of it as being only one, then the aspect of ultimate reality can be revealed. This interpretation is not inconsistent with what is currently proclaimed.
I concur. However, the language is concise while the meaning is profound, making the intent of the sutra difficult to manifest.

This commentary further elaborates through detailed analysis, even employing the methods of "using three to reveal one," "using one to reveal three," "using three to reveal three," and "using one to reveal one.

It further cites fifteen locations concerning the meanings of the gates of illumination and so forth; these are not cited in full here. Having concluded the narration of the ancient interpretations, the Master now provides the correct interpretation to open up the method.
Regarding the "gateways of skillful means": that which was not previously taught is now all taught.

Previously, it was taught that all worldly livelihoods and productive enterprises were never truly skillful means; now, they are all opened up as being non-contradictory with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Previously, the provisional means of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and its fruits were taught; yet even the fruit of the Lesser Vehicle is not the true mark.
How much more so for minor expedient means? That which should be this gate is now all opened; this is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). What you all practice is the bodhisattva path.
This definitive resolution of the *śrāvaka* teachings is the king of all sutras.
As for what was previously taught as two gates of expedient means, they are now all opened; this is the true reality. How could it still be merely a "gate"? [I] cause them all to...
To cause sentient beings to open, realize, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision: in every form and every fragrance, there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma.
Whether they be gates or non-gates, all are opened to reveal the true mark and manifest the water of the Buddha-nature.
Had these not been opened, they would have remained deep, firm, obscure, and remote, such that no one could reach them; now that they are opened, one immediately perceives the water. There is none.

It is dry soil. Furthermore, it is explained again by means of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). That "all things belong to this sutra" refers to the perfect *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing).

This sutra’s "opening up of expedient means" refers to the perfect *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection). Its "revealing of the true mark" refers to the perfect *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation).
These three are profound and remote; that the Buddha now reveals them allows one to behold the truth.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this Lotus Sūtra, are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
If there are śrāvakas who, upon hearing this sūtra, are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are those of overweening pride.
This is the fifth exclusion of what is not [the true teaching]. If a bodhisattva hears this teaching and becomes startled or doubtful, such a person is a śrāvaka of overweening pride;
they are like dry earth—neither even moist soil, let alone water that can be seen. This concludes the section praising the Dharma of the sutra.
From here below is the second part, which briefly shows the method for propagating the sutra. This is further divided into two: first, showing the method; second, clarifying the benefits.
Furthermore, there are three methods.
Medicine King: if there are good sons or good daughters who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, wish to preach this Lotus Sūtra for the fourfold assembly, [they should do so as follows].
First, the introductory heading is stated:

"How should it be taught? This son of good family or daughter of good family, having entered the Tathāgata’s chamber, donned the Tathāgata’s robe, and sat upon the Tathāgata’s seat, should then extensively expound this sūtra for the fourfold assembly."
The second explanation:
The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings. The Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and patience.
The Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all phenomena. Having established oneself therein, one may then...
With a mind free from indolence, he extensively expounded this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly;

this is the third exhortation to practice. To cultivate the Tathāgata’s chamber is to cultivate great compassion. If one approaches it from the perspective of the same essence (*samatā*), it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
if it extends to sentient beings, it is liberation (*vimukti*). It is able to cause sentient beings to realize their identity with that same essence.
This is precisely Prajñā. Regarding those who cultivate the robe of the Tathāgata: if one considers that which is covered, it is the Dharmakāya;

if one considers that which covers and adorns the body, it is the patience of cessation (śānti-kṣānti); if one considers its harmonizing with the light to benefit all beings, it is liberation (vimukti).
Regarding the seat of the Tathāgata: if considered from the perspective of that which sits upon it, it is Prajñā; if considered from the perspective of that which is sat upon, it is the Dharmakāya.
The correspondence between the body and the seat is Vimukti. Furthermore, great compassion and peaceful bliss constitute the *zicheng gui* (the track of supportive accomplishment).

Gentleness that subdues anger and severs delusions is the track of contemplation and illumination (*vipaśyanā-yoga*). Sitting upon the seat is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the track of true nature (*tathatā-yoga*).
Within the "Peaceful and Joyful Practices" (*sukhavihāra*), these three dharmas are further elaborated. As for the aforementioned "Adornments of the Tathāgata," this refers to the robe (*cīvara*).
The aforementioned statement that "that which is borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata" refers precisely to this seat. "Borne" (dàn) carries the meaning of carrying and transporting;
it signifies entering the chamber. Furthermore, this exhortation to practice abides in three dharmas and continues to urge a mind free from indolence.

That the subsequent explanation identifies these as merely the first two stages within the position of contemplative practice (guanxing-wei) indicates that one should therefore propagate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Benefiting others, one transforms that merit back to oneself. Upon reaching the stage of "Similarity" (Sādṛśa-bhūmi), wondrous sounds manifest spontaneously and pervade the three thousandfold world-systems without waiting for exhortation.
Thus, when these three dharmas are compared with one another, each possesses these three virtues and three tracks (*triyāna*).
Although the Great Parinirvāṇa likewise possesses them, it is merely a single triad; since even "three" is not truly three, how could they be divided into nine? One should...
Know that the Bodhisattva constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, the Buddha exhorted those who propagate the sutras to constantly contemplate it;

he wished for those who propagate the sutras to propagate them through contemplation. Without contemplating the mind that propagates [the teaching], how can one understand the principle being propagated?
Thus, the Buddha commanded them to enter my room, wear my robes, and sit upon my seat. If these three dharmas are lacking, what can be called "propagating the sutras"?
Yes. △ Below, "I [shall go] to other lands" refers to the second section, which enumerates five benefits to encourage the circulation [of this teaching]:

first, dispatching emanated persons; second, dispatching emanated members of the fourfold assembly; third, dispatching the eight classes of supernatural beings; fourth, enabling them to see the Buddha; and fifth, bestowing upon them dharanis.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands I shall dispatch emanated beings to assemble for them a congregation to hear the Dharma.

When first dispatching emanated beings, if their initial resolve is not yet pure, one may only dispatch emanated beings; one must not yet dispatch emanations of the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings.
This is because if they were to see devas and nāgas, they might rely on this to become arrogant, which would obstruct and damage their path; therefore, it is not permitted.
This is to cause them to see. If the mind is free from attachment, one is capable of seeing the Buddha; how much more so the devas and nāgas?

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

It is like a person who, thirsty and needing water, digs into a high plateau; seeing only dry soil, they know the water is still far off.

The above two sections of the sūtra merely summarize the fifth of the five textual passages praising the Dharma of the sūtra, which praises it in terms of its fruit. Furthermore, it omits summarizing the preceding passage concerning the person, the Dharma, and the locus.

"Great compassion is the chamber; gentleness and patience are the robe; the emptiness of all phenomena is the seat. Abiding therein, he preaches the Dharma."

The first three lines praise the exhortation to practice. The following nine lines praise the second benefit:

dispatching the fourfold assembly of emanations to guide all sentient beings, gathering them together to listen to the Dharma. Even if someone should wish to inflict harm with swords, staves, tiles, or stones—

These one and a half lines constitute the first verse concerning the dispatching of transformation-beings.
If a person who preaches the Dharma is alone in a secluded place, where it is silent and devoid of human sound, and recites this sutra—
At that time, I shall manifest for them a body of pure radiance; if they should forget any passages, I shall explain them so that they may master them.
These two lines above summarize the fifth point: enabling the attainment of dhāraṇī.
If a person possesses these virtues, whether they preach for the fourfold assembly or recite the sutras in a secluded place, they shall all behold my body.

If one draws near to the Dharma Master, one will swiftly attain the path of a bodhisattva; by following and training under this teacher, one shall behold buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

This constitutes the first of the five chapters on the independent circulation [of the sutra], namely the "Dharma Master" chapter, in which Śākyamuni Buddha himself speaks of his own merits and virtues, concluding with his command to seek out its circulation.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.
This chapter also clarifies that the merit of propagating this sutra is profound and its blessings are weighty, thereby encouraging its circulation.

Within this encouragement for circulation, it clarifies how the Many Treasures Buddha and his emanations both bear witness to and assist in the propagation of the teaching. First, the specific title shall be explained; next, the scriptural text shall be explained. Part One: [The Specific Title]...

Regarding the explanation of the title: first, it is explained in terms of causes and conditions; second, in terms of the teaching’s origin and its ultimate manifestation; and third, in terms of contemplation of the mind. First, the name is translated;

second, the meaning of the realization and its symbolic significance is explained. Regarding the initial translation of the name: the Sanskrit term is *stūpa*, or *thūpa*, which is translated here as "square mound" (*fangfen*).
It is also called a "spiritual temple" (*lingmiao*), and further referred to as a *caitya*, which refers to that which has no bones or physical remains. This stūpa...
Since the entire body remains undispersed, it is not termed a *caitya*. The Āgamas clarify four sites of significance (*sthāna*), namely:

the place of birth, the place where the Way was attained, the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned, and the place of entry into extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). Stūpas were erected at these four locations.
The present precious stūpa is the site of the entry into extinction of a previous Buddha. The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "The three bodies of the Buddha arise from this sūtra."
It is here that all Buddhas sit at the site of enlightenment; it is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma;
it is here that all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa. This very Lotus Sūtra is the fourfold seal of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

The Buddhas of the past have already resided [therein]; the Buddhas of the present sit together [therein]; and it will be the same for the Buddhas of the future. The *Mūla-śāstra* also states that this sutra concerns the bodhi of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Therefore, we know that this sutra has already explained the causes and effects of both teacher and disciple. Thus, the Buddhas of antiquity bear witness to it. This sutra assembles the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas;
whereas the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* adds four Bodhisattvas to explain the causes and effects of the Bodhisattvas. As for those who are able to add [these elements]:

However, because these are the *traces* (manifestations) of Buddhas acting as principal and associates, it does not require the gathering of Buddhas; it simply states that those in the ten directions act as mutual principals and associates.
Furthermore, it does not say that the associates are emanations of a Buddha, but refers to them merely as "retinues.
Throughout the various chapters of the text, it is consistently said that bodhisattvas have gathered. Now, this stūpa has emerged to clarify this matter, so that all four assemblies may behold it.
All were filled with joy; hence it is called the "Chapter on Seeing the Jewel Stupa. This is an explanation of the chapter title based on the world-system.

The commentators state: "The Way is neither existent nor non-existent; past and present are of one principle. Thus, the earth split and the stupa surged forth to manifest that the Twin Śāla trees do not perish;
the seats intersect and the shadows join to subtly reveal that the sixteen-foot form is not born. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Seeing the Jewel Stupa. This is the interpretation.
Not so. To say that the present Buddha sits within an ancient Buddha stupa signifies that the true Way is non-arising throughout past and present;

it does not necessarily prefigure the non-extinction at the Twin Trees. Superficially observed, one might say that the present manifest Buddha entering the stupa of the ancient extinct Buddha represents extinction yet non-extinction.
Now, this is not the case. The manifestation of the ancient Buddha stupa demonstrates extinction yet non-extinction.

Extinction. Śākyamuni entered the stūpa to demonstrate that though he appears to be born, he is not born; he is neither born nor extinguished. Therefore, his sitting side-by-side with Vairocana symbolizes this.
He gathered his emanations and summoned those belonging to him to reveal that Vairocana is not something newly accomplished—how could it be that only the sixteen-foot form demonstrates extinction?
In the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (瓔珞經), Subhūti asked: "Are the merits of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), the whole body, and the fragmented body equal? The Buddha replied:
"To enshrine the relics of a single Buddha and erect stupas filling an entire four-continent world-system is not as meritorious as making offerings to the birth-body.

This is because the relics exist by virtue of the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*). Furthermore, to erect stupas filling a great trichiliocosm and make offerings to the physical body is not as meritorious as [making offerings to the birth-body]."
One nurtures the Dharma-body. Because the Dharma-body possesses a form-body, one should know that seeing the form is inferior to hearing the sutras;

for it is through hearing the sutras that the Dharma-body exists. Thus, the sutras are partial or complete, and the Dharma-body is accordingly whole or fragmented, such that their merits are not equal.
Question: The Tathāgata Śikhin preached the Dharma and transformed beings for twelve nayuta kalpas, and his śarīra relics were likewise so.
"These must be [relics]," they said. The Buddha declared, "They are all produced by the supernatural power of Tathāgata Śikhin.
Now, while the *kāyika-janma* (physical body) relics are completely fragmented, the *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body) relics are perfectly round;

both emerge from this sutra to manifest its merit and the great power of its propagation and upholding. They have surged forth from the earth to testify to this matter, so that the fourfold assembly may all behold it. Thus it was.

Regarding the chapter titled "The Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa," it was brought forth for the sake of the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of human benefit). The masters of the Northern Region say:

"When the Buddha was preaching the sūtra to Śāriputra, the jeweled stūpa had already appeared to serve as a witness. If [it were to appear] only after the preaching of the sūtra was finished, what would it come to witness?
The compilers of the sūtra established the sequence by placing it after the three turnings [of the wheel]. The Master said: "This is merely a matter of human sentiment."

This cannot be trusted. Now, according to the *Sākyamuni-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when the Buddha was preaching the *Lotus Sūtra* with countless verses, a stupa made of the seven precious substances suddenly emerged from the earth. Within it was a golden couch, and upon the couch sat a Buddha.
The characters *pao-hsiu-lan-lo* mean "Great Treasure" (*mahāratna*) in the Han language. He praised the World-Honored One, saying: "I have come specifically to make offerings;
I pray that you will sit upon my golden couch and further preach for me the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Based on the evidence of this sutra, it is clear that after the three rounds of preaching, he requested [the Buddha] to further discourse on his lifespan. That the Sage spoke these explicit words yet was unwilling to accept them—this is a person’s piercing [of the truth].

"How can it be supported? This stupa emerged from the earth specifically to testify to what preceded and what followed; since the fourfold assembly all witnessed it, it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.
This is an explanation of the chapter according to the method of counteracting [afflictions]. The Master Di (Dharmatrāta) says that Prabhūtaratna is the Dharmakāya Buddha.
The *Śāstra* states that by virtue of Prabhūtaratna’s vow, an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) comes to testify to the sutra. This passage is also [to that effect].
The Master said: "The Dharma-body neither comes nor goes; the Reward-body is majestic and sublime; the Response-body universally responds to all.
If one were to claim that these [three manifestations] are themselves the three Buddhas, one has not yet exhausted their essence.

One should know that this present chapter merely serves as a symbolic representation: Muchika represents the Dharma-Buddha, Śākyamuni represents the Reward-Buddha, and the emanated bodies represent..."
The Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. Although these three Buddhas are three, they are neither identical nor different; one should speak in this way and understand them thus.

This is the explanation of the chapter according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). An ancient asked: "When the great assembly sees the stūpa, is it the sense organ (*indriya*) or consciousness (*vijñāna*) that sees?
Or does the stūpa cause it to see? Extensively employing analogies and categories, he refutes both self and other. This is profoundly difficult to comprehend within the sūtra.
The general purport is as follows: After three cycles [of teaching], even ordinary beings have all transcended mundane views.

However, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*’s contemplation of phenomena was intended for those of dull faculties in the final age; since the Buddha’s own time was the appropriate occasion, why would he have needed to establish this?

Such would be the logical conclusion regarding the contemplative practice that interprets the sutras. Generally, if there is no comprehensive insight in the exegesis of sutras, it causes later students to remain unacquainted with the path of the school. Now...
This is primarily for the purpose of verifying the sūtra, while the ancillary discussion serves to clarify what is implied therein. An ancient questioner asked:

"When the past Buddhas were summoned and their emanations assembled, why were there so many bodies, yet only one stūpa? Now, I shall answer this; since the meaning of the sūtra is fully established, the precious stūpas are not numerous.
In accordance with the vow of Prabhūtaratna, the emanated bodies are not limited to one. Even if one were to verify this through the sutra, many stupas would need to be assembled;

how could the stupas not be numerous? Since he is able to manifest throughout the ten directions, we know for certain that the stupas are likewise not one. Therefore, the emanated bodies are transformations.

The stūpa is also a provisional device; yet, we now follow what it symbolizes. Here, the single body of the present Buddha embodies many bodies, secretly symbolizing that the manifestations of his activity are not one.
In the case of the many stūpas of ancient Buddhas, they display only a single stūpa, clearly symbolizing that the ultimate principle is non-dual.
Furthermore, the fact that the stūpa rises from the earth into the air, along with its various ornaments, is by no means in vain. Moreover, the stūpa emerges as two.
First, by uttering a single sound, he validates what preceded; second, by opening the stupa, he initiates what follows. Regarding the validation of what preceded:
it validates that the teachings of the three assemblies are all true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). To speak of this reality briefly, it is that which accords with the true mark (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

To speak of it extensively, it is that which transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and cuts off the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*). To speak of it from the middle way, it is the "eight negations" (*aṣṭāpavāda*).
It is called "Reality. The stupa emerging from the earth demonstrates non-extinction. Sharing a seat and sitting together demonstrates non-arising.
Entering the stupa demonstrates non-permanence. Manifesting the stupa demonstrates non-interruption. The division of the body demonstrates non-identity. The whole body demonstrates non-difference.
Many Treasures yielding his seat demonstrates non-coming. Śākyamuni sitting on half the seat demonstrates non-going. Thus, the eight negations are made manifest. Therefore—

This is the truth. Because the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Proof within the Stupa) praises the reality through the "Eight Negations," the event of the stupa’s emergence likewise symbolizes the Eight Negations;

their meaning is identical. Furthermore, it serves as proof for the circulation of the Trace Gate (*ji-men*), demonstrating that the merit of upholding this sutra is profound and the power of its propagation is great—all of which is true.
Question: What is the relationship between "equal great wisdom" (*pingdeng dahui*) and *prajñā*? Answer: The *Śāstra* states: *Prajñā*... [text continues]

This is the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Just as one enters a city through its gates from any of the four directions, one should know that Prajñā is likewise called the wondrous Dharma.
This sutra refers to it as "Equal Great Wisdom" (*samatā-mahāprajñā*); the mutual reference between these two texts makes the intended meaning clear.

Regarding "arising after": if one wishes to open the stupa, it is necessary to assemble the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), clarify the profound entrustment, and let the sound reach the lower realms.
One summons the original disciples and discusses the measure of the lifespan.

The stupa of long antiquity emerges from the earth, manifesting the power of sovereign supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*) and revealing how it benefited sentient beings in past lives. Emitting a great voice, it displays the lion’s roar.
The power of swiftness manifests throughout the ten directions to reveal the provisional and manifest the ultimate.

Possessing great vows, whenever future Buddhas preach this sutra, my jeweled stupa shall arrive at their respective locations to serve as a witness, manifesting the power of great majesty and ferocity to reveal that the future is eternally abiding and indestructible. Furthermore, the stupa remains suspended in mid-air.

This also proves that what arises later was already present before. For those at the seven stages of expedient means, the principle of the *pitaka* has not yet been opened; they are obscured by ignorance, like a stupa remaining on the ground.

Upon hearing the three turnings of the wheel, which open the three [vehicles] to reveal the reality, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened and the *dharmakāya* is manifested—like a stupa surging into the air.
This is the proof of what preceded: the *dharmakāya* attained through cultivation has long been manifest, like a stupa already in the air. It is without...

"Being able to open [the stupa]" signifies that his original ground has long been perfected, yet it was unrecognized by the multitude. If he reveals his traces to manifest his original ground, one will understand and reach certainty without doubt;
this refers to what follows. If the stupa emerges from the earth, it signifies the manifestation of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

This is both the same as and different from other sutras. It is the same in that a Bodhisattva manifests the Dharma-body; it is different in that a follower of the Two Vehicles manifests the Dharma-body. If...

The stupa is in the air; opening the door, one sees the Buddha. This signifies the manifestation of the traces and the revelation of the fundamental source, which is forever distinct from other sutras.

If the stupa comes to testify before the event has occurred, the matter is already manifest and there is no need for doubt. If the stupa comes after the event has transpired, it possesses a hidden significance unknown to the multitude.
Now, we correctly adopt the latter meaning. To provide this explanation in advance is likewise without fault. This is based on the fundamental [source].
The Chapter on Explaining the Traces. Regarding those who understand through contemplation of the mind: by practicing contemplation in reliance upon the sutras, they correspond with the Dharma-body;

thus, object and wisdom must necessarily meet, just as the stupa came to bear witness to the sutra. Since object and wisdom have met, the great retribution is perfected, just as Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna sat together upon a single seat.
Because the great retribution is perfected, he manifests responses according to the capacities of beings, just as the emanated bodies all do.
[The assembly] gathers because the Many Treasures [Buddha] emerges; thus, the three Buddhas become manifest. Because one upholds this sutra, one is endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*).
This is precisely the meaning of what the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* says: "The three kinds of Buddha-bodies arise from the Vaipulya [sūtras]. Jingxi said:
One should know that every sūtra is capable of being cultivated. Yet, other commentaries and sub-commentaries do not touch upon this at all.

Therefore, for the followers of this school, both practice and realization remain unimpaired; their textual analysis and contemplative observation are both free from deficiency. I hope that those who cherish the Way will honor and revere this.
Whenever I behold this principle, I regret that I have not yet partaken of it myself. I shall linger over these thoughts with deep reflection, upholding them forever upon my head.
The above concludes the fourfold explanation of the title of the chapter. △ Next, the explanation of the sutra text follows. It consists of prose and verse. The prose section has three parts:
first, the manifestation of Prabhūtaratna; second, the distant gathering of the emanated bodies; and third, Śākyamuni’s proclamation of the invitation.
The first section also has six parts: 1. the manifestation of the stupa; 2. the offerings of the devas; 3. the praise of Prabhūtaratna; 4.
the astonishment and doubt of the assembly; 5. the inquiry of Mahāpraṇidhāna; 6. the Tathāgata’s response.
At that time, before the Buddha, there was a stupa made of the seven treasures, five hundred yojanas in height and two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
It surged forth from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air. It was adorned with various precious objects, featuring five thousand railings and ten million chambers.
It was magnificently decorated with countless banners and streamers, and hung with precious necklaces and ten thousand jeweled bells.
A hundred million [parasols] hung above it. From all four sides, the fragrance of *tāmālapatra* sandalwood issued forth, pervading the entire world.

Those various banners and canopies were composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby—and reached as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.
First, the characteristics of the stupa are explained. That the stupa is made of the seven treasures clarifies the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

it takes the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven sages of inherent virtue as its material wealth. A "stupa" is the realm of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), the locus upon which the Dharma-body relies.

Its height of five hundred *yojanas*—equivalent to twenty thousand *li*—vertically symbolizes the ten thousand practices within the causal stage and the ten thousand virtues within the resultant stage.
It is two hundred and fifty *yojanas* wide, which is ten thousand *li*. It is adorned horizontally by ten thousand virtues.
