This is explained in the first section on "Characteristics of Vision" within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Regarding the thirty-two marks: the soles of the feet are as level as the bottom of a cosmetic box;
the insteps are as prominent as the shell of a tortoise—these two marks are cultivated together through firm and steadfast generosity.

The wheels with a thousand spokes are cultivated as a single mark through the act of comforting those who are afraid. The heels are long; the fingers and toes are long; and the body is rounded and straight—these three marks are cultivated together.
One cultivation: namely, the precept of non-killing. Seven parts are full: the shoulders, the neck, the arms, and the feet. One cultivation: constantly acting as a donor.

The hands and feet have webbed fingers and toes, and both palms and soles are soft and supple. One cultivation: namely, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). The heels are broad and straight; the ankles do not protrude;
and the body hair curls to the right—these three marks share one cultivation: constantly benefiting sentient beings with wholesome dharmas. The calves are like those of a deer.
(Shi Yuan) First, he cultivates the mark of intestines that are uniform and well-ordered by teaching people through the scriptures and treatises without parsimony.

Second, he cultivates the mark of skin that does not receive dust or grime by answering questions as they are asked. Third, he cultivates the golden-hued mark by practicing patience and giving fine garments.

Fourth, he cultivates the mark of the concealed male organ by reconciling disputes. Fifth, he cultivates the mark of the Brahma-body being perfectly symmetrical and the mark of the hands reaching the knees; these two are counted as one.

The cultivation of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth; the rounded shoulders; the halo around the neck (*ūrṇā-kośa*); and the lion-like chest—these three marks are cultivated together. Constantly causing the merit of giving to increase;
the *svastika* mark on the palms and soles—this is cultivated as one. Not harming sentient beings; the deep blue eyes; and eyelashes like those of a bull king.

The two marks of being free from illness and regarding sentient beings with loving-kindness are cultivated together as one. The mark of the uṣṇīṣa and the mark of blue-black hair are cultivated together as one.
All meritorious qualities manifest before the multitude; the mark of a single hair per pore and the mark of the white ūrṇā-kośa are cultivated together as one.

Abstaining from false speech: forty teeth, white and even—these two marks are cultivated together. Abstaining from divisive speech: broad and long tongue, Brahma-voice—these two marks are cultivated together.
Abstaining from harsh speech: lion-like jaw—one mark is cultivated. Abstaining from frivolous speech: four canine teeth—one mark is cultivated.
Being free from wrong livelihood: the merit of all sentient beings is equal to a single hair of the Buddha—the Buddha.

The merit of all the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) is equal to that of one primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*); the merit of all the primary marks is equal to that of one *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft) and *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance).
One hundred thousand million times the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* and *uṣṇīṣa* constitutes the Brahma-voice.

Although the causes for each of the thirty-two marks are distinct, if one discusses their true cause, it is the upholding of the precepts and diligence; for without the precepts, even diligence cannot lead to rebirth among humans or devas.

How much more so for other marks? This is the fundamental basis for the marks of the Buddha in the Tripiṭaka Teaching. Emptiness and non-arising are the fundamental basis for the marks in the Shared Teaching.
The Knowledge of the Modes of the Path is the fundamental basis for the marks in the Distinct Teaching. The True Mark is the fundamental basis for the marks of the Buddha in the Perfect Teaching.

The eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) are as follows: the twenty fingers and toes; the eight surfaces of the hands and feet are flat and full; the six locations—the ankles, knees, and thighs—are excellent and marvelous;
the six locations—the shoulders, elbows, and wrists—are full; the three locations—the two hips and the crotch—are excellent; the two locations—the loins and buttocks;

the one location—the male organ concealed within a sheath like that of a horse; the two locations—the two shoulder blades; the two locations—the waist and navel; the six locations—the sides, armpits, breasts, abdomen, chest, and back; and the neck.
Fourth: the upper and lower teeth; the upper and lower lips and palate; the two cheeks; the two temples; the two eyes; the two eyebrows; the two nostrils; the forehead; the two ears;

and the rounded head—these are the eighty minor marks (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*). If one distinguishes four types of these eighty minor marks according to the Four Teachings, the principles are all consistent with what was stated above.
△ Below, second, it clarifies that the Teacher’s wondrous fruition shall result in Buddhahood.
Within the assembly of teachers,
there were again three who addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas,
shall attain Buddhahood, to be known as Tathāgata Devendra, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara."
The Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. The world was named Devamārga.
When he first attained the fruit of perfect enlightenment, it was said in the Puṇḍarīka Sūtra: "Devadatta shall become a Buddha, titled Tivara-ya;
in the Han language, this means 'Heavenly King. His kingdom shall be named Tivara-vat; in the Han language, this means 'Heaven and Earth.'"
At that time, the Buddha Devendra remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively preaching the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds toward Pratyekabuddhahood;

and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges resolved their minds toward the Unsurpassed Way, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.
The second [section] clarifies his transformation and deliverance while remaining in the world.
After the Tathāgata Devendra entered parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas. His entire body was preserved as śarīra relics.
They erected a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels, sixty yojanas in height and forty yojanas in length and breadth.

All the devas and human beings offered worship and service to this wondrous stūpa of the seven jewels with various flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, unguents, garments, necklaces, banners, pennants, precious parasols, musical instruments, and songs of praise.
Through this, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of arhatship; they were beyond counting.
Sentient beings awaken to the state of a pratyekabuddha; inconceivable sentient beings resolve their minds on bodhi and reach the stage of non-retrogression.
This third section clarifies the benefits after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa.

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In future ages, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, believe and revere it with a pure heart and do not give rise to doubt or confusion, they shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
They will be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions, and in every place where they are born, they will constantly hear this sūtra. If they are born among humans..."
In the heavens, one experiences supreme and wondrous bliss; if one is before the Buddha, one is born through transformation within a lotus flower.
The third exhortation for practice is as written in the text. Regarding "born through transformation within a lotus flower," the *Tāi jīng* (Womb Sutra) states:

"Those born from a lotus flower are not among the transformations of the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, or transformation. They are transformed without being [subjected to] transformation. In reality, they are not like those within the four modes of birth.

They are born by transformation (*upapāduka*). Just as the various devas are born by transformation, they still arise upon the laps of their parents and so forth; how much more so in the case of those within the four realms of existence? The *Avalokiteśvara-vinaya* states:
"Born by transformation from a lotus flower, they take it as their father and mother. The *Contemplation of Infinite Life* states:

"Those who remain for a long time upon the lotus pedestal are called 'womb-born' (*garbhaja*), yet in reality they are not born from a womb; they are merely categorized as such by analogy with lotus-birth, and are also termed 'moisture-born' (*saṃsvedaja*) or 'egg-born' (*aṇḍaja*)."
It is not born from moisture or an egg; rather, it appears suddenly, like the miraculous birth within the house of King Śuddhodana.
It is merely that a lotus flower remains unopened amidst the moisture, appearing as if moist or like an egg, contained within the flower like a fetus.
As stated in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*: "If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they shall be miraculously born upon a lotus flower before all Buddhas."
Birth. First, not to speak of the faults of others even at the cost of one’s life. Second, to transform people so that they take refuge in the Three Jewels.
Third, to establish all beings in the bodhicitta. Fourth, to remain untainted by the brahma-conduct.

Fifth, to fashion images of the Buddha and place them upon flowered seats. Sixth, to be able to remove the grief and affliction of sentient beings. Seventh, regarding those who are arrogant and haughty...
He is always humble. Eighth, he does not vex others. Although it is thus in the *Ratnakūṭa*, the various sūtras and śāstras speak according to what is appropriate.

Even if all that is set forth in the sūtras and śāstras regarding the causes for the birth of lotuses were listed together, they would all be surpassed by the merit of this present "Chapter on Hearing.
Therefore, although the birth of the flowers is the same, the original conditions for each are distinct. △ Below.
At that time, he departed. Second, the explanation of how Mañjuśrī today attained mastery of the sūtras and brought benefit to others. This section also has two parts:

first, the explanation of Mañjuśrī’s attainment of mastery over the sūtras; second, from the words "Mañjuśrī said: 'In the midst of the ocean... onwards, the explanation of the benefits brought. The first part further contains five sections.
At that time, from below, the bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakoṣa), who had followed the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, requesting to return to his own land.
This is the first of the five sections clarifying the penetration of the sutra: the request for withdrawal by Jñānakoṣa. The *Pundarika Sutra* states: "From below..."
The Bodhisattva who follows the Buddha is named Prajñākūṭa; in the Han language, this means "Accumulated Wisdom.
Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Prajñākūṭa, saying: "Good son, wait but a moment. Here is a bodhisattva..."
"He is named Mañjuśrī; you may meet with him and discuss the sublime Dharma. You may now return to your own land.

A second time, Śākyamuni stopped him, commanding him to wait for the proof of the benefit derived from the circulation of the sutra. Zhijī said, "The Many Treasures Buddha appeared for the sake of providing testimony for the sutra;
now that he has exhorted the dharma to be circulated and his purpose is fulfilled, he requests to return. This is why Śākyamuni stopped him.

Although the events of the Trace Gate (Jimen) have concluded, the Essential Gate (Benmen) has not yet been revealed; therefore, [the Buddha] entrusts it to Mañjuśrī and causes Prabhūtaratna to remain.
The Buddha’s secret intention is not something known by bodhisattvas, nor is the meaning of this "secret intention" understood by various masters.
At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel; the bodhisattvas who had come with him likewise sat upon precious lotus flowers.
They emerged spontaneously from the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King in the great ocean and remained suspended in mid-air.
Proceeding to Vulture Peak Mountain, they descended from their lotuses and arrived before the Buddha, where they paid homage by bowing their heads to the feet of the two World-Honored Ones.
Having completed his prostrations, he went to where Zhijī (Jñānākara) was and exchanged greetings with him. He then withdrew to sit on one side.
Shortly thereafter, the third Mañjuśrī arrived. Someone asked: "In the introduction, he was said to be in the assembly; why is it now said that he has come from the sea?"

I shall now answer this. How could one measure the realm of the sages with ordinary sentiments? It would be of no fault for him not to arise from this assembly, as he continues to transform sentient beings throughout the ocean-like world.
Furthermore, once his benefit for this single period has been completed, why would it be necessary to inform him of his departure?

When [the assembly] arrived, great benefit arose. They came from the sea together with the multitude. If one were to compare this with the eulogies of the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth, this sutra is extremely concise;
perhaps there exists a more extensive version there that fully contains the words regarding their emergence from the assembly, whereas what has been transmitted here is merely an abridgment.
Question: Beyond the trichiliocosm, there are four million billion lands in each of the ten directions.
The earth is purified as lapis lazuli, and there is no longer a great ocean. Why, then, does Mañjuśrī still say that the ocean has come?
Answer: The literal explanation is not incorrect; moreover, it is inconceivable. Now, three meanings apply to this:

first, since both humans and devas have been moved and the great ocean has been transformed, the ocean must have come from the place they were moved from, and thus there should be no fault regarding distance. Second, even if the various oceans were moved, the dragons... [text fragment ends].

The palace remains unmoved; the dragon calls it "unmoved," yet that which is inhabited has already changed. What is there that is improper in coming from a place that changes while remaining unchanged?
Thirdly, those without a karmic connection were moved away, while those with a karmic connection have now arrived.
This inconceivable mountain and sea are made entirely invisible to the multitude; this is merely a transformation of perception, not a change in substance. — Mañjuśrī.
Since he did not rise to go, that land was simultaneously transformed from impurity to purity. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"He transported [the assembly] to another land without causing anyone to have the perception of coming or going. Here, however, they are made to have the perception of coming and going while, in fact, there is no movement at all.

Therefore, we know that when there are those with the karmic capacity (*yōki*), the land transforms; yet even as the multitude is moved, they still perceive themselves as coming, whereas for those who lack the conditions (*muen*), there is no such perception.
Furthermore, although the essence of reality is motionless, the manifestation of transformative deeds follows established patterns;

thus, what is perceived differs, and the timing of coming and going varies. If even the ritual manifestations of a Bodhisattva are such as this, how could the transformations devised by a Buddha be the same as those of ordinary beings?
Question: If he departs without arising, why is it said that he "comes"? Answer: It is to show both groups of beings so that they may know the merit of the sutra.

The power of consciousness receives the benefit of the teaching; therefore, it must be said that it "comes. To go where one has not gone, and to come from where one has not come, is entirely for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Why then should this objection be raised? Thus we know that in other lands, one does not necessarily see them coming. If they do not see them coming there, one does not see them departing here.
Without coming or going, the manifestation of the event is nonetheless complete, just as when Vimalakīrti pressed the earth with his toe.
At that time, the great assembly saw themselves seated upon precious lotus flowers, yet the ground remained as defiled as before. These are all records from the text;
they were analyzed and their meanings clarified by Jingxi [Zhiyi].
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa asked Mañjuśrī: "Virtuous One, as for the number of sentient beings you have converted while visiting the Dragon Palace, how many were there?
Thus did Jñānakūṭa pose his question. △ Fifth, Mañjuśrī’s response: "It cannot be proclaimed by words. This fifth section is further divided into seven parts.
Mañjuśrī said: "Their number is immeasurable, beyond calculation, not to be proclaimed by speech, nor fathomed by the mind.
Wait but a moment, and there shall naturally be testimony."
The first answer given by Mañjuśrī brought benefit to a vast multitude.
Before he had finished speaking, innumerable bodhisattvas, seated upon precious lotus flowers, emerged from the ocean and proceeded to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
They dwell in the void.
Those who have received the benefit for the second time all assemble to realize it.
These bodhisattvas are all those transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī; they are fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva and all together...
The treatise explains the six pāramitās.
It is stated that Mañjuśrī transformed three śrāvakas who were originally practitioners of the śrāvaka vehicle; they remained in the void, expounding the conduct of the śrāvakas.
Fourth, those who first received the provisional teachings and abide in the path of the two vehicles:

the *Puṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that a lotus flower emerging from a pond represents one who originally resolved upon the bodhisattva mind; when that flower is in the air, it speaks of the matters of the Mahāyāna.
One who originally resolved upon the śrāvaka mind is represented by a flower in the air that speaks only of the matter of severing birth and death.
Now they all practice the Mahāyāna meaning of emptiness.
Fifth, it clarifies that having now heard the teaching of reality, they all abide in the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
Mañjuśrī said to Zhiji: "Such were the events of his teaching and transformation in the ocean."
The sixth section concerns Mañjuśrī’s summary of the benefits.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa praised him in verse, saying:
“O one of great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor, who has transformed and delivered immeasurable multitudes! Now this entire great assembly, as well as I myself, have all witnessed it.”

He eloquently expounds the meaning of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) and elucidates the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), widely guiding all sentient beings so that they may swiftly attain *bodhi*.
Seventh, Zhizhi (Jñānakūṭa) praises him in verse. △ From the departure of Mañjuśrī, the second section clarifies the benefits; this consists of nine parts.
Mañjuśrī said, "In the midst of the ocean, I have always expounded only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This is the first instance of Mañjuśrī’s own account.
Then, the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa asked Mañjuśrī, "This sūtra is extremely profound and subtle; it is a treasure among all sūtras."
"It is rare in this world. Are there any sentient beings who, by applying themselves with diligent vigor, practice this sutra and quickly attain Buddhahood?
Thus did the second, Jñatikūṭa, pose his question.
Mañjuśrī said, "There is the daughter of the Naga King Sāgara, who is eight years of age.

She possesses sharp faculties and wisdom, well understands the faculties, karma, and practices of sentient beings, and has attained dhāraṇīs regarding the profound, secret treasury taught by all Buddhas."

They are able to receive and uphold [the teachings] in their entirety. They enter deeply into meditative concentration and thoroughly comprehend all phenomena. In a single kṣaṇa, they give rise to the bodhicitta and attain non-retrogression.
Their eloquence is unimpeded, and they regard all sentient beings with compassion as if they were their own infants. Thus, they are fully endowed with merit and virtue.

Mentally contemplating and verbally expounding that which is subtle, wondrous, vast, and great; possessing compassion, benevolence, and humility; with a mind that is harmonious and refined—one can thus reach Bodhi.
This is the third part of Mañjuśrī’s direct response.

The Bodhisattva Jñānakośa said: "I have seen that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable kalpas, performed difficult practices and ascetic austerities, accumulating merit and virtue while seeking the bodhisattva path without ever ceasing.
He surveyed the trichiliocosm and found not even a space the size of a mustard seed where he had not sacrificed his body and life for the sake of sentient beings. Then...

Thus she was able to accomplish the path to Bodhi. Not believing that this girl could, in the space of a single moment, attain Perfect Enlightenment, the fourth [section] features Zhijizhang, who clings to the Separate Teaching to raise doubts.
△ The fifth [section] clarifies these doubts through the Dragon Girl’s demonstration of perfection.
First is the prose, followed by the verses; these constitute three sections.

Before the discourse had concluded, the daughter of the Dragon King suddenly appeared before them. She prostrated herself with her head at their feet in respectful salutation and withdrew to stand to one side.
First, this is the sūtra compiler’s account of how [the Buddha] suddenly appeared and [the assembly] offered their respects.
He praised him with verses.
These verses are further divided into three parts.
"Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, they shine universally throughout the ten directions.

The first half-verse clarifies that by upholding this sutra, one attains liberation. Regarding "sin and merit," these are conventionally established according to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).

Now, this verse speaks of profoundly penetrating the state where there is neither sin nor merit, entering into the single true reality (*eka-tattva-lakṣaṇa*); this is called "profound penetration. "The ten directions" refers to the ten... [text continues].
The Dharma-realm is likewise illuminated by true wisdom; therefore, it is called "universal illumination.
The subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body possesses the thirty-two marks and is adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics.
He is venerated by gods and humans; dragons and spirits all pay him homage. Among all classes of sentient beings, there are none who do not revere him.

The following two verses clarify the accomplishment of the two bodies. One who possesses the thirty-two marks has profoundly attained the principle of the Dharma-body and is thus fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "If one wishes to attain all dharmas, one should study Prajñā. As...
One obtains the wish-fulfilling jewel; the followers of the Two Vehicles obtain only emptiness, which lacks the marks and signs of excellence.
Furthermore, I have heard that the attainment of Bodhi is realized only by a Buddha. I shall propagate the Mahāyāna teachings to deliver suffering sentient beings.
Third, citing the Buddha as witness. △ Sixth, the provisional objection of Śāriputra regarding the narrowness of the Tripiṭaka. This is divided into two parts.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the dragon girl: "That you say you will attain the unsurpassed path before long—this is difficult to believe."
First, Śāriputra raised another objection. He first stated in general that [the teaching] is difficult to believe.
Why is this? "The female body is defiled and impure; it is not a vessel for the Dharma. How, then, could she attain unsurpassed bodhi?"

The path of the Buddha is vast and remote; it requires traversing immeasurable kalpas, accumulating practices through diligent toil, and fully cultivating all the pāramitās before one finally achieves success.
Furthermore, the female body still possesses five obstacles: first, one cannot become a Brahmā King; second, [one cannot become] Śakra.
Third, the Māra kings; fourth, the wheel-turning sage-kings (cakravartin); fifth, the Buddha-body. How can a female body swiftly attain Buddhahood?
This is the second instance where Śāriputra explains that there are five obstacles.
At that time, the dragon girl possessed a precious jewel worth as much as the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system.
She held it up and offered it to the Buddha, who immediately accepted it.
Within the section on the seventh dragon girl’s removal of doubts through reality and her manifestation of clear proof, the initial offering of the jewel symbolizes the attainment of perfection.

Explanation: The round pearl symbolizes the cultivation and attainment of the perfect cause. Offering it to the Buddha signifies bringing that cause to fruition. That the Buddha accepts it quickly indicates the swiftness of attaining the fruit.
This is precisely what is meant by sitting at the site of enlightenment in a single thought-moment and becoming a Buddha without fail. Such clear evidence is as follows.
The Dragon Girl said to the Bodhisattva Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa) and the Venerable Śāriputra: "I offered a precious jewel to the World-Honored One, and he accepted it.
Was this matter not swift? They replied, "It was exceedingly swift. The girl said, "By means of your supernatural power, observe me attaining Buddhahood;
it shall be even swifter than this."

Next, the perfection of the cause and the fulfillment of the fruit are correctly demonstrated. The *Tāi jīng* (Womb Sūtra) states: "Māras, Brahmās, Śakras, and their daughters all do not discard their bodies nor receive new bodies;
they all attain Buddhahood in their present forms. Therefore, the verse says: "The Dharma-nature is like a great ocean; it does not speak of right or wrong.
Whether ordinary person or sage, they are equal with no high or low. It depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements. To take [this as the meaning]:
Realizing suchness is as easy as turning over one's palm. Question: Does this dragon girl attain Buddhahood without abandoning the *pariccheda* (segmented) existence?
If she does not attain Buddhahood in this very body, how can this text and the *T'ai-ching* (Womb Sutra) be reconciled? Answer:

The passage concerning the dragon girl here is spoken from the perspective of the provisional (*upāya*) that shares the same essence, in order to demonstrate the swiftness of attaining Buddhahood according to the Perfect Teaching (*vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*). If actual practice were not swift, it would be the provisional practice.

This is merely an introduction. Thus, the meanings of the provisional and the real are equal; the principle is not in vain. Therefore, the verse from the *Tāizàng jīng* (Garbha Sūtra) speaks of "attaining the real.
If one attains the real, it is by purifying the six sense organs and attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

One should know that the Dragon Girl, responding to the inclinations of sentient beings, manifested spiritual transformations, manifested her body as a Buddha, and realized the Perfect Sūtra. Since she has already realized non-arising, how could...
If one cannot know that there is originally no [state of] equanimity to be abandoned, what prevents one from abandoning this and proceeding to that?

When those at the stage of ordinary beings in other teachings reach this assembly, their further severing of ignorance is likewise so. In all such cases, one must necessarily resolve doubts and obstacles by means of the non-duality of the provisional and the ultimate.
At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform into a man, fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva.

She immediately proceeded to the stainless world in the southern quarter, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained equal and perfect enlightenment, manifesting the thirty-two marks of a great being.
Possessing the eighty secondary marks, he universally expounds the sublime Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

This is the first instance within the eighth [chapter] perceived and heard by the assembly. Those residing in the southern region had their conditions ripened such that it was appropriate for him to manifest the Eightfold Path to Enlightenment;
however, as the conditions in this land were thin, he taught solely through the dragon girl. This is an expedient skillful means.
This is the power [of the Buddha]. It is the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body, by which one attains a single body that is all bodies.

How much more so for those who employ skillful means (*upāya*)! It is not necessary to interpret this exclusively as a provisional explanation; it simply states that the dragon girl has already attained non-arising (*anutpāda*).

This discusses skillful means in terms of essence and function (*tǐ-yòng*), rather than referring solely to the provisional and the real (*běn-jì*) as skillful means. Therefore, regarding the two aspects of the provisional and the real...
The meaning and the power of the sutra are both established [here]. When others explain this, some claim that the dragon girl was at the seventh or tenth stage;
however, such views fail to manifest the power and function of the sutra.

At that time, in the Sahā world, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others—both human and non-human—all saw from afar that the dragon girl had attained buddhahood and was preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly of humans and devas. Their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage from afar.
Immeasurable sentient beings, having heard the Dharma, attained realization and reached the stage of non-retrogression; immeasurable sentient beings received [the precepts].
The Record of the Path: The stainless world shook in six ways. In the Sahā world, three thousand sentient beings dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression;
three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions of enlightenment.
This was the eighth chapter. Next, humans and devas rejoiced; both sides received benefit.
Bodhisattva Jñatikūṭa, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly silently accepted this with faith.
The ninth chapter, "Jñānakūṭa and Śāriputra," concludes with them remaining silent in faith and submission. This marks the end of Mañjuśrī’s exposition of the sutra.
Following the account of the Dragon Girl attaining Buddhahood, this "Sadāprarudita" chapter serves to lead others toward the propagation of the sutra, benefiting both self and others.
It clarifies that the efficacy of the current teachings and transformations is not in vain, thereby encouraging its circulation. The text is finished.
The Thirteenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "Exhortation to Uphold.

This chapter belongs to the third of the five chapters on the single circulation of the Trace Gate (*jimen*), concerning eighty thousand great beings who have newly received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to propagate this sūtra in this land;
it concerns their propagation in other lands as well. Some versions read "Exhortation to Uphold" (*quanchi*); in terms of meaning, it must...
Both [titles] are acceptable according to the respective headings. However, it is not as good as following the original; therefore, the title is "Chapter on Upholding" (*Cih-p'in*).

Because twenty thousand bodhisattvas received the command to propagate the sutra, it is named the "Chapter on Upholding. Because they were further exhorted to propagate the sutra by eighty quadrillion *nayutas*, it is named the "Chapter on Exhorting to Uphold.
Question: Why is this so? Answer: The twenty thousand [bodhisattvas] were specifically commanded at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Master."
Because [the number] was so vast, I received the imperial decree to uphold it. Previously, there had been no separate command; it merely involved seeking [the scripture].
Now, the Buddha has looked upon me with his Buddha-eye and commanded me to make a vow to propagate this sutra in this land.

The verification of its efficacy is profound and grave, and the Buddha’s intention is earnest. Therefore, having received this exhortation, I propagate it. Thus, there are two intentions. Regarding the text, there are two parts. First—
This clarifies the upholding [of the teaching]. Next, it clarifies the exhortation to uphold it. The initial section is further divided into three parts.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna, together with a retinue of twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all made this vow before the Buddha: "We pray only that the World-Honored One..."
We resolve that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and expound this sutra.

For in the future evil age, sentient beings will have diminished roots of goodness and will largely increase in overweening pride; they will covet profit and offerings, increase unwholesome roots, and remain far removed from liberation.
Although they are difficult to transform, we shall arouse the power of great patience to read, recite, uphold, and proclaim this sutra.
They transcribed [the sutra] and made various offerings, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.
Twenty-two thousand bodhisattvas first received this command and upheld the sutra in this land.
At that time, among the assembly, five hundred arhats who had received predictions of enlightenment addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we..."
They also made a vow themselves: "In other lands, we shall extensively expound this sutra.

Furthermore, eight thousand persons, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who had received their predictions of enlightenment, rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and made this vow:
"World-Honored One, we too shall extensively expound this sutra in other lands. Why is this? Because in this Sahā world, the people..."
There will be many who are corrupt and evil, harboring overweening pride, possessing meager merit, and being turbid with anger and crooked through deceit; for their minds are not sincere.
Subsequently, five hundred and eighty thousand śrāvakas made a vow to circulate [this teaching] in other lands.
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs— both those in training and those beyond training—
rose from their seats, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, their eyes never for a moment turning away.
There are three instances in which these bhikṣuṇīs requested a prophecy. First is the request for a prophecy made by Mahāprajāpatī.
Regarding her being the maternal aunt, the *Sūtra on Past Deeds* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*) states: "Among the Śākya clan, there was an elder named Suprabuddha who fathered eight daughters.

At that time, King Śuddhodana and his three younger brothers—four men in total—each took two of the daughters as wives. King Śuddhodana’s queen was Māyā; this is what is called [the 'Heavenly Mother'] here."
Afterwards, once the Crown Prince had been born, he passed away seven days later and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The next queen was the eighth daughter, named Mahāprajāpatī, also known as Mahāmāyā; she was his maternal aunt, hence she is called "Aunt-Mother.
Question: These śrāvakas have already become great beings (mahāsattvas); for what reason were they unable to propagate [the Dharma] in this land?
Question: Is this based on the sutra? Answer: It is for the sake of guiding beginner bodhisattvas who are unable to practice asceticism in this degenerate age;
furthermore, it is intended to reveal the "Chapter on the Practice of Peaceful Ease" for those beginners.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī: "For what reason do you look upon the Tathāgata with such a sorrowful countenance?
Does it not occur to your mind that I have failed to mention your name when bestowing the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"Gautamī," he continued, "I previously spoke in general terms that all śrāvakas had already received their predictions. Now, if you wish to know your own prediction, listen."

In a future age, you shall become a great Dharma teacher among the teachings of sixty-eight thousand billion Buddhas, and together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs—both those in training and those beyond training—you shall all serve as Dharma teachers. In this manner, you will gradually fulfill the path of a bodhisattva.
"You shall attain Buddhahood, named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha Bhagavān. Gautamī,
this Buddha Sarvasattvapriyadarśana and six thousand bodhisattvas shall successively receive their predictions of enlightenment."
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Tathāgata next bestowed a prediction [of enlightenment].
*Kauṇḍinya* is here translated as "Most Victorious" (*zuìshèng*); she is also known as *Prajāpatī*.

She was also called Gautamī; this was her clan name. Having bestowed the predictions upon Pāṭalī and the six thousand others in their entirety, at that time, Yaśodharā Bhikṣuṇī, the mother of Rāhula, had this thought:
"Among those for whom the World-Honored One has bestowed predictions, he alone has not mentioned my name."
Second is Yaśodharā’s request for a prediction. *Yaśodharā* here means "Renowned.

The Buddha told Yaśodharā: "In the future, amidst the teachings of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, you shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices and become a great Dharma teacher.
Gradually perfecting the path to Buddhahood, you shall attain Buddhahood in the land of *Kṣema*, and your name shall be *Samantaprabhāsa* (Universal Radiance)."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha,
Bhagavān named Footprint of Ten Million Radiant Marks. The lifespan of this Buddha shall be immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Next, the bestowal of predictions is explained.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, along with the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā and their retinues, were all filled with great joy at having attained what they had never experienced before. They then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“O World-Honored One, O Guide, who brings peace and security to devas and humans! Having heard this prediction, our minds are fully satisfied.
Thus did the bhikṣuṇīs express their understanding and rejoice.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, they addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, we too are able [to go] to other regions.”
Throughout the lands, they shall widely proclaim this sutra.
This is the section on the bhikṣuṇīs making vows to propagate the sutra. △ Second, the exhortation to uphold [the sutra], which consists of both prose and verse.
The prose section has five parts.
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eighty trillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
All these bodhisattvas were avaivartika, turning the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma and having attained all dhāraṇīs.

The Buddha’s initial gaze with his Buddha-eye was itself a silent exhortation. As for why he did not speak, although he had not specifically commanded them above, he had already demonstrated the profound depth of the merit of upholding this sutra through clear scriptural citations;
furthermore, the Many Treasures Buddha and his emanations had traveled from afar to urge them toward enlightenment.
This diligent effort has already fulfilled its purpose. Those who wish to respond to this call should immediately make their vows; there is no need for further prolixity.
Furthermore, out of consideration for the aspirations of the śrāvakas in other directions, the World-Honored One does not wait to proclaim them.
He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, joined his palms with single-minded devotion, and thought to himself:
"If the World-Honored One commands us to uphold and proclaim this sutra, we shall, in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, widely propagate this Dharma."
The second bodhisattva addressed him, thinking again: "The Buddha now remains silent; we see no instruction.
Now the Buddha is silent."

"What should I do? At that time, the bodhisattvas, out of reverence for and compliance with the Buddha’s intention, and desiring to fulfill their own original vows, let out a lion's roar before the Buddha.
The fourth bodhisattva, understanding their intention,
made this vow: "World-Honored One, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions and enable sentient beings to copy,
uphold, read, recite, explain the meaning of, and practice according to the Dharma this sutra."

Practicing and maintaining right mindfulness—all this is through the Buddha’s majestic power. We only pray that the World-Honored One, while remaining in another land, will behold us from afar and protect us.
Fifth, the vow to propagate the sutra. △ The following verses are independent (gūqi) verses; they concern all the bodhisattvas and others.
"Please protect the propagation of the sutra" means that he is here describing the method for propagating the sutra himself. Why?

Because the Buddha, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," has already finished explaining the methods; the Ratnastūpa sought out those who employ these methods, and Sadāprarudita was led forth by employing these methods.
The "Peaceful Practices" (*Anrakugyō*) are the methods for a beginner; therefore, it says, "abiding in patience."
The details regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth are as explained in subsequent chapters. If it were otherwise, there would be no method for propagating the sutra;
and for one to propagate the sutra without a method is impossible—just as entering a battle naked inevitably leads to self-injury. Thus, the words concerning "donning the armor" are not in vain.
There are twenty lines of verse requesting the protection and upholding of the sutra; of these, the first seventeen lines concern propagating [the teaching] by donning the garment of patience.
The Sūtra. Second, one line: entering the room to propagate the sūtra. Third, one line: sitting upon the seat to propagate the sūtra.
Fourth, one line: concluding summary and request for understanding.
Immediately, all the bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison and spoke these verses:
"Within this lower robe of the first patience (*kṣānti*), we shall divide the detailed exposition into three parts.
We pray that you do not worry: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the midst of a terrifying and evil age, we shall widely proclaim [the Dharma]."
The first part generally clarifies the timing. △ Next, regarding the objects of endurance, there are three [points].
When there are ignorant people who revile us with harsh words and even attack us with knives and staves, we should endure all of this.
The first line generally clarifies the worldly multitude—those people who hold wrong views and whom [the Buddha] endures.
In this evil age, there are bhikṣus whose minds of false wisdom are crooked and deceitful; they claim to have attained what they have not attained, and their hearts are filled with pride.
The next line clarifies those with overweening pride regarding renunciation; this is even worse than the former.
There may be some forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*) who wear patched robes in secluded places and, claiming to practice the true path, look down upon those in the human world.
Because of their greed for gain and offerings, they preach the Dharma to laypeople and are venerated by the world as if they were arhats with the six supernormal powers.
Yet these people harbor evil intentions and constantly dwell on worldly matters; they falsely claim to be forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka) and take pleasure in exposing our faults.
And they spoke these words: "These bhikṣus, for the sake of craving gain and offerings, preach the doctrines of external paths;
they have composed this sūtra themselves to delude the people of the world, and for the sake of seeking fame and renown, they analyze and preach this scripture."
Constantly amidst the great assembly, because they wish to disparage us, they slander us before kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and other groups of monks,
speaking ill of us by saying we are people of false views who preach the doctrines of non-Buddhist paths.
The seven verses above constitute the third [category]: those who falsely claim to have attained the state of an *ārya* due to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This fault is more severe than the preceding one, because each subsequent stage becomes increasingly difficult to recognize. The *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle 6, states:

"Araṇya" is translated here as "without affairs," which is to say, "without contention. Where there are affairs, there is inevitably contention. "Dhūta" is translated as "shaking off. (From the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*)
It is said: "The place of the forest-dweller (āraṇyaka). One who dwells in an araṇya does not contend with the world.

It should be neither too near nor too far, convenient for alms-gathering, possessing the shade of trees, abundant flowers and fruits, sufficient pure water, free from difficulties, and not rugged or treacherous."
It was easy to ascend, yet he was alone without a companion. He recited what he had heard.
When the *aranyaka* bhikṣu saw the king, the prince, the brāhmaṇas, and all the people approaching, the bhikṣu cried out, "Welcome, welcome! Please come and sit here. They then sat down together;
if they did not sit, the bhikṣu likewise could not sit. He should preach the Dharma in various ways to comfort them and lead them [to faith].

Joy! At the end of the time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this degenerate age, one will not conform to the precepts. Although bhikṣus may recite the dharma of the precepts in order to sustain their lives, they take no pleasure in practicing those precepts.
This applies likewise to all other dharmas of the Path, including the fivefold body of the Dharma (pañcadharmakāya).
It is like a person with a runny nose who speaks of sandalwood; having no fragrance themselves, they do not even perceive it. Thus it is for devas and humans.
The nāgas and devas, as well as the kumbhāṇḍas, will never make offerings to one who lacks the precepts; the same applies to the other four parts [of the path].

There is no one capable of bringing forth the sublime Dharma; it must necessarily arise from pure ethical discipline (*śīla*). The same holds true for concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and liberation (*vimukti*).
Even if one encounters the most grievous illness of impending death, and is oppressed by pain and affliction to the point of utter despondency, one should recollect the Buddha.

One should not abandon the constant practice of mindfulness. When all manner of bitter sufferings seize one's heart, that person, by personally understanding these dharmas, realizes that all dharmas are empty.
If it were otherwise, it would not be the practice of an araṇya-dweller. Those who reside in an araṇya do so to subdue their afflictions;
to exalt oneself and despise others is not the practice of non-contention (araṇā). If you do not understand this, what is the purpose of your sitting with hands folded in stillness?

He treats his teachers and friends with contempt and shows arrogance toward kings and ministers; how much more so does he cause the ignorant to claim him a sage, making those with eyes shudder with cold.
Rāhula’s conduct is forever at odds [with his reputation], and where is the virtue of Śāriputra?

This arises solely because his inner mind is not sincere, devoting himself exclusively to outward pretenses while neglecting the internal. To discuss the Way earnestly, there is nothing to be said; it is truly as Piṇḍola has stated.
Luo has known the kingdom for seven years; as for whether Master Chou should advance or retire, it depends on the King.
Therefore, one’s conduct must adapt to the times—how could one remain fixed in a single direction?

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* clarifies that a forest-dwelling bhikṣu must possess fifty qualities before he is fit to reside [there], and even the twelve dhūta practices each require ten qualities. Otherwise, for the time being—

Seeking a teacher to advance on the Path—how could one so hastily cling to ignorance? Having left the household life and departed from the world to sever attachments and pursue the Way, one ought to take the fivefold discipline as the correct standard.
If one already violates the regulations of the Hīnayāna and yet treats the Mahāyāna teachings with contempt, this is an especially grave harm.
If these [Hīnayāna] names were equated with those of the Mahāyāna, then the three trainings and two liberations of the Mahāyāna could [be disregarded].

They use this as a self-regulation, claiming it should be the standard for those who have gone forth to dwell in forest hermitages (*araṇya*). Yet, while adhering to what they profess, they do not diligently practice it;

their sole concern is how to sustain themselves. Such individuals as these are said to possess "semblance-trainings," to be hypocrites regarding the three trainings, and to be thieves of the three trainings.

While the three trainings are permitted, those who wish to disparage those who master the scriptures are thereby required that the propagators wear the garment of patience and single-mindedly propagate the True Dharma.

Only when one who possesses the precepts further increases the three trainings can they be called one who "increases the precepts" (vṛddha-śīla); to merely maintain one [precept] without practicing [the others] does not suffice.
I know with certainty that their precepts have diminished; since they do not even practice the precepts, how could they practice concentration and wisdom?
Therefore, one must examine them by means of the five factors. Out of reverence for the Buddha, we endure all these evils and accept these words of contempt: "You are all Buddhas."
Such words of contempt and disdain—these we shall all endure. In this defiled age of evil, there are many terrors;
malevolent spirits may enter their bodies and revile, abuse, and humiliate us. We, who revere and trust in the Buddha, shall don the armor of patience.
For the sake of expounding this sutra, we endure these various hardships; we do not cherish our own bodies or lives, but only hold dear the unsurpassed Way.
In future ages, we shall protect and uphold what the Buddha has entrusted to us. The World-Honored One himself shall know that there will be evil bhikṣus in the turbid world.

Not understanding the Buddha’s skillful means and the teachings he spoke according to what was appropriate, they will speak with harsh words and knit their brows, repeatedly seeing them expelled and driven far away from the stupas and monasteries.
For all such evils as these, one should endure them all by recollecting the Buddha’s injunctions.
This third section clarifies the intention behind donning the robes. Regarding the "armor of patience," one must explain patience through four teachings.
First, within the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna, the fifth *Āgama* states: The bhikṣu Kālaka complained to the Buddha, saying, "Śāriputra reviled me and spoke ill of me.
The Buddha quickly summoned Śāriputra and asked, "Did you truly revile him and speak ill of him? Śāriputra replied, "In my mind..."
Regarding the "undetermined": one might say, "I have already resolved my mind; why then do I speak insults?
Just as a bull with broken horns does not gore or harass people, and just as a castrated youth, out of shame, does not trouble others, so too is my mind like earth, water, fire, and wind.
Whether pure or impure, whether it be feces, urine, vomit, or saliva, I accept them without reviling; my mind is like a broom, accepting both the clean and the unclean.
Cleanse them both together. Furthermore, it is like a broken vessel filled with fat placed in the sun; it leaks drop by drop constantly.
When you observe your own nine orifices, which are constantly leaking impurities, how can you revile others?
Moreover, if a dead snake or dog were tied around the neck of a pure youth, he would feel shame and self-reproach, yet he would not revile others. The Buddha asked, "Such an evil person as you—"

What is contemplation? The answer is: there are five types of persons. First, one who is virtuous in body but unvirtuous in speech and mind. One should contemplate only their virtue and not their non-virtue.

This is like the patchwork-robed bhikṣu who, seeing a heap of refuse and tattered rags, grasps them with his left hand, spreads them out with his right, cuts away the impurities, and takes what is pure;
he contemplates using the purity of that body as a model for his own body, while discarding its speech and mind.

Use this to admonish your speech and mind. Furthermore, if your verbal conduct is pure while your physical and mental conduct are impure, you should likewise attend to your speech and cast aside your body and mind;
it is like one suffering from heat and thirst who encounters a large grassy pond, parts the grass, scoops up water, cools their body, and quenches their thirst.
Again, if your mind is pure while your body and speech are impure, you should likewise attend to your mind and not employ your body and speech; it is like a traveler in the heat.
I am thirsty; there is but a small amount of water in a cow’s footprint. If I were to take it with my cupped hands or my palms, the water would become turbid.
I should instead kneel on both knees, rest upon them with both hands, and draw the water up with my mouth to quench this parching thirst. Furthermore, as all three of my karmas are impure—
Although there may be nothing further to be done for them, one should feel deep compassion for them.

Just as one would see a sick person on the road and settle them so they are secure, one should contemplate their impurity so that they may encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) who will rectify their three karmas and prevent them from falling into the three miserable realms.

Furthermore, regarding those whose three karmas are all pure, one should constantly keep them in mind, using them as a model for self-training. In this way, one’s mindfulness and vows shall be equalized, like the Pure Cool Mountain (Sītavana).

There is a pond abounding with various flowers and grasses. One who is parched with heat and thirst enters into it to refresh themselves. Constantly recollecting the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) serves to remove one's evil.
This is the armor of patience within the Tripiṭaka teaching, which employs suffering, impermanence, impurity, non-self, and true emptiness.
The *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle eight, states: "The recollection of being reviled is a single word; the rest are all merely sounds."
What does it matter to me that someone calls out such words all day long? Furthermore, these words are disparaging in this region, yet they would be words of praise in another region;

if I dwell upon these disparaging words, I shall find no place for happiness. Moreover, when observing these syllables, if the insults were reversed, these very same syllables would become words of praise.
Furthermore, "insult" is merely a small portion of one element (*dhātu*), a small portion of one sense-base (*āyatana*), and a small portion of one aggregate (*skandha*).
It is a minor portion. One reviles a few, not many. Furthermore, who accomplishes the reviling? It is the reviler who accomplishes it.

Since that accomplishment belongs to him, what does it matter to me? Moreover, reviling consists of a single syllable; a single syllable does not constitute reviling. Two syllables constitute reviling.
There is never a time when two characters are uttered simultaneously. If one utters the latter character, the former has already ceased.
Furthermore, the one who reviles and the one who is reviled perish together at the same moment, within a single *kṣaṇa*; what, then, can this do to me?

Contemplating things in this way as empty, like illusions and transformations, one takes the penetration of emptiness as armor. The details are as explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* within the contemplation of emptiness and non-arising.
It is explained in detail. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 17, states: "Both ordinary beings and noble ones possess three types of sensation (*vedanā*);
they are also said to possess five sensations, namely: sorrow, joy, suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. Regarding the three sensations of ordinary beings and noble ones, what is their distinction?

For ordinary beings, there are two aspects to the sensation of suffering: first, physical suffering; second, mental suffering consisting of grief and lamentation. Like the arrows of the three poisons, they become angry when they lose pleasure."

Upon attaining pleasure, one feels joy; in the absence of both suffering and pleasure, one is deluded. The Noble One possesses only bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*) and lacks mental sensation (*caitasika-vedanā*).
Thus, they feel no hatred toward suffering, no craving for pleasure, and no delusion in the absence of both suffering and pleasure. The three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) cannot enslave them;
they have attained liberation from these tendencies. Therefore, there is the distinction between the ordinary person and the Noble One, based on the presence or absence of such [afflictions].
As for "descending," this refers to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), which serves as the armor of patience (*kṣānti*). The three teachings mentioned above clarify that their armor is not wondrous.
In the present sutra, the armor is clarified as follows: taking the mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*) as the armor of patience.

This is the perfect mindfulness of the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*), who is the Buddha of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*). Because he is the Dharma itself, the text says: "The Buddha’s admonition is mindfulness; the Buddha is [the Dharma] itself."
This is the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha is the harmony of both principle and phenomena. Vairocana pervades all places;

such armor is the single armor that is all armors—the armor of the Perfect Teaching (Eonkyo). It receives the names of the various teachings based on the distinctions of the contemplative perspectives.
Regarding the five feelings that are observed, their characteristics are not distinct; therefore, the practitioner should observe the three feelings. Thus it is said:
"One is able to endure all evil deeds," and so forth. This concludes the first section, from the beginning of the verse up to this point, which clarifies the garment of patience.
In all villages and cities, wherever there are those who seek the Dharma, I shall go to each of their places and preach the teachings entrusted by the Buddha.
Second, this clarifies the method for entering the Tathāgata’s chamber to propagate the sūtra.
"I am the messenger of the World-Honored One; dwelling among the assembly, I am without fear. I shall skillfully expound the Dharma; may the Buddha dwell in peace.
This third verse clarifies sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat to propagate the Dharma.
In the presence of the World-Honored One and all the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions, I have made this solemn vow. The Buddha himself knows my heart.

This is the fourth summary, requesting that he take cognizance. This concludes the chapter on Upholding, wherein eighty thousand great beings, having received their mandate, have finished propagating this sutra in this land.
