Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
The *Anrakugyō-hon* (Chapter Fourteen: The Course of Ease and Bliss) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
with the Commentary and Notes by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe,
and the Sub-commentary by the Shamon Daicheng of Siming.

This "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (Anlehangpin) is the fourth section within the "Circulation Division" (Lingchongfen) of the Trace Gate (Jimen), clarifying the method for those at the initial stage of the outer ordinary person (wailan chuxin) to propagate the sutra.

In both ancient and modern commentaries on this chapter, there are invariably expositions on the "arising" of the teaching, the ten conditions and five conditions, as well as the clarification of the purpose of its inclusion—namely, the three purposes and five purposes.
Here, however, it is not so; rather, I shall explain it by following the momentum of the chapter's text and pursuing its meaning as it unfolds.
This is not necessarily uniform. Therefore, upon reaching the commentary on this chapter, one should comprehensively expound the meaning of the preceding four chapters.

Specifically, from the section "The Dharma Master" (*dharmabhāṇaka*) onwards, there are three points through which the robe, the seat, and the chamber of the Dharma Master serve as the standard for the propagation of the teaching.

Thus, the explanation of the titles of the first three chapters and the analysis of their text are all based on these three elements to clarify the original intent of the chapters. If one follows the literal text...
The distinctions between the characteristics and their modes of arising differ; this is merely the beginning and end of the text.

Since the Dharma Master is the starting point for its dissemination, these three dharmas are fully set forth as a standard. Furthermore, regarding dissemination: it consists of expounding and spreading the correct teaching so that the speaker may rely upon these three to establish their resolve.
Only then can they illuminate the scripture being propagated, causing sentient beings to admire and look up to it, whereby the Dharma can be widely circulated.
Providing secret support and manifest benefit—this is the work of the Tathāgata’s emissaries.

Were it not so, for what reason would the World-Honored One command those who propagate the sutras to assess their capacities and determine who is fit to hold this responsibility? Therefore, he dispatches them to this land and other lands, to the zenith and the nadir.
Advancement and stagnation follow divergent paths. If one acts for oneself alone, one does not foster the faith of others; it would be like prescribing cold medicine to one suffering from a fever.
Therefore, the scriptures must not be transmitted haphazardly. Thus, the threefold revelation unfolds through both doctrine and parable, never exceeding the three virtues (triguṇa).
Whether regarding cultivation or inherent nature, one should apply these as the standard. As for the virtue of nature, it is neither something to be opened nor something not to be opened.
Cultivation and attainment are timely; when transformed, they are called "responding to things. In the present, whether identical or different, there is nothing that is not the One Vehicle.
The One Vehicle is Buddha-nature. This is fully detailed in the three types of Buddha-nature in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which is precisely the Secret Treasury.
Therefore, at the beginning of its circulation, this Treasury is again taken as the standard. This is why the Dharma Master named his room, robes, and seat [after it], and upon their arrangement—
This is for the sake of facilitating the propagation of the meaning. In the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," if one speaks from the perspective of the stupa:

the stupa surging up into the void represents the seat; its appearing in various places as proof of the sutra represents the chamber; and its adornment with various jewels represents the robes. If one speaks from the perspective of Śākyamuni:

his being in the void represents the seat; his entering the stupa represents the robes; and his commissioning [the disciples] to propagate [the Dharma] represents the chamber. Furthermore, the three Buddhas symbolize the three bodies (trikāya); this is also the case here.
The three ears are the robe of Prabhūtaratna, the seat of Śākyamuni, and the chamber of the emanated bodies. If explained according to what these three transformations symbolize:

the first transformation symbolizes the destruction of *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* (afflictions of views) and *kleśa-āsrava* (afflictions of passion), which is the seat; the second transformation symbolizes the destruction of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the chamber.

The subsequent transformation represents the shattering of ignorance; it is the robe. Therefore, those who propagate [the teaching] are commanded to rely on these three dharmas to propagate this wondrous triad.
If, within the midst of Devadatta, the body serves as the form of the seat—if one does not profoundly penetrate these three, how could one possibly hold life lightly and the Dharma heavy?
Thus, the body of marks and signs must necessarily possess the Dharma-body and the Reward-body: the Dharma-body is the robe, and the Reward-body is the seat.
The response body (nirmāṇakāya) is the chamber. If one follows the causal practices of Devadatta, the five pāramitās are the robes; the prajñāpāramitā is the seat;
and loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity are the chamber. How much more so when master and disciple have attained the Way and are fully endowed with the three bodies!
Upon reaching the verses of the "Chapter on Upholding," it is clearly revealed that one propagates this sutra by means of the three dharmas.

Although this "Chapter on Peace and Bliss" is intended for beginners, its title likewise employs the three virtues; for within this single chapter, there is nothing that is not comprised of the three virtues and the practices of the three virtues.
This is divided into five parts: first, a general explanation based on three meanings; second, clarifying the purpose of the four practices.
The sequence of the Three Clarities (三明) and Four Practices (四行). The essence of the Four Clarities and Four Practices differs. Fifth is the formal explanation.

△ Within the first section, the general explanation of the three meanings, there are two parts. First, the brief commentary on the title; second, the extensive explanation of each of the three [meanings].

First, according to the facts (依事); second, following the text (附文); third, regarding the three dharma-gates (約三法門). Within the initial brief explanation, first is the explanation according to the facts: the body is without...
Because it is free from danger, there is peace; because the mind is without sorrow or affliction, there is joy. Because body and mind are peaceful and joyful, one is able to proceed.
These two constitute the peace and joy of karma. To advance in the propagation of the sutra is the practice of verbal karma (*vākkarman*). Next, regarding the commentary on the text: the Sutra says:
By donning the Tathāgata’s robe, the Dharma-body is at peace; by entering the Tathāgata’s chamber, the mind of liberation finds joy;

by sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat, Prajñā guides the advancement of practice. This follows the preceding text, as it is explained in terms of the three virtues and the three tracks (*trividhā-mārga*).
If the Dharma-body possesses the practice of these two virtues, it causes the adorned Dharma-body to be at peace.

If the essence of the Dharma-body were merely simple, it would be disregarded and treated as inferior by devas and nāgas; therefore, one must possess the three dharmas to jointly guide the practice of propagating the sūtra.
Regarding the present text, the subsequent sūtra says: "Because one dwells on the ground of patience, the body is at peace; because one does not act with sudden violence, the mind [is at peace]."

Joy. Because one contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one practices progress; thus, progress itself constitutes practice. It is solely through this self-progress that one extensively propagates the sutra.
Third, the explanation of "peaceful and joyful practice" (*sukha-vihāra*) by way of the Dharma-gate: "Peace" (*an-*) means immovability; "joy" (*-laya*) means non-sensation (*an-upādāna*).
"Practice" is called "non-practice. As for "immovability," it cannot be moved by either the birth-and-death of the six realms or the nirvana of the two types of noble ones.
Since one does not take the two extremes as objects of perception, the body is without agitation. As the preceding text states:
"The body, along with the hands and feet, is tranquil, settled, and unmoving; the mind is always serene and never distracted. Thus, one dwells securely in immovability.
Like the summit of Mount Sumeru, it is the Dharma-gate of eternal immobility; therefore, it is called "Peace" (An).

As for "Bliss" (Le), it is the vast function of non-reception samādhi. It does not receive the five sensations of ordinary beings, nor even the views arising from the five sensations within the perfect [middle way].

They are all equally not received. Where there is receiving, there is suffering; where there is no receiving, there is no suffering. Absence of suffering and absence of pleasure is what is called "Great Bliss.
Regarding "non-practice": if there is anything received, then there is something practiced. When there is no receiving, there is nothing to practice.

One does not practice the conduct of ordinary worldlings, nor does one practice the conduct of sages and saints; therefore, it is called "non-practice. Yet, within this non-practice, one practices the Middle Way.
Therefore, it is called "practice" (*caryā*); this is precisely a Dharma-gate. Now, let us further explain this through its details. That which is "peaceful bliss" (*sukha*) is Great Nirvana;
this name is established from the perspective of the fruit. "Practice" refers to the path to Nirvana; this name is derived from the perspective of the cause.

All other causes and fruits are characterized by suffering, such as when followers of eternalist non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) engage in ascetic practices and instead obtain the fruit of suffering. If [the cause is]...
Pleasure as the fruit of suffering is like the non-Buddhist heretics who hold the view of annihilation; they indulge their desires to seek pleasure, yet later receive the retribution of suffering.

Suffering as the cause of pleasure is like the two vehicles of the Dharma-breakers; through their impermanent and clumsy methods, they must exert arduous effort until suffering reaches its limit before they finally enter nirvana.

What is now called "the practice of peace and bliss" (an-lè xíng) refers to the simultaneous bliss of both cause and fruit; this is precisely the skillful and authentic deliverance described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
As the Great Sutra states: "Those who exclusively practice asceticism are the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); those who practice both suffering and bliss are the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
those who exclusively practice bliss are the Bodhisattvas. All coarse causes and coarse fruits belonging to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are not [this] peace and bliss.
"Joyful Practice" (*sukha-caryā*). Because it is uniquely sublime in both cause and fruit, it is called "Peaceful and Joyful Practice. This concludes the detailed explanation of the subject matter.

To further provide a detailed explanation based on the text itself: Peaceful and Joyful Practice is the path to *nirvāṇa*. There are three meanings of *nirvāṇa*, namely, the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*).

There are three meanings of "practice," namely, the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*), the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*), and the practice of compassion (*karuṇā*). Regarding the practice of tranquility, it concerns the three types of action (*tri-karma*).
Gentleness and flexibility, wherein both compliance and opposition are quiescent, constitute the practice of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); this is the aforementioned "Tathāgata’s robe.
The practitioner of contemplation, possessing the wisdom of the single true reality and the light of non-discrimination, constitutes the practice of Prajñā;
this is the aforementioned "Tathāgata’s seat. The practitioner of compassion, through the four great vows to deliver all beings, constitutes the practice of liberation (*vimukti*).

This refers to the "Tathāgata’s Chamber" mentioned above. These three practices collectively constitute the path to *nirvāṇa*. Collectively, the three virtues serve as the objective domain (*viṣaya*) of these practices.

Because the domain is termed "peaceful bliss" (*anurakṣita-sukha*) and the path is termed "practice," they are called the "Peaceful and Blissful Practices" (*anurakṣita-pratipatti*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, the bodhisattva constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa* while practicing the path; during this causal stage, he employs these three..."
The practice of the Dharma: taking the three karmas as the path of practice, because these two [body and speech] karmas are purified, it is equivalent to purifying the six sense faculties.

If the six sense faculties are purified, one gives rise to a corresponding understanding and attains entry into the Truth. At the stage of fruition, these are called the Buddha’s eyes, ears, and so forth; at the causal stage, they are called the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*).

At the stage of fruition, they are called the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); at the causal stage, they are called the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*). At the stage of fruition, they are called the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); at the causal stage, they are called the practice of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*).

The fruit is called "graceful virtue" (*guṇa*). Furthermore, the causes are called the "three karmas," and the fruits are called the "three mysteries. During the four periods, compassion guides the three karmas to benefit others;
at the time of the fruit, this is called the "inconceivable transformation of the three wheels. When viewed in this way, there is no further conceptual discrimination.
Within all phenomena, there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss; all sentient beings are themselves Great Nirvāṇa.

It cannot be extinguished again. Practicing what is not the Way, one penetrates the Buddha-way; this is precisely the absolute, unconditioned practice of peaceful and blissful conduct (*anurakṣita-pratipatti*).
This practice accords with the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. As it says: "Furthermore, there is one practice, which is the practice of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is the person; peace and bliss are the Dharma. The Tathāgata is the person of peace and bliss; peace and bliss are the Dharma of the Tathāgata."

In summary, their meaning is not different; even in their particulars, they do not differ. This clarifies that the seat of the emptiness of the Dharma of the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*) is the Tathāgata’s chamber.
That [passage] clarifies the precious trees of gold and silver; these precious trees are the forest of untainted jewels (*anāsrava-ratna-vana*).

The untainted is conjoined with emptiness and the patience of quiescent extinction. The great river of golden sand flowing directly into the Western Sea is the wisdom of the single reality (*eka-tattva-prajñā*). It is with this...
All dharmas are in accord with emptiness. A woman who has attained the Way is free from flattery and crookedness; this unconditional great compassion accords with the Tathāgata’s chamber.
That is called the meaning of "without remainder," while here it is called the "Unsurpassed Way. Furthermore, there is the meaning of the five practices.

This is also consistent with the intent regarding robes, seats, and dwellings. Question: The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies that one should associate closely with kings, carrying bows and arrows to subdue evil people;

whereas this sutra teaches distancing oneself from power and influence, practicing humility, kindness, and compassion. Since these two approaches—harshness and gentleness—are so diametrically opposed, how can they not be different?

Answer: The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* specifically discusses the method of subduing [through force], yet while dwelling in the stage of regarding all beings as one's only child, how could it ever lack the quality of gathering and sustaining them?

This sutra emphasizes *saṃgraha* (gathering/acceptance), yet it is not that *vidāraṇa* (subduing) is absent; each is cited as a single aspect, appropriate to the occasion. In principle, all four must be present. Why?
To be timely and appropriate is the *loka-saṃvṛti-arthas* (worldly intention); gathering is the *puruṣa-arthas* (human intention);
subduing is the *pratipakṣa-arthas* (remedial intention); and awakening to the Way is the *paramārtha-arthas* (ultimate intention). [The details are] extensive.

Regarding the explanation of the Dharma-gates: one should clarify the gate of immovability, the gate of non-reception, and the gate of non-practice. These various sets of three dharmas collectively explain this text;
they are fully detailed in the "Ten Sets of Three Dharmas" and may be understood by analogy, so they are not recorded here in detail.

The above constitutes the first three meanings, completing the general explanation of the title. Next, regarding the purpose for which the four modes of peaceful conduct (*caturvidha-sukhavihāra*) are presented, first:

It is explained that those of profound practice do not require [the teaching]. Next, it is correctly explained that those who are beginning their practice do require it; therefore, this section follows. First, regarding the explanation that those of profound practice do not require it:
these are the twenty thousand eighty billion nayutas who received the mandate to propagate the sutra.

Having deeply realized the provisional and the real, they did not allow themselves to dwell together with those of the two vehicles, fearing they might receive provisional teachings. They possessed extensive knowledge of both the gradual and the sudden, and...

One does not speak of the faults of the gradual teaching, so as not to cause those who rely on the perfect [teaching] to despise the partial. Furthermore, by understanding the capacities and conditions of beings, one does not require the third practice;

this is to protect the followers of the two vehicles from disparaging the distinct [teaching] because of the perfect. Moreover, through mastery of spiritual powers, one does not require the fourth practice;
rather, one causes them to enter the reality [of the ultimate] only after they have subsequently attained supernatural faculties. This is the power of profound practice.
This method may be employed amidst the disturbances of a turbid age without obstructing the mastery of the sutra; there is no need to further demonstrate other techniques.

This refers to those who practice the profound path—those whom the World-Honored One beheld among the eight billion bodhisattvas in the "Chapter on the Encouragement of Bodhisattvas" as being individuals for whom such profound practice is unnecessary.
Next, to clarify that beginners must employ the four kinds of peaceful dwelling, this is the first reliance for the beginner.

The Mind. Desiring to cultivate perfect practice and enter the turbid age to propagate the sūtra, one is afflicted by that turbidity; thus, one's own practice fails to be established, and there is no merit in transforming others.
For the sake of such people, it is necessary to demonstrate the method for clear and peaceful practice; this is the intended purpose for the arrival of this chapter.
Third, regarding the sequence of the three clarifications and four practices: as for this "Peaceful Practice," what is its sequence? Now...
The perfect practice of the Lotus Sūtra consists of one practice that is immeasurable practices; it is inconceivable. How could there be a fixed sequence of before and after?
For now, we shall provisionally rely on the "Dharma Master" chapter to clarify how the various stages differ while remaining of a single essence.

The "Dharma Master" chapter briefly demonstrates the propagation of the sūtra, taking the benefit of others as its fundamental principle. It first clarifies "entering the room," wherein the propagation of the Dharma during the Final Dharma Age is distinguished.
The Sūtra says: "To settle all afflictions, first don the Tathāgata’s robe; this is merely a matter of manifesting [the sequence] before and after. If one follows the order of practice:
"All dharmas from the very beginning have always been characterized by quiescence. If one deviates from quiescence and gives rise to signs, one should first use Prajñā to dispel entanglements.
Thus, when first taking one's seat, while all dharmas do not arise, Prajñā arises—this is the compassion of same essence (sahaja-karuṇā).

Compassion: One practices the Way out of pity for sentient beings. Next, one enters the Tathāgata’s chamber; since one transforms the world through compassion and kindness, one will inevitably encounter both opposition and compliance, and must therefore practice patient endurance (*kṣānti*).
Next, one dons the Tathāgata’s robe. Although these stages are presented in this sequence, this is the time of explanation, not the time of practice.

At the time of practice, one enters emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wherein all dharmas are fully present. Furthermore, since compassion and patience are themselves [emptiness], this clarifies the four practices.

The sequential intention is concluded. Regarding the four clarifications on the distinct natures of the four practices: first, physical action (*kāyakarman*); second, verbal action (*vākkarman*); third, mental action (*manaskarman*);
and fourth, the practice of the vow for peaceful bliss. Among these four practices, one must employ *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and compassion to guide the three types of action as well as the vow;
only then will they accord with the Buddha’s intent. Why is this? Because physical action possesses *śamatha*, it is free from coarse physical karma.
Because there is contemplation, one does not grasp at the body. Because one does not grasp at the body, one does not grasp at the body that could be abandoned.
Because of this non-apprehension, one does not fall among the ordinary worldlings. Because of the presence of compassion, one diligently cultivates bodily karma to extensively benefit all beings.
One does not fall into the stages of the two vehicles; this is the body’s non-falling into the error of the two extremes.
Because the body possesses the practice of *śamatha*, one dons the robe of patience. Because the body possesses the practice of *vipaśyanā*, one sits upon the Tathāgata’s seat.

Because of compassion, one enters the Tathāgata’s chamber. This body is thus endowed with the three methods of training. When the body possesses the practice of *śamatha* and is free from faults, it constitutes the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

When the body possesses contemplative practice and non-attachment, one immediately accomplishes the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). When the body possesses compassion and benefits others, one immediately accomplishes the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*).

This constitutes the possession of the three virtues within bodily action (*kāya-karman*). Furthermore, the virtue of grace supports and perfects the virtue of wisdom, and the virtue of wisdom is able to penetrate the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*);

this is called the "peaceful and blissful practice" (*sukha-carita*) of bodily action. The same applies to the remaining actions of speech (*vāk-karman*) and mind (*manas-karman*), as well as to vows.
The same applies to the vows and the three types of peaceful conduct (*anurakṣaṇā-pratipatti*).

One should know that the three karmas are all endowed with compassion (*karuṇā*), and that the vows likewise possess both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, it is understood that the three tracks (*mārga*) from the preceding chapter are employed here as the modes of practice.
Were it otherwise, one would not be skillfully propagating the sutra. The above constitutes the general explanation of the title. Next follows the word-by-word commentary on the text of the sutra.

First, by abiding in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice and sphere of intimacy, one is able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
First, the two are presented together as the "sphere of practice" (*caryā-viṣaya*) and the "proximate sphere" (*upaniṣad*). △ Second, in the explanation, there are again two parts:
namely, the sphere of practice and the proximate sphere. Mañjuśrī, what is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha first provided a general indication; now, based on three dharmas, he clarifies the sphere of practice.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the ground of patience, being gentle, compliant, and not impetuous, their mind is likewise unstartled.
Furthermore, regarding all dharmas, they do not engage in any [discursive] activity, yet they contemplate all dharmas as they truly are, neither engaging nor disengaging.
Analysis: To explain the method for practicing this, one must interpret it by means of three categories of dharmas. First, the place of practice is clarified by means of a single dharma;

second, the place of practice is clarified by means of two dharmas; third, the place of practice is clarified by means of three dharmas. Only then does it accord with the Buddha’s intention. First, the initial [category]...
