He was constantly provided with offerings, honored, respected, revered, and praised by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, commoners, brahmins, householders, and others.
Furthermore, the devas of the void always attended upon him in order to hear the Dharma. Whether he was in a village, a city, or a secluded forest, whenever someone came to him...
Regarding those who wish to pose difficult questions, the devas constantly protect them day and night for the sake of the Dharma, enabling all listeners to attain joy.

Second, the distinct conclusion of the accomplishment of the practice of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*): because it is accomplished through loving-kindness and compassion, one gathers the fourfold assembly and the gods and humans.
Because they made offerings and listened to the Dharma with the vow to achieve [enlightenment], they were moved by the Buddha’s supernormal powers and protected by the various devas;
thus the Tathāgata’s seat was established, for the listeners were filled with joy.
Why is this so? Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
This is the third explanation of the fulfillment of the vow of practice: if even the Buddhas of the three periods protect it, how much more so the devas? Hereafter follows...
Second, the praise of the difficulty of hearing this sutra. This also has two parts: the explanation by way of dharma and the explanation by way of parable.
Regarding the explanation by way of dharma, there are again two parts: "Mañjuśrī, in immeasurable lands, even the name of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* cannot be heard."
In the past, this was never previously revealed;
therefore, it was not obtained then—how much less could it have been seen, upheld, read, or recited?
Today, for the second time, it is finally obtained. △ Next, the illustrative parable also has two parts. First, the parable of not giving the jewel, which illustrates the past.
It has never been explicitly taught. Second, there is the analogy of the jewel, which illustrates what is heard today. Each of these two analogies has both an opening and a closing section.
Regarding the "not giving the jewel," the opening analogy is divided into six parts.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful universal monarch who, wishing to subdue various kingdoms through his majesty, first brings those kingdoms under his awe-inspiring control.
The Universal Monarch is like the Tathāgata transforming the world; the subduing of the various kingdoms is like the subduing of the realms of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Yet the various minor kings do not obey his command.
The disobedience of these two minor kings is analogous to afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like; failing to attain the taming of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) wisdom is termed "not obeying his command."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King raised various armies and went forth to wage war.
He raised these various armies in three divisions: those who practice the methods of the seven stages of worthiness (*saptakṛdbhava-parama*) formed the vanguard;
those who practice the methods of the *srotāpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin* formed the middle army; and those who practice the methods of the *anāgāmin* and *arhat* formed the rear guard.
That which is to be destroyed consists of the three poisons and eighty-four thousand bandits of equal proportion.

That which is capable of destroying them consists of the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates as the army of officers. The "eighty thousand" and so forth refer merely to the eighty thousand [dharmaskandhas] of the former Hīnayāna.
As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma; this does not pertain to the Mahāyāna."
When the king sees that his troops have achieved merit in battle, he is greatly delighted.
Recognizing their merit with joy, he bestows rewards according to their service:
he may grant them fields, houses, villages, or towns; or he may give them clothing and articles for adorning the body.
Or they may give various kinds of precious treasures— gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber— as well as elephants, horses, carriages, and conveyances,
along with male and female slaves and subjects.
Fifth, regarding rewards according to merit: "departing" refers to samādhi; the "house" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*);

the "village" refers to the first and second fruits of the path; the "town" refers to the third fruit; and the "city" refers to nirvāṇa. "Clothing" refers to the wholesome dharmas of shame (*hrī*) and patience (*kṣānti*).

"Adornments for the body" refer to the wholesome dharmas that assist the path. The "various seven treasures" refer to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) and so forth. The "elephants, horses, and carriages" [refer to the vehicles of the various stages].
The "two vehicles" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). "Slaves and servants" refers to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"Possessing wholesome dharmas with outflows" is like the "people," which refers to the dharmas of the stage of worthiness (*ārya-bhūmi*).
Only the bright pearl from within the topknot shall not be given to him. Why is this? This single pearl exists solely upon the crown of the King's head;
if it were given to him, the King’s entire retinue would surely be greatly shocked and amazed.
The sixth [jewel] was not given to him. There are those with the capacity for the *paricchinna* (segmented) [rebirth], for whom it constitutes a minor merit;

there are those with the capacity for the *pariṇāma* (transformative) [rebirth], for whom it constitutes a great merit. As for those who were astonished: when no great merit had yet been achieved, the topknot jewel was suddenly bestowed, and all the ministers were struck with wonder.

This is analogous to sentient beings whose great capacity has not yet been stirred, yet this sutra is suddenly preached, causing the followers of the two vehicles to harbor doubts and the Bodhisattvas to be amazed.
This expresses wonder and amazement. △ Below follows the six similes.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is also like this: by the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he has attained the kingdom of Dharma.
The King was at the head of the three realms;
initially, he combined his supreme majesty to subdue all nations,
yet the various Mara kings refused to submit in obedience.
In the second stage, the subordinate minor kings disobey;
the Tathāgata’s noble and holy generals engage them in battle.
In the third stage, he mobilizes his armies to launch a punitive expedition.
Those who have performed meritorious deeds also rejoice in their hearts.
Having rejoiced in the merit of these four groups,

he preaches various sutras among the fourfold assembly to gladden their minds, bestowing upon them meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).

The faculties and powers are the wealth of all dharmas; furthermore, he bestows upon them the city of nirvana, declaring that they have attained extinction, guiding their minds so that they all rejoice.
Fifth, although he combined [the teachings] and bestowed rewards according to merit, he did not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for him.

Sixth, although he combined [the teachings], he did not grant him the parable of the jewel. Thus, there are six instances each of "opening" and "combining," all of which were previously unprovided analogies.
[End. △ Below this is the analogy of giving the jewel today; there are two sections each for opening and closing.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a wheel-turning monarch who, seeing among his troops those who have performed great service, feels profound joy in his heart.
The initial opening of the parable concerns the bestowing of the jewel. At first, there was great merit;
this jewel, so difficult to believe in, had long remained within [the Buddha's] topknot and was not given to others at random, yet now it is bestowed.
The second part is the correct analogy for giving the jewel. "Bright jewel" means that brightness is a metaphor for the wisdom of the Middle Way, and roundness is a metaphor for permanence.
"On the crown" means it is the primary object of veneration at the ultimate fruit. "In the topknot" means the Real is concealed by the Provisional.
"Untying the topknot" means opening the Provisional; "giving the jewel" means revealing the Real. △ Below, the analogy of giving the jewel is applied to the teaching.
The Tathāgata is likewise so. Within the triple world, he is the Great Dharma King who teaches and transforms all sentient beings through the Dharma.
Seeing the army of the noble ones engaged in battle with the Māra of the five aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, and the Māra of death, he achieves great merit and renown;
he extinguishes the three poisons, emerges from the triple world, and shatters the net of Māra.

In the second section on the analogy, there is first the "meritorious achievement. Regarding "seeing the noble ones," the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states: "Knowing suffering destroys the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*);

severing the origin [of suffering] leaves one free from the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*); realizing cessation leaves one free from the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*); and cultivating the path destroys the demon of the deva-sons (*devaputramāra*).
The reason it does not mention the demon of the deva-sons here is that while followers of the Hīnayāna mostly sever the three demons, they have not yet destroyed the demon of the deva-sons.
Because it is the work of Māra. Nevertheless, there is also the sense of "destruction," as in the phrase "great merit" (*mahāpuṇya*) and so forth.

When the Tathāgata sees these worthy sages of the Hīnayāna who have already eliminated the causes and effects within the realms, it is called "waging war against the aggregates" (*skandha-yuddha*). Upon reaching the Prajñāpāramitā, it is called "great meritorious achievement.
Therefore, one should know that expressions such as "the three poisons" were merely spoken for the sake of the former Hīnayāna.
At that time, the Tathāgata was also greatly rejoiced. This Lotus Sūtra can cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
In all worlds, it is met with many enmities and is difficult to believe; though not previously preached, it is now being taught.
It leads to all-knowledge. "Knowledge" is the name for the fruit; "practice" is the same as the path.
Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas among all their teachings.
It is most profound and is bestowed at the very end, just as a powerful king who has long guarded a bright jewel finally grants it to someone.
This "first teaching" refers to the instruction on a single passage.
Mañjuśrī, this Lotus Sūtra is the secret treasury of all the Tathāgatas. Among all sūtras, it stands supreme;
for a long night it has been guarded and not recklessly proclaimed. Only today do I now expound it for you and others.

The second pair is the analogy of the jewel and the secret treasury. The "secret treasury" represents the oneness of principle; it also encompasses the oneness of the person. Thus, there are two pairs each for the opening and closing [of the analogy].
This concludes the current section on the analogy of the jewel.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.

There were fourteen and a half lines of verse, divided into two parts: the first four lines versify the aforementioned methods of practice; the subsequent ten and a half lines [versify the following].
The Verse Praise Sūtra. First, regarding the method of practice for the verses, it is further divided into two parts:
constantly practicing patience and having compassion for all beings; only then can one expound this sūtra praised by the Buddha.
The first line [of the verse] transcends the prose to express the accomplishment of practice. Above, the accomplishment of practice was explained in general; now, the verse specifically reveals it.

"Constantly practicing patience" expresses the accomplishment of the practice of wearing robes. "Compassionately pitying all beings" expresses the accomplishment of the practice of entering the chamber.

"Then being able to expound [the Dharma]" expresses the accomplishment of the practice of sitting upon the seat. This corresponds to what was stated above: "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, one accomplishes the fourth [practice]," up until the point where it says "reaching the place."

Because of protection. △ Below is the second section, consisting of three lines, which provides a verse-explanation of the methods of practice. Above, there were three [points]: the object, the vow, and so forth;
now, this verse fully summarizes them as three.
"In the future, at the end of the age, those who uphold this sutra—whether householders or renunciants, and whether they are bodhisattvas or not"—this refers to the object of the initial verse’s vow.
It corresponds to the passage mentioned above: "toward householders and renunciants, one gives rise to a mind of great compassion."
One should give rise to compassion. That these people do not hear this sutra and do not believe it constitutes a great loss.
These two verses constitute the general vow; they correspond to the passage from "one should act" up to "not understanding," as mentioned above.
"When I attain the Way of the Buddha, I shall use various skillful means to preach this Dharma for them, causing them to abide within it.
These three verses constitute the formal expression of the vow. This refers to what was stated above: "Even though those people do not [yet] reach it, they shall abide in this Dharma.
The foregoing concludes the verses on the practice of the Dharma. Next, the second section below consists of ten and a half lines, which are verses praising what was mentioned above.

The sūtra is difficult to hear; it contains [sections on] the Dharma, analogies, and their synthesis. Now, however, we only recite the analogies and their syntheses. There are two parts to the recitation of the analogies.
First is the opening of the parable, which further has two parts. First, the verse on not giving the jewel, which is divided into three sections.
It is like the powerful Wheel-Turning King;
the first verse concerns his initial subjugation of the various kingdoms, which corresponds to the aforementioned passage where Mañjuśrī arrives in those lands.
The soldiers have achieved merit in battle.
The second verse concerns the fourth [type of] joy regarding this achievement of merit; it refers to what was stated above: "When the King sees their arrival, he is filled with great joy."
He bestowed various gifts: elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles; articles for adorning the body; as well as fields, houses, villages, and cities;
or else he gave garments, various kinds of precious jewels, male and female slaves, and wealth, bestowing them all with great joy.
The three verses [of the fifth section] concern rewards bestowed according to merit; they correspond to the passage above beginning with "according to merit" and ending with "the people," etc.
Above, there were six analogies, but here only three are versified. The second, third, and sixth [analogies] are not versified at all.
△ Second, the bestowal of verses. The jewels constitute two [parts].
Just as one who is courageous and brave is able to perform difficult deeds, the first verse possesses meritorious achievement.
As stated above, from Mañjuśrī’s arrival up to his reaching of joy.
The King untied the bright pearl from within his topknot and gave it to him.

These two verses concern the pearl; the preceding text, from "By this" up to "gave it to him," explains this. △ Below is the second section, the application of the analogy (*upamāna-saṃyojana*), which has two parts.
First, the verse applying the analogy of not giving the pearl, which is divided into three sections.
The Tathāgata is likewise: he is the sovereign king of all dharmas, possessing the great power of forbearance and the precious treasury of wisdom;
with great compassion, he transforms the world in accordance with the Dharma.
The first verse above corresponds to the subduing of all kingdoms through majestic power. This refers to what was stated previously: "The Tathāgata is also like this...
reaching the sovereignty over the three realms.
He beholds all people undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, seeking liberation, and waging war against the various māras.

The two verses together describe how the minor kings were disobedient and how [the Buddha] went forth to subdue them; this corresponds to the passage above beginning with "the various Māra kings" and ending with "engaged in battle with them.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he preached various dharmas and, through great skillful means, taught these various sūtras.

The three verses together accord with the reward for merit. This refers to the passage above beginning with "He preached various sutras among the fourfold assembly" up to "causing all to rejoice," and so forth.
Regarding the fourth [case] where there was merit and the sixth where the jewel was not given, both lack these verses.
△ Second, the verses accord with the giving of the jewel; this is further divided into six parts.
Having already known the sentient beings and obtained their power, this marks the initial fulfillment of meritorious achievement.
This corresponds to what was stated above, from "The Tathāgata likewise" up to "is also greatly rejoiced."
It was only at the very end that he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
"Two combined with a jewel" (二合與珠) refers to what was mentioned above as "this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*," which has now been preached.
It is like a king who unties his topknot and gives the bright jewel to him;
the three unions above are like that powerful long-reigning king protecting the bright jewel.
This sutra is the most honored, the highest among all sutras.
This is the secret treasury of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the four directions above.
I constantly guard it and do not reveal it recklessly.
For a long night, I have guarded it and have not proclaimed it recklessly.
Now is precisely the right time. I shall speak for you;

I shall expound this from this very day throughout the six realms of existence. The above constitutes the opening and closing [of the section], which concludes the verses praising the rarity of hearing this sutra.
From here below, these twenty-three lines constitute the third part of this chapter, serving as a summary.
The practice achieves signs of spiritual response to encourage cultivation. This text consists of three parts.
After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way and desire to attain peace and security should approach and study this sutra.
These four dharmas constitute the first section, which exhorts one toward the four practices for peace and happiness. Next, for twenty and a half lines, he exhorts by citing the three retributions;

this is also called the purification of the three obstacles. Through the transformation of the purification of the three obstacles, the evil karma of the present life and future lives is exhausted. Thus:
One obtains superior rewards in the present life and in future births. The text consists of three parts:
those who read this sutra will always be free from sorrow and affliction, will have no illness or pain, and their complexion will be bright and pure.

The first clarifies the transformation of karmic retribution. This refers to the transformation of present retribution; by extinguishing the anxieties and afflictions of the present life, one eliminates the retribution of painful sensations (*duḥkhavedanā*).
When this mind that transforms present retribution is free from illness and pain, this is the transformation of the physical form of retribution (*vipākavarṇa*).
One will not be born into poverty, lowliness, or ugliness.

Second, it clarifies the transformation of karmic obstructions: transforming the retribution to be experienced and transforming evil karma. Although the cause of evil karma ought to result in an evil fruit, [it is transformed].

By the power of the sutra, evil causes are transformed so that one obtains good fruits; that is, the retribution of birth is transformed so that it does not arise. Thus, there will be no karma for an evil birth.
By upholding the sutra in the present life, one does not create the karma for poverty, and in future lives, one will not be born into a lowly or base condition.

△ Third, the transformation of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which transforms the subsequent retribution. This is further divided into two parts. First, the specific explanation of the transformation of the three obstacles of affliction. There is...
3. Sentient beings delight in seeing [him], as if yearning for a sage or noble one. Celestial youths serve as his attendants.

First, to clarify specifically the transformation of the obstacle of greed: those with excessive desire are treated with contempt by others; furthermore, it obstructs rebirth in the Brahma heavens. Desire—
Because their hindrances have been transformed, they are pleasing for others to behold and are served by celestial youths.
Weapons do not strike them, and poisons cannot harm them. If someone reviles them with evil words, that person's mouth becomes sealed shut. They wander about without fear.
Like the lion king:

secondly, this specifically clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of anger. By abandoning anger, one removes the internal sword and arrows; when entering the fray, one is not wounded by external blades.
The light of wisdom is like the shining of the sun;

this specifically clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of ignorance. △ Below, the second section consists of sixteen lines, which collectively clarify the transformation of all obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
This is also the transformation of subsequent retribution (*paścād-vipāka*); one should know that these signs manifest as a present response to upholding the sutra.
That which was accomplished in the distant past now merely arises by virtue of conditions.
Furthermore, there are signs such as the causes and effects of attaining Buddhahood, all of which pertain to future retribution. Therefore, within a dream, one sees the signs of future retribution;

events spanning hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas are manifested within a single moment of dreaming to illustrate the inconceivability of the wondrous Dharma—how the infinite is contained within the one.

One among the immeasurable [signs] appears first; later, it shall bear fruit. Furthermore, there are six stages: from the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā*) up to the attainment of Buddhahood through the eight marks (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*) of the wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
All these are the adornments of the Tathāgata by which one adorns oneself; this is the retribution for patience (*kṣānti*).

With reference to the initial dream, one enters the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Within this context, one should clearly understand faith, diligence (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth.
The five faculties (*pañcendriya*). As for the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), one attains firm faith in the Three Jewels that cannot be undermined by anything.

The faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*) consists in attaining the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*). The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) consists in attaining the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), observing diligent skillful means, and subduing greed and sorrow.

The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) consists in attaining the four dhyānas. The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is the analytical understanding of the Four Noble Truths as they truly are. Furthermore,
The faculty of faith: the pure faith attained by generating the bodhicitta toward the Tathāgata.
The faculty of vigor: the vigor initiated by the resolve generated toward the Tathāgata. The faculty of mindfulness: the mindfulness initiated by the resolve generated toward the Tathāgata.
The faculty of concentration: the samādhi initiated by the resolve generated toward the Tathāgata. The faculty of wisdom: the knowledge initiated toward the Tathāgata.
Wisdom. Therefore, this is the entry into dreams. Furthermore, the ten stages of faith are divided into two.
If, within a dream, one sees only wondrous things—seeing all the Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones, surrounded by assemblies of bhikṣus.
They surrounded him as he preached the Dharma. Furthermore, he saw nāgas, devas, asuras, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, reverently joining their palms.
This was the first retribution of his compassion. As for dreams, everyone from stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) up to pratyekabuddhas has them;
only a Buddha does not dream. Because he is free from doubt and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he does not dream. Dreams arise from five causes, as stated in the verse:
It is said that dreams arise from five factors: conceptualizing with a doubting mind; learning based on present events; being addressed by non-human beings;
and [the impressions of] what has been previously heard or seen, as well as various afflictions—thus there are seven causes for dreams. Question:

Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the present moment does not yet perceive visible forms (*rūpa*), how can it perceive visible forms within the dream state? Answer: All of these are [based on] what was previously [experienced].
One merely perceives it through the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) of what has been previously heard; furthermore, it is merely a sign of auspiciousness or inauspiciousness. Question:

Since there is no supernormal power (*abhijñā*) or knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) within a dream, how can one perceive events of the future? Answer: This is not the domain of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*);
rather, it is known through inference (*anumāna*). People have previously had such dreams and experienced such results; now, one simply infers [the future] based on this. Question:

Who sleeps? Answer: Those in the five realms of existence and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) all sleep; even those in the womb whose sense faculties are fully developed sleep, and even the Buddha sleeps.
Question: Sleep is delusion and an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*); how is this [statement] to be reconciled with that? Answer: It refers to the Buddha’s arising [from sleep].
Sleeping in order to compose the body when it is present before one is not an *nīvaraṇa* (hindrance); it is sleep that is not characterized by delusion (*moha*).
He sees his own body and preaches the Dharma for its sake.
Second, right view is the retribution of non-delusion. Since he speaks of both compassion (*maitrī*) and right view as well as non-delusion, [it follows that] compassion...

Compassion is like the initial arousal of the great vow; right view is free from delusion, which constitutes true accomplishment within the realm [of reality], for it is devoid of both the afflictions of views and those cultivated through meditation.
Furthermore, one beholds all Buddhas, their bodies golden in color, emitting immeasurable light that illuminates all things, and speaking with the voice of Brahmā.
He expounded all dharmas. For the fourfold assembly, the Buddha preached the unsurpassed Dharma. Seeing himself standing amidst them, he joined his palms in praise of the Buddha;
hearing the Dharma, he rejoiced and made offerings. He attained dhāraṇīs and realized non-retrogressive wisdom. The Buddha, knowing his mind, [granted him this].
Having deeply entered the Buddha-way, you shall immediately receive the prediction that you will attain supreme perfect enlightenment.

"O son of good family, in a future age, you shall obtain immeasurable wisdom and the Great Way of the Buddhas; your buddha-field will be adorned and pure, vast and beyond compare, and it shall likewise have a fourfold assembly."

Joining their palms to listen to the Dharma, they dream of entering the Ten Abodes and realizing the wisdom of non-retrogression; this signifies that they have attained the stage of the first abode where one receives the prediction of enlightenment through the realization of non-arising.
Seeing the Buddha represents that they shall themselves attain the eight aspects of a Buddha’s manifestation, which is the stage of partial realization of truth.

This is the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Seeing the body situated in the center signifies entry into reality. "Joy" signifies entry into the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);
because the arousal of the mind and the vision of the center are equal to the first stage, it is also called "joy. One attains the three *dhāraṇīs* and possesses the three types of non-retrogression.
The "Buddha-wisdom" is the cause for receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); the subsequent attainment of the prediction may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, one sees oneself in mountain forests practicing wholesome dharmas.
Among the three dreams of cultivating the ten practices, seeing one's body in mountain forests signifies the cultivation of wholesome dharmas through the ten practices.

Regarding the practice of "cultivating conduct": it is not that there was no conduct previously; rather, what was not distinct becomes distinct, for at this stage one most fully attains the name of "conduct.
Thus, one realizes all true marks (*dharmatā*).

The four dreams awaken one to the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). Having realized all true marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one knows these to be the ten dedications, which are the stage of the Middle Way in correct contemplation.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "having realized all": the word "all" (*sarva*) specifically indicates the severance of the thirty categories of afflictions.
He enters deeply into meditative concentration and beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions;
his five dreams signify entry into the ten stages (*bhūmi*). "Entering deeply into meditative concentration" refers to the stainless samādhi (*vimala-samādhi*) within the tenth stage.

Entering the Vajra-samādhi, one receives the empowerment by being touched on the crown of the head by all Buddhas. As for the term "stainless" (*vimalā*), it is already attained at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*);

however, to accord with the Great Sutra, it is here associated with the first stage. If one speaks of entering the Vajra-samādhi, its meaning corresponds to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which properly belongs to the tenth stage.
The bodies of all Buddhas are golden in color, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings; hearing the Dharma and preaching it for others, one constantly has such auspicious dreams.
Furthermore, one dreams of becoming a king who renounces his palace, his retinue, and the five exquisite sensual pleasures, proceeding on foot to the site of enlightenment.
Beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon the lion throne, he sought the Way for seven days until he attained the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Having realized the Unsurpassed Way, he arose and turned the wheel of Dharma, preaching the teaching to the fourfold assembly for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
He preached the sublime Dharma of the untainted, delivering immeasurable sentient beings, and was destined to enter nirvana, like a lamp extinguished when the smoke has ended.
This is the sixth dream, entering wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Dreaming of the Buddha in his eight aspects is to know wondrous enlightenment;

this refers to the stage of the first abode (*prathama-bhūmi*), which possesses the characteristics of being able to achieve Buddhahood through the eight aspects, yet it is still discussed here as the ultimate enlightenment within the sequence of preceding stages.
If, in a future evil age, one speaks of this foremost Dharma, that person shall obtain great benefit, including all the aforementioned merits.

This is the third summary, which establishes the completion of the practice. Regarding "establishing the completion," it reveals that the merit of the four practices has been perfected. One who can perform these practices, while simultaneously exerting the power to propagate the sutra, attributes the merit of transformation to themselves;
thus, the signs of the fruit manifest first, enabling the Great Being to surpass [others] in a single moment, even in a dream.
"Ten billion eons. This indicates that the merit of propagating the teaching for a single lifetime transcends many kalpas.

Since peace and bliss (*anālaya*) are the practice of the Tathāgata, those who propagate the sutra prefigure the attainment of its fruition. Thus, one knows that the power of the merit of propagation is not small.

Question: Why is it that at this point one praises the teaching? Answer: This occurs at the end of the section on the circulation of the *Jiemo* (Trace Gate). Previously, the Buddha [was already discussed].
After the World-Honored One passed into extinction, the merit of propagating the sutra was profound. Ancient Buddhas certified the sutra, and the present Buddha attained enlightenment.

The benefits of its proclamation and dissemination throughout this land and other directions—numbering twenty thousand and eighty trillion—are immeasurable. That people obtain such wondrous merit is truly due to the reality of the Dharma;
therefore, at the end of its circulation, I shall again clarify that which is propagated. What is it that is propagated? It is the revelation and clarification through the three stages.

Therefore, the wheel-turning king is cited as an example of subduing through majesty; the military hosts obtain merit, and because there are small and great degrees of merit, the rewards bestowed are not the same.
The above concludes the third summary of the signs manifested by the attainment of practice.

This marks the end of the fourth chapter, "The Practice of Peaceful Conduct," which completes the methods for propagating the sutra for beginners among those outside the ranks of the sages. From the "Dharma Master" chapter up to this point [the first part is concluded].
Chapter. This concludes the five chapters of the third section on the Trace Gate (*traces-mén*), ending the single passage on the Propagation of the Teaching.
