*The Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
with commentary and notes by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe;
and further annotated by the Śramaṇa Daowei of Siming.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Fifteen: The Emergence from the Earth.
This chapter concludes the fourteenth section of the sutra; this major division constitutes the "Root Gate," which reveals the recent manifestations of the Master’s gate.
This section reveals the Buddha-ground’s realization of the fundamental source. The text is divided into three parts.

First, from this point onward until “you yourselves shall, by means of this, come to hear it,” constitutes the introductory section of the Fundamental Gate (Honmon). Second, from “At that time, Śākyamuni addressed Maitreya”... [and so forth].
This concludes up to the nineteen verses spoken by Maitreya in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," which constitutes the section of the formal exposition (*samyag-deśanā*).

Third, from the verse following this until the middle of the third chapter, "The Unconquerable One" (*Anatimanyana*), is the section of the single circulation (*pravartana*) for the Root Gate (*mūla-mukha*).

These constitute the three divisions of the introduction (*nidāna*), the formal exposition (*samyag-deśanā*), and the circulation (*pravartana*) for the Root Gate. This is the introduction to the Root [Text].

Since there was no general preface (sūtra-opening formula) previously, it is profoundly significant that the meaning of dividing this single work into three sections is applied as a general heading at the beginning of the scripture.
Furthermore, the textual divisions of the "Half-Chapter" (Bunpō-hon) are not fixed in their inclusion or exclusion;

moreover, the intent for the circulation of the two sections—Original (Hon) and Trace (Jaku)—is distinct, and the Original Section is eternally different from all other parts. Thus ends the section on the Preface, the Main Body, and the Circulation of the Original Section.
[End. △ The title states: "Emerging from the Earth. Because the Master is venerable and the Way is honored, one bows deeply and serves with reverence;

at a single command from the Tathāgata, they rush forth from all four directions. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Emerging from the Earth. This is the meaning of the term *loka-dhātu* (the world-realm).
One should know that because the Master possesses the Way, he is venerable; because the Master is venerable, his command must not be disobeyed. Because the Way is honored, there is a command.
They will certainly respond, for the Teacher possesses both [aspects]. With bowed bodies and reverent service, he guides and transforms throughout the three periods of time;

his wisdom and benefit are boundless. Like a single moon reflected in ten thousand waters, who could fathom it? He summons past transgressions to manifest [the truth], and expounds the sutra to benefit those of the present.

Therefore, it is said that [this occurs] from the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth. This is the *puruṣa-saṃvṛti-tantra* (the teaching for the benefit of individuals). If the *puruṣa-saṃvṛti-tantra* does not reveal the traces [of the Buddha's manifestation], [it would be incomplete].

The Buddha has already descended and returned; none are able to know this. Now, wishing to reveal the origin, I shall first bring forth its fundamental attribution. This possesses the growth of roots of goodness from two lifetimes:
it summons the person of the origin to manifest to the person of the present, causing the person of the present to give rise to present goodness;

it causes the person of the origin to propagate the present sutra, causing the person of the future to give rise to future goodness. Furthermore, empty space is profound and still, with neither early nor late.

Those who are deluded cling to the traces while remaining ignorant of the source. By invoking the past to illustrate the present, and by shattering the near to reveal the distant, the principle is manifested beyond the void;

the source and the trace manifest the phenomena. Phenomena possess both source and trace, yet the principle is without beginning or end. Thus, the deluded are confused about the principle and remain ignorant of the source and the trace;
consequently, they cling to the near traces and thereby lose the distant source. If they are still confused regarding the source and the trace, how much more so regarding the inconceivable oneness?

Therefore, the original disciple dwelt in the void below, while the original master of that ground remained in the void for a long duration. The present master and disciple now exist in the void of the present.

Though the void of the past and the void of the present, as well as the void below and the void above, are identical in essence, the original disciple fundamentally understood the immediate traces, whereas the present disciple still remains deluded regarding the distant origin. Thus, it is to shatter their attachment to the immediate that [this teaching is given].

The past is summoned to reveal the present. Now, this disciple, having fallen into doubt, has presented a request; only upon hearing the teaching will that doubt be shattered. To shatter attachment to what is near and evil, this serves as an antidote.

Yet, the one at the site of enlightenment (Śākyamuni) is the younger father, while the one in the realm of tranquil light (Vairocana) is the elder son. The power of their medicine is revealed so that all may come to know it.

Śākyamuni, the one at the site of enlightenment, manifests the initial attainment of Buddhahood and is thus the "younger father. Vairocana, the Bodhisattva of tranquil light, has practiced for a long time and is thus the "elder son."
[The father] is attached; therefore, while the child grows old, the father remains young. Regarding the analogy of the medicinal power: why is the father young while the son is old?

According to the meaning of the subsequent analogy of father and son: the father has long since taken the medicine of the seed of wisdom (*tathāgatagarbha*) that restores youth, so though he is old, he appears as if young.
The son has likewise long received the prescription for eternal non-death, so though he is young, he appears as if old. Although each has indeed partaken of such nourishment...
The merit of this [is such that] father and son have long been settled; this is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).

Now, although these four *siddhāntas* (fourfold methods of interpretation) generally explain the present text, their intent simultaneously encompasses the subsequent chapters. However, while the first *siddhānta* is explicitly in the text of this chapter, the second has its intent encompassing the subsequent chapters, and the third and fourth *siddhāntas* draw upon the subsequent chapters;
all serve to assist the latter [chapters] in order to manifest and clarify the profound. Thus, Śubhananda was born.
This refutes the [view of] evil. It is because one perceives the source. Therefore, we know that the world is precisely the basis for the three *siddhi*s (the three types of success).
Thus, the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" focuses specifically on the world. The text asks: "From where do they come? By what causes and conditions have they gathered?

Now, by explaining this chapter through various meanings, I shall clarify the understanding of the causes and conditions of the four *siddhi*s. Therefore, it says: "They emerge from the earth. This is the explanation.
Title completed. △ The initial preface consists of two parts: first, the emergence; second, the questions and doubts. The emergence consists of three sections:
first, bodhisattvas from other directions requesting the propagation of the sutra; second, the Tathāgata’s refusal; third, the emergence from below.
At that time, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from other lands, numbering more than eight times the sands of the Ganges River,
rose from their places within the great assembly, joined their palms in homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if you would permit us, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha,
to remain diligently and with great vigor in this Sahā world to protect, uphold, recite, copy, and make offerings [to this teaching],"
Those who uphold this sutra shall extensively expound it in this land.
At first, bodhisattvas from other regions, hearing that the merit of transmitting this sutra is vast, all desired to make vows to dwell here and propagate it;
therefore, they requested [the Buddha] to do so for their sake.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: "Cease, sons of good family! There is no need for you to protect and uphold this sutra. Why is this?
In my Sahā world, there are naturally sixty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
each of these bodhisattvas has a retinue of sixty thousand followers, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. These...
"O people, if you are able, after my parinirvāṇa, to protect, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound this sutra"—this second request the Tathāgata declined and did not permit.
There are three reasons for this refusal: first, each of you has your own respective place of residence;
if you remain in this land, it would neglect the benefit of those other realms. Second, [the needs of] both other regions and this land [would be compromised].

The conditions for establishing a karmic connection are shallow; though one may wish to proclaim and transmit [the teaching], there will certainly be no great benefit. Third, if permission were granted, it would be impossible to summon those from the lower realms.
If those from the lower realms do not come, their traces cannot be destroyed and the Dharma cannot be manifested in the distant future.
These are the three reasons why the Tathāgata forbade it. There are also three reasons why he summoned those from the lower realms: they are my disciples, and they ought to propagate my [teaching].
The Dharma, by virtue of its profound and vast conditions, is able to benefit this land universally, benefit all the lands of the manifested bodies universally, and benefit other lands universally.
Furthermore, it enables the near to be opened up and the distant to be revealed; for this reason, it stops at that [near] point and summons those below. Question:

Regarding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who together mature the unripe—what distinction exists between them? If their manifested bodies and scattered reflections pervade the ten directions, why do they speak of "self"?

"Does this mean that they abide in them or abandon them? The answer is: "For all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there is truly no distinction between 'this' and 'that. It is simply that the capacity of sentient beings exists or does not exist;
this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) from beginningless time. Therefore, by means of the second meaning, the first meaning is revealed: the matter of forming a karmic connection (*kemyō*) is shallow.
One first forms a karmic connection with these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and subsequently achieves realization through those same Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the earth throughout the Sahā world—the trichiliocosm—trembled and split asunder.
From within it, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously surged forth.
First, it clarifies their emergence.
These bodhisattvas all have golden bodies, possess the thirty-two marks, and emit immeasurable radiance;
this is the second [section on] bodily characteristics.
First, it is located beneath the Sahā world, dwelling in the void of this realm.
Third, as for its dwelling place: it is the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsvara*). "Eternal" refers to the virtue of permanence;

"quiescent" refers to the virtue of bliss; and "light" refers to purity and selfhood. This is the secret treasury of the four virtues; such is its dwelling place, by means of the dharma of non-abiding.
It dwells within the secret treasury. "The lower realm" refers to the abyssal depths of the *dharmatā* and the ultimate ground of the profound mystery;
hence it is called the "lower. It does not belong to this world below, nor does it belong to that space above. Being neither this nor that, it is precisely the Middle Way.
Emerging from here, it is not in the realm above, nor is it in this realm below. Neither above nor below, it abides in the midst of space. Furthermore—

This is the Middle Way. However, fundamentally there are four virtues that serve as the supported (the environment), while the four virtues attained through cultivation serve as the supporter (the body).
Both the supporter and the supported possess a body that serves as the supporter, which in turn relies upon the land that serves as both the supporter and the supported.
Only when these two meanings are equal is this the true nature of the body and land of Vairocana. If one speaks of the "interpenetration of successive layers of atoms and lands," [it is because]...
There is a multilayered existence, multilayered phenomena, and multilayered teachings. For those who have not yet attained realization, these phenomena are used to manifest the underlying principle.
If one does not understand this single point, who can comprehend the ten directions of the Dharma-realm? There is but one Buddha, yet other Buddhas are also permitted.
If other Buddhas are permitted, then those other Buddhas likewise possess multilayered bodies and lands that mutually manifest, mutually enter, and mutually merge.
It should be understood that this refers to a single discourse being applied universally.
These bodhisattvas heard the sounds spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha and came forth from below;
each and every one of these bodhisattvas was a leader who exhorted the great assembly.
Regarding the fourth point, the account of the reason for coming: I have come because I heard your command; I have come to propagate the Dharma; I have come to shatter attachments;
and I have come to reveal the fundamental source—all as explained above.

Each leads a retinue of sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [Ganges-sand] equals; how much more so those leading fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* equals?

How much more so even down to one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, half a *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, a quarter, or even down to a ten-millionth, a billionth, a hundred-billionth, or a trillionth part of a *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*? How much more so those leading ten million?
There are those with retinues of hundreds of millions and billions; how much more so those with retinues of tens of millions, or thousands of millions, or hundreds of millions, down to ten thousand;
how much more so those with one thousand, one hundred, or even ten; how much more so those who lead four, five, four, three, two, or one disciple;
and how much more so those who dwell alone, delighting in the practice of seclusion. Such as these are immeasurable and boundless beyond calculation.
This cannot be known through calculation or analogies.

Fifth, regarding the description of the retinues they lead: if one judges by common human sentiment, one would say that leading sixty thousand, fifty thousand, or as many as the sands of the Ganges constitutes "many," while leading three, two, or one constitutes "few. To be alone is to be solitary and single. However, according to the text:
I went to seek them out. Those numbering sixty thousand or fifty thousand were few; those who were alone were many. The text says:
"Those who dwell alone and solitary are even more numerous than the aforementioned. If one relies upon this Dharma-gate, every single one of them is the virtue of the Teacher."
It can lead all people to the place of treasure. One should know that "one" does not mean solitary, nor does "sixty thousand" mean many.
"One" refers to the single path of purity; "two" refers to concentration and wisdom; "three" refers to precepts, concentration, and wisdom;

"four" refers to the Four Noble Truths; "five" refers to the five eyes; and "six" refers to the six perfections. Each perfection encompasses the ten dharma realms, and within each realm there are [further divisions].
Ten makes a hundred; a hundred possesses a thousand. Ten wholesome deeds make ten thousand. One *pāramitā* possesses ten thousand;
six *pāramitās* thus possess sixty thousand dharma-gates. Many are not many; one is not few. It is neither many nor few.

Whether many or few, this is precisely the contemplative practice (*guanxing*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*). Practice relies upon the wondrous object; therefore, while the degrees reach ten thousand, the degrees themselves are not actually ten thousand.
Within each of the six [teachings], there are ten thousand, yet these are merely a single ten thousand—there are no separate ten thousands. The six are entirely the ten thousand.
There is no distinction among the six. Each and every practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*) is none other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The realm is devoid of the characteristics of a realm; it is but a single instant, which is itself the Single Path. As it is with one and six, so it may be understood by analogy for two, three, four, and five.
Thus, within the six, there is not one that does not fully possess both the one and the many. One should know that from the Single Path up to the arrival of the Five Eyes, it is all one.
The eye is a single truth; all possess ten thousand [qualities], none of which fail to be the contemplation of the Dharma-realm through the three contemplations.
△ The above concludes the narrative by the scribe. From here on, the second section, the inquiry, consists of five parts: first, offerings of the three karmas; second, the words of the inquiry;
third, the Buddha’s response regarding peace and well-being; fourth, verses of sympathetic joy; fifth, the Tathāgata’s discourse.
They sighed in admiration.
Once these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, they each proceeded through the air to the seven-jeweled, wondrous stupa where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha were located.
Upon arrival, they bowed their heads at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones, and so forth, [prostrating] before all the jewels.

Before the Buddha on the lion throne beneath the tree, they likewise prostrated, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined in reverence, praised him with various bodhisattva methods of eulogy.
Standing to one side, they gazed upon the two World-Honored Ones with joyful devotion.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had emerged from the earth, [endowed] with the various qualities of bodhisattvas.
He praised the Buddha with various eulogies of the Dharma. Thus, a period of fifty intermediate kalpas elapsed.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha sat in silence, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for those fifty intermediate kalpas.

By the Buddha’s supernatural power, he caused the great assembly to perceive the time as being like half a day. At that moment, the fourfold assembly, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, [also perceived it thus].

Therefore, they saw bodhisattvas filling the empty space of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lands, making offerings with their first three karmas for fifty minor kalpas, which felt like half a day. The fourfold assembly saw this everywhere;
this was achieved by concealing the long and manifesting the short, and by borrowing his supernatural power to make the narrow appear vast—all of which is inconceivable.
This discourse clarifies the Tathāgata’s inconceivable power over the extension and contraction of time, manifesting the sovereign might of the Tathāgata.
To prostrate and circumambulate is the body; to praise the Dharma is the speech; and to gaze with reverence is the mind.
That fifty intermediate kalpas are equivalent to half a day is the inconceivability of time as perceived by the Tathāgata, which is not based on duality.
Regarding the signs: the Bodhisattvas below constantly face [the Buddha] and offer praise, while the Tathāgata remains silent, always receiving their commendation.
To those who understand, what is short is made long—meaning fifty minor kalpas; to those who are deluded, what is long is made short—meaning as if it were half a day.
This serves as a prologue to the fundamental and the phenomenal. Before the Tathāgata had preached [the truth], people were ignorant of the fundamental and clung to the phenomenal;
yet when the Buddha reveals and clarifies it, they awaken to the near and reach the far, realizing that the inconceivable is one.
That the fourfold assembly sees the Bodhisattvas everywhere is likewise inconceivable. Indeed, what is seen by the fleshly eye and the divine eye does not extend far, but now—
That which is beheld fills the void. Seeing the rain fall fiercely, one knows the dragon is great; seeing the flowers flourish, one knows the pond is deep.
Seeing that they should fill the void, one then knows the true *maitreya* pervades the *dharmadhātu*. This secretly indicates that ignorance shall soon be shattered;
therefore, for the time being, only a single portion is suppressed.

Within this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four guiding teachers: the first was named Upariṣṭacārin (Upward-Walking), the second Anantacārin (Boundless-Walking), the third Śuddhacārin (Pure-Walking), and the fourth Supratiṣṭhitacārin (Well-Established-Walking). These four bodhisattvas were the foremost leaders and preceptors among that multitude.
The second part consists of the words of inquiry, which include both prose and verse. Within the initial prose section, the four guides are first designated.
The reason only these four individuals are mentioned is that they are intended to represent the forty stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
This is analogous to how the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* mentions only Dharmamati, Guṇakara, Vajradhvaja, and Ratnagarbha to expound upon the forty stages.
Before the great assembly, they each joined their palms together, gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha, and inquired after him, saying:
"World-Honored One, are you free from illness and affliction? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?"
First, he inquired whether [the World-Honored One] was dwelling in peace and happiness,
whether those to be delivered were easy to instruct, and whether he caused the World-Honored One any fatigue.
Next, he asked whether sentient beings were easy to deliver.
At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"World-Honored One, are you at ease? Are you free from illness and affliction? In teaching and transforming sentient beings, do you experience no weariness?"
The first line asks whether [the Buddha] is at ease and whether it is easy for sentient beings to be transformed, so as not to cause the World-Honored One any weariness.
The next line is a verse asking whether sentient beings are easy to deliver.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas, spoke these words:
"So it is, so it is, sons of good family. The Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction."
Third, the Tathāgata initially answered me: "I am at ease;
these sentient beings are easy to transform and deliver, and there is no weariness. Why is this? Because these sentient beings..."
From lifetime to lifetime, they have constantly received my transformation; they have also reverently made offerings to and honored the Buddhas of the past, planting various roots of goodness.
As soon as these sentient beings see my body and hear what I preach, they all believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
From the beginning, their faculties were sharp and their merit was profound; throughout successive lifetimes, they have constantly received the Great Transformation.

Upon first seeing my body, they immediately received the *Avataṃsaka* and entered the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Since the fruit has ripened and is ready to fall, these sentient beings are easy to deliver.

Question: By what do you mean when you say the *Avataṃsaka* is "first seen"? Answer: That sutra itself states, "Just now, I have attained perfect enlightenment. All subsequent passages are merely an expansion [of this initial realization].
This clarifies the characteristics of cause and effect, wherein the primary and secondary [realms] are universally identical. Therefore, within this single sutra, there are three explicit passages:

at the beginning of the "Chapter on the World-Ruling King," the beginning of the "Chapter on Names and Titles," and the beginning of the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," all state that he first attained perfect enlightenment at the site of bodhi.
Because it was his initial attainment, those who see it are established in the beginning. Now, I shall briefly cite ten points to explain this.

Regarding "first seeing" and "seeing now": when one first attains the Way, it is called "first seeing"; the true reality at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, occurring long thereafter, is called "seeing now.
One must understand that today, in this royal city, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened.

As for the seer and the seen, what difference is there between the object and the wisdom? Second, regarding "opening and closing" versus "not opening and not closing": the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is like the sun shining upon high peaks.
The "Mountain" refers to the Sudden teaching, which is neither opened nor joined. Compared to the *Avataṃsaka*, the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is termed "unopened";

because it still retains elements of the Gradual, it is termed "unjoined. For those who have not yet entered [the Great Vehicle], the Sudden is opened by means of the Gradual, using the five flavors to subdue them and lead them gradually back to the Sudden.
To enable them to practice and enter now, the Lesser Vehicle is further opened; only with this present sutra are they finally joined. How much more so for that which was previously unjoined?
Now we also synthesize them; thus we know that the opening [of the teaching] in that sutra was not universal, and its accommodation to capacities was insufficient.

Its synthesis, too, was not exhaustive, as it still retained traces of expedient means (*upāya*). One should know that what was opened there is also opened here, yet what is synthesized here is no different from what was synthesized there.
In the transformative work of a single Buddha, similarities and differences are perfectly distinct; however, because that [sutra] lacked those of small capacity, it was called "Sudden" at the outset.
Since the opening of the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, the name has gradually returned to the Sudden [teaching]. Although the opening and closing differ, the two forms of the Sudden are not distinct.

Third, "vertical breadth and horizontal brevity": the Sudden directly enters the Dharma-realm vertically; hence it is called "vertically broad. Because it does not pass through expedient means, it is "horizontally brief.
Now, passing through the five flavors constitutes "horizontal breadth," and attaining entry into the Buddha-wisdom is likewise "vertical breadth."

The fourth point concerns "the one reality with its many manifestations. Regarding the fact that the manifestations are shared while the reality is unique: because there is but a single pedestal, the reality is one;

because there are a thousand petals, the manifestations are many. The manifestations are "shared" because they are common to all other sutras, whereas the reality is "unique" because it differs from all other sutras.
Even if the ten directions act as mutual principals and companions, the ten directions do not depart from a single atom, and that single atom resides precisely upon this pedestal.
One should know that these leaves concern only the environment and its inhabitants within the *迹門* (the Gate of Traces); they expand upon that.

However, since the mutual interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants has already been extensively expounded, what remains unclear regarding the primordial basis of the distant past? If one discusses the *本門* (the Gate of the Origin) of this sutra, it differs from all other scriptures.

The *Avataṃsaka* is both identical to and different from that *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Although the latter contains causes for practice over a long period, it refers only to a single instance of such causes on this present day;
it has never yet spoken of an intermediate instance of fruition. Much less does it mention becoming a Buddha repeatedly during the interim.
One should know that this difference makes it distinct from that [Lotus Sūtra]; thus, one knows that the present text differs from the various other sūtras.
Therefore, it is said that [the Lotus Sūtra] alone is wondrous. If one says they are not different, then Gayāśīrṣa is still [part of it];

how could the Flower Treasury (Huá-zàng) not be so? When opened, both are opened; in their inconceivability, they are one. This is because the remote origin of the *Dharmapada* (Fǎhuá) differs from the proximate manifestation of the *Avataṃsaka* (Huáyán).
Thus, we know that the gates of the teachings cannot but differ. Fifth, those four bodhisattvas were empowered, and forty [verses] were spoken.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, most of the teachings are spoken by the added bodhisattvas; even those up to Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, as well as the entry into the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), are still spoken by the bodhisattvas themselves.
One does not see any text therein that bears the Buddha’s seal of approval.

In the present sutra, both the provisional and the ultimate, the primary and the secondary, are all spoken by the Buddha himself to reveal, instruct, awaken, and enter [the truth], without adding anything from others—except for the introductory section where Mañjuśrī resolves doubts and the account of the transmission.

Among those who transmit [this teaching], there are bodhisattvas who have made vows to propagate it extensively; these are all endorsed by the Buddha. Furthermore, when they address the Buddha directly, they are thereby considered to possess the seal (mudrā) of approval.

Whether this seal is explicitly added or not, all such acts constitute the wisdom of the Buddha. Although the ritual manifestations of transformation differ according to time and place, the principle regarding whether something is sealed or not remains one and the same.
This is because the sixth transformation of the land—the Flower King World—is a non-transformed land.

It is said that [the Buddha’s] words do not change, yet he transforms his lands three times; therefore, it is called "transforming the land. However, purity and defilement are inherently distinct and always differentiated.

That which is now called "transformation" refers to the defiled as the manifestation of provisional means (*upāya*) and the transformation as the revelation of the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*). Defilement belongs to the five turbidities and originally pertains to those of limited capacity (*hīnayāna-śrāvaka*).

When the opportunity arises for these limited-capacity practitioners, the provisional is opened; the transformation of the land serves as the sign of this opening. Thus, having revealed the original ground, it becomes purely [real].
For all Bodhisattvas, the Pure Land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes perceive it as burning. Furthermore, those various worlds are different from one another:
purity does not obstruct impurity, for there are jeweled trees, flowers, fruits, and places of recreation; and impurity does not obstruct purity.

How much more so in the land of the eternally quiescent light, where beauty and ugliness are both transcended. Yet, in relation to the quiescent light, there still exist both purity and impurity, whether they manifest through transformation or remain unchanging.

How can the Buddha’s wisdom be considered distinct? Could it be that the difference in the Buddha’s wisdom arises from a distinction between change and non-change based on the sequence of beginning and end?

If one disregards the teaching of "neither believing nor disparaging," yet stubbornly clings to the passage concerning the burning of the eyes, using the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to disparage the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it is like someone who insults their own body while praising their arms.
Thus, we know that the discussion of change refers only to the provisional traces [of the teaching].
Transformation. Purity and impurity are inconceivable; their substance is identical while their names differ. Regarding the seventh [point], "many locations" versus "not many locations":

the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra has seven locations and eight assemblies, which constitutes "many locations. This present sūtra is located at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and in the distant void, and thus does not have "many locations.
Although they differ in being more or fewer, what difference is there in that which is taught? How could a difference in number cause the Buddha’s wisdom to be distinct?
If it were the same reward land (*vipākabhūmi*), it would likewise not be in multiple locations; yet here, when contrasted horizontally with the four lands, the locations indeed become many.

By taking those many and contrasting them with this Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsabhūmi*), even "many" becomes "one. Since these two are of one essence, how could the Buddha’s wisdom differ? Eighth, regarding the refutation:
because the illusory city is extinguished and the status of a hired laborer is changed, there is a refutation herein. Furthermore...

They are like those who are deaf and mute; therefore, there is rejection and exclusion. They do not possess these qualities; therefore, there is no rejection or exclusion. These are all given the prediction by the Buddha;
therefore, there is no rejection or exclusion. Ninth, they practice the Great Straight Path, which is called "Directly Revealing the Real.
This definitive understanding of the Śrāvaka Dharma is called "Opening the Expedient to Reveal the Real. Tenth, with sharp faculties and mature conditions, they first enter the Buddha’s [teaching].
Regarding wisdom: those with dull faculties mature later. Now they enter the Buddha-wisdom; because their conditions and capacities differ, there are briefly ten points of distinction.
In the *sarvajñajñāna* (all-encompassing wisdom) and the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), there is no difference whatsoever. Therefore, this sutra says:

"As soon as they see my body and hear what I preach, they all believe and accept it, entering the Tathāgata’s wisdom—except for those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna. Now, regarding this sutra...

Entering the Buddha’s wisdom is clearly set forth herein; there is no need for doubt. Various masters, seeing that the conditions differ, follow those differing conditions with divergent interpretations;
thus they remain lost and fail to return, moving further and further away from the Way. If one recognizes that the underlying principle is the same, then a thousand chariots will share the same ruts.
The Buddha’s wisdom is without distinction. Question: Since the principle of all sutras, even down to grasses and trees, is equally non-dual, why is it unique to the *Lotus Sūtra*?

Answer: The similarities and differences among the teachings are fully explained in the *Xuánwén*. Although the underlying principle is the same in all cases, the teaching being discussed here is the present one.
What is praised here is the capacity of the expressive teaching; therefore, it is not found within other teachings. This is detailed as in the *Fāngguǎn*.
This is clarified in the "Chapter on Expedients. Formerly it was said: "The *Avataṃsaka* is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), possesses full letters (*pūrṇākṣara*), and is eternal;
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*), lacks full letters, and is not eternal. Now, let us compare these scriptural passages.

If entering [the path] at the beginning were definitive meaning, and entering it now were non-definitive meaning, then entering at the beginning would be the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*), while entering now would not be the Buddha-wisdom. If the Buddha-wisdom is indeed identical [in both cases], then [the distinction between] definitive and... [is untenable].

The meaning is likewise equal; the permanence of the *maṃtra* (full letters) is entirely so. The followers of the [Ten] Stages school call the *Avataṃsaka* the "Perfect Doctrine" (*yuanzong*) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* the "Not-True Doctrine.
Now, I shall also employ this text to place them side by side.
Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Lesser Vehicle— such persons I shall now also cause to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom. Furthermore,
for the sake of those whose faculties are dull and whose merit is meager, who throughout successive lifetimes have not received the Great Transformation, it is necessary...
The Buddha opens up the sudden teaching and explains the gradual. In the *Avataṃsaka*, there is no "Lesser Vehicle" (Hīnayāna); being at the very beginning, it is called "sudden.
He then opens the three gradual stages—the Tripiṭaka, Vaipulya, and Prajñā—to discipline them. He also causes these people, who have now heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, to enter the Buddha’s wisdom.

Although this is more difficult than the former [gradual stages], for the Buddha it is extremely easy. The Buddha recognizes what is appropriate and employs skillful means to reach the right point; it is like applying a thin layer of ointment and using a hot iron to cauterize.
The Buddha’s wisdom and realization are identical.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke these verses:
"Excellent, excellent! O Great Hero, World-Honored One! These sentient beings are easily transformed and can inquire of the Buddhas."
This profound wisdom, having heard it, we believe and understand; we rejoice in it.
The fourth Bodhisattva spoke a verse to express his understanding and rejoice.

As for those who are able to ask, they are the four great beings in the *Avataṃsaka* and Śāriputra’s three requests in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; both are capable questioners. As for that which is asked, it is the inquiry.
This is the wisdom of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the foremost great bodhisattvas, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Sons of good family, you are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata."

Regarding the fifth point, the Tathāgata’s expression of praise, it differs from the question. In the section on the question, those who rejoice in the one who asks are all bodhisattvas and those being taught;
having heard [the teaching], they practice with faith, and we likewise rejoice. This is what the Tathāgata praises.

Regarding the statement that "the one capable of transforming others gives rise to sympathetic joy (anumodana)," what is the meaning of this? Indeed, those who are able to inquire are all ancient Buddhas;
that you are able to give rise to sympathetic joy means you are a Tathāgata. The Bodhisattva gives sympathetic joy to their traces, while the Tathāgata praises their source.
This also secretly indicates the measure of their lifespan. As for this secret indication: by now praising the Bodhisattva, it is shown that he is already an ancient Buddha.
This "Secret Manifestation" indicates that the present Buddha did not achieve enlightenment at this very moment. If he was not accomplished at this time, there must have been a distant origin;
because it has not yet been clearly revealed, it is called a "secret manifestation. The above concludes the Prologue on Assembling the Multitude.

From here, starting with "At that time," begins the second section: the Prologue of Questions concerning the Root Gate. From the time of the site of tranquility (Vaiśālī) down to the present seat, the Great Beings from the ten directions have come...
The assembly is unceasing; though it cannot be limited, by the power of my wisdom as one in the final birth before Buddhahood, I see and know them all.

Yet, among this multitude, I do not recognize a single person. Nevertheless, as I travel and transform beings throughout the ten directions, visiting and honoring the Buddhas, I clearly recognize the great assemblies of those Buddhas.
Even regarding the places I have traversed, I do not recognize them. Whether coming or going, it is as if—
This is because they do not recognize him. Furthermore, those various Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) are predecessors who have gone before;
Maitreya is a junior student of a later generation. Because the latter does not know the former, he does not recognize them.

Moreover, those Great Beings abide in the fundamental reality (dharmatā) and manifest throughout the ten directions, teaching and transforming beings individually. All their true and responsive manifestations are beyond the scope of Maitreya’s perception.
The realm. For this reason, they do not recognize it. Furthermore, the Buddha, entrusting the propagation of the sutra, summoned the great bodhisattvas (*mahāsattva*).

Because these great beings came upon hearing their teacher’s command, he secretly revealed his lifespan; it was not something known by the assembly at that time, and thus it is said they did not recognize it.

This concludes the explanation of the introductory section regarding doubts and questions according to the four *siddhāntas*. There are two types of doubts and questions: first, the doubts of the bodhisattvas of this land; second, [the doubts] of those from other lands.
The Bodhisattvas had doubts; furthermore, there were two kinds of doubts among the Bodhisattvas of this land.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and a multitude of Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers all thought to themselves:
"Since ancient times, we have neither seen nor heard of such a multitude of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these,
who have surged forth from the earth, standing before the World-Honored One with palms joined in worship and inquiring after the Tathāgata’s well-being.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya knew the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, and also desired for himself— "
Having resolved their doubts, they joined their palms toward the Buddha and asked him in verse:
"From the beginning, these bodhisattvas of this land have harbored long-standing doubts.

There are immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of great assemblies of bodhisattvas whom none of us have ever seen before. We pray that the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings will explain [this]."
"From where have you come?
This first line and phrase asks from where one has come and by what causes and conditions one has gathered [this assembly].
Possessing a vast body and great supernormal powers, your wisdom is inconceivable; your resolve and mindfulness are firm and steadfast.
Possessing the power of great patience, he is one whom sentient beings delight to behold. From where has he come?
[This consists of] two lines and three phrases, asking by what causes and conditions he has come.
Each and every bodhisattva was accompanied by a retinue of immeasurable number, as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Some great bodhisattvas led retinues as numerous as sixty thousand times the sands of the Ganges; such a great assembly sought the Buddha-way with single-minded devotion.
These great masters, numbering as many as sixty thousand Ganges-sands, have all come together to make offerings to the Buddha and to protect and uphold this sutra;
there are also those numbering fifty thousand Ganges-sands, whose count exceeds even that, as well as forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, down to ten thousand.
One thousand one hundred, and so on, up to as many as the sands of a single Ganges River; half, or three-quarters, or four-fifths; a ten-millionth part of a billion;
a hundred-thousand-nayuta; ten-thousand-billion disciples; even down to fifty million—these numbers exceed even those mentioned above.
From one million down to ten thousand, from one thousand and one hundred, to fifty and ten, even down to three, two, or one—
those who are alone without retinue and delight in solitary dwelling all came to the presence of the Buddha, their number exceeding even those mentioned above.
If one were to count these great assemblies by casting tally-sticks, even after more kalpas than the sands of the Ganges River, one would still be unable to know them all.
This third section of nine lines describes their numerical magnitude.
These assemblies of bodhisattvas of great majesty and vigor—who taught them the Dharma, by whom were they instructed and brought to fulfillment?

From whom did they first resolve their minds for enlightenment? Whose Buddha-dharma did they extol? Whose sutras did they receive, uphold, and practice? And which path of the Buddhas did they cultivate?
The fourth section consists of two lines, asking who their teacher is;
"Such bodhisattvas as these, with supernatural powers and great wisdom.
The fifth section consists of five and a half lines, concluding the request; it further contains five parts, the first half-line of which concludes the praise.
The earth in the four directions quaked and split open, and [beings] all surged forth from within. "World-Honored One, since the past, I have never seen such a thing.
I pray that you will tell us whence they come and the names of their lands. I have constantly traveled through various countries, yet I have never before seen such a phenomenon."
Second, he requested an answer regarding his place of origin:
"Among this assembly, I do not recognize a single person. Having suddenly emerged from the earth, I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions thereof."
The third line requests an answer regarding the circumstances of this coming:
"In this great assembly today, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions; all these bodhisattvas and others desire to know this matter."
Regarding the causes and conditions concerning the origins and ends of this assembly of Bodhisattvas,
in the fourth section of one and a half lines,
the great assembly together entreats the World-Honored One of Immeasurable Virtue: "We pray that you will resolve the doubts of the multitude."
The fifth section consists of two phrases; please respond to the Master. △ From this point downward is the doubt of the bodhisattvas from other lands.

At that time, the various Buddhas who were emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha, having come from immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands in other directions, were seated cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath the various jeweled trees in the eight directions. Their...
The attendants of each of those Buddhas saw these great assemblies of bodhisattvas emerging from the earth in the four directions of the trichiliocosm and remaining in the air.
Each addressed his own Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, from where have these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) assemblies of bodhisattvas come?"
First, regarding those bodhisattvas from other lands who harbored doubts: their manifested bodies and retinues were situated throughout the ten directions, sharing the same doubts as Maitreya.

Since both groups were unaware of their original lands, [the Buddha] wished to manifest that his attainment of enlightenment had occurred long ago; thus, each of them presented their doubts to their own Buddha.
At that time, each of the Buddhas addressed their respective attendants: "Good sons, wait but a moment.
There is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Maitreya, who has been prophesied by Śākyamuni Buddha to become a Buddha immediately after him.
He has already asked about this matter, and the Buddha is now answering it. You yourselves shall hear it through his account."
Regarding the statement that "the Buddhas all withheld [their answers] to wait for Maitreya," this means that the benefit of answering questions does not reside in me;

therefore, I did not answer. Why did they withhold [their answers] to wait for Śākyamuni to answer Maitreya’s questions? It is because the matters and deeds concerning which Maitreya inquired were no trivial ones.

Throughout his entire life, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni had never explicitly taught this; it is only now, in response to these questions, that he extensively reveals the longevity [of the Buddha].
This profound mystery of his entire career shall be revealed by the Buddha himself, and you shall hear it.

I should not answer [otherwise]. The above concludes the introduction to the two questions. This concludes the two introductions to the Root Chapter. From here on, starting with "At that time," is the second [part].
The Section on the True Teaching of the Essential Gate consists of two parts: first, the prose introduction followed by the verses of admonition and permission;
second, the formal exposition itself.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, Ajita! Thus it begins.
That you are able to ask the Buddha such a great matter is indeed rare.
First, Śākyamuni answers by first praising them himself:
"You all should be of one mind, don the armor of diligence, and resolve with firm intent."
Next, the Buddha exhorted Maitreya and the others, commanding them not to be distracted, not to be indolent, and not to retreat.
The Tathāgata now wishes to manifest and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas.

Within the subsequent section on the Buddha’s permission, he first designates the wisdom of the fruit. As for the wisdom of the fruit, it is the knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata’s original ground; it is knowledge and vision.
It is the wondrous fruit.
It is the power of the sovereign spiritual transformations of all Buddhas; the power of the lion’s majestic display of all Buddhas;
the power of the fierce and great might of all Buddhas.

Next, regarding the opening of the teachings that transform beings across the three periods of time: this refers to their proclamation and manifestation. "Mastery of supernatural powers" refers to benefiting sentient beings in the past.
"The Lion’s Vigorous Stride" refers to the places reached by his manifested bodies throughout the ten directions in the present. Alternatively, it is said:
The manner of the "Vigorous Advance" (*vaiśāradya*) represents the sign of the future, permanent benefit for sentient beings. "Great Power and Fierce Majesty" refers to the future benefit of beings.
Alternatively, this may be taken as the present shaking of the ten directions, functioning according to the intentions of people;
however, it is best to rely on the sequential order of the text. Furthermore, I privately maintain that the "sovereignty of the Tathāgata" is [the state of] the self.

It is also the joy of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). It is the purity resulting from the lion’s vigorous exertion (*siṃhavikrīḍita*) that removes all defilements. Its great power and majesty bring benefit to sentient beings in the future;
this is the eternal (*nitya*). These points constitute the meaning of the four virtues (*guṇa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
These stanzas contain both admonitions and permissions:
"You should be diligent and single-minded; I wish to speak of this matter, so do not harbor any doubt or regret."
The first three lines of the verse praise the three admonitions.
"The Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable" is the first line,
which praises the fruit of wisdom as indicated at the beginning of the intermediate section.
Now you must exert the power of faith and abide in the goodness of patience. The Dharma never heard before shall now all be heard by you.
I now comfort you: do not harbor doubt or fear. The Buddha’s words are never untrue; his wisdom is immeasurable.
The supreme dharma attained is profound and difficult to discern; this I shall now explain—listen with a single mind.

Regarding the three verses on the "three times" that follow, although the preceding section on the "lion’s sport" (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*) and so forth clarifies the three times, the text itself does not contain the expression "three times";
it is simply by the force of the meaning that they correspond to the three times. These present verses are likewise direct [in their application].

This is explained by means of one and a half verses beginning with "Because the Buddha has no speech that is not true. Since his words are not false, it must be known that his benefit across the three periods of time is likewise real and true.
△ From here, starting with "At that time, the World-Honored One... and extending to the end of the *Juryō-hon* (Life Span Chapter), is the second section:

the formal exposition of the Original Gate (*Honmon*). This section is divided into three parts. First, from this point until the end of the *Juryō-hon*, there is the formal opening of the near [teaching] to reveal the far [reality]. Second...

At the beginning of the "Chapter on Analysis," there is a general bestowal of the prediction of the Dharma-body. Maitreya then provides a general summary of his understanding. This section consists of two parts:

first, a brief opening that reveals the distant by means of the near, which stirs attachments and gives rise to doubt; second, an extensive opening that reveals the distant by means of the near, which cuts off delusions and engenders faith.
The brief opening further consists of two parts: first, the brief opening itself; second, a further request due to doubt. Regarding the brief opening, there are both prose and verse.
Verse: Herein, only two questions are answered; the question regarding the causes and conditions for their accumulation is not answered.
Because it is not answered, [Maitreya] requests it again.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "I shall now, before this great assembly, proclaim..."
I tell you, Ajita: these great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable,
who have surged forth from the earth— those whom you have never seen before— I,
after attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this Sahā world, have taught, guided, and disciplined these bodhisattvas.
He caused their minds to resolve upon the path.
First, he answered the fourth question as to who their teacher was:
"These bodhisattvas all dwell in the space beneath this Sahā world."

Next, the answer to the first question, "From where have you come? regarding those who dwell in the lower space of the atmosphere: the *Śāstra* clarifies that this refers to the *Aghaniṣṭha-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Ultimate Limit), which is precisely the lower space.
This should be explained according to the Four Teachings. Furthermore, "existence" (*yu*) refers to the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*).

"Limit" (*di*) refers to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naiva-saṃjñā-nāsaṃjñāyatana*). It is called the "limit" because it is profound and supreme. Moreover, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception is the limit of the tainted (*sāsrava*). Furthermore...
"Existence" (*yu*) refers to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). "Bottom" (*di*) refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); because it is empty and quiescent, it is the bottom. This is the general meaning.

Furthermore, "existence" refers to the two extremes of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). "Bottom" refers to the fulfillment of ultimate knowledge; thus it is the bottom. This is the bottom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

This refers to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*). In the present sutra, the "bottom" is taken to be the space below; it is neither the upper realm nor the lower realm, but represents the Middle Way as the foundation.

This is the method of "opening the near to reveal the far. In the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*), the Middle Way itself is taken as the foundation. This is the interpretation according to the commentary.

△ Regarding the passage "In all the various scriptures," etc., this is the explanation. The Master knew that his disciple was fully endowed with the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and the severance of afflictions (*prahāṇa*). First...
This is the simultaneous cultivation of wisdom and abandonment; it is followed by the simultaneous realization of wisdom and abandonment.
Regarding the various sūtras, one should read and recite them until they are mastered, contemplate and analyze them, and maintain right mindfulness.

First, the simultaneous cultivation of wisdom and abandonment is explained by way of distinction in the sūtras: right mindfulness is the cultivation of the virtue of wisdom; right recollection (*samyak-smṛti*) is the cultivation of the virtue of abandonment.
Ajita, these sons of good family do not delight in being among the multitude and speaking much; they always delight in solitude.
Abiding therein, he practices with diligent vigor without ever resting.

Next, the dual realization of wisdom and abandonment is explained: not delighting in being among the multitude is the realization of abandonment; practicing with diligent vigor is the realization of wisdom.

Nor do they dwell relying upon gods or humans; they always delight in profound wisdom that is free from obstruction, and they also constantly delight in the teachings of all Buddhas, seeking unsurpassed insight with single-minded diligence.
The second part answers the question regarding the place of dwelling. "Human and celestial" refers to the two extremes; [the Bodhisattva] dwells in neither and clings to neither.
"Profound wisdom that is unimpeded" means relying on inconceivable wisdom (*acintya-jñāna*). "Delighting in the Buddha-dharma" means delighting in the inconceivable realm.
Since both the realm and the wisdom are exceedingly subtle, they are not within the reach of Bodhisattvas of limited practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
The verses consist of eight and a half lines; the first five and a half lines are in verse-form answers to two questions, while the subsequent three lines provide a dual explanation.
Ajita, you should know that these great bodhisattvas, who have practiced the Buddha’s wisdom for incalculable kalpas, have all been transformed by me;
I have caused them to resolve upon the mind of the Great Way. These are my sons, who rely upon this world.
They constantly practice the dhūta austerities and take delight in secluded places. Having abandoned the clamor of the great assembly, they do not enjoy much speaking.
Such sons as these study my Way and Dharma; day and night they are always diligent for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
The first four lines answer regarding the master and disciple residing in the space below the Sahā world;
the first half-line specifically answers the location.
With the power of resolve and mindfulness firm and steadfast, they constantly and diligently seek wisdom. They preach various sublime dharmas, their minds free from all fear.
The next line praises the virtues of the bodhisattvas.
At the city of Gayā, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, I attained supreme perfect enlightenment and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma;
it was then that I taught and transformed them, causing them to first resolve upon the path. Now they all abide in non-retrogression and shall all attain Buddhahood.
I now speak these words of truth; you all should believe them with one mind.
The first two and a half verses explain the teacher and his disciples:
"From long ago, I have been teaching and transforming this assembly."

Next, the half-verse explains the location. Although the Sūtra does not mention "location," but rather speaks of "teaching for a long duration," the preceding direct answer has already concluded the discussion of location;
therefore, it explains location solely by means of time. Regarding the distant past, in what location was he taught?
He taught them so that they might enter reality—namely, emptiness. One should thus resolve the two questions in the Sūtra text.
The meaning of the double explanation: the preceding verse-text concludes the brief opening of the "Proximity" (Upāya) chapter. △ From the passage beginning with "At that time, Maitreya...
onwards, there is a prose section followed by verses. The prose section is divided into two parts: first, the doubt; second, the request.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and countless other bodhisattvas felt doubt and wonder at this unprecedented occurrence.

They thought to themselves: "How is it that in such a short interval, the World-Honored One has taught and transformed such immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable numbers of great bodhisattvas, causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

"Bodhi. Having heard that he first taught them beneath the Bodhi tree and that they now all abide in the stage of non-retrogression, and further hearing that I have been teaching these multitudes since time immemorial—upon hearing these two accounts, their attachments were shaken and doubt arose. △ [They] said:

The Buddha descends. As below. First, the raising of doubts; second, the request for an answer. The first, the raising of doubts, is divided into two parts: first, the teaching (dharma); second, the analogy.
The teaching is further divided into three sections.

He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata was still a prince, he departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
From that time until now, barely more than forty years have passed. World-Honored One, how is it that within this short span of time you have performed such great deeds of a Buddha?"
By the power of the Buddha and through the Buddha’s merit, he teaches and transforms such an immeasurable assembly of great bodhisattvas,
so that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At first, they suspected that his attainment of enlightenment was recent, yet those he had transformed were so numerous that they clung to the idea of its proximity while doubting its distance.
"World-Honored One, if someone were to spend thousands of millions of billions of kalpas counting this great assembly of bodhisattvas, they could not exhaustively enumerate them."

They have not reached its limit. For a long time past, these beings have planted roots of goodness under immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, accomplished the path of a bodhisattva, and constantly cultivated pure conduct.
Secondly, because those to be converted are numerous, and their stages of practice are profound and subtle, they hold that which is distant to be near while doubting that which is close. Question:
Since Maitreya neither knows their number nor recognizes a single individual among them, how can he know that [certain beings] have long planted roots of goodness? Answer:

It is precisely because Maitreya does not know or recognize them—and because the Buddha has praised them—that it is known. Their virtues and deeds in their place of dwelling are both many and profound.
"Could this be a transformation manifested by one who has recently attained Buddhahood?
World-Honored One, such a matter is difficult for the world to believe.

This is the third request for clarification. The sutra merely cites what is difficult to believe; it uses a metaphorical object to illustrate disbelief, thereby rejecting and refuting [the opponent's position].
The Buddha must certainly have given an answer.

When object and wisdom are in union, there is cause and fruit. To illuminate the object without yet exhausting it is called the cause; to exhaust the source is [the fruit].
The fruit is the accomplishment of the meaning of awakening to the path; that is, one comes to achieve perfect awakening by riding the path of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-mārga*).

This Tathāgata of the true body (*dharmakāya*) uses the wisdom of reality as it is to ride the path of reality as it is and manifest birth within the three realms of existence (*trabhava*) to demonstrate the achievement of perfect awakening—this is the Tathāgata of the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because one understands according to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and speaks according to the characteristics of phenomena, one is called a Tathāgata.

It is 'thus' because it pervades all places without variation; it is 'come' (*āgata*) because it arrives without moving. Pointing to this is what is meant by the Dharmakāya Tathāgata."

The three bodies (trikāya) realized at the site of awakening under the Bodhi tree and throughout the intermediate stages are all termed "traces" (*ji*).

Taking the three bodies attained at the original site of the Way in the past, they are termed the "source" (*ben*). Therefore, this differs from other sutras. Without the source, there would be no way to manifest the traces;
without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the source. Although the source and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability. This is the Master Zhaolun’s [view].

The meaning of these words lies in the fundamental reality of the site of enlightenment (Vajrāsana). Furthermore, regarding the fundamental and manifested aspects of the site of enlightenment, there are many varieties.

For instance, one may take *nirvāṇa* as the fundamental, while the arising of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) from that truth as the manifested. Both the manifested and the fundamental are empty; both speech and thought are severed.
Therefore, it is one in its inconceivability. Alternatively, the conventional is taken as the fundamental essence, and the arising of responses from the conventional constitutes the traces.
These traces and their essence are so profound and vast that those on lower stages cannot describe or conceive their limits; thus, they are said to be one in their inconceivability.

Alternatively, the Middle Way is taken as the fundamental essence, and the arising of responses from the Middle constitutes the traces. Both these traces and their essence transcend the path of language and the sphere of mental activity.
Because the locus of cessation is extinguished, it is called the "Inconceivable One. Furthermore, these three are not three, nor are they one;

being neither three nor one constitutes the fundamental (hon), while being three and one constitutes the phenomenal manifestation (ji). All are beyond the path of language and where the movements of the mind cease—this is the Inconceivable One.
I do not yet know upon which fundamental and phenomenal manifestations the various masters point when they speak of the "Inconceivable One."
First: the four instances of the "Gathering of the Venerable One" (Shēxiè) now presented are all merely manifestations within the realm of the inconceivable.

The essential core of this ocean is the responsive wisdom of the *dharmatā*, which serves as its vital throat.

first, the exhortation to believe; second, the formal response. This includes both prose and verse. The prose section consists of two parts: the teaching (*dharma*) and the analogy (*upamā*). The teaching further has three sections.
Within the first [section], regarding the benefit of beings throughout the three periods of time, the first clarifies the benefit of beings in the past. First, it presents...
There are three [types of] attachment to what is near.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly: "O sons of good family, you should have faith and resolve in the true and sincere words of the Tathāgata.
He further addressed the great assembly: "You should have faith and resolve in the true and sincere [words] of the Tathāgata."
These words. Furthermore, he addressed the great assembly: "You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, with Maitreya at their head, joined their palms and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, we only pray that you will speak of it."
"We shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words. Having made this request three times, they further said, "We pray only that you will speak it;
we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words. At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas would not cease their triple entreaty, addressed them, saying, "Listen attentively."
First, to clarify the admonitions for faith: the Buddha’s intent is to admonish, and the assembly receives it as faith.

This text contains three admonitions, three requests, a repeated request, and a repeated admonition. In the Trace Gate (*jimen*), there are three requests and one admonition; here, there are four requests and four admonitions.

Altogether, before and after, there are five admonitions and seven requests. These are matters of extraordinary significance, treated with great earnestness and gravity. An admonition is sincerity and truthfulness.

This is thorough and real; it does not deceive things, and its words reach the truth. Previously, during the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*), he spoke according to the intentions of others and did not speak with sincere honesty.
Now, speaking according to his own intention, he reveals the essential; therefore, his words are called "sincere and true" (*satya*).
Since the Bodhisattva has received these sincere admonitions, he dares not harbor doubt; upon hearing them, he must take them in faith, receiving and accepting these sincere words.
This is the Tathāgata’s power of secret supernormal knowledge (*ṛddhi*).
This is that which emerges from the deluded dharmas. "Secret" (*guhya*) means that the one body is itself the three bodies; this is called "secret.

That the three bodies are themselves the one body is called "mystery" (*rahasya*). Furthermore, that which was not previously taught is called "secret. That which only the Buddha himself knows is called [mystery].
"Esoteric" refers to the power of spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*), which is the function of the three bodies (*trikāya*). "Spiritual" (*shen*) is the principle of natural immovability;
it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). "Penetration" (*tong*) is unobstructed, inconceivable wisdom; it is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). "Power" (*li*) is sovereign mastery in its functioning;
it is the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The Buddha possesses these three bodies equally throughout the three periods of time across all teachings.
It was kept secret and not transmitted. Therefore, one must further extensively synthesize the various flavors; having done so, one must again synthesize the provisional and the ultimate.
Only through such synthesis will the three bodies and supernatural powers of the Original Ground be revealed.

Regarding the two ways in which all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras are deluded: all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras believe that the Buddha has only now, at the Bodhi tree, attained these three bodies;
thus, they cling to what is near and doubt what is far. In this fundamental exposition, [this matter] is not further...
When referring to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), it is done only in contrast to the bodhisattvas.

Bodhisattvas are included within the three wholesome realms of existence—devas, humans, and asuras—whereas the other three evil destinies involve heavy karmic offenses, dull faculties, and meager wisdom; they do not know how to engage in such [bodhisattva] practices.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* simply states that the Mahāyāna excels over devas, humans, and asuras, and likewise does not mention the three miserable paths.
All of these refer to the present Śākyamuni Buddha, who departed from the palace of the Śākya clan and, not far from the city of Gayā,
sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Regarding the phrase "the three who emerge from what they were deluded by," there are three types of bodhisattvas: first, those from the lower direction; second, those from other directions; and third, those who have long resided [here].
Those from the lower direction are those originally transformed [by the Buddha]; therefore, they lack the notion of being attached to what is near.

As for those from other directions and those who have long resided, both possess two kinds: first, those who should be born as emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*) from the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), who previously attained [realization] in past lives.
Regarding those who have been born: some have already previously heard the revelation of the manifested traces and the manifestation of the fundamental source;

even if they have not yet heard it, when their retribution is exhausted and they receive the Dharma-nature body, they will naturally hear this discourse on the long duration [of the Buddha's life] within the stage of the Dharma-body. Therefore, Bodhisattvas should not give rise to the notion that [the Buddha] is merely manifesting what is near.
Second, there are those who have now for the first time attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), as well as those who have not yet attained it.
"All have this attachment" refers to what is near. △ "Good son, since I truly attained Buddhahood...
and so forth, is the second section, which clarifies the destruction of attachments and the removal of delusions to reveal the fundamental reality of long antiquity.

The exhortation regarding "truthful reality" in the preceding passage is precisely this. Within this section, there are two parts: first, revealing the distance; second, from "Since that time until now... onwards.
[This section] clarifies the appropriateness of benefiting sentient beings in the past. This initial part is further divided into two: first, an exposition of the Dharma to reveal the remote [past];
second, citing analogies for comparison.
"Furthermore, son of good family, since I truly attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas."
"Another kalpa.

This refers to the initial section within the "refutation of the near to reveal the far," which uses the Dharma-exposition to reveal the distant [past], thereby refuting attachments and dispelling delusions to manifest the primordial origin from long ago.
The exhortation regarding "truthful reality" in the preceding text is precisely this. It is the Dharma-exposition concerning the time since attaining Buddhahood.
It is exceedingly vast and remote. "Gaya" refers to what is near; by refuting the near, the remote is revealed. Briefly stated, there are ten meanings, as detailed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
This text specifically employs the method of refuting the near to reveal the remote. Refuting the near refers to emotional attachment; abandoning the near reveals the remote.
This is because it is sublated by the proximate teaching. △ Below follows the illustrative parable for comparative measurement, which is further divided into three parts.
For example, suppose there were five hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of trichiliocosms, and someone were to grind them into fine dust.
Suppose one were to pass beyond five hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas [of worlds] to the east...
"In the *Saṃghāṭa* world-system, he drops down a single mote of dust. Continuing thus toward the east until all these motes of dust are exhausted—sons of good family, what do you think?
Is it possible to conceive of, calculate, or know the number of those world-systems?"

The initial presentation of the analogy reveals the immense duration. While other sutras may clarify the number as being "unspeakable" (anabhilāpya) by using metaphors such as atoms of dust or sands of rivers, compared to this [present case], those are still few;
for even the realms directly beneath a single speck of dust are already unspeakable in number.
How much more so for that which is not even a point! How could it possibly be described? Even "lower dust" and "non-lower-dust realms" cannot be described;
how much less can "lower dust" and "non-lower-dust particles" be described? How much more so for that which exceeds this—how could it ever be described?

One should know that the measure of its lifespan cannot be known through description. As the commentator says: "The beginningless lifespan is obscure and has not yet been manifested. This is not... [the end of the fragment].
It must be so. Why? Because here the long duration of antiquity is explicitly clarified in order to refute the short duration of recent accomplishment at Gayā;
this is manifest and evident—how could it be obscure? Furthermore, as for the statement "which Buddha would not do so," that too is not the case.
Because their durations differ—being long or short—the Bodhisattvas, headed by Maitreya, all addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these worlds are immeasurable and boundless;
they cannot be known through calculation, nor can they be reached by the power of the mind. All Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, by means of their outflow-free [wisdom]..."
Even with wisdom, one cannot contemplate or know their limited number.
We who dwell on the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) do not reach the limit of such matters either, World-Honored One. Thus, these worlds are immeasurable and boundless.
In the second response, three individuals who do not know [this] are cited: namely, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Maitreya.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas: "O sons of good family, I shall now clearly declare this to you."
If all these worlds— both those where atoms are placed and those where they are not— were entirely reduced to dust, and if one were to count one kalpa for each atom,
the time since I attained Buddhahood would exceed even that by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

The third point concerns the harmonization of metaphors. The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*) states that according to Kumārajīva’s earlier translation, the four characters "a single speck of dust" and "a single kalpa" were absent.

However, the Qi dynasty eminent monk Tánfù, while reciting the sutra, was moved by a dream which said that one phrase was missing; he subsequently recovered it. This is as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:
"The number of drops in all the oceans of the world may be known, but there is no one who can know [the measure] of the Tathāgata..."
"Life span. This also clarifies future life span, not past life span. If one were to cite this as proof, it would be entirely irrelevant.
△ From "From here on" below, the suitability for benefiting sentient beings is clarified. This is further divided into three parts.
Since that time, I have constantly remained in this Sahā world, preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings;
I have also guided and benefited living beings in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya lands in other places.
