First, the place where he benefits sentient beings is clarified. Now, it is necessary to manifest this location; for the preceding analogies have been cited at great length, and one may ask: "Where has he resided for so long?
Therefore, it is said that he constantly performs buddha-work in this land as well as in other lands. Furthermore, regarding this Sahā world:

This is precisely the land where the original *saṃbhogakāya* resides; today it is the land where the *nirmāṇakāya* manifests. It does not depart from its original state, but only the times of past and present differ.
Those who perceive the burning see what is near; those who illuminate the fundamental reality reach the distant. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "My land is not destroyed."

I have always been on Vulture Peak; how could I ever leave Gayā? To seek eternal quiescence elsewhere is not outside the Land of Peaceful Light (Sukhāvatī). Apart from this, there is no separate Sahā world.
O sons of good family, during this interval, I spoke of Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others, and further said that he had entered [nirvāṇa].
Nirvana. Thus, all these are distinguished through skillful means.
Second, it clarifies the removal of doubts regarding the traces left behind. These doubts concern both cause and effect:

the causes were the various practices taught in the former teachings, and the "predictions" (vyākaraṇa) received at various stages constitute the doubt regarding the result. Now, this doubt is dispelled by pointing back to Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
This dispels doubts regarding the cause. Furthermore, to say that he entered nirvana dispels doubts regarding the result.
Such matters of cause and effect are not of a single strand; they are all my skillful means (*upāya*) and not literal teachings. Therefore, they are called "dispelling doubts.
Or, as some may say, it was taught through skillful means that Dīpaṃkara Buddha was my teacher, yet in reality, it was Śākyamuni who appeared [as him].
It is not that what has not arisen appears to arise, nor that what has not ceased appears to cease; therefore, it is further said that there is "nirvāṇa. Now, I say this is not so;
one should simply adopt the previous explanation. Why? At that time, when the conditions for Dīpaṃkara Buddha were ripe, he transformed himself into the form of a Buddha to teach him.
As for me, my conditions were not yet ripe, so I remained a bodhisattva and received a prediction from the Buddha. To receive a prediction is precisely the meaning of "fruit" (phala).
The practice of each practice is itself the cause; this suffices for the interpretation of the text.

As for the word "that" (其), it refers to the "that" of the transformative teachings given during the intermediate period, and does not refer to Dīpaṃkara. Furthermore, the benefitting of beings during that intermediate period consists of both material and vocal benefits.
If one says they encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, this refers to a material benefit. Moreover, as for the statement that he entered nirvāṇa:
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who assist in propagating his teachings bring immediate benefit through both voice and form.
If this is so, these dual benefits of form and voice both belong to the intermediate causes. Since there is the arising of form and voice, there must necessarily be death;
upon death, one enters nirvana, which is designated as the fruit. One cannot say it belongs to the intermediate stage. Why? Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: [text follows].
Prior to this, it had not yet been stated that he would attain Buddhahood; how, then, could there have been any doubt regarding the fruit of Buddhahood?
The previous interpretation—that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was a manifestation of myself—is also incorrect.

Since the sutras prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* did not discuss his having already attained Buddhahood in the past, what teaching could have said that Dīpaṃkara was a manifestation of myself, thereby dispelling such a doubt? △ Below follows the third section: The Benefit of Sentient Beings.
It is appropriate. Furthermore, there are two [points].

Sons of good family, if there are sentient beings who come to me, I observe with my Buddha-eye the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, such as faith and so forth, and deliver them according to what is appropriate for each.

The first section clarifies the response to resonance. "Those who come to my place" refers to the gradual and sudden capacities of sentient beings in past lives, who have silently struck the Dharma-body.
"Observing with the Buddha-eye" means that having long since attained Buddhahood, one uses the Buddha-eye to discern and illuminate.
There is no omission or error. He intends to give rise to two types of responses—both inferior and superior—to benefit [beings]. There are generally two powers of the excellent opportunity:
first, to elicit the flowery retribution of humans and devas; second, to elicit the fruit-retribution of the Buddha-way. If one views this with the Dharma-eye...
One observes and knows the myriad virtues; according to their gravity or lightness, each receives a provisional reward (*puṇya-phala*).

However, one cannot ultimately know that they will finally attain the fruit of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*). If one uses the Buddha-eye to perfectly illumine the myriad virtues, one knows their beginning and end.

This sutra consistently clarifies that the Buddha-eye observes and knows that sentient beings, through their myriad virtues, will ultimately attain Buddhahood; this is the emergence of the One Great Matter.
This is the correct intention of the world. Regarding the "faculties such as faith" (*śraddhādi-indriya*), these refer to the five faculties beginning with faith.

The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is the cause of realization (*vijñapti-hetu*), while the remaining faculties are the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*). These two types of wholesome faculties each possess degrees of sharpness and dullness, encompassing the capacities and conditions of both sudden and gradual approaches.

The sharp and dull capacities of the sudden approach correspond to the faculties of the Perfect (*yuan*) and Separate (*bie*) vehicles; the sharp and dull faculties of the gradual approach correspond to those of the Treasury (*zang*) and Penetrating (*tong*) vehicles.

Regarding the conditions of capacity (*ki-en*): furthermore, the faculties of the Hīnayāna are termed "dull," while those of the Mahāyāna are termed "sharp. Alternatively, the faculties of the Hīnayāna are termed "sharp," while those of the Human and Celestial Vehicles are termed "dull.
The sharpness or dullness of all the roots of goodness possessed by sentient beings within the ten dharma realms constitutes the capacity.

Evil dharmas are not included; it refers specifically to the roots of goodness that are not the two causes of the conditioned (*yu-in*) or the penetrating (*ryō-in*). The Tathāgata fully illumines the good capacities of the ten realms.

According to those who are to be saved, he manifests forms and sounds to provide them with benefit. △ Below, the second section correctly clarifies what is appropriate for responding through transformation.
This is divided into two parts: first, the benefit of form and sound; second, the joy derived from that benefit. Regarding the benefit of form, there are further two sections:
first, manifesting birth where there is no birth; second, manifesting extinction where there is no extinction.
In various places, he speaks of his own names as being different and his age as being greater or smaller;
yet from the beginning, it was not that he was born who now manifests birth. Regarding "speaking of his own names as being different": since the physical form has manifested, there are names;
one invokes the essence by means of the name. Because capacities have degrees of excellence or deficiency, and forms have superiority or inferiority, the names differ because the forms differ.

Regarding "the same": this refers to the difference in age; that is, the distinction between form. The victor is the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (Response Body), while the vanquished is the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (Transformation Body).
Regarding "different names": this refers to the manifested lifespans of the two Buddhas, which are either finite or infinite. Regarding "in every place": [this refers to...]
Discussed vertically, it refers to the causes and lands traversed throughout successive lifetimes. Discussed horizontally, it refers to the lands of the ten directions.
Although the names differ, even regarding vertical locations, there are differences in the names of the dharmas of birth;
for example, as when the present *nirmāṇakāya* is compared to past Buddhas such as Dīpaṃkara. Regarding horizontal lands as well, there are likewise [differences in] the dharmas of birth.

Names. Just as the present *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) differs from its emanations (*nirmāṇakāyas*), so too are there numerous different names for Śākyamuni listed among the ten titles in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, as explained in various sūtras, the Buddha has three bodies with differing names, and the dharmatā (dharma-body) they designate is distinct in each case;
some refer to it as Vairocana, some as Śākyamuni, and some as Lokeśvararāja. The Dharma...
The "Body-Buddha" (kāya-buddha), or what is termed the *tathatā* (suchness), the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), *prajñā*, the *Śūraṅgama*, and so forth, are all comparable.
These are different names for the manifestation of the Buddha’s Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*).

If one considers the manifestations of the bodies of the nine realms, their names are likewise diverse and are immeasurable and boundless, which can be understood through the power of the mind. Regarding the "greatness or smallness of age," this clarifies [the Buddha’s] lifespan.
Regarding the length of life, the manifested *nirmāṇakāya* that appears accordingly may be said to have a lifespan of twenty thousand years, as was the case during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha;

or it may be said to have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, as will be the case during the time of Maitreya Buddha. These accounts are transmitted alternately to clarify the relative scale of the [Buddhas]. Whether viewed vertically or horizontally, this can be understood.

As for the respective lifespans of the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas, they are fully detailed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). Alternatively, one may consider them in relation to the three bodies (*trikāya*) in comparison to one another.

Distinguishing between the Small and the Great: Alternatively, when the three bodies are each treated individually, they are all considered "small"; when explained collectively, they are termed "great.
This is analogous to the three dots [of the *i* vowel]. All of these manifest bodies and the length of their lifespans are merely in accordance with those to be saved.
Furthermore, he manifests by saying that he shall enter *nirvāṇa*.
Second, it clarifies that although there is no extinction, he manifests extinction. Regarding "manifesting by saying that he shall enter *nirvāṇa*":

for those who are to be delivered through final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*), he immediately manifests that final liberation, causing them to feel longing and reverence so that they may attain deliverance. This is the meaning.
This is currently within the section on analogies.
Furthermore, by means of various skillful means, he expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Second, this clarifies the benefit of sound. Regarding "by means of various skillful means, he expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma," this refers to manifest sound.
This is for the benefit [of others]. A small body and short lifespan refer to the teaching of gradual instruction; thus it is called "various skillful means.
A large body and long lifespan refer to the teaching of sudden instruction; thus it is called "expounding the subtle and wondrous Dharma."
It can cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy.
Second, they gain the joy of benefit. Although it begins gradually, it ultimately causes them to enter the Great [Vehicle]. Thus, it is said that all are made to attain joy.
This very state of joy is precisely the benefit obtained through transformative teaching. The Buddha, relying on the four *siddhāntas*, bestows both physical and vocal benefits.
Sentient beings thereby obtain these four advantages; they rejoice when [the teaching] accords with their capacities and are distressed when it does not.

The subsequent text states, "All is real and not false," which refers to this very meaning. Next, the explanation of benefiting beings in the present is divided into two parts. First, the response of the capacity (*indriya*).
Second is the response through transformation.

Good sons, when the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings and whose virtue is meager while their defilements are heavy, he first clarifies the resonance of their spiritual capacity (*mūka*).
This is the present manifestation of the Lion’s Vigorous Stride (*siṃhavikrīḍita*) for the benefit of beings; this samādhi possesses ten merits.
Virtue: First, discerning the faculties of others—whether they are mature or immature, pure or impure;

second, using the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma to teach those not yet liberated, causing them all to enter the Dharma and Vinaya; third, his great vows pervade the ten directions, and his voice is likewise:
whether as a single sound or as hundreds of thousands of millions of sounds, it pervades everywhere, universally teaching all beings.
1. Turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma four times; transforming sentient beings so that they all attain parinirvāṇa—others cannot turn this wheel, only the Buddha can. 2.
Being able to demonstrate leaving the household life, shaving the head, and upholding the pure precepts, while also enabling others to find joy therein.

3. Having a nature and conduct that accord with emptiness (*śūnyatā*). 4. Emitting light to manifest extinction; appearing to exist or to perish; manifesting the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), or remaining hidden.
The marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Eighth, subduing the four māras. Ninth, enabling others to enter the essential point and increasing their *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Tenth, being fully endowed with the roots of the ten wholesome paths of action, such as the three of body and four of speech. When the Tathāgata beholds them, it is the illumination of the Buddha-eye.
Those among all sentient beings who delight in minor teachings are the specific capacities (*indriya*) perceived [by him]. As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "The great assembly..."
Although [the teaching] is pure, others who delight in inferior dharmas may give rise to doubt and regret, leading to long-term decline and affliction.

Out of compassion for them, [the Buddha] remained silent. As the verse says: "Others have not practiced for long; their wisdom is not yet clear. They rely on consciousness rather than relying on wisdom."
Having heard this, they will give rise to anxiety and distress; fearing that they will fall into the evil realms, I do not speak [of it].
According to that sutra, there are no śrāvakas or followers of the two vehicles; it merely refers to those who have not long practiced as "persons who delight in the lesser Dharma.

The Master said: "Those who delight in the lesser Dharma are not people of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna); rather, it is because they delight in what is near [to them] that they are called 'lesser'. Now, it should be...
To explain this generally: those who crave the twenty-five realms of existence—namely, the capacities of humans and devas—who come to me, are said to "delight in the Lesser Dharma.
Those who crave the bliss of nirvana and seek their own liberation—the capacities of the two vehicles—who come to me, are likewise said to "delight in the Lesser Dharma.
Those who delight in gradual progression and take a circuitous path to the Buddha-way... [the capacities of the three vehicles]... are likewise said to "delight in the Lesser Dharma."

The bodhisattvas who come to me are also said to "delight in the lesser Dharma. Those of "meager virtue" have weak and inferior capacity in their application of the two virtues of the conditioned and the unconditioned;
as the text below says, "the sons are still young. Those with "heavy defilements" have not yet eliminated the afflictions of views and thought.

Question: Is it not the case that by manifesting birth where there is no actual birth, you fully employ both gradual and sudden transformations for those at the seven stages of the expedient means and so forth?

Regarding those who delight in the Lesser Dharma (*hīnayāna*): while the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] accords with the capacities of those who should delight in the Great Dharma, why is it that they are all collectively judged to delight in the Lesser Dharma?
Answer: Previously, I briefly indicated the meaning; now I shall explain it extensively. There are four points in total. First, regarding the past:

although they may have resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), they were unable to apply themselves with single-minded diligence. Because they were largely attached to base desires and failed to transcend the mundane world, they are termed "defiled" (*pāpa*).
Desire is a minor teaching (*hīna-dharma*). Second, regarding the present:

as when the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, although various devas and humans possessed great spiritual capacities (*mahā-yāna-śakti*), their minds were defiled by worldly pleasures and attached to false views; therefore, they are said to "delight in minor teachings.
These two meanings are identical in intent to the subsequent analogy of "rolling about on the ground. Third, regarding practice: although one does not delight in...
The base desires of the three realms are called "lesser teachings" (hīnayāna). Furthermore, delighting in the extinction of the three vehicles is also termed a "lesser teaching.

Although one does not delight in the proximate fruits of the three vehicles, yet delights in practicing the One Vehicle through gradual stages rather than being able to practice it universally and suddenly within a single mind, this is therefore called "delighting in the lesser.
These three points clarify the delight in lesser teachings from the perspective of the causal gate. Fourthly...

Regarding the gate of the fruit: they take pleasure in hearing about the minor [attainment] achieved through proximity—leaving the palace of the Śākyas and initially attaining bodhi—but do not desire to hear with joy the long-distant, great, and enduring Way;
thus it is said they "delight in the small. Such a narrow-mindedness is not something that begins only today.

If [beings] first delight in the Great [Vehicle], the Buddha does not speak of "initially attaining" [enlightenment]. Those who speak of "initially attaining" do so solely for the sake of those who delight in the Lesser Dharma.
△ Second, the present responsive manifestations, which also has two parts: first, manifesting birth where there is no birth; second, manifesting extinction where there is no extinction.
Manifesting birth also has two parts: first, manifesting birth; second, benefiting [others]. Manifesting birth also has two parts: first, manifesting...
There are two kinds of birth: manifest birth and non-birth. Manifest birth refers to the appearance of traces in birth; non-birth means that there was no original manifestation of birth.
For the sake of such people, I said: "I left home at a young age and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
For these beings, it is said that I have only now attained Bodhi. Previously, it was explained that two types of capacities—the sharp and the dull—come to evoke the Dharmakāya;

now, two corresponding manifestations—the superior and the inferior—are revealed. The inferior manifestation responds to those of dull faculties, while the superior manifestation responds to those of sharp faculties.

Both of these manifestations possess both the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*). Regarding the production of the two bodies of the inferior manifestation: through right wisdom, [the Buddha] takes conception in a womb.
Regarding his birth, he took seven steps; as described by Kātyāyanīputra, this continues until his return from six years of ascetic practice.

This is called the "birth of the physical body" (*janmakāya*). As for the "birth of the Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*), it refers to the complete severance of the fetters through the thirty-four moments of mind.
This refers to the attainment of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*). Regarding the birth of the superior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*):

as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other texts, [the Buddha] dwells within the womb of Māyā together with the various bodhisattvas, constantly preaching the Mahāyāna, and proceeding in each of the ten directions, taking seven steps in each.

This is called the birth of the response-body. Regarding the birth of the Dharma-body: at the site of the terrace of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), in the state of quiescence... the gold... [text continues].
Following the adamantine mind, ignorance is severed and exhausted, and one attains the wisdom corresponding to wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

This wisdom thoroughly illuminates the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the seeds of myriad virtues and all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) become perfectly bright and universally complete; this is called the birth of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). As for those who leave the household life:

the inferior response-body (*pratibhāsa-kāya*) leaves the house of the segmented existence (*bhavāgra-viccheda*), while the superior response-body leaves the house of the two deaths (*dvimaraṇa*). As for those who attain *bodhi*: the inferior response-body attains the four noble truths with effort (*sābhisamskāra*).

The untainted knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) that is thus produced is called *bodhi*. Furthermore, the supreme *saṃbhoga-kāya* illuminates the path of the three truths as one reality;
this is the *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all modes) which constitutes *bodhi*.

However, in truth, it has been for such a vast duration since I truly attained Buddhahood. It is only by means of skillful expedients that I have taught and transformed sentient beings, leading them to enter the Buddha-way, and thus I have made such a statement.
Next, it is clarified that the fundamental reality is non-arising; that is, it is not birth.
It is only humans, devas, and asuras who perceive these two kinds of arising dharmas and two bodies, claiming they have newly arisen.

This is not so. For I have long since attained these two bodies of the dharma of arising; the "birth" of today is not a real birth. Therefore it is said: "For such a vast duration, for such a vast duration."

The phrase "as above" refers to the previous analogy regarding long duration. From the words "but by means of skillful means" (*upāya*) downwards, it clarifies that since this is not a real birth, for what reason does he manifest birth?
It is for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and joy to those who follow the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle—those of meager virtue and heavy defilements—so that they may attain the Buddha-way.
Therefore, it is said: "He merely uses skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, making such a statement. This means that although there is no actual birth, he manifests birth.
Therefore, it is said that he speaks thus. Other sutras merely refute the arising and non-arising of the inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*);

they do not yet refute the arising and non-arising of the inferior response-dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This present sutra, however, correctly refutes the arising and non-arising of the superior response-dharma-body.
Why? Because I have truly been a Buddha for a duration as long as this. Thus, one knows that today [the distinction between] the inferior and the superior...
Both theories regarding the arising of the *dharmakāya* are refuted; therefore, its arising is non-arising. This stands in perpetual contrast to other sutras.

One should know that when these two positions are compared, one cannot equate the sandalwood pavilion with the sun-piercing essence, nor can one equate the perfect clarity of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) with the total exhaustion of both correct habits and residual tendencies. Furthermore, there is a difference between the ten directions and the seven steps.
Thus, the superior and inferior [capacities] are manifested. Therefore, one should know that in both cases there is no long-term accomplishment.
△ Below, secondly, it clarifies the benefits of the forms and sounds manifested in this life. First, it clarifies the forms and sounds; next, it clarifies their non-futility.
"Good sons, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of delivering and liberating sentient beings. He may speak of his own person or speak of the persons of others;
he may manifest his own person or manifest the persons of others; he may demonstrate his own affairs or demonstrate the affairs of others."
First, the benefits of form and sound are clarified: "speaking" refers to vocal teaching (*śabda-śāsana*), and "indicating" refers to formal regulations (*rūpa-vyavasthā*).

Form and sound do not transcend the categories of self and other. If one speaks of the *dharmakāya*, this is speaking of one's own body; if one speaks of the *nirmāṇakāya*, this is speaking of another's body.

Regarding the benefit of speech, saying "I encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha" is speaking of one's own body; saying "Dīpaṃkara was my teacher" is speaking of another's body. This indicates the correct [distinction].
"Retribution" refers to one's own affairs; "manifesting the dependent retribution" refers to the affairs of others. Speech that accords with the intentions of others describes the bodies of others;
speech that accords with one's own intentions describes one's own body. Manifesting both one's own and others' affairs is likewise of this nature.

△ Below, regarding all that is gone, it clarifies that [the teaching] is not empty. This further has two parts: first, the heading indicating it is not empty; second, the explanation of why it is not empty. First, the specific [heading].
According to the explanation that "sound is not in vain," both [form and sound] are explained as being not in vain.
All that is spoken is truly not in vain. Regarding the first point, "not in vain":
for those of both gradual and sudden capacities, receiving these two kinds of forms and sounds, the benefit is entirely not in vain. Above.
The Chapter on the Past clarifies that all [teachings] are joyful, appearing as benefits for the world. Now it is clarified that all are not in vain:
superior and inferior forms and sounds are adapted to two types of capacities, and by attaining the four *siddhāntas*, they are all not in vain.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that the four *siddhāntas* are all real: the worldly is real; the remedial and the person-directed are real. To speak with earnestness, these three...

This is real according to the world, yet this reality is empty. Within the conditions [of dependent origination], there are likewise three realities of the mundane world, while the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is empty.
If one considers this emptiness and reality through the two gates of the fundamental and the provisional, regarding the emptiness and reality of gradual and sudden benefits:
the practice of former expedient means has not yet attained the benefit of the true path; this is its emptiness as a cause. Clinging to the proximate provisional traces, one has not yet attained...

The benefit of the reality of the original ground is that it is empty of fruit. Now, by hearing the teaching of the Trace Gate, one enters the same true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and thereby attains the real benefit within the cause.
By hearing the teaching of the Origin Gate, one eliminates the attachment to the near and attains the real benefit of the long-distant ground of fruition.
Having now attained these two realities in contrast to the previous two emptinesses, this is explained according to the Perfect and Sudden [teaching].
Sentient beings, regarding the two gates of the trace and the source—one real and one illusory—attain the practice of the Middle Way; this is obtaining the real benefit within the cause.
Yet, by clinging to the proximate fruit, they are illusory with respect to the fruit. Now, hearing the teaching on the cause, they do not obtain any further separate benefit of reality;
yet hearing the teaching on the distant fruit, they immediately obtain the benefit of the real fruit. Previously, there was one [aspect] that was illusory.

Now that one reality has been attained, it is said that "all is real and not false. Question: Regarding the true mark (*dharmatā*) revealed by the Mahāyāna of the present and the past, must there not be a difference between those who realize it earlier and those who realize it later?
Answer: There is a distinction between the initial entry and the subsequent entry, even as far as the destruction of the grass hut.
Both penetrate the Middle Way; however, because there are gradual and sudden modes of entry, the two teachings are distinguished.

By analogy with the entry into the True Truth (*satyadharma*), those of dull faculties rely on the contemplation of the impermanence of analyzed phenomena (*prabheda-dharma-anityatā-vipaśyanā*), while those of sharp faculties employ the contemplation of the emptiness of the essence of phenomena (*tattva-dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); thus, the distinction between the *Hīnayāna* (Zàng) and *Mahāyāna* (Tōng) is made.

△ Second, a general explanation that benefiting sentient beings is not in vain. First, the benefit of form (*rūpa-anugraha*) is explained; subsequently, the benefit of speech (*vāk-anugraha*) is explained as being not in vain.
Herein, these six phrases reveal that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not separate from the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The dharma-body has no form, nor does it have arising or ceasing.
Yet, when sentient beings possess the capacity for arising and ceasing, they evoke the dharma-body through the power of the Tathāgata’s vows, such that the response [body] accords with them.
Arising and ceasing; the view of arising and ceasing originates from sentient beings. Therefore, the various phrases are clarified by way of the three realms.

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, that the illumination of principle is not in vain; second, from the phrase "following all sentient beings" onwards, it clarifies that responding to their capacities is not in vain.

The principles are realized in accordance with capacities; the establishment of teachings to transform sentient beings is certainly not in vain. However, "original" and "traced" (honji-suijaku) are explained by means of provisional events, as in the following explanation of "knowing and seeing as they truly are" (*yathābhūta-jñānadarśana*).
The *Śāstra* states: "When the Tathāgata knows and sees the characteristics of the triple world..."
This means that the realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of nirvāṇa; it is not separate from the realm of sentient beings because the tathāgatagarbha exists within them.
There is no such thing as saṃsāra and so forth, for the treatise states: "Because its meaning is eternally constant, pure, and unchanging.

Furthermore, there is no such thing as abiding in the world and so forth, for the treatise states: "The essence of the tathāgatagarbha-tathatā is neither identical to nor separate from the realm of sentient beings."
Therefore, regarding the "not real" and so forth, the treatise states: "Because one is free from the four kinds of characteristics, for those four kinds of characteristics are impermanent.

One should know that the intent of the treatise is that all phrases are complete. For this reason, each phrase states that [the Buddha-nature] is neither identical to nor separate from the realm of sentient beings.
Therefore, I shall now explain them all as the Middle Way of Perfectly Constant Buddha-nature; I do not interpret them otherwise.
Commentary: If one cannot yet perceive the reality within the teachings of the past, how much less can one perceive the revealed reality, let alone the reality of the distant past?
Therefore, it is necessary here to point to the fundamental wisdom that illuminates its object. Without perceiving this principle, one merely wastes the "Root" chapter in vain.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the three realms as they truly are. Therein is no birth-and-death, neither retreating nor emerging;
there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa. It is neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different.
He does not perceive the three realms as the three realms are perceived by those within them. Such matters the Tathāgata sees clearly, without error or delusion.
First, regarding the explanation that "illuminating the principle is not in vain," we first explain the first four lines of the sutra, from "the Tathāgata" up to "neither like nor different.
To know and see according to reality is precisely the wisdom of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), which illuminates the reality of the triple world (*tridhātu*).
Since reality is such, there are no causal marks of the triple world; how much more so when the Tathāgata perceives clearly—this should be called the *dharmadhātu*.

Why is it said only that the three realms (*tridhātu*) are equal? It is so that sentient beings may know that the places where [the Buddha] manifests his traces are none other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is eternally abiding; therefore, it is called "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*). There should be no two kinds of causes for the three realms.

To speak directly of the "three realms," that which is able to know and see them is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*); that which is known and seen is "suchness" (*tathatā*); suchness is precisely the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*).

As for the "object" (*viṣaya*), it does not transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*). Within that which is perceived, since both ordinary beings and sages are included, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are entirely real;
all other perceptions and cognitions, when compared to the Buddha's, are entirely empty.

Yet, because there is still a cause, and the Buddha perceives it as it truly is, it is said to be "without cause. Since there is no separate principle apart from the triple world, there is no such thing as birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). There is none.
There are two kinds of suffering of death: arising and accumulating is called "retrogression," while the manifestation of the fruit of impermanence is called "emergence.
This concludes the explanation of the first phrase. Furthermore, there is neither abiding in the world of saṃsāra nor entering the extinction of nirvāṇa;
since both of these are extinguished, it is said that "there is neither one who remains in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa. Moreover, where there is no saṃsāra, there is no duality.
The "fruit" refers to death. The "arising," "accumulation," and so forth, are simply the cause and effect of the two types of death.
Therefore, the five abodes of accumulation are called "receding," while the two fruits of death are called "emerging. This concludes the explanation of the second phrase.

It is not regarding the reality of extinction (*nirvāṇa*), nor is it regarding the unreality of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); thus it is said to be "neither real nor unreal. This explains [the third phrase].
This is the third phrase. It is not the differentiation of the mundane world, nor is it the *tathatā* (suchness) of the supramundane.
Therefore, it is said to be "neither like [the mundane] nor different [from the supramundane]. This concludes the explanation of the fourth phrase. These four clarify the Middle Way.
If one employs a double negation of the two extremes yet concludes by fixing upon a single extreme, such cases all belong to the provisional teachings; for example, "neither birth nor death."
The phrase "birth" is for the sake of generating; "this is birth" is for the sake of death. The phrase "death" is for the sake of retreating; "this is retreating" is for the sake of emerging.
The phrase "emerging" is for the sake of neither retreating nor emerging. The phrase "neither false nor real" is for the sake of the real;
"this is false" and "this is real" are for the sake of the false. All such instances as these are now rejected, extending even to the single, the double, and the complete.

The [opponent’s] position is also refuted by this; it serves merely to reveal the meaning of the Middle Way. Nevertheless, when these phrases are used as conclusions, each has its specific application:
thus, all views are concluded only as "existence," while the various propositions of the Two Vehicles are concluded only as "non-existence.

This "existence" and this "non-existence" merely constitute distinct conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*); they do not constitute a distinct Middle Way. Now, in order to clarify the Perfect Principle (*yuanli*), it is necessary...

Analyze this in detail. The Sūtra states that the Tathāgata knows and sees things as they truly are; if one were to explain this using the perspective of the Two Vehicles and so forth, one would incur the fault of disparaging the Buddha.
However, this concluding statement belongs exclusively to our own school (*ekagṛha*), which adjudicates all modes of phrasing across the various sūtras and śāstras.
To distinguish the different meanings, textual structures, and essential purports, the fifth phrase is explained as follows: "Not as the three realms are seen by those within the three realms.
"Not as" means not in the manner of the marks of the three realms as perceived by sentient beings within the two kinds of triple-world systems. "As" (如) means "the same as";

it indicates that this is not the same as how other people see the three realms, thereby describing the vision of the Buddha. The Buddha necessarily possesses both provisional and ultimate wisdom (*upāya-jñāna* and *paramārtha-jñāna*).
It is fully endowed. It must certainly not be the same as those two types of causes for the two extremes seen within the three realms.

One should know that the name "three realms" is pervasive; it extends both inside and outside the realms. If the name "three realms" is established for what is outside the realms, it is because the external is modeled upon the internal.
Since the Middle Way principle has not yet been fully exhausted, it is generally termed "view-delusion," which pervades the three realms. [This applies to] the land of transformation.
The superior and wondrous five sense-objects are called the "volition of the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-cetanā*); the inconceivable dharma-object is called the "volition of the upper realms.
The *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Pure Name) details their characteristics therein. To explain the sixth phrase: it refers to that which ranges from "thus" (*evam*) to "error" (*viparyāsa*).
Only the Buddha alone, as he truly and exhaustively illumines the reality of the three realms, possesses within himself the functioning of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
This is also speech according to one's own intention; it is also a discourse on matters concerning oneself. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no conceptual discrimination. This is an explanation based on actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). As for the Tathāgata’s skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), he knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world (*tridhātu*) according to their measure;
that is, he knows and perceives them as they truly are, in accordance with the perceptions of sentient beings within the triple world. There is no... [omission].
There are no two deaths, yet in accordance with the intentions of others, he manifests the bodies of two deaths and teaches that there are two deaths;
though there is neither falling back nor emerging, in accordance with the intentions of others, he speaks of falling back and emerging;

likewise, though there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has attained extinction, in accordance with the intentions of others, he manifests birth in the world and entry into nirvana, and says that there are those remaining in the world and those who have attained extinction—yet these are not real.
Yet he speaks of the reality of nirvāṇa; he speaks of the emptiness of the triple world without falsehood.
There is no distinction between the three periods of time, yet he speaks of there being distinctions; there is no suchness of ultimate truth, yet he speaks of there being suchness.

To view the triple world as identical to the triple world—all these are words spoken in accordance with the intentions of others, termed "speaking of the matters of another’s body to demonstrate the matters of another’s body."
This is precisely skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). The Tathāgata has realized both skillful and ultimate wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*) and clearly discerns the two truths (*satya-dvaya*).

Therefore, both his physical manifestations and verbal teachings benefit beings; all are real and not false. △ Below, the second section explains that [the teaching] accords with capacities and is not false. This also has two parts.
Because sentient beings possess various natures, various inclinations, various modes of conduct, and various conceptualizations and discriminations,
[the Buddha] first clarifies the responsive capacity of their faculties. Since the faculties of sentient beings vary in being sharp or dull, and differ in being gradual or sudden,

with diverse distinctions in their dispositions, inclinations, conduct, and wisdom, he taught [the distinction between] self and other in order to cause each to increase their respective roots of goodness.
The teaching does not rely on empty causes and conditions or mere metaphors. As for the gradual and sudden capacities of sentient beings, each possesses various types;

this must employ the *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta* (the standpoint established for the benefit of individuals). The *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta* is precisely intended to give rise to various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

These roots of goodness are still essentially dispositions (*gotra*); through the cultivation of desires, they become established as dispositions. Why, then, is it said here that disposition comes first and desire follows? The explanation states: because there exists the "original-day root" (*mūladina-gotra*).
Nature (*prakṛti*) is that which can give rise to the desires and pleasures of today.

Just as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) exist because of afflictions (*kleśa*), and further afflictions arise because of the five aggregates—neither preceding nor following one another—the nature of desire is likewise. One must first practice desire before it becomes one's nature.
As for desire, there are two types of capacities: gradual and sudden. If various desires and pleasures differ, this requires the use of worldly [means].
This refers to the *dhātu-siddhānta* (the standpoint of elements). As for "practice," it means initiating the practice of karma and cultivating various deeds according to one's inclinations;
this requires the use of the *pudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint of persons). Within such practice, there is often much attachment and craving, which leads to obstructions;

this requires the use of the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedies). That which is recollection and conceptualization is wisdom—that is, a semblance understanding—arising from the process of cultivation.
One is able to attain the arising of understanding; this is the skillful means (*upāya*). Yet it still does not accord with the principle of the path beyond words (*avācya-mārga*);

it remains a contemplation based on conceptual thought (*saṃjñā-vipaśyanā*). Sentient beings, whether gradualist or sudden, abide at the stage of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)—both external and internal—and possess various roots of goodness and aspirations.

One practices because of a desire for joy; through practice, one attains a conceptual understanding that accords with that [desire]. This must employ the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint).
According to the conceptual understanding attained, one further preaches the Dharma for them, whereby they immediately attain a clear awakening to the *paramārtha*.
Even when one desires to practice for the second stage (*bhūmi*) after having practiced for the first stage, one likewise conceptualizes the objects of the second stage.
This is precisely conceptualization. If one gives rise to true understanding on the second stage, this conceptualization and contemplation are eliminated;
the dharmas of speech cease, and only upon reaching Buddhahood does one finally achieve ultimate liberation from recollection and conceptualization, attaining eternal, quiescent illumination.
Desiring to cause various roots of goodness to arise, he employs various causes, conditions, parables, and modes of speech to teach the Dharma in manifold ways.
Next, he clarifies the application of transformation (*pariṇāmanā*): directly confronting the capacities of beings, he bestows benefit through his own and others' forms and voices.

Because he causes various roots of goodness to arise within the diverse faculties of gradual and sudden practitioners, he manifests various deeds involving his own and others' bodies, as well as various [manifestations] of himself and others.

Regarding the vocal teachings, there are various causes, conditions, and parables. When addressing those with gradual capacities, one employs the four gates within the Tripiṭaka, each containing various causes, conditions, and parables;
within each gate, there are further variations, such as those provided for the indolent.

For those who speak of the patience regarding suffering, and for those with the conceit of "I-am-ness," one speaks of the patience regarding impermanence and so forth. The four gates of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*) are likewise.

If addressing those of sudden capacity, as in the Distinct and Complete Teachings, there are also four gates for each, in various and manifold ways, such as the thirty-two bodhisattvas each speaking on entering the gate of non-duality, or the various types of practices and characteristics found within the *Avataṃsaka*.
For the sake of various capacities and dispositions, he employs numerous analogies and verbal expressions to preach the Dharma.
His performance of Buddha-activities has never been suspended for even a moment.
Third, the summary concluding that [the teachings] are not in vain: all the aforementioned forms, sounds, and voices—whether pertaining to oneself or others—cause sentient beings to...
This is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It is not for the sake of the minor matters of humans, devas, or the two vehicles; therefore, it is called the "Buddha-work performed.
If only a single person were to attain extinction while others did not, the Buddha-work performed would be rendered incomplete.
Such incompleteness would cause the multitude to fail to obtain true benefit. How could it then be said that all have attained reality and nothing is in vain? How so?
Indeed. It was previously said: "While sitting at the site of enlightenment, I did not obtain even a single dharma as real. The seven expedient means (*upāya*) are all not ultimate cessation;
the two types of *nirvāṇa* are but empty fists of expedient means, and thus one knows they are merely provisional and have not yet seen the universal reality.

If the seven provisional [teachings] had been bestowed in the past and one consequently could not enter the one reality, then one might say they were false. But since the false leads one out [to the real], there is no... [falsehood].
There are cases where something appears to be empty but is actually substantial; thus we know that what was previously empty has become substantial.

That all things are substantial and not empty, such that the Buddha’s work is never abandoned—this is precisely the meaning [of this passage]. △ Second, clarifying that there is no extinction yet extinction is manifested. This also has two parts.

First, clarifying that what appears to be extinction is not actually extinction; second, clarifying the benefits of manifesting extinction. The first section also has two parts: first, clarifying that the fundamental reality is not extinguished;
next, from the phrase "However, now," onwards, clarifying the proclamation of extinction within the provisional traces.
In this way, since my attainment of Buddhahood, a very long time has passed; my lifespan is immeasurable, spanning incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, as I abide eternally without extinction.
First, I clarify the permanence of the stage of fruition: because it is permanent, it does not perish. By means of these four characters, I manifest the great power and majesty of the future.
The Fierce One constantly dwells to benefit sentient beings.
O sons of good family, the lifespan I attained while originally practicing the bodhisattva path is still not exhausted even now; it is twice as long as the number mentioned above.
Second, citing the cause to illustrate the effect, it clarifies that even those who have long resided [in this world] are impermanent. Based on this, it is used to prove impermanence, stating:

"Those before [the Buddha] were more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, and those after him were twice that number; though they extended their lifespans through supernatural powers, they were nonetheless impermanent. This is a biased interpretation of the scriptural meaning.
This is a great error. One should know that the ancient masters, seeing the phrase "accomplished lifespan" (*siddha-āyus*) in the sutra, took it to mean "resultant lifespan.

They then pointed to the preceding passage regarding "exceeding the realm of dust" (*atikrānta-rajas-kalpa*), interpreting "exceeding the sands of the Ganges" as referring to what precedes those [kalpas], because the sands of the Ganges cannot serve as a sufficient analogy.
Thus, they employed "world-systems" (*lokadhātu*) as the analogy; this [lifespan] remains unexhausted even now, serving as the subsequent [measure].
Twice the aforementioned number. Furthermore, because ancient sages saw the expression "doubling again," they took it to be finite.

Moreover, not knowing that this was actually due to lifespan, they claimed it was due to supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), implying: "Although it has not yet been exhausted now, there must come a time when it is exhausted.

We say this is not so. The Sūtra cites the cause as an illustration of the result; the result is not a numerical quantity. As the Sūtra says: "That which is obtained through long-cultivated practice."
The lifespan is for incalculable kalpas; this is not a prolonging of life through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Why?

Because when the Buddha cultivated the perfect cause and ascended to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), he had already attained eternal life. Since eternal life is inexhaustible, it is already many times greater than the aforementioned number;
how much more so, then, is the fruition (*phala*)! Why then discard that which is illustrated by the fruition and insist only upon the illustrating cause? Even if this cause were already...

It is eternal; it is not impermanent. For example, the stipends of a crown prince cannot be exhausted even during his time as a prince, let alone once he has ascended to the highest position of honor—how could his stipends ever be exhausted?
The clear evidence lies right here; why must you distort the meaning and mislead future generations with such doubts?
However, at present, there is no actual parinirvāṇa, yet he proclaims that he shall attain parinirvāṇa.

Within the second trace (the nirmāṇakāya), he proclaims extinction; yet within all three bodies, there is the principle of proclaiming extinction despite not being extinguished. As it says in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
Phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; now they are not extinguished. This is the Dharma-body, which is non-extinguishable.

Furthermore, it is said that this is the meaning of "quiescent extinction" (nirvāṇa), which is the proclamation of extinction. Because phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, there is nothing that can be extinguished; this is the meaning of quiescent extinction.
As for the term "proclamation of extinction," this proclaims quiescent extinction; it is the extinction of arising, not the extinction of that which is already arisen. That is, arising...
Because this cessation is non-cessation, one should know that this cessation is called "non-cessation. The Dharma-body is eternally abiding; it is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished.

Now, when we speak of "quiescent extinction" (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), its meaning is actually to proclaim extinction. Why? If one has already fully realized [this truth], one does not proclaim "quiescent extinction";
it is for those who have not yet realized it that one proclaims "quiescent extinction. If one has realized quiescent extinction, one points back to birth itself.
If one refers exclusively to arising, there is no benefit for those who are indolent; therefore, one must proclaim "quiescence. If one says "illumination-quiescence," this is proclaiming cessation.
If one says "quiescence-illumination," this is proclaiming arising. Now, although the Dharma-body is neither arising nor ceasing, it nonetheless possesses arising and ceasing.
Because of the proclamation of cessation, wisdom arises and delusion ceases; this is explained in terms of phenomena and principle.
It is also relative. If the deluded mind clings, afflictions arise and wisdom perishes. If the understanding mind is untainted, wisdom arises and afflictions perish.
As for the mention of the "deluded mind" and so forth, it resembles the *sāmbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body).

The meaning here, however, is distinct. This section primarily clarifies that the delusions which are extinguished constitute the essence of the Dharma-body. That this essence possesses arising and ceasing is truly due to wisdom;

therefore, by relying on the manifesting agent (the capacity), the manifested object (the essence) is revealed. When delusions are extinguished and understanding arises, this is "impermanence-extinction.
If understanding arises and delusions are extinguished, this is "quiescent extinction. Both of these instances of arising and ceasing are predicated entirely upon the Dharma.
The nature is thus distinguished. Although both [wisdom and delusion] arise and perish, this is entirely based upon the principle of nature (*dharmatā*).

If the two conditions of delusion and awakening did not exist, one would not speak of these arising and perishing. As for the claim that the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) does not perish yet speaks of perishing: who possesses wisdom? Who possesses afflictions?
To say that wisdom can destroy [afflictions] is to take the fact that delusion and wisdom are fundamentally without arising or perishing as the basis for the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The body has no essence of arising or ceasing; this means that light and darkness do not exclude one another. This is the meaning of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) being imperishable.
Sentient beings, failing to understand this, hear it and immediately claim, "This is the Buddha," thereby giving rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, and no longer practicing the Way.
Therefore, it is further proclaimed that the Path is able to extinguish delusions. When afflictions exist, there is no wisdom; when wisdom exists, there are no afflictions.
Is it not the case, then, that wisdom can extinguish afflictions? Regarding the statement that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is not what is extinguished but rather proclaims extinction:

this must be the function of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). Since their essence is without extinction, how could their function have an end? This refers precisely to the *nirmāṇakāya*.
He does not pass into extinction; it is only for the sake of sentient beings. If they were to see the Buddha constantly, they would give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence;
therefore, he proclaims, "I shall attain parinirvāṇa this very night. The above concludes the explanation of the proclamation of extinction based on the three bodies (trikāya) being non-extinct.
Second, regarding the interpretation that the three bodies are eternally abiding and non-extinct: as for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), its essential nature is clearly non-extinct.

One does not look to other bodies; rather, regarding those other two bodies, one must look to the Dharma. If one considers the essence in relation to its function, the function would instead become subject to extinction.
This clarifies that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and does not perish. If the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) is said to be imperishable, it must be in reference to the Dharma-body.
Since the Dharma does not perish, the Reward-body likewise does not perish. According to principle, wisdom is able to destroy [delusion].

Whether [the wisdom] reaches [the afflictions] or does not reach them, whether it acts in conjunction with them or independently—when one investigates through such reasoning, there is no capacity for it to destroy [them].
This is the meaning that wisdom does not destroy delusions. Since when wisdom exists, there are no afflictions, it is precisely wisdom that can eliminate delusions;
thus, "wisdom" itself is not termed "destruction. This explains, in terms of phenomena, that the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) is eternally abiding and indestructible.

Furthermore, if it is said that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is imperishable, this must be understood in relation to the *dharmakāya* (truth body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). Since the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are eternally constant, their functional application (*prayoga*) is uninterrupted.
As long as sentient beings are not exhausted, there is no final extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). Now, this *nirmāṇakāya* does not cease its benefitting of beings;

this is precisely what is meant by "imperishability. Regarding the uninterruptedness of its functional application: because the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are all-pervasive, the essence of the response body is likewise pervasive. Thus, the capacity for response is spontaneously and freely present without limit.
The Dharma must always be thus. If it were otherwise, then even if one explained it as perfect and eternal, it would still be identical to arising and ceasing.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "if sentient beings are not exhausted, then there is no nirvana": at the time of nirvana, if birth has truly not yet been exhausted, what is the meaning of this?

One should counter-argue as follows: If it were the case that birth had not yet ceased, then there would be no nirvāṇa; therefore, the proclamation of nirvāṇa is intended to inspire the thought that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter because he does not arise again, rather than because his births have been exhausted.
Thus we know that the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is eternally present and does not perish—not only the dharma-body (dharmakāya).

If one fails to understand this, then even the dharma-body and the enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya) would perish; how could it be only the response-body? This is the eternal abiding of the response-body.

It is not extinguished. Third, regarding the clarification that the three bodies are neither born nor extinguished: if one speaks of the Dharma-body in terms of its own essence, it is neither born nor extinguished;
the Reward-body, having fully realized this, is incapable of birth or extinction; and the Response-body, in its continuity, is neither born nor extinguished.

The Dharma-body is as previously described; it is subject neither to arising nor to ceasing. As for the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), its wisdom is self-aware wisdom; there is nothing capable of extinguishing it.

Since wisdom belongs to the category of the "capable," and it is itself neither arising nor ceasing, how could it cause delusions to arise or cease? The Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is continuous, and therefore does not arise;
it is continuous, and therefore does not cease. Thus we know that, based on the Response-body, it is not the case that it proclaims cessation while being subject to extinction.
A single phrase of the text extensively elucidates that the three bodies (trikāya) are both subject to extinction and non-extinction, and neither arising nor ceasing.

If it were not so, then arising and ceasing would be fixed; how then could the three bodies be described as neither identical nor separate? If one grasps this meaning, it applies throughout the entire teaching of a lifetime;
upon hearing even a single utterance regarding extinction, one immediately understands the significance of all that is extinguished and non-extinguished. This is complete.

Regarding the extent of the body, there is the distinction between extinction and non-extinction. Only upon reaching the original ground does one realize that it is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished.
Only upon reaching the intermediate stage does one realize that today’s transformative teachings involve both extinction and non-extinction.

This is because all traces and teachings from the original ground to the intermediate stage today do not transcend the three bodies and the four propositions. △ From here on, the second section clarifies the manifestation of extinction.
Benefiting sentient beings is twofold: first, not entering extinction results in harm to sentient beings; second, if one were to proclaim entry into extinction, it would benefit all things.
The first [point] is also twofold: first, the harm resulting from not entering extinction; second, the detailed explanation thereof.

The Tathāgata employs these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings. Why is this? If the Buddha were to remain in the world for a long time, those of meager virtue would fail to plant roots of goodness;
being poor, lowly, and base, they would become greedily attached to the five desires and fall into the net of discursive thoughts and false views.
First, it clarifies that there is detriment in not attaining extinction. As for "detriment," it refers to those people who, as mentioned before, delight in inferior dharmas;
although they see the Buddha as ever-present, they do not plant roots of goodness. Being poor, lowly, and base, they do not give rise to the two kinds of goodness, and thus it is of no benefit.

Because their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are not severed, and the two evils are not abandoned, there is indeed detriment. They are greedily attached to the five desires and enter into discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Discursive thought...

This refers to the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). The five desires refer to the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). Because the defilements of sentient beings are thus heavy, it is necessary to proclaim extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
If extinction were not proclaimed, then the two evils would arise and not be extinguished, and the two virtues would be diminished and not arise.

If one relies on the four *siddhāntas*, manifesting extinction causes the two evils to cease and the two virtues to arise. For the purpose of extinguishing the two evils, the [teaching] is employed as an antidote.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) counteracts and extinguishes unarisen evil; the conventional (*loka*) counteracts and extinguishes arisen evil.
For the sake of people, the conventional gives rise to two kinds of goodness: it gives rise to unarisen goodness for people, and it brings about arisen goodness for people.

Furthermore, the conventional extinguishes arisen evil, while the counteractive [ultimate truth] extinguishes unarisen evil; this is like how the five aggregates of dhyāna extinguish the evils of the desire realm.

This refers to the arising of evil after the world has perished, the arising of good once a person is born, and the arising of the unconditioned good of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that has not yet arisen.
Since these are discussed in terms of the three bodies (*trikāya*) regarding what perishes and what does not perish, the responses of the four *siddhāntas* must also be deeply understood;
it is precisely for this reason that there have been many successive expositions.
If one perceives the Tathāgata as eternally present and imperishable, one will give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence,
and will be unable to conceive the thought that such a being is difficult to encounter, nor develop a heart of reverence.
Next, the reason why [the Buddha] does not perish despite being subject to decline is explained in detail by means of the three types of Buddhas, each being correctly demonstrated.
If one perceives the Buddha as being eternally present, one gives rise to a mind of arrogance and self-indulgence; thus, there is decline. Because one cannot generate reverence, there is no benefit.

Arrogance and self-indulgence increase the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); weariness and indolence give rise to the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). Furthermore, failing to conceive the thought that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter—[is detrimental].
One cannot give rise to the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*), nor can one give rise to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) due to a lack of reverence;

for this reason, it is appropriate that [the Buddha] manifest extinction. This is the general indication of the underlying cause. Below, the benefits and harms are further explained by way of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

As for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is fundamentally without the designation "nirvāṇa. For those with overweening pride who reckon that [the Buddha's] nature is no different from [that of ordinary beings], [it is taught otherwise].
It refers to the suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of Maitreya—this single suchness is non-dual suchness; this equality is itself the truth.

Based on this, pride and arrogance arise in their hearts, leading them to claim that all afflictions are fundamentally unarisen and now likewise non-extinguished, so what need is there to cultivate the path?
They then indulge in self-indulgence and negligence, proclaiming that this is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. This refers to...
This explains the reason for the manifestation of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Next, regarding the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*):

those who are conceited, upon hearing that all sentient beings are the very mark of Bodhi, and that the mark of Bodhi is the very mark of afflictions (*kleśa*), and that light and darkness do not exclude one another to manifest the Buddha’s Bodhi—when sentient beings hear this, they again give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, no longer cultivating goodness, becoming indolent and lax.
Yi: For the sake of those such as these, it is proclaimed that the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* can extinguish afflictions;

yet the power of ignorance is so great that it can only be extinguished by the *bodhi*-wisdom of a Buddha. One should know that the former refers to those who are conceited and claim for themselves [the status of] a Tathāgata, while this refers to those who claim for themselves [the possession of] wisdom.
These two are both cases of conceit regarding the Mahāyāna. Nevertheless, there is no lack of difference in the degree of shallowness and depth between these two forms of conceit.
That which is called "identical" (ji) refers to one who has become a person of great shamelessness. That which is called "wisdom" (zhi) means that by means of it, wisdom must illuminate delusion.

Due to these two forms of overweening pride, because of a lack of understanding, one does not comprehend what is meant by "identical. Generally speaking, the term "identical" is used to manifest separation.
Just as ice is not separate from water, it is logically necessary to melt the ice; only when the meaning of "separation" is established can "identity" (*ji*) be revealed.

Furthermore, the mention of "separation" is for the purpose of establishing "identity. If there were no separation, sentient beings would already be Buddhas—what need would there be to cultivate the Path?

Because they do not recognize the aspect of separation, one speaks directly of "identity"; therefore, it is necessary to proclaim the extinction [of delusion], for even the single grade of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is still merely the Buddha-wisdom.

How could one, based on the common ground of ordinary beings, claim that this is precisely it? I say: Those who study and investigate this commentary should examine it again and scrutinize it once more to reach a profound accord with the Buddha’s intent.
This exposition clarifies why the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is not extinguished, even though there are instances where it appears to diminish.

That the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is not extinguished yet manifests as if extinguished is easy to understand, as explained previously. This passage generally explains the [nature of] the three bodies (*trikāya*).
This concludes [the section on the Dharmakāya]. Third, regarding the specific exposition of the Sambhogakāya, explaining the source of its benefit:

if one proclaims that "the Dharma is fundamentally unborn and even now does not perish," yet insists that one must first extinguish delusions before attaining quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), this is a case of using the Dharmakāya to clarify the necessity of wisdom.
As the Sūtra asks: "If wisdom does not extinguish afflictions, what is the proof? The answer is: it is evident that when there is light, there is no darkness. This serves as the verification.
One knows that darkness is ignorance; therefore, one uses wisdom to sever the darkness of afflictions. You now possess afflictions in abundance—how could you possibly possess wisdom?
One should know that wisdom is able to extinguish obstructing delusions.

When sentient beings hear this proclamation of extinction, they conceive the thought that the Three Buddhas are difficult to encounter, and they give rise to a mind of reverence. The above concludes the explanation on how non-extinction is detrimental.
△ Second, the explanation that the proclamation of extinction is beneficial, in two parts. First, praising the difficulty of encountering a Buddha; second, explaining that difficulty.
Therefore, the Tathāgata spoke by means of skillful expedients: "Bhikṣus, you should know that the appearance of Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter."

First, to clarify that [the Buddhas] are difficult to encounter: it is difficult to encounter all three Buddhas. Sentient beings delight in and are attached to the Lesser Dharma, and their hindrances of views and afflictions are heavy;
thus, upon hearing that the Three Bodies are imperishable, they do not cultivate the Way, making it difficult to achieve a harmonious meeting.
Why is this? Because those of little merit may, after the passing of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, either behold a Buddha or not behold one.
For this reason, I say to the bhikṣus: "The Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.
When these sentient beings hear such words, they will certainly conceive the thought that he is hard to meet, and their hearts will be filled with longing.
They yearn for and thirst for the Buddha, thereby planting roots of goodness. For this reason, although the Tathāgata does not truly pass away, he speaks of "extinction" (parinirvāṇa).

Next, [the text] explains the difficulty of encountering him. If one were to see three Buddhas, that person would have much merit and little evil; such a person would not [be subject to the aforementioned suffering].

He proclaims the cessation [of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa]. Those who see the Buddha as always dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa do so because their obstacles are light and their roots of goodness are heavy.

As for those who do not see the Buddha, their obstacles are heavy and their roots of goodness are light; for them, he explains that the three bodies (trikāya) are difficult to realize. Upon hearing this, sentient beings think:
"Although the three Buddhas are neither born nor extinguished, one must necessarily give rise to goodness and extinguish delusions before one can realize and see them. This matter is not easy."
Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter. Regarding "those who harbor longing and yearn with thirst": this clarifies that his manifest extinction causes no loss.

To extinguish the afflictions of views and thoughts is called "no loss"; to plant roots of goodness is called "beneficial. The above constitutes the first section, which concludes the explanation of how he benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
The second major section below summarizes that the benefits of the three periods of time are not in vain. This is further divided into three parts.
Furthermore, noble son, such is the nature of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas:
when first clarifying how the Buddhas appear in the five turbidities, they must first speak of three and then of one; first the near and then the distant.
In order to deliver sentient beings,
it is next clarified that all [these teachings] are for the purpose of transforming sentient beings;
they are entirely real and not false.

The three knowledges (*vidyā*) are all free from falsehood. The above concludes the explanation by way of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*). Next follows the second part: the explanation by way of analogy (*aupamyadeśanā*).

This consists of the introduction of the analogies and their application. The introduction of the analogies is divided into two parts: 1. The analogy of the skilled physician treating his sons, which illustrates what is appropriate for the manifestations and transformations (*nirmāṇa*) throughout the three periods of time.

2. The analogy of the actual benefit derived from treating the sons, which illustrates that the benefiting of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is not in vain. The above [section] was not yet...

The preceding text was brief; this section contains it in full. It is divided into three parts: first, the analogy of the skilled physician’s departure, which illustrates the benefit of beings in the past;

second, the analogy of returning and departing again, which illustrates the responsive transformation in the present; third, the analogy of seeking and then returning home, which illustrates the responsive transformation in the future.
The text concerning the past is further divided into two: first, setting aside the near to reveal the distant; second, clarifying the responsive transformation in the past.

This concerns what is appropriate for transformation (*nirmāṇa*). For now, we shall merely use analogies for what is appropriate for responding to transformation. There are three such appropriatenesses: first, the location;

second, the clearing away of traces and doubts; and third, the actual response to transformation. For now, we shall only provide analogies for the response to transformation. Furthermore, this response to transformation has two aspects: first, the stimulus of the capacity (*indriya*);

and second, the actual response to transformation. We shall provide analogies for both. For example, "there being a skilled physician" surpasses the previous analogy by employing the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) to represent the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
"Contemplation" refers to the wisdom capable of responding [to sentient beings]. "From many sons" is a further analogy for the aforementioned:

"If there are sentient beings who come to me," which represents the capacity of the beings to be moved [by the teaching]. Regarding the suitability of the response and transformation, there are two aspects:

first, benefiting beings; second, clarifying joy. Here, we only take up the analogy for benefiting beings. Regarding the benefit of beings, there are again two parts: first, manifesting as what is not born; [and so forth].
First, arising; second, that which is not extinguished appearing as extinguished. Here, we shall merely use it as an analogy for appearing as extinguished.
It is like a skilled physician, wise and discerning, who is thoroughly practiced in prescriptions and medicines and is adept at curing all manner of ailments.
In the initial opening of the parables, the first—concerning the skilled physician treating his son—illustrates the benefit to sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.

Within this, the initial metaphor of the skilled physician at a distance illustrates the resonance between the capacity for benefit and the response [of the Buddha] in the past; specifically, it serves as a simile for that responsive capacity. As for the "skilled physician," there are ten types of physicians.

The first type treats illnesses such that the ailments increase without being alleviated, or even leads to death; this is a simile for the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) who hold views of nihilism (*śūnyadṛṣṭi*), acting according to their own whims.
When the mind practices evil, it teaches others to give rise to deviance, severs the roots of goodness, causes the Dharma-body to perish, and likewise brings the life of wisdom to death.

Second, there is the case of treating illness where there is neither increase nor decrease; this is like seeing an ascetic non-Buddhist who practices austerities such as throwing himself from cliffs or leaping into fire.

Though he practices good through these austerities, he does not attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and cannot sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*); thus, there is no benefit, yet there is also no harm. Furthermore, he is unable to sever them.
"Good; this is precisely 'no increase. Third, there is the treatment of illness that diminishes it without increasing it. However, when treated by worldly physicians, once cured, the disease returns;
this refers to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Fourth, there is the treatment of illness that can cause it to be cured such that it does not recur, yet the treatment is not universal; this refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*), who treat only one or two [categories of afflictions]."
