First, those who possess specific conditions are unable to treat all [sicknesses] universally. Second, although they can treat them universally, they lack skillful means in the application of treatment for pain;
the *Śāstra* calls this "clumsy pāramitā," which refers to the Bodhisattvas' broad and compassionate treatment via the six pāramitās.
Third, there is the wondrous art of treating illness which treats [sicknesses] where there is no pain or affliction, yet cannot treat those that are inevitable.
The person who dies is like a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) who realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);

however, they treat only those ordinary people (pṛthagjana) who have regressed from their practice, and do not treat the "burnt seed" (jiaozhong) practitioners of the Two Vehicles. Seventh, although one treats diseases that are difficult to cure, one does not treat all diseases at once;
this refers to the Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao). Eighth, one is able to treat all diseases at once, yet...
It cannot restore [the patient] to their original state; this refers to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) at the initial stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Ninth, it can universally treat all illnesses and also restore them to their original state, yet it cannot cause them to exceed their original state; this refers to the final stage of the Perfect Teaching.
Tenth, it treats all illnesses simultaneously, being able to restore them and furthermore cause them to exceed their original state.
This is the Tathāgata. The first three types of physicians are like the old physicians in the Great Sūtra who used milk medicine;
the latter seven are all guest physicians without skill, merely employing dharmas such as impermanence and suffering, which is like using bitter, pungent, or sour medicine.
When a skilled physician arrives from afar and causes [the patient] to take milk once again, he is the final, ultimate, and excellent physician. Excellent.

This is excellent. Internally, there are the three penetrations and the five eyes, which constitute the eight arts. One who skillfully masters the nature of medicine and treats effectively is one who externally recognizes the source of the illness and is thus able to employ the medicine.
"Wisdom" refers to the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, through which one deeply understands the two truths.

"Eloquence" refers to the five eyes that discern capacities, ensuring that the sudden and gradual teachings do not deviate from their proper application. As for the twelve divisions of the teaching, the text—

The principle is profoundly deep. It is like skillfully compounding prescriptions and medicines; relying on the four *siddhāntas*, it treats the illnesses of sentient beings, just as one who is adept at curing various ailments.
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* says: "He is a great physician, a king among physicians. Because he is a great physician, he is called a skilled healer."
That person has many children—perhaps ten, twenty, or even up to a hundred.
The second [part] clarifies the metaphor for the capacities of those to be converted: ten śrāvakas, twenty pratyekabuddhas, and a hundred bodhisattvas.
Regarding the "children of the Bodhisattva," there are generally three meanings of the term "seed": first, with respect to all sentient beings, they are all...
There are three kinds of Buddha-nature as the nature of virtue; these are the sons of the Buddha. Therefore it is said, "The sentient beings therein are all my children.
This text says, "there are many children," which, when reckoned according to the ten mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*), amounts to one hundred children.
The mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the direct cause of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the revealing cause of Buddha-nature.

The remaining nine [mental factors] support one another and belong to the conditional cause of Buddha-nature. When one number arises, the other nine numbers provide assistance; thus, they constitute a hundred.

These ten numbers, along with the mind-king, are the Buddha-sons of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*); they are neither good nor evil, yet they pervade both good and evil. Therefore, these ten numbers and the mind-king serve as...
This encompasses the mental factors (*caitta*). Therefore, the three causes of the nature-merit (*prakṛti-guṇa*) all belong to the true children of the Buddha.

Second, regarding those who became children of the Buddha through past connections, such as the sixteen princes: when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was being expounded again, those who heard the Dharma also gave rise to a slight understanding;

this immediately constituted the nature of the accomplishing cause (*niṣpatti-hetu*). Their former ability to practice constituted the nature of the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). The primary nature [is]...
Fundamentally, these three causes all belong to the category of "causes as conditions" (*pratyaya-hetu*). They provide the support and impetus for the realization of the single reality today;

therefore, the karmic connections established in the past serve as the causal condition for becoming a son of the Buddha. These are precisely the thirty children within the burning house. This refers to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*);

when a single faith arises, it already encompasses the remaining nine, thereby constituting the hundred faiths. Thus, one attains the status of a son of the Buddha through the establishment of these karmic connections.
They are sons. These three are the sons of the *nirvedhika-hetu* (the cause of penetration); that is, those who today hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, abide in true wisdom, and are certain:
"I shall surely become a Buddha. Having definitively realized the *śrāvaka-dharma*, they know it to be the king of all sūtras;

born from the Buddha’s own mouth and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-dharma, they are therefore called "true sons. These likewise possess the nature of the three causes, which are now manifested.

"Attainment" refers to seeing the Buddha-nature; both belong to the Buddha-sons as the "cause of attainment. Regarding the meaning of the "hundred sons," one again employs the number ten to enter into the ten wholesome dharmas.
The ten faiths enter into the first dwelling (bhūmi). Therefore, the direct cause (正因) pervades both the fundamental and the derivative.
This passage clarifies the three causes of the hundred sons. It does not take up the "cause as the factor of realization" (了因) and the "cause as the factor of production" (生因).

These two belong to the section below on "not losing the mind," where they are explained within the context of taking medicine. However, the three causes of cultivation and nature (*xiùxìng sānyīn*) are present in both the *Miaoxuan* and the *Zhiguan*;

it is only in this commentary that their textual characteristics are so clearly manifest. This is because one desires that the power of hearing the sutra in the past be great, and thus the three natures are bound together.
They serve as the direct cause (*hetu*), while the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the consummation (*pariniṣpatti*) each combine with them; thus, all are designated as "one.

Therefore, one should know that various texts speak of the conditions and consummation as being threefold each in terms of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), or discuss only the nature (*prakṛti*), which possesses all three from beginning to end—such as when it is said that the three paths, the three virtues, and the three Buddha-natures are identical.
This is explained in detail in the *Xiuxing-bu’er-men* (The Gate of the Non-duality of Cultivation and Nature). Only when these nine gates are combined is this [truth] fully realized.

The essential point is this: if one grasps this meaning, the skeletal framework of the practice and principle of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) will be naturally established; the skin, fur, and colors will then emerge from the various scriptures.
Thus, one should know that this sutra is the teaching that records the great outline, and it cannot be explained through the fine mesh of detailed categories.
If one grasps this meaning, then the doctrinal principles of our school can be understood as a whole. This is for those who wish to cultivate the gates of contemplation.

In the practice of cultivation, there are stages. Upon hearing various strange accounts, one’s mind remains composed; upon examining the various provisional scriptures, one grasps their intent without error.
One penetrates names and characteristics with clarity until doubt vanishes. The increase and decrease of dharmic categories, as well as their separation and conjunction, become evident.
By refuting other interpretations, one causes others to return to the Great Path, for these matters were absent from the three previous teachings.
On account of certain affairs, he traveled far away to another country.
This second simile illustrates the manifestation of parinirvāṇa within the past responsive transformations.
Subsequently, the sons drank a poisonous drug; when the drug took effect, they became delirious and rolled about upon the ground.
Among these good physicians, the second returns and then departs again. This is analogous to the present manifestation of the Buddha’s response to beings:
the first metaphor illustrates the mutual resonance between the superior faculties [of the Buddha] and the capacity [of the beings].

Seeing that sentient beings have meager virtue and heavy defilements, and that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa they take pleasure in and cling to the teachings of heterodox teachers within the triple world, it is said that they "drink the poisonous medicine of others"—that is, they wander and visit others.
The kingdom revolves through the various realms of existence and falls within the three worlds; thus it is said that they "wallow upon the ground.
At that time, their father returns home. Among his sons, some have drunk poison and lost their original minds, while others have not.
Seeing their father from afar, they were all filled with great joy; they prostrated themselves, knelt, and inquired after his well-being, saying, "We have returned safely and in peace.
We were foolish and mistakenly took poison; we pray that you will save and heal us, and grant us our lives once more."
This second parable does not concern birth or appearing to be born; it illustrates the benefit of manifesting physical form. It refers to my earlier departure from home and attainment of *sambodhi*.
In the preceding Dharma discourse, there was mention of having a physical form and voice, as well as the non-falsity of the benefits conferred.

Now, the statement that "the sons have drunk poison and departed" illustrates the aforementioned benefit of physical form. Believing and accepting the teachings of false teachers is called "drinking poison," which leads to the loss of one's mind.

This is because there is no arising of karmic resonance through either great or small capacities. Not losing one's mind means that there is an arising of karmic resonance through either great or small capacities.

Furthermore, "losing one's mind" refers to those who are greedily attached to the three realms and lose the roots of goodness of the Three Vehicles previously planted; it is for such people [that this is taught].

It is not that they extinguish what has not been extinguished; rather, it is the proclamation of extinction. One who does not lose their mind, though attached to the five desires, does not lose the roots of goodness of the Three Vehicles.

For such a person, it is not that they are born where they have not been born; for their goodness is strong and their evil is light, so upon seeing the Buddha, they are able to cultivate the Way and sever their fetters, like a child seeing his father, or a patient finding medicine and being cured. Even if one's goodness is light and their evil is heavy, upon seeing the Buddha...
They seek rescue and protection, yet do not cultivate the Way; they are like a child who sees his father and cries out for help, yet refuses to take the medicine.
For the sake of such a child, the father declares that he must die. Those who see from afar refer to the time when a Buddha appears in the world:

sentient beings likewise behold the form-body (*rūpakāya*), yet because they are obstructed by the five hindrances and the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they cannot personally receive the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); hence it is said they "see from afar."

Upon seeing or hearing of the Buddha’s appearance, there are always matters of joy and reverence; the manifestation of various sūtra texts, such as the invitation by Brahmā, are all instances of words seeking salvation.
Seeing his sons suffering in such a manner, the father, relying on various medical scriptures, sought out excellent medicinal herbs that were fully endowed with fine color, fragrance, and flavor;
he then ground, sifted, and compounded them together, giving them to his sons to take as medicine.
In this second analogy regarding the benefit of the sound, the first part illustrates the Buddha accepting an invitation to turn the wheel of Dharma.
"The scriptures" refers to the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). "Medicinal herbs" refers to the eighty thousand dharma-gates (*dharmamukha*) expounded by those teachings.

From the Buddha emerge the twelve divisions of scripture, and so forth, up to the emergence of *nirvāṇa*; this represents the gradual and sudden emergence of the medicinal herbs. It proceeds directly from the Buddha.

The twelve divisions emerge from it; this refers to the emergence of the medicinal herbs of sudden [teaching]. From the Buddha emerge the *sūtras*; this refers to the emergence of the medicinal herbs of gradual [teaching].
This follows the sequence of their arising: the five flavors all emerge from the Buddha. For now, setting aside the sudden, we shall speak according to the gradual.

One should know that the name "medicinal herb" is universal and its excellent meaning is not restricted; thus, even the sudden [teachings] are collectively termed "scriptures" (*jing*). There is no...
"Not [the objects of] sight, etc. Here, "form" (*rūpa*) is a metaphor for precepts (*śīla*); the precepts guard body and speech, and their characteristics gradually become manifest.

"Fragrance" is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the fragrance of its merit perfumes all things. "Flavor" is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*); it is able to attain the flavor of principle.

These—precepts, concentration, and wisdom—are precisely the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). By cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path, one can perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Furthermore, form is *pāramitā*.
If one clearly perceives the color of the dharma-nature (dharmatā), it is distinct and unimpeded. Fragrance is liberation, the virtue of severance that is free from stench;
flavor is the essential taste of the dharma-body (dharmakāya). These three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal; this is called the Secret Treasury (guhyagarbha).

By practicing according to the teaching, one attains entry into this treasury. Through the power of the samādhi of emptiness of the Three Vehicles, one is like [grain] being pounded; it is signless (animitta).
The *sieve* is like non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), and the *blend* is like each individual samādhi, which is endowed with morality, concentration, and wisdom.

Furthermore, the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is like pounding, the contemplation of the conventional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) is like sifting, and the contemplation of the middle way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*) is like blending. These three contemplations are each inseparable from morality, concentration, and wisdom.
To bestow this Dharma upon sentient beings of both gradual and sudden capacities and cause them to practice it is called "ingesting" it.
"This is a great and excellent medicine, fully endowed with color, fragrance, and fine flavor. You should take it;
it will swiftly eliminate suffering and affliction, so that you shall no longer have any further ailments. This is the first analogy, the gate of exhortation.
This is the parable of the admonition.
Among those sons, those who had not lost their minds saw that this excellent medicine was both fine in color and fragrance, and they immediately took it;
thus their illnesses were entirely eliminated and they were healed.
The two metaphors demonstrate that the benefit obtained is not in vain. There are two parts above: first, the non-falsity; second, the explanation of that non-falsity. Now it says:
"Among those sons, he whose mind was not lost recovered from his illness by taking the medicine. This immediately illustrates that what was stated above is entirely real and not false.
This explains the metaphor of "not being false" within the sutra. What has been discussed above is the metaphor for the manifested response (nirmāṇa) which is not a true birth.
The section on the present life concludes. △ Next follows the second analogy: "the non-extinction of what is presently extinguished.

This first part also has two sections. Regarding those who have lost their minds: when they see their father coming, although they joyfully greet him and seek treatment for their illness, when he gives them medicine, they refuse to take it.
Why is this? Because the toxic vapors have penetrated deeply and they have lost their original mind. In this regard—
These excellent medicinal herbs with fine scents he calls unpalatable. The father thought to himself: "This son is pitiable;
he has been struck by poison and his mind is completely inverted. Although he sees my joy and seeks a cure, he refuses to take such excellent medicine."
The initial manifestation of extinction is precisely because sentient beings lack merit; seeing the Buddha, they do not practice, which is equivalent to being unwilling to take medicine.
△ "I now," etc., correctly proclaims that [the Buddha] should die; it is not a proclamation of extinction when there is no actual extinction.
Within this, the clarification of senility is further divided into two parts.
"I shall now employ a skillful means to cause you to take this medicine.
At first, it is appropriate to depart from staying, just as staying at a high elevation may be harmful while descending is beneficial.
He then spoke these words: "You should know that I am now old and decrepit; the time of my death has arrived. This is an excellent and wholesome medicine."

"I remain here now; you may take this medicine. Do not worry that you will not recover. Having given these instructions, he went again to another country and sent a messenger back to announce: "Your father has already died."
The second proclamation, "He is to die," is a direct metaphor for the present cessation [of his life] and the impending end of his period of transformation.
"The time of death has arrived" means that he is about to enter *nirvāṇa*. Because he leaves behind the teaching, it is said: "This excellent medicine is now left here.
"Furthermore, going to another land" refers to manifesting cessation in this region while manifesting birth in another region. As stated in the preceding text: "I vow to remain..."

On the other hand, "seeing from afar while protecting" is precisely that meaning. Regarding the dispatching of messengers: one may take the great voice universally proclaiming within *nirvāṇa* as the messenger;
or one may employ supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), or relics (*śarīra*), or the teachings of the sūtras (*sūtra-śāsana*) and so forth as messengers.
Now, employing the four reliances (*catuḥ-pratisaraṇa*) Bodhisattvas, they speak to sentient beings, saying: "The Buddha has already entered *parinirvāṇa*; he has left behind only..."

"I now proclaim and propagate this Dharma; you should receive and practice it. In future times, if sentient beings lack the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) for the transmission of the sūtras and the Dharma, how could they possibly know for themselves?
Since the Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa, these four reliances are therefore the messengers.
"2. As for 'All the sons,' etc.: The awakening of all the sons is a metaphor for the benefits realized upon the manifestation of [the Buddha's] passing away. In the preceding text, there is..."
Two parts: first, clarifying loss and gain; second, explaining loss and gain. Here, we merely provide analogies for the attainment of benefit.

From the passage "In this life, one reflects upon being solitary and exposed" onwards, it clarifies the attainment of benefit after death, such as the case of those converted by Upagupta. This, too, has two parts.
At that time, the sons, hearing that their father had passed away, were filled with great sorrow and distress, and they thought to themselves:
"If our father were still alive, he would have compassion for us and been able to protect and save us; but now he has abandoned us and died far away in another land."
The first part clarifies the benefit of manifesting the cessation [of suffering].
Thinking to myself that I am solitary and exposed, with no one left to rely upon, I was constantly filled with sorrow and emotion; my mind then became awakened.
I realized that this medicine possessed a fine color, fragrance, and flavor, so I took it immediately, and my toxic illness was entirely cured.

The second clarifies the karmic resonance of future beings. This is truly because sentient beings, after the [Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa, awaken and practice the Way by taking up the medicine, thereby creating the causes and conditions that can evoke the manifestation of the responsive transformation [of the Buddha].
As the *Śāriputra-prakaraṇa* (Teaching Left Behind) says: "For those who have not yet been delivered, one creates the causes and conditions for their deliverance.

Furthermore, there are instances where one attains such a vision in the present. As the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* says: "Through diligent effort and reaching the limit of suffering, one attains..."
He beheld the emanations of Śākyamuni, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, the Buddha Bhadraśrī of the East, and the other World-Honored Ones of the seven Buddhas.
When his father heard that his son had fully recovered, he immediately returned home and allowed him to see them all.

This is the third clarification concerning the future benefit of sentient beings. As for the power of majestic ferocity: when the father heard that his son had recovered, it was an immediate response to his karmic resonance.
To cause all to witness this is precisely to initiate a responsive transformation for the future, whereby both form and voice shall provide dual benefit.
"Good sons, what do you think? Could anyone say that this good physician has committed a falsehood?
"No, World-Honored One.

This second treatment for the son is truly beneficial; it serves as a metaphor for how the [Buddha] benefits beings throughout the three periods of time without fail. The illustration is now concluded. △
The second part, the analogy, is divided into three sections.

The Buddha said: "I am also like this. Since I attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, nayutas, and asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed for the sake of sentient beings."
The first "combination" refers to the past, wherein he benefited sentient beings;
by the power of skillful means, he declared that he would enter parinirvāṇa.
The second "combination" refers to the present.
Furthermore, there is no one capable of rightfully accusing me of the fault of speaking falsely.
This third point confirms that benefiting sentient beings is not in vain.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The following verses consist of twenty-five and a half lines. They eulogize the preceding teachings on the Dharma and its analogies. The first nineteen and a half lines eulogize the discourse on the Dharma;
the subsequent five lines eulogize the discourse on the analogies. Regarding the discourse on the Dharma above, there were two parts; now, the eulogy likewise has two parts.

The first nineteen and a half lines eulogize the benefiting of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time; the final one line eulogizes that all is real and not false. The first four lines eulogize...
In past lives, he benefited sentient beings in three ways.
Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed is immeasurable—hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and asankhyeyas.
The first verse states: It has been long since he attained the Way;
constantly preaching the Dharma to transform and teach countless billions of sentient beings, leading them to enter the Buddha-way. This has continued for immeasurable kalpas.
The second [verse] concerns the single practice.

In the middle of the verse, it says that for the sake of benefiting beings and delivering sentient beings, he manifests nirvāṇa through skillful means, yet in reality he does not pass into extinction; he eternally abides here preaching the Dharma.
I always abide here. By means of various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), I cause sentient beings who are subject to delusion not to see me, even though I am near them.
These three verses concern the dwelling place for benefiting beings. △ Below, the second section consists of five lines; it concerns the present and is divided into two parts.
The multitude sees my parinirvāṇa and makes extensive offerings to my relics; all harbor longing and affection, giving rise to hearts of thirsty adoration.

Once sentient beings have gained faith and submission, their natures becoming upright and their minds supple, they desire with single-minded devotion to see the Buddha, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.
At that time, I and the assembly of monks together departed from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
The first two and a half lines of the verse concern how that which is not born appears to be born.
At that time, I spoke to sentient beings: "I am always here and do not perish; yet, through the power of skillful means, I manifest both death and non-death."
In other lands there are sentient beings who revere, believe in, and delight in [the Dharma]; for them as well, I further preach the unsurpassed Dharma.
You do not hear this, and thus you merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa.

The second section consists of two and a half lines; this verse praises the non-extinction of that which is currently extinguished. △ Below, the third section consists of ten and a half lines; this verse praises the aforementioned future.
The previous section merely alluded to the four characters "constantly abiding and not extinguished," whereas the present verse is extensive. The text is divided into four parts.
I see all sentient beings submerged in the ocean of suffering; therefore, I do not manifest my body before them to cause them to give rise to longing and veneration.
Because their hearts are filled with yearning and devotion, I then appear and preach the Dharma for them.
The first one and a half lines clarify the response to future capacities:
such is the power of his supernormal knowledges that he remains constantly on Vulture Peak and at other various dwelling places throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa, when it is consumed by a great conflagration, my land remains peaceful and secure, always filled with devas and humans.

Its gardens, groves, and various halls and pavilions are adorned with every kind of jewel; its jeweled trees abound with flowers and fruit, providing places of delight for all sentient beings to roam and enjoy.
The various devas beat celestial drums and constantly perform manifold musical entertainments. They rain down *māndārava* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
These two four-line verses praise the aforementioned eternal abiding and non-extinction; he eternally dwells on Vulture Peak Mountain. This is called the Land of True Retribution (*sambhoga-kāya*).
One must refer to the *parabhogakṣetra* (land of enjoyment for others). If one relies on the expression "always abiding," it belongs to the *svabhogakṣetra* (land of enjoyment for oneself).
As for "other various dwelling places," this refers to the *upāyaśeṣabhūmi* (land of remaining skillful means), which carries the meaning of a "remaining realm" above.
If one follows the verse’s mention of "jewel-adorned," then it is not the self-land (*svabhūmi*), but rather the other land (*parabhūmi*) from the original time, such as the [Padma]buddhakṣetra.
In the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, it is mostly explained as the *parasaṃbhoga-kāya* (body of enjoyment for others). Furthermore, this refers specifically to the *vipākakṣetra* (retribution land);

however, generally speaking, it extends everywhere throughout the ten directions, whether pure or impure. Regarding "humans and devas filling [the land]": the thirty stages of mind (*triṃśaccitta*) are humans, and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are devas.
Regarding "beating the celestial drum": this refers to the spontaneous preaching (*anunaya-vyākaraṇa*). Regarding "Mandārava flowers": these refer to the teaching of the *Bhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*.
This is the stage of the sages.
My Pure Land is never destroyed, yet the multitudes perceive it as being consumed by flames, filled everywhere with grief, fear, and various afflictions.
These sentient beings of sinful karma, due to the causes and conditions of their evil deeds, will pass through incalculable kalpas without hearing the names of the Triple Gem.
The third two lines clarify that there are no causes or conditions for not seeing [the Buddha].
All those who cultivate merit and are gentle, upright, and sincere shall all see my body here, preaching the Dharma.
At times, for the sake of this assembly, I speak of the Buddha’s lifespan as immeasurable; for those who see the Buddha only after a long time, I speak of how difficult it is to encounter a Buddha.
Such is my power of wisdom, and the light of my insight shines immeasurably; my life-span lasts for incalculable eons, attained through the practice cultivated over a long period.

The fourth section, consisting of three lines, clarifies the causes and conditions for attaining vision. "One who cultivates merit" refers to the fulfillment of both the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Tranquil and in accord with principle" refers to being gentle, supple, and upright. "Then all see my body" refers to the *sahōkai* (Real Reward Land).
"Sometimes for this assembly" refers to those at the first stage (*bhūmi*) or the first dwelling (*vihāra*). "Only after a long time do they see the Buddha" refers to...
"The five turbidities are heavy indeed; such is the power of my wisdom. This summarizes his great majesty.
"You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this; you should sever them so that they are forever exhausted. The Buddha’s words are true and not false."

The next single verse is not empty. The above concludes the verses on the Dharma-exposition (dharmadeśanā). △ The following five verses concern the parable-exposition (aupamyadeśanā), which is divided into two parts.
First, the initial single verse opens the parable, which is further divided into three sections.
Just as a skilled physician employs skillful means—
initially praising his past benefits to sentient beings,
and for the sake of curing his wayward son, saying he was truly dead when he was actually alive.
The next two lines praise the benefit of beings in the present;
"unable to speak falsely" praises the aforementioned lack of falsehood.
△ The second section below consists of four lines, praising the application of the analogy, which is divided into three parts.
I am also the Father of the World, rescuing all who suffer.
The first half-verse combines with the past to show the benefit [of my teaching]:

for the sake of ordinary people who are inverted, I speak of extinction when it truly exists, because they perceive me through the lens of eternalism and thus give rise to a mind of arrogance and indulgence.
Those who are heedless and attached to the five desires fall into the evil realms. I always know whether sentient beings practice the Path or do not practice it;
according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, I preach various Dharmas for them.
The second section consists of two and a half lines, which combine to describe the benefits in the present life:
"I constantly reflect upon this: by what means may I cause sentient beings to enter the unsurpassed path and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body?"
The third line of the verse combines the preceding metaphors. In the Trace Gate (*jimen*), the three are opened to reveal the One; in the Origin Gate (*benmen*), the near is opened to reveal the far.
In both cases, it is intended that sentient beings may swiftly enter the Buddha-way. This matter will certainly be attained; it is by no means in vain.
The combination of metaphors is hereby concluded.
The Seventeenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "Distinguishing Merits" (*Puṇyaparyāya-parivarta*).

This chapter contains the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), the comprehension of the teaching (*anujñāna*), and the propagation (*saṃprakāśana*). Because it distinguishes these attributes, starting from the beginning, it is called the "Chapter on Distinguishing.
Since the Buddha spoke of the span of his life (*āyuṣpramāṇa*), the disciples of the two periods obtained various benefits; therefore, it is said:

As their merits differ in degree—whether shallow or deep—they are said to be "distinguished. However, regarding the two periods: the emergence from the earth refers to the past, while Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa refers to the present.
This constitutes the second section on the bestowing of predictions within the *Honmon* (Original Teaching).

If one were to judge solely by the merit of hearing this sutra, these cases would merely belong to the "residual" category; yet, according to the words that they shall "attain [enlightenment] in the future," they are likewise granted predictions. Thus, the treatise analyzes this passage.

There is the power of the Dharma and the power of practice. Regarding the power of the Dharma, there are five aspects: first, realization; second, faith; third, making offerings—all as explained in the current text;

fourth, hearing the Dharma, as in the "Chapter on Rejoicing"; and fifth, reading, reciting, upholding, and explaining. Reading and reciting are as described in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master.
Upholding refers back to the three chapters of the "Dharma Master’s Chapter," the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices," and the "Chapter on Encouraging Upholding. Explaining [the Dharma]...
As for these, they are like the "Entrustment" chapter regarding the power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*). As for the power of practice: the power of conduct is like Bhaiṣajyarāja;
teaching and transforming others is like Gadgadasvara; protecting against difficulties is like Avalokiteśvara’s dhāraṇī; and manifesting merit is like King Susaṃskṛtarāja.

The "Dharmapāla" [chapter] is like the "Samantabhadra" chapter. Regarding the interpretation of this chapter by Guanzhi and the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra), their extensive citations are all inappropriate, as detailed in the commentary (*shu*).
Now, the Master [Zhiyi] adjudges that the *lun* considers the former [chapters] deep and the latter shallow, whereas Guanzhi considers the former shallow and the latter deep;

these two views contradict one another, so who in the world can judge between them? Furthermore, regarding the "patience with the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the sutras and treatises differ.
Kātyāyanīputra, the stage of the Bodhisattva who has attained non-retrogression through the accomplishment of the five dharmas is the level of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

Whether it be the wisdom or the abandonment of a *srotāpanna*, these constitute the stage common to the three vehicles (*triyāna*), which is the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
To attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) upon ascending to the first stage (*bhūmi*) refers to the distinct (*pratyeka*) bodhisattva position;

to attain the patience of non-arising upon ascending to the first dwelling (*vihāra*) refers to the perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) bodhisattva position. Both are explicit statements in the sacred teachings and must not be conflated.

Guangzhai’s [interpretation] is merely speculative and fails to grasp the scriptural text. Vasubandhu takes the first stage to be the patience of non-arising, relying exclusively on the specific meaning [of the *Pratyekabuddhabhūmi*]. Furthermore...

This is not found in the sutras. However, Guangzhai’s interpretation is not yet appropriate; one should not harbor doubt where there is faith. How could the Master of the Treatise, Vasubandhu, have composed it in vain?

It is merely feared that the translators may have interpreted it according to their own private sentiments—such as the division of consciousness into eight or nine in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, or the sixteen characters in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*—all of which depend on the discretion of the person involved.
What concern does this have with the holy intent [of the Buddha]? The explanatory notes are very extensive; they are not included here.
Detailed exposition: Now, the text is divided into three sections: first, the general introduction by the sūtra compiler; second, the Tathāgata’s formal analysis and bestowal of predictions;
and third, the offerings of the assembly at that time.
At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha’s teaching on the length of his lifespan, which was so vast and far-reaching;
immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings attained great benefit.

The initial passage is the general introduction by the scribe. However, regarding its detailed analysis: the Buddha’s words are perfect and subtle, and thus cannot be explained using provisional stages.

Therefore, while the preceding section presented the opening, showing, awakening, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the present section on the "increase of the Way and decrease of birth" in the Essential Gate is explained entirely in terms of the perfect stages.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Ajita, when I spoke of the long duration of this Tathāgata’s lifespan,
six hundred and eighty million *koṭis* of *nayutas* of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."

One attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and enters the stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*). Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "In the first dwelling of the initial resolve, one resolve gives rise to all resolves;
one attains the Tathāgata’s single body that is infinite bodies, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body, which responds to all things with profound stillness.
This is precisely that meaning.
Furthermore, there are a thousandfold more bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attain the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining, and who,
having attained this dhāraṇī of hearing, enter the stage of the ten perfected practices.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition;
these had entered the tenth stage of the Perfect Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who attained hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of immeasurable *āvartana-dhāraṇīs*;
this marks their entry into the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world systems who were able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma;
these had entered the second stage of the Perfect [Teaching].
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in two thousand central lands, who were able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma;
these had entered the third stage of the Perfect [Grounds].
Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm,
who shall attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment after eight more births.
Regarding the "eight births" mentioned in this sutra, they collectively comprise four stages:
namely, entering the fourth stage in eight births, entering the fifth stage in seven births, entering the sixth stage in six births, and entering the seventh stage in five births.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in four sets of four continents who, through four more births,
shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
These four [types of beings] enter the eighth stage.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in three sets of four continents,
who shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after three births.
Those who have entered the nine stages over three lifetimes;
furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in two sets of four-continent worlds,
who shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after two more lifetimes.
Second, those who will enter the ten stages in their next birth.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in one four-continent world-system,
who shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in their next life.
In one lifetime, they entered the vajra-mind of equal enlightenment.
Furthermore, sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Those among these eight worlds who have resolved their minds are individuals whose six sense-faculties are purified; they are those who have first entered the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Thus, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states: "The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Wholesome Actions resolve their great mind and forever depart from the ocean of suffering and cyclic existence within the triple world.

This refers precisely to this meaning. This clarifies the Ten Faiths; the Ten Faiths universally and fully possess the ten wholesome actions, and it does not mean that one is defined solely by the human realm.
The heavens do not [restrain] killing, stealing, and so forth; these are used to correspond to the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Since it is said that one "permanently departs from the wheel of suffering of the triple world," and since various sutras regarding the stage of faith state that one "permanently departs from the ocean of the wheel of suffering of the triple world," this cannot be used to judge the stages of Abiding, Practice, and Direction (*vihāra-pratipatti-mukha*).

One must know that this refers to the Ten Faiths as the severing of delusions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*). This is not something that could be determined by other schools except for our own tradition, which relies upon the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The Dharma Master’s statement that the six faculties function interchangeably (*ṣaḍindriya-samprayoga*) constitutes the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), which is the inner ordinary person (*adhyātma-prthagjana*).

Prior to the Ten Faiths, based on the section concerning the "final stage of differentiated merit" (*vibhakta-guṇa-paryanta*) from the passage beginning with "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa," he establishes the Five Ranks (*pañca-vipākabhūmi*) as the outer ordinary person (*bāhya-prthagjana*).
How can it be reconciled with the intent of the *Ratnaketu-parikarman-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra* (Renwang jing) to judge that the Ten Faiths sever the suffering of the triple world? If...
Otherwise, how could one determine that the first *bhūmi* of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* belongs to the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*)?

If one were to judge the ten Brahma-words of the *Avataṃsaka* by equating the merit of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā-citta*) with the ultimate stage, it would result in an excessive conclusion. If the first *bhūmi* is classified as belonging to the noble ones, how could the ten stages of faith not be considered the stage of internal cultivation (*adhyātma-pratipanna*)?
This corresponds to the suppression of afflictions prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi-pūrva*), while the first ground constitutes the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
These are never related. Therefore, I shall now interpret the text according to the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), further citing scriptures as evidence for each point.
Thus, the six stages of "identity" (*liu ji*) are established to define the levels; the underlying principle must not be lost.

As for the increase of the Path and the diminution of birth, it is not like Guangzhai’s view of severing the "birth of causes," nor like Vasubandhu’s view of severing the "birth of karmic retribution. Rather, it concerns only the virtues of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).

Regarding increase: it is discussed in terms of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); regarding decrease: it is discussed in terms of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); regarding birth: it is discussed in terms of ignorance (*avidyā*); regarding cessation: it is discussed in terms of the same.
This is, for example, like the analogy of the moon in the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra: from the first day to the fifteenth day, its radiance and color gradually increase;

from the sixteenth day to the thirtieth day, its radiance and color gradually decrease. While the body of the moon remains constant, increase and decrease are spoken of in relation to it; this serves as an analogy.
When discussing wisdom and abandonment from the perspective of the *dharmakāya*, there may be eightfold increments or decrements occurring within a single individual;

or they may occur over one lifetime, eight lifetimes, or immeasurable lifetimes; or they may occur over eight moments of mindfulness, or immeasurable moments of mindfulness, or even across a multitude of beings, including those as numerous as atoms.
Therefore, one must not restrict this to the arising of causes or the arising of effects.
This cannot be understood apart from Zhang Zhi’s commentary. However, the attainment of the Way in this Root Chapter exceeds that of all other sutras by several multiples;

it is not only more numerous in count, but its cultivation has also been practiced for a long time. Its original source has manifested traces everywhere to guide and lead beings, and we have encountered it here in the interim.
They have been ripened again and again. In this present age, through the five flavors, they have been tamed stage by stage, gathered together, and brought back to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
It is like a farmer’s work: spring growth and summer cultivation, plowing, sowing, weeding, autumn harvest, and winter storage;
all are finally reaped at once. From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* onwards, those who attain the Way are like those who gather what has been left behind. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* itself points to this.

Eight thousand śrāvakas received their predictions of enlightenment within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Just as one harvests in autumn and stores away in winter, having nothing further to do, we know that the great harvest must take place in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Thus, regarding those who attained the Way in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the end of the "Brahmacarya-parivarta" states:
"In the kingdom of Magadha, immeasurable people resolved upon bodhicitta," continuing through to the "Ājñātakauṇḍinya-parivarta."
At the end, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of a single lifetime; fifty thousand bodhisattvas attained the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of two lifetimes;
twenty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained ultimate wisdom (*atyanta-jñāna*); thirty-five thousand bodhisattvas awakened to the primary truth (*paramārtha*);
forty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the space-like samādhi (*ākāśa-samādhi*); and fifty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained...
They attained non-retrogressive patience, which is also called the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). Sixty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained *dhāraṇī*;
seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the *siṃhanāda-samādhi*;

and eighty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the *samatā-samādhi* and resolved their minds upon *bodhicitta*, as well as the minds of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), each numbering as many as immeasurable Ganges sands, totaling twenty-two billion.

This person has now manifested the transformation of female form. The preceding eight sections of the text, beginning from "one birth" and ending with "equality," are all not yet at the stage prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*).

Although they are profound and numerous, when compared to the dust motes of the four continents or the dust motes of a great trichiliocosm mentioned in the present sutra, they are truly insufficient to mention.
The three applications of the main body of the present sutra, as well as the benefits obtained in the "Root Chapter," are in no way comparable to those of other sutras.

This is likewise true. Furthermore, within the section on the circulation [of the teaching], from the "Medicine King" chapter downward through six chapters, each chapter contains those who attained the Way, all numbering more than eighty thousand.
In the "Encouraging Devotion" chapter, the beings as numerous as the dust motes of a great trichiliocosm are endowed with the path of Samantabhadra.
Thus we know that even the supplementary portions of this sutra are so; yet prior to these, the provisional texts of the various flavors were intended for such purposes.
The skillful means of this present sutra subsequently gather in those of such capacity through the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, even supporting the Vinaya to clarify the permanence of the One Vehicle.
Having grasped the purport of this sutra, every minute action and every single phrase of the Dharma is none other than the Dharma-realm.

One gives rise to the vision of equality regarding the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions, yet constantly discerns the various modes of the Buddhas' transformations; only then does one accord with this sutra.
Regarding the purport of this vehicle, one should reflect upon what we ourselves rely upon, so as to accord with the manner in which this sutra is widely proclaimed.
When the Buddha spoke of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attaining the great benefit of the Dharma,
mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers rained down from the void, scattering over the countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jewel-trees.

He scattered [flowers] upon all the Buddhas on the lion thrones within the stūpas made of the seven treasures, as well as upon Śākyamuni Buddha on the lion throne and the long-extinguished Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna; he also scattered them upon all the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, fine powdered sandalwood, aloeswood, and other incenses rained down from the sky, where celestial drums resounded spontaneously with exquisite sounds.

The sound was deep and far-reaching. Furthermore, a rain of a thousand kinds of celestial garments fell, with various necklaces—pearl necklaces, maṇi-jewel necklaces, and wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) necklaces—hanging down, pervading the nine directions.

Myriad precious incense burners burned priceless incense, which naturally reached everywhere to make offerings to the great assembly. Above each Buddha, there were bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies. Next...
Ascending further up to the Brahma Heaven, these bodhisattvas used wondrous voices to sing immeasurable verses in praise of the Buddhas.
This third period of the assembly’s offerings represents the section on the general realization and understanding of Maitreya and others from the Original Gate. Having heard the profound...
The distant Dharma brings great benefit; desiring to repay the Buddha’s kindness, one establishes offerings. This is also a means of expressing understanding by means of external acts.
Although the Bodhisattvas of the "Chapter on the Past Deeds" (Jōshaku-mon) also attained awakening, they did not present [offerings] because their great task was not yet complete.

The exposition of the Essential Gate having concluded, Maitreya offered a comprehensive summary of his understanding. He clarified that the various bodhisattvas hold aloft banners and canopies, ascending in succession as far as the Brahma Heaven.
"Banners" (dhvaja) signify the meaning of turning [the wheel of Dharma]; "canopies" (chattra) signify the meaning of covering; and "ground" (bhūmi) signifies the meaning of the beginning.
"Brahma" (梵) signifies purity. Wisdom and severance progress step by step; compassion and protection unfold stage by stage.

High and low, deep and shallow, they do not lose their proper sequence, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven to manifest the Bodhisattvas' increase in the Path and decrease in birth, bordering upon Wondrous Enlightenment (妙覺).
It reaches the ultimate purity. If one were to interpret this according to Vasubandhu’s commentary, it would only apply to a single instance of the first bhūmi;
how could that possibly accord with this text?
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke.
The verse says:
There are nineteen lines in this verse, which further divide into three parts.
The Buddha has preached a rare Dharma, the likes of which has never been heard before. The World-Honored One possesses great power; his lifespan is immeasurable.
Countless sons of the Buddha, hearing the World-Honored One’s detailed exposition on those who have attained the benefits of the Dharma, were filled with joy throughout their bodies.
These first two lines of verse describe how the assembly attained understanding at that time.
"Or they abide on the stage of non-retrogression.
This first line praises the aforementioned patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which corresponds to the stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).
"Or they attain *dhāraṇī*s."
The second line [of the verse] praises the aforementioned attainment of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retention (*śrutadhāraṇī*). The ten practices are inconceivable and provisional;
for now, they are correlated with hearing and retention, or alternatively, with unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
This single line praises the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
"The dharani of ten billion revolutions" praises the first stage (*bhūmi*) mentioned above.
Or there may be as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a great trichiliocosm, each of whom is able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma;
this single verse refers to the second bhūmi.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a medium chiliocosm, each of whom is able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma;
this single verse describes the third stage.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm who have each had eight more births remaining before they shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
This one verse refers to the fourth stage (bhūmi).

Furthermore, there are four, three, and two [times]. Just as with these four continents, there are bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms [in them] who attain Buddhahood according to those numbers.
This single line of verse summarizes the four births for the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the three births for the ninth stage, and the two births for the tenth stage.
Or there may be bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a single four-continent world-system, who have but one birth remaining before they shall attain all-knowledge;
such beings, upon hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, obtain immeasurable, untainted, and pure karmic fruition.
These two verses describe Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Regarding the phrase "attaining immeasurable, outflow-free, and pure retribution":

it is called "immeasurable" to distinguish it from the limited [retribution] of the Two Vehicles; it is called "pure" because it is evoked by sublime causes; and it refers to the unobstructed land (*anāvaraṇa-kṣetra*).
Therefore, it is called "retribution" (vipāka); this differs from the two vehicles, for whom there is no such retribution.
Since the text definitively determines that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable, how can one employ the old interpretation that it is measurable?
Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who, upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse on his lifespan, all resolved their minds upon the Unsurpassed Way.
The World-Honored One has expounded immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas, bringing vast benefit to many, as boundless as empty space.
These two lines summarize the ten stages of faith mentioned above.
It rains *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers; Śakras, Brahmās, and others as numerous as the sands of the Ganges come from countless Buddha-fields.
Sandalwood and aloeswood rain down in profusion, scattering in disarray like birds flying from the sky to alight below, as offerings strewn before all the Buddhas.
In the midst of the void, celestial drums spontaneously produce wondrous sounds, while thousands of millions of heavenly robes swirl and descend.
With exquisite incense burners made of various jewels, they burned priceless incense that naturally pervaded everywhere as an offering to all the World-Honored Ones.
The assembly of great bodhisattvas held banners and canopies made of the seven treasures, of ten trillion varieties of sublime height, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven.
Before each and every Buddha, jeweled banners were suspended with excellent streamers; they also sang praises of all the Tathāgatas with ten million verses.
Such various deeds as these had never occurred before. Hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan was immeasurable, everyone rejoiced.
"The Buddha's name is heard throughout the ten directions; he extensively benefits sentient beings. All possess roots of goodness, which assist the unsurpassed mind. (Third eight-line verse).
This verse describes the offerings made by the assembly at that time to signify their understanding. The above concludes the revelation of the main body of the text according to the Original Gate.
△ Now, following the Master of the South, the eleven and a half chapters following the verse are divided into two parts.

From this point downward, up to the middle of the third fascicle of the "Never-Disparaging" chapter, the profound merit of propagating the sutra is explained solely to encourage the single circulation of the Root Chapter.
From the "Divine Power" chapter downward through eight chapters, the entrustment is explained by clarifying both the Root and the Trace gates for their circulation.
Each of these further contains three parts. This half-chapter, along with the "Rejoicing" chapter, clarifies the causes of the first chapter.

First, by means of the merit [of the teaching], it exhorts its circulation. Second, by means of the merit of the Dharma Master, it clarifies the fruit-merit of the first chapter to exhort its circulation.
Third, the "Chapter on Not Disparaging" cites the offenses and blessings of those who believe or slander, thereby providing testimony to exhort its circulation. These are the latter three.

The entrustment through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and the entrustment for the propagation [of the teaching] comprise the five chapters from "Bhaiṣajyarāja" downward. These are categorized as exhortations for propagation regarding the transformation of others;

the chapter on Samantabhadra is categorized as an exhortation for propagation regarding one's own practice. As for the arising [of benefit]: those who hear this sutra in the present obtain both the true and the semblance benefits of understanding, as explained above.
Even if one merely hears a single phrase and gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), it is like the four kinds of faith in the present.

To evaluate his merit: fearing that people might doubt the smallness of their own blessings because there will be no Buddhas in the future, he speaks of the five grades of merit after the extinction [of the Buddha].
Because the merit of the cause is subtle and hidden, it does not compare to the manifest brilliance of the merit of the fruit; therefore, he speaks of the "Chapter on the Merit of the Dharma Master.

Although both cause and fruit are presented together, they do not compare to the clarity of citing scriptural evidence; therefore, he speaks of "Never-Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta). Even though he is mentioned...

The past [manifestations] of the person were not equal to the present transformations; therefore, it is called "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi*). Although he displayed spiritual power, it was not equal to the placing of hands upon their heads and the entrustment;
therefore, it is called "entrustment" (*parindanā*). Although there was general entrustment, it was not equal to revealing the essential method of discarding the body to preserve the Way;

therefore, it is called "Bhaiṣajyarāja. Although he admonished those who transform others, it was not equal to admonishing those who are transformed; wherever they hear the Dharma, [they shall follow].

One should conceive the thought that [the teacher] is a Buddha; therefore, it speaks of Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound) and Guanyin (Avalokiteśvara). If one who has newly resolved to propagate the sutra lacks supernatural powers, they must rely on internal prohibitions;
therefore, it speaks of dhāraṇīs. Furthermore, external protection is required; therefore, it speaks of King Vaideha and Samantabhadra.
These are linked and layered so that the Great Dharma may be widely propagated. Following the verses, there are two sections in prose: first, the four kinds of faith during the present age;

second, the five grades after the extinction [of the Buddha]. Question: What are the four kinds of faith? Answer: Briefly explained, there are three types of persons; explained in detail, there are two;
and for one who has perfected contemplation, there is faith. Since faith applies to all four, they are called the "four kinds of faith. As for these four kinds of faith:

The first is the initial moment of faith and understanding, which is not yet capable of exposition. The second is a brief explanation of the meaning of the words. The third is explaining it extensively for others.

The fourth is the accomplishment of profound faith and contemplation. Regarding the first, the initial moment of faith and understanding, there are both prose and verse; the prose consists of three parts.
First, he identifies the person; second, he clarifies their merit; third, he explains the non-retrogression of their practice and realization.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Ajita, if there are sentient beings who, hearing that the lifespan of the Buddha is thus long and far-reaching, are able to give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding..."
First, he identifies the person: one who possesses faith and understanding in a single thought-moment, wherever they hear [the teaching], is suddenly enlightened;
entering according to the words, they encounter no obstruction. They believe that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, and they further believe that the Buddha-dharma is not separate from all dharmas.
Not attaining the Buddha-dharma, yet not attaining any dharma, they perceive all dharmas.
They also see the Buddha-dharma as being three in one and one in three. They practice non-ways to penetrate the Buddha-way;
they practice the Buddha-way to penetrate all ways; yet they neither attain the Buddha-way nor any way.
Yet one penetrates the Buddha-way and all paths: that which is non-existent yet exists, and that which exists yet is non-existent;

it is neither existent nor non-existent. Just as a road before a gate leads everywhere—east, west, and north—with no obstructions, so too it is with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: whatever they encounter is entirely like this, without doubt.
It is said: faith is clarity; understanding is lucidity. This constitutes the mind of one-moment faith and understanding (*ekakṣaṇa-śraddhādhimukti*).

If, while sitting in contemplation, one follows whatever is contemplated and suddenly attains awakening, penetrating the three truths (*tisraḥ satya*), it is likewise so. Such faith and understanding is called the stage of the iron wheel (*ayaścakra-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, this single understanding is not yet the full-fledged iron wheel stage; rather, it is the initial mind of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Since that person has not yet attained the purity of the six sense faculties, they do not yet occupy the formal rank of the Iron Wheel-turning King.
The merit they have acquired is immeasurable;
this first section provides a general comparison.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, practice the five pāramitās—
the pāramitā of dāna, the pāramitā of śīla, the pāramitā of kṣānti, the pāramitā of vīrya,
and the pāramitā of dhyāna— for eighty million nayuta koṭis of kalpas, excluding the prajñā-pāramitā.
Regarding the *pāramitās*:
first, the five perfections are cited as the standard for comparison. Since *prajñā* is the very wisdom that is the subject at hand, it is said that [the others] exclude *prajñā*.
Question: If they are separated from *prajñā*, then the five cannot be called "perfections" (*pāramitā*). Answer: They are all for the purpose of seeking the Buddha-wisdom.
Exhausting the limits of giving and precepts may also be called "crossing over"; this is intended to show their sequential relationship.
Compared with the former merit by means of these merits, even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part does not equal one part of it;
indeed, it is beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
Second, this is the correct measure of the quantity.
If a son of good family possesses such merit as this, it is impossible for him to fall back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Third, the clarification of non-retrogression in the stages of practice: in the distinct [teaching], one may still retrogress up to the sixth mind, whereas from the seventh mind onward there is no retrogression;

in the Perfect [teaching], from the very first stage of faith (*śraddhā*) there is no retrogression. This is because, externally, one is sustained by hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan and merits; internally, one is perfumed by a compliant faith and understanding (*adhimukti*) that accords with the Perfect [teaching].
Therefore, there is no retrogression. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "There are bodhisattvas who retrogress and those who do not; there are Māras and there are none."

All these refer to this same meaning. Furthermore, from the first stage of faith up to the seventh stage of faith constitutes "non-retrogression in position"; from the eighth stage of faith onward constitutes "non-retrogression in practice.

As for "non-retrogression in the seven minds," this refers to the seventh abode (*vihāra*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyākaraṇa*), wherein both *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* (afflictions of views) and *bhāvanā-kleśa* (afflictions of cultivation) are eliminated together.

This refers to non-retrogression from name and rank. Furthermore, regarding the mention of "Māras and the like," the intent is to clarify that for Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra*), there are Māras when they retrogress, but no Māras when they do not retrogress.
For those at the initial stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), Māras cannot find an opportunity; how much less so for those who have attained non-retrogression?

From the first *bhūmi* onward, they analytically destroy the eight Māras, because they are able to realize that Māras and all such phenomena are identical to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, even when the name of the *Śūraṅgama* is invoked, the Māras [are unable to prevail].

If even those who are bound are not subject to such [disturbance], how much less so for those who practice contemplation, and how much less so for those who have attained self-realization? How could Māra cause them to regress?
One should know that for a person of perfect capacity, Māra has already retreated far away from the very beginning of the five stages of practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
There were nineteen and a half lines, divided into three parts:
"If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom, For eighty quadrillion nayutas of kalpas, They practice the five pāramitās."
Throughout all these kalpas, they made offerings of food and drink of rare excellence, superior garments, and bedding,
as well as sandalwood monasteries adorned with gardens and groves, to the Buddhas, the pratyekabuddhas and their disciples, and the assemblies of bodhisattvas.
Such acts of giving as these, all of them subtle and wondrous, throughout the entirety of these kalpas, are dedicated toward the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, if one upholds the prohibitive precepts, pure and without flaw, seeking the unsurpassed path, one is praised by all Buddhas.
If one further practices patience and dwells on the stage of gentleness, even if various evils are heaped upon them, their mind remains unshaken.
Even when those who have attained some degree of realization harbor overweening pride and thus treat one with contempt or cause distress, one is likewise able to endure it.
If one further applies diligent effort, with a mind and mindfulness always firm and steadfast, for immeasurable billions of kalpas, remaining single-mindedly without slackening;
and furthermore, throughout countless kalpas, dwelling in secluded places, whether sitting or walking, constantly restraining the mind and removing sleepiness.
By these causes and conditions, one is able to give rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). For eighty billion *koṭi* of kalpas, one dwells peacefully with an undisturbed mind.
Taking this merit of single-mindedness, one vows to seek the unsurpassed path; may I attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and reach the ultimate limit of all meditative concentrations.
For hundreds of thousands, ten millions, and billions of kalpas, this person practices these various merits as described above.
The first twelve lines of verse weigh and compare the magnitude of these amounts.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing me speak of the lifespan [of the Buddha], have faith for even a single thought-moment, their merit shall exceed that of the former.
If a person is entirely free from all doubts and regrets, and has deep-seated faith for even a brief moment, their merit shall be just like this.
The next two lines are a recapitulation of the marks of the superior person:
"Those bodhisattvas who have practiced the Way for immeasurable kalpas will be able to believe and accept this when they hear me speak of the lifespan."
May all such people as these receive this sutra upon the crowns of their heads;

may I, in the future, possess long life to deliver sentient beings, just as the World-Honored One today—the King among the Śākyas—roars the lion’s roar at the site of enlightenment and preaches the Dharma without fear.
"In future ages, we shall be honored by all; when seated at the site of enlightenment, our lifespan shall be proclaimed in this same way.
If there are those with profound resolve, pure and upright, who are learned and capable of perfect retention, they will understand the Buddha’s words according to their true meaning."
"Such persons as these have no doubt regarding this.

These five lines and a half concern the stage of practice and non-retrogression. "Those who have practiced the Way for immeasurable eons" refers to those who have long cultivated the various perfections (*pāramitās*).
"May I, in the future... expresses the arising of the vow of compassion. By relying on the long-standing practice of vows, one hears the sutra and gains faith.

Commentary: In this first chapter, at the very beginning of hearing this sutra, to have even a single thought of faith and understanding is a merit equal to that of long-term practice—and indeed surpasses it.
△ Below, in the second section on "Faith," each is divided into two parts: first, the manifestation of the signs; second, the comparative evaluation.

Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching and understand the meaning of these words—this being the second stage of faith, which briefly explains the meaning of the words—it first presents the characteristics of human beings; in the preceding initial stage, one merely has faith and understanding.

It has not yet been fully expounded. Such exposition involves names and numerical categories and requires proficiency in local dialects; since this chapter is complete, it is said that one "explains it for others.
It receives its name from what is most eminent and is called the Second Chapter. By the power of this exposition, one is able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of both oneself and others.
The merit obtained by such a person is immeasurable; it can give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This is the formal calculation.
How much more so for one who extensively hears this sutra, or causes others to hear it, or upholds it themselves, or causes others to uphold it, or writes it out themselves?
Whether teaching others to write it, or making offerings to the scripture scrolls with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, silk canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps—
this refers to the third [category], extensively explaining it for others, wherein one first manifests the marks of a human being.
The merit of this person is immeasurable and boundless; it can give rise to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This concludes the comparative evaluation. Third, [the stage of] extensive faith, extensive hearing, extensive understanding, extensively teaching it to others, and extensively practicing offerings.
By making offerings to external conditions, one causes internal wisdom to enter swiftly and be able to give rise to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Ajita, if good sons or good daughters hear me speak of the long duration of my lifespan, [they shall attain this].
In the fourth stage, the position of perfected profound contemplation, one first gives rise to the perception of the human form.
With deep mental faith and understanding, one then perceives the Buddha constantly dwelling on Vulture Peak, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as he preaches the Dharma.
Furthermore, one sees this Sahā world, its ground made of lapis lazuli, level and smooth.
It is correct. Jambūnada gold demarcates the eight paths, with rows of jewel trees and all the terraces and towers made entirely of jewels.
The assembly of bodhisattvas all dwell therein. If there is anyone who can contemplate it in this way, you should know that this is the mark of profound faith and understanding.

Next is the evaluation. Regarding the phrase "profound mind" (*gambhīracitta*) and so forth: within this *Yuanmen* (Perfect Gate) of the *Benji* (Original Ground), one must still possess five dharmas before doubt can be severed.
First is generating faith upon hearing [the teaching] from afar. Second is the profound mind, which exhaustively realizes that principle is non-dual.
Third is the direct mind; "direct" means that the beginning and end are of one accord. Fourth is extensive learning. Fifth is explaining it for others. This...

The fourth type of person is one who possesses the three aforementioned grades and further cultivates contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and employing wisdom, they bring forth the manifestation of the signs (*nimitta*).
These signs are inherently complete within the principle (*tattva*); by relying on this principle, the mental image arises, and thus the image is perfected. Consequently, they perceive these signs.

From the initial stage of practicing contemplation, it is merely termed "mental imaging" because the contemplative practice is still shallow; furthermore, it accords with the mental image and accords with the principle. As for the principle...

The signs then manifest. In other teachings, one cultivates contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), but such contemplation may conflict with the ultimate principle; even if there is a partial realization of its energy, it does not accord with the Middle Way.
If even when such skillful means of contemplation are accomplished, it is still merely a sign, how much more so when they are not yet accomplished?

Furthermore, although seeing these signs does not constitute true realization, by the power of contemplation one temporarily beholds the two lands. Only when the three delusions are partially extinguished will one be in permanent correspondence with them.

This is not yet called "conceptualization. Now, as conceptualization forms, signs arise, enabling one to see the characteristics of the two lands: the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder and the Land of True Retribution.
To see the Buddha together with the assembly of bhikṣus constantly residing on Mount Grdhrakūṭa is the characteristic of the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder.

Furthermore, to see the Sahā world consisting purely of bodhisattvas is the characteristic of the Land of True Retribution. Moreover, there is the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder, where [beings of] both small and large capacities coexist.

Regarding the two vehicles of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* (the *Zangtong*): those who have severed the delusions common [to both vehicles] are still designated by their original names, as seen according to their respective capacities.

As for the Pure Land of the Bodhisattvas alone, it is also a land of "other-enjoyment" (*parasaṃbhoga*). It is merely that, based on this perception, [the land] gradually deepens and becomes fully realized.

Upon entering the stage of the first abode (*prathamā bhūmi*), one spontaneously and universally perceives applications that are boundless. Question: Since one gives rise to conceptions in accordance with principle, why is it necessary to have the conception of a land (*kṣetra-saṃjñā*)?

It would suffice merely to contemplate a single thought-moment, for the wondrous principle is immediately present. Answer: For those at the initial stage of both teachings, all must extinguish the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*).
