How much more so for the land itself? In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), even the initial mind is still obscured by the shadows [of ignorance], though the final mind is able to perceive the lands of the Indra’s Net (*indrājāla*).

Only in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) does one immediately contemplate that within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), the three thousand realms and the three truths (*tisraḥ satya*) are fully present.

This means that within a single mind are all minds; within a single body are all bodies; and within a single land are all lands—all observed simultaneously within a single thought-moment, whether it be body, mind, or land.
If emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are without further sequence of before or after, then when contemplation is perfected, with a single mind one sees all minds;
with a single body one sees all bodies; and with a single land one sees all lands—the Buddhas of all ten directions and the three periods of time.
Because they manifest within one's own body, one constantly perceives all lands and bodies of the ten directions and the three periods of time within the tranquil light of one’s own mind.
If one contemplates only the land of the other [Vairocana], one will inevitably become deluded regarding one's own realm; however, if one understands that the mind is the realm, [one realizes this].
Because self is other, and other is self; if one does not understand this realm, even the self becomes other—how much more so when observing others?
Since it is thus with the observation of the land, it is the same for the body, the Buddha, and the mind. Therefore, upon hearing of "longevity," one must understand the essential principle.

Thus, one knows that while names and concepts are identical, their referents differ. According to the previous explanation within the four *siddhāntas*, even the first principle (*paramārtha*) is still inclusive.
This is because it is designated by a name and concept. Therefore, hearing of the lifespan in the Original Chapter brings benefit twice as great as that of other sutras;

this is truly due to the fact that what is heard here is extraordinary. The above constitutes the first section, clarifying the circulation of the four levels of faith. △ Below follows the second section, clarifying the five grades after the extinction [of the Buddha].
This is divided into two parts: first, listing the five grades and comparing their merits with those of the four grades; second, the "Chapter on Rejoicing," which compares them with the first grade.
Regarding the merit: Question—Why is this so? Answer—There are four grades of coarse estimation. The first grade is the extensive estimation.
Once the extensive estimation has been made, those who surpass it can be understood by implication. The Buddha does not employ redundant phrasing; his skillful teaching is like this.
Regarding the five grades: first, those who simply give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; second, those who add the practice of personally receiving, upholding, and reciting [the teachings];

third, those who further add exhorting others to receive, uphold, and recite them; fourth, those who further add the concurrent practice of the six perfections; and fifth, those who further add the correct practice of the six perfections.
These five types of persons, in general discussion, all practice for themselves and transform others. As the subsequent text states: "The fifty people successively transform one another..."

This is the teaching. Since all possess their own practice (*sva-caryā*), they are collectively termed "disciples" (*śrāvaka*). Since all possess the transformation of others (*para-parivartana*), they are collectively termed "Dharma Masters" (*dharma-bhāṇaka*).
To discuss them specifically: the first two types [of practitioners] engage only in their own practice, while the latter three possess both the transformation of others and act as Dharma Masters.
Previously, these were categorized as being among the "three" [groups], not the "five. Therefore, they are all referred to as disciples.
Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, if one hears this sutra and does not disparage it, but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy,
you should know that this is already a sign of profound faith and understanding.
The first chapter merely identifies the person and directly expresses sympathetic joy;
how much more so for those who read, recite, receive, and uphold [the text].
Next, the second grade of practitioners is clarified. First, the person is identified; "how much more so" refers to those capable of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it. This is it.

Such a person shall be one who carries the Tathāgata upon their head. Ajita, these sons and daughters of good family need not further erect stūpas or temples for my sake, nor construct monasteries, nor provide the four requisites as offerings to the Saṃgha. Why is this?
Because those sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sūtra have already erected a stūpa.

To construct monasteries and provide offerings to the community of monks is equivalent to erecting a stupa of the seven precious gems for the relics of the Buddha, high and wide, gradually tapering upward until reaching the Brahma Heaven, adorned with hanging banners, canopies, and various jeweled bells;

with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, and burning incense; and with various drums, music, flutes, pipes, lutes, and all manner of dances and performances, accompanied by exquisite sounds.
To sing hymns and offer praises is equivalent to having performed such offerings for immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
Second, to weigh the merit of the second grade of practitioners: those at the initial stage fear being distracted by external conditions, which hinders their cultivation of the primary practice;

yet, if they simply and exclusively uphold this sutra, that itself constitutes the highest offering. By setting aside ritualistic activities to preserve the underlying principle, the benefit is vast and great. Hereafter—

As for the mind: if the contemplation of principle (*li*) becomes mature, external involvement will not hinder the internal; affairs will assist the Way, just as when there is abundant oil, the fire burns fiercely.
It is like sailing with the current while raising the sails and adding further effort—the momentum becomes even swifter.

Referring to the scriptural text: this is the *dharmakāya* śarīra; it is unnecessary to enshrine the *janmakāya* śarīra. The text is the means of expression (*vyañjana*), and that which is expressed (*artha*) is the stūpa.
There is no need to attend to the stupas. This is because that which is elucidated by the Great Teaching is the Dharma-body and the true mark (*dharmatā*).

It is simply within the place where the sutra resides that there is the relic of the Dharma-body; thus, one builds a stupa. This is because the scriptural text is capable of elucidating [the truth], just as a stupa is capable of containing it.
Furthermore, the scriptural text can accommodate the ultimate precepts and the Sangha; there is no need to follow the conventional Sangha. Question:
If that is so, then upholding the sūtras is itself the ultimate precept (*paramārtha-śīla*). Why, then, is it further said that one "is able to uphold the precepts"?
And why even mention "making offerings to the Saṃgha"? Answer: This clarifies the meaning of the first chapter.

One should not raise objections based on subsequent chapters. Since those in the first chapter have not yet been able to enter into the practice, they provisionally take the principle as their object of refuge.
To take the sutra as a stupa: if one wishes to explain this, upholding the sutra is precisely to accord with the precepts of principle.

This also spontaneously results in upholding the first two sections. What is now called "being able to uphold the precepts" refers to the third section; the first two sections merely constitute the first two chapters.
Therefore, one should not raise the objection that [this applies only to] being able to uphold the three chapters of the lower section. All who practice...

Regarding the practitioner of the Perfect Course (yuanxingzhe): please examine this text. If one belongs to the first two categories of persons, their initial mind and every moment of thought shall always abide in the four kinds of samādhi;

they may occasionally slightly contravene the dharmas pertaining to the three lower groups. As for those in the three lower categories, they maintain both the prohibitions and the active precepts (zhizuo erchi).

The two modes of practice—collective and individual—must not be transgressed even by the slightest hair’s breadth, as detailed in the section on the purity of precept-keeping within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Only when both phenomena and principle are harmoniously perfected can one truly be fit to advance toward the Way; how much more so for those who have already entered the Way—how could they allow their conduct to be deficient?

If one has not yet become single-mindedly devoted to the four types of samādhi, one must not violate even slightly the five categories and seven groups of offenses, nor the grave and light transgressions of a Bodhisattva; only then can one be called "one."

This is the essential purport of our teaching. Why is this so? For a renunciant bodhisattva, the complete and steadfast observance of the *vinaya* articles and clusters is entirely consistent with the intent of the Mahāyāna teachings.
However, merely guarding these articles does not yet constitute the mark of upholding the eighty thousand monastic regulations of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
It is simply because the capacities of those in this land are inferior that we provisionally employ minor restraints to assist in the fulfillment of the great code.

Furthermore, one must understand the conditions for opening and closing [the precepts], the gravity of offenses, and their underlying substance; the gradual and sudden nature of the regulations, the presence or absence of the principle of relinquishment, the different lineages of seating order, and the vast differences between various methods of repentance.

Moreover, there are distinctions regarding whether the seven classes of followers share these practices, and whether the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions are common or distinct—only then can one proceed with one's own practice.
Measure your own level and capacity; let your acceptance and rejection be appropriate to the occasion. Some may admire lofty principles while remaining oblivious to their own survival or ruin;

others may rely on minor textual fragments while losing sight of the path of contemplation. If you wish to grasp the present meaning, first establish it through principle and teaching, and subsequently verify it through rank and practice.

If it were not so, they would be like birds, rats, or humans; how could they be established in the ranks of the noble? I respectfully entreat you to receive the Buddha’s final testament and to honor it even in small measure.
Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there are those who hear this sutra and are able to receive and uphold it—whether by writing it themselves or by teaching others to do so—
"Human Writing.
This clarifies the third grade of attainment. First, the characteristics of the person are indicated; furthermore, because they are able to teach others, they surpass the preceding stage.
Thus, they establish monasteries and construct thirty-two halls using red sandalwood, eight *zhang* in height.
There were *tāla* trees, tall, broad, and magnificent. Within them resided hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus. Gardens, groves, bathing ponds, walking paths, and meditation caves were present;
clothing, food, drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions—all such articles of comfort—were abundant therein.
Such monasteries, halls, and pavilions numbered in the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions, their count being immeasurable. With these, he made offerings before him.

They shall be sustained by me and the community of bhikṣus. Therefore, I say that after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain it to others;

whether they write it themselves or instruct others to write it; and honor the physical scrolls—there is no further need for them to build stūpas or monasteries, nor to construct vihāras to provide offerings to the Saṃgha.
This is the measure of the merit of a person of the third grade;
how much more so for one who can uphold this sutra while simultaneously practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration,
and wisdom?
This clarifies the person of the fourth category. Furthermore, they are able to practice the six perfections concurrently. First, their personal characteristics are defined:
their virtue is most supreme, immeasurable and boundless, like space—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Immeasurable and boundless is the merit of this person; it is likewise immeasurable and boundless. They will swiftly reach all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is the most supreme among the merits of the persons compared in the fourth category.
If a person reads, recites, receives, and upholds this sutra, and explains it for others; or if they write it themselves, or instruct others to write it;

and further, if they are able to erect stupas and construct monasteries, making offerings and praises to the assembly of śrāvakas, and likewise praise the merits of bodhisattvas with hundreds of thousands of millions of methods of praise;
and furthermore, for the sake of others, through various causes and conditions, according to—

They explain the meaning of this Lotus Sūtra; furthermore, they are able to maintain the precepts with purity, dwell together with those who are gentle and mild, practice patience without anger, and possess firm resolve and mindfulness.
They always value seated meditation and attain various profound concentrations.
With diligent vigor, they gather all wholesome dharmas; possessing sharp faculties and wisdom, they are skilled in answering difficult questions.
This clarifies that those in the fifth stage of practice are further able to correctly cultivate the six perfections. First, the characteristics of such persons are indicated:

"Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there are sons or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and who furthermore possess such virtuous merits as these, you should know that these persons have already set out for the site of enlightenment and are close to [Buddhahood]."

Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Ānanda, beneath the Bodhi tree, wherever these sons and daughters of good family sit, stand, or practice walking meditation, a stūpa should be erected there; all devas and humans [should honor it].
All should be honored as if they were stupas of the Buddha.

This concludes the fifth section on the merit of those in the five grades of practice. Regarding these five grades of practitioners: the first three are at the stage of wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);

the next [two] are at the stage of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), wherein they concurrently practice the six perfections; and the final [grade] is at the stage of wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), wherein they correctly practice the six perfections. All of them are...
This refers to the stage prior to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). Alternatively, it is said that the first "Stage of Rejoicing" (*pramuditā*) constitutes the entry into the stage of faith;

this single stage is divided into two minds. These five stages are the ten minds of faith, which correspond to the stage of the "Iron Wheel" and the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
There are nineteen and a half lines, divided into four parts; these do not recite the first chapter, but rather concern those who rejoice with approval.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, one is able to uphold this sutra, that person’s merit will be immeasurable, as has been described above;
indeed, such a person is fully endowed with all forms of offering, including the building of stupas for relics adorned with the seven treasures.
The spire and banner are exceedingly high and vast, gradually tapering as they reach the Brahma-heaven. With billions of precious bells, stirred by the wind, they emit wondrous sounds.
Furthermore, throughout immeasurable kalpas, one makes offerings to this stupa with flowers, incense, various necklaces, celestial garments, and manifold music.

Furthermore, with fragrant oil and butter lamps, let them constantly illuminate all around. In this evil age of the final Dharma, one who can uphold this sutra has already, as described above, fully provided all manner of offerings.
The first five and a half lines of the verse refer to the second category of persons mentioned above:
if one can uphold this sutra, it is as if the Buddha were present; one may then construct a monastic dwelling out of gośīrṣa-candana to make offerings to him.
There are thirty-two halls, each eight *tāla* trees in height. They are provided with exquisite food and fine garments, and are fully equipped with couches and bedding.
These dwellings for hundreds of thousands of beings feature gardens, groves, various bathing pools, walking paths, and meditation caves—all of which are magnificently adorned.
The next three lines are a verse summarizing the third chapter:
"If one possesses a mind of faith and understanding, and upholds, recites, and transcribes [this sutra], or further teaches others to transcribe it, and makes offerings to the scripture scrolls."

Scattering flowers, incense, and powdered incense, and constantly burning fragrant oils such as those of sumana, campaka, and atimuktaka—those who make such offerings shall attain immeasurable merit, as boundless as space; their blessings shall likewise be so.

How much more so for one who upholds this sutra, while simultaneously practicing giving, maintaining the precepts, enduring with patience, delighting in meditative concentration, being free from anger, and refraining from harsh speech—
these latter four practices summarize the fourth chapter above.
One should show reverence to stupas and temples, be humble toward all bhikṣus, remain far removed from pride, and constantly contemplate wisdom.
When questioned or challenged, one should not become angry, but explain the teachings in accordance with the truth. If one can practice such conduct, their merit will be immeasurable.
If one sees this Dharma-master who has accomplished such virtues, one should scatter celestial flowers over him and cover his body with celestial robes;
bowing head-to-foot, one should give rise to the thought of regarding him as a Buddha. Furthermore, one should form this thought: "Before long, he shall proceed to the site of enlightenment."
Having attained the untainted and unconditioned state, they bring vast benefit to all devas and humans.

Wherever they dwell—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—even where they utter a single verse, a stūpa should be erected there, adorned with exquisite beauty and offered various kinds of worship.
The Buddha-sons dwell in this stage; it is the enjoyment of the Buddhas. They are constantly within it, whether walking, sitting, or lying down.

(Next, seven lines of verse describe the person of the fifth grade of practice. Those who give rise to a mind that conceives of themselves as Buddhas belong to the five grades and the ten stages of faith.
This refers first to the person, who is designated as a Tathāgata. "Before long he shall go to the tree of enlightenment" means that his station is at the stage of the iron wheel;
before long he shall enter the copper wheel and be able to manifest the eight phases of a Buddha. "Having already proceeded toward the site of enlightenment" refers to the place of practice.

"Tripiṭaka-sambodhi" (Threefold Enlightenment) refers to the proximate stage. It may also be understood as the practice of contemplation and its proximity; both are accessible to those at a shallow level.
It is profound. This fifth stage is equal to the fourth stage of faith; both belong to the level of wisdom attained through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

If one discusses their entry into the stages, they are both identical to the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*). The difference lies merely in whether it pertains to the time when a Buddha is present in the world or after his parinirvāṇa. Question:
For what reason are there four grades of faith during the Buddha’s presence, while five grades are established after his passing? Answer: Its...

Since the meaning is identical, there is no distinction between the fourth and fifth [periods]; it is simply that after the extinction [of the Buddha], recitation and chanting are added as the second category.
The above prose and verse sections collectively constitute the five categories following the extinction, having completed the weighing of merits to encourage the circulation [of the teaching].
*The Wondrous Sutra Entering the Commentary*, Scroll Ten.
Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Eleven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
Exegesis and Records by Tiantai Zhizhe.
The Śramaṇa Daowei of Siming entered this commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Eighteen: “Merit of Rejoicing.
This chapter concerns the merit of rejoicing after the [Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa; it compares this merit with that of the first chapter in order to encourage its circulation.
However, all the chapters from this point onward constitute the two gates of the dissemination of the Trace and the Origin.

Since they are all augmented by hearing the "Chapter on Increasing the Ranks of Longevity," it is necessary to describe both the present and the past gates together. Furthermore, these chapters extol the five kinds of Dharma-preachers.
Regarding the functional efficacy (*kāritra*): it is able to enter the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) and is identical to the stage of the four faiths (*catur-adhimukti*) in the present.

Since the section beginning with "Not Disparaging" (*Adhyāśaya-parivarta*) is collectively referred to as the *Lotus Sūtra*, how could it pertain solely to the Trace [Teaching]? First, the title is explained; second, the sūtra is interpreted.

In the explanation of the title, there are the causal conditions (*nidāna*) and the doctrinal analysis (*yathā-śāsana*). Within the causal conditions, first, the Worldly Universal Truth (*loka-siddhānta*) has three parts: first, a brief explanation; second, an extensive exposition.
Regarding the names of the three fetters: "following" (anuloma) means to accord with principle and phenomena such that there is neither duality nor distinction.

One should know that phenomena and principle are merely different names for the provisional and the real. When one realizes this provisional and real, they are no longer provisional or real; thus, there is neither duality nor distinction.

This is precisely following the principle and phenomena of opening up the provisional to reveal the real. "Joy" (prīti) is to rejoice for oneself and rejoice for others—rejoicing for both oneself and others.

This is precisely the power of the principle and phenomena within the traces. Because principle possesses phenomena, it can bring joy to others; because phenomena possess principle, one can rejoice in oneself.
Furthermore, because they are non-dual yet dual, one rejoices in both self and others; because they are dual yet non-dual, [one rejoices in their unity].

Therefore, one realizes that [the self] is neither oneself nor another. This concludes the brief explanation. As for the detailed explanation: upon hearing the profound and subtle Dharma, there is the merit of reality in accordance with principle, and the merit of skillful means in accordance with phenomena.
One rejoices in oneself through wisdom and rejoices in others through compassion.

Because one has heard the sutras oneself and is further able to teach them to others, it is only when both compassion and wisdom are fully possessed that it is called "joy" (*muditā*). How much more so when hearing the sutras!
At the very beginning, practice and vows arise simultaneously; thus, each phrase and each verse benefits both oneself and others.

Now, at this initial stage, one establishes the path of self-cultivation exclusively, yet through the power of one's vows, one rejoices in the welfare of others. Because the provisional and the ultimate, as well as wisdom and severance, are taught in conjunction, it is called the "Chapter on Rejoicing in Merit.
This is the world-encompassing perspective (*loka-saṃvṛti*). Furthermore, for those who accord with principle, upon hearing the Buddha—
The fundamental ground is profoundly deep, exceedingly deep. One believes and complies with it without opposition, without a single hair’s breadth of doubt or obstruction.

If one’s faith is directed toward the long-distant, that faith must necessarily rely upon principle; this principle is no different from the wondrous principle within the traces. It merely points to what has existed for a long time in the origin, where merit is attributed to actual realization.

Since the principle is profound and the time is remote, and since one has long heard of this principle, how could one dare to harbor secret doubts? Thus, there is not a single hair’s breadth of doubt.

Regarding the profound principle (*paramārtha*), one who accords with the facts hears that the Buddha benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, encompassing both the horizontal and vertical dimensions, pervading all places without a single hair’s breadth of doubt or obstruction.
Thus, they penetrate the profound principle through extensive phenomena, and penetrate extensive phenomena through the profound principle.
They are non-dual yet dual; they are undifferentiated yet differentiated. Although dual and differentiated, they are neither dual nor differentiated. It is as follows:
This faith and understanding is called "conformity. For more than forty years since the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he did not reveal the ultimate reality;

nor did he speak of the true truth to those at the seven stages of expedient means. Today, I and others rejoice, for with the minds of ordinary beings we have attained what the Buddha knows, and with our born eyes we have become equal to the vision of the Tathāgata.
Through such knowledge and vision, we have reached the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm, which is vast and boundless.
At the base of the precipice, it is peerless and equal to the peerless; there is nothing superior to it.
Because the Buddha now speaks this and I have heard this, it is named the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing. This is an explanation based on the perspective of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*).

Furthermore, the fiftieth person is at the beginning of the first chapter; at the outset, they possess only a single thought of understanding and realization, and only a single thought of rejoicing for themselves and rejoicing for others.

As for those who have not yet engaged in such practice and whose kindness has not reached others, even the merit they obtain—as skillfully illustrated by the Tathāgata—surpasses that of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
How much more so for those who first heard this in the assembly; how much more so for those who have heard it through two, three, four, or five stages;

Yet they do not admire it. The Tathāgata spoke this in order to cause beings to revere it; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Rejoicing in Merit.
This is an explanation from the perspective of benefiting others (*parārtha*).

Such is the view of worldly people.
Those with erroneous understanding fail to fathom the greatness of the merit of the initial resolve, yet they attribute that merit to higher stages and disparage this initial resolve.

Therefore, I now demonstrate that although their practice is shallow, its merit is profound, thereby revealing the power of the sutra. Suddenly hearing this, they will firmly abide in the ground of faith.

The sprouts have already reached a circumference of a hundred spans; the *piṅgala* bird dwells within the egg, its voice surpassing that of all other birds. The Holy One has personally praised it as rare and extraordinary;
light doubts are thus dispelled, and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is revealed. Therefore, this is named the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing.

Now, those among the non-Buddhists who have attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) can move mountains and dry up the oceans, yet they do not subdue the views and cravings (*dṛṣṭi-tṛṣṇā*), nor do they reach the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

Ordinary people and those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning are both liberated from cause and fruit; yet they remain bound by *nirvāṇa*, for they do not realize that both cause and fruit are provisional.
Although those of the Shared Teaching are skillful in their cultivation of the cause, they fail to recognize the five hundred *yojanas* when they first resolve their minds;

upon attaining the fruit, they merely eliminate the four abiding delusions. Although the Separate Teaching surpasses the Two Vehicles, its cultivation of the cause is partial and its gateway is clumsy; it is not [the ultimate].
The praise bestowed by the Buddha does not equal that of the first person who rejoices. Now, the Buddha cites the "Gate of the Letter A" (*akāra-mukha*);

how much more so for the subsequent "Letter Ca" (*cakāra*). This is because it surpasses all other teachings; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing. The explanation of the chapter title is complete.

comparing the latter with the former, the former is even more so. This is now divided into two parts: first, a horizontal comparison across the fourfold assemblies of all teachings; second, a direct calculation based on the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa).

therefore, I shall now assist them. For the time being, we rely upon the gates of the teachings to establish the number of persons. Within the Tripiṭaka there are four gates, and within each gate there are four assemblies.
If one further distinguishes between śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, there are six types of persons per gate; thus, across the four gates, there are twenty-four.

Within the great sevens, there are seven times seven, which makes forty-nine; all of these consist of teachers and disciples, fully embodying both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.

As for "virtue," this refers to the very last person; they possess only the virtue of self-liberation and lacks the virtue of teaching others. Therefore, by comparing them with those below, the superiority of those above is revealed.
This concludes the explanation of the initial stage of successive mutual instruction.
Ajita, I shall now describe the merit of the rejoicing performed by that fiftieth son or daughter of good family;
you should listen well. Suppose there were sentient beings within four hundred million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds—beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth:
those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether they have form or are formless, possess thought or are without thought, or are neither... [non-percipient].

Whether they possess perception or lack perception; whether they have no feet, two feet, four feet, or many feet—regarding all such beings included within the category of sentient beings, there may be someone seeking merit who provides them with whatever articles of enjoyment they desire, granting these to each and every being.

and having practiced such giving for eighty full years, he then thought: "I have already provided these amusements for sentient beings."
"Let it be as you wish. However, these sentient beings have all already grown old; they are over eighty years of age, with white hair and wrinkled faces, and death will soon come for them.

I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma. He then gathered these sentient beings together, proclaimed the transformative teaching of the Dharma, and instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them.
In that single moment, they all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, and the stage of *anāgāmin*.

The path of the Anāgāmin and the path of the Arhat exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*). They attain mastery over profound meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and possess the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).

This clarifies that within the process of evaluation: first, one bestows worldly happiness and uproots the suffering of the fruits [of existence]; subsequently, one bestows the bliss of *nirvāṇa* and uproots birth.
The suffering of death. This has been a brief enumeration of Brahma-merit. Now, let us further examine it in detail according to the *Mahāśāstra*.

The merit of all people filling Jambudvīpa does not equal the merit of a single person in Aparagoyānī. The merit of all people filling Aparagoyānī does not equal the merit of a single person in Pūrvavideha.
The merit of all people filling these three continents does not equal [the merit of] one person in Uttarakuru.
The merit of a single person exceeds the merit of all beings filling the four continents; yet this does not equal the merit of one of the Four Heavenly Kings (*cāturmahārājika*).

The merit of the Four Heavenly Kings does not equal that of one Śakra, and so on up to the sixth heaven. Even this does not equal the merit of a single Brahmā. This merit of Brahmā consists of both concentrated (*samāhita*) and dispersed (*vyutthita*) types.
To build a stūpa where none exists; to repair a ruined stūpa; to bring together a harmonious Saṃgha;
and to invite them to turn the Wheel of Dharma, so that those who have dispersed may be reunited—these are the four merits. Because they are equal to those of Brahmā, they are called "Brahma-merits.
As for "Noble merits," this refers to Arhats who, dwelling in their final body, have attained *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. This is it.

Furthermore, there are those of the three vehicles who take the Dharma as their essence. They study together the non-arising of phenomena and exhaust their afflictions, like wood being burned into charcoal.

Moreover, there are *sattvas* of noble merit who, through both self-cultivation and the transformation of others, sever afflictions by means of the path beyond words and enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Furthermore, there are *sattvas* of merit who, from the moment they first resolve their minds, gradually transform others and lead them into the Great [Vehicle].
Nirvāṇa. Measuring them in this way, the merit of Brahmā does not equal the merit of the Noble Ones; the merit of the Noble Ones does not equal the merit of the essence of the Noble Ones;
the merit of the essence of the Noble Ones does not equal the merit of a minor *sattva*; and the merit of a minor *sattva* does not equal the merit of a great *sattva*.
The merit of a great *mahāsattva* does not equal the merit of a person who, upon first hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, rejoices in it for the very first time.

Why is this? Because that [merit] is not the Buddha-dharma; it is not real; it is not perfect. Although they abide in a subsequent fruit, they do not equal those of us who possess the initial resolve.
Such is the meaning. Therefore, when people see a wish-fulfilling gem before their eyes, they instead strive to seek out ordinary crystal.
Having already encountered the sunlight, they yet compete to plot for lamps and candles; thus, even Bodhisattvas at the ultimate stage of skillful means cannot surpass the fiftieth person.
Nevertheless, when the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra uses the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) as a point of comparison, the matter remains relatively easy.

Now, to compare the merit of the sages with that of an ordinary person at the initial stage of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), were it not for the profound intent of the Great Sage, how could this be possible?
Believe this rare and marvelous thing; this is the basis for calculation.
What do you think? Is the merit obtained by this great donor not indeed vast?
These three Tathāgatas asked him about the merit of his sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the merit of this person is exceedingly great, immeasurable and boundless.
If a donor were merely to bestow all instruments of happiness upon sentient beings, their merit would be immeasurable; how much more so if they cause them to attain arhatship?"
[The Buddha spoke of] the fruit. Fourth, Maitreya answered that the merit of his sympathetic rejoicing was exceedingly great.
The Buddha told Maitreya: "I shall now speak to you clearly: this person, by means of all manner of articles of enjoyment, gives them as a gift to the four [assemblies]."

The merit obtained by causing hundreds of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* worlds of sentient beings in the six realms of existence to attain the fruit of arhatship is not equal to the merit of rejoicing upon hearing even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* by the fiftieth person.
A hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-billionth part—none of these can equal even a single fraction of it. Even by means of calculation or analogy, it cannot be known.
Ajita, such is the merit of the fifty-first person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* through successive transmission and rejoices in it;
it is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). How much more so for those who hear it at the very beginning within the assembly and rejoice?

This is the fifth correct calculation regarding the merit of rejoicing in the first category. The above constitutes the Buddha’s answer to Maitreya concerning the supreme merit of one who rejoices in their own heart.
Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, goes to a monastery and listens to or receives it for even a brief moment—

If there is a person sitting at a place where the Dharma is being preached, and another person comes and encourages them to sit and listen, or offers them half of their seat to sit upon, the merit of that person is such that, upon changing bodies, they will obtain the seat of Śakra, or the seat of Brahmā, or [the seat of a Cakravartin].
Regarding the place where a wheel-turning sage king sits, and the merit obtained by sharing a seat with him:

He immediately accepted the instruction. By hearing it for even a brief moment, the merit of this person is such that, upon changing bodies, he will be reborn in the same place as a *dhāraṇī*-possessing Bodhisattva.
With keen faculties and wisdom, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, he shall never be mute;
his breath shall not be foul; his tongue shall always be free from disease, as shall his mouth; his teeth shall not be stained black, nor yellow, nor sparse. Furthermore—
It is not deficient or missing; it is neither distorted nor crooked. The lips do not hang down, nor are they drawn back or shriveled;

this constitutes fifty merits in total, from being born in the same place as a Bodhisattva who possesses *dhāraṇī* up to the perfection of the marks of a Great Man (*puruṣalakṣaṇa*). These merits are used to characterize the person, thus also forming fifty.

This is the second chapter on the dharma-preacher, clarifying the merits of the fruit of the first chapter in order to encourage its circulation. First, the explanation:

Chapter. Next, the explanation of the sutra. First, regarding the "Teacher of the Dharma" (Dharmabhāṇaka): the meaning of this term has already been explained above in the passage concerning the five kinds of teachers of the Dharma.

Question: Since this chapter states that this is the fruit of sympathetic joy (anumodanā), why does it refer back to the title "Teacher of the Dharma"? Answer: [The text continues:]... [as previously stated].

The disciple penetrates both the beginning and the end; the Dharma Master [penetrates] only two or three. The meaning also encompasses the latter two, or perhaps has not yet entered the categories at all.
Why is this? If one considers the five stages as entering into the six faculties, then the five masters serve merely as causes for the six faculties.
Even if the five grades were situated outside the six faculties, the Five Teachers did not say they practiced contemplative cultivation (*vipaśyanā*);

they merely designated them as "penetrating" (*tong*) through recitation and exposition. Furthermore, this designation of "penetration" applies to the second and third grades, while also encompassing the fourth and fifth. Thus, at first glance, it appears to be a general term.

However, if one distinguishes them according to their stages, they have not yet entered the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). This is because they bear the title of "Dharma Master. Regarding that...
This chapter’s commentary is extensive; therefore, one must refer back to that [text] to explain the title of this present section.

Since the designation "Dharma Master" applies universally and is not restricted to the four levels of faith or the five stages (*pañca-varga*), we shall refer to that passage to clarify the heading of this chapter. Regarding "merit" (*guṇa*): previously, it referred to the merit at the beginning of the first stage;
now, it refers to what stands above the five stages—namely, the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and their internal and external adornment. Five...
Purity of the sense faculties is called external adornment; purity of the mental faculty is called internal adornment.
Furthermore, the manifestation of all forms and images—from those in the hells up to and including the Buddhas—within one's own body is called internal adornment.
From the hells above to the Buddhas below, all forms and images are manifested externally through the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation;
this is called external adornment. As it is with the faculty of the body, so it is with the other five. As it is with recitation and chanting, so it is with all else.
The four types are likewise so. As it was with the first category, it is even more so for the other four; as it was with the semblance [stage], it is twofold so for the partially true [stage].
This is the explanation of the meaning of "this world. When the practitioner hears this teaching on the benefits of these merits, they are overcome with joy beyond measure.
Seeking with tireless diligence, one contemplates and cultivates the four kinds of samādhi, causing one to swiftly enter subsequent faith and causing faith and progress to increase manifold;

this is the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of human benefit). Clearly recognizing that the Mahāyāna possesses great power, one becomes resolute and free from the net of doubt, suddenly casting away suspicions regarding provisional teachings;
this is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial counteraction). This marks the very beginning of semblance-understanding, surpassing the two vehicles.

This ultimate limit exceeds [the former] by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, as calculated previously. It points to the beginning to reveal the end, providing a definitive understanding of the ultimate.
The resolve of an ordinary person is equal to that of the Wondrous Enlightenment; this is the First Noble Truth, which is inconceivable.
This chapter elucidates these four meanings, and is therefore called the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master. Regarding the merits of the six sense faculties:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dapin) states: "Because form (*rūpa*) is pure, Prajñā is pure; because Prajñā is pure, form is pure. Because form is pure, the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are pure;
because Prajñā is pure, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is pure. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Zhengfahua) states that [the Buddha] is fully endowed with six thousand merits.

The *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* (Dajing) states: "A single sense-faculty of the Tathāgata is capable of seeing forms, hearing sounds, smelling fragrances, distinguishing tastes, perceiving tangibles, and cognizing phenomena (*dharma*)."
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states: "Ordinary people, by the power of the sutra, attain superior faculties;

although they have not yet entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), they can see both the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm with the physical eyes born of their parents. Now, in this sutra, the six sense organs are purified.
It is the same as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. By means of these merits, it adorns the six sense faculties, which is the same as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The nose seeing forms, the ears hearing sounds, and the consciousness of objects is the same as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. The fleshly eye possessing the functions of the divine eye, the wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye is the same as the treatises (*śāstra*).
Such are the words and their meanings. How can various masters, with their biased views, suppress the authentic scripture?

Now, according to this analysis: the three karmas of peaceful and blissful practice constitute the ten wholesome deeds (*daśakuśala*). Each of these ten wholesome deeds contains ten [factors], thus forming one hundred wholesome deeds.

Within each of these wholesome deeds there are ten suchnesses (*tathatā*), thus forming one thousand wholesome deeds. When these are applied to the transformation of others, they become two thousand. This is reckoned in relation to the Tathāgata’s chamber.
The robes of the Tathāgata and the seat of the Tathāgata thus become six thousand. The five kinds of Dharma-preachers all possess the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*);
each individual organ possesses one thousand merits. Furthermore, within a single mind, the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*) are complete;
as each realm possesses the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*), they constitute one hundred. Each sense organ universally apprehends the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Thus...
There are six hundred; when combined with the two adornments of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they constitute one thousand two hundred.

Each and every faculty (*indriya*) is adorned with both concentration and wisdom, thus equaling one thousand two hundred. If one discusses the purity of the six faculties, such purity does not concern whether merit is few or many.
If one speaks of adornment, it can be full, it can be diminished, and it can be equal—this is what is meant by "equal adornment."

Regarding "rigorous" (*yan*): each faculty has six thousand [aspects]. If one says "twelve hundred," it reveals its capacity for expansion; if one says "eight hundred," it reveals its capacity for contraction.
If one says "pure," there is neither expansion nor contraction, neither equality nor inequality, as the six faculties function interchangeably because the faculties are sovereign and inconceivable.
To judge this unilaterally is to lose the essential meaning. As for the stage of "semblance": if...
According to the four wheels, this refers to the stage of the iron wheel. According to the fifty-two stages, it refers to the ten levels of faith.
According to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, it refers to the ten great minds of goodness. Here, in relation to the "Ever-Diligent One," it refers to the third of the ten levels of faith.
Although the names differ across various sūtras, they are all identical in being the stage of semblance within the Perfect Teaching.
The text consists of two parts.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constantly Diligent:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this Lotus Sūtra, such a person shall obtain eight [qualities]."
The merit of a hundred eyes; the merit of twelve hundred ears; the merit of eight hundred noses; the merit of twelve hundred tongues;
the merit of eight hundred bodies; and the merit of twelve hundred minds. By means of these merits, one adorns the six sense faculties.
All are rendered pure.
First, there is a general enumeration of the numerical merits of the expansion and contraction of the six sense faculties.
Next, each is explained in detail through six chapters, each consisting of both prose and verse.
These sons and daughters of good family, with the pure physical eyes born of their parents,
see all the mountains, forests, rivers, and oceans within and without the trichiliocosm; from below, reaching down to the Avīci Hell, and from above,

reaching up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they also see all sentient beings therein, as well as the places where they are born through the causal conditions of karma and their resulting retributions— seeing them all completely.

[The Buddha] said, "Understood. In the first chapter on the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), it is explained that what is produced by one's parents is called the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). Yet, its range of vision exceeds that of the "divine eye" (*divya-cakṣus*).

The Brahmā King possesses a divine eye obtained as a karmic reward (*vipākaja*); within his own realm, he sees throughout the great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*). Beyond this great trichiliocosm lies the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
It acts as an obstruction to the eye, preventing one from seeing what is outside. If one is in another realm, one cannot see the entire trichiliocosm because it is not under one's governance;
a Lesser Arhat sees a small chiliocosm, a Great Arhat sees a trichiliocosm, and a Pratyekabuddha sees a hundred Buddha-worlds.
It is not obstructed by the wind-wheel, nor is there any separation between one's own realm and others'. Now, according to the sutras and treatises...
The eye that can see both the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm must be the celestial eye (*divyacakṣus*); why then is it called the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*)?

This refers to the stage of semblance (*sadr̥śabhūmi*) within the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). By the power of the sutras, it possesses the superior function of a faculty; however, as true realization has not yet been manifested, it cannot be termed the celestial eye.

It is still called the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). For example, it is like the provisional means (*upāya*) of the Hīnayāna: as long as one has not attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one does not yet possess what is termed the "divine eye" (*divya-cakṣus*) or "divine ear" (*divya-śrotra*).
It remains a body subject to segmentation (*paricchinna-kāya*), and is therefore called "born of father and mother. Although it is called the fleshly eye, it possesses the functions of the five eyes:
through the function of the divine eye, it sees all sentient beings and their karmic causes and conditions throughout the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm.
The function of the Dharma-eye: its vision is exceedingly pure. The function of the wisdom-eye: it perceives all at once the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm;
it perceives karma and perceives purity, and further completely subdues the afflictions above the dharma-realm. The function of the Buddha-eye:

as the Great Sūtra says, "Though one possesses the fleshly eye, it is called the Buddha-eye. Because it is the Buddha-eye, it is called pure. Because it is endowed with the five eyes, it is thus said.
Adorned with the ability to expand and contract, it is called the superior function of the faculties (indriya) and the mastery over the faculties.
How could it be understood merely as eight hundred or twelve hundred?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, amidst the great assembly, one preaches this Lotus Sūtra with a mind free from fear, listen now to its merits."
This person attains eight hundred meritorious and sublime eyes. Because they are thus adorned, their vision is exceedingly pure.
With the eyes born of their parents, they see the entirety of the triple-thousandfold world system, including the inner and outer Mount Merus, Sumeru, and the Iron Ring Mountains.

Together with all other mountain forests, the great oceans, and the rivers and streams—reaching downward as far as the Avīci Hell and upward as far as the Peak of Existence—all the sentient beings therein are seen by him entirely.
Although he has not yet attained the divine eye, the power of his physical eye is such as this.
This verse concludes the preceding chapter on the faculty of the eye.
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, or recites this sutra, [they shall obtain such merit].
If one explains or writes it down, one shall obtain twelve hundred merits of the ear. With this purified ear,
one hears all various kinds of speech and sounds within and without the trichiliocosm— from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra)—
including the sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and chariots, as well as the sounds of weeping and lamentation.
Sounds: the sound of conchs, the sound of drums, the sound of bells, the sound of gongs, the sound of laughter, the sound of speech, the voices of men, the voices of women, the voices of boys,

the voices of girls, the sound of the Dharma, the sound of what is not the Dharma, the sound of suffering, the sound of pleasure, the voices of ordinary persons, the voices of noble ones, the sound of joy,
the sound of lack of joy, the voices of devas, the voices of nāgas, the voices of yakṣas, the voices of gandharvas, the voices of asuras, and the voices of garuḍas.
The sound of rākṣasas; the sound of kiṃnaras; the sound of mahoragas; the sounds of fire, water, and wind;
the sounds of the hells; the sounds of animals; the sounds of hungry ghosts; the sounds of bhikṣus; the sounds of bhikṣuṇīs; the sounds of śrāvakas; and the sounds of pratyekabuddhas.
The voices of bodhisattvas and the voices of Buddhas— to speak briefly— whatever sounds exist, both internal and external, throughout the trichiliocosm,
he hears and knows them all with the pure, natural ears born of his parents, even though he has not yet attained the divine ear.
Thus he discriminates these various sounds without impairing his faculty of hearing.
Next is the Chapter on the Ear Faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). It universally hears the sounds of the ten dharma-realms, both internal and external, throughout the great trichiliocosm.

Hearing the sounds of the six realms of existence constitutes the two ears of flesh and heaven; hearing those of the two vehicles constitutes the wisdom ear (*prajñā-śrotra*); hearing those of the bodhisattvas constitutes the dharma ear (*dharma-śrotra*); and hearing those of the Buddhas constitutes the Buddha ear (*buddha-śrotra*).
Furthermore, the fleshly ear born of one's parents that can hear both the internal and external is the heavenly ear (*divya-śrotra*). To listen to it...
Attachment is the ear of wisdom (*prajñā-śrotra*). Non-delusion is the ear of the Dharma (*dharma-śrotra*). Hearing simultaneously and mutually is the ear of the Buddha (*buddha-śrotra*).
Applying this analogy to the eye, the eye is also like this: seeing humans and devas is the two eyes; seeing the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*) is the eye of wisdom;
seeing bodhisattvas is the eye of the Dharma; and seeing the Buddha is the eye of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The ears born of one's parents are pure and free from turbidity or defilement; with these constant ears, one hears the sounds throughout the three thousandfold world-system."
The sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen; the sounds of bells, gongs, conchs, and drums; the sounds of zithers, lutes, and harps; the sounds of flutes and pipes;
and the pure, beautiful voices of song—he hears them all without attachment. He is able to fully comprehend and discern the countless varieties of human voices.
Furthermore, they hear the voices of the various devas and their subtle, wondrous songs; they hear the voices of men and women, as well as the voices of boys and girls.
Within the mountains, rivers, and steep valleys, they hear the calls of the kalaviṅka birds and all the various birds such as the jīvañjīvaka, perceiving every one of their sounds.
The various sounds of agonizing pain from the hells; the cries of suffering from the many kinds of torment; the sounds of hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, seeking food and drink;
and the great voices that emerge when the asuras and others dwelling on the shores of the great ocean converse among themselves.
Thus, the one who preaches the Dharma dwells here in this world, yet hears those various sounds from afar without his faculty of hearing being impaired.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the cries and calls of birds and beasts—all these the preacher of the Dharma hears entirely from this place.
The sounds of speech from all the Brahma heavens—the Ābhāsvara, the Śubhakṛtsna, and even up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven—the Dharma Master dwelling here hears them all.
So too does he hear the voices of the entire assembly of bhikṣus and all the bhikṣuṇīs.
Whether one recites and chants the scriptures, or explains them to others, the Dharma Master abiding here hears them all.
Furthermore, there are various bodhisattvas who read and chant the scriptural teachings, or explain them to others, and compile commentaries to elucidate their meanings.

All such sounds and voices they shall hear: the Great Holy Sages, the Buddhas who transform sentient beings, as they expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma within the great assemblies; those who uphold this Lotus Sutra shall hear them all.
Throughout the trichiliocosm, all sounds—both internal and external—from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above, are heard by them without their faculty of hearing being impaired;
because their hearing is so keen and sharp, they are able to discern and know them all.
"Those who uphold this Lotus Sutra, though they have not yet attained the divine ear, possess such merit even with their ordinary ears.
This verse summarizes the preceding chapter on the faculty of hearing.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra,
they will accomplish eight hundred merits of the nose. With this purified faculty of the nose,
they will smell the various kinds of fragrances throughout the trichiliocosm— above, below, and in between, both inside and out— such as the fragrance of the sumanā flower.
The fragrance of *jāti* flowers, the fragrance of *mallikā* flowers, the fragrance of *campaka* flowers, the fragrance of *pāṭala* flowers,
the fragrance of red lotuses, the fragrance of blue lotuses, the fragrance of white lotuses; the fragrance of flowering trees, the fragrance of fruit trees,
the fragrance of sandalwood, the fragrance of aloeswood, the fragrance of *tamarapada*, the fragrance of *tagara*, and ten million kinds of blended incenses, whether in powder or in pills.
If one who upholds this sutra dwells in this world, they will be able to distinguish all types of scented unguents. Furthermore, they will specifically know the scents of sentient beings:
the scent of elephants, the scent of horses, the scent of oxen and sheep, and so forth; the scent of men, the scent of women, the scent of boys, and the scent of girls;
as well as the scents of grasses, trees, thickets, and forests. Whether near or far, all such scents shall be perceived and distinguished.
It is not so. Those who uphold this sutra, even while dwelling here, shall also smell the fragrances of the various devas in the heavens:
the fragrance of the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees, as well as the fragrance of māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, sandalwood, and aloeswood.
He perceives every scent produced from blended celestial incenses, such as powdered incense and various mixed floral perfumes;
furthermore, he perceives the bodily fragrance of the devas, including Śakra Devānām Indra, who is sporting in the five desires within his magnificent palace.
The fragrance when they sport; the fragrance when they preach the Dharma for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven atop the Hall of the Sublime Dharma;
the fragrance when they play in the various gardens; and the fragrances from the bodies of the male and female deities of other heavens—all these are smelled from afar.
In this manner, it extends successively even to the Brahma-world, and reaching as far as the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), the bodily fragrances of all those gods are likewise smelled. And...
They smell the incense burned by the devas, as well as the fragrance of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the bodily fragrance of the Buddhas;
they smell them all from afar and know their locations. Although they smell these fragrances, their faculty of the nose is neither impaired nor confused.
If they wish to distinguish them and explain them to others, their recollection is unerring.

The Chapter on the Nose Faculty is also like this. That which is born of one's parents is the fleshly nose; that which reaches throughout the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm is the celestial nose;
being unstained and unattached is the wisdom nose; discerning without error is the Dharma nose; and their simultaneous mutual functioning is the universal nose.

This refers to the Buddha’s nose. This chapter clarifies the mutual functioning [of the sense organs]: when the nose perceives what is pleasant or unpleasant, distinguishes between the noble and the lowly, and beholds the adornments of celestial palaces and the like, then the nose possesses the function of the eye.
When reading scriptures or preaching the Dharma, being able to know [the meaning] by smelling the fragrance, then the nose possesses the function of the ear.

When perceiving the flowers, fruits, and seeds of various trees, as well as the aroma of ghee and oil, then the nose possesses the function of the tongue. When entering or emerging from meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), [the nose functions].
In dhyāna there are eight contacts (*spraṣṭavya*). The playful indulgence in the five desires is likewise a phenomenon of contact. The nose has a physical function;

it knows the minds of those who are stained by desire, delusion, or anger, as well as those who cultivate goodness. The nose also has a mental function. Such is the sovereign and superior function of the nose faculty.
The five sense organs are likewise thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The nose of this person is pure; within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul things, he perceives and knows them all in their various forms."
Sumanā, Jāti, Tamāla, sandalwood, aloeswood, and cinnamon;

the fragrances of various flowers and fruits, as well as the scents of sentient beings—whether male or female—the teacher of the Dharma, though dwelling afar, perceives their presence by smelling these fragrances.
The great universal monarch, the minor wheel-turning kings and their sons, the ministers, and all the palace attendants—their locations are known by the scent.
The precious jewels worn upon their bodies, as well as the treasures hidden within the earth, and the precious women of the wheel-turning king—all are known by the scent.
The various articles for adorning the body—robes, necklaces, and the many kinds of scented ointments—one knows their bodies upon smelling them.
Whether the devas are walking, sitting, sporting, or performing miraculous transformations, those who uphold this Lotus Sūtra can know them all by smelling their fragrance.
The flowers, fruits, and seeds of all trees, as well as the fragrance of ghee and oil—wherever the upholder of this sutra dwells, he knows them all.
Even in deep and perilous mountain recesses where sandalwood trees are in full bloom, he can perceive by their scent all sentient beings dwelling therein.
Within the Iron Ring Mountains and the great oceans, among all sentient beings dwelling upon the earth, those who uphold this sutra will perceive their fragrance and know precisely where they are.
When the male and female asuras, along with their various retinues, are engaged in combat or sporting, those who uphold the sutra will likewise perceive their fragrance and be able to know them all.
In vast wildernesses and perilous narrow passes, lions, elephants, tigers, wolves, wild oxen, water buffaloes, and the like—he perceives their locations by their scent.
If there is one who is pregnant, he knows whether it is male or female; even those without sense organs or non-human beings, he can know them all by their scent.

By the power of smelling fragrances, they know when one has first conceived, whether the pregnancy will be successful or unsuccessful, and whether it will result in the birth of a son who brings peace and merit.
By the power of smelling fragrances, they know the thoughts of men and women—whether their minds are stained by desire, delusion, or anger—and they also know those who cultivate virtue.
The various hidden treasures within the earth—gold, silver, and all manner of precious gems contained in copper vessels—he can know them all by their scent.
Regarding the various kinds of necklaces whose value no one can discern, he knows their worth, high or low, as well as their origins and locations, simply by smelling their fragrance.
The various celestial flowers, such as the māndārava, mañjūṣaka, and pārijātaka trees—hearing their fragrance, he can know them all.
Regarding the celestial palaces, with their distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, and adorned with various precious flowers—hearing their fragrance, he can know them all.

In the celestial gardens, the sublime palaces, and the various halls for contemplating the wondrous Dharma, he dwells in the midst of them and enjoys himself; by smelling their fragrance, he knows them all.
Whether the devas are listening to the Dharma or indulging in the five desires, whether they are coming or going, walking, sitting, or lying down—he smells their fragrance and knows them all.
When celestial maidens are adorned with fine garments and fragrant flowers, as they move about and sport, one can know them all by their scent.
In this manner, proceeding further upward, even unto the Brahma world, one can know by scent those who enter and emerge from meditative absorption.
From the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), he can perceive through the scent of their initial birth and their passing away.
As for the assembly of bhikṣus who are ever diligent in the Dharma—whether sitting, walking in meditation, or reading and reciting the scriptures—he likewise knows them all.
Or perhaps beneath forest trees, sitting in meditation with single-minded concentration; those who uphold the sutras will perceive their fragrance and know exactly where they are.
Whether the Bodhisattvas’ resolve is firm as they sit in meditation, recite the scriptures, or preach the Dharma to others, they can all be known by means of their fragrance.
Wherever the World-Honored One dwells, revered by all, he preaches the Dharma out of compassion for sentient beings; by smelling their fragrance, he knows them all.
Sentient beings standing before the Buddha hear the sutras and are filled with joy; as they practice according to the Dharma, he knows them all by smelling their fragrance.
Although they have not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted (anāsrava) dharma that gives rise to the nose, this upholder of the sutra first attains this mark of the nose.
This verse concludes the preceding chapter on the faculty of the nose.
Furthermore, Nityodyukta, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra,
they will obtain twelve hundred merits of the tongue. Whether things be pleasant or unpleasant, delicious or not delicious,
or even bitter and astringent substances, when they come into contact with their tongue-root, they all transform into a supreme flavor, like the nectar of the gods.

There is nothing that is not beautiful. If, by means of the faculty of the tongue, one preaches amidst a great assembly, producing a profound and wondrous voice that can penetrate their hearts, causing them all to rejoice and experience happiness;
and furthermore, among the sons of gods, daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and all other devas.
Hearing this profound and wondrous sound, all those who had teachings to expound and discourses to deliver came to listen,
including the nāgas and nāga daughters, yakṣas and yakṣa daughters, gandharvas and gandharva daughters,
asuras and asura daughters, garuḍas and garuḍa daughters, kiṃnaras and kiṃnara daughters, and mahoragas.
The mahoraga women, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, all came to approach, pay respect, and make offerings.
Likewise, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; kings, princes, ministers, and their retinues;

minor wheel-turning kings and great wheel-turning kings, along with their seven treasures, their thousand sons, and their inner and outer attendants—all mounted their palaces and came together to listen.
Because this bodhisattva skillfully expounds the Dharma, brahmins, householders, and all the people within the kingdom will serve and make offerings to him for as long as they live.
Furthermore, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas always delight in seeing him.
In whichever direction this person resides, all buddhas will turn toward that place and preach the Dharma; he is fully able to receive and uphold it all.
All Buddha-dharmas. Furthermore, it can produce the profound and wondrous sound of the Dharma.
The same applies to the chapter on the tongue-organ (*jihvendriya*). That which is born of one's parents is the physical tongue of flesh;

it is able to produce the speech of the ten dharma-realms. Based on this, the meaning of the five tongues is clarified. Being able to produce the speech of the ten dharma-realms is precisely the [tongue of] Heaven.
It is the tongue. That which is unimpaired is the tongue of wisdom. That which is non-erroneous is the tongue of Dharma.

That which functions simultaneously and interchangeably is the tongue of the Buddha. Question: If bitter and foul flavors reach the tongue, they all transform into supreme flavors; when various forms reach the eye...
"Why does it not transform into a wondrous color? The previous answer was not analogous. Flavors can be either harmful or beneficial;
that which is harmful transforms, while that which is not harmful does not. Since various colors do not impair the eye, they are not analogous. Now, the explanation is not thus:
all forms are identical to the Buddha’s form, and all sounds are identical to the Buddha’s sound; all are equally pure. Thus, there is no impediment to the analogy. This is universal knowledge.
All phenomena of form and sound are without confusion or error; even their differentiation does not present any obstruction.
Since these are faculties of sovereign mastery, why would you conceive of them as being dull and obstructive?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The tongue-faculty of such a person is pure; they shall never experience foul flavors. Whatever they consume or eat shall all become nectar."
With a profound, pure, and wondrous voice, he preached the Dharma to the great assembly. Using various causes, conditions, and parables, he guided the minds of sentient beings;
all who heard him rejoiced and offered supreme offerings. So too did the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and asuras.
All come together with a mind of reverence to listen to the Dharma. If this person who preaches the Dharma wishes to fill the trichiliocosm with a sublime voice, they can achieve it at will.
Great and small wheel-turning kings, along with their retinues of a thousand sons, [all gather].
With palms joined in a heart of reverence, they constantly come to listen to and receive the Dharma.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas likewise, with joyful hearts, always delight in coming to make offerings. The Brahmā kings, the Māras, Īśvara, and Maheśvara—

Thus, the hosts of devas constantly come to where they are; the Buddhas and their disciples, hearing the sound of their preaching the Dharma, always keep them in mind and protect them, sometimes even manifesting themselves before them.
This verse concludes the preceding chapter on the tongue faculty.
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, or recites this sutra...

If one explains it or writes it down, one will obtain eight hundred merits of the body and attain a pure body like clear lapis lazuli, which all sentient beings will joyfully behold because of its purity.
Throughout the great trichiliocosm, whenever sentient beings are born or die, [they shall see this body].
The superior and inferior, the beautiful and the ugly, those born in good realms and those born in evil realms—all appear therein.
Furthermore, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Mount Meru, Mount Mahāmeru, and all other kings of mountains, as well as the sentient beings within them, all appear therein.
From the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence above, everything and all sentient beings therein appear within it.
Manifestation: Whether it be the preaching of the Dharma by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Buddhas, their physical forms and images all appear within the body.
It is the same for the chapter on the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*): everything that exists in the world appears within the body; this is the function of the fleshly body.

Extending upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it manifests within the body; this is the function of the celestial body (*devakāya*). When it manifests within the bodies of those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is the function of the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).

When it manifests within the bodies of Bodhisattvas, it is the function of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). When it manifests within the body of a Buddha, it is the function of the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*).
These manifest simultaneously and perfectly; they are mutually functional at once—this is the "Middle" (*madhya*). They are simultaneously without error—this is the "Provisional" (*upāya*).
At that time, there was no attachment; it was emptiness.
Then the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one upholds the Lotus Sutra, their body will be exceedingly pure, like that clear lapis lazuli; all sentient beings will joyfully behold them."
Furthermore, just as a pure, bright mirror reflects all forms and images, so too does the Bodhisattva, within his purified body, perceive everything that exists in the world.
He alone perceives with perfect clarity; what others do not see, he sees. Within the three thousandfold world system, he beholds all living beings.
Devas, asuras, hell-beings, pretas, and animals—all such forms appear within his body.
The palaces of the devas and so forth, up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), as well as the Cakravāḍa mountains, Mount Meru, and Mahāmeru—all are manifested therein.
The waters of all great oceans appear entirely within their bodies. Buddhas, śrāvakas, and the sons of the Buddha—bodhisattvas—whether alone or in assembly, all appear preaching the Dharma.
Although they have not yet attained the subtle body of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) that is free from outflows (anāsrava), [all these things manifest].
"By means of the pure, eternal essence, all things manifest within it.
This verse concludes the chapter on the body and faculties.
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if any son or daughter of good family should receive, uphold, and recite this sutra after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, [they shall attain these benefits].
Whether reading, reciting, explaining, or transcribing it, one attains twelve hundred merits of the mental faculty.
By means of this purified mental faculty, even upon hearing a single verse or a single phrase, one penetrates immeasurable and boundless meanings.
Having understood these meanings, one is able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse for as long as one month, four months, or even up to a year. All...
The teachings he expounds accord with their underlying meaning and do not contradict the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Whether he speaks of worldly scriptures, secular discourse, or the means of livelihood, all are in accordance with the True Dharma.

He fully knows the mental activities, the movements of the mind, and the conceptual proliferations of the minds of all sentient beings throughout the six realms within the trichiliocosm; even though...
Although they have not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), their faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is thus pure.
Whatever this person contemplates, deliberates, or speaks is entirely the Buddha-dharma; it is all true and without exception, and is also that which was spoken in the sūtras of previous Buddhas.

As for those who cite from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* the passage regarding "paying homage to those who know the Dharma," and from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* the account of a bhikṣu paying homage to a layperson—this interpretation is not correct.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the constant ritual serves to manifest the resolve to revere the Dharma; because one seeks instruction from such a person, one temporarily sets aside formal etiquette to pay homage to an inferior.
In the *Vimalakīrti*, having already received the profound grace of hearing the Dharma, one thus forgets the transgression [of violating monastic decorum].
One should pay respect, yet not adhere to worldly conventions. If one follows the correct ritual of the Mahāyāna, which transcends worldly norms, one must not cause the Way to bow before the secular.
Do not lightly establish such practices; all [other views] differ from this. It is not for the sake of propagating [such views], as they are neither the Great nor the Small Vehicle’s teaching.
Some say that if a Bodhisattva does not perform this prostration, it constitutes an offense. Now, I say that if there is an offense, it must...

According to the established regulations, there is no textual basis in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* for minor offenses; thus, there is no formal restraint regarding them. Furthermore, it is said that a Bodhisattva must necessarily guard against natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), whereas they may occasionally exceed the prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
