Now, I maintain that one must certainly not exceed these prohibitions. If one exceeds them, can it be called "maintaining"? If one exceeds them, it cannot be called "maintaining. One who breaks [the precepts] is no longer a Bodhisattva.
When forgetting an offense while saving sentient beings, the priority lies in the peace and security of those beings. If the beings are secure, why make such distinctions?

Regarding the nature of prohibition: we now pay homage to the fourfold assembly. What fault has the salvation of the masses committed? Therefore, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools universally prohibit the practice of secular prostration.
Since the ritual itself would not even accept it, the principle of salvation cannot be established.
Among the fourfold assembly, there were those who gave rise to thoughts of anger and impurity, speaking with harsh words and insults, saying:
"This ignorant bhikṣu, from where has he come? He says of himself, 'I do not slight you,' and grants us the prediction that we shall become Buddhas.
We have no need for such false predictions. Thus it continued for many years, and they were constantly...
Even when reviled, he did not give rise to anger, but constantly spoke these words: "You shall become Buddhas.
While he was speaking these words, the multitude sometimes struck and pelted him with sticks, wood, tiles, and stones; yet even as they fled and stayed far away, he still cried out in a loud voice:
"I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas. Because he constantly spoke these words, [his merit] increased.
The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who were arrogant toward him were called "Never-Disparaging.

Second, this clarifies the fault of those who disparage him not receiving even one of the four [teachings]. Because they were filled with anger and impurity, they reviled him, saying he was "without wisdom.
Since wisdom knows the principle, and they called him "without wisdom," they did not accept even a single teaching; thus, the monks did not accept them.
The person is one and the same. From where have they come? They do not accept practice; this is the first "one" of non-acceptance. They receive false prophecies; they do not accept the teaching;

this is the second "one" of non-acceptance. Having passed through many years, they are constantly reviled; this is the fourth "one" of non-acceptance regarding the binding of the provisional and the revealing of the real.
They flee and dwell far away, shouting aloud; they likewise do not accept. This is the non-acceptance of the revelation of the near.
This clarifies that the first of the four [aspects] of the original ground is the constant utterance of these words; thus, it concludes that those who believe do so with unceasing deep faith.
That the fourfold assembly bestowed upon him the name "Not-Disparaging" (Adhimātra) concludes that those who disparage him did not cease their insults.
Question: When Śākyamuni appeared in the world, he hesitated and did not speak; yet Viśeṣacintin saw him and spoke without hesitation. Why was this? Answer:

Those who already possessed goodness were protected by Śākyamuni through his subtle means. Those who originally lacked goodness were strengthened and transformed by Viśeṣacintin through his powerful methods.
This forceful transformation served as the condition for them to hear the Dharma in the future, as detailed below.

Following the sutra text: "He encountered the teaching of Constantly Not Disparaging regarding the three types of bodhi. △ Below, the third section clarifies the retributions for both praise and disparagement.
The initial text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the retribution; second, correlating the past with the present.

When this bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard in the midst of the empty sky the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—previously taught by the Buddha King of Majestic Voice—as twenty quadrillion verses.

He was able to receive and uphold them all, and immediately attained the aforementioned purification of the faculty of the eye, as well as the purification of the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Having attained this purification of the six faculties, his lifespan was further increased.
For two hundred trillion nayuta years, he extensively preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of others.
At that time, the fourfold assembly of those with overweening pride—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—despised this man who had been given the name "Not-Disdainful" (*Adhimāna*).
However, they saw that he had attained the power of great supernormal faculties, the power of eloquence in joyful exposition, and the power of great sublime tranquility. Upon hearing this...

All who heard what he taught believed, submitted, and followed him. This Bodhisattva further transformed and guided thousands of millions of billions of beings, causing them to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After his life ended, he encountered two thousand billion Buddhas, all of whom were named Candrasūryapradīpa.
Within their teachings, they preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. By these causes and conditions, he again encountered two...
There were ten billion Buddhas, all equally named Cloud Sovereign Lamp King (*Meghasvararāja*).

Within the teachings of these Buddhas, because he upheld, recited, and read this sutra, and expounded it for the fourfold assembly, he attained this constant purity of the eye, as well as the purity of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
With his faculties purified, he preached the Dharma among the fourfold assembly with a mind free from fear and attained great power;
this was the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Never-Disparaging, who made offerings to, reverently honored, respected, and praised such a multitude of Buddhas.
Having planted various roots of goodness, they will later encounter thousands of millions of billions of buddhas, and under the teachings of those buddhas as well, they will preach this sutra.
Having accomplished such merit, they shall attain buddhahood.

First, the explanation of the karmic retribution for those who possess faith. Regarding the discourse on the three types of retribution for the faithful: attaining the purification of the six sense faculties in the present life is the retribution in the present (*drstadharma-vedanīya*).

Encountering Dīpaṃkara Buddha is the retribution in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*). Encountering two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas is the retribution in subsequent lives (*aparāpariya-vedanīya*). This is the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
This purity of bodily action is the power of eloquence; this purity of verbal action is the power of sublime tranquility;
this purity of mental action is the attainment of great majesty. What do you think? Was the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging at that time anyone else?
It was none other than myself.
This connects the ancient and the modern.
Had I not, in past lives, upheld, recited, and read this sutra, and had I not explained it to others, I would not have been able to quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
It was at the abodes of former Buddhas that I upheld, recited, and read this [sutra].
Sūtra: Because one explains it for others, one will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Second, having already cited those who benefited from past faith, this serves to encourage compliance. Next, the retribution for those who disparage [the teaching] is explained.
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, explaining the attainment of the fruit; second, correlating the past with the present.

Because those four assemblies—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—of that time treated me with contempt out of a mind of anger, for two hundred billion kalpas they never encountered a Buddha, did not hear the Dharma, and did not see the Saṃgha.

For a thousand kalpas, they will undergo great suffering and affliction in the Avīci Hell. Once these karmic retributions are exhausted, they will again encounter the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who will instruct and transform them in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
First, it is explained that those who disparage [the teaching] obtain both good and evil fruits. Because they slander, they fall into the evil realms;

yet because they have heard the name of Buddha-nature, by the power of the "poisoned drum," they obtain a good retribution. Thus, striking the two drums of faith and disparagement serves as the dual causes for future births. Question:
If one falls into suffering due to slandering, why does a Bodhisattva act as a cause for such suffering? Answer: It is because they lack goodness.
Because of this cause, one who does not slander yet falls [into evil] will certainly gain benefit by slandering and thus falling into evil. It is like a person who has fallen to the ground;
they must rise back up from that very ground. Therefore, through "righteous slander," one is brought out of "erroneous falling."

"O Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? Were those four assemblies who constantly disparaged this bodhisattva at that time anyone other than these five hundred bodhisattvas in this assembly, such as Bhadrapāla and the others; these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, such as Siṃhacandrā and the others;
and these five hundred upāsakas, such as Buddhamati and the others—all of whom are now established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Regarding the three types of awakening, those who are non-retrogressive are the ones who first convened the fourfold assembly throughout the past and present.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings great benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and is able to cause them [to attain it].
Regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for this reason all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should,
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, constantly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe this sutra.

Next, by citing the contrary to manifest the compliant, and by exhorting to uphold [the teaching] to preclude its disparagement: the sutra possesses great power and will ultimately bring about great fruit.
One must strive to diligently practice the five kinds of conduct.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.

The verses consist of nineteen and a half lines; the first fifteen and a half lines merely recite the causes and effects of faith and slander, while the final four lines recite the exhortation to uphold [the teaching].
Within the former section, there are again two parts.

In the past, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja). His spiritual wisdom was immeasurable; he guided all beings and was venerated by devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits alike.
The first one and a half lines provide the fundamental basis for the events described above.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, at a time when the Dharma was about to perish, there was a bodhisattva named Sadāparibhūta. At that time, the fourfold assembly...
Regarding attachment to dharmas:
in the third section of the *Pūrva-kalpa*, there are three parts. The first, consisting of one and a half lines, introduces both individuals together.

As for those who "attach to dharmas," it is said that this dharma cannot be demonstrated; if one definitively asserts that it exists, this is attachment to dharmas, and so on, up to definitively asserting that it does not exist.
It is not non-existent; it is also called "one who adheres to dharmas. The *Buddhapiṭaka* states:

"The sin of one who harms the people of Jambudvīpa with a wheel of swords is still slight compared to the sin of one who, possessing a mind of attainment, preaches the Mahāyāna. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"To dispute 'existence' with 'non-existence,' or even to dispute 'neither existence nor non-existence' with 'existence' and 'non-existence,' is like a leather bag [struggling against] a dragon."
Even with a rope, one cannot avoid suffering. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Buddhas teach the Dharma of emptiness primarily to transform those attached to existence.
If there are those attached to emptiness, the Buddhas cannot transform them. If one definitively asserts that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, [one remains untransformed].

This is called the discourse of the deluded. If one loses the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, then whether acting for oneself or transforming others, all such acts are termed "attachment to dharmas.
If one attains the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, then both self and others are free from attachment.

Therefore, those who receive the teachings of skillful means do not yet escape the charge of slander during the stage of the ordinary person (*bālapṛthagjana*). Thus, there are words of the perfect and true [teaching] that speak of neither receiving nor slighting.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa (Not-Disparaging) went to where they were and said to them, "I do not disparage you;

all of you who practice the Way shall surely become Buddhas. When the people heard this, they treated him with contempt, reviled, and abused him; yet the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa was able to endure it all.
The next two and a half lines of verse describe the gains of those who do not disparage [the teaching] and the losses of the fourfold assembly.
Once their transgressions are exhausted, at the time of death, they shall hear this sutra; by the power of their supernormal faculties, their six sense organs will become pure.

His lifespan was increased. Furthermore, he extensively preached this sutra for the sake of all people. All those who were attached to dharmas received the Bodhisattva’s instruction and transformation, being brought to fulfillment and established in the Buddha-way.
After his passing, the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging encountered countless Buddhas because he had preached this sutra.
They attained immeasurable merit, gradually perfected their virtues, and swiftly realized the Buddha-way. At that time, "Not Disparaging" was none other than myself.

As for the fourfold assembly who were attached to the Dharma at that time, they heard the words of Not Disparaging: "You shall become Buddhas. By these causes and conditions, [they attained liberation].

They have encountered innumerable Buddhas. These five hundred bodhisattvas in this assembly, as well as the fourfold assembly of laymen and laywomen of pure faith who are now listening to the Dharma before me, were all encouraged by me in previous lives to hear and receive this sutra.
The foremost Dharma: to reveal and instruct others so that they may abide in nirvana. One should uphold such a sutra as this from lifetime to lifetime.
These ten lines of verse summarize the above results of faith and slander, and conclude the discussion of the past and present.
For billions upon billions of kalpas, until an inconceivable time has passed, one may finally hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

For billions upon billions of kalpas, until an inconceivable time has passed, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach this sūtra at such times. Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the practitioner—

Having heard this sutra, do not give rise to doubt or confusion; you should with single-minded devotion widely expound this sutra. Thus, in life after life, you shall encounter the Buddhas and swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.

The four verses above exhort one to uphold [the teaching]. This concludes the third chapter, "Never Disparaging," which cites those who abide in faith and those who disparage it—both their transgressions and blessings—as proof, and thus completes the exhortation to circulate [the sutra].
Commentary on the Title of Chapter Twenty-one, "The Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata," of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the term "Tathāgata," it is explained as above in the "Life Span" chapter. As for "supernatural powers" (*ṛddhi*):

"supernatural" (*shen*) means unfathomable, and "power" (*li*) refers to efficacious function. That which is unfathomable is the profound, natural essence; the supernatural resides within, which is the fundamental substance (*ti*). This is the primary principle (*zong*).

When applied to function, the power of transformation is great; this is precisely "function" (yòng). The Buddha’s exposition of the fundamental and the manifested (benji) through the power and function of the Wheel of Speech has already been completed previously.
Now, through the Wheel of Body, he manifests this supreme function to cause the teaching of the fundamental and the manifested to circulate among the masses.
Therefore, it is said that "the essence is profound and the power is great. Within this, the profound Dharma is entrusted, manifesting ten kinds of great powers.

Therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on Spiritual Powers" (Rddhy-abhisamskāra-parivarta). From here below, there are eight chapters in total concerning the entrustment and circulation [of the teaching]. This section is divided into three parts:

first, the two chapters on spiritual powers and entrustment, which constitute the formal entrustment and circulation; second, the five chapters beginning with Bhaiṣajyarāja, which concern circulation through the transformation of others;
and third, the Samantabhadra chapter, which concerns circulation through one's own practice. The present chapter clarifies how the bodhisattvas receive [the teaching].

The entrustment to propagate the sutra follows. In this chapter, the Tathāgata places his hand upon [the bodhisattvas'] heads to confer the charge. This chapter consists of both prose and verse. The prose section is divided into three parts: first, the bodhisattvas receive the command;
second, the Buddha manifests his supernatural powers; and third, the essential points are summarized and they are exhorted to uphold the teaching.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds, who had emerged from the earth,
all stood before the Buddha with single-minded palms joined, gazing up at his venerable countenance and addressed the Buddha, saying:
First, the sūtra narrator describes the ritual of veneration. △ Second, the aspiration to propagate the sūtra, which is divided into three parts.
"World-Honored One, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, at one time"—this refers to the period following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Wherever the emanations of the World-Honored One reside, in those two locations, and at the place of his parinirvāṇa, this sutra should be extensively preached. Why is this? Because we ourselves also desire to obtain this.
The True and Pure Great Dharma: to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and make offerings to it.

Regarding the three vows, it is not merely that one obeys the command to benefit others; one also personally vows that this True and Pure Great Dharma shall provide universal relief and shared excellence.
△ From "At that time" onwards is the second section, manifesting ten spiritual powers, which is divided into two parts. First, the object [of the manifestation].
Next, he manifested his supernormal powers.

At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] Mañjuśrī and the rest— immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had long resided in the Sahā world, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Before all the assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.

First, the assembly addressed is clarified. Regarding Mañjuśrī: he is the assembly manifested through his provisional traces. Regarding those who have long resided [there]: they are the primary assembly from the lower direction.
They should not be identified as merely the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of supernatural beings. Regarding "all":

this refers to those who have come from other directions and those who have come following the emanation-bodies of the Buddha; these are precisely the subjects of the subsequent passage beginning with "and all. Question: Why is it that only those from below are seen?
When he was about to make his vow, why did he not see Mañjuśrī and the others making their vows? Answer:

The previous passage states, "In my land there are naturally bodhisattvas who are able to uphold this sutra," which means that [the vows] were simultaneously attained by them as well. △ From here below, the supernatural powers are truly manifested.
There are ten [reasons].
He manifests great supernatural power and extends his broad and long tongue upward as far as the Brahma-world.

Regarding this single manifestation of the tongue: the teaching expounded in the present sutra opens up the three to reveal the one; this refers to the description of the preceding traces to explain this opening.

This is the manifestation. Internally secret and externally revealed, it sets aside the immediate to manifest the remote, clarifying how [the Buddha] benefits sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—all of which is truthful and not false.
This explains its function during the intermediate period. As for those of merit, their tongue-attribute reaches the nose; for the Buddhas of the Tripitaka, it reaches the hairline;
now, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven, it transcends both the ordinary and the sage, extending to the summit of the Pure Heavens. Since the mark is thus...
This extraordinary account is all the more worthy of belief. I privately remark that what is expressed here differs from the intent of the *Smaller Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra*,
for it states that from every single pore, immeasurable and innumerable rays of light are emitted, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions in their entirety.
The Buddhas upon lion thrones beneath the various jewel trees did likewise; they extended their broad and long tongues and emitted immeasurable light.
When Śākyamuni Buddha and the Buddhas beneath the jewel trees manifested these supernatural powers, it lasted for a full hundred thousand years.
Second, light radiates from all the pores of his body, illuminating the ten directions everywhere until there is no place that is not bright;

this signifies that the realm of wisdom is exhaustive. Previously, the brilliance emitted from the white tuft of hair began in the east, signifying the seven stages of expedient means by which one first perceives the single principle.
Now that the present "Root Chapter" has concluded, he emits all-encompassing light to illuminate all lands, enabling those at the initial stage of cause to reach their ultimate fulfillment.

Regarding the Perfectly Awakened One, they ultimately attain the Buddha-wisdom; this is because they perceive the profound principle, thereby increasing their path and diminishing their births until they reach the vicinity of the ultimate.
The emanations of the various Buddhas are likewise so. Since these characteristics are identical, each within their own land—
The benefit was likewise so.
Thereafter, he withdrew his tongue-organ. He cleared his throat three times;
this is the manner of one about to speak, and it is also a sign of clearing the channels. [It lasted] forty-odd...
For many years, the truth was concealed; now it has been fully unfolded without any lingering obstruction.

This is the great matter of my appearance in the world reaching full realization; therefore, I clear my throat. This is precisely to manifest the outward sign of my desire to entrust this Dharma to the various Bodhisattvas.
To guide and benefit sentient beings in future generations, he was about to speak of this matter; therefore, he cleared his throat. This signifies the entrustment of the fundamental [teaching].
Clearing the throat carries two meanings: first, clearing the throat to conclude the matter; second, clearing the throat to entrust it to others. Regarding these two meanings:
"the matter" refers to the fundamental and the manifested, while "entrusting to others" means to ensure its transmission throughout future ages.
Together they snap their fingers. These two sounds reach throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions.

The four finger-snaps signify rejoicing (*anumodana*): rejoicing in the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*) as they collectively enter the perfect path; this represents the traces (*traces of manifestation*).
Rejoicing in the perfect path that increases wisdom and diminishes birth; this represents the fundamental nature (*the root*). Rejoicing in all bodhisattvas who uphold...

The Great Dharma of True Purity brings forth rejoicing for future generations, who shall obtain the unsurpassed treasure. In this single snap of the fingers, one penetrates vertically through the three periods of time and extends horizontally throughout the ten directions.
The earth shook in six ways.
Regarding the shaking of the five stages in six ways: this symbolizes the progression from the initial mind to the final mind, shaking ignorance six times.
Now, it is clarified that [the light] further shakes the six sense faculties of all people, causing them to attain purity.
Among them, the sentient beings— devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth— all saw this Sahā world by the spiritual power of the Buddha.
He saw immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas beneath various jeweled trees, seated upon lion thrones;
he also saw Śākyamuni Buddha together with the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, seated upon a lion throne within a jeweled stupa.
Furthermore, he saw immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly, surrounding them with reverence.
They circumambulated Śākyamuni Buddha. Having seen this, they were all filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.
This sixth "Universal Vision" assembly generally clarifies the four "Ones," signifying that the Way of all Buddhas is identical.
From now on, it shall likewise be so. The five thousand [monks] rose and departed; though moved by the three transformations, they had already lost their original resolve.

This is the manifestation of benefit. It is appropriate to manifest extinction where there is no extinction. By following the various bodhisattvas who propagate the sutras, one attains the Way and enters the Buddha-wisdom, no different from those present in this assembly today.
This also signifies that there is a single capacity for those in the future. As for what is called "capacity" (or "potential"):
The significance of this opportunity should be understood as comprehensive. In the future, it will bring about four kinds of singular benefits for all.
At that moment, the various devas in the void cried out with a loud voice:
"Beyond these immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there is a land named Sahā. Within it dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
“Nī, now for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he shall preach the Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the teaching of the bodhisattvas,
which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas. You all should rejoice with a profound heart, and you should also pay homage and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.”
The sound proclaimed from within the seven voids signifies that there shall be a single teaching in the future.
Upon hearing this voice from the void, those sentient beings join their palms toward the Sahā world and speak these words:
"Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha! Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha!"
Eighth, we take refuge and pay homage as disciples of the Buddha. This signifies that there shall be one person among humanity in the future.

With various flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and all manner of ornaments for the body, as well as rare jewels and exquisite objects, we all together scatter them from afar toward the Sahā world.
These scattered offerings come from the ten directions, gathering like clouds and transforming—
They formed a jeweled canopy that completely covered all the Buddhas present.
As for the various objects that came from afar like gathering clouds, they symbolize that there will be those in the future who practice the One Vehicle.
At that time, the worlds of the ten directions were unimpededly pervasive, as if they were a single buddha-field.
That the ten directions are identical and unified like a single buddha-field expresses the oneness of principle. Question:

How is it known that the manifestation of the ten signs expresses both the present intention and the future intention? Answer: The text states: "By means of the Tathāgata’s supernormal power, I [entrust this] as a commission."
Because of the accumulation of this sutra, even if one were to express and manifest it, its meaning would remain clear and inexhaustible.

△ From "At that time, the Buddha addressed the Superior Practice Bodhisattva" (爾時佛告上行) onwards is the third section, the Essential Summary and Entrustment. This text consists of four parts: first, the praise and entrustment;
second, the essential summary and entrustment; third, the exhortation and entrustment; fourth, the explanation of the entrustment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, including Śikhin and the others: "The spiritual power of the Buddhas is thus immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
If, by means of such spiritual power, I were to [manifest] throughout immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis..."
Even if one were to spend incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) to proclaim the merits of this sutra for the sake of entrustment, one could not exhaust them.
This was the initial praise and entrustment.
To state the essentials: all the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata, and all the sovereign spiritual powers (*vibhūti-rddhi*) of the Tathāgata—
All the secret treasuries of the Tathāgata and all the most profound matters of the Tathāgata are proclaimed and clearly expounded within this sutra.

Second, regarding the summary of the essential entrustment, there are four points: the two gates of the fundamental and the manifested each have their own essential principle and function; these constitute the two gates.
The essence of these two locations is no different; their names crown these three and encompass them all. As for the essentials of this single section, how could they exceed this?
Therefore, they are gathered together to ensure their circulation. "All dharmas" means that everything is the Buddha-dharma.
This concludes the designation of "all as wondrous. "All powers" refers to unimpeded penetration and mastery.
The eight masteries are the wondrous function of this knot. "All secret treasuries" means that throughout all places, everything is the true reality (*dharmatā*);
this is the wondrous essence of this knot. "All profound matters" refers to cause and effect as profound matters;
this is the wondrous core doctrine of this knot. "All of these are proclaimed and clearly explained in this sutra" summarizes the entire scripture, which consists of nothing other than these four.
Having done so, I grasp its essential pivot and hand it over to you.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you all should with one mind receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and practice according to the teaching.
In whatever land there may be those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe [this], and practice according to the teaching...
Regarding the practice of cultivation: wherever this scripture is kept— whether in a garden, a grove, beneath a tree, in a monastery,
in a layperson’s house, in a hall, or in mountain valleys and wildernesses—
one should erect a stūpa at those places to make offerings.
Third is the exhortation and entrustment.
Why is this so? You should know that this very place is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
It is here that all Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma; and it is here that all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa.

Nirvāṇa. Fourth, the entrustment. As stated above: "Wherever this scripture is located, one should erect a stūpa there. Regarding the essential teachings within the scripture, they consist of four matters:
the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) explains the profound matters mentioned above; and the attainment of *bodhi* explains the secret matters mentioned above.

The entry into the womb, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the explanation of all dharmas mentioned above, and the entry into nirvana, which explains the supernormal powers mentioned above—these four essentials encompass the entirety of the sūtra’s text;
therefore, stūpas should be erected for each of them. As for what is meant by "essentials":
attaining bodhi is the Dharmakāya, turning the wheel of Dharma is Prajñā, and entering nirvana is Vimukti. These three dharmas constitute the secret.

The "Treasury" (garbha) is that in which the Buddha dwells; this is precisely the meaning of a *stūpa*. The *Āgama* states: "When a Buddha appears in the world, *stūpas* are erected at only four places:

the place of birth, the place of attaining the Way (*bodhi*), the place of turning the wheel of the Dharma, and the place of entering *nirvāṇa*. The sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is the place where the Dharma-body is born.
However, as for using the small to certify the great: by opening the small, it is immediately the great; therefore, it can serve as proof. That [text] then proceeds from...
This concerns the facts; here, they are borrowed to illustrate the underlying principle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse.
There are sixteen lines of verse: the first four lines eulogize the ten supernormal powers, and the subsequent twelve lines eulogize the summary of the essential points.
The entrustment [concludes with] the following two lines, which summarize the merit of such a person by praising the four dharmas in general.
From "If one can uphold them, it is as if I have already seen them" onwards, the second section consisting of eight and a half lines praises the four dharmas individually.
The Buddhas, saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers; for the sake of gladdening sentient beings, they manifest immeasurable spiritual transformations.
Their tongues reach up to the Brahma-heaven, and their bodies emit countless rays of light; for those who seek the Buddha-way, they manifest these rare and wondrous events.
The sound of the Buddhas’ coughing and the sound of their snapping fingers resound throughout the lands of the ten directions, and the earth quakes in six ways;
because they are able to uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all the Buddhas rejoice and manifest immeasurable supernatural powers.
The first four verses extol the ten supernatural powers mentioned above;
because they entrust this sutra, the praise for those who receive and uphold it cannot be fully exhausted even throughout immeasurable kalpas.
The merit of this person is boundless and inexhaustible; it is like the empty space of the ten directions, whose limits cannot be found.
Regarding the summary verse that concludes [the section], the first two lines provide a general summary of the four dharmas by simply stating that [the Buddha] entrusts this sutra.
This continues until the phrase "whose limits cannot be found," which fully encompasses the four meanings; for all four meanings are themselves without limit.
Furthermore: △ Next, the four dharmas are separately versified in four [stanzas]:
"Those who are able to uphold this sutra have already seen me, as well as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and all his manifested bodies."
Furthermore, it is seen that today I am teaching and transforming various bodhisattvas.
The first one and a half verses praise all dharmas; these are precisely the praises of the "Sublime Names" mentioned above.
To uphold the Dharma is to uphold the body of the Buddha, for there is no other [dharma] mixed with it. That Dharma is secret and wondrous.
Those who are able to uphold this sutra shall cause me, my emanations, and the Buddha Prabhūtaratna who has entered parinirvāṇa, all to rejoice.
They shall also behold and make offerings to the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions, as well as those of the past and future, and likewise cause them to attain joy.
This verse describes the wondrous function. My own verse and the two verses concerning my emanations praise his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).

This supernormal power exhorts the Buddhas to rejoice, thereby fully expressing that those Buddhas who sit at the site of enlightenment have attained a secret and essential Dharma, which those who can uphold this sutra shall likewise attain before long.
The third single verse praises the sublime essence:
those who are able to uphold this sutra will possess inexhaustible eloquence in explaining the meanings, names, and phrases of all dharmas.

Like the wind in the sky, they shall be entirely without obstruction. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, they will understand the sūtras spoken by the Buddha—their causes, conditions, and sequence—and explain them according to their meaning as it truly is. Like the light of the sun and moon, they will be able to dispel all darkness.
This person, walking through the world, is able to extinguish the darkness of sentient beings. He instructs immeasurable bodhisattvas so that they ultimately abide in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
These four verses are the sublime essence; these four stanzas praise the profoundly deep matters. They teach and transform all bodhisattvas so that they ultimately abide in the One Vehicle.
This One Vehicle is the sublime essence of cause and effect.
Therefore, those who possess wisdom, having heard these merits and benefits, should uphold this sutra after my parinirvāṇa.
Such persons will have no doubt whatsoever regarding the Buddha-way.

One line and a half of verse serve as the summary. The above constitutes the first chapter, "The Supernatural Powers," which concludes the account of the Bodhisattvas receiving their mandates to propagate the sutra.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Twenty-two: "Entrustment."
This chapter constitutes the second instance of the Tathāgata’s touching of the crown of the head (mūrdhābhiṣeka) and the entrustment for its circulation.
Regarding the commentary on this text, first, others have distinguished the sequence of the chapters; only then does the present sub-commentary provide the correct explanation.

First, both Ci'en and An-guo maintain that this chapter should be moved to follow the "Chapter on Encouraging the Aspiration" (*Kuan-fa pin*). If it were placed here, there would be eight contradictions and ten impossibilities.

Although my vision is but that of one looking through a tube, I have received considerable instruction. At every lecture assembly, I have had the honor of receiving your compassionate teachings and the guidance you bestowed for our salvation;
thus, I have had deep grounds for reliance. Recently, I observed Master Xiu’s *Fahua Yuanjing*, which extensively establishes challenging arguments that do not overstep the established rules.
Now, combining my former learning with these recent insights, I shall provide a comprehensive and detailed refutation—likewise consisting of eight "impossibilities."
First, regarding the general rescue: after the emergence from the stupa, all subsequent mentions of Prabhūtaratna refer exclusively to being "within the stupa" and do not mention "seeing the Buddha.

If this passage were moved to a later section, there would be no place for his emergence from the stupa; thus, the first point is untenable. Furthermore, after the dispersal of the emanated bodies, all subsequent accounts discuss only the Buddha’s stupa and do not involve the emanated bodies.
If this passage were moved to a later section, there would be no context for the dispersal of the Buddha’s bodies; thus, the second point is untenable.
It is acceptable [to place it here]. In the *Zhulei wen* (Text on Entrustment), after the Buddha has scattered the impure soil, the subsequent scriptural passages do not mention purity.

If it were moved to a later position, there would be no further reference to impurity. This is the third reason it is unacceptable. According to the *Huiben* (Concordant Text), he was originally on the ground and ascended into the air because of the stupa.
If [the passage] "The Buddha scattered [flowers] and departed from the stupa" were moved to the end, there would be no place for it to return to on the ground;
this is the fourth impossibility. After the "Entrustment Chapter," the scripture is not yet finished; it merely describes the joy of the assembly and does not state that they departed.

If it were moved to the end, one would have to add the words "and departed"; this is the fifth impossibility. After the "Encouragement to Resolve Chapter," there is no further text remaining in the scripture.
Once [the Buddha] has passed away, he departs; if it were moved to a later section, it would have to be removed, which is the sixth impossibility.
Since the two gates of the fundamental and the trace have completed their Buddha-work, there must be something entrusted; this constitutes the "entrustment" (parīndanā).

If it were moved to a later section, the Dharma would have no place of return, which is the seventh impossibility. After the entrustment, the vehicle, the person of the vehicle, and the propagation of the sutra are clarified.
Regarding the *Pūrvayoga* (Past Deeds): these matters must be entrusted [to you]. If they were moved to a later section, the master and disciples would become intermingled;

this is the eighth impossibility. Next, as for the separate refutations: I have fully set forth the original points of refutation and shall address each one individually. First, regarding the claim that "the various versions contradict one another":
according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as well as the *Saṃyukta-ratna-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnarakṣa of the Sui dynasty, within this [text]...
The supplementary chapters (*parivarta*) are all located at the end of the sutra. [Daoshi] said: "In the *Zheng* and *Miao* versions, the translators were different, and thus what they saw varied.

It would be impossible to make them entirely identical. As for the term 'supplementary chapters' (*tiānpǐn*), according to the *Nanshan Neidian Lu*, it is said that Kumārajīva arbitrarily moved the *Parīndanā* chapter to the end.
Since Kumārajīva made this arbitrary alteration, Dharmarakṣa had not yet..."
This may serve as a reliable basis for judgment. Since the original text (zhengben) takes precedence, the "Augmented Version" (tianpin) cannot be called a revised edition.

As Master Nanshan has already rejected the Augmented Version, it stands to reason that both versions are equally invalid. Why is this? Although Kumārajīva was born in Kucha, he traveled extensively throughout the five regions of India;
how could he alone have failed to see the original Sanskrit *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? Having resided in Chang’an for a long time, how could he not have seen the version translated by Dharmarakṣa?
Regarding those [versions] that were translated and yet not used for a re-translation, one should know that Dharmarakṣa was not fit to serve as a guide.

If he were fit to serve as a guide, why would both the phrasing and the meaning not have been based entirely upon the original text? If you object that the phrasing and meaning of the later translations are diluted and thin, then those translated during the Tang dynasty are even thinner than the former.
Now, we rely on the translation by Kumārajīva; its principles are worthy of being taken as a standard. Thus, Master Rui said:
Where the Sanskrit sounds were erroneous, they were corrected according to those of India; where the Qin (Chinese) terminology was mistaken, it was rectified through the meaning of the characters;

and that which could not be translated was transcribed as it stood. Was it that Master Kumārajīva and his four disciples were suddenly devoid of discernment that they would arbitrarily shift a chapter and place it within the scripture?
If one does not fathom the ultimate intent, one should simply revere it; how can one [proceed otherwise]?
Is one measuring the great ocean or empty space with a measuring rod?
Second, regarding the claim that the sutras and śāstras contradict one another: the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that there are five powers of cultivation.

Within the fifth, the power of protecting the Dharma, it says: "As in the 'Exhortation of Samantabhadra' chapter and the subsequent chapter. The "subsequent chapter" refers here to the "Entrustment" (*parindanā*) chapter.
[This is] a chapter. Jiu said: "The treatise (*śāstra*) was also translated by a person. Why do you harbor doubts based on a mere indication?

Furthermore, although the treatise came from the West, since its translation occurred after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it was simply because the translator followed the sequence of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The primary scripture was translated during the Western Jin period, while the treatise was translated during the Later Wei period. It is like when Guptaka of the Sui dynasty saw the 'Medicinal Herbs' chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."

Regarding the "Later Additions": there was a prose section followed by verses, and the "Entrustment" (parīndanā) was placed at the end. Consequently, the main sūtra was inserted into the chapter, and the "Entrustment" was moved to follow the "Exhortation.
Nothing else was said [in the original], which led later generations to refer to it as the "Addition-Chapter Lotus Sūtra" (Tiānpǐn Fǎhuá).
Thus we know that the translator did not hesitate to act according to what he saw; the "Miaofa" and "Zhengfa" versions were both derived from the same Sanskrit original.
[The author] comments: At first glance, one might trust Kumārajīva while setting aside Dharmarakṣa; how then could one set aside the wondrous original text and rely exclusively on the treatise?

Master Xiū said: "As for what is called the 'later chapter,' it refers to the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra*, because both are initiated by Samantabhadra, and [the treatise] intends for one to cultivate the visualization based on that sūtra.
Furthermore, as for what is called the "later chapter," since its title is not mentioned therein, then...

It appears that the sutra’s transcription was not yet complete. If this were not the case, why would it not state "and the Chapter on Entrustment" (*parīndanā-parivarta*), but instead simply say "the latter part"?

This is one perspective. However, according to Tiantai, this is judged to be the conclusion of the sutra; he does not say it belongs to the section following the Chapter on Exhortation (*anuparīndanā*).
Third, regarding the contradiction with other teachings: it is said that all other sutras have their colophons at the end of the text; how is it that this sutra alone is placed here?

To resolve this, one might argue that it follows the pattern of other sutras; however, such a defense would lead to even greater contradictions and obstacles. For instance, in the middle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*...
There is a "Chapter on Entrustment" (*parindanā-parivarta*), and at the end of the sutra there is again a "Chapter on Entrustment. It is not permissible for these to be placed in both locations.

For example, in the *Mahāratnakūṭa* Sūtra, there are entrustment passages in every one of its forty-nine assemblies; yet how could it be required that all sutras be exactly like this? Take, for instance, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
the inquiries regarding the name and the inquiries regarding the upholding are situated within the body of the sutra itself; they cannot [be placed elsewhere].
It causes all to abide in the Middle Way. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the provisional is opened to reveal the fundamental, and the śrāvakas are granted predictions of enlightenment.
How could this mean that all are made to manifest the ultimate reality? There are numerous instances where cases do not conform to one another.
Regarding the fourth point, concerning the contradiction between two matters: if the manifested bodies were to return, this land would again become defiled.

Based on the admonition addressed to Gadgadasvara, we know that the land was indeed defiled. Furthermore, within the section on the entrustment (*parindanā*), it is stated that Prabhūtaratna should also return.

It is not logical for Avalokiteśvara to bestow the jewels and then divide them into two parts; if they were divided into two, then Prabhūtaratna would not have returned. Since their departure was identical, there should be no contradiction. [This is] the rescue.

It is said: It is precisely because [the Buddha] has not yet returned that the jewels are divided into two. Therefore, it is only stated that "one portion is offered to the stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna," and it is not stated that he is "offered to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
Thus we know that those whose business is finished depart, while those who have a karmic connection remain;

what harm is there in this according to principle? If Prabhūtaratna were still present, it would be improper for the emanated bodies to disperse; had the sutra text merely said "the stūpa may be as it was," [it would have been sufficient].
Therefore, as before, it simply returns to its original state and closes; this causes the manifested bodies to disperse, whereupon it is said that they each return to their own lands.
Thus we know that although the stūpa is made to return, because the hearing of other sūtras is permitted, the stūpa remains closed as it was when not yet opened.
It is merely said that "Prabhūtaratna issues a great sound from within the jeweled stūpa," and it is further said that "the fourfold assembly hears [it]."
Regarding the sound that issued forth from within the jeweled stūpa, Mahāpratibhāna said: "From within that stūpa, this sound was uttered.
Furthermore, the Buddha told Mahāpratibhāna: "Within this jeweled stūpa, there is a Tathāgata and others;
therefore, before the stūpa was opened, the great assembly spoke only of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. After the jeweled stūpa was subsequently opened, the entire assembly spoke thus:"

He saw two Tathāgatas within the jeweled stūpa. After the stūpa was closed, as stated at the end of the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta," it says that the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna was within the jeweled stūpa when the Tathāgata Gadgadasvara arrived there;
he merely placed his jeweled necklace upon Śākyamuni to offer greetings, and only then did he inquire:
"This Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who entered parinirvāṇa long ago, is within this jeweled stūpa. Why has he come?
"Are you listening to the Dharma? He then addressed Śākyamuni on behalf of that Buddha, asking: "Are you at ease, enduring well, and remaining for a long time?
You should know that the stupa remained closed; he stayed there and did not depart. Furthermore, he said: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will show me so that I may see him.
How could two Buddhas sit side by side? Thus he said, "Please let me see him. Then, from within the precious stupa, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed Gadgadasvara.
It says: "It merely states that you are making offerings to Śākyamuni and the others; it does not say 'emanated bodies. How could the emanated bodies be within one's sight and yet not be offered to?
Furthermore, when Gadgadasvara was about to return, he simply said that he had made offerings to Śākyamuni and the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna;
he did not say he had seen the Buddha. Upon arriving there and seeing Śubhavyūha Tathāgata, he simply said he had made offerings to Śākyamuni and..."
Regarding the Many Treasures Stūpa, it does not state that he saw the Tathāgata Many Treasures or his emanations.
Furthermore, when Mañjuśrī arrived, it immediately states that he prostrated with his head at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones; yet after the entrustment, this passage is entirely absent.

Therefore, the original stupa has already been sealed and the emanated bodies have already dispersed. If the emanated bodies were still present, it would be logical to offer worship to both Avalokiteśvara and Śāntamati;
it should not be limited to these two alone.

Regarding the fifty-second point on the inequality of their lifespans: for what reason does Śākyamuni divide his body while Prabhūtaratna remains whole? Why do the two both proclaim the dispersal [of the assembly], yet their departure and remaining are unequal?
If it is said that the stupa was merely made to close and is as it was before, why then does the primary body [of Śākyamuni] say he returns to his own land?

Jiù said: "Though the two lives are identical, their objects of focus differ. The jeweled stūpa came for the sake of hearing the sūtra; the manifested bodies gathered for the sake of opening the stūpa.
Since the stūpa has already closed, the manifested bodies must disperse. Because the sūtra is not yet finished, the stūpa has not yet returned.
Once the manifested bodies have dispersed, the earth shall merge back into its original state. Therefore, the preceding text says: 'For the sake of all Buddhas who are to come...'"
Because they were seated, each purified the eight directions. How much more so when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that one may return to one's own land?
It is simply that Dharmarakṣa’s translation was not correct; how could one judge Kumārajīva’s version and require it to conform to the "correct" scripture?

If the "correct" scripture were truly correct, there would have been no need for a re-translation; it should have merely stated "as before. If you wish to rely on the "correct" scripture, why do you not lecture on the original text? Examine the "correct" text thoroughly.

The original text contains contradictions in various places and errors; since the preceding and succeeding sections are not consistent, one need not take the canonical scriptures as the sole standard.
Furthermore, it is asked: "When Śākyamuni emerges from the stūpa, why must the stūpa be closed? And when the stūpa is closed, why must the emanated bodies necessarily disperse? The answer is:

The fundamental vow of Prabhūtaratna merely states that he would listen to the sutra from within the stūpa. If he were to manifest his own body to the fourfold assembly, [the stūpa would have to open].

[He] causes the emanated bodies to assemble. It should be known that the emanated bodies assemble because the stupa is to be opened. Śākyamuni likewise remains in the air for the sake of opening the stupa;

because he remains in the air, the stupa is opened; because the stupa is opened, [the Buddha] commands them to sit; because of the entrustment, they emerge from the stupa; because they emerge from the stupa, the stupa closes;
because the stupa closes, the business of the emanated bodies is finished; because the business is finished, they must disperse. Thus, the stupa is opened and closed.

The emanated bodies disperse and gather according to their respective causes and conditions. Why must you raise the objection that "the two lives are not equal," claiming that while the emanated Buddhas are made to return to their original places, the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna has no place to which it returns by the end of the sutra?

If this chapter were placed later in the text, then at the time of the proclamation of dispersal, [the stūpa] would return. To this, the [author of the] *Jiujing* (Explanatory Commentary) replies: [The text continues: "The emanated Buddhas are made to go and all return; the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna, however, until the conclusion of the sutra, has no further place to return to.

If the chapter were situated later, then upon the chanting of the dispersal, it would return. To this, the *Jiujing* says: [The text continues... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary discussing the structural placement of a specific chapter—likely the "Stūpa" chapter (*Dabaocha jing pin*)—within the *Lotus Sutra*. The argument concerns the consistency of the narrative regarding the dispersal of the emanated Buddhas versus the finality of the Prabhūtaratna Stūpa.)
He will naturally return; why need one seek his whereabouts? Once the exhortation to arouse the aspiration has concluded, the entire assembly shall pay homage and depart.
Although this act of homage does not specifically address the Precious Stupa, its departure encompasses all [the Buddhas].

Since the Original Vow of Prabhūtaratna was to come for the sake of hearing the sutra, once the sutra is finished, why worry that he would not depart? One need only worry that there is no textual passage concerning the stupa’s return.

There is no mention of the land becoming defiled again, nor of any words expressing concern over such defilement. If the land were to become defiled later on, how could it be that there would likewise be no arrival of humans or devas?

Regarding the seventh point, concerning the difference between the pure and the impure: since even the Land of Wonderful Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*) was subject to warnings and was not a pure land, we know that the emanation bodies have long [resided there].
Those who had already returned to their own lands were gathered on the day of the assembly.

He commanded his attendants to go to Mount Ling (Vulture Peak), yet they reported that none of the other mountains were there, while Mount Ling alone remained. Mañjuśrī emerged from the ocean and it was also called Mount Ling; suddenly, flowers appeared.
Therefore, when Gadgadasvara arrived, he returned to the original admonition. He said: "The scriptural text is brilliant and clear, yet readers do not perceive it.

The Sūtra says: 'All devas and humans were moved and placed in other lands; only the assembly of this gathering was left behind. Thus we know that the purification of the land was intended to provide peace for all Buddhas.
It is logical that the original assembly on Vulture Peak would not be moved. Even when Mañjuśrī arrived, it was immediately stated:"
When he went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and dwelt in mid-air, his wondrous voice did not say, "I dwell in mid-air.
Thus we know that when pure, he was in the void, and when defiled, he was on the ground. Now that his divided bodies have dispersed, all are defiled.
This, however, subverts the principle that [the Pure Land] is submerged and yet remains defiled. It is a stubborn insistence that only Vulture Peak is defiled.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra) states that "Miao-yin was cautioned," using the term "cautioned land" (*jèi-tǔ*) rather than referring exclusively to the mountain. Therefore, it says, "Do not despise that land," and so forth.
Thus, when the two, Mañjuśrī and Miao-yin, arrived, their circumstances were not equal. To attempt to treat them as one case is a principle difficult to reconcile.

Regarding the eighth point, "The assembly rejoices while their hearts feel alienated": In the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment), the Buddha instructs his emanations to return, yet the stūpas do not depart.
If it were not for the mention of "entrustment" at the end of the sūtra, one might think that the asuras and others rejoiced too soon.

Since their joy was not born from hearing the Dharma, but rather from seeing the guest Buddhas depart, which brought them comfort, this is truly strange. To address this, [the author] says: "It reaches..."
This joy was felt, yet it was considered too early. At the end of each of the three cycles, there was likewise joy, even earlier than this;
why should it not be considered strange? Having concluded the discourse on the lifespan, within the section analyzing the merits, it says: "Hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable..."
All were filled with joy. Now that both the fundamental and the manifested have been completed, we hear further that following these matters brings little effort but great merit.

We also hear of the profound efficacy of listening to and upholding the Dharma Master’s teachings. Furthermore, we hear how the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging was able to transform both himself and others, benefiting them in the present and for the future.

The method for propagating the Dharma has no fixed or permanent ritual. Furthermore, one observes that the World-Honored Śākyamuni manifested the ten supernatural powers, bestowed the four essential points of the summary, and entrusted the Three Samādhis.
Having received these three times, the great task was completed; how could one not rejoice?
To say it is "too early" is to know that such a person has not yet rejoiced even by the end of the sutra—how then can they propagate the Dharma?
"Does this mean he causes others to rejoice? As for the statement that 'the Guest Buddha departs,' it is moved to the subsequent passage.
Furthermore, to claim that one generates joy by adding 'departing for the stūpa' is even more preposterous. Examining these cases, all are merely measuring the Sage with ordinary sentiments;

they are nothing but idle scribbling of words, using a single instance to obscure the whole. It further states: "This is simply because he first exercised his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), and thus manifested the Pure Land."
The land is fundamentally defiled. Fearing that Gadgadasvara might see the defiled appearance of his own native land and give rise to derision, the Buddha cautioned him.
It was not that the land remained defiled only after the emanations had returned and Gadgadasvara arrived; rather, even though it is a pure land, one still sees Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Its transformation is not exclusively pure, as it simultaneously manifests defilement. This is because one perceives the lower from the higher. To this, the opponent replies: "Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is the Buddha."

He retained it for himself and thus caused the great assembly to see it together. The Tathāgata himself spoke of the Pure Land; yet you provide a forced interpretation, claiming it is not merely pure.
The Buddha said he causes all to be purified, yet you say that the original impurity still remains. If you claim that those above can see what is below...
If you perceive impurity within purity, why does Gadgadasvara perceive purity within impurity? Furthermore, he is able to see impurity because his mind is pure;
therefore, the Buddha-land is pure. If one still perceives impurity, it is known that Gadgadasvara’s mind was not yet pure, which is why the Buddha still cautioned him.
Since Gadgadasvara perceived impurity and still gave rise to disparagement, how can he be called "supreme in vision"?

[If you say it is] inferior, then it is inferior; one who gives rise to such thoughts is not a superior person (ārya). Since they still give rise to derision and disparagement, how could they be a superior person?

Next, Master Shi [Seng]jie raised two further difficulties, totaling ten difficulties; thus they are called the "Ten Impossibilities. First, he refutes the general introduction; second, he overturns the two specific difficulties.

Regarding the refutation of the introduction: he first states the introduction as follows: "In the 'Entrusting' chapter (Parīndanā-parivarta) of Master Kumārajīva’s [translation of the Lotus Sūtra]..."
After the section on supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), from that point onward, all have collectively accepted and received [this arrangement], unanimously stating that it was moved to this location;
they rightly grasp the intent of the sūtra. If it were placed later, the various objections previously enumerated would apply, as briefly described above.

To claim that one should determine the textual placement based solely on the meaning is precisely why it ought to be situated here. Only the Master Ci'en of our Tang dynasty did not approve of this interpretation. The Dharma...
The Master further said: "If Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound) were defiled when he was cautioned, how could there be Mount Ling (Gṛdhrakūṭa) when Mañjuśrī comes from the ocean?
The text simply says 'only this assembly remains,' it does not say 'only Mount Ling remains. One should know that both the internal and external are pure;
it is merely stated as it was before. Furthermore, he said: 'The emanated bodies are Śākyamuni himself; if the entire body of Prabhūtaratna [is present], it is likewise [Śākyamuni]."

[The Buddha] bestowed only one portion. As for the emanations of Śākyamuni, he bestowed only one portion. If he had accepted many portions, it would mean that Śākyamuni alone would long receive offerings and sustenance.
How could this be appropriate when practicing the six points of harmonious respect? Therefore, he bestowed only one portion. Furthermore, it is said:
"If the entrustment were to remain here, the Tathāgata would not have risen from his seat and said, 'Do not sit again,' nor would the emanation Buddhas have departed."
One should stand when offering [the food] and stand when receiving the offerings of Avalokiteśvara; one should not receive them while seated. Furthermore, it is said:

"The great assembly all rejoice, yet few practice accordingly. One should not establish this [position]. It is also said: "Spiritual power removes impurities, though it may not necessarily eliminate them entirely.
If they were to be completely eliminated, where would they be gathered? What pure land could contain such a defiled land? To this, the defense says: This is precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

From the Western Jin dynasty until the Tang, this *Sūtra of the Sublime Dharma* was never practiced or employed. However, once the Later Qin translation was completed, it spread widely throughout the four seas and became an object of veneration for all under heaven.
Moreover, wherever it circulates, it must rely upon invisible grace; yet now that such invisible grace has departed, [the text has fallen into neglect].

How could this be subject to debate? Moreover, the efficacy of its reception and maintenance has been immeasurable. Even Samantabhadra transmitted it word by word without requiring the removal of chapters;

how much less so for the generations thereafter? Renowned monks have succeeded one another, and eminent scholars have gathered like a forest, all of whom collectively authorized the entrustment and included it herein.
How could it be that by the Tang dynasty, what was seen had diverged from the past? For this sutra is eternal.
Taking the abiding in the Buddha-nature as the throat; taking the wondrous practice of the One Vehicle as the eyes; taking the seeds of rebirth and ruin as the heart and viscera;

and taking the manifestation of the fundamental long life as one’s vitality—yet you instead use the extinction of seeds through *vijñapti-mātra* to kill that heart, use the *Vibhāṣā* Bodhisattva to blind the eyes, and use the *Āyuḥpramāṇa* Sūtra to resolve doubts and sever the life-force.
Because it is eternally abiding yet not all-pervasive, it severs its own throat. Taking the three realms and eight hells as the primary categories renders this [Pure Land] small;
taking the One Vehicle and four virtues as minor meanings leaves nothing toward which one can ultimately return. Based on this analysis, various precedents may be understood.
As for those who insist on the old explanations, the Sublime Voice (Ghoṣadatta) has never harbored pride regarding this birth; if the land remains pure, [the teaching remains valid].
The Buddhas filling the space, Śākyamuni, as well as the stūpas and the assembly, are further present in the sky, manifested through supernatural power and pervading the ten directions.

Why must you still insist on using your marvelous voice to offer such misguided admonitions? Those Buddhas clearly perceive that the terrain is uneven and high and low, yet they conceal their Buddha-wisdom by claiming the land is already pure;
they claim that Śākyamuni does not long receive benefits, merely to conform to the six points of harmonious respect.

This would mean making the holy conform to the mundane. If you say that the manifested bodies are Śākyamuni himself, then since Śākyamuni opened the stūpa, he would have already manifested those bodies;

why then would it be necessary for them to assemble again? If we rely on the fact that these responsive traces are distinct individuals, then if they were manifestations of Śākyamuni, one fears that Śākyamuni would be too numerous and thus unable to receive the offering.
If they were Avalokiteśvara, one fears that there would be too many Buddhas to receive it, and thus [Śākyamuni] would not grant it. If...
Avalokiteśvara did not accept it; this merely demonstrates Avalokiteśvara’s partiality in giving. How does this relate to the six points of concordance or having few desires?
If the emanations had not accepted it, they should have first received the gift and then yielded it back; why, then, was it divided into only two portions?

Therefore, we know that dividing it into two parts now manifests both the past and the present; its significance is thus complete. Once the emanations have departed, the principle is perfectly established.

Why is this objection necessary? If you claim that one should not establish the ritual for sending forth the emanations (*vibhāga-pratimā*) nor the ritual for receiving offerings, and that even if the section were moved to the end, these faults would be avoided—then while it might be permissible to remain seated while receiving the offerings from Avalokiteśvara, at the moment of the touching of the crown (*mūrdha-mārjana*), the ritual for dispersing [the assembly] must still be established.

Thus, at the very conclusion of the sutra, one would still incur the fault of failing to send forth the emanations; to laboriously set up such a frivolous argument is merely to mock the venerable ritual.

Regarding this sublime sutra, its widespread praise has not yet been fully realized. If one were merely to follow the sentiments of ordinary people, placing Śākyamuni side-by-side with his emanations while sitting to see them off would constitute a neglect of propriety;
therefore, standing to see the guests off is established as being precisely in accordance with ritual decorum.

Furthermore, regarding standing to receive and standing to offer, what scriptural injunction prescribes that such receiving and offering are invalid? Moreover, it is said: "The assembly already rejoices, lacking only the act of offering."
[The passage] says: "It is improper to place this here. It is merely because [the practitioner] has not practiced it sufficiently that it should not be placed at the end.

Furthermore, it asks: "In which Pure Land could such a defiled land be contained? Why not ask why the grass carried through the kalpa-fire does not become ash, or how the pores can contain the ocean while the body does not follow its waves?
All such explanations are merely products of one's own mind; they do not accord with the scriptural text.

The examples are as follows. Next, we shall specifically refute the ninth and tenth [objections]. Regarding the ninth objection—that the Buddha has no seat—the challenge is stated as follows: "When the stūpa was opened, he received the invitation;

Śākyamuni entered and sat down. When the stūpa was closed, he emerged. It would likewise be appropriate for him to return to his seat. How could he then preach while standing? Below this, [the refutation of] the various [points] follows.
Is it not recorded in the sutras? For instance, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tathāgata manifested lying down and then rose from his reclining position;
when the Tathāgata was cremated, he rose from the golden coffin and ascended to the Brahma Palace, and after descending from the Brahma Palace, he returned once more to his original seat.

This case should be understood in the same way. Why would this not be so? [The opponent] replies: "If [the Buddha] has already bestowed the empowerment by stroking the crown of the head, logically he must return to his seat. If you claim there is no scriptural authority for this..."
Regarding the phrase "causing the Buddha to stand eternally": after Mañjuśrī has finished answering the questions, there is no mention of entering the sea.
Why, then, does the text suddenly state that the sea comes here? Furthermore, it says that he constantly preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the sea.

If the words "constantly preaches" imply he must always be in the sea, and if he were originally in the sea, he should not have been listed in the introduction (*nidāna*). How could he then be the subject of Maitreya’s subsequent inquiry? Moreover, it says:

The sutra concludes. The Buddha merely instructs the assembly to disperse; there is originally no textual passage regarding them sitting again. Therefore, the Buddha should have escorted the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings as they departed.
Why would he escort only the multiple manifestations of Prabhūtaratna? Escorting the manifestations while standing is somewhat more consistent with propriety.
To dispatch the Eight Classes [of Devas] as messengers creates a doubling of the discrepancy between the honorable and the humble.
Furthermore, why not instead hold the various emanation Buddhas accountable and merely have their attendants carry flowers to convey greetings?

Moreover, when it is said that "a certain Buddha [among them] gives his consent (*chandam dadāti*) for this jeweled stūpa to be opened," one immediately speaks of Śākyamuni at that time seeing the assembled emanations give their consent to open the stūpa, yet one does not mention the attendants.

When it comes to the discussion of desire (*kāma*), desire should not be established [as a valid category]. Although the Dharma Master was somewhat close to him, one should side with principle rather than kinship;

this is an ancient standard to rely upon. Furthermore, why not hold the Teaching Gate accountable for saying that Upatiṣya (Da-da) committed evil in life after life, yet suddenly declaring him to be the Teacher of the Buddha?
It is further claimed that he received a prophecy from the Teacher—such contradictions cannot be fully recounted.
Why not reproach the Dragon Girl for becoming a Buddha too quickly? Why not reproach the Śrāvakas for becoming Buddhas too slowly?
Regarding the tenth assembly, there was no command for them to sit. The objection states: "The Buddha occupies a high and remote place; the multitude requested that he descend.

Now that he has returned to the ground, he should likewise issue a command for them to resume their seats. How can he allow them to remain standing for so long without granting them a place to rest? Therefore, it is known that...
Regarding the entrustment (*parindanā*): following the establishment of the sūtra, it was translated as follows: "Whenever one relies on the power of another, one must request their empowerment.

If one relies on one's own power and does not seek the assistance of others, one remains in emptiness beyond the reach of one's own strength; therefore, one requests the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Once one returns to one's original state and acts according to the capacity of one's own power, there is no need to await the Buddha’s command. Moreover, since the original cause for entering the stūpa was the Buddha, the request is made [at that point]."

[The assembly was] in the air. Now that the Buddha has risen from his seat, how could they remain seated? Therefore, it says, "with even greater reverence, they bowed their bodies and lowered their heads.

Since the Buddha sat down again and preached the Dharma, it stands to reason that the assembly should likewise return to their seats; this should be understood by inferring the meaning where there is no explicit text.
Furthermore, if the assembly neither rose nor sat, they should still remain in the air. For what reason, then, [does the text say they returned to their seats] in the Universal Gate Chapter?
The *Akṣayamati-parivarta* begins with the passage, "Akṣayamati rose from his seat," while the *Dhāraṇī-parivarta* begins with, "Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat.
From this, we know that the text concerning "the invisible [deities] returning to their seats" and so forth cannot be omitted; rather, it should be moved to the end of the chapter.

Furthermore, since the title of the chapter contains the phrase "entrustment" (*parindanā*), those elements intended for the end—namely, the meaning of entrustment found within the chapter—should likewise all be moved [to the end].
However, although the title of the "Chapter on Entrustment" (Parindanā-parivarta) is "Entrustment," within the chapter it simply states:
"I have practiced for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas to attain this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is difficult to obtain; I now entrust it to you.

Likewise, although the title of the "Chapter on Supernatural Power" (Rddhy-abhisamskāra-parivarta) is "Supernatural Power," within the chapter it says: "In order to entrust this sutra... Thus, by means of the Tathāgata...

Regarding the four dharmas, they concern the entrustment (*parindanā*) and the superior practices (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and so forth. Therefore, one should first transpose the entrustment, followed by the transposition of the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
[The entrustment] is placed after [the supernatural power]. Furthermore, the beginning of the "Chapter on Entrustment" states: "He manifested great supernatural power.

Since there is a mention of entrustment within the "Chapter on Supernatural Power," it is said that both chapters should be moved toward the end. If both were moved toward the end, the two chapters could not [be arranged as they are].
It is re-established. It is not permissible for two chapters to follow one another [in this manner]. If there were such a sequence, it would again lose its finality.

If you claim that the order of the sūtra’s text places the "Chapter on Encouraging the Retention" after the "Chapter on Never Disparaging," why then is it interspersed with the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers"?
The "Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa" should have been followed immediately by the "Chapter on Encouraging the Retention"; how could it be otherwise?
It is permitted to insert [the passage] within the "Tie-da" (Devadatta) chapter; as for its position in the sequence of chapters, it does not follow Kumārajīva’s version.
In principle, all such matters must conform to the authentic sūtra. In the present sūtra, there are twelve thousand śrāvakas, whereas in the authentic sūtra, there are only one thousand two hundred.
The praise of the śrāvakas’ virtues consists of eleven phrases, while the praise of the bodhisattvas’ virtues consists of twenty-eight phrases.

These do not correspond with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* or its commentary. Why do you not blame the commentary for contradicting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, yet instead resent the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for contradicting the commentary?
Furthermore, within the listing of names in the authentic scripture, it says "Guangshiyin" (Prabhūtaratna-śrī-garbha), where "guang" (light) is a transliteration of "prabhu" (sound/voice).
