The same. He then immediately wrote it down. Why do those of later generations not rely on this luminous interpretation? Bodhisattva Baozhang separates [the figures] into two, adding Baoyinshou (Jewel-Seal Head).
Since "palm" (*zhǎng*) already refers to the hand, to further add "head" (*tóushǒu*) and separate them into two individuals is redundant.
As for the Sovereign Deva King, he has the Great Brahmā as his head-ornament; it is also said that thirty thousand devas are present together with him. This is...
The Sanskrit original contains the term *mahābrahmālipyakṣara* (the great Brahma-syllable), which is not fully translated here.

In the introductory section, it does not state that he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra named the *Anantārtha*; rather, it simply says that after preaching this sūtra, he ascended the seat and entered samādhi. Furthermore, the *Anantārthavihāra-samādhi* is missing.
One does not know what sūtra was preached prior to this, nor what dhyāna-concentration was entered. Why not inquire about the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? This increases [the confusion].
Furthermore, does it add the "Infinite Meanings" [Sūtra]? Again, regarding the emission of light, it merely states that it ascends as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
For what reason did Dharmarakṣa suppress the Buddha’s radiance? The *Miaojing* (Wondrous Sūtra) speaks of eight hundred disciples, whereas the authentic sūtra speaks of eighteen persons among them.
Whenever it says "like the sands of the Ganges," all instances should say "like the sands of the rivers.
Since this is the case in the Prologue, there are countless errors throughout the Main Body of the text; why not rely on them? Yet you cite only the Chapter on Entrustment.
Therefore, the main scripture cannot be relied upon at all. Even if these were moved by Master Kumārajīva, one ought to have seen the profound intent of the Sanskrit original. If...
Why not simply move it to the end of another chapter instead of necessarily placing it here?
If there were no such hindrances as mentioned above, would moving it later cause further hindrances? Therefore, wherever this text circulates, the various sages secretly bestow their grace.
The preceding passages are entirely from Jingxi [Zhiyi]’s critique of the errors of the ancient commentaries regarding the relocation of chapters. This concludes the record.
The Wise One’s Commentary provides a correct explanation of the title of this chapter. Regarding "Entrustment" (*zhùlèi*): "entrust" (*zhù*) refers to what the Buddha has entrusted;

"burden" (*lèi*) means to trouble you with its propagation. This name is derived from the Sage’s intent; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Entrustment," which corresponds to the *loka-prasāda* (worldly standpoint).

Furthermore, "entrust" refers to receiving the entrustment upon one's head [with reverence], and "burden" refers to doing so with delight rather than weariness. This is derived from the Bodhisattvas' respect.
It is named "Following the Attainment" (Shun de ming). Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Entrustment" (Zhulei pin). This constitutes the *siddhānta* of generating wholesome roots (*shanshan*).

Furthermore, "entrustment" (*zhuchi*) refers to what was entrusted by the Tathāgata’s golden mouth, while "cumulative burden" (*leilei*) refers to what is borne upon the head with a sincere heart by the Bodhisattvas.

Since this is discussed in terms of both the bestowal and the reception, it is called the "Chapter on Entrustment. This constitutes the *siddhānta* of remedial treatment (*duizhi shan-tan*). For this reason, the Tathāgata rose from his seat in person and extended his hand.

[The Buddha] stroked [the crown of his head] and bestowed upon him the Dharma that is difficult to encounter. The great assembly bowed their bodies and joined their palms, saying, "As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall reverently practice it in its entirety.

Because they received and transmitted [the teaching] with such earnest devotion, this is called the "Chapter on Entrustment" (Zhūlèi Pǐn). This concludes the explanation of the chapter. The subsequent scripture is divided into two parts:
first, the entrustment; second, the joy of the assembly. The first part is further divided into three sections. First, the Tathāgata’s entrustment.
[The Buddha] entrusts [the teaching]. The two bodhisattvas receive it. Third, the conclusion of the assembly is announced. The first section further consists of three parts.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha rose from his Dharma-seat and manifested great supernormal power;

with his right hand, he stroked the crowns of the heads of immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and spoke these words: "I, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas..."
"Throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, you have cultivated this Dharma of the attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is so difficult to obtain. I now entrust it to you.
You should, with a single mind, propagate this Dharma and cause it to increase and flourish extensively.
Having thus placed his hand upon the heads of all these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he spoke these words: "I, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions..."
For billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have cultivated this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is so difficult to attain.
I now entrust it to you all. You should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and widely proclaim this Dharma so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it.
In this first section on the Tathāgata’s entrustment, this is the primary text of the actual entrustment. As for the "actual entrustment":

with the skillful hand of his single expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), the Buddha strokes the crowns of the heads of the bodhisattvas of true wisdom—those who dwell in the three thousand three hundred million *nayuta* worlds below, including those from other lands—who fill the void of space. Thus does the Tathāgata transmit the Way and transform them.
Therefore, it is called the "Hand of Expedient Wisdom. Because the Bodhisattva personally practices and receives the Way, it is called the "Crown of Real Wisdom.
When he extends his hand and strokes the crown of the head, this is the entrustment of the body. When expedient wisdom approaches real wisdom, this is the entrustment of the mind.
To speak these words is the entrustment of the mouth. This precisely symbolizes the threefold entrustment of body, speech, and mind. The text states: [The text continues...]

The intention behind the four *siddhāntas* is as follows: "I have cultivated this dharma so difficult to attain throughout immeasurable kalpas" refers to having received and studied it from previous Buddhas;
"now I entrust it to you" means that you, daughter, shall transmit it to the successors of the three periods—this is the *loka-siddhānta*.
"Circulate it with a single mind" is the *pudgala-siddhānta*. "Extensively cause it to increase" is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*.
This is the *siddhānta*. "Benefiting" refers specifically to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion, is free from all stinginess, and has no fear;
he is able to bestow upon sentient beings the Buddha’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and natural wisdom. The Tathāgata is the [refuge] for all sentient beings.
The Great Benefactor of all beings: you all should likewise train yourselves in the Dharma of the Tathāgata;
do not give rise to stinginess or parsimony. This second point explains the intent behind the entrustment. Those who possess great compassion are the dwelling place of the Tathāgata;
those who are free from all stinginess and parsimony are the robe of the Tathāgata; and those who are without fear are the seat of the Tathāgata. This is the wisdom of the Buddha.
"Wisdom" refers to the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*). "The Tathāgata’s wisdom" refers to the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
"Self-existent wisdom" refers to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Within the chamber of the Tathāgata, he is able to bestow these three kinds of wisdom upon sentient beings.
It is likewise with the seats within the hall. Therefore, one should know that if the chamber were not non-dual, the great vows would not be universal;
if the robes were not non-dual, the Dharma-body would not be complete; if the seats were not non-dual, the destruction of delusions would not be thorough.
Because the donor is thus, they are free from stinginess and free from fear. With these three dharmas lacking nothing, both self and others are not in vain. Such is the donor.
Therefore, possessing great compassion, he himself enters the chamber and causes others to enter the chamber because he is free from stinginess;

he himself puts on the robes and causes others to put on the robes because he is free from fear; he himself sits upon the seat and causes others to sit upon the seat—this may also be said to be because he is free from stinginess.
Thus, being free from fear, he bestows these three things and explains these three things. If...
If one speaks of giving, it must be endowed with compassion; this refers to the three dharmas for entering the chamber.
You all should study these dharmas of the Tathāgata and propagate them through these three dharmas. With these three sets of three, you should bestow them upon all.

This clarifies the efficacy of the sūtra: one must necessarily possess these three sets of three. How much more so regarding the three sets of three dharmas that one propagates—only then can it be called [the true teaching].
To cause others to attain that which has been propagated is called explaining and delivering the Buddha’s intent.
To those in future ages who are good sons or good daughters and who have faith in the Tathāgata’s wisdom, one should expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* so that they may hear and know it;
this is for the sake of causing such persons to attain the Buddha’s wisdom. If there are...
As for those sentient beings who do not believe or accept [this], you should instruct, benefit, and gladden them by means of other profound teachings of the Tathāgata.
If you are able to act in this way, you will have repaid the kindness of all Buddhas.
Regarding the threefold entrustment: if one has deep roots and sharp faculties, one may directly expound the Buddha-wisdom.

If they are not yet capable, one should instruct, benefit, and gladden them within other profound dharmas. The Buddha-wisdom is profound but not "other"; the six stages of skillful means are "other" but not profound;
the sequential teaching of the Separate Vehicle (Bie-jiao) is both "other" and profound. You are able, by means of these other profound dharmas...
To assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s wisdom is precisely to skillfully repay the Buddha’s kindness; this is called the admonition and entrustment.
The three sections are concluded.
At that time, when the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had heard the Buddha speak thus, they were all filled with great joy. Their [joy] pervaded them entirely.
They increased their reverence even further, bowing their bodies and lowering their heads, joining their palms toward the Buddha, and together they spoke with one voice:
"As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall carry it out in full. Indeed, World-Honored One, may you have no further concern. Thus spoke the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Thus they repeated this three times, all raising their voices together and saying: "As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall carry it out in full. So be it, World-Honored One;
may you have no further concern."
Second, the Bodhisattva’s acceptance is explained: acceptance with a joyful mind; acceptance through the body by bowing and lowering the head;
and acceptance through the mouth by uttering words aloud—this includes acceptance through the mind as well.

"As the World-Honored One has commanded," [the Bodhisattva] accepts the intention of the Great Benefactor, the Tathāgata’s chamber, and shall practice it fully. He accepts the Tathāgata who is free from stinginess.
Regarding the intention of the robes: may you have no anxiety. Receive the intention of the Tathāgata’s seat of fearlessness.

Since the Buddha has thus entrusted [the Dharma] three times and the Bodhisattva has accepted it three times, one must not cite the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*—which speaks of the five types of stinginess and the seven retributions for stinginess—to explain this passage;
they are entirely unrelated. One must not use this to prove that the Buddha is the same as ordinary beings; this is profoundly unacceptable.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha commanded the various emanated Buddhas who had come from the ten directions to each return to their own lands, saying:
"May the Buddhas each abide as they please; let the stupa of Prabhūtaratna return to its former state."

The third matter being concluded, the assembly is dismissed. Many Treasures came to bear witness to this sutra; now that the two gates of the Trace and the Source have been completed, he must respectfully depart as before.
He manifested his divided body for the purpose of opening the stupa, and since the task of opening the stupa is finished, [he departs].
He commanded the emanated bodies to return to their original forms. Since the stūpa could not be opened again, the emanated bodies departed and did not appear within it;
yet because they continued to listen to the Dharma, it remained closed even though they were still present. Question: If the stūpa listens to the Dharma, it should likewise not be closed. Answer:
Because [the Buddha] has already realized the truth, the stūpa is closed; because he listens for the sake of its circulation, the stūpa remains there.
When these words were spoken, the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions who were seated upon lion thrones beneath jeweled trees,
as well as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, the boundless assembly of bodhisattvas such as Uṣṇīṣa,
the fourfold assembly of śrāvakas such as Śāriputra, and all the world— including devas, humans, and asuras— heard what the Buddha had said.
All were greatly rejoiced.
Second, it clarifies the joy of the great assembly. The Buddhas rejoice because they have accomplished the task of transforming others;

the Bodhisattvas rejoice because they have attained the Dharma for their own practice; furthermore, they rejoice because they speak of the purity of persons—the Buddha is such a person—and because they hear the purity [of the Dharma].

They rejoice because of the Dharma; this refers to the wondrous sutra. They rejoice because they have heard the Dharma and attained realization; this refers to those who will benefit in the present and future.
Because these three matters are fully complete, there is great joy. This explains the second instance of the Tathāgata’s touching of their heads.
The formal entrustment for the circulation [of the sutra] is concluded.

From this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," the twenty-third, through the following five chapters, the text exhorts the circulation [of the sutra] by means of transforming others. This "Bhaiṣajyarāja Chapter" admonishes the [practitioner].

The Teacher of Transformation. This is the vehicle of ascetic practice (*duṣkara-caryā-yāna*). First, the title is explained; second, the general purpose of its appearance is clarified. Regarding the explanation of the title:
the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states that formerly named Starlight (*Jyotirasa*), he heard the exposition of the Buddha’s wisdom from the Venerable Sūryagarbha.

He offered medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains to the assembly of monks, vowing: "In the future, may I be able to cure the two types of illness—those of body and mind—for all sentient beings. Thus it is raised.
The world rejoiced and called him "Medicine King. This passage clarifies that Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (All-Beings-Love-to-See) suddenly sacrificed his body and further burned both his arms;

he regarded life as light and the Dharma as heavy, so that while his life ended, the Way remained. By citing the past to illuminate the present, it is therefore called the "Chapter on Past Deeds" (*Pūrvayoga-parivarta*).
If one pursues this meaning, Starlight (*Jyotīrasā*) should follow after Love-to-See, from the point of his renouncing the medicine.
Since making this vow, he has been named "Medicine King. This concludes the explanation of the title of this chapter. Next, regarding the purpose of the following five chapters:

this present chapter clarifies the teacher who transforms others, who solely wishes that the Great Dharma may be widely proclaimed and that all sentient beings may obtain great benefit through their great vows.
Therefore, he exhausts his supernatural powers and his very life, remaining earnest and reverent in his resolve.

It is like the case of the wood [in the previous analogy]. I hope to cause my disciples to revere the Dharma as they did their teacher. I transmit this clarity to you; you, in turn, shall transmit this clarity.
This unending succession of clarity is the will of the Teacher. Therefore, one should know that this chapter exhorts the masters who propagate the Dharma.

The subsequent two chapters, "The Marvelous Sound" and "Avalokiteśvara," clarify how the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) from other directions receive the mandate to propagate the sutra and universally manifest their physical forms.
The form has no fixed standard; it cannot be viewed with the eyes of cattle or sheep, nor can it be fathomed by the common intellect.

Regarding what you have heard, do not give rise to thoughts of contempt. If such thoughts arise, the Dharma will not permeate the mind; thus one is known to be of inferior capacity. This is an exhortation for disciples who receive the Dharma.
Now, the "Expedient Means" chapter is clarified: the three vehicles are opened to reveal the One. The perfect cause is hereby completed. Peace and Bliss.
Chapter on Practice (*Caryā-varga*). The exposition of the Dharma of the vehicle (*yāna*) is concluded. The exposition of the lifespan, which clarified the fruit of the vehicle, is also concluded.

This chapter correctly clarifies the person who rides the vehicle of vehicles (*yānayāna*), and their transformation of others for the sake of its circulation. Thus, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states: "The Mahāyāna is that which is ridden by great beings such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī;
therefore, it is called the 'vehicle of vehicles' (*yānayāna*). King Bhaiṣajyarāja [attained this] through the vehicle of ascetic practice.
As for the "Vehicles": Samantaghoṣa and Avalokiteśvara ride upon the vehicle of samādhi; Dhāraṇī rides upon the vehicle of total retention (dhāraṇī); Subhavyūha rides upon the vehicle of vows;
and Samantabhadra rides upon the vehicle of supernormal powers (abhijñā). Those who understand it in this way find it convenient for the purpose of transforming others and circulating [the teaching].
This concludes the explanation of the intent of the passage. From here below is the exegesis of the scripture, which is divided into four parts.

“Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain this briefly.

The third section consists of the request for an answer. △ The text of the answer is divided into two parts:

in that land, there are no women, nor are there hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, or any of the various difficulties.
The ground is as level as the palm of a hand and is composed of lapis lazuli. It is adorned with jewel trees, covered above by jeweled canopies, and hung with jeweled flower banners.

Jewel vases and incense burners are distributed throughout the realm. There are pedestals made of the seven precious substances; beneath each tree is a pedestal, and the distance between each tree and its pedestal is [one krośa].

The three types of lands and so forth; this concludes the section on the fundamental matters. The fundamental narrative consists of three parts.

The Buddha first expounded the Dharma; yet, since the Buddha universally acts for the sake of all beings, why address it solely to Priyadarśana?
This was intended as a response to him, necessitating that the teaching be entrusted for circulation—just as in the present case of Śāriputra, where one person is used to represent the many.
II. Regarding the offerings, there are two parts: I. those for the present, and II. those for the future. Regarding the present, there are again two parts.
This was the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, who delighted in practicing ascetic austerities.
Within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he practiced walking meditation with diligence and sought Buddhahood with a single-minded focus for twelve thousand years.
Having completed this period, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms. Upon attaining this samādhi, his heart was filled with great joy.
First, it clarifies attaining the Dharma through present practice. △ Next, one reflects upon repaying their debt of gratitude.

This is further divided into two parts, wherein one reflects, saying: "That I have attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies is entirely due to the power of having heard the Lotus Sūtra.

In samādhi, within the void of space, there rained down *māndārava* flowers and great *māndārava* flowers, along with fine powder of black *kālānusāri* sandalwood, filling the sky and descending like clouds;
furthermore, there rained down the fragrance of *gośīrṣa* sandalwood from the shore of the ocean.
This incense weighs six *zhū* and is worth as much as the Sahā world; it is used for making offerings to the Buddha.

Having poured various fragrant oils over himself, he used his supernatural powers and vows to spontaneously ignite his own body,
its radiance illuminating worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty billion Ganges Rivers.
First, it clarifies the burning of the body.
Within that assembly, all the Buddhas simultaneously praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Good son, this is true diligence;
this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgatas."
I said: "The Wise One, the Patriarch, reached this point and became silent, without a sound. He attained great enlightenment and was about to report his realization to his teacher.
The teacher said: 'It is not you who does not realize it; it is not I who cannot recognize it. The meditative concentration you have entered is the Lotus Samādhi;
the eloquence you have manifested is the Revolving Dhāraṇī. The sub-commentary explains: 'Both the one who makes the offering and that which is offered are..."*
It is unattainable. As for the current practices of meditation and lecturing, how can one erroneously attempt to conjecture about it with mind and mouth?

Even if one were to offer various items such as flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, powdered incense, ointment incense, celestial silks, banners, and canopies, as well as the sandalwood from the "this-side of the sea"—none of these could equal it. Even if a kingdom...
Even the giving of one's city, wife, and children cannot equal it. Good son, this is called the foremost gift;
among all gifts, it is the most honored and supreme, because it is the offering of the Dharma to all Tathāgatas. Having spoken these words, they each became silent.

Second, to clarify that the Buddhas praise ascetic practices and the burning of the body: what is called "the true Dharma offering" must refer to the internal application of bodily wisdom (*kāyajñāna*) in contemplation.
One contemplates the causes and effects of afflictions (*kleśa*), using the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*) to dissolve them;
therefore, it is called the "true Dharma. The reason burning the body is named the "true Dharma" is due to this internal contemplation. What is the object of this contemplation? It is precisely this—

The physical body arises due to the cause of delusion, thereby bringing about this fruit of delusion. Since both are eliminated by the wisdom of emptiness, it is evident that both cause and effect are simultaneously eradicated.
Furthermore, one contemplates that whether it be the body or the fire, the offerer or the offering—all are the true reality (dharmatā).

This clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Since it is the true reality (*bhūtala-kṣaṇa*), and in true reality there is no fire for burning the body, nor the subject and object [of that act], how could there be burning or subject and object?
Ultimately, who burns and what is burned? Both the offerer and the offering are unobtainable.
This is according to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Not only are the body and so forth all true reality; even the master of the body and so forth—all [are likewise].
Since all these are non-existent, they are called "who. One should know that the burner is the fire that burns; the fuel is the body that is burned.
Both the body and the fire are that which can perform the service. The Buddha and the Dharma of the sutras are the field to which offerings are made.
The presiding master is the observer who is capable of contemplation. The body and fire are the objects of both the subject and object of contemplation.

When object and wisdom are non-dual, the distinction between subject and object perishes. By means of non-dual contemplation, one contemplates the non-dual object, accomplishes non-dual practice, and realizes non-dual emptiness.
At the time of performing this contemplation, suffering becomes the Dharma-realm, benefiting all who see and hear it; therefore, it is called the "Vehicle of Vehicles" and is so named.
This is the true offering of the Dharma. Were it otherwise, it would become a fruitless ascetic practice. The Buddha has sincere admonitions that should truly be contemplated beforehand.
Thus, by leaping from cliffs, one does not invite the criticism of external practitioners; by entering fire, one does not incur the censure of the internal community.
This is truly because internally there is contemplation of principle and externally there is clarity regarding the intended mind. Therefore, Śūra (the Fierce One) brought peace to Sudhana’s...
Doubt. The Nirgranthas give rise to the interpretation that [ascetic] austerity is fierce; they earnestly discourse upon their path, claiming that only through such practice will there be success.

If the mind is upright, the conduct will be upright; if the wisdom is deviant, the affairs will be deviant. Conduct must not be abandoned, and wisdom must not be lost. Thus, those of later generations shall not forfeit the benefits of the Dharma. Someone asked:
"The Vinaya regulations state that burning one's own body constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense, while burning a finger constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense. This..."
Regarding the praise for cremation: what is its significance? I shall now answer this. The regulations and prohibitions differ between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.

The Hīnayāna establishes it as a transgression, while the Mahāyāna mandates cremation. Thus, in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, it states that if one does not cremate [the body], one is not an ordained bodhisattva.
How could it be that this applies only to the laity while failing to regulate those on the Path? Therefore, we know that following the Hīnayāna makes practice easy; why then would one not cremate?

Difficult! It is difficult from the perspective of the Great Truth (Mahāyāna). To burn [the precepts] is not easy. If the world regards "not holding" [the precepts] as great, then both the small and the great will collapse together.

If one believes that the capacities and conditions (*indriya-pratyaya*) of this land are such that all are deluded regarding the Small and the Great, they do not know that one first takes the Small and later the Great. According to what sequence of summer retreats (*varṣa*) would this be?

If one first takes the Great and later the Small, with what intention does one receive them? If one first takes the Small and later the Great, does this open up the prohibitions of the Hīnayāna? First...
The great [precepts] follow the small. Does this not exclude the Bodhisattvas? Within a single realm, how can there be two assemblies? Within a single body, how can there be two distinct entities?
If the great governs the small, from where does one derive benefit? If the small recites for the great, who can fathom the resulting harm?
One must diligently discriminate these matters to serve as seeds for the future. For the vehicle upon which one rides is entirely the Sublime Dharma. Therefore—
Because the names "cause" and "effect" are established based on a single reality; because one mounts what is to be mounted in order to benefit sentient beings;

and because one merely examines one's own virtues, observing the mind through various objects so as to be in accord with that mind—one should follow the prescriptions and prohibitions accordingly. Now, Bhaiṣajyarāja has long since realized this.

In both cases, he manifested methods for opening and regulating [the Dharma], cherishing the profound Law above all else. He gave rise to vows of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to serve as a guide for ordinary beings;
this can be understood through reflection.
His body remained ablaze with fire for twelve hundred years, after which his physical form was finally exhausted.

Eight hundred thousand million billion nayutas of *viṃvara*, *bimbara*, and *amapa* verses.

"Your countenance is most wondrous and sublime; your radiance illuminates the ten directions. I have previously made offerings to you, and now I come once more to draw near.

The World-Honored One was still in the world.

"The time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived; the moment of cessation has come. You should prepare a seat; tonight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
He further commanded the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana: "Good son, by means of the Buddha-dharma..."

After my parinirvāṇa, all my relics shall likewise be entrusted to you; you must cause them—

How much more so in that Pure Land—what is there to find difficult about it? Nevertheless, the simultaneous presentation of the pure and the impure is not something found in the mundane world; they are all...

This is likewise true in this land.
He caused countless seekers of the śrāvaka vehicle and immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
enabling them all to abide in the samādhi of manifesting all physical forms.
The third is the benefit.

Now, having burned his arms, his body was no longer complete. At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana made this vow before the great assembly:
"I have sacrificed both my arms; I shall certainly attain the golden-hued body of a Buddha.
If this is true and not false, let my two arms be restored as they were before. Having made this vow, they were naturally restored once more. Because of this...
This was brought about by the profound purity of the Bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom.
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down precious flowers; all devas and humans attained what they had never experienced before.

The fourth clarifies the present retribution. Regarding the phrase "the golden-hued body," since it was previously stated that he has already attained the ability to universally manifest all forms, this refers specifically to the golden hue of the eightfold marks;
thus, one knows that this must pertain to the ultimate fruition (*phala*). △ Below is the third section, which reconciles the ancient and the modern, and is further divided into two parts.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Ratnaśrī): "What do you think?
Is the Bodhisattva一切衆生憙見 (Sarvasattvapriyadarśana) anyone else? He is none other than the present Bodhisattva藥王 (Bhaiṣajyarāja).

First, the summary of the connection:
"O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there should be one who resolves their mind to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and is able to burn a finger,
or even a single toe, as an offering to a Buddha-stūpa, this surpasses [the merit of] using kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and the three..."

To offer the mountains, forests, rivers, and ponds of a thousand great trichiliocosm worlds, along with all manner of rare treasures, as an act of worship—this is secondly, the exhortation to practice.
Regarding this exhortation to practice: to burn even a single finger is superior to the sacrifice of one's external body; for the external is light while the internal is weighty.
Therefore, there is a distinction between merit and blessings. Wives and children are external to the self; kingdoms, cities, and the like are external wealth.
This concludes the section on ascetic practices. Part Two: Praising the Sūtra. This is divided into three sections.
Furthermore, if there were a person who filled a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offered them as alms to the Buddhas,
great bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats, the merit obtained by that person would not equal that of one who receives,
maintains, and recites even a single four-line verse of this Lotus Sūtra; the latter’s merit is far greater.
First, there is praise for the person capable of upholding [the Dharma]: offering the seven precious jewels to the four types of noble ones is not equal to upholding a single verse.
The Dharma is the noble teacher; in its ability to give birth, to nourish, to bring to completion, and to cause to flourish, nothing surpasses the Dharma.

Just as parents inevitably protect their child with the four kinds of protection, now that the aspiration has been generated, one takes the Dharma as the means of birth; following it from beginning to end constitutes nourishment, causing it to reach full perfection.

The fruit is accomplished; its capacity corresponds to the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as its glory. Although these four differ, they take the Dharma as their foundation. Therefore, people regard persons lightly while regarding the Dharma heavily.
This is precisely the four *siddhāntas* from beginning to end. Question: The opening chapter states that one praises the person who can uphold [the Dharma].
Why, then, does the sutra say it is not equal to a single verse, or say such things as "The Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha"? Answer: The former...

The previous section praised the person who possesses the Dharma; this section praises the Dharma that resides within the person. Part Two: Praising the Dharma that is Upheld, which has two subsections:
first, praising the essence of the Dharma; second, praising the function of the Dharma. The "essence" being praised here is not the essence of the central thesis (*zong*);

the "function" being praised here is not the function of the central thesis. This refers generally to the entire treatise as the essence. Within the treatise, there are three aspects: essence, thesis, and function.
It possesses such functions as uprooting [afflictions] and so forth; thus, the essence of the Dharma is praised as being eightfold.
O Śrīgarbha, just as among all streams, rivers, and great waters, the ocean is foremost, so too is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* likewise:
among all the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgatas, it is the most profound and vast.

First, it praises the profundity of the essence as being like the ocean. Regarding the statement that among all waters—such as streams, rivers, and torrents—the ocean is foremost, the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (*Wuliangyi jing*) states:
"The four waters are a metaphor for the teachings; the parable of the medicinal herbs describes how a single cloud can rain down [upon them].

Now, while "all waters" collectively represent the entirety of the teachings, the specific mention of these four serves as a metaphor for the four flavors of the teachings: milk, curd, raw [milk], and cooked [milk].
This teaching of the Lotus Sūtra is like an ocean of *amṛta* (clarified butter). Its profundity lies in its exhaustive exposition of the fundamental ground;

its vastness lies in its pervasion of all places. It is an "ocean" because it exclusively elucidates the Buddha-dharma without mentioning other teachings; thus, it is the most profound and vast. Such is its meaning.
Furthermore, just as among all mountains— the Earth Mountains, the Black Mountains, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains,
and the Ten Treasure Mountains— Mount Sumeru is the foremost, so too is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* among all sūtras.
It is the most supreme among them.
Second, as for the analogy of its substance being high like a mountain: the names of the ten jewel-mountains appear in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures.

Because the earth is black iron and the perimeter mountains (*cakravāḍa*) are likewise, they are not made of jewels. Although these ten mountains are made of jewels, they exist either individually or in pairs, and various divine dragons dwell within them. As for Mount Sumeru—
It is composed of the four jewels and is the dwelling place of pure devas.

This serves as an analogy for other teachings that describe the "supported"—namely, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and forty mental states—which may be mundane or supramundane, ordinary or noble, and which describe the "support"—whether conventional, ultimate, or intermediate. These are considered inferior.
The truth of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—the eternal, blissful, self, and pure—is like that which is composed of the four jewels; it reveals [the ultimate].
It is the basis for those who demonstrate, awaken, and enter [the truth]. For this reason, this meaning is the most supreme.
Furthermore, just as among all the stars the Moon Deity is the foremost, so too is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*;
among the thousands of millions of various sūtras and teachings, it is the most illuminating.

The three bodies are as perfect as the moon. Both stars and the moon are of the same yin essence and both appear at night; yet while the stars have no waxing or waning, they cannot compare to the moon.
Other sutras speak of expedient wisdom as being unable to attain mastery, whereas this sutra clarifies that the expedient is itself the real.
Reality is itself expedient means; fullness and deficiency refer to one another. Though non-dual, they appear as two. To speak of expedient wisdom in this manner surpasses other teachings.
Furthermore, just as the Sun Deity is able to dispel all darkness, so too is this sutra: it is able to shatter all [ignorance].
The darkness of goodness.
The four clarities (vidyā) have as their essence illumination like the sun; the sun is the quintessence of yang, capable alone of dispelling darkness.

While the various sutras clarify that true wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) dispels delusion, this still does not equal [the teaching of] the provisional within the real; how then could it be equal to the real within the provisional? Previously, this was the provisional.
Because it reveals external reality, it shatters doubt; because it is not partial, one knows that this sutra’s elucidation of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is the most supreme.
How much more so for the present sutra, which fundamentally aims to manifest reality and sever all doubts; thus it is said that "the provisional is identical with the real.
Therefore, the terminology of the provisional and the real is not unique to this sutra alone, but the expression of their mutual identity originates here.
Furthermore, just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King is the most supreme, so too is this sutra;
it is the most honored among all the various sutras. Just as Śakra is the king among the Thirty-three Heavens, so too is this sutra;
it is the king among all sutras. And just as the Great Brahmā King is [the sovereign] of all sentient beings...

Father, this sutra is likewise so. It is the father of all those in the stages of learning and no-more-learning among the noble ones, as well as those who have resolved their minds toward bodhisattvahood.

The five masteries are like the wheel-turning kings, Śakra, and Brahmā; the commands of a wheel-turning king extend only over the four continents, while Śakra’s authority encompasses the three [realms].

Thirteen. The Sanskrit title serves as a general heading for both the preceding and following sections. For example, other sutras speak of the three truths and the three samādhis as being mutually exclusive and lacking in sovereign mastery.
What this sutra teaches is that by entering the ultimate through the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), one definitively realizes the Dharma of the śrāvakas;
it is the king of all sutras. Furthermore, by entering the conventional through the true mark, all activities of livelihood and production do not conflict with it.
Turning back, one enters into the true reality (*dharmatā*). There are no phenomena that are not the Buddha-dharma; thus the text says:
"The father of all those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as those who have resolved to attain the Bodhisattva mind. The meaning is as follows:
this present sutra is the father of the three teachings and three vehicles of the past, for it is able to give birth to them. What was previously considered not a son is now finally known to be so.
Furthermore, just as among all ordinary persons, the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*,
and *pratyekabuddha* are the foremost, so too is this sutra the most supreme among all the sūtras and teachings spoken by all Tathāgatas,
whether spoken by Bodhisattvas or by Śrāvakas. Any who are able to receive and uphold it [shall attain the same].
This sutra is likewise so: among all sentient beings, it is also the foremost.

That it is the foremost for the six classes of *śrāvakas*, the *pratyekabuddhas*, all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), and those who have attained the four fruits of the *śrāvaka* path, clarifies that it functions spontaneously and without effort (*anābhoga*).
Other sutras require effort to enter the stream [of the Dharma], like those who attain the four fruits.

It is only through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation that one attains awakening. This sutra elucidates the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), unmixed with expedient means, whereby one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñatā*.
Like a great white ox, fat, strong, and full of power, moving as swiftly as the wind, once one has entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), one attains effortlessness (*anābhoga*).
Just as among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is the foremost,
so too is this sutra likewise the most supreme among all sutras and dharmas.
Among the seven types of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is the foremost; this clarifies that he is foremost in terms of the cause.

While other sutras clarify the causes as being the seven stages of expedient means (*upāya*), the present sutra clarifies a cause that transcends these expedient means; therefore, it is foremost in terms of the cause.
Just as the Buddha is the king of all dharmas, so too is this sutra; it is the king among all sutras.

Regarding the "first" of the eight Tathāgatas, this clarifies the fruit. While other sutras clarify the fruit as being proximate to the site of enlightenment (Śīla-mañca), this sutra clarifies the fruit by pointing distantly to the original ground;
therefore, it is the most supreme. Next, the second section praises the function of the Dharma. For...
3. Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, this sutra is able to save all sentient beings;
this sutra is able to cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and affliction; this sutra is able to greatly benefit all sentient beings and fulfill their aspirations.
First, the praise of the function of uprooting suffering:
It is like a cool pond that can satisfy all who are parched with thirst; like fire for one who is cold; like clothing for one who is naked;
like a master for a merchant; like a mother for a child; like a boat for one crossing over; like a physician for one who is ill. As...
It is like finding a lamp in the darkness, like a poor person finding treasure, like a subject gaining a king, like a merchant reaching the sea, or like a torch dispelling the dark.
Next, twelve matters are clarified to praise its utility in bestowing happiness.
This Lotus Sutra is also like this: it can cause sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and all illness and pain, and it can untie all the bonds of birth and death.
Third, uprooting suffering and bestowing joy. △ Second, the profound merit of upholding the sutra, which is divided into two parts.
If those in suffering hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, whether they write it themselves or cause others to write it, the amount of merit obtained cannot be measured even by the Buddha’s wisdom;
its limit cannot be reached. If one writes out this sutra scroll and offers it with flowers, incense, and necklaces of jewels...
By offering incense, powdered incense, and unguents; banners, canopies, and robes;

and various kinds of lamps—ghee lamps, oil lamps, lamps of various fragrant oils, lamps of *campaka* oil, lamps of *sumana* oil, lamps of *pāṭala* oil, lamps of *bāliśika* oil, and lamps of *navamālikā* oil—one shall likewise obtain immeasurable merit.
First, the merit of hearing the entire sutra is set forth. △ Second, the merit of hearing this chapter is divided into two parts.
"Sudāntaśrī, if there be anyone who hears this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja,' they shall likewise attain immeasurable and boundless merit.
If there be a woman who hears this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja' and is able to receive and uphold it..."
These [beings] shall all be female bodies; thereafter, they will no longer receive such births.

If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there should be women who hear this sutra and practice according to its teachings, at the end of their lives here, they will immediately go to the Land of Peace and Bliss, to the place where Amitābha Buddha dwells surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas, and be born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne.
Above, he was no longer afflicted by desire, nor was he afflicted by anger or delusion, nor was he afflicted by the defilements of pride and envy.
He attained the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, his faculty of sight became pure. With this purified faculty of sight, he saw seven million two thousand billion [buddhas].
At that time, as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in ten billion Ganges Rivers spoke from afar in unison, praising him:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha."
If one contemplates this sutra and explains it to others, the merit obtained will be immeasurable and boundless. Fire cannot burn it;
water cannot wash it away. Your merit is such that even if a thousand Buddhas were to speak of it together, they could not exhaust it.
You have now been able to destroy the thieves of Māra, shatter the army of birth and death, and utterly annihilate all other enemies. Good son, [a hundred...]
A thousand Buddhas, by means of their supernatural powers, shall together protect you.
Among all the devas and humans in every world, there is no one like you, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata.
As for the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas, none possess wisdom or meditative concentration equal to yours. Sarvaratnatejarāja, this bodhisattva has accomplished such merit as this.
By the power of virtue and wisdom, if there is anyone who hears this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" and is able to rejoice in it and praise it as excellent,
that person shall, in their present life, constantly have the fragrance of blue lotuses issue from their mouth,
and constantly have the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood issue from the pores of their body. The merit they obtain shall be as described above.
First, the measure of the merit of hearing this chapter is presented. Regarding the period of the "last five hundred years," it has already been explained as before.

If there should be women who hear this sutra and practice according to its teachings, this itself constitutes the cause for birth in the Pure Land; it is unnecessary to further point to texts such as the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Contemplation Sutra).
Question: How does one practice? Answer: Since it is said, "practice according to the teaching," one establishes practice based upon the sutras, as detailed in the "Chapter on the Analysis of Merit.
One directly contemplates that this land is fully endowed with the four lands; therefore, this Buddha-body is itself the three bodies.
Therefore, this great assembly is itself the universal assembly. Because delusions have not yet been severed, [the land] is called "Peaceful Bliss" (Anle).

Practice. This is the aspect of the practice for the Land of Shared Residence that is Pure. Therefore, without leaving the defilement of shared residence, one perceives the purity of shared residence.

Question: There are many types of lands of shared residence; why must it be *Sukhāvatī* (Ultimate Bliss)? Answer: Because the teachings speak of it extensively; because of the capacity of sentient beings; because it gathers in and sustains living beings;
because it causes them to focus their minds single-mindedly; because of the thickness of past affinities; and because it is taken as the primary portion. As stated in the following text:

The case of Tuṣita is different; both depend upon the resonance between the capacity of the recipient and the response of the Buddha. That fragrance issues from the mouth is a reward received in the present life, while the others are rewards to be received in future lives.
For this reason, Śrīkūṭarāja, I entrust to you this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja. After my parinirvāṇa...

After my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, you must widely proclaim and disseminate this [sūtra] throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted, lest evil Māras, the followers of Māra, or various devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others find an opportunity to exploit it.
Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, you should use the power of your supernormal faculties to protect this sūtra. Why is this? Because this sūtra is for Jambudvīpa...
It is the excellent medicine for the illness of humanity. If a person who is ill hears this sutra, their illness will immediately be extinguished, and they shall neither age nor die.
Suvarnapuṣpa, if you see anyone who upholds this sutra, you should take blue lotuses filled with powdered incense and scatter them upon them.
Having scattered them, you should form this thought: "This person will, before long, surely attain [enlightenment]."
Seated upon grass at the site of enlightenment, one shall shatter the armies of Māra, blow the Dharma conch, and beat the great Dharma drum,
delivering all sentient beings from the ocean of old age, sickness, and death. Therefore, those who seek the Buddha-way, upon seeing anyone who receives and upholds this sutra,
should give rise to a heart of such reverence.
Second, the entrustment: "To hear this sutra and attain neither aging nor death" must be understood through contemplative insight. "Not aging" is bliss;
"not dying" is permanence. By hearing this sutra, one attains the realization of permanence and bliss, which rests serenely within the heart.
They were free from all fear and hesitation.

When this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" was being preached, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the dhāraṇī for understanding the languages of all sentient beings.
Third, the benefits gained from hearing [the teaching].
Within the precious stupa, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna praised the Bodhisattva Rājādhiṣṭhānavaśavartin, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Rājādhiṣṭhānavaśavartin!
You have accomplished inconceivable merit, for you are able to question Śākyamuni Buddha thus."
This matter benefits all sentient beings immeasurably.
Fourth, the praise of Prabhūtaratna. The above concludes the initial clarification of the admonition against ascetic practices and the propagation of the vehicle.

The *Sūtra of the Lotus Blossom of the Fine Dharma*, Chapter Twenty-Four:
The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara. Commentary by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe, with annotations by the Shramana Daowei of Siming. Including the original record (*ji*).

The second section consists of two chapters on the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Sublime Sound (*Ghoṣeśvara*), which instructs the disciples to be transformed. Regarding the vehicle of the samādhi-vehicle, the first part explains "Sublime Sound" in two sections:

first, the explanation of the chapter title; second, the explanation of the scriptural text. Regarding the initial explanation of the title by way of its causal conditions, the text itself provides the explanation:
formerly, he offered one hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments to the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound King (*Meghadundubhisvararāja*); now, he travels to transform sentient beings in other lands.
Music follows him spontaneously. Formerly he offered eighty-four thousand precious bowls; now he is surrounded by such a retinue of ritual implements.
Formerly he attained the dhāraṇī of the languages of all sentient beings; now he manifests his body universally.
Because he roars with his voice throughout the ten directions to widely proclaim this teaching, it is named the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound.

This chapter clarifies that the Bodhisattva, by means of inconceivable power, communicates the sutras according to the various types of beings. Creatures perceive only his traces and cannot fathom his source;
they merely savor the flavor without discriminating against his form. This is like [the case of] one who deprecates the ground while damming up its own flow. It is thus.
This is the second meaning within the section on transforming others. The text is divided into six parts: first, emitting light to summon from the east;
second, coming from the west in obedience to the command; third, propagating the sutra in the ten directions; fourth, the benefits received in the two lands; fifth, returning to one's native land.
Chapter Six: Advancing on the Path through Hearing.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the radiance from the *uṣṇīṣa*—the mark of a great man—and emitted the light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which shone throughout the east, pervading as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in one hundred and eight million *nayuta* Ganges Rivers.
Beyond this number of worlds, there is a world named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhā-vyūha*).
In that land dwells a Buddha named Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom Tathāgata (*Vimalapuṣpa-nakṣatrarāja-jñāna-tathāgata*), Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid,
Anuttara-puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who [teaches] for the sake of immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas.
The assembly respectfully surrounded him as he preached the Dharma for them. The radiance from the white tuft between the eyebrows of Śākyamuni Buddha shone throughout that land.
When he first emitted light to summon it from the east, it was the mark of a great man—the ocean of great marks—and the merit of the hairs on his entire body. It was inexhaustible.

Furthermore, the merit of a single minor mark (*anuvyañjana*) surpasses that of all the minor marks combined; the merit of all the minor marks does not equal that of a single primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

These primary marks, proceeding from the lower parts upward, each successively surpass the preceding one, yet they do not equal the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows).

The merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* does not equal the merit of the *uṣṇīṣa* (the cranial protuberance); therefore, these are the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). As for the karma that produces these marks, it arises from filial obedience toward teachers and elders.
Now, this light is emitted to summon his original disciples and cause them to propagate the sutras of the Middle Way for the benefit of those with great capacity.
The white tuft of hair arises from the single path of purity; now, by emitting this light, he causes this Dharma to be propagated. Question:
Since each and every mark of the Buddha is the ocean of the Dharma-realm, why is there talk of superiority and inferiority? Answer: As clarified in other sutras, it should be understood as follows...

This is what was said. Question: The Buddha has disciples who extend throughout the ten directions; why then does he summon those in the east and speak of the west, rather than addressing all eight directions?
Answer: This has a symbolic meaning. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* asks: "For what purpose do the sun and moon travel across Jambudvīpa?
It is because they wish to use their radiance to dispel the darkness of the masses. The east is the beginning of the light, and the west is its end. There is...
To have a beginning and an end—can this be anything other than the Sage? He causes those who have not yet resolved their minds to resolve them;
he causes those who have not yet reached the ultimate goal to reach it. As it is with one bodhisattva, so it is with all beings;

as it is in one direction, so it is in all directions. The Sage does not employ redundant elaborations; by citing a single instance, he refutes all others, speaking merely of "east" and "west. △ Below this:

The second [section] concerns the journey westward in accordance with a command. The initial account of the departure consists of two parts. The first is the circumstances of the departure, which further comprises six sections.

At that time, in the land of Universal Pure Light Adornment, there was a bodhisattva named Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣa*), who had long since planted the roots of all virtues and had made offerings to and drawn near countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas.
Initially, within the narrative of the Sūtra regarding merit and wisdom, first is the account of the causes of merit,
which arises from having encountered many previous Buddhas;
and second is the accomplishment of profound wisdom, which is precisely the adornment of wisdom.
He attained the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner Mark, the Lotus Samādhi, the Samādhi of Pure Virtue, the Samādhi of Constellation King’s Play,
the Samādhi of the Objectless, the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom, the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings,
the Samādhi of Accumulating All Merit, the Samādhi of Purity, the Samādhi of the Play of Supernatural Powers, the Samādhi of the Wisdom Torch, and the Samādhi of the Adorned King.
The samādhi of pure light, the samādhi of the pure treasury, the uncommon samādhi, the sun-turning samādhi—
attaining such hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great samādhis, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The thirty-six samādhis constitute the adornment of merit. Having concluded the narrative of the sūtra compiler,
Śākyamuni Buddha’s light shone upon his body,
and the two [Buddhas] of Wondrous Sound were likewise illumined.
He then addressed the Buddha Śubhavyūhapadmottararāja, saying: "World-Honored One, I shall go to the Sahā world to pay homage, draw near to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha;

and to see the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the Bodhisattva Sūradatta, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, the Bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritramati, and the Bodhisattva Prabhāvyūha."
When the Bodhisattvas King of Adornment and Medicine King had taken their third leave of the Buddha and were about to come to this land,
at that time the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom addressed the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound: "Do not look down upon that land and give rise to inferior thoughts."
"Inferior perception. Good son, that Sahā world is uneven with highs and lows; it is filled with mountains of earth and stone and is replete with filth and impurity.
The Buddha’s body is short and small, and the forms of the assembly of bodhisattvas are likewise small.
Yet your body is forty-two thousand yojanas in height, while my body is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas. Your body is the most upright and handsome among hundreds of thousands."

Ten thousand blessings! Its radiance is sublime and wondrous; therefore, you should go. Do not hold that land in contempt, nor conceive thoughts of inferiority toward the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or their lands.
Regarding the fourth point, that the Buddha issued this admonition: because he is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body, things are accomplished without the need for strict enforcement.

Since there may be those among his retinue who have not yet attained full realization, he relies on that [external authority] to provide a model for this [internal practice]. Indeed, the Buddha’s body is in perfect accord with the ultimate principle.
One must not see the humble and small and thereby forget their majesty; this is an admonition regarding the Tathāgata’s seat.
Yet, while relying on emptiness, phenomena lack inherent characteristics, whereas the body possesses characteristics. In principle, it is wondrous emptiness;

even a body as small as a single speck of dust is entirely equal to that principle, let alone a physical form sixteen feet tall—how could one conceive of inferiority? Indeed, both teacher and disciple are fully endowed with wisdom and the severance of afflictions.
Since the Master has already employed skillful means (*upāya*), the disciple must likewise conceal his own reality; this is a warning based on the Tathāgata’s robe.
Both conceal their silent endurance (*kṣānti*) and tolerate such clumsiness. Now, the land of the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) is entirely what is evoked by the primary retribution (*mūla-vipāka*).
Since the Tathāgata approaches the great trichiliocosm with compassion, one must attend to both the high and the low; do not look only at the environmental realm and neglect the primary retribution.
This is an exhortation based on the Tathāgata’s chamber: one should abide in objectless compassion and settle within this defiled land.
This Buddha’s propagation of the sutra also enjoins these three intentions. That Honored One’s exhortation is based on the fact that the path of all Buddhas is identical.

In every place where the traces of the various manifestations of the *nirmāṇakāya* appear to teach the Dharma, these three are fully present; they exhort the assembly for the purpose of propagating the sutra.
This is the rule.

The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara addressed his Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, that I now go to the Sahā world is entirely through the power of the Tathāgata, the playful mastery of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers, and the adornment of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom."

Regarding the five who received the mandate of the Sublime Sound: the power of the Tathāgata is the power of this seat; the power of supernormal faculties is the power of this chamber; the power of adornment is the power of these robes.
These individuals have received the great purport of propagating the sūtra and the essential core for benefiting sentient beings;
therefore, they are able to travel and transform throughout the ten directions without moving from this assembly. Nevertheless, it is not that all bodhisattvas do not share in the merit.

Regarding the Master of Transformation: the Tathāgata first instructed that the Bodhisattva should exert himself personally. When the Bodhisattva hesitated, [the Tathāgata noted] that going there alone is already difficult;
how much more so must the coming and going involve benefiting others? Thus, one knows that all coming and going is by the power of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, while the Tathāgata bestows empowerment upon those who are capable of receiving it, and the Bodhisattva possesses a share in this, they have not yet reached the ultimate limit. Therefore, [the Tathāgata] applies the three ultimates as an empowerment.
This is divided into three parts: the robe, the seat, and the chamber, which serve as the means for propagating the essential tenets of the Sūtra.

Thus we know that all these arise through the power of the Tathāgata and his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*); only through such manifold adornments can he benefit sentient beings. This is because the Tathāgata is empty within and without.
Because he is able to bestow compassion upon all bodhisattvas and is fully endowed with adornments, he benefits beings according to their capacities.
As for what is called "adornment," it refers to the myriad practices during the causal stage; this assembly is that very land. △ Sixth, the manifestation of signs preceding his arrival.
This passage consists of six parts.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat and without moving his body, entered a samādhi.
By the power of this samādhi, not far from the Dharma-seat on Vulture Peak Mountain, he manifested eighty-four thousand multitudes of precious jewels.
There was a lotus flower with a stem of Jāmbūnada gold, leaves of white silver, filaments of diamond,
and a pericarp made of karketana gems.
First, lotus flowers appeared.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, seeing these lotus flowers, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen first appeared? There are many tens of millions of lotus flowers, with stems made of Jāmbūnada gold.”
The petals are made of white silver, the filaments are made of diamond, and the pedestal is made of *kiṃśuka* jewels.
This is the second inquiry of Mañjuśrī. Question: If Mañjuśrī’s rank were lower, his words would not have been such as to seek an audience;
if his rank were higher, how could he fail to recognize him upon their meeting? Answer: Although they share the same rank, there are distinctions of beginning, middle, and end; it stops here.
"If one does not know even a single matter, one brings no shame upon a high station. Furthermore, seeing an auspicious omen among the assembly, I did not understand it;
I asked the Buddha in order to give rise to knowledge of it.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara."
He wishes to come from the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña, surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas,
to this Sahā world in order to make offerings to, attend upon, and pay homage to me, and also to make offerings to and listen to the Lotus Sutra.
The Buddha replied.

Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness has this bodhisattva planted, and what merits has he cultivated, such that he is able to possess such great supernatural powers?
What samādhi does he practice? We pray that you will explain this samādhi for our sake."
"World-Honored One, we also wish to diligently practice this samādhi so that we may behold the physical appearance, stature, and dignified deportment of this bodhisattva.
We pray only that the World-Honored One, by means of your supernormal powers, cause that bodhisattva to come here."
"Grant that I may behold him.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa."
I shall manifest that sign for you all.
