At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land and, together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, set out.
As he traveled through the various countries he visited, the earth shook in six ways, and everywhere there fell rains of seven-jeweled lotuses;
hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
First, the description of his retinue and his journey:

the eyes of this Bodhisattva are like the petals of a vast blue lotus; even if one were to combine hundreds of thousands of millions of moons, his countenance would be more upright and handsome than that.
His body is the color of pure gold, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits.
With majestic power blazing forth and radiance shining brightly, his various marks were fully perfected like the solid body of Nārāyaṇa.
He entered a pavilion of the seven treasures and ascended into the void, remaining at a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground.
Surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas who paid him respectful homage, he came to this Sahā world, to Vulture Peak Mountain.
Second, the description of ascending the platform:

Having arrived, he descended from the seven-jeweled platform, took a necklace worth hundreds of thousands, went to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, offered the necklace, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom..."

The Buddha asked after the World-Honored One: "Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness? Are the four great elements in harmony?
Can you endure worldly affairs? Are sentient beings easy to deliver? Are they free from excessive greed, anger, ignorance, envy, stinginess, and pride?
Are there none among them who are unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward śramaṇas, or possessed of wrong views and unwholesome minds?"
"Does he restrain the five sense-faculties? World-Honored One, are sentient beings able to subdue all demonic adversaries?

Has the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who entered parinirvāṇa long ago, come from within his stupa made of the seven treasures to listen to the Dharma? Furthermore, I inquire after the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna:
is he at ease, free from affliction, and able to endure remaining for a long time?"
The third *vidyādhara* inquired after the World-Honored One’s health and transmitted this message:
“World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna. I only pray that the World-Honored One will show it to me so that I may behold it.
The fourth *vidyādhara* likewise requested to see Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha said to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, "This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wishes to see you;
World-Honored One, please grant him passage."
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed Gadgadasvara, saying: “Excellent, excellent!
It is for the sake of making offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, for hearing the Lotus Sutra, and for seeing Mañjuśrī and the others that you have come here.”
Sixth, it is well known that within the stupa, he is called "Good. △ Third, the propagation of the sutra throughout the ten directions consists of two parts:
question and answer. At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness did this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound plant?"
What merit has been cultivated?
First, it clarifies Puṣpākṣa’s question regarding what roots of goodness he planted in the past to possess such supernormal power.

Regarding the second question on present supernatural power, the Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Cloud Thunder Sound King (*Meghadundubhisvararāja*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
His land was named Manifesting All Worlds (*Sarvalokadarśana*), and his eon was named Joyful to Behold (*Priyadarśana*)."

The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, for twelve thousand years, made offerings to the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja with one hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments and presented him with eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven precious gems.

By virtue of these causes and conditions and their karmic retribution, he has now been born in the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūhapadmottarajñānarāja and possesses such supernormal powers. Flower Virtue, what do you think? At that time, the Buddha Megha...
Was the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, who at the abode of the Buddha Ghoṣarāja made offerings of music and presented precious vessels, anyone else?
It was none other than this present Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara.

Flower Virtue, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has already made offerings to and attended upon immeasurable Buddhas, long planting the roots of merit; furthermore, he encountered as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

"Of the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, he first answered [their questions] and planted roots of goodness in the past by offering music and presenting ritual vessels. Thus, he connects the present with the past.
Flower Virtue, you see only that the body of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara is here; yet this Bodhisattva manifests in various forms."
In various places, for the sake of all sentient beings, he preaches this sutra. He may manifest in the body of Brahmā,
or manifest in the body of Śakra, or manifest in the body of Īśvara, or manifest in the body of Maheśvara, or manifest in the body of a celestial general,
or manifest in the body of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, or manifest in the body of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or manifest in the bodies of various minor [deities].
He may manifest as the body of a king; or manifest as the body of a householder; or manifest as the body of a lay official;
or manifest as the body of a brahmin; or manifest as the body of a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā;
or manifest as the body of a householder or lay official’s wife; or manifest as the body of a brahmin’s wife.

He manifests in the body of a boy or a girl; or he manifests in the bodies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, and preaches this sutra.
He is able to rescue and deliver all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and all places of great hardship, even unto the king’s palace.
In the palace, he transformed into a female body and preached this sutra. Flower Virtue, this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound is one who can rescue and protect all sentient beings in the Sahā world.
This Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound manifests such various transformations of his physical form.
In this Sahā world-system, for the sake of all sentient beings, he preaches this sutra; yet his supernormal powers, transformations, and wisdom suffer no diminution.
By means of various forms of wisdom, this bodhisattva illuminates the Sahā world, causing all sentient beings to each attain understanding.
It is likewise in the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It is so. If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.
If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the form of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests the form of a pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them.

If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the form of a bodhisattva, he manifests the form of a bodhisattva and preaches the Dharma for them. If there are those who are to be delivered by means of the form of a Buddha, then...
He manifests in the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them. In such various ways, he manifests forms according to those who are to be saved;
even for those who are to be saved through parinirvāṇa, he manifests parinirvāṇa.
Flower Virtue, such is the manner in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara has accomplished the power of great supernormal faculties and wisdom.
Second, the answer concerning his present supernatural power. △ Second, the question and answer. This also has two parts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound has deeply planted roots of goodness."
"Bhagavān, in what samādhi does this bodhisattva abide to be able to manifest such transformations and deliver sentient beings?
My initial question concerns which concentration he currently dwells in to be thus able to provide such sovereign benefit."
The Buddha told Flower-Virtue Bodhisattva: "Good son, this samādhi is named 'Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
It is by abiding in this samādhi that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings in such a manner."
Second, as for the answer regarding abiding in the Buddha-samādhi:

when this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, the eighty-four thousand people who had come together with the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara all attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
Furthermore, immeasurable bodhisattvas in this Sahā world also [attained it].
One attains these samādhis and dhāraṇīs.
Regarding the fourth point, there is the attainment of benefit in two lands. Samādhi and dhāraṇī are one in essence but differ in function:
quiescence is samādhi, while the function of retention is called dhāraṇī. Furthermore, the manifestation of the form-body is called samādhi; [the manifestation of] sound...
Discursive explanation is called *dhāraṇī*. The *Upadeśa* (Shangpin) states: "Initially, one attains the *samādhi* of all physical forms;
upon transforming the body, one attains the *dhāraṇī* of all speech and language. One should know that sound is still a phenomenon of form (*rūpa-dharma*);

therefore, it is said that while their essence is one, their functions differ. Furthermore, the purification of the tongue faculty is called *dhāraṇī*, while the purification of the other faculties is called *samādhi*.
All of these are dharma-gates for the purification of the six sense faculties. This, then, is the samādhi and dhāraṇī of the Perfect Teaching (yuanmen).

They must be identical in essence though different in name: samādhi arises from concentration (samāpatti), while dhāraṇī arises from wisdom (prajñā). These are precisely the inconceivable concentration and wisdom;
therefore, they may be employed interchangeably.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara, having made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha, returned to his own land.

As he passed through various kingdoms, the earth shook in six ways, precious lotus flowers rained down, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of musical instruments were played.
Having arrived in his own country, he was surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.
He went to the presence of the Buddha Śubhavyūha-puṣpadhvajarāja-jñāna and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have gone to the Sahā world to benefit sentient beings;
there I saw Śākyamuni Buddha and the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, where I paid homage and made offerings.
Furthermore, I saw the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, through whom I attained diligent vigor."
The Bodhisattvas Balin and Śūradatta, as well as these eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, also attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
Upon their fifth return to their own lands, they caused the earth to tremble and flowers to rain down; even as they traveled through these realms, they were still able to provide incidental benefit.
Moreover, when the Buddha emitted light before him, it shone sideways upon one hundred and eight myriads of koṭis of nayutas of lands in the eastern direction;
this, too, was spoken of in terms of benefiting others.
At the time when he preached this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara’s Coming and Going," forty-two thousand devaputras attained the dharma of non-arising.
Endurance. The Bodhisattva Flower Virtue (Huade) attains the Lotus Samādhi.

Chapter Six: Hearing and Advancing on the Path. Above this, from the "Exquisite Sound" (Miaoyin) chapter onward, the instruction for the disciples to be transformed regarding the vehicle of samādhi is concluded.
The Universal Gate Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Twenty-fifth Chapter of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma.
This second chapter, the "Avalokiteśvara Chapter," clarifies the disciples to be converted and the vehicle of samādhi; it is divided into three parts: first, an explanation of the chapter title;

second, an indication of the section’s intent; and third, an explanation of the sutra text. Within the explanation of the chapter title, there are two sections: first, distinguishing [the subject] from others to highlight its essential nature; second, [an explanation of the title].
A summary explanation of the title: First, it is clarified that this chapter belongs to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, for which there have been many commentators.
My current interpretation does not accord with others; rather, I have a private record in two fascicles. Herein, I shall briefly extract from that work to explain this title.
There are both general and specific [categories]. There are ten pairs in the general category and five groups in the specific category, as will be explained in detail below.
Regarding the first, the ten general pairs: the first is the person, Avalokiteśvara; the second is the Dharma, the Universal Gate (Samantamukha).

As for the persons, there are many types, all of which are manifestations of the one reality along with the seven expedient means. As for the Dharmas, there are many types, namely the preceding and succeeding questions and answers. How so?
He performs such deeds as preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. Based on the preceding dialogue, the person of Avalokiteśvara is discussed;

based on the subsequent dialogue, the *Pumen* (Universal Gate) Dharma is discussed. Because the title combines both the person and the Dharma, it is called the "Avalokiteśvara *Pumen* Chapter. Second, regarding the clarification of "extracting suffering and bestowing happiness":

"Avalokiteśvara" refers to the Great Compassion that extracts suffering, based on the preceding dialogue. [The text continues with] "hundreds of thousands... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*. The translation reflects the structure and intent of the original Chinese.)
All who suffer and are distressed attain liberation. As for the "Universal Gate" (Pumen): it bestows happiness through great compassion.

According to the subsequent dialogue, one should preach the Dharma according to those who are to be saved. Third, this is explained by way of the two adornments of merit and wisdom. "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the adornment of wisdom;
wisdom can sever delusions, just as there is no darkness when it is bright. The "Universal Gate" refers to the adornment of merit.
Merit can transform longevity, just as a jewel rains down treasures. Fourth, the clarification of the four truths and the two bodies:

"Avalokiteśvara" (the Observer) refers to observing the profound within the objective realm; this is the Dharmakāya. "Universal Gate" refers to manifesting according to what is appropriate for beings;

this is the Nirmāṇakāya. Fifth, the clarification by way of the medicinal tree and the king of jewels: "Avalokiteśvara" is likened to the King of Medicinal Trees, whose entire body heals [all ailments].
"Regarding 'the sick': as for the Universal Gate (Pumen), it is like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*), which grants whatever one desires.

The two benefits—subtle and manifest—are clarified here. As for Avalokiteśvara: he provides subtle benefit such that nothing is seen or heard, yet the three poisons and seven calamities are all eliminated, and the two kinds of seeking and the two kinds of wishes are both fulfilled.
As for the Universal Gate: he provides manifest benefit, such that one beholds the thirty-three holy ones with one's own eyes."
I have heard these nineteen expositions from my teacher. Seventh, the explanation by way of the two wisdoms of provisional and real:
"Avalokiteśvara" refers to the illumination of real wisdom according to one's own intention; "Universal Gate" refers to the illumination of provisional wisdom according to the intentions of others.

Eighth, the explanation by way of the fundamental and the trace: "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the unmoving fundamental limit; "Universal Gate" refers to the trace that adapts to all forms and circumstances.
The nine conditions clarify the two causes; "Avalokiteśvara" refers to the fundamental seed of the cause of understanding (*parijñā-hetu*).
"Universal Gate" (*Samantamukha*) refers to the fundamental seed of the condition-cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). The ten knowledges clarify the two virtues of abandonment; "Avalokiteśvara" refers to...
The ultimate nature of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is like the moonlight on the fourteenth night;

"universal gate" (*samantamukha*) refers to the ultimate nature of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), like the moon on the twenty-ninth night when its false radiance is about to end. These two question-and-answer passages in the sutra contain immeasurable meanings;
I shall briefly employ ten pairs of categories, beginning with person and dharma and ending with wisdom and cessation, to explain the general title of this chapter. Such is their meaning.
Thus it is. Regarding the second distinct discussion on the five aspects: first, explaining "contemplation" (*guan*). There are many kinds of contemplation, namely:

analytical contemplation (*xi guan*), essential contemplation (*ti guan*), sequential contemplation (*ci di guan*), and perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*). Analytical contemplation means destroying form to enter emptiness. Essential contemplation means...
Form itself is emptiness. As for "contemplation in successive stages," this refers to everything from analytical contemplation up to perfect contemplation.

Regarding perfect contemplation, it means that analytical contemplation is itself the true reality (*dharmatā*), and even successive contemplation is likewise the true reality. Now, setting aside the three types of contemplation, we discuss only perfect contemplation;
the text refers to it as the "Universal Gate" (*samantamukha*). If the contemplation were not perfect, the gate would not be called universal. Thus...

This is the meaning. Regarding the second [point], the explanation of "world" (*loka*): if one proceeds from practice, one first contemplates the past world; if one proceeds from verbal expression, one first contemplates the future world.
Now, following the convenience of explanation, we discuss the world last. Furthermore, there are many kinds of worlds:

namely, the conditioned world (*saṃskṛta-loka*), the unconditioned world (*asaṃskṛta-loka*), the world of the two extremes, and the inconceivable world. The conditioned world refers to the worlds of the three realms.
The "unconditioned world" refers to the two types of *nirvāṇa*. The "world of the two extremes" refers to *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*.

The "inconceivable world" refers to the realm of the true nature (*dharmatā*). One sets aside all other worlds and takes up only the inconceivable world. Regarding the third [point], the "releasing sound" refers to the spiritual capacity (*indriya*).
There are many kinds of capacities: the capacity of humans and devas, the capacity of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), the capacity of bodhisattvas, and the capacity of Buddhas.

Regarding capacities: those with the capacity of humans and devas are told, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Those with the capacity of the Two Vehicles are told, "Loathe and fear birth-and-death;
rejoice in and esteem the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Those with the capacity of Bodhisattvas are told, "Put others before oneself; be compassionate, benevolent, and yielding.
Those with the capacity of Buddhas are told, "Among all dharmas, enter by means of universal contemplation; be entirely without obstruction."
A person is one who transcends birth and death through a single path. Discarding the capacities for all other sounds, one responds only by taking up the capacity for the Buddha’s sound.

Because of this causal relationship between the capacity and the response, it is called "Avalokiteśvara" (Contemplating the Sounds of the World). Fourth, regarding the explanation of "Universal" (Samantabhadra):

"Universal" (*paryanta*) means all-pervasive. All phenomena (*dharma*) are immeasurable. If one does not attain universality, it is a partial phenomenon; if one attains universality, it is a perfect phenomenon.
Thus, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* states: "All phenomena are deviant; all phenomena are correct. To briefly illustrate universality by way of ten phenomena:
once this principle is grasped, one can categorize all phenomena such that there is none that is not universal—namely, compassion.

Universality: universality of the great vows, universality of practice, universality of detachment from delusion, universality of entering the Dharma-gates, universality of supernormal powers, universality of skillful means, universality of preaching the Dharma, universality of maturing sentient beings, and universality of making offerings to all Buddhas.

From humans and devas up to Bodhisattvas, all possess compassion; yet there is both universal and non-universal [compassion]. Regarding the two conditions—sentient beings and phenomena—the essence of compassion is as follows:
Since it is partial, its conditions are not extensive and thus cannot be called universal. When there is no [discriminative] object, it is identical in essence to the true mark (*dharmatā*);
since its principle is perfect, compassion is all-pervasive. Like a magnet attracting iron, it accords spontaneously; such is this compassion.
Pervading all things is called "universal compassion. Regarding "universal great vow" (*mahāpraṇidhāna*): "great" (*maha*) means vast; "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) means to restrain.
Because it is a vast restraint of the essential mind, it is termed a "great vow. This great vow arises in relation to the Four Noble Truths.

If it were restricted to the four truths of conditioned arising, non-arising, or the immeasurable, it would not encompass all phenomena exhaustively and thus could not be called "universal. However, if it is based on the unconditioned Four Noble Truths (*anabhisaṃskṛta-satya*), [it encompasses all].

This is called the universality of the great vows. As for the universality of practice: for example, before the Buddha encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha, whatever he practiced was not in accord with principle.
After receiving the prediction of enlightenment, every encounter was immediately in accord with principle;
as his wisdom and principle permeated all phenomena, there was no practice that was not universal. As for the universality of severing delusions: if one employs all...

The knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of the modes sever the delusions of the four abodes, the dust-like afflictions, and so forth, like pruning away branches; thus it is not called the universal severing of delusions.
If one employs the knowledge of all modes to sever ignorance, then the five abodes are entirely exhausted, like removing the root itself.
This is called the universality of severing delusions. Regarding the universality of entering the Dharma-gates: that which precedes the Path is called the cultivation of skillful means;

that which is entered after the Path is called entering the Dharma-gates. If those of the Two Vehicles enter a single concentration with a single mind and perform a single act with a single mind, they cannot attain the manifold;
furthermore, because they are bound by their concentration, it is not called universal. If one traverses the various stages individually, from shallow to deep...
There are no gradations, nor is it called "universal" in a limited sense. When one enters the King Samādhi, all samādhis are entirely contained within it;

yet, without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation, one manifests all modes of dignified conduct. Therefore, it is called the universality of entering the Dharma-gate. As for the universality of supernormal powers:
The great arhats’ divine eye illuminates a trichiliocosm; pratyekabuddhas illuminate a hundred buddha-worlds; and bodhisattvas illuminate worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

In all these cases, because the objects of their focus are narrow, the supernormal powers they manifest are likewise partial. However, for one who cultivates by taking the true nature (*dharmatā*) as the object, when one power is manifested, all are manifested—this applies even to what are called "semblance" supernormal powers, as will be explained below;
how much more so for true supernormal powers, which would not be universal? Thus it is said: [Text follows]

Regarding "universal pervasion," there are two kinds: those subsumed within the preliminary preparations for the Path and those during the practice of the Path. Furthermore, there are two kinds subsequent to the Path:

first, the essence of the Dharma, as explained in the section on entering the Dharma-gates; second, the transformative function, as explained here, which accords with the capacities of beings to benefit them.

It accords with conditions and suitability, being perfectly pervasive all at once; yet, although it manifests various activities, there is no diminution within the reality-limit (dharmatā-bhūtakoṭi) of the dharma-nature.
This is called the universality of skillful means. As for the universality of preaching the Dharma, one is able to use a single sublime voice.
It accords with the capacities of the ten dharma realms; according to their respective natures and types, it causes all to attain liberation.

Like the lute of the asuras, it is therefore called "universal in preaching the Dharma. Regarding "universality in maturing sentient beings," all activities, both mundane and supramundane, are performed by the Bodhisattva:
digging wells, constructing boats, Shen Nong tasting medicinal herbs, and clouds shading the sun.

Illuminating and benefiting sentient beings, even unto benefiting all worthies and sages; instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening them, causing them to enter into *sambodhi*—this is called the universality of accomplishing sentient beings.
Regarding the universality of making offerings to the Buddhas:
if one performs external offerings, by means of a single meal at a single time, or a single flower or a single incense, one makes offerings to all Buddhas. There is no...
There is no before and no after; they are simultaneously and equally offered. Within a single atom, the manifestation of various kinds of atoms is likewise so.
For one who practices internal contemplation, perfect wisdom guides all practices; this perfect wisdom is called the Buddha.
When all practices support perfect wisdom, that is the offering to the Buddha. If practices support other forms of wisdom, it is not called the universal offering. All practices [support...]
Perfect wisdom is what is called "universal offering. Regarding the five gates of the Śramaṇa: from the provisional entering emptiness, emptiness is unobstructed while the provisional is obstructed;
from emptiness entering the provisional, the provisional is unobstructed while emptiness is obstructed. If one is unobstructed in only one direction, it is not universal;

because it is obstructed, it is not a gate. The Middle Way is neither empty nor provisional; it correctly penetrates the true reality (dharmatā) and simultaneously illuminates the two truths, and is therefore called "universal. It is correct...

Because they provide access, they are called "gates" (*mukha*). The universal gates of perfect penetration have immeasurable meanings; here, ten pairs and five single items are briefly cited, by which the other categories may be inferred.

This concludes the explanation of the title. Next, to demonstrate the intent of the chapters: this chapter still concerns the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation, specifically its circulation for the sake of transforming others.
Third, the formal explanation of the sūtra text. The text is divided into three parts: first, the question; second, [the answer]; third, [the conclusion]. (The second part follows.)

Answer: This is the third section, on the benefits gained from hearing [the teaching]. It consists of two rounds of questions and answers. The first round of questions and answers is divided into two parts. The initial question is further divided into two.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and...
He spoke these words.
First, when the narrator describes the time, it is when he has finished speaking of the Bodhisattvas of the East and proceeds to speak of the Bodhisattvas of the West;

this is the *loka-prasiddha-tantra* (the standpoint of worldly convention). When he has finished speaking of the arising of goodness in the East and proceeds to speak of the masters of goodness in the West, it is for the sake of...
The *puruṣa-siddhānta* (human standpoint) concludes with the resolution of doubts regarding the East. Next, when resolving doubts regarding the West, this is the *pratipakṣa* (antidote).
When the attainment of the Way regarding the East is concluded, next is the time for attaining the Way regarding the West; this is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate standpoint).

As for the term "Inexhaustible Intent" (*Akṣayamati*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that emptiness is inexhaustible, while the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* clarifies the eighty [inexhaustible] dharmas.
The Gate of Exhaustion (*kṣayamukha*). The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "That which is inexhaustible is neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion; therefore, it is called 'inexhaustible.

Taking these three sūtras as a whole, one explains "inexhaustibility" by means of the three contemplations (*trividhā vipaśyanā*) and the three knowledges (*trividha-jñāna*). Here, "intention" (*abhiprāya*) refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), while "inexhaustibility" refers to the object (*viṣaya*).
When wisdom accords with the object, if one follows the object alone, it should be called "inexhaustible. If one follows wisdom alone, it should be called... [text ends].

△ The Buddha’s response consists of three parts: first, a general response; second, a specific response; third, a response encouraging the holding of the name. The general response comprises four sub-sections.

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, suppose there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings—'one person' here refers to a single individual—who each experience much suffering;

that is, many people undergo one kind of suffering, one person undergoes much suffering, and one person undergoes little suffering. In the present text, 'hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings' refers to many people."

"Undergoing various sufferings and afflictions" clarifies the second point: encountering suffering. "Undergoing various sufferings and afflictions" refers to many sufferings. By citing the many, the few are made manifest;
if even many can be saved, how much more so the few?
Upon hearing of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, one calls upon his name with a single mind.
"Hearing" refers to the perception of the name. Encountering suffering is evil; calling upon the name is good. The union of good and evil constitutes the meaning of the "stimulus" (ki).
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately observes their voices, and all obtain liberation.

This refers to obtaining liberation through the four clarities (*caturvidha-abhijñā*). "All obtain liberation" is the response; this is the causal condition of the stimulus and the resonance, and thus he is named Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, it is the causal condition of person and dharma, and even the causal condition of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*); for these reasons, he is named Avalokiteśvara.

Akṣayamati, suppose there were someone who received and upheld the names of sixty-two billion Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River,

The first section clarifies the basis for comparison. The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "The Dharma-body is one, while the manifested forms are many;
comparing the sixty-two billion manifested forms, they are equal to a single Dharma-body. Zhiyi says: "The person of the Perfect [Teaching] is one, while those of the Partial [Teachings] are many;
comparing the sixty-two billion partial bodhisattvas, they are equal to a single perfect bodhisattva. If the mind...
Regarding the correlation of objects, there is a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*). This present case belongs to the category of the "both [sides]" clause:

upholding [the teachings] of sixty-two billion [deities], both mind and object are inferior; upholding Avalokiteśvara, both mind and object are superior. This is the contemplation according to the definitive teaching of this very teaching.
If it were the "mutual interaction" clause, both would follow the transformation of the mind. Question: Why is it that in the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra) [it says...]?
Is it then by means of upholding the names of sixty-two billion *Ganges-sand* Buddhas that this is being compared?
Answer: Some say the treatise (*śāstra*) is erroneous; we now say it is not so. First, I shall cite the treatise, and next, I shall briefly explain it. The treatise says:
"The merit of upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara is equal to the merit of [upholding] the names of the sixty-two billion *Ganges-sand* Buddhas. There is...
There are two kinds of meanings: first, by the power of faith; second, by ultimate knowledge. The power of faith is further twofold:
first, seeking to become like Avalokiteśvara through ultimate faith; second, generating a mind of reverence, thinking that one may likewise attain those same qualities.
As for "ultimate knowledge," it is the definitive knowledge of the *dharmadhātu*. *Dharmadhātu* is termed "Dharma."

Regarding the nature [of this]: because a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) is able to realize and enter the equal body (*samatā-kāya*) of all Buddhas—and that "equal body" refers to the *dharmakāya* of True Suchness (*tathatā*)—therefore, upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara is no different in merit from [upholding the names of] sixty-two billion Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Now, it is said: by this evidence, one should know that one must rely on the "perfect" (*yuan*) interpretation. Why is this?

Regarding these two meanings, the power of faith pertains to phenomena (*dharma*), while ultimate [faith] pertains to principle (*li*). Phenomena and principle support one another; only when they are mutually integrated is what is recollected fully accomplished.
As in the two aspects of the power of faith, it is stated: "I seek to make my body like that of Avalokiteśvara," which refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).

Furthermore, it is stated: "The merits of Avalokiteśvara, I too shall attain," which refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). Only when one aspires to equalize the reward and response bodies is [the goal] achieved.

It is established that one who merely recollects the virtues of the fruit need not necessarily understand the underlying principle; therefore, the subsequent meaning states "knowing the dharma-realm" and so forth.
Next, the stage of realization is cited, which is the first bhūmi. This is done by citing a partial realization to enable others to recognize it.

Thus, we know that when recollecting the three bodies of Avalokiteśvara, one must further compare this to the practice of recollecting the Buddha. If one discusses this in terms of recollecting the dharma-body, even though...
The merit of invoking all Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise equal; why then mention only sixty-two?
Thus, although the treatise appears to cite the sutra, it is actually an augmented sentence intended to explain the meaning, much like the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter.

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there are sentient beings in any land who are to be liberated by means of a Buddha-body, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them.

If they are to be liberated by means of a Pratyekabuddha-body, he immediately manifests a Pratyekabuddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them. If they are to be liberated by means of a Śrāvaka-body..."
To those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests in the body of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma to them.
To those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of a Brahmā king, he manifests in the body of a Brahmā king and preaches the Dharma to them.

To those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of Śakra, he manifests in the body of Śakra and preaches the Dharma to them. To those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of Maheśvara, he manifests in the body of Maheśvara...
He preaches the Dharma to them. To those who are to be liberated by means of the body of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma to them.
To those who are to be liberated by means of the body of a Heavenly General, he manifests the body of a Heavenly General and preaches the Dharma to them.
To those who are to be liberated by means of the body of Vaiśravaṇa, he manifests the body of Vaiśravaṇa...
He enters their gates and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be saved by the body of a minor king, he manifests as a minor king and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by the body of an elder, he manifests as an elder and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by means of a householder’s body, he manifests a householder’s body and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by means of a minister’s body, he manifests a minister’s body and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by means of a Brahmin’s body, he manifests a Brahmin’s body and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be saved by means of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī...
To those who are to be liberated through the bodies of upāsakas or upāsikās, he manifests the body of an upāsaka or upāsikā and preaches the Dharma for them.

To those who are to be liberated through the bodies of elders, householders, officials, brahmins, or women, he manifests the body of a woman and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be liberated through the bodies of boys or girls...
To those who are to be delivered through the form of a boy or a girl, he manifests in the body of a boy or a girl and preaches the Dharma for them.

To those who are to be delivered through the forms of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans, he manifests all such bodies and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be delivered by means of the Vajrapāṇi deity...
The "Deliverer" (Tāraka) is none other than the present Vajrapāṇi, who preaches the Dharma for him.

2. Dual presentation of the agent and the object. 3. The skillful means of the transformer. 4. The benefits gained by those being transformed. 5. Concluding by correlating the past with the present. 6. Hearing this chapter.
Awakening to the Way.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly:

"In ages past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom (*Meghadundubhisvararāja-puṣpajñāna*), a Tathāgata, Arhat..."
Rāhula, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. The land is named Radiant Adornment; the eon is named Joyful Vision.
First, the original narrative is clarified. △ Second, the two aspects of the agent and the object are indicated.
In that Buddha-dharma there was a king named Wondrous Adornment (Miaozhuangyan). The king’s queen was named Pure Virtue (Jingde), and they had two sons:
the first was named Pure Treasury (Jingzang), and the second was named Pure Eye (Jingyan).
At the outset, both the subject and the object are indicated: one person who is to be converted and three persons who convert them, all of whom have their names mentioned.
These two sons possess great supernormal powers, merit, and wisdom; they have long cultivated the path practiced by Bodhisattvas, namely:
the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, and vīrya-pāramitā.

He thoroughly understood and mastered the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of skillful means, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, up to and including the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Furthermore, he attained the Bodhisattva’s Pure Samādhi, the Constellation Samādhi, the Pure Light Samādhi, the Pure Color Samādhi, and the Pure Illumination Samādhi. Long...
He has also fully mastered the Samādhi of Adornment and the Samādhi of the Treasury of Great Majestic Virtue.
These two specifically manifest the merit and wisdom of the two sons. The six perfections and the four great vows—referred to in other sutras as the ten pāramitās—are the horizontal dharma-gates.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the vertical dharma-gates. In other sutras, these are designated as the "right path."
The practice of conduct serves as an aid to the Path. In this sutra, the ten perfections (pāramitās) are designated as the primary [Path], while these [practices] are called "aids to the Path.
Within the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), samādhis are fully present; within the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas), there are samādhis at every stage.
To further specify the seven samādhis is merely to extensively manifest the various Dharma-gates. △ Third, the skillful means of the transformer (the teacher). This also has three parts.

At that time, that Buddha, wishing to guide King Subhavyūha and out of compassion for sentient beings, preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Regarding the initial clarification of "the time having arrived":
when that Buddha appeared in the world, he constantly proclaimed the True Dharma; however, because his karmic affinity with the king was weak, it was not yet the right time [to preach it].
If one were to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, then indeed it would be the right time. The text states: "That Buddha, being about to guide [him], preached..."
The Lotus Sūtra is precisely its meaning. △ Second, the Discussion. This also has four parts.
At that time, the two sons, Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra, went to their mother’s place and, joining their ten fingers and palms together, said:
"We pray that you, Mother, will go to the presence of the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña. We, too, shall attend upon and draw near to him, making offerings."
They paid their respects and made offerings. Why was this? Because this Buddha was preaching the Lotus Sūtra amidst the assembly of all devas and humans;
it was fitting that they should listen to and receive it.
It was now time for them to first inform their mother.
The mother said to her sons, "Your father has faith in and accepts the teachings of the non-Buddhists and is deeply attached to the Brahmanical dharma.
You should go and inform your father; we shall go together."
The two mothers urged them to transform their father.
Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra joined their ten fingers and palms together and said to their mothers: "We are sons of the Dharma King, yet we have been born into this family of wrong views."
The three sons were born into a heterodox family and harbored resentment.
Their mother said to them, "You should take concern for your father and manifest supernatural transformations for him. If he sees them, his mind will surely become pure;
or else, you should allow us to go to where the Buddha is."
The four mothers exhorted them to remember their father.
Thereupon, because the two sons remembered their father, they surged up into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and manifested various supernatural transformations.
While in mid-air, they walked, stood, sat, and lay down; water issued from the upper part of their bodies and fire issued from the lower part of their bodies. From the lower part of their bodies...
He emerged from the water; fire issued from his body. He manifested a massive form that filled the void of space, and then again appeared small; having been small, he again appeared large.
He vanished in mid-air and suddenly reappeared on the ground. He entered the earth as if it were water, and walked upon the water as if it were solid ground.
By manifesting such various supernatural transformations, he caused his father, the king, to attain pure faith and understanding.

Third, the manifestation of transformations. One should clearly explain the eighteen transformations, providing a detailed commentary as an illustration. △ Fourth, the benefits obtained by those transformed. This also has ten parts.

At that time, the father saw his son’s supernatural powers were such as this; his heart was filled with great joy, having attained what he had never experienced before. He joined his palms toward his son.

They said, "Who is your teacher? Whose disciple are you? The two sons replied, "Great King, that Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Wisdom is currently seated upon the Dharma throne beneath the Bodhi tree made of the seven precious gems.
In the midst of all the world’s devas and humans, he is extensively preaching the Lotus Sūtra; he is our teacher, and we are his disciples."

At first, the father believed and the son submitted to the Master. When the King witnessed the supernatural transformations—whether one or two of them, though narrow and humble—and saw what his son had accomplished, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Believing his son, he submitted to the Master and asked, "Who is this teacher?
I too wish to see him."
The father said to his sons, "I too now wish to see your teachers; let us go together.

The two fathers and the king already had faith, and eighty-four thousand others within the palace were also prepared. They informed their mother and offered congratulations, saying, "We pray that you will permit us to leave the household life.
The mother also granted her consent.
Thereupon, the two sons descended from mid-air and approached their mother. Joining their palms, they said to her: "The Father King has now attained faith and understanding;
he is capable of giving rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. We have already performed the work of a Buddha for our father’s sake.
We pray that you will grant us leave to leave the household life and cultivate the Way under that Buddha. At that time, the two sons, wishing—
To restate his intention, he addressed his mother in verse:
"I pray that you, Mother, will release us so that we may leave the home life and become śramaṇas. Buddhas are exceedingly difficult to encounter; we shall follow the Buddha and train."

"As rare as the udumbara flower, it is even more difficult to encounter a Buddha; it is likewise difficult to be liberated from all calamities. I pray that you grant me permission to leave the household life.
His mother then replied, "I grant you permission to leave the household life. Why is this? Because a Buddha is so difficult to encounter."
The parents were repeatedly urged three times, for now was precisely the right time, as it is difficult to encounter a Buddha.
Thereupon, the two sons said to their father, "Excellent, father and mother!

We pray that you will go at once to the presence of the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom to behold him in person and make offerings. Why is this? Because a Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower."
It is like a one-eyed turtle encountering the hole of a floating log. Because our past merit is so profound and vast, we have been born at a time when the Buddha-dharma exists.
Therefore, parents, you should grant us permission to leave the household life. Why is this?
The Buddhas are difficult to encounter, and their times are likewise hard to meet.

At that time, the eighty-four thousand women in the inner palace of King Subhavyūha were all capable of receiving and upholding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. The Bodhisattva Viśuddhanetra [was established] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

He has long since attained mastery. The Bodhisattva Viśuddhagarbha has, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, attained mastery in the samādhi of transcending all evil destinies, desiring to cause all sentient beings to leave behind all evil destinies. As for the king’s consort:
They attained the Samādhi of the Assembly of All Buddhas and were able to know the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
These two sons, through such skillful means, skillfully transformed their father, causing his mind to develop faith and understanding, and to take delight in the Buddha-dharma.

Fourth, the transformative merit having been fully manifested, the Buddha praised his meritorious virtues. As previously explained, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* subsumes all phenomena and returns them to the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding "leaving behind the evil destinies": first, one abides [in the view] that the three paths are the evil destinies;

however, when discussed in full, the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) all deviate from the truth and give rise to delusion, and are thus entirely evil destinies. Now, he has left them all behind. That is to say:
The twenty-five samādhis shatter the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*). The "Samādhi of the Buddha’s Assembly" is the secret treasury;
the Buddha is assembled therein. It is the sphere of practice for the Buddha alone, not for others. △ Fifth, all go together to the Buddha's abode.
This also has five parts.
Thereupon, King Wonderful Adornment, together with his ministers and retinue; Lady Pure Virtue, together with her ladies-in-waiting and retinue;
and the king’s two sons, together with forty-two thousand people, all went at once to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.
First, it clarifies that they all went there at one time.
At that moment, that Buddha was preaching the Dharma for the king, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; the king was filled with great joy.
Both kings, having heard the Dharma, were filled with delight.
At that time, King Wonderful Adornment and his queen took off from their necks pearl necklaces worth hundreds of thousands and scattered them over the Buddha as a threefold offering.

In the midst of the void, there manifested a precious pavilion supported by four pillars. Within the pavilion was a great jeweled couch, spread with hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial robes.
Upon it sat a Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture, emitting a great radiance.
The four quarters manifested auspicious omens.
At that time, King Wonderful Adornment had this thought: "The Buddha’s body is rare and extraordinary; it is upright, majestic, and unique, having achieved the foremost and most subtle of forms."
The five classes of beings were filled with joy.
Having thus all arrived at the Buddha’s presence, the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom addressed the fourfold assembly, saying:
"Do you see this King Sublime Adornment standing before me with palms joined? This king shall become a bhikṣu within my Dharma and shall cultivate it with diligent effort."
He shall practice the dharmas that assist the path to Buddhahood and will surely attain buddhahood, named Śālarāja. His land shall be called Mahāprabha, and his eon shall be named Mahocchrayarāja.
That Buddha Śālarāja will have an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas as well as an immeasurable number of śrāvakas.
That land was level and upright; such were its merits.
The six Buddhas bestowed upon him a prophecy.
Thereupon, the king immediately entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother. The king, together with his queen, two sons, and all his retinue, [proceeded] to the Buddha.

Within the Dharma, he left the household life to practice the Way. After the king had left the household life, for eighty-four thousand years he constantly applied himself with diligent vigor, practicing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Following this period, he attained the Samādhi Adorned with All Pure Merits.
He immediately ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees.
Having practiced the religious life with the sevenfold clarity, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, these two sons of mine have already performed the work of a Buddha; by means of their supernormal powers and transformations, they have turned [the wheel of Dharma]."
"With my mind previously set on what is false, they have caused me to dwell securely within the Buddha-dharma and enabled me to behold the World-Honored One.
These two sons are my true spiritual friends; desiring to arouse the roots of goodness from my past lives and to benefit me, they have come to be born in my family."
King Śubhavyūha sighed over his two sons.
At that time, the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja-puṣpadhvaja-jñāna addressed King Śubhavyūha, saying: "So it is, so it is."
It is as you have said. If good sons or good daughters plant roots of goodness, they will encounter spiritual friends from life to life.
These spiritual friends are able to perform the work of a Buddha, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening them, leading them into *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Great King, you should know that a spiritual friend is a great causal condition; that is to say, they provide transformation and guidance.
They were enabled to see the Buddha and resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Great King, do you see these two sons? These two sons have already made offerings to sixty-five hundred thousand million billion *nayutas* [of Buddhas].

He has personally approached and paid homage to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; in the presence of those Buddhas, he has upheld the Lotus Sūtra and, out of compassion for sentient beings with wrong views, has caused them to abide in right view.

When the nine Buddhas had thus recounted their sublime practices, King Subhavyūha descended from the midst of the sky and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata is most rare and extraordinary.
By virtue of his merit and wisdom, the fleshly protuberance upon his crown radiates brilliant light, and his eyes are long and wide."
His complexion was a deep azure-blue. The tuft of hair between his eyebrows was as white as a conch shell or the moon. His teeth were white, even, and closely set, and he constantly radiated light.
The color of his lips was a beautiful red, like the *bimba* fruit.

At that time, King Subhavyūha, having praised the Buddha for such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of merits, joined his palms with single-minded devotion before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
“World-Honored One, it is unprecedented! The Dharma of the Tathāgata is fully endowed with inconceivable, subtle, and wondrous merits.
The practice of its teachings and precepts brings peace, security, and well-being. From this day forward, I shall no longer act according to my own whims.”
He did not give rise to any evil thoughts such as wrong views, arrogance, or anger. Having spoken these words, he prostrated to the Buddha and departed.

[The Buddha] ten times praised the Buddha’s own vow and commended the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), saying that there is great significance in this; the spiritual friend is able to perform the work of a Buddha.
This refers to the external protector spiritual friend. As for "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening," this refers to the instructional spiritual friend.
Consciousness. That which is called "transforming and guiding so that one may attain the vision of the Buddha" refers to the spiritual friend of shared practice (*sahāyaka-kalyāṇamitra*).

That which causes one to enter into Bodhi refers to the spiritual friend of the reality-limit and the true mark (*bhūtakoṭi-bhūtalakṣaṇa-kalyāṇamitra*). The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "The spiritual friend..."
If she is a virtuous and faithful wife, this is the meaning of external protection. Furthermore, a spiritual friend is like kinsmen or wealth;
this is the meaning of practicing together. Furthermore, a spiritual friend is like a merchant leader; this is the meaning of instruction.
Furthermore, a spiritual friend is like a child lying in his father’s lap; this is the meaning of the ultimate reality.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly: "What do you think? Was the King Subhavyūha anyone else?
He is none other than the present Bodhisattva Padmaśrī. As for the Lady Viśuddhaguṇā, she is the present Bodhisattva Prabhāvyūha who shines before the Buddha.
Out of compassion for King Subhavyūha and his retinue, she was born there. As for those two sons, they are the present Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja..."
The Bodhisattva is Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
Within the fifth section, which correlates the ancient and the present, the initial formal correlation identifies these as the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
Having already accomplished such great merits as these, [they have done so] for immeasurable hundreds...
Under the presence of billions of Buddhas, they have planted the roots of all virtues and accomplished inconceivable, manifold wholesome merits.
If there are those who know the names of these two Bodhisattvas, all the world— including the devas and human beings—
should likewise pay them homage.
Second, the praise of the two bodhisattvas:
When the Buddha spoke this "Chapter on the Former Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment," eighty-four thousand people were distanced from dust and freed from defilement,
attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
In the sixth chapter, "On Hearing," regarding the purification of the Dharma-eye within the context of awakening to the Way, some say this refers to the first fruit (srotāpanna).
When King Śrī’s consort and the eighty thousand others all upheld this sutra, they were all destined to become Buddhas; how could those who heard this chapter have attained only the minor fruits?
While the names are the same, their meanings differ, and one must carefully discern this, as has already been explained previously. The commentator also states that this is what he has observed.

"Pure. This does not refer to the first fruit of the Hīnayāna. The above constitutes the entirety of the fourth chapter, "The King of Sublime Adornment," which concludes the section on the vow for external protection and the vehicle of the vehicle.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Encouragement of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Third, the Chapter on the Encouragement of Samantabhadra.

This section covers both self-practice and the exhortation to transmit [the teaching] to others. First, the title of the chapter will be explained; second, the scriptural text will be analyzed. Regarding the initial explanation of the title:
in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Avalokana-sūtra*, he is named "Universal Auspiciousness" (Pianji); in this sutra, he is called "Samantabhadra. Both are...
In the Chinese language: *Puxian*. In the Sanskrit sound: *Vasubhadra*. This is translated as "Universal Worthy" (*Samantabhadra*). The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:

"I vow to practice the bodhisattva path within this defiled and evil world so that it may be made pure and adorned. My practice must surely surpass that of all other bodhisattvas. The Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
"For these reasons, I now change your name and call you Universal Worthy (*Samantabhadra*). This is precisely...
This is the intention of the three *siddhāntas*. Furthermore, it is explained through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), as well as the origin of its name based on practice and vows.
From the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), it is collectively termed "Universal Good" (*Samantabhadra*).

Specifically, regarding the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), which borders upon the Truth and approaches the state of a Sage, it is called "Good" (*bhadra*); this is what is taught within the Tripitaka. Now, we clarify that it is the summit of the path of subduing (*vītarāga-mārga*).
Its cause is called "Universal" (*pu*) because it is all-pervasive. Following the path of severance, one who is adjacent to the ultimate Sage is called "Worthy" (*xian*).

As for the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), they represent the beginning of the path of suppression; they are neither the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) nor the "Universal. Being adjacent to the first stage of the Sage, they are neither subsequent nor ultimate.
Even up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), it is not yet all-encompassing; how much less so for the preceding stages?

Now, we discuss the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). It occupies the summit of all subdued states; because the path of subduing is all-pervasive, it is called "Universal" (*Samantabhadra*). Because the path of abandonment has just been exhausted, there is very little remaining to be compared;
as it borders the ultimate limit, it is called "Worthy" (*Bhadra*). As the *Śāstra* quotes regarding the moon on the fourteenth night: [as follows].
The moon on the fifteenth night—this meaning is clear. This explanation is based on the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); the subsequent stage refers to Samantabhadra.
"Exhorting and inspiring" is a term expressing devotion to the Dharma. Although he resides afar in that land, he has heard this sutra in its entirety from beginning to end.
Desiring to cause both his own practice and the transformation of others to continue forever without end, he comes from the east and from the west to offer this exhortation.
[He] sets forth [the teaching], possessing the intent of the four *siddhāntas* (and so forth). The text says:
"For the sake of making offerings to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, I manifest my own body. If one sees my body, they will experience great joy" (1).
"Because of seeing me, they will further increase their diligence and immediately attain *samādhi* and *dhāraṇī*" (2). "Because of attaining this *dhāraṇī*, there shall be no..."
Those who are able to destroy [this] shall likewise not be deluded or disturbed by women (verse three).

Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within the three thousandfold world-system, fully endowed with the path of Samantabhadra (verse four), come forth to exhort and inspire according to these explicit texts, which constitute the four *siddhāntas*.
△ Above, the circulation [of this teaching] was divided into three parts; from the nineteenth verse onwards...
The latter five chapters and a half cite the great power of the sutra itself to encourage its circulation.

The final five chapters, beginning with the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter, cite the great power of the bodhisattvas' transformative path to encourage its circulation. This one chapter cites the great power of Samantabhadra’s vow to encourage its circulation.
The text is divided into four sections: first, the emergence; second, the exhortation to emerge; third, the description of emergence; and fourth...

The Arising of Benefits. First, the narrator describes the arrival [of the assembly] in three parts: first, making offerings to those above; second, transforming those below; and third, practicing reverence.

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, by means of his sovereign supernormal powers, majestic virtue, and renown, arrived from the east together with immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable great bodhisattvas. All the lands through which he passed were universally shaken.
It rained precious lotus flowers, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of music were performed.

This was the supreme offering made during his initial arrival. As for "sovereignty," it refers to the oneness of principle (*li*). As for "spiritual powers" (*abhijñā*), it refers to the oneness of practice (*xing*).
As for "majestic virtue," it refers to the oneness of the person (*ren*). As for "fame," it refers to the oneness of the teaching (*jiao*). Furthermore, "sovereignty" is constant...
The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are bliss (*sukha*). The majestic virtue (*mahātmya*) is the self (*ātman*). The renown (*yaśas*) is purity (*viśuddhi*).

Such is the explanation; thus, while being one, they are four. Their virtues are fully complete, which is the meaning of sovereignty (*vaśitā*). By the power of purity, flowers rain down. By the power of bliss, music is performed.
By the power of supernormal faculties, the earth shakes. By the power of sovereignty, it rains according to one's wish. Following...
They followed the rain as it fell and accompanied the movement as it stirred; they were like great dragons flying without ceasing, from whose bodies clouds and rain flowed forth endlessly.
Samantabhadra and his retinue, in the form of bodhisattvas, employed the power of the four virtues to come and exhort the realization of the "Four Ones.
In every place they passed through, they personally presented the highest offerings, and their deeds were thus.
Furthermore, surrounded by a great assembly of countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, each manifesting their majestic power and supernormal faculties,
he arrived at the world of Sahā, at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Second is the benefit of downward transformation. According to what is appropriate for others, he manifests the forms of the eight classes of beings.
Briefly employing two powers, he acts according to their respective capacities; such are his deeds.
He prostrated with his head at the feet of Śākyamuni Buddha, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and performed three circumambulations while facing the Buddha;
this constitutes the practice of reverence. △ The exhortation to resolve has two parts:
first, the exhortation through inquiry; second, the exhortation through vow. There is both question and answer.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, from the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, I have heard from afar that in this Sahā world the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached.
Together with immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas, I have come to hear and receive it.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for us: if a good man or a good woman, regarding the Tathāgata..."
"After his parinirvāṇa, how can one obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

This was the initial inquiry. As for the questioner: having heard that the sutra had been concluded from afar, his longing for the Dharma remained insatiable, and thus he resolved to travel a great distance.

His intention lies in exhortation and inspiration. Therefore, he requests the correct teaching once more to inspire his own practice; he requests the circulation [of the teaching] once more to inspire others.
If the Tathāgata permits these two paths to be expounded again, their radiance will be infinitely boundless;
thus, he makes this dual request. The Buddha’s response consists of three parts: first, the general; second, the specific; third, the conclusion.
The Buddha told Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: "If good men or good women accomplish four dharmas, they shall obtain this Lotus Sutra after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata."
The first Buddha gave a general answer:
first, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, encountering the roots of all virtues; third, entering the stage of right determination;
and fourth, giving rise to the mind that seeks to save all sentient beings.
Second, the specific response. The names of four dharmas are listed. Since Samantabhadra made his request in pairs, the Tathāgata skillfully responded by briefly citing four to encompass all.
Why? Because the essentials of these four dharmas include both the orthodox teaching and its dissemination. Why?

Although the Buddha is without partiality, if one can distance oneself from evil and follow what is good, turn back from delusion toward the correct, and open up the provisional means—[one attains liberation].
Regarding "knowledge and vision": to manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision accords with the holy mind and is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.

If the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened, then Prajñā provides illumination; this is the planting of the roots of all virtues and is also the entry into the stage of the right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).
It is neither distracted nor savoring; it neither grasps nor abandons. It is also the arousal of the resolve to rescue sentient beings.

One should know that these four [aspects] share the same essence as the "opening of the provisional and revealing of the real," differing only in name; they are non-dual and without distinction. Furthermore, "being protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
"planting the roots of all virtues" is the showing of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; and "arousing the resolve to rescue sentient beings" is the awakening to it.
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision; entering the stage of right determination—this is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

These four points encompass the essentials of the "Trace Gate. Furthermore, the Trace has its Origin; from the Origin come the opening, showing, awakening, and entry. Thus, there is the opening, showing, awakening, and entry within the Trace.
Now, by revealing the Origin through the Trace, the Origin and the Trace are shown to be non-dual and without distinction. With these four dharmas, he answers their request.
